News.title: New Airbnb ban dubbed ‘ludicrous’ and ‘absolutely absurd’ comes into force from TODAY
News.content:
Next

NEW Airbnb rules that hosts have described as”ludicrous” have officially come into force today.

The controversial new changes will see guests no longer face a list of chores when it is time to check out – including washing dishes.

Airbnb has changed its rules on what is expected of guests when they check-out after facing complaints from travellers.



From today, Airbnb hosts will have to select rules for guests from seven standard house rules and then add additional “reasonable” requests.



Included in the seven standard rules are specifying a maximum number of overnight guests, whether pets are permitted and rules on smoking.

Airbnb will now review any additional rules set, which, for example, dictate washing, laundry, rubbish and utilities.

For washing up, Airbnb writes: “You can ask guests to put washing up in the sink, but they shouldn’t be asked to do the washing up and put it away.”



When it comes to laundry, “you can ask guests to gather used towels, but they shouldn’t be asked to remove sheets from the bed or start a load of laundry.”

Guests are also expected to follow additional ground rules regardless of the changes, which include putting rubbish in the bin and not causing damage that is beyond normal wear and tear.

The announcement of the new rule changes sparked uproar amongst hosts, with many calling the policy “ludicrous”, “absurd” and “out of touch with society”.

Airbnb's example of additional rules for guests Airbnb says that rules on listings will be reviewed Washing up: You can ask guests to put washing up in the sink, but they shouldn’t be asked to do the washing up and put it away.

You can ask guests to put washing up in the sink, but they shouldn’t be asked to do the washing up and put it away. Laundry: You can ask guests to gather used towels, but they shouldn’t be asked to remove sheets from the bed or start a load of laundry.

You can ask guests to gather used towels, but they shouldn’t be asked to remove sheets from the bed or start a load of laundry. Rubbish: You can ask guests to separate rubbish and recycling into designated indoor bins, but they shouldn’t be asked to take rubbish off-site.

You can ask guests to separate rubbish and recycling into designated indoor bins, but they shouldn’t be asked to take rubbish off-site. Utilities: You can ask guests to turn off air conditioning when they leave, but they shouldn’t be asked to avoid using a listed amenity.

One host from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, wrote: “Sorry, you think it’s unreasonable to ask your guests to wash their own dishes? That’s utter nonsense and ludicrous.



“In self-catering accommodation, it’s a requirement and it’s not the cleaner’s job to wash people’s dishes. Airbnb have lost touch with society.”

At the time of the announcement, an Airbnb spokesperson said: “House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage.

“So we’ve redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”

News.title: Bikes and games consoles are most memorable childhood Christmas presents, survey finds
News.content:
Next

BIKES are the most memorable childhood Christmas present, a survey has found – but only fifth of youngsters have one on their wish list.

A poll of 1,200 parents of children aged four to 16 revealed 37 per cent believe a bicycle produced their most endearing festive memories when they were younger.

This is ahead of games consoles (26 per cent), dolls and dolls’ houses (21 per cent), and board games (20 per cent).

Among parents who received a bike for Christmas as a child, 71 per cent claimed it was their most memorable present.





However, children’s Christmas lists today look rather different, with toys (40 per cent), clothes and trainers (38 per cent), and video games (34 per cent) the most requested gifts this year.

Just 18 per cent are asking for a bicycle – putting bikes behind money or gift cards, games consoles, books, headphones and tablets.

Pippa Wibberley from Halfords, which commissioned the study, said: “While a bike might not appear at the top of every child’s Christmas list, parents know the gifts that create the biggest initial reaction aren’t always those that leave the most lasting impression.

“For generations, receiving a first bike has meant far more than simply unwrapping another present.

“It represents freedom, independence and the chance to start exploring the world beyond the front door.

“Parents remember getting their own bike for Christmas. Now they get to see that same excitement on their child’s face, run alongside them as they find their balance and cheer when they pedal off on their own.

“Those are the moments both of you remember, and they’re a good reason to put a bike back on the Christmas list.”

The research also found 81 per cent of parents believed their child’s Christmas wish list has changed when compared with their own.



And 83 per cent reckon youngsters today are more interested in technology-based presents than they were at the same age.

Despite this, 46 per cent would rather buy their son or daughter a practical present that encourages them to spend time outdoors.

It also emerged 68 per cent feel they know better than their children which presents they will enjoy in the long term.

As a result, 83 per cent admit they would buy their child a gift they hadn’t specifically requested if they thought it would benefit them.

The research, carried out via OnePoll, also found 53 per cent think Christmas presents were more exciting when they were young, while 51 per cent thought today’s children aren’t having traditional childhood experiences.



Toys (50 per cent), board games (44 per cent), books (37 per cent) and outdoor toys (35 per cent) and bikes (23 per cent) were among the gifts parents feel modern youngsters are missing out on.

Despite not being at the top of most modern wish lists, 21 per cent would personally most like their child to receive a bike this year, making it the most popular specific gift among mums and dads.

Two thirds (66 per cent) also admitted the prospect of giving their child their first bicycle makes them feel excited.

What’s more, 65 per cent believe learning to ride a bike is an important life skill, while 57 per cent described getting a bike and learning to ride as a childhood rite of passage.

Pippa Wibberley of Halfords added: “A first bike is one of the few Christmas presents that can genuinely open up a child’s world.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Parents recognise the wider benefits too, as many feel owning a bike encourages exercise and gets children outdoors, while others highlighted the confidence, independence and reduction in screen time it can bring.

“Whether it’s the first wobbly ride without stabilisers, cycling to see friends or heading out together as a family, these are experiences children can carry with them long after this year’s must-have toys have been forgotten.”

News.title: Moment cops ram wrong-way driver after ‘careering’ onto A-road with ‘stolen motorbike in boot’ – as boy, 17, arrested
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment cops plough into wrong-way driver on a major road as a 17-year-old boy is arrested.

Dashcam footage captures the van speeding past cops in Ashford with a stolen motorbike in the back.



It refused to pull over, jumped red lights and hit 70mph on 30mph roads. before swerving into the wrong lane and attempting a three-point turn.

Officers use “tactical force” to stop the vehicle following the pursuit on November 12.



The driver then makes a run for it from the vehicle as police continue the pursuit on foot.

A 17-year-old boy was arrested and the stolen motorbike has since been returned to its rightful owner.



It comes after a separate horror chase where a driver leapt from a moving car in Nottingham City Centre as police pursued him.

Dashcam footage from that incident showed the suspect jump from a black Nissan while it was still moving.



This left the whole vehicle to roll onto a pedestrian crossing.

Three pedestrians were forced to scramble out of the way as the runaway car rolled into their path.

Halit Gjoni, 21, of no fixed address, was arrested minutes later by Nottinghamshire Police’s knife crime team.

He has since pleaded guilty to four offences, including dangerous driving.

News.title: The £300k ‘golden phones’ helping Albanian drug gangs become Britain’s new cocaine kingpins…who scoff at our lax borders
News.content:
Next

BRITAIN’S porous borders are being exploited by Albanian gang bosses to smuggle criminals into the country to deal drugs – and back out again if they come under police investigation.

Godfathers from the former communist state are using the people smuggling tactic to make millions of pounds from the UK’s booming drug trade and take control of the lucrative cocaine market.





Undercover TV investigators infiltrated Albanian organised crime groups, exposing how they recruit street-level dealers.

The probe shows how they operate sophisticated cocaine delivery networks and trade mobile phones containing thousands of customers’ details for as much as £300,000.

Investigators also discovered people smugglers advertising their services on TikTok, offering to transport Albanian drug dealers in trouble with the law across the Channel to Europe for £2,500.

A Sky News documentary – The Drug Lords Next Door – reveals how the Albanian mafia has become the dominant force in Britain’s cocaine market.

The documentary includes an interview with an Albanian migrant who admitted crossing the Channel illegally to work in Britain’s drugs trade.

The man, known as Granit, told Sky News that his relatives paid for his journey to Britain on the condition that he work for Albanian drug dealers.

He said: “We used a motorboat to head to Britain.”

Asked whether other passengers aboard the boat had also intended to join the drugs trade, he replied: “Yes. The majority of them had set off with this idea in mind.”





Granit was given accommodation at an asylum hotel but quickly left and began working at a cannabis farm near Manchester.

He has since returned to Albania, where he works in construction, and spoke anonymously for fear of reprisals from the gangs.

But he said others were continuing to make the dangerous crossing to join criminal networks operating in Britain.

In 2022, Albanians accounted for almost a third of small boat arrivals to Britain, making them the largest national group crossing the Channel that year.

Frank Stewart, from the National Crime Agency, warned that Albanian drug gangs and organised immigration crime were closely connected.

He said: “There’s an unknown number here illegally.”

Mr Stewart explained that Albanian drug dealers preferred “working with Albanians that they can trust.”

He added: “You cannot untwine them from those involved in organised immigration crime, and there are Albanian organised crime groups who do their own trafficking of bringing people in illegally into the UK.”



Investigators discovered that illicit routes across the Channel also operate in the opposite direction.

A TikTok account advertising in Albanian stated: “We transport boys with problems from the UK to Europe. Safe trip every week.”

The account operator told undercover journalists that people in trouble with the British police could be transported back to Albania in trucks for £2,500 per person.

Hundreds of TikTok s offering drug-dealing jobs in towns and cities across the UK were also uncovered.

Reporters applied for the positions and were offered jobs selling cocaine, including one paying £280 a day in Wigan and another providing accommodation in Exeter.

“It’s as if it’s a major corporation advertising and recruiting for staff,” said former Met police officer David McKelvey, who helped pioneer undercover operations against Albanian gangs in Britain.

The documentary also reveals how the gangs have revolutionised drug dealing through dedicated mobile phones containing customers’ contact details.

Investigators found such phones being advertised on social media for as much as £300,000 and contacted an Albanian seller undercover.

“The phone is the business. All of your clients are on your phone. You’re effectively buying a business,” Mr McKelvey explained.

The investigation traces the gangs’ rise to their ability to bypass European middlemen and establish direct cocaine supply networks stretching to South America.



“We estimate the Albanian organised crime groups have primary control over the importation of cocaine into the country,” the NCA’s Mr Stewart said.

The documentary – made by Sky’s in-house documentary team with Quicksilver Media – also investigates Franc Copja, a former Tottenham resident accused by Albanian prosecutors of running one of Europe’s biggest cocaine networks.

His criminal empire became embroiled in a bloody gang war after 50kg of cocaine disappeared in London.

Kathryn Westmore, director of financial crime at UK Finance, warned of the human consequences of Britain’s booming cocaine market.

She said: “This is not a victimless crime, somebody buying cocaine for their night out.

“There’s a whole history in that one transaction which takes you back to exploited people, vulnerable people, violence.

“This is all part of the same ecosystem, and it touches all of our lives.”

TV investigator Chris Matthews said: “These gangsters are posting on TikTok openly.



“They may not be saying we’re selling cocaine, but a few snowflakes and you know hint, hint, wink, wink, nudge, nudge. We all know what they’re doing.”

Chris went on: “I personally reached out as an undercover on TikTok to a number of accounts that advertise opportunities for drivers in UK cities.

“I reached out in Albanian because they don’t trust you if you reach out in English.

“I didn’t speak the language so I’ve sent just very short brief messages like “any word bro?”

“And and and then they would reply and say, “Yeah, sure, let’s have a chat on the phone.”

Chris said: “At that point, I obviously had a difficult situation because I couldn’t pick up the phone and talk to them. I needed someone who could speak Albanian.

“The issue with that is that many Albanians do not want to speak to the Albanian mafia.

“Albania is a very small place; everyone knows everyone. And the Albanian mafia are incredibly dangerous. They have a propensity towards violence

“It took a great deal of bravery from the person that ended up doing those calls.

“They then spoke to the gangsters and said, “Look, I’ve got a guy in the UK.



“‘He’s been out of work, but he’s previously worked in the game. He wants to get back into it.

“He’s not Albanian, but he’s good for it. You know, he’s worked with me before. He’s a good guy.

“The undercover journalist knew what to do, but he was English.

“So there was always that fear that they wouldn’t like him specifically because he’s not Albanian, and the Albanians want to work with other Albanians because it’s a thing about trust.

“It’s also about fear. You know, they can get back to their families because they know who they are.

“They know where they come from, and they can put pressure on them that way.

“It used to be very much who they knew, so they went down to the local Albanian bar, and then someone would say, “Oh, I’d like a job,” and they’d work it through that.

“But the Albanians have got so big now that they just don’t have enough dealers.

“They need more and more and more, and so what they’re having to do is go on TikTok and basically put out an open call for for drivers saying: ‘Please, please contact us. We’ve got jobs all over the UK in pretty much

every UK town’.

“The only place that they don’t really go is Merseyside because the Merseyside gangs are so violent.”



Chris said there is no shortage of people willing to work for the Albanian gangs, who are exploiting the UK’s faltering job market to recruit.

He went on: “Everyone knows it’s tough in the UK at the moment to make money.

“Everything’s expensive. The only thing that’s decreased in price in the last 10 years is cocaine.

“And then these guys are offering 280 quid a day to do a driving job, and you’ll be making about 2k a week, obviously not paying any tax

“If you want to have that take-home pay, you really need to be earning something along the lines of £140k a year… accountants, doctors’[pay].

“You could train for however many years to become a doctor or an accountant and make that sort of money…

“Or you could just become the lowest rank of the Albanian mafia. Drive around, give people cocaine.”

News.title: Diabetic woman, 66, kills both parents, 94, by injecting them with insulin after claiming it was ‘perfect murder weapon’
News.content:
'CRUEL END' Diabetic woman, 66, kills both parents, 94, by injecting them with insulin after claiming it was ‘perfect murder weapon’







Next

A DIABETIC woman killed both of her elderly parents by injecting them with lethal doses of insulin after boasting the hormone was “the perfect murder weapon”.

Raelene Polymiadis, 66, faces two mandatory life sentences behind bars after a jury unanimously convicted her of two counts of murder following a marathon four-month trial in Australia.



Polymiadis – who suffers from type 1 diabetes – reportedly clutched the edge of the dock as the first guilty verdict was read out at the South Australian Supreme Court on Friday.

She then began dabbing her eyes with a tissue, shaking her head and blinking rapidly as the second guilty verdict was delivered.



Jurors took less than five hours to accept that Polymiadis murdered her parents, Brenda and Lynton Anderson, in separate attacks in March 2022 and April 2023.

The victims, neither of whom suffered from diabetes, were both aged 94 when they were murdered.

Prosecutors suggested their daughter may have been driven to kill by a misguided belief that it would spare her mum and dad from being forced into a nursing home.

The court heard Brenda had been recovering at Noarlunga Hospital, near Adelaide, following a fall, a fractured vertebra and pneumonia in early 2022.

However, after Polymiadis visited her mum on March 12, nurses discovered Brenda “largely unresponsive”.

Prosecutors alleged her daughter injected her with a high dose of insulin on two separate occasions between March 12 and March 15.



Following his wife’s death, Lynton continued to live at home while his four children took turns staying overnight to care for him.

On April 30, 2023, Polymiadis left the property after spending the weekend looking after her dad.

However, he was found unconscious by a carer just two hours later – and died the following day from insulin toxicity.



During the trial, Polymiadis’ ex-boyfriend Ian Edward Willcourt told jurors she had boasted to him that “insulin was the perfect murder weapon because it’s natural in the body and it can’t be detected”.

Cops also planted a covert listening device inside her car that secretly recorded Polymiadis confessing to God that she had killed her parents.

Detectives even uncovered handwritten notes penned by the killer as she tried in vain to outsmart investigators.

One note read: “What they will do is wait for a few weeks, months, year to see if I ‘think I got away with it’ and I get cocky and slip up.

“Hang on buddy, it could be a long ride, otherwise the suspect would be arrested now.”



Polymiadis had her bail revoked following the verdict and will remain in custody ahead of a directions hearing on December 16.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Her son and husband Michael, who supported her throughout the trial, refused to comment as they left the courthouse.

Justice Sandi McDonald thanked the jury for their service during the “long and difficult trial”, which began in June but was hit by a slew of illnesses and other delays.

News.title: Mom accused of faking toddler’s illnesses after 2-year-old underwent invasive surgery & 175 doctor appointments
News.content:
Next

A MOTHER has been accused of faking her two-year-old child’s illnesses after the toddler underwent invasive surgery and attended a staggering 175 medical appointments.

Emilee Guzman, 29, allegedly fed doctors false information about her child’s health, leading to a painful procedure that investigators say may never have been necessary.



The West Virginia mom was arrested on Wednesday and charged with child neglect resulting in serious bodily injury.

Investigators claim Guzman deliberately exaggerated her toddler’s feeding difficulties, prompting doctors to surgically insert a feeding tube into the child’s stomach.



The shocking allegations emerged after detectives launched an investigation into suspected medical child abuse involving the toddler and a nine-year-old child living in the same home.

According to a criminal complaint obtained by People, the two-year-old had attended approximately 175 medical appointments over just two years.

Read more crime stories FAMILY MURDER Wife & daughter arrested 4 years after man’s SEVERED HEAD found in trash bag



And investigators warned that the staggering figure did not even include visits to healthcare providers outside WVU Medicine.

Guzman allegedly convinced doctors that her child suffered from Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID), a condition involving severe restrictions around eating.

She also reportedly claimed the toddler had microgastria, an extremely rare birth defect that causes an abnormally small stomach.

Based on the mother’s account of the child’s eating difficulties, doctors performed surgery to insert a gastrostomy tube, known as a G-tube, on October 1.



But investigators claim the procedure could have been avoided entirely.

During an October 13 interview with detectives, Guzman allegedly admitted deliberately misrepresenting how much food her child consumed.

She reportedly feared being reported to Child Protective Services for neglect if doctors discovered the toddler’s actual food intake.

“Emilee further acknowledged that had the physicians known the truth regarding S.G.’s dietary intake, the surgical placement of the G-tube likely would not have occurred,” the complaint states.

The child’s pediatric surgeon later told investigators he had not been given accurate medical information.



He reportedly said he would have been recommended less invasive treatment had he known the truth, given the potential harm caused by the painful surgery.

The toddler’s dietitian also told detectives she would never have recommended a surgical evaluation if she had known the mother’s claims were misleading.

Foster parents subsequently reported that the child appeared uncomfortable with the feeding tube and resisted anyone attempting to clean the area.

Despite the alleged feeding problems, the toddler was reportedly able to eat a wide variety of foods.

The Monongalia County Sheriff’s Office said its investigation ultimately led to a diagnosis of medical child abuse, CBS reported.



Guzman was accused of Munchausen syndrome by proxy, now known as factitious disorder imposed on another.

The condition involves a caregiver falsely presenting someone in their care as sick or deliberately causing symptoms to obtain medical attention.

Meanwhile, a search of the family’s Morgantown home allegedly uncovered horrifying living conditions.

Detectives reportedly discovered cockroaches, swarms of flies and gnats, scattered garbage and dried feces believed to belong to both cats and humans.

“An overwhelming odor of garbage permeated the residence,” the complaint stated.



Investigators also uncovered allegations of physical punishment and threats involving the nine-year-old child.

In one disturbing exchange, Caitlin Jean Meredith, 32, allegedly sent Guzman a photograph of her bruised hand, claiming the injuries came from repeatedly striking the older child.

Meredith, who lived at the property, was arrested alongside Guzman’s husband, Milton Alexander Guzman Cisneros, 47.

Both face two counts of child neglect creating risk of bodily injury.

Authorities allege that Cisneros failed to ensure the children’s safety and hygiene despite having limited involvement in the toddler’s medical appointments.



The sheriff’s office said the investigation began on October 8 after concerns were raised about the children’s welfare and discrepancies in the toddler’s reported medical history.

If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call or text the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline at 800-422-4453 or live chat at childhelphotline.org.

If a child or other person is in immediate danger, contact 911 immediately.

News.title: TK Maxx urgently recalls children’s product due to serious risk of choking with users warned ‘stop using immediately’
News.content:
Next

TK MAXX has extended its recall on a collection of bag charms and key rings over fears they present a serious choking risk.

Shoppers have been urged to stop using the accessories immediately and to return them to stores for a refund.

TK Maxx has recalled 10 bag charms made by the brand Piper K after the metal spring clip was found to be a major choking hazard.



Earlier this month, the retailer pulled the Seal Lifeguard and Duck in Dungarees bag charms, but the recall has now been extended to eight more products.



The crochet charms, designed by American accessory brand Piper K, were recalled because the metal spring clip can detach with a force below the minimum requirement, causing the O-ring to open.

If a young child was to put the detached small O-ring into their mouth, it could obstruct the airway and lead to choking.

As a result, all 10 of the bag charms have been pulled from TK Maxx as they were found not to pass relevant regulations.

As well as the previously recalled items, new items include a Fluffy Cherry Scarf Black Charm, a Hedgehog Heart Bag Charm, a crochet Lobster Charm and a Fox with Hat Bag Charm.

Others include a Bat Key Charm, Crochet Coffee Donut Bag, Spider Skull Key Charm, and Nightmare Character Key Charm.

Customers who have previously bought the hazardous charms have been urged to stop using all of the products immediately and keep them out of reach of children.

News.title: EU chiefs threaten Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset unless Labour caves on tuition fees
News.content:
HOLD EU TO RANSOM EU chiefs threaten Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset unless Labour caves on tuition fees







Next

EUROCRATS are threatening to hold Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset to ransom in a row over tuition fees.

Last-minute demands from Brussels have put the Prime Minister under pressure to bring costs down to the same level as British students.



Concerns have already been raised over being a rule-taker of food standards and allowing 100,000 young Europeans to work and study in Britain.

But student fees could see a cut from fees of up to £38,000 a year to £9,970 which the UK has resisted because of the financial knock-on effect on university finances.



A six-month-deadline has been put on talks to find an agreement on the costs with the rest of the deal may not be implemented until a solution is found.

An EU source said: “It is an important element of the deal. Let’s hope that everything can go ahead. The agreement should come into force in a balanced way.”



An EU Official also added: “I can confirm that we have not yet reached an agreement on tuition fees and we have given ourselves six months to reach that agreement and we envisage being able to sign the several agreements in parallel.”

Under the proposed deal, Britain will sign up to European rules on food, carbon trading and youth mobility in return for closer access to the single market.

In a further setback, it was confirmed that 100,000 young Europeans will be able to come to the UK under the new youth mobility scheme.

The PM had pushed for a lower cap of around 80,000, but the Government caved at the last minute.



No10 insists it has landed huge agreements that will cut costs for businesses and bring down prices at the shops, and believes the deal is as good as done.

Downing Street will also continue talks on Channel cooperation and the EU’s Made in Europe plans.

A Number 10 spokeswoman said the deal is done and negotiations have concluded between Britain and the EU.

Both sides will work towards putting into force agreements on food and drink, youth mobility and the emissions trading scheme.

News.title: Secret UK cyber operation protected tens of thousands of fridges from hackers
News.content:
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.

Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.

France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies.

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.

In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.

The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.

News.title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish
News.content:
Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a targeted inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US. It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS, external, found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.

Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.

Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."

He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTCâNCIâAACR Symposium 2026, external where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."

Pancreatic cancer accounts for about 3% of all cancers in the United States and about 8% of all cancer deaths, killing around 53,000 people a year, external.

In Britain, there are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.

Actor Alan Rickman died of the disease in 2016, five months after diagnosis.

Symptoms can include, external jaundice, itchy skin, darker pee, paler poo, unexplained weight loss, tiredness and high temperature.

News.title: Calls for consent law change after Joanne Young rape case
News.content:
The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change to the law on consent.

Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period, using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.

The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials of this nature.

Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"

Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse

Philip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers without her knowledge.

During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.

The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.

In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone.

"We live in a world where someone's partner can consent for them, and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law.

"This is simply unacceptable."

News.title: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad
News.content:
Phil had no idea the flat he rents had been sold to overseas investors in May 2025 until the BBC contacted him. But there were clues: bills addressed to someone called Jan HÃ¡la had been coming through the letterbox for months.

Lee Jones told us that the properties his companies provide are "good quality accommodation" and he has no responsibility for the communal areas of Castleview House since he sold the freehold in 2021. He denied his relationship with Chris Smith amounted to a conflict of interest, but did not respond to questions about his role in marketing the properties.

Jan HÃ¡la, the Czech investor who now owns Phil's flat, and the BritskÃ© Reality estate agency did not respond to requests for comment.

We spoke to several other people living in flats run by Nurture Housing Association in Castleview House who said they were in supported accommodation. They reported receiving little or no help from Nurture but were afraid to speak out publicly for fear of eviction and becoming homeless.

There is also evidence that marketing materials for investors buying flats in Castleview were misleading. Investors were told Nurture was providing "specialist supported housing" - a claim which is repeated on its website.

According to the Regulator of Social Housing, this would mean it was providing a high level of care, equivalent to living in a care home.

But Nurture had not been registered as a specialised supported housing provider, the regulator said, and its claim to be providing this was "shocking".

In a statement, Nurture acknowledged that Castleview House is managed under a "general housing management model" and does not form part of its supported housing portfolio. It said it provided supported housing elsewhere through partners which were registered providers.

It said the Czech advert found by the BBC related to "historic marketing material" produced by third parties.

However, the BBC has seen marketing material from several other agents selling flats in Castleview House to investors, which also claim that Nurture is providing supported housing to the residents on a 25-year lease.

Nurture said it is not directly involved with the companies marketing the properties. But it said: "We will be reviewing communications with relevant agents and reminding them of the importance of ensuring that any information relating to Nurture is accurate, transparent and does not create misunderstanding regarding the accommodation or services provided."

News.title: UK braces for coldest night of autumn so far with temperature of -10C forecast
News.content:
The coldest night of the autumn so far was on Thursday night when the temperature got down to minus 8.4C (18F) at Tulloch Bridge, Highland.

Temperatures for many of us have been up and down recently due to cold Arctic air temporarily sweeping southward across the UK.

Southern areas of the UK have mostly held onto milder air from the Atlantic.

During Friday though a northerly wind will once again bring some of the colder air from the Arctic, and bring a colder day for most of the UK.

Any early cloud and rain in southern England will clear and for most of the UK it will be a bright day with some sunshine. A few wintry showers are possible across Scotland.

By night, temperatures will drop with frost expected widely, mostly across the Midlands, northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.

Although it is likely to be the coldest night of the autumn so far, with minus 10C predicted in rural Scotland, we are a long way off the coldest November night on record, when a temperature of minus 16.1C was recorded in Cumbria in 1912.

We came closer to that record low temperature in 2025, when the UK experienced the coldest November night in 12 years with minus 12.6C in Moray.

News.title: Next round of BBC cuts will be more noticeable to audiences, report warns
News.content:
Further job losses and programme cuts at the BBC will be more noticeable to audiences than previous savings measures, a new report has warned.

The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach its Â£500m target.

In its report, the National Audit Office (NAO) anticipated the BBC's next round of cost-cutting measures would be more difficult to deliver and more perceptible to audiences.

The BBC welcomed the report, saying it had "consistently argued that the current funding model is not sustainable and needs reform".

The NAO report, external also said the BBC's current measures were expected to reduce the BBC's workforce by 11% over three years.

Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "As the BBC approaches charter renewal in just over a year's time, there is no doubt that there are difficult choices ahead."

The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.

The organisation has so far achieved savings by reducing staffing levels, rationalising its estate, modernising technology, simplifying processes and changing the mix and scope of content and services, the public spending watchdog said.

News.title: Guests no longer asked to wash up as new Airbnb rules come into force
News.content:
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.

Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.

Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".

But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.

The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.

Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said.

Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.

If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

News.title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
News.content:
Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures.

Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser.

The latest official sales figures, external from the ONS add to the evidence that the public has begun stockpiling.

"Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said.

"Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again."

The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the increase came after a 0.6% decline in September.

As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October.

News.title: New EU-UK deal should reduce 'Irish Sea border' impact
News.content:
A new deal between the UK and the EU on food, plants and animals is likely to be significant for Northern Ireland by reducing the impact of the "Irish Sea border".

The agreement is expected to be confirmed later when Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels.

Since Brexit, Northern Ireland has continued to follow EU rules for agri-food products while the rest of the UK has not.

The new deal will see the whole UK realigning with EU rules on those products, meaning goods being sent from Great Britain to Northern Ireland will no longer need to be checked at ports.

It will also mean a reduction but not elimination of the paperwork required to move agri-food goods from Great Britain to Northern Ireland.

News.title: More young hikers lost using Google Maps, say rescuers
News.content:
More young people are getting caught out on the fells due to relying on Google Maps for navigation, rescuers have said.

After a full-team rescue on Sunday, Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team (WMRT) said an increasing amount of young people, mostly aged 18 to 24, were getting lost or into trouble after using Google Maps on their phones.

WMRT said Google Maps was "not made for the mountains", because unlike a paper map, the app does not display steep rocky outcrops, fell paths and contours, which show three-dimensional shape of the land.

The advice to use a paper map - which is echoed by Google - has been repeated by rescue teams for years, so how can navigation be made more available to young people?

"It's a tricky one," mountaineering and climbing instructor (MCI) Pippa Archer, who lives in Kendal, said.

"I can see the appeal of using something that is free and readily available on your phone, however, a map and compass won't set you back too much," she said.

Archer, who guides and helps people develop their skills in the mountains, said the detail on a paper map was "crucial for staying safe" and "gives a picture of what to expect on your walk, and this is the key to not getting lost".

"A walking map will show you where the ground gets really steep, where there are cliffs to avoid, or streams that need to be crossed," she said.

News.title: Girls as young as five targeted for upskirting as charges continue to rise
News.content:
Girls as young as five have been targeted for upskirting, new police figures show.

Over the past three years, Wales' four forces received 219 complaints from people up to the age of 87, with 18 people charged, results of Freedom of Information (FOI) requests, external reveal.

Upskirting involves taking a photo or video, external beneath someone's clothing - without their knowledge - with the intention of viewing their genitals, buttocks or underwear.

It was made a criminal offence under the Voyeurism (Offences) Act 2019, external and carries a maximum sentence of two years in prison.

The Crown Prosecution Service, external urged people to report incidents immediately, saying those that led to charges almost doubled between 2022 and 2026.

"As well as being an extremely damaging offence in its own right, our prosecutors often see upskirting forming part of a wider pattern of sexual offending," said national lead for sexual offence prosecutions Siobhan Blake.

Between January 2023 and June 2026, Wales' four police forces received 219 complaints, with the highest being 159 in the Dyfed-Powys area and the lowest, six in Gwent, according to the FOI figures.

Where ages were recorded, 11 involved under-10s, 67 came from girls aged 11 to 17, 35 from those 18 to 24, and 12 from over-55s.

From these 219 complaints, nine people were charged in the north Wales force area, six in Dyfed-Powys, three in south Wales, while Gwent had no data.

A previous FOI to Greater Manchester Police, external showed it received 146 reports between 2019 and 2025, leading to 41 arrests and 10 people being charged.

West Midlands Police received 75 reports between 2022 and 2026, with 23 charged, according to another FOI, external.

News.title: Northern line upgrades give green light to colour blind London tube drivers
News.content:
Osman Hassan has worked for TfL for eight years - including in customer service roles - but it was only relatively recently that he was able to achieve his dream of becoming a Tube train driver.

Hassan has colour vision deficiency (CVD), a condition commonly known as colour blindness.

London Underground has historically depended on red and green lights for its signalling system meaning a career as a train driver on most of the network has not been possible for people with CVD for safety reasons.

However, the Northern line has now become the second line to be fully upgraded in a way which allows for those with CVD to drive its trains.

"It's wonderful," says Hassan.

"I love my job. I love the responsibility of getting people in London safely from A to B and the interaction I have with the public.

"It's brilliant that TfL has been able to make these changes and I hope it prompts other companies to look at what they might be able to do to help employees with CVD."

Around three million people in the UK have CVD. It is much more common in men with around one in 12 affected, compared to one in 200 women.

CVD is not automatically considered a disability but for some people who have it, it can be a significant impairment, especially if it affects their career choices or prospects.

Back in 2018 the Jubilee line became the first â and until now â only line which drivers with CVD could work on.

Now though, the Northern line is able to welcome drivers with CVD too, meaning greater opportunities for employees with the condition.

Hassan - who previously had a stint driving on the Jubilee line - is one of two drivers with CVD working on the Northern line.

A key figure behind the upgrade has been TfL strategy and change manager, Joe Brown.

News.title: Babydoll singer Jamie Miller covers Christmas classic
News.content:
After spending four weeks at number one in the UK singles charts, Jamie Miller is releasing his take on the festive classic It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas.

In October, Miller became the first artist from Wales to top the UK singles chart since 2011 with his TikTok-viral song Babydoll.

The success transformed Miller's career, but he revealed that his "made it" moment was telling his taxi driver dad and cleaner mum they could retire.

While Babydoll's popularity continues, Miller teased the release of his next track on social media, telling fans: "You guys asked for a Christmas song..."

His cover arrives as artists compete for this year's Christmas number one.

Among those in the running is singer Sam Fender, who covered the Rolling Stones' You Can't Always Get What You Want in this year's John Lewis Christmas advert.

Other festive releases include Olivia Rodrigo's original Christmas song Take me Home (4 Christmas).

Classic Christmas songs also tend to return to the charts in the lead-up to the holiday, like the 1984 Wham! hit Last Christmas which is currently sitting at number 22.

The song made history in 2023 when, 39 years after release, it reached the Christmas number one spot for the first time, only to do so again the following year.

News.title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'
News.content:
The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.

Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.

NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.

In the end, more than Â£30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.

Once established, it was effective.

But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

News.title: England fined for fans' anti-Catholic chants in Spain
News.content:
England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.

European football's governing body have fined the Football Association Â£12,572 (15,000 euros) and imposed a suspended one-match ban for England away supporters.

BBC Sport understands the charge of 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour' relates to chants that were deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish.

"We will not tolerate this unacceptable and deeply offensive chanting, and will work with the police, who attend all England home and away matches, to identify the perpetrators and take the necessary action," an FA spokesperson said.

A further offence within the next two years would mean a ban on away fans is enforced.

Free Lions - the Football Supporters' Association Fans' Embassy for travelling England fans - says the team will be put at a disadvantage because of the actions of supporters in Spain.

"There is no place for offensive chants aimed at religious figures. The time for these chants is over," a statement read.

"The behaviour and reputation of England supporters abroad has improved significantly over the years but these chants undermine that progress.

"If the chants continue then thousands of travelling fans will miss out on future away games and players will miss that backing in the ground, putting our own team at a disadvantage, at one of the best times to be an England fan."

There had been concerns of the prospect of racist chanting from Spain fans before the game in Madrid with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.

Tuchel stressed he didn't expect any incidents, but the visit was England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.

That led to a firm response from Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

England won the match 3-2 to end Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and top League A Group 3.

News.title: Scientists find hidden fungal toxins in 212 plant-based foods
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Scientists who tested 212 plant-based food and drink products found a fungal toxin in every single one.

The research team detected at least one of 19 mycotoxins in each product, and many of the items carried multiple toxins.

The study was led by scientists at the University of Parma in Italy, with contributions from Cranfield University in Bedfordshire. Their findings were published in the journal Food Control.

The 212 products analysed included vegan burgers, vegetarian chicken pieces, vegan sausages, and oat, almond, and soy milk.

Despite the widespread presence of the contaminants, the concentrations in every product fell below recommended European Union guideline levels.

The team said this reflected the high food quality standards maintained by the UK food industry.

open image in gallery The scientists analysed 212 plant-based food and drink products, including vegan sausages and burger patties ( Getty/iStock )

What are mycotoxins?

Mycotoxins are poisonous substances produced by certain fungi, including moulds. They can enter the food supply when agricultural crops become contaminated during growing, harvesting, or storage.

Many of the ingredients used to manufacture plant-based foods are particularly susceptible to fungal contamination.

Grains, legumes, and seeds can encounter mould in fields or storage facilities, creating opportunities for mycotoxins to develop before the ingredients reach food manufacturers.

Mycotoxins’ presence in food does not necessarily mean the product contains living mould, and detecting a toxin does not automatically mean the food is unsafe, Cranfield University said.

The potential health risk depends on factors such as the type of toxin, its concentration, and how much a person consumes over time.

open image in gallery The study also found mycotoxins in almond, oat, and soy milk ( Getty )

That distinction is especially important for people who eat plant-based products frequently, the university said. Someone whose diet regularly includes meat substitutes, dairy alternatives, grains, and legumes may encounter the substances through several different foods rather than a single source.

Earlier studies have suggested that consuming small amounts of mycotoxins regularly may contribute to cumulative exposure and potentially increase health risks.

At sufficiently high or harmful exposure levels, certain mycotoxins can damage the liver and kidneys, interfere with normal immune system function, and increase the risk of cancer.

Andrea Patriarca, a senior lecturer in mycology at Cranfield University, said that mycotoxins are a natural part of the food environment and should not discourage people from eating a varied diet.

"Mycotoxins occur naturally in foods and cannot be completely avoided. As consumers, we should not be frightened or deterred from enjoying a variety of products.

“However, a significant concern arises when new foods enter the market, as there are currently no established regulations to monitor mycotoxins.”

News.title: Nations League draw LIVE: England discover quarter-final opponents
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

England were fired up by Spain waving the World Cup around

England are set to discover their opponents for the Nations League quarter-finals in March.

Thomas Tuchel’s side topped Group A3 with a sensational 3-2 win over Spain despite seeing out the last half-hour with only 10 men after Elliot Anderson’s straight red card.

That means the Three Lions enter the last-eight draw as one of the top seeds, along with France, Germany and Portugal, and will play either Belgium, the Netherlands or Norway - who all finished runner-up in their groups - in the two-legged quarter-finals.

Topping the group also means they will have the advantage of a home tie for the second leg, while they cannot be drawn against Spain despite the world champions finishing second in Group A3, as they have already played each other.

News.title: Mapped: Where temperatures will plunge to -9C as Britain big freeze
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Temperatures are set to plummet to the coldest point of the autumn this week after the first weather warning for snow was activated.

Sub-zero temperatures will be widespread overnight, forecasters have warned, with lows possibly reaching minus-9C in more northern regions and Scotland.

Thursday night was the coldest of the autumn so far, the Met Office confirmed on Friday, reaching a low of minus-8.4C in Tulloch Bridge, Scotland.

Cold health alerts from the UK Healthy Security Agency will remain in place across northern England until Monday morning.

Overnight frost can be expected in many places, alongside rain and a possibility for more snow.

Here’s where the coldest temperatures can be expected over the weekend:

The Met Office issued its snow warning on Tuesday, covering northern regions. Up to 3cm fell in some locations, threatening to cause some travel disruption in the affected areas.

Temperatures will begin to pick up overnight on Saturday, the forecaster has said, but more rainfall will then begin to be seen largely in the Southwest on Sunday.

This is due to a “weather front [that is] moving in from the Atlantic,” Met Office meteorologist Aidan McGivern said on Thursday, adding that “as it encounters the cold and drier weather towards the north east, a large area of high pressure sitting to the north, it slows down.”

“It's going to become increasingly heavy in terms of the rainfall. But also it will slow it down... In fact, it stalls across southwestern parts throughout Sunday, leading to a very wet day in the southwest, but mostly the rain not making much further,” he said.

Bringing uncertainty to this winter’s weather is the activity of the polar vortex – strong winds in the stratosphere above the Arctic.

These winds weakened last week, the earliest time this has happened on record, which the Met Office confirmed on Wednesday to be a ‘sudden stratospheric warming’ event.

The current cold snap is not thought to be driven by this activity, but experts warn that disruptions to the polar vortex can cause cold air to be pushed further south, threatening lower temperatures.

Met Office five day weather forecast

Friday

Cloud and rain clears the south through the morning, with some sunny spells developing later. Chillier, but brighter further North, with a few scattered showers along North Sea coasts, turning wintery in the far north. A chillier day for most.

Largely dry, though some showers in the far north. Clear skies allow for widespread frost development. With light winds, fog patches develop across central and southern England and Northern Ireland.

Saturday

A crisp start to the weekend, with long sunny spells through the day. Skies turn cloudier in the southwest with rain later and strong winds developing towards the coast overnight.

Sunday to Tuesday

Rain persists across the southwest with strong winds on Sunday, drier elsewhere with sunny spells. Frosty overnight. Winds ease Monday, before strengthening again as rain arrives from the west Tuesday.

News.title: F1 to introduce ‘professionalised officiating’ for 2027 season
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The FIA have announced the introduction of permanent race stewards for the 2027 Formula 1 season.

The sport’s governing body, which runs all F1 race operations, has faced pressure to appoint full-time officials after several contentious decisions in recent years. Currently, each grand prix has a group of four voluntary stewards, one of whom is an ex-driver.

Yet from next season, the FIA will recruit a “small number” of full-time stewards, aiming to reach a roster of 12-15 permanent stewards by the 2028 season, a move it has described as “professionalising officiating.”

The FIA statement added: "The introduction of dedicated full-time stewards to the FIA's flagship championship will provide continuity and expertise within the stewarding structure, further advancing the FIA's commitment to fairness through the ongoing review and continuous improvement of sporting regulations and stewarding guidelines.

"It will also allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making."

Carlos Sainz, a director of the drivers’ body, Grand Prix Drivers’ Association (GPDA), has previously called for full-time stewards to improve decision-making, with rulings on driver standards and racing errors failing to be applied on a consistent basis. McLaren CEO Zak Brown has also long called for this implementation.

Sainz said in 2025: "F1 and the FIA all agree that [permanent stewards] should be the way forward, where at least two of the three stewards are permanent and we have one rotational for teaching purposes."

Of the new change, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula 1 World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport."

News.title: Resident doctors strike across Northern Ireland over pay dispute
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Resident doctors across Northern Ireland are on strike on Friday amid an ongoing dispute over pay.

The 24-hour walkout will run from 7am on Friday until 7am on Saturday 21 November, as resident doctors withdraw their labour from both GP surgeries and hospitals.

This industrial action will be followed by specialist and consultant doctors in the region, who are set to stage a strike on Monday 23 November.

It marks a second round of strikes over demands for full pay restoration, following a previous 24-hour walkout held by doctors in June this year.

open image in gallery Dr Rita Sushil joins striking NHS resident doctors on the picket line outside Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast during a 24-hour walkout over pay ( PA )

According to Dr Steven Montgomery, chairman of BMA NI resident doctors’ committee, doctors "should not have to take strike action for a second time", though the problem leading them to picket lines during the summer remains unresolved.

“Our pay is eroding, and we need to address that in order to retain young doctors in Northern Ireland,” he said.

“When I talk to colleagues, it’s clear they want the best for the health service in Northern Ireland and for our patients.

“But it is also clear that they are facing burnout and moral injury, and what we are paid does not reflect that.

open image in gallery Striking NHS resident doctors on the picket line outside Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast ( PA )

“Doctors train for many years, carry enormous responsibility and are asking for the value of their pay to be restored.

“Our members have been very clear that this dispute is about full pay restoration. Receiving the pay award doctors are overdue for this year will not restore the value of the pay that has been lost over many years.

“We are more than willing to discuss with the minister and the department how we can address pay erosion and the steps they need to take to satisfy our members that they are committed to addressing the issue.”

Over the summer, resident doctors in England voted to accept a government offer on pay and working conditions, bringing an end to a year of industrial action.

The decision concludes a dispute that saw the British Medical Association (BMA) Resident Doctor Committee (RDC) orchestrate 21 days of strikes since July 2025.

open image in gallery The 24-hour strike will run from 7am on Friday until 7am on Saturday 21 November ( PA )

Resident doctors in England had threatened a four-day strike in June but called it off at the last minute after the government’s offer.

Dr Jack Fletcher, chairman of the BMA’s resident doctors committee (RDC), expressed the union’s long-standing position on industrial action.

He said: "We have always been clear that no strikes needed to go ahead if we received an offer appropriate to put to our members."

News.title: Léa Seydoux says she doesn’t care about James Bond casting: ‘How can you?’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The speculation over who will play the next Bond girl has drawn a notably unbothered response from Léa Seydoux.

The French actress, 41, played Dr Madeleine Swann opposite Daniel Craig, 58, in Spectre and No Time to Die.

Asked on The Runthrough podcast who she thought should take on the role of the next Bond girl, or Bond woman, Léa laughed and said: “I don’t really care.”

She added: “I don’t really care, guys. How can you?”

Léa discussed the future of the spy franchise during her podcast appearance, and also addressed the changes behind the scenes following Amazon MGM Studios’ takeover of creative control of the franchise.

open image in gallery Lea Seydoux played Madeleine Swann in two Bond movies ( Sony Pictures )

She said: “It became American. But I’m sure the movie will be great because it’s directed by Denis Villeneuve, who’s a very talented director. I’m sure he will do something great.”

The change in ownership saw longtime Bond custodians Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson relinquish creative control of the film series, with Seydoux previously expressing disappointment about the change.

Speaking to Variety before the Cannes Film Festival, Léa said: “I was a bit sad when I heard that it was sold… but now that it’s Denis, I was like, ‘Oh, at least it’s him, so it will be cinema’.”

She has already worked with Villeneuve on the science-fiction blockbuster Dune: Part Two, in which she played Lady Margot Fenring alongside an ensemble cast including Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya, Florence Pugh and Austin Butler.

She also revealed she had sent the director a congratulatory note after learning he would take charge of the next Bond film.

Speaking to Variety, she said: “He’s super cultured – he knows so much about cinema, but not only cinema.”

Léa also questioned whether younger actors possess the qualities needed to portray the famous secret agent.

She said on The Runthrough: “It’s really difficult to cast James Bond, because you need to find an actor with a depth and with many layers, and I don’t think that the young generation really has that.”

Her interview was recorded before reports emerged naming Robert Pattinson, 40, as the new 007, prompting widespread discussion and debate.

In a statement released by Amazon MGM Studios, Robert said: “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime.”

He added: “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

open image in gallery Robert Pattinson will take on the role of James Bond in the next film about 007 ( Amazon MGM Studios )

Pattinson rose to international fame playing vampire Edward Cullen in The Twilight Saga and later took on the title role in The Batman. He will succeed Daniel in the as-yet-untitled 26th Bond film.

The next instalment is being developed under Amazon MGM Studios, with Dune director Denis Villeneuve, 59, attached to direct.

The appointment of Denis marks a significant change for the long-running franchise following Daniel’s departure after five films spanning Casino Royale, Quantum of Solace, Skyfall, Spectre and No Time to Die.

The new Bond film will be written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight, 67, with Amy Pascal, 68, and David Heyman, 65, producing.

A release date has not yet been announced.

News.title: Could hackers gain access to my fridge? Concerns grow after supermarket cyber attacks
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A slew of cyber attacks targeting refrigeration systems across Europe has prompted fresh concern about smart fridges found throughout many homes.

Attacks on European supermarkets spread across the continent earlier this month, hitting fridges and ​freezers from Sweden to Belgium, and forcing stores to throw away food.

It followed a similar incident in France in October, where police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures as high as 50C.

A British cybersecurity operation has since fixed a flaw in the operating systems of commercial fridges and freezers used by supermarkets, warehouses and restaurants, helping to protect them from hacks, as reported by the BBC.

But could Britons with internet-connected fridges be the next victims?

Could a hacker gain access to my fridge?

Fridges were once among the simplest of appliances, vulnerable to little more than someone leaving the door open. But in the era of smart technology, the fridge now sits alongside locks, thermostats and a host of other mechanical devices that are all connected to our WiFi.

Being able to monitor and control a fridge remotely can be convenient, particularly when you are away from home. But there are fears those same useful features could potentially be used in a cyber attack.

open image in gallery Your smart fridge could be vulnerable to a cyber attack ( PA )

The reality is that any device that uses the internet can potentially be targeted by hackers. In 2015, researchers at a hacking conference in Las Vegas used a Samsung smart refrigerator to demonstrate how these devices could be compromised.

Whether a fridge is connected directly to your home's internet, or via an app or cloud service, it could be at risk. Hackers are usually interested in stealing data, using devices to access a larger network, or disrupting services, which is why smart devices are targeted.

However, three-quarters of attacks were focused on routers rather than appliances, according to data from the security industry.

What can a hacker do if they access my fridge?

A hacker may not appear to have much to gain from breaking into a fridge, but once inside they can potentially either control the device or gather information from it.

As the French supermarket hacks showed, accessing devices can give hackers control, allowing them to potentially cause chaos by raising temperatures and spoiling food.

Devices with cameras could pick up images and sound, while a compromised router could show any information that passes through the network.

open image in gallery A hack saw French supermarket fridges heated to 50C ( AFP/Getty )

Users could see their devices being switched on or off, settings changed, or even end up being locked out of their devices.

More serious attacks could see hackers use poorly secured devices to access other systems on the network or steal personal information from online accounts.

Could hackers take over cars?

Cybersecurity researchers have demonstrated vulnerabilities in connected vehicles. In 2015, researchers remotely took control of a moving Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, forcing the recall of about 1.4 million vehicles and the deployment of software fixes.

Nearly ten years later, researchers disclosed a flaw that allowed them to track, unlock and start certain Kia vehicles using only number plate information.

The researchers said they reported the vulnerabilities to Kia, which fixed them within months, and there was no evidence they had been exploited ‌in real-world attacks. However, modern vehicles and aircraft are also designed with extensive safety and backup systems.

Critical infrastructure such as power and water networks generally has multiple layers of security, monitoring and regulation that consumer devices don't offer.

That does not mean they are immune from cyber attacks, but they are typically much harder targets than a household appliance connected to a home Wi-Fi network.

News.title: EasyJet flight met by police after passenger smokes in toilet
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A passenger was removed from an easyJet flight from London to Scotland by police after allegedly smoking in an aircraft toilet.

Flight U2404 from Luton to Glasgow was delayed by an hour on Monday while a “disruptive” passenger was taken off the aircraft for smoking onboard.

According to aviation news network AirLive, before the aircraft left the gate, a passenger lit a cigarette in an onboard restroom, triggering the lavatory smoke alarm.

The Airbus A320 had been scheduled to depart Luton airport at 1pm, but ended up leaving shortly before 2pm, landing in Glasgow at 2.54pm – around 40 minutes late, per Flightradar24 data.

Smoking and vaping are “prohibited on all UK airlines”, said the UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA).

The act is a criminal offence under Article 243 of the Air Navigation Order 2016, and can carry fines of £2,500.

An easyJet spokesperson said: “Flight EZY404 from Luton to Glasgow on 16th November was met by police before departure due to a passenger behaving disruptively onboard.

“Our cabin crew are trained to assess all situations and to act quickly and appropriately to ensure the safety of the flight. We take these incidents seriously and do not tolerate disruptive behaviour onboard.

“The safety and wellbeing of our customers and crew is always easyJet's highest priority.”

On Wednesday, an easyJet flight was forced to divert back to Bristol airport after the plane suffered a bird strike during take-off.

Flight EZY213 departed Bristol airport at 9.24am on Wednesday, 18 November, for a domestic flight to Edinburgh that usually lasts under an hour.

Yet passengers found themselves reaching only as far as the Brecon Beacons in Wales before turning back south after 10 minutes of flying.

The Airbus A320 circled the air above the Bristol Channel a few times before landing back at Bristol airport, around 40 minutes after it took off.

The plane suffered a bird strike as it left the airport, and was forced to turn back.
