News.title: Anthropic achieves $2tn valuation as shares soar
News.content:
Anthropic has surged to a $2tn (£1.5tn) valuation as the Claude-maker defied a tech sell-off with a record-breaking float.

Shares in the Silicon Valley AI lab soared as high as $111.50 in opening trading on the Nasdaq exchange in New York on Thursday. The stock traded up around a third on its initial price of $83, before falling back to $97 per share at close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 closed 2.3pc lower, with investors cashing-in on the excitement, analysts say.

Dow Jones ended the session 2.2pc lower, while the S&P 500 closed down 2pc.

The AI lab raised a record $107bn in the stock market listing, smashing a previous $86bn record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June.

Many investors had been concerned about the backdrop to the blockbuster listing after a Chinese spying scandal engulfed US chip giant Nvidia and Jensen Huang, its former chief executive.

Nvidia is a major investor in Anthropic, but it has suffered a $900bn share price wide-out since Mr Huang admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an alleged Chinese spy earlier this month.

The US midterm elections, meanwhile, wiped trillions of dollars from the stock market earlier this month over concerns about a Democrat-led crackdown on AI companies and data centres.

Anthropic is likely to emerge as a bellwether for the wider AI industry. The AI giant plans to spend more than $1tn on technology infrastructure to power its digital chatbot and its pursuit of superintelligence, which its founders claim could lead to unprecedented growth and an “age of miracles”.

The float also sees Anthropic leap ahead of its main rival, ChatGPT-developer OpenAI, which is plotting its own trillion-dollar float next year.

The deal cements the status of Anthropic’s seven founders, including chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela, and British policy boss Jack Clark, as multi-billionaires.

The seven were worth around $19bn at the initial float price, which valued Anthropic at $1.4tn late on Wednesday, but could be worth as much as $26bn based on its latest valuation.

It also catapults Mr Clark, a 37-year-old former journalist from Brighton, into the ranks of the richest Britons.

Anthropic was founded just six years ago with a promise that it would pursue superintelligent AI while focusing on safety. It was launched after Mr Amodei quit OpenAI amid a bitter split over its approach to safety with founder Sam Altman.

The company’s founders have been deeply concerned about the potential risks of AI, including that an uncontrollable future AI system could spell disaster for humanity.

Mr Amodei said on Thursday that AI carried “real risks” but that the company would be “obsessed with safety”.

Anthropic launched its Claude AI as a helpful chatbot in 2023, but it has since found widespread use among businesses for coding or acting as an AI “agent”, a kind of digital co-worker.

The company reported revenues from its AI tool of around $33bn in the first nine months of the year, although it lost $104bn.

The deal also mints nearly all of Anthropic’s staff as millionaires. Private market data company Hill estimated that, at its initial float price, some 5,100 out of its 5,300 staff would become overnight millionaires. Some 580 will have fortunes of more than $100m.

It will provide a stunning return for many of Anthropic’s early investors, who include Ashton Kutcher, the actor, and Jaan Tallinn, the founder of Skype.

XTX Ventures, a fund launched by British billionaire trader Alex Gerko, is also set for significant gains after a $10m investment in Anthropic three years ago.

Dan Ives, a technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, said after trading began that the deal would help “restore some investor confidence” that the “AI revolution” is not waning.

However, Joe Maher, an analyst at Capital Economics, warned the deal may not be enough to “save the AI trade” as stocks fell on Thursday.

Elsewhere, a short-seller report targeting AMD, a chip company led by Lisa Hsu, the cousin of Nvidia chief Mr Huang, prompted an 8pc share price fall. The report claimed AMD had deeper ties to China than widely believed.

An AMD spokesman said the report “misrepresents” its business practices.

As the float got underway, there were protests outside the Nasdaq exchange, with several anti-AI demonstrators arrested.

In recent months, Anthropic’s own researchers have warned of the risk of an AI disaster that could destroy humanity. One suggested the risk was as high as 10pc.

The protests in New York called for a “a freeze to reckless AI development and destruction”.

News.title: Myanmar guilty of genocide, International Court of Justice rules
News.content:
Myanmar’s military junta has been found guilty of committing genocide in a ruling that could have implications for Israel and its war on Gaza.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, the UN’s highest court, said Myanmar had systematically attempted to destroy the Muslim minority Rohingya population. It is the first time in its 81-year history that the ICJ has found a state guilty of genocide.

The 2017 attacks led to one of the largest movements of people in modern history, with hundreds of thousands fleeing violence across the border to Bangladesh. The court said the attacks constituted more than an attempt to contain unrest in the region through military means.

The judges said: “The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations.”

The judges ruled by nine votes to six that it had been genocide.

News.title: England feast on Australia chaos to land early Ashes blow
News.content:
Good morning from idyllic Hobart, where there is not a cloud in the sky, and England are having a belting time batting first.

They zipped along all day in lovely batting conditions, moving to 137 for two from 20 overs.

The wickets to fall have been Tom Banton, well caught by a juggling Mitch Marsh running back from mid-off, and Joe Root, who had a horrible heave at Matt Renshaw, and was bowled. He has never made an ODI hundred on Australian soil and is unlikely to get another chance.

Ben Duckett initially cruised along in Banton’s slip stream, but has hit a blaze of boundaries since. He has feasted on some Australia’s bowling and fielding that has been pretty ordinary, as they say in these parts. Duckett was the beneficiary of a terrible drop at square leg by Alex Carey, who is back in the side but not keeping.

The other big talking point, inevitably, is sandpapergate. Usman Khawaja, who lit the fire for the reopening of the public debate, is here commentating, and Cricket Australia have announced an independent forum for players and staff from the tour of South Africa in 2018 to come forward and share their memories. CA will not be reopening the investigation, and or issuing any new punishments, though. They haven’t even decided how much of forum’s findings they will make public. So it is unclear exactly what the point of the whole thing is.

News.title: Households face back-to-back interest rate rises
News.content:
Mortgage borrowers face another rise in interest rates before Christmas after official figures showed inflation rose to its highest level in a year.

The Bank of England is expected to raise borrowing costs again in December, after increasing rates for the first time in three years earlier this month.

It comes after consumer prices index (CPI) inflation rose from 3.5pc in September to 3.6pc in October, according to the Office for National Statistics.

In a rare intervention after the publication of inflation data, the Bank underlined its commitment to slowing down the pace of price rises.

A spokesman for the Bank said: “The conflict in the Middle East has caused energy prices and inflation to rise in recent months, and inflation is expected to rise further by the middle of next year due to cost pressures already in the pipeline.

“The Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2pc target and stays there.”

Rob Wood of Pantheon Macroeconomics said it was a “very close call” over whether policymakers raise rates in December or February, but favoured a jump before Christmas.

Traders are betting there is a 74pc chance of a December rate rise, down from 77pc on Tuesday, after services inflation rose slightly less than expected to 3.7pc in October.

Mr Wood said: “The headlines provide some relief, but underlying inflation remains too high, and airfares may be beginning to show some effect from higher energy costs.

“We expect at least two further rate hikes and now bring our calls forward to December and February, from February and April.”

Inflation increased in October as a result of surging fuel prices for motorists.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October to 174.7p, the highest level since August 2022.

The ONS said diesel rose by 7p to 199.5p per litre last month – the highest since records began in 1996.

News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. When a mother survives childbirth, her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

An expectant mother receives an ultrasound scan at an MSF hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Sierra Leone’s success is largely due to the roll-out of free healthcare to pregnant women and children in 2010, and a more recent push to reach zero preventable maternal deaths. The 300 days of Activism for Triple Zero campaign – which also aims to tackle preventable child deaths and unvaccinated children – began in March.

According to the government, maternal deaths have dropped by 31.4 per cent since last year. There remains, however, deep inequality for pregnant women, mostly because of geographical inequity.

The United States charity Partners in Health, the lead funder for the Maternal Center of Excellence, points out that women in Sierra Leone have a one in 74 chance of dying in pregnancy or childbirth in their reproductive years. By comparison, the risk for UK women is around one in 7,500.

Despite the unparalleled progress of recent years, the happy ending which Adama and her baby have experienced is by no means universal across Sierra Leone.

A mother and her newborn recover from birth at the Maternal Center of Excellence at the Koidu Government Hospital Credit : Simon Townsley

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

An ambulance that was due to visit the village during our visit never arrives because the driver is afraid it will get stuck.

It is evident that a woman needing a team of midwives and expensive monitoring equipment to assist with a complicated birth can be totally cut off during the rainy season.

On our hike, we pass women washing clothes in a flooded river while, further along, a group of men escapes the full blast of the sweltering heat in the shade of a mango tree.

Betty Abu prepares for the birth of her third child; Only two of Isha Sheriff’s four children survived Credit : Simon Townsley

Nine-months pregnant Betty Abu, 26, is sheltering inside the village clinic, preparing to give birth for the third time.

“I walked here from my own village because the road is so bad,” Betty tells me. “It took me three hours. I’ve been doing the same thing regularly for appointments because I’ve had a lot of pain.

“Even though it’s not great here it’s better than where I come from. Many women there have had miscarriages and stillbirths.”

Beside her, 29-year-old Isha Sheriff echoes this view, testifying that only two of her four children were born alive. Isha, like others, bears her tragedy with stoicism, recognising her own survival is entirely thanks to modern medicine.

Sebatu Kamara with baby Moses Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I had a blockage in my stomach, which caused the baby to die inside me. I also had sepsis,” explains Isha, a teacher in the village school. “They had to operate on me.

“My whole body was swollen. I could barely walk because I was so weak. But I know that I definitely would have lost my life without the treatment I was given in hospital.”

As we leave the village, I meet 23-year-old Sebatu Kamara carrying her eight-month-old baby Moses in a sling on her back.

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu faces the prospect of motorcycle transport Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I feel very lucky to have got through my pregnancy,” admits Sebatu. “There are no guarantees in a place like this. Now I can focus on my child.”

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu, 19, is less settled, desperately hoping that she can avoid an excruciating motorcycle trip to Koidu. She counts down the days to her admission into Ponduru’s delivery room.

If she does stay, the facilities in the clinic will be minimal. The village has a pump from a borehole, but no running water.

Community midwife Margaret Messie Seppeh admits the power supply is so unstable that she regularly depends on mobile phone torches to see during a nocturnal delivery.

The Maternal Center of Excellence is now the country’s main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

For those with the means to get there, the Maternal Center of Excellence, which is five and a half hours from the capital and biggest city Freetown, offers exemplary care.

Attached to the existing Government Hospital, it is now the main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies for the whole country.

From the six-bed delivery ward to the intensive care unit, every part of the hospital boasts the latest foetal and maternal monitoring technology.

The facilities are so much better than other regional delivery wards that some patients travel for days on the back of a motorbike taxi to use it, including some from neighbouring Guinea. Admission is free of charge, mostly thanks to financial support from Partners in Health.

The centre boasts state-of-the-art hospital facilities Credit : Simon Townsley

Nearly half of the 2,375 women to give birth in the Maternal Center of Excellence since it opened have had emergency caesarean sections, for which a blood transfusion is routinely required.

The reason for this is that many patients – often still teenagers – have had no check-ups, so potential complications are only identified as they go into labour.

Nurse Kamara says another significant challenge is that the majority of expectant mothers have been subjected to female genital mutilation, making a natural birth more problematic.

Midwife Fatu Josephine Musa with foetal heart-rate monitors in the centre’s delivery suite Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most mothers who come here have undergone this procedure,” she explains. “We can have up to 14 c-section operations a day, not including emergencies.

“Many of them had no antenatal appointments so when they arrive it is already too late for a natural birth.

“The young mothers often just don’t know what they are doing. They arrive here with a variety of obstetric problems. They are usually exhausted from the long journey too.”

A mother watches over her newborn in Sierra Leone’s first-ever neonatal intensive care unit Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Another issue which affects maternal health is the nutritionally limited diet of mothers who depend on staples like cassava and plantain. A lack of vitamins and minerals can increase the risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and complications after delivery.

Lack of income prevents many from making the long journey to Koidu. For them, motorcycle taxi fares are unaffordable.

But for now, the successful results of the facility mean pregnant women are gravitating there. With no equivalent anywhere nearby, it could soon be over-capacity.

In the antenatal ward, Kadiatu Jawara, 26, says it has taken her two days to reach the sanctuary of the region’s outstanding maternity hospital from her village in Guinea.

After suffering a miscarriage in her first pregnancy, she was desperate for the reassurance it provides.

“The pregnancy has been fine, but I know there is always risk,” admits Kadiatu. “I will need a caesarean, so I feel much more confident about it being here.”

Blood donors in Ponduru – including the village chief (centre) – play a crucial role in maternal healthcare Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At the heart of the multi-pronged approach to tackling maternal deaths in Sierra Leone is blood donation.

A scheme called Gi4SaveLife is addressing postpartum haemorrhage – when a mother loses a large quantity of blood after delivery – one of the leading causes of maternal death.

Clinics previously relied on blood donated by family members for transfusions.

Community blood donors in Ponduru Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

This precarious dependence was further complicated by cultural suspicion around blood donation in the rural areas where it is most needed.

Now, instead of desperately finding relatives willing to accompany a patient to give blood during an emergency, villages are building up their own supply.

Isatu Jimmysam, 27, discloses that she is alive only because she received two pints of blood from stocks donated by her neighbours when she delivered her baby boy Hassan earlier this year.

At a blood drive in another village outside Koidu, backed by the local Lifeline organisation, 28-year-old Kadaitu Balgale tells me she feels obliged to donate following her own experience during childbirth.

“I was given a transfusion because of complications when I had my baby,” she reveals. “My pressure went right up during labour and I collapsed. The nurses had to perform a C-section.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village after losing his sister to childbirth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Now my baby is three and we are both healthy. I was lucky. I’m very happy to give blood to make sure there is enough stock for other women who have the same problem.”

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most of these pregnant girls don’t want to go to clinic appointments because they are embarrassed, so one of our main jobs is to ensure that they do.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“There were so many girls dying in the past,” she continues. “My own niece died from bleeding because she was not taken to hospital in time.

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. When a mother survives childbirth, her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

An expectant mother receives an ultrasound scan at an MSF hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Sierra Leone’s success is largely due to the roll-out of free healthcare to pregnant women and children in 2010, and a more recent push to reach zero preventable maternal deaths. The 300 days of Activism for Triple Zero campaign – which also aims to tackle preventable child deaths and unvaccinated children – began in March.

According to the government, maternal deaths have dropped by 31.4 per cent since last year. There remains, however, deep inequality for pregnant women, mostly because of geographical inequity.

The United States charity Partners in Health, the lead funder for the Maternal Center of Excellence, points out that women in Sierra Leone have a one in 74 chance of dying in pregnancy or childbirth in their reproductive years. By comparison, the risk for UK women is around one in 7,500.

Despite the unparalleled progress of recent years, the happy ending which Adama and her baby have experienced is by no means universal across Sierra Leone.

A mother and her newborn recover from birth at the Maternal Center of Excellence at the Koidu Government Hospital Credit : Simon Townsley

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

An ambulance that was due to visit the village during our visit never arrives because the driver is afraid it will get stuck.

It is evident that a woman needing a team of midwives and expensive monitoring equipment to assist with a complicated birth can be totally cut off during the rainy season.

On our hike, we pass women washing clothes in a flooded river while, further along, a group of men escapes the full blast of the sweltering heat in the shade of a mango tree.

Betty Abu prepares for the birth of her third child; Only two of Isha Sheriff’s four children survived Credit : Simon Townsley

Nine-months pregnant Betty Abu, 26, is sheltering inside the village clinic, preparing to give birth for the third time.

“I walked here from my own village because the road is so bad,” Betty tells me. “It took me three hours. I’ve been doing the same thing regularly for appointments because I’ve had a lot of pain.

“Even though it’s not great here it’s better than where I come from. Many women there have had miscarriages and stillbirths.”

Beside her, 29-year-old Isha Sheriff echoes this view, testifying that only two of her four children were born alive. Isha, like others, bears her tragedy with stoicism, recognising her own survival is entirely thanks to modern medicine.

Sebatu Kamara with baby Moses Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I had a blockage in my stomach, which caused the baby to die inside me. I also had sepsis,” explains Isha, a teacher in the village school. “They had to operate on me.

“My whole body was swollen. I could barely walk because I was so weak. But I know that I definitely would have lost my life without the treatment I was given in hospital.”

As we leave the village, I meet 23-year-old Sebatu Kamara carrying her eight-month-old baby Moses in a sling on her back.

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu faces the prospect of motorcycle transport Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I feel very lucky to have got through my pregnancy,” admits Sebatu. “There are no guarantees in a place like this. Now I can focus on my child.”

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu, 19, is less settled, desperately hoping that she can avoid an excruciating motorcycle trip to Koidu. She counts down the days to her admission into Ponduru’s delivery room.

If she does stay, the facilities in the clinic will be minimal. The village has a pump from a borehole, but no running water.

Community midwife Margaret Messie Seppeh admits the power supply is so unstable that she regularly depends on mobile phone torches to see during a nocturnal delivery.

The Maternal Center of Excellence is now the country’s main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

For those with the means to get there, the Maternal Center of Excellence, which is five and a half hours from the capital and biggest city Freetown, offers exemplary care.

Attached to the existing Government Hospital, it is now the main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies for the whole country.

From the six-bed delivery ward to the intensive care unit, every part of the hospital boasts the latest foetal and maternal monitoring technology.

The facilities are so much better than other regional delivery wards that some patients travel for days on the back of a motorbike taxi to use it, including some from neighbouring Guinea. Admission is free of charge, mostly thanks to financial support from Partners in Health.

The centre boasts state-of-the-art hospital facilities Credit : Simon Townsley

Nearly half of the 2,375 women to give birth in the Maternal Center of Excellence since it opened have had emergency caesarean sections, for which a blood transfusion is routinely required.

The reason for this is that many patients – often still teenagers – have had no check-ups, so potential complications are only identified as they go into labour.

Nurse Kamara says another significant challenge is that the majority of expectant mothers have been subjected to female genital mutilation, making a natural birth more problematic.

Midwife Fatu Josephine Musa with foetal heart-rate monitors in the centre’s delivery suite Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most mothers who come here have undergone this procedure,” she explains. “We can have up to 14 c-section operations a day, not including emergencies.

“Many of them had no antenatal appointments so when they arrive it is already too late for a natural birth.

“The young mothers often just don’t know what they are doing. They arrive here with a variety of obstetric problems. They are usually exhausted from the long journey too.”

A mother watches over her newborn in Sierra Leone’s first-ever neonatal intensive care unit Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Another issue which affects maternal health is the nutritionally limited diet of mothers who depend on staples like cassava and plantain. A lack of vitamins and minerals can increase the risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and complications after delivery.

Lack of income prevents many from making the long journey to Koidu. For them, motorcycle taxi fares are unaffordable.

But for now, the successful results of the facility mean pregnant women are gravitating there. With no equivalent anywhere nearby, it could soon be over-capacity.

In the antenatal ward, Kadiatu Jawara, 26, says it has taken her two days to reach the sanctuary of the region’s outstanding maternity hospital from her village in Guinea.

After suffering a miscarriage in her first pregnancy, she was desperate for the reassurance it provides.

“The pregnancy has been fine, but I know there is always risk,” admits Kadiatu. “I will need a caesarean, so I feel much more confident about it being here.”

Blood donors in Ponduru – including the village chief (centre) – play a crucial role in maternal healthcare Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At the heart of the multi-pronged approach to tackling maternal deaths in Sierra Leone is blood donation.

A scheme called Gi4SaveLife is addressing postpartum haemorrhage – when a mother loses a large quantity of blood after delivery – one of the leading causes of maternal death.

Clinics previously relied on blood donated by family members for transfusions.

Community blood donors in Ponduru Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

This precarious dependence was further complicated by cultural suspicion around blood donation in the rural areas where it is most needed.

Now, instead of desperately finding relatives willing to accompany a patient to give blood during an emergency, villages are building up their own supply.

Isatu Jimmysam, 27, discloses that she is alive only because she received two pints of blood from stocks donated by her neighbours when she delivered her baby boy Hassan earlier this year.

At a blood drive in another village outside Koidu, backed by the local Lifeline organisation, 28-year-old Kadaitu Balgale tells me she feels obliged to donate following her own experience during childbirth.

“I was given a transfusion because of complications when I had my baby,” she reveals. “My pressure went right up during labour and I collapsed. The nurses had to perform a C-section.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village after losing his sister to childbirth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Now my baby is three and we are both healthy. I was lucky. I’m very happy to give blood to make sure there is enough stock for other women who have the same problem.”

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most of these pregnant girls don’t want to go to clinic appointments because they are embarrassed, so one of our main jobs is to ensure that they do.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“There were so many girls dying in the past,” she continues. “My own niece died from bleeding because she was not taken to hospital in time.

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

Additional reporting by Saidu Bah

News.title: Testosterone ads banned over low sex drive claims
News.content:
Five adverts that claimed symptoms such as low energy and lack of sex drive were linked to low testosterone levels have been banned by the UK’s advertising watchdog.

An investigation by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), published on Wednesday, found that the adverts exaggerated the link between low testosterone and several common symptoms, including loss of motivation and changes in mood, which could have many possible causes.

The adverts, which included three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads, were created by Voy, an online health platform and prominent seller of weight loss jabs like Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The ASA said: “While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn’t have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation”.

It also ruled that one Facebook ad, claiming that low testosterone affects one in four men over 30, was “misleading and not supported by the evidence Voy provided”. Voy disputed this.

“We’ve banned the ads and have told Voy to ensure that future ads don’t mislead people about the symptoms or prevalence of low testosterone,” added the ASA, who launched its investigation after receiving multiple public complaints.

Catherine Drewett, investigations manager at the ASA, said: “People should be able to trust the health claims they see in ads. This ruling makes clear the standards we expect from advertisers promoting health tests and services and the importance of ensuring their claims are supported by strong evidence”.

In response, Voy said the language in the ads was “deliberately conditional”, arguing it “did not state or imply that the advertised symptoms were definitively caused by low testosterone”.

Voy said the ads were retracted while the investigation was underway, adding that they will not run them again.

Dr Earim Chaudry, Chief Medical Officer at Voy, said: “Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance”.

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney forced Man Utd to keep promise about son Kai, 17, that could have seen academy ace RELEASED
Sports.content:
Next

WAYNE ROONEY has revealed he urged Manchester United staff to treat son Kai the same as every other academy prospect.

The Manchester United legend is hoping to see his son follow in his footsteps but wants him to succeed off his own back.



Kai, 17, joined the Red Devils academy aged six back in 2016 before moving to rivals Man City just months later.

He eventually returned to United aged 11 in 2020 and has established himself as a top young player.



Kai – who is the eldest of four sons Rooney had with wife Colleen – has been prolific for the youth teams and made his debut for the United Under-21s last month.

He agreed a one-year scholarship with United at the start of the year – which will turn into a pro deal – and fans have high hopes for the youngster.



But Rooney wants Kai to be given a fair assessment at United – and has even told staff to release him if he’s not good enough.

The legendary striker – who is currently on I’m a Celebrity Get Me Out Of Here – explained how it wouldn’t be fair if Kai was kept on just because of his own reputation.

He told Gabby Logan‘s Life At The Midpoint podcast: “Firstly, going up through the academy, I didn’t want the parents or anyone to think that he was there because of me. I actually spoke to the coaches and said, ‘If he’s not good enough, release him’.

“I don’t want him there because it’s not fair on him if he’s there and he’s not good enough and the club are keeping him on because of me.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“And thankfully he has turned out to be good enough; he has been good enough.”

Rooney added that Kai must learn to deal with the finer details of his career on his own.

He said: “What I don’t want is to always be there– he has to go through these moments in life.

“Because all of a sudden he is going to have a wife, he is going to have his own kids, etc., and we can’t always be there for him.”



Rooney himself has become a cult figure at United after netting 253 goals in 559 appearances for the club.

He lifted five Premier League titles and also won four domestic cups and the Champions League.

Kai is already making big steps towards emulating his dad after bagging FOUR goals in a recent youth match against Burnley.

That already led to calls from United fans for the youngster to start games for the senior team amid their woeful start to the season.

Sports.title: What shock drone spying footage reveals about Pochettino’s line-up and tactics for Man Utd’s visit to Liverpool
Sports.content:
Next

MAURICIO POCHETTINO has a lot of leaks to plug at Manchester United, and drone footage publicly revealing his first training session isn’t the best way to get started.

The Argentine coach flew in to Manchester after the curtain came down on his time with the USA, and got straight to work with his Red Devils squad ahead of their clash with Liverpool on Sunday.



There has been plenty of talk about how much the 54-year-old will change the intensity of training for these United flops.

Around 12 minutes of his first training session at Carrington was secretly recorded and then shared on YouTube before it was deleted by the channel owner, CC Overview, with an apology following.



However, the damage was already done, with fans, analysts and doubtless Liverpool coaches including boss Andoni Iraola gratefully looking through the footage to see what tactical secrets Pochettino could conjure up.

The footage saw Pochettino and coaches working with a full starting XI on a full-size pitch with players spread out between mannequins that appear to represent the opposition.



Faces of players could be clearly made out, though some of the players involved – Ayden Heaven, Andrey Santos, Joshua Zirkzee, Harry Amass – have not been regular starters this season.

That could suggest Pochettino is treating this squad with a clean slate and with all of them able to earn a spot in team, or that he is drilling tactics to get the whole squad in shape.

What it almost certainly did show is the tactical set-up Pochettino could take to Anfield in a bid to get United their first Premier League win since August.

On the full-size pitch footage, one group of United stars are seen setting up in a three-at-the-back shape and passing the ball between the lines and moving it from left to right before shifting it forward for an attack.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

The ball comes out wide to Mbeumo on the wing before it is whipped centrally towards two players in the area.

That drill is later seen being repeated in wide-shot footage, indicating it is something Liverpool will need to be wary of.

Another pair of groups with first-team stars including Bruno Fernandes, and Diogo Dalot were seen doing rondos with two defenders in the middle.

Pochettino’s No2 Jesus Perez was also seen across both groups in the video, cementing the idea of his heavily-involved approach.



The splitting of his captain to the group also rubbishes the idea of him having a set starting XI which he works with in training.

But while the United line-up at Anfield remains guesswork, one thing is for certain, United chiefs have a security problem that has now been exposed publicly.

And that could create an even bigger headache given the club are already in the relegation battle.

SunSport’s hit series Tactics Exposed has also examined how United could set-up against Liverpool, featuring a “midfield flex”.

Sports.title: ‘Total error of judgment’ – Drone footage filmer removes video and issues grovelling apology to Pochettino and Man Utd
Sports.content:
Next

FOOTAGE of Mauricio Pochettino’s first Manchester United training session has been DELETED from YouTube.

And the user that posted the video has issued an apology.



The Red Devils were left stunned on Thursday after the secret drone film emerged online.

Twelve minutes of footage was captured before being uploaded to YouTube.



The clip showed Pochettino putting his new players through their paces along with commentary from the drone operator, whose bio said he had previous footage used in a promotional video for Old Trafford.

YouTube user CC Overview, who uploaded the controversial film, deleted it from the platform before issuing a statement.



It read: “I would like to speak about yesterday’s incident.

“A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Manchester United training session at Carrington, whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part.

“My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time.

“I had wrongly presumed that with it being close to the start of the session that no meaningful training sessions would have started so would have been some harmless warming up shown.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

“I also wrongly assumed that the training session would have been open to various media outlets.

“I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match.

“I would also like to state that Liverpool Football club or any other football club were not involved in my decision to film at Carrington yesterday.

The video has been removed from my channel.

“I have spent the past 4 years building up my YouTube channel and were well regarded in the fields I film and would now like to get back to building up my damaged reputation and making well received responsible videos. Thank you.”

Man Utd declined to comment on the incident.



The operator initially said while filming: “For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it.

“The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn’t fly over anyone or even near anyone, so it was a perfectly legal flight according to the Civil Aviation Authority rules that regulate drone usage.

“The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required.



“As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the manager’s first training session, there are many media outlets there, so it certainly won’t be the only footage of training released.”

Civil Aviation Authority guidelines say: “If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you’re likely to be breaking data protection laws.”

Pochettino arrived at Man Utd this week after signing a two-and-a-half year contract.

His first match in charge will come against Liverpool at Anfield this Sunday.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino, 54, sent his first message to United fans on Wednesday evening just hours after arriving at Carrington.



The Argentine insisted that the team’s players will “fight on the field” under his management.

THE knockout stage of the Nations League is quickly approaching and the draw for it gets underway THIS MORNING!

The top two teams from each of the four League A groups will progress to the quarter-finals.

Sports.title: ‘Respect me, you f***ing small team’ – Neymar in extraordinary X-rated outburst at rival fans on live TV
Sports.content:
Next

FURIOUS Neymar launched an X-rated outburst at goading fans and demanded: Respect me!

The outburst took place following a 1-0 win over Coritiba which moved Neymar’s Santos up to eighth in the Brazilian Serie A table.



Gabriel Barbosa scored the winner in added time to seal the points on Wednesday.

It came as a huge relief to Neymar, who was provoked by rival fans throughout the match.



The 34-year-old lashed out at the Coritiba supporters in front of TV cameras at full-time.

Gesturing towards the fans, he said: “Don’t f*** around! You’re going to Serie B, you idiots.

“Suck it! You have to respect me, respect me, you f****** small team.”

The forward’s contract expires at the end of next month and it remains to be seen if he will continue at the club.

Santos’ chief executive – who is also Neymar’s dad – is keen for him to extend.

He said: “We know that in every transfer window, offers come in for him to leave. Yet Neymar always chooses to stay at Santos.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“What I’m anticipating is that, first and foremost, I need to keep Neymar happy. Do you understand?

“And if he’s happy here, I can keep him here. So, look, down this final stretch, the work we’ve done to structure the squad and open up positive possibilities has given us the license to dream.”

Sports.title: Lionel Messi moment that helped launch Mauricio Pochettino’s managerial career in Premier League
Sports.content:
Next

MAURICIO POCHETTINO once gained immediate respect from Southampton stars after being embraced by Lionel Messi and his Barcelona team-mates.

The Argentine is gearing up for his first game in charge of Manchester United ahead of a massive trip to Liverpool on Sunday.



He will have a major task on his hands rebuilding a fractured squad that has slipped into the relegation zone following one win all season.

Pochettino will also have to manage some big characters and personalities after some outspoken behaviour from the squad.



But former Southampton star Charlie Austin believes he will make a quick impression after sharing a story from the manager’s time on the south coast.

Austin joined the Saints two years after Pochettino left Southampton for Tottenham but was told about a time when he impressed the players on tour in Barcelona.



He said Poch had bumped into Messi, who embraced him alongside a raft of other big-name Barca stars.

The ex-striker told talkSport: “The players see the first or second meeting, how he addresses you and the group and how he kind of speaks, if it’s a firm chat or if the manager is going to be a pushover or not. There’s the odd player…

“Pochettino when he came to Southampton… he gained the respect straight away.

“He was an unknown manager. Southampton went over to Barcelona for a tour and when all the players came off the bus the manager was greeted by Lionel Messi, Carlos Puyol, Xavi, Andres Iniesta and embraced him there.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“So if you’re an unknown manager and you don’t know what he’s going to be like, well if the greatest player of all time is embracing your manager and Carlos Puyol… straight away he’s won them over.

“He may have done that intentionally but without even wanting to say anything to the players.

“He knew they would be watching because Barcelona were there training.



“To see how they had those players reacted to seeing him speaks volumes.”

Pochettino went on to manage Messi for a short period when he was in charge of a star-studded PSG side between 2021 and 2022.

It’s not been an ideal start for Pochettino at United after his first training session was filmed by a drone.

The drone captured 12 minutes of the session and the video has since been uploaded to YouTube.

Poch has already spoken out on becoming United boss after giving his first interview since joining the club – with his full focus on beating Liverpool.



He told the official club media channel: “It’s a privilege to be head coach of Manchester United and I think we cannot be wasting time.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We need to be ready to compete Sunday. Now it’s not thinking about rest, it’s not thinking to sleep.

“It’s to be ready and to prepare everything to be sure that we are going to compete in the best condition at Anfield.”

Sports.title: Champions League club set to build stunning 40,116-seater new stadium as agreement is reached
Sports.content:
Next

CLUB BRUGGE are closing in on new digs.

The Belgian giants have held promising talks with local authorities over securing land for a 40,000-seater stadium.



Construction is due to begin in January.

The Club currently share the Jan Breydel Stadion with Cercle.



It was built in 1975 and houses under 30,000 fans.

Thew new stadium would be built next door in the Sint-Andries district.

Mayor Dirk De Fauw confirmed that outstanding issues had been resolved over the long-term use of the land and approved by the city executive.

Next up, the municipal council will hold a vote before the end of the month in the last stage before the deal is finalised.

Local outlets suggest that FC Bruges will pay £65,000 a year to use the land, but varying reports suggest the term is between 50 and 100 years.

On non-matchdays, public land in the park will be accessible and a new park is being planned around the arena.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

The city will create and maintain the area, but litter generated by fans will be the responsibility of the club.

In order to reach a deal, it was agreed that the stadium would include space for tractors and other equipment needed by the city, as well as a staff room.

The £165million project still faces opposition and legal proceedings could yet cause an issue, although construction is not expected to be delayed.

A 2029 completion date has been proposed.

FC Brugges are second in the Pro League with nine wins in 11 matches.



Things are also going well in Europe with three victories in four Champions League outings despite a 3-2 loss to Aston Villa.

Liverpool are travelling to Belgium for a clash on November 25 after taking on Mauricio Pochettino‘s Manchester United on Sunday.

Sports.title: Will Frank turn things around at Crystal Palace?
Sports.content:
One of the Premier League's most charismatic managers is back.

On November 16, Thomas Frank signed a deal running until the summer of 2029 to take over the vacant managerial role at Crystal Palace, following the conclusion of Pierre Sage's short spell at Selhurst Park.

His return to the top flight comes nine months after he was sacked by Tottenham after a run of just seven wins in 26 Premier League games.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Thomas Frank tells PALACETV why the word PATH is his recipe for success at Crystal Palace (Pictures: PALACETV)

Before that, he had four successful Premier League seasons with Brentford, after guiding them to promotion in 2020/21.

Here, Sky Sports takes a look at what Frank needs to change, what to expect in terms of style and shape and whether he can keep Palace in the Premier League...

What situation has he walked into?

Palace won the Conference League last season, so it's easy to forget they also only finished six points above the Premier League relegation zone.

Sage was unable to build on the legacy left by Oliver Glasner, so the Eagles again find themselves in a spot of bother.

The Premier League's bottom side have lost four in succession and have the worst defensive record in the division, having conceded an average of 2.4 goals per game.

They are through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup, however, and have taken five points from four Europa League league phase matches so far, which has them currently on course to qualify for the knockout rounds.

Frank highlights issues to address

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Thomas Frank speaks for the first time since becoming the new Crystal Palace boss

Speaking in his first interview with the club, Frank identified the problems his new side need to address.

"There's no doubt - to state the obvious - we need to stabilise things. We need to work incredibly hard," he said.

"We are conceding too many goals, so we need to work on the defensive side of things, with principles, attitude. We need to work on set-pieces, which are key in both boxes. We need to work on defensive transitions, as we are conceding too many situations there.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from Crystal Palace’s match against Liverpool in the Premier League

"We need to bring energy, belief, confidence because this is a very, very good team and very good players, but they need to believe in themselves.

"We need to balance a lot of things with aiming high in Europe and two fantastic cup tournaments, but the Premier League is the most important, if we need to prioritise."

What needs to change then?

Analysis by Sky Sports News' Chris Reidy:

Frank will see areas all over the pitch he can improve for Crystal Palace, but undoubtedly his priority will be to stop them conceding as many goals and as many chances as they have so far this season.

Crystal Palace have kept one clean sheet in the Premier League this season and too often look vulnerable on transitions and weak on set-pieces.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol explains why Crystal Palace sacked Pierre Sage

Frank will have to review whether the personnel he has suits playing three centre-halves or if a change to four is necessary. Time and time again teams have exploited space between defenders against Crystal Palace which leads to shots or good chances created for the opposition.

Away from the defence, Frank will need to rejuvenate Adam Wharton. The midfielder has been way off his best this season, and perhaps finding the right partner for him will be key to that. Quinten Timber has shown plenty of energy and will in his early days at Palace perhaps without giving stability in the middle, and Daichi Kamada has been used higher up the pitch due to Ismaila Sarr's absence from the team.

Image: x

What has gone under the radar in recent weeks because of Crystal Palace's defending, is their struggles up top. Eddie Nketiah's fortunate penalty with the last kick of the game against Liverpool spared Palace a record of four Premier League games without a goal.

Crystal Palace have spent the most time trailing in the league and have also only taken the lead in three games this season. A mentality shift is needed, because Palace have good players who aren't responding well to adversity.

What should fans expect in terms of style?

Based on his previous jobs, Frank has shown he is a pragmatic manager, not wedded to one shape or style and comfortable finding different ways to win.

His most used formation in the Premier League is a 4-3-3 (59), but he has also heavily used a 4-2-3-1 (35) or - importantly for Crystal Palace - a 3-5-2 (53).

Across his four top-flight seasons at Brentford, the Bees scored 80 set-piece goals, with only Arsenal, Liverpool and Man City scoring more across that period.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports’ Kaveh Solhekol and Dave Reed analyse Thomas Frank’s arrival at Crystal Palace, his challenge to keep the Eagles in the Premier League and whether or not his Brentford success can be replicated at Selhurst Park

He is reportedly close to adding Bernardo Cueva - his former set-piece coach at Brentford - to his coaching staff, which suggests a similar approach is likely at Selhurst Park.

Elsewhere, while the Bees became markedly more direct after promotion from the Championship, there was still a particular focus on high quality chances, meaning fewer shots were taken from outside the box.

From 1763 shots across their first four seasons in the Premier League, Frank's Brentford created 225.0 worth of Expected Goals, which equated to a league-high 0.128 xG per shot.

So why didn't it work out at Spurs?

Analysis by Sky Sports News' Michael Bridge:

"It just didn't seem the right fit from the start. It didn't get off to the best of starts in terms of the press conference when he said: 'We will 100 per cent lose football matches.' Then he turned to the press office and said: 'Apart from Arsenal.' The problem is, when you say something at a club like Spurs, it stays.

"There were some really tough defeats for Spurs fans to look at. The defeat at home to Chelsea, when they generated 0.1 xG. Then there was the 4-1 reverse at Arsenal, 0.07 xG.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the Transfer Talk podcast, Michael Bridge discusses what went wrong for Thomas Frank at Tottenham Hotspur as the Dane has been announced as the new manager of Crystal Palace

"Spurs had come off the back of winning the Europa League, but they'd finished 17th in the league with 22 league defeats. They weren't as good as the Europa League trophy suggested.

"It wasn't a great squad. It was a squad littered with injuries. It was also a squad of players who then thought, well, we've won the European trophy. I think a couple of them thought, 'Who's this guy?'

"Then he picked Cristian Romero to be the club captain. Romero spoke out on a number of occasions during that season, criticising the board, criticising the hierarchy. He was sent off in two key games against Liverpool and Man Utd, so there was a real discipline issue there as well.

Image: Thomas Frank was seen drinking from an Arsenal cup before a game against Bournemouth

"Then there was that really unfortunate incident away to Bournemouth where he was walking around pre-match holding an Arsenal cup because Arsenal played in the previous match.

"He needs to prove that Spurs was a one-off and not Brentford."

Can he keep Palace in the Premier League?

It's clear Frank and Palace have a significant battle on their hands.

They have collected 0.7 points per game this season - the lowest in the Premier League. Maintaining that average would see them pick up 20 more points, finish on 28 and almost certainly be relegated to the Sky Bet Championship.

Unsurprisingly, they are currently priced at Evens by Sky Bet to be relegated from the Premier League, while Opta Analyst's predicted table shows them finishing bottom of the pile with 38 points.

Frank's own points-per-game average in the Premier League, however, stands at 1.3.

If Palace replicate that average across the remaining 28 games of the season, they would collect another 36.4 points, taking them to 44, which would almost certainly be enough to survive. In a 38-game Premier League season, no side has ever collected as many as 43 points and gone down.

Frank has already shown he can build a successful Premier League team. He now has 28 games to show he can save one.

Sports.title: Guimaraes growing at Arsenal - but Arteta still wants more
Sports.content:
It's all eyes on Bruno Guimaraes this Saturday. The Newcastle hero who captained the team to cup success returns in Arsenal colours. And he returns as a growing cog in the Gunners' system.

Despite being Newcastle's key man, the Brazilian endured a slow start to life at Arsenal. An early-season injury did not help, nor did the early-season form of Myles Lewis-Skelly in the Brazilian's absence.

But now he is back in the North East as a first-choice option, having impressed in Arsenal's recent league wins over Liverpool and Hull, while also scoring crucial goals against Sunderland and Leeds.

But is Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta satisfied? Not yet.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Harvey Barnes insists the return of Guimaraes to St James' Park, along with the visit of champions Arsenal, is just what Newcastle need to kickstart their season

"He's still not there," said Arteta after the 1-0 win over Hull last time out. "He's much better, he's hitting serious levels now, but we can still take the player to another level."

The comments were a surprise, given Guimaraes had just received a standing ovation from the Arsenal crowd as he was substituted following an impressive display.

In a largely frustrating game for the Gunners before Martin Odegaard's second-half winner, the Brazilian was at the heart of the action. He recorded more touches and passes than any other Arsenal player, while he was equally effective in the defensive side of the game.

When Arteta made attacking substitutions in search of a winner, he took Declan Rice off before Guimaraes. That is how well he was playing - but it is still not enough for the Arsenal manager.

"I told him in the dressing room - he's very good, he had a massive impact, he owned a lot of moments in the game," said Arteta. "But there is still much more to come."

Pushed on those comments this week, he said: "It's about impact, the amount of things he can do to influence the game and own the game."

To work out what Arteta is getting at, it is worth going back to the analysis the Spaniard made of his £75m signing when he first joined.

Image: Guimaraes has more to do to improve, says Mikel Arteta

"A player which obviously has tremendous timing and intuition to win the ball back and progress play very, very fast," said Arteta back in August.

"He's a player that is very comfortable putting people through, moving between the lines, moving in behind."

Winning the ball back and playing it forward very fast are two areas where Guimaraes has excelled so far this season.

From a defensive point of view, only Chelsea's Romeo Lavia has a better ground-duel success rate this season among Premier League midfielders.
