Sports.title: Drone operator apologises for filming Mauricio Pochettino's first Man United training session and clarifies Liverpool were not involved in embarrassing security breach
Sports.content:
Drone operator apologises for filming Mauricio Pochettino's first Man United training session and clarifies Liverpool were not involved in embarrassing security breach

The drone operator who filmed Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session at Manchester United has removed the video from his YouTube account and apologised to the club.

United suffered the embarrassing security breach on Pochettino’s first day as head coach after the 12-minute footage showing the Argentine and his staff working with the players at Carrington was posted online.

The owner of the account called CC Overview, who is known only as Colin, justified the intrusion by saying that the airspace over Carrington is unrestricted and the drone was operating legally within Civil Aviation Authority rules.

However, he took the video down on Friday morning insisting that he was unaware of the significance of his actions.

He also clarified that neither Liverpool – who are United’s opponents in Pochettino’s first game at Anfield on Sunday – nor any other club were involved in the filming.

United have declined to comment over the incident and it’s unclear if the club have made contact with him or involved Greater Manchester Police.

Mauricio Pochettino's first Man United training session was filmed by a drone and the operator has now apologised

The drone user, who is known only as Colin, said he had not broken laws but apologised

His statement read: ‘I would like to speak about yesterday’s incident. A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Manchester United training session at Carrington, whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part.

‘My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time.

'I had wrongly presumed that with it being close to the start of the session that no meaningful training sessions would have started so would have been some harmless warming up shown.

‘I also wrongly assumed that the training session would have been open to various media outlets.

'I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match.

‘I would also like to state that Liverpool Football club or any other football club were not involved in my decision to film at Carrington yesterday.

‘The video has been removed from my channel. I have spent the past four years building up my YouTube channel and were well regarded in the fields I film and would now like to get back to building up my damaged reputation and making well received responsible videos. Thank you.’

The incident is a major embarrassment for United on Pochettino’s first full day in charge after the club paid £10million to buy the Argentine and his staff out of their contracts with the US Soccer Federation.

Footage of the session was captured close to Carrington and uploaded online

United regularly use their own drones to film training sessions, but put up signs six years ago banning the use of them near the training ground in case they could reveal top-secret information to their opponents.

The video was taken half an hour into Pochettino’s training session and clearly shows the 54-year-old instructing the United squad along with his coaching team of No.2 Jesus Perez, first-team coach Miguel D’Agostino, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez, his son and fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya.

Pochettino only flew into Manchester on Wednesday with D’Agostino, Tuya and analyst Alec Scott after taking charge of his last game as US coach against Haiti in Cincinnati.

They caught a private jet provided by United after the game and he went straight to Carrington after landing in the UK shortly before noon.

Perez, Jimenez and Sebastiano Pochettino have been at the training ground since the weekend after being given permission by the US Soccer Federation to leave after the first-leg against Haiti in Miami.

Man United installed signs in 2018 warning that the use of drones over Carrington was 'strictly prohibited' and would be reported for prosecution

Pochettino addressed the Man United's internal media team for the first time on Thursday, outlining how he plans to drag this underperforming squad up the table.

'The culture is the most important,' Pochettino explained.

'Create the habits, the principles, and I think that is what we want to create.

'We need to [be] looking forward and to find a way to create the best habits and the culture that makes us to be close to winning every single game.'

'The players need to express their talent. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now – it's to work with them and try to take the pressure.'

Pochettino has stressed he is focused on the potential of his squad, rather than their present position in the Premier League.

'It's a mistake to see the [current] situation. We need to see the potential of this club,' a defiant Pochettino added.

Sports.title: Rassie Erasmus is GOOD for rugby - yes he went too far this time, but he's a box-office pantomime villain shaking up a sport bogged down by stuffy bores, writes NIK SIMON
Sports.content:
Rassie Erasmus is GOOD for rugby - yes he went too far this time, but he's a box-office pantomime villain shaking up a sport bogged down by stuffy bores, writes NIK SIMON

In March 2022, I met Rassie Erasmus for dinner at the Fat Butcher in Stellenbosch. Being the alpha Afrikaner, he took charge of the order. Bone marrow, tomahawk steaks and brandy.

He was compelling company. Locals approached him, asking for selfies. ‘Thank you for everything you’ve done for our country,’ said one diner to the man who was then in the middle of a long ban for criticising match officials.

Four years later, Erasmus has still not learnt his lesson. He has been handed a six-match suspension for his comments about match-fixing following South Africa's defeat by France and, outside of South Africa, the popular opinion is that rugby would be better off without him.

I disagree. Yes, Erasmus overstepped the mark. Yes, Erasmus is a bad loser. Yes, his comments incited a social media hate mob we could all do without.

Referees cop the worst of it. Coincidentally, Christophe Ridley, who will officiate the Springboks Test this weekend, is someone I went to school with. So I can see the human side. It is worth noting, however, that online pile-ons – including pathetic threats – are a societal problem that extend far beyond South African rugby.

In a sport that is dominated by traditionalists, I have always been drawn to the non-conformists. Retired prop Joe Marler was a prime example. He made outlandish comments about governance and officiating, pushing the boundaries of acceptability. There are many people in rugby who would have been happy to see him cancelled.

Rassie Erasmus has been handed a six-match suspension for his comments about match-fixing following South Africa's defeat by France

I met Erasmus for dinner in South Africa not long ago and he was compelling company

Yet look at Marler now, adored by the non-rugby world after his starring role on last year’s Celebrity Traitors.

Like Marler, Erasmus is one of rugby’s lovable rogues. The sport’s press conferences are full of bland platitudes. In the Test arena, only Erasmus and Eddie Jones say what they really think. I have sat through hundreds of hours of media sessions with other coaches that have done nothing to generate headlines or capture the attention of the outside world.

As a rugby man, I have sometimes looked enviously towards Premier League football and the storylines generated by the likes of Jurgen Klopp, Pep Guardiola and Jose Mourinho. In the world of rugby values, they would likely be cast out in the same way as Erasmus.

Sport, lest we forget, is an entertainment business. It needs pantomime villains. Erasmus crossed the line with his remarks after South Africa’s defeat by France. But it is only a game.

Yes, he has a populist, Trumpian following, but his words and actions have nothing like the impact of the American president. Put simply, he creates a sporting narrative that doesn’t always sit comfortably in rugby’s paradigm of right and wrong.

Take the outrage, for example, when he changed his entire front row an hour before kick-off in Paris last week. No rules were broken, yet it was as if he had committed a war crime. The 48 hours between team announcement and kick-off can sometimes leave a deathly void to fill and, personally, I quite enjoy a late plot twist.

There is a strong case that some of rugby’s most centralised policies are more damaging than any Erasmus rant. The powerful Six Nations and SANZAAR boards recently joined forces to create the F10 group that will share the riches of the Nations Championship Tests while other proud rugby nations are left to rot.

Erasmus has dressed as a water boy in the past so he could get his message across to the South African players

Erasmus, pictured on a paintball session in Edinburgh while at the 1999 World Cup as a player, has never been afraid to fire a few shots

Many of those decision-makers are the same people who think rugby would be better off without Erasmus.

While Erasmus won’t be at the Aviva Stadium on Saturday for South Africa’s game against Ireland, he will be watching on TV from his hotel room. Tens of thousands have signed up for his cheeky watch-along party.

Registrations crashed and sponsors – predominantly South African, you suspect – are apparently keen to get on board.

I will be tuning in. I suspect some of his haters will, too, although they may be too embarrassed to admit it. The Rassie Roadshow is the performance that keeps on giving.

Sports.title: Inside the crime epidemic striking fear into Premier League stars: Terrified players paying 'protection money' and buying £20,000 guard dogs, WAGs targeted in violent carjackings and the fall of the crime family who targeted Alexander Isak
Sports.content:
The man parked up in a nondescript green Ford Fiesta cut an incongruous sight in the affluent residential neighbourhood of Casal Palocco, in south-west Rome, but no one paid him much notice. He made no eye contact and at no stage stepped from the car.

It was only after the street’s famous resident, AS Roma’s Belgian midfielder Radja Nainggolan, had his home burgled and an extraordinary £400,000 worth of possessions stolen that the player’s then wife, Claudia, six months pregnant at that time in April 2016, recalled the Eastern European-looking man in the battered vehicle up their street.

He was Vlada Djuric, a 50-year-old Macedonian of Romani descent and part of the wider Nikolov family, including his wife Zora Jovanovic, their two sons and daughter, whose highly organised thefts from the homes of top footballers would continue for more than a decade, with imprisonment deemed only a minor setback.

While the Nainggolans were blithely unaware of the criminal family’s lookout man – they’d gone to visit friends nearby for a couple of hours and hadn't even bothered to activate the burglar alarm – the assailants were primed to seize the chance.

The two sons, Valentino and Giacomo, mounted the villa’s perimeter wall, opening one door with a magnetic card and jimmying another with a screwdriver, and proceeded undisturbed through the house in 27 minutes, throwing the proceeds of their burglary into a bag as they went.

There were 15 watches (Rolex, Patek Philippe and others) valued at £250,000 and 20 pieces of jewellery, including a diamond worth £25,000. Security cameras on a landing and in an internal room filmed them but such was their confidence, they only partially covered their faces.

Former Roma midfielder Radja Nainggolan and his then wife Claudia, who was six months pregnant, were the targets of a burglary in 2016 (Source: Instagram/Claudia_lai_82)

Nainggolan had an extraordinary £400,000 worth of possessions taken, including 15 watches

It was old-fashioned detective work from a local officer, Bruno Failla, which led police to a rambling home at Lurano, a small town six hours drive away in Lombardy, at which the Nikolovs would lavishly entertain other members of the Romani community.

The watches matched the descriptions of those stolen from the Nainggolans, though it was a necklace with a Roma logo, and the pair of red shoes with Nainggolan's initials, which really gave the game away.

‘I ask again for vigilance and watchfulness, please,’ Failla said at the time, because this was the fourth time that footballers' properties in Casal Palocco had been targeted in the space of five years. But the challenge of placing footballers in a state of constant vigilance became clear fully seven years on, when another Nainggolan residence, in Antwerp, Belgium, was burgled while his relatives held a party there.

‘It is one of the most complicated and consistently challenging parts of our security work,’ one former special forces soldier now providing security for footballers tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘It’s been a big sector of our work for years now, but the movements of these clients are so public and that’s irresistible to criminals. The wealth is very evident.’

One of the sons, Valentino, was jailed for two years in 2016 and other members of his family also did time, but once out, they all set their sights on the Premier League. In 2024, they arrived in the UK via a ferry to Dover from Calais, stopped off in London and made their way north, sleeping in a Ford motorhome and travelling to target homes in a Citroen C3.

A spree of attacks ensued from them on the homes of Alexander Isak, then a Newcastle player, Wolves’ Matheus Cunha (who has subsequently been burgled again while at Manchester United), Birmingham City’s Neil Etheridge and Leon Bailey, with Aston Villa at the time.

A number of Premier League clubs, including Liverpool, Everton and United, are known to have appointed their own security teams to provide an around-the-clock presence at the homes of players who are in squads playing away from home – rather than have that in the hands of a range of private operators.

Some of the top football TV analysts are known to have sought the same security cover outside their houses when away at games.

A number of Premier League clubs, including Liverpool, have appointed their own security teams to provide an around-the-clock presence at the homes of stars who are playing away

Three masked criminals managed to slip over Bruno Fernandes' security fence and into his home in Nether Alderley, Cheshire, last month and made off with jewellery

It didn’t work in the case of Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes. Three masked criminals still managed to slip over the security fence into his home in Nether Alderley, Cheshire, last month and make off with jewellery.

It was one of the player’s neighbours who spotted them on their CCTV system and alerted police, who arrived five minutes after the burglars had left. Some in this security sector feel that it takes the private firms' former military and special services experience to cope with the criminal gangs’ level of sophistication.

Clubs using security staff in this way is a relatively recent development. In the days of security officers like United’s Ned Kelly, who wrote a book about his 14 years with the club, the job entailed ensuring the team were protected in public, or ferrying managers and new signings around.

Many clubs still leave it to players. ‘Player-liaison staff will recommend vetted security providers but it’s down to player personal choice for obvious reasons,’ says one player agent.

'That's not always been easy,' says a former Premier League player-liaison officer. 'The players have a huge entourage: so-called experts who want a seat at the table and think they know best. Of course, social media enhances the security problem.'

The house burglars’ modus operandi pales by comparison with some of violence displayed by others who prey on the footballer set. One footballer's wife in Cheshire was driving a top-of-the-range vehicle when a moped took up a position in front of her and slowed. In her rear-view mirror, she saw a second. The driver of the third then arrived at her side window, assessing what there was to steal.

On any given day, there could have been £200,000 worth of jewellery in the car, though she was wearing neither rings nor a watch on this occasion. The three drove off.

The episode had echoes of the attempted heist which saw Arsenal’s Mesut Ozil and Sead Kolasinac carjacked in broad daylight in north London, seven years ago.

Sead Kolasinac, then of Arsenal, thwarts an attempted carjacking in broad daylight in north London, seven years ago. Kolasinac was with his team-mate Mesut Ozil at the time

Attackers go for Kolasinac after his car was 'boxed in' when approaching traffic lights

Paul Hughes, managing director of Benchmark Security Group, a leading Manchester-based protection firm, employs former police and Royal security drivers to train his clients in the art of 'defensive driving'.

In a two-hour session, they learn how to avoid being 'boxed in' – as Ozil and Kolasinac were – when approaching traffic lights. Techniques include never taking up a position in the middle lane, avoiding the outside lane if there is a central barrier, and always maintaining sight of the tyres of the vehicle in front when you slow.

'If you can see the tyres, you will always have room to manoeuvre right or left of the car in front, at speed, without hitting it,' Hughes says.

His staff are often asked to escort clients in their fleet of vehicles, which includes two Land Rovers with blacked-out windows. The firm acquired a Darkfighter Dome – a night-vision camera which is mounted on to the roof of its security vehicles – allowing them to see would-be assailants in the dark. Escorted school runs are also part of the protection they offer.

A screen which dominates Benchmark's underground headquarters, at anonymous premises in Manchester, revealed the fortresses that players' houses have become, when I visited.

It showed live feeds from the gardens of mansions which are criss-crossed by infra-red beams. An alarm is triggered in the control room if anyone not approved through face-recognition software is picked up by up to 18 pan, tilt and zoom cameras at a property.

Loudspeakers, operated from the control room, warn off intruders. A team of security staff is never more than six minutes away. A patrol is on the scene of an alert, usually within 90 seconds.

A number of Manchester United players have invested in specialised security dogs from the Leicester-based firm Chaperone K9 at a cost of up to £20,000 each, though some sources suggest demand has receded as many players have young children. Security firms have their own dogs.

Benchmark are one of Britain's most trusted operators – industry-accredited, with former senior police officers on their staff. But this is also a world in which some unsavoury individuals are looking to extract gain.

Daily Mail Sport is aware that a number of current players have paid protection money to ensure they remain safe and are not venturing out socially without having done so. The ‘panic rooms’ some install in their homes, with security card access, are a place to hide valuables.

The family who preyed on footballers for a decade will be behind bars for some time. Valentino Nikolov (pictured) is serving an initial 10-year sentence, which has since been extended

Kolasinac fought off the carjackers. Everton's Duncan Ferguson put an assailant in hospital when he tried to burgle his home at Ormskirk, Lancashire, in January 2001. ‘I’m not a hard man off the pitch...unless you try to break into my house,’ he said recently.

But the assailants in the Ozil and Kolasinac attack were part of Eastern European gangs. 'The criminal demographic has changed,' one former senior detective tells me. 'We are now talking about gangs who lack the slightest compunction about taking a life.'

The Italian family who have preyed on footballers for a decade will be behind bars for some time. The Rome lookout man’s two sons were jailed for 10 years and eight years respectively at Newcastle Crown Court last year, for burglaries including the Isak attack – sentences since extended. Their mother is doing seven years.

That court case revealed how the family had moved on from the days of old cars, screwdrivers and shinning over walls in Rome – using Isak’s own vehicle as a battering ram to force entry to his Newcastle home.

'None of the property stolen from my home was ever recovered,’ Isak related. 'The attack left me with a sense of unease and a fear it could reoccur.'

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino gets straight to work: New Man United boss meets struggling stars for the first time and vows to shift losing mentality as he takes training with players back from international duty
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino gets straight to work: New Man United boss meets struggling stars for the first time and vows to shift losing mentality as he takes training with players back from international duty

Mauricio Pochettino has vowed to reset the culture at Manchester United as he lifted the lid on being in the stands in 1999 to see the club's greatest triumph.

Pochettino was officially appointed as United's new head coach on Wednesday and took charge of training for the first time on Thursday.

The Argentine was pictured greeting his new squad, with several stars having returned from international duty, before attentions turned to preparing the Red Devils for Sunday's trip to Anfield.

Pochettino also addressed the club's internal media team for the first time, outlining how he plans to drag this underperforming squad up the table.

'The culture is the most important,' Pochettino explained.

'Create the habits, the principles, and I think that is what we want to create.

Mauricio Pochettino took Man United first team training for the first time on Thursday

Matheus Cunha and Lisandro Martinez were among those to report back after international duty

Man United will hope to hit the ground running under Pochettino when they face Liverpool on Sunday

'We need to [be] looking forward and to find a way to create the best habits and the culture that makes us to be close to winning every single game.'

'The players need to express their talent. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now – it's to work with them and try to take the pressure.'

Pochettino's determination to be the man to bring winning football back to Old Trafford is in large part due to one of his founding memories of the club back in 1999 when he was a player at Espanyol.

Alongside his now trusted goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez, Pochettino was at the Nou Camp to see United clinch the Champions League, thus sealing a famous Treble, against Bayern Munich.

'In 1999, I was in Barcelona for that final. That was an iconic final,' he added.

'Toni Jimenez [was there] too. We were shouting for Manchester United from there. I was so excited to see Manchester United.

'This [is the] type of game that you stay sitting in your place [for] and you're so excited because you are watching the game. That was an amazing game.

'And then what happened in the end... it's like it's impossible not to empathise with that team, no?

'That was an amazing memory that made me pay more attention to United, to [Sir Alex] Ferguson and the players that were there, that are all legends.'

That level of success feels a lifetime away from the current squad, which emerges from the international break for a trip to face bitter rivals Liverpool at Anfield slumped 18th in the Premier League.

Pochettino wants to focus on the potential of his Man United squad, rather than their current Premier League plight

Pochettino is determined to shift the culture at Manchester United back to winning

The Argentine head coach was in the stands in Barcelona cheering for United back in 1999

While there are those who may be daunted trying to turn around the ship which sunk so far it cost Michael Carrick his job, Pochettino wants to focus on potential, rather than the present.

'It's a mistake to see the [current] situation. We need to see the potential of this club,' a defiant Pochettino added.

'Of course, the circumstances are the circumstances, and we need to be responsible for the circumstances. But at the same time, we need to understand that it's a game and, to connect with the game, we need to feel free.

'The players need to express their talent. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now – it's to work with them and try to take the pressure [off].

'Pressure needs to bring energy, responsibility needs to bring energy. Because if not, it's too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back.

'When you connect with the game, you connect through your talent and when you feel freedom, when you feel happy, when you want to play for your team-mates, when you want to play for your family, when you want to play for your club, your fans.

'That is what we need to create all together and I think we have an amazing staff - we were talking a lot today. Then [we need to] settle all the principles and the ideas and to create our own philosophy and start from zero.

'I think with the power of this club and the fans supporting us, I think we will get in the place that we deserve to be.'

Pochettino touched down in Manchester on Wednesday morning after his overnight flight

Pochettino poses at his unveiling with United director of football Jason Wilcox on Wednesday

Pochettino knows that time is not on his side ahead of an upcoming week that sees United travel to face Liverpool on Sunday, followed by a Champions League trip to face Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday. The week is rounded out by a home match a week on Saturday against Brentford.

The Argentine head coach touched down in Manchester on Wednesday morning, taking a private jet straight after the final whistle of United States versus Haiti in Cincinnati.

From there he immediately headed to their Carrington training base where he took a tour and met players and staff, including Tom Heaton, Luke Shaw, Mason Mount and Bruno Fernandes. It is understood he left a good first impression on the players.

And yet, in spite of such a packed schedule, which saw him leave Carrington very late at night on Wednesday and reappear bright and early on Thursday for training, Pochettino is raring to go and is eager for his players to head to Anfield on Sunday convinced they can win.

'I have plenty of energy. It's a privilege to be head coach of Manchester United,' he said.

'And we are not wasting time. We need to be ready to compete on Sunday.

'Now it's not time to think about rest, it's not time to think about sleep. It's about being ready and to prepare everything to be sure that we are going to compete in the best condition at Anfield.'

Sports.title: Inside the deadly world of bodybuilding: Athletes dying at an alarming rate, rampant drug use and why thousands still risk everything in fatal obsession with the perfect body
Sports.content:
We're at the Vaillant, a mid-sized arena in Derby. It’s the Sunday before last and a bronzed man with a grey beard is discussing his new identity.

His name is Jake Bourne and he’s 48, three years removed from the 26 he spent in the military. First, he was in the parachute regiment and then he worked in intelligence, serving in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, Kosovo and Sierra Leone. ‘Some interesting stuff,’ he tells me, while snacking on a small rice cake.

In a couple of hours, he’ll head away from this corridor by the toilets and onto the stage, where he will compete in the men’s physique category of the UK Open, an amateur bodybuilding contest run by the Physical Culture Association (PCA).

This has been part of his life since 2024 and it has dominated his thoughts in the past 16 weeks of hard preparations. If today goes well, he’ll win his pro card, so he talks about discipline, sacrifice and sustaining himself on chicken and a bit of rice to make it happen.

Bourne is an intense guy, but likeable and honest enough to list his other ingredients – doses of testosterone and human growth hormone. In this realm, it is often the case that anything goes, including the kind of performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) banned in conventional sport.

But bodybuilding isn’t conventional. And whatever he tries, Bourne is still unhappy with his legs. ‘They are so used to working under load in the military that I can’t push them hard enough to grow,’ he adds. Everyone in this corridor has something similar to say. For Harry Taylor, a personal trainer who competes clean, it’s his ‘love handles’, and Kyle Davies, another ‘natural’, isn’t getting what he wants from his pecs.

Competitors strike a pose for bodybuilding's UK Open, which took place this month in Derby

Jake Bourne (left) has been bodybuilding since 2024 after 26 years in the military, while Harry Taylor (right) wants to get rid of his 'love handles'

To Tom Reynolds, who has ‘enhanced’ himself with peptides and other substances, it’s his ‘extended gut’, which he ascribes to cocaine and alcohol addictions in his younger years.

He says bodybuilding improved his life, mimicking the sentiment of Phil Vickery, a 2003 Rugby World Cup winner for England who has been struggling with brain injury. He wasn’t in Derby but strongly dislikes his glutes. Of the 150 or so competitors in this arena, each has a problem to fix.

But there’s an edge to it and it’s darker than two coats of tan. Because what about deeper issues, like overloaded hearts, kidneys and livers? What about the tragedy that happened 55 miles away a few weeks ago? And what about the role drugs might play in a terrifying trend?

Daily Mail Sport has spoken to dozens of athletes, event organisers, medical experts and the author of a landmark study to explore the extremities of an extreme sport. What we found was a warm community filled with good and intelligent people. But it is also a place where the protagonists are dying at a truly astonishing rate. In this space of thongs and flexes, serious questions need to be posed.

The initial assumption of at least one witness was that Mateusz Chmura had fainted last month. In a sport where athletes want a dryer, more toned appearance, dehydration is common, so there wasn’t an immediate assumption of the worst when he collapsed on stage at the PCA’s British Finals in Telford.

But it rapidly became apparent on Sunday, October 18 that the situation was far more severe for Chmura, a newlywed from Wakefield who had made his amateur debut a fortnight earlier.

Within moments, he received CPR from an attending paramedic. He was then airlifted to New Cross Hospital in Wolverhampton.

While that was unfolding, a crowd of several hundred was ushered from the hall of the Telford International Centre. A statement from the PCA a day later, on what would have been Chmura’s 34th birthday, announced he had died.

Mateusz Chmura died at the age of 33 after collapsing on stage at an event in Telford

Chmura was a newlywed from Wakefield who had made his amateur debut a fortnight earlier (Source: Instagram/mateusz.chmura.92)

‘It was horrible,’ says Nick, a 40-year-old bodybuilder and coach who was present in the arena and declines to give his surname. ‘I’d never known anything like it to happen in the UK. We all went outside for a couple of hours and a decision was made to continue the event, but I believe he was still alive at that point. If he had died on stage, it would have been cancelled.’

A formal cause of death has not been publicised by Chmura’s family. Nor is it known if he was using any performance-enhancing substances in a sport where they are not banned in many categories and legal to possess under UK law.

But the events of October 18 do blend into an established pattern. And the figures make for shocking reading.

A study published last year by the European Heart Journal tracked 20,286 amateur and professional male bodybuilders from databases belonging to the International Federation of Bodybuilding and Fitness (IFBB) and MuscleMemory.org, following the criteria that they had competed in at least one of 730 events between 2005 and 2020. Within that sample, 121 deaths were recorded at an average age of 45.

Some involved suicide, homicide or vehicle accidents, and many lacked quantifiable data. But 46 fatalities fell into the largest category of ‘sudden cardiac deaths’ (SCD) and 11 of those occurred within one year of the athlete’s last competition. Drilling further, the study said one bodybuilder collapsed on stage, two suffered SCD during training and four athletes did so less than a week after an official event.

Discoveries from the pinnacle of professional bodybuilding were the most eye-catching. The ‘open’ category of Mr Olympia was won seven times by a steroid-infused Arnold Schwarzenegger and is sanctioned by the IFBB Pro League (a separate organisation to the IFBB), with prizes of up to £450,000.

It’s where the best want to be. It’s also where the study found seven deaths from just 100 competitors. The average age was 36.

Daily Mail Sport consulted the lead author of the study, Dr Marco Vecchiato, a specialist in sports and exercise medicine, to discuss the scenario. Among the details he shared was a troubling admission – none of the sport’s many federations, leagues or athletes had been in contact to better understand his research.

Bodybuilding has a warm community filled with good and intelligent people. But it is also a place where the protagonists are dying at a truly astonishing rate

The ‘open’ category of Mr Olympia was won seven times by a steroid-infused Arnold Schwarzenegger. It’s also where a study found seven deaths from just 100 competitors

‘My personal impression is that the study has generated considerable media attention,’ says Dr Vecchiato. ‘Its impact on practical measures to protect athletes has been less apparent.’

Dr Vecchiato has continued to monitor mortality in bodybuilding beyond 2020 for an updated report in 2027 and confirmed the subsequent number of deaths is ‘substantial’, involving both men and women.

That might include the case of Neil Currey, an Englishman who contested the men’s classic physique at Mr Olympia in 2022 and died a year later, aged 34. His parents were clear on why – in a written statement to the inquest, they said their ‘firm belief’ was that his use of steroids was responsible.

The study isn’t alone in exploring this trend. A detailed story in BoxLife Magazine claimed there were as many as 56 fatalities worldwide in 2025. Even without cataloguing the consequences that fall short of death, these numbers would indicate bodybuilding is one of the most dangerous sporting pursuits on the planet.

Naturally, a significant conversation here will discuss the rampant use of performance-enhancing drugs – Dr Vecchiato’s study found ‘at least’ 19 of the 121 deceased carried evidence of PED use. On the ground level of the sport, in places like this hall in Derby, there is a level of cognitive dissonance on that front, among even the more knowledgeable practitioners.

It’s a space where Nick, our coach and competitor from earlier, will comfortably share with me that he might ‘blast and cruise’ on testosterone. That can mean ticking over on anywhere between 125-150ml of testosterone per week, he says, and then upping the dose for competitions with oral compounds that add a couple of hundred extra millilitres.

A point to add here – Nick is not some shadowy figure. He was very pleasant, actually. And open about the entire operation – the testosterone is relatively cheap at £50 for a bottle that can last 12 weeks, and his growth hormone is dearer at £300 for a month.

‘I know guys who have gone IFBB Pro and take nothing – they have great genetics,’ he says. ‘But you’ve got to be sensible (if you do use drugs). Some just go silly with it. Around competition time, it is usually diuretic use (removing excess fluids) that can cause them problems. I get my blood work done, heart scans, but some don’t. If you’re not getting your heart checked, something serious can happen.’

Neil Currey, who contested the men’s classic physique at Mr Olympia in 2022 and died a year later aged 34. His parents had a ‘firm belief’ that his use of steroids was responsible

To talk to Nick is to hear a man who is significantly better informed than a layman and isn’t blindly following a coach’s advice.

But, aside from legal questions about the supply of substances that are prescription-only in the UK, not to mention health concerns about what might be contained in black-market equivalents, can there be a sensible approach, especially if no medical need has been diagnosed?

Perhaps inadvertently, Nick answers that himself several hours later, when he tells me his plan is to only do one more year on his drug cycles because he is mindful of potential heart complications down the line.

On these high wires, bodybuilders exist in vast numbers. And, as experts have explained in the course of researching this article, it is easy to overlook one salient fact – the sport places more stress on the body than most, even before you supercharge the fuel.

One England-based source contacted by Daily Mail Sport remains convinced her brother took no performance-enhancing drugs prior to his death following a stroke last year. He was in his mid-twenties and training hard for his first competition as an amateur; a doctor shared with the family his belief that the strain of workouts was influential.

We spoke to multiple bodybuilders who claim to be clean. But it has long been known that substances are endemic in the sport, including events reserved for ‘naturals’ on the global calendar. Daily Mail Sport studied the most recent testing figures compiled by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and discovered a remarkable statistic: of 1,217 samples collected on behalf of the Madrid-based IFBB in 2024, 162 returned adverse findings.

That's a fail rate of 13 per cent, more than four times greater than the next highest among 39 sports that supplied more than 1,000 samples. WADA deemed the IFBB non-compliant in 2022 and confirmed that status is ongoing. The IFBB told me they are ‘committed’ to clean sport and ‘actively working to resolve’ their non-compliance.

That bodybuilding shares a symbiotic relationship with performance-enhancing drugs is no surprise. But it is only recently that the wider risks of the sport have been quantified by a peer-reviewed fatality toll. The existence of which begs a pair of key questions: why do it? And should the Wild West do more to make itself safer?

‹ Slide me › Phil Vickery was a Rugby World Cup-winning prop for England in 2003 before turning his hand to bodybuilding in retirement (swipe for transformation)

The ‘why’ is easier to answer. According to the aspiring cast of amateurs in Derby, it’s an obsession rooted closer to perceptions of improvement rather than money.

For those who might win a PCA pro card, the prizes at the subsequent PCA World Championships in Spain were listed at £2,500. That’s far more indicative of the landscape than the rewards at Mr Olympia.

As Bourne puts it: ‘You want to see what you can do. Push yourself. It becomes a bug.’

Some of his subsequent equivocations around drug use contain kernels of truth.

‘My caveat would be that people come back after a stressful day at work and won't exercise, might have four cans of lager,’ he says. ‘I take a bit of testosterone, a bit of growth hormone, but I don't drink, my food is measured and clean. I do my blood work every six weeks, my blood pressure each morning. I know what's going on in my body. We're going to identify problems in our health much sooner than somebody that's doing what is socially acceptable.’

It’s an interesting perspective but hardly bulletproof. Dr Vecchiato directed us to a Danish study in 2025 that found ‘steroid exposure was associated with approximately three times the risk of myocardial infarction, almost nine times the risk of cardiomyopathy and more than three times the risk of heart failure’.

He has serious misgivings about the level of understanding among bodybuilders around what they are taking.

‘There are important gaps in knowledge particularly about lifetime exposure, repeated combinations, newer compounds and outcomes after people stop using them,’ he says.

Tom Reynolds, who has ‘enhanced’ himself with peptides and other substances, is targeting his ‘extended gut’, which he ascribes to cocaine and alcohol addictions in his younger years

Dr Vecchiato believes three areas need addressing urgently. First is an independent registry of deaths in bodybuilding, and secondly an education programme in gyms. His third objective is fascinating – a ‘structured pre-participation medical assessment’ including family medical history, substance disclosures and physical examination.

The latter is common in other sports – think of the medicals required for a boxing licence. As with much in bodybuilding, the picture is far less clear.

The PCA, for instance, require competitors to sign a waiver with their entry fee (£70 for Derby) that declares ‘to the best of their knowledge’ that they are fit and well. They also have to notify organisers of any medical conditions or prescribed medication, while remaining ‘responsible for decisions concerning their personal preparation’.

Those disclosures can trigger a refusal of entry, but the PCA did not respond to a Daily Mail Sport request for more detail.

One question asked if a bodybuilder would be required to supply proof of a professional health assessment, and another enquired how many would-be participants had been refused entry in the past 12 months.

As the waiver on the PCA website stated it was ‘effective’ from October 30, 12 days after Chmura’s passing, we also asked if there was an earlier version. No answers were forthcoming.

Similar questions were sent to the IFBB, the separate IFBB Pro League, which sanctions Mr Olympia, and the US-based National Physique Committee to ask if their athletes are required to supply proof of having undergone a professional health assessment prior to competing.

Only the IFBB replied, stating the health of their athletes is a ‘fundamental priority’ and supported by their medical commission, but they do not require a ‘specific medical examination certificate’.

Chmura's passing is the latest entry in the sport's catalogue of tragedy (Source: Instagram/mateusz.chmura.92)

At the PCA in Derby, Bourne would go on to win his pro card. Beaming a grin on stage with a glistening tan that will take a full two weeks to wash off, he is satisfied with his sacrifices. By exercising his free will, he is making strides.

Meanwhile, the organisation’s owner, Ryan Alexander, would later tell me that Chmura’s death was the first since their formation 10 years ago, and that they have a medical team and defibrillator at their shows.

‘The safety of our athletes is paramount,’ Alexander said. ‘When we find out (the cause of Chmura’s death), if there’s something that needs to be reviewed additionally, that's of course something we would do.’

For now, the detail of Chmura’s passing is unknown. But one fact is inescapable - this extreme sport has become dangerously familiar with tragedy and remains some distance short of a solution.

Sports.title: 'F*** the Pope and the IRA' chant lands England in hot water as fans are given suspended one-game stadium ban and FA fined
Sports.content:
'F*** the Pope and the IRA' chant lands England in hot water as fans are given suspended one-game stadium ban and FA fined

UEFA have slapped the FA with a £12,500 fine and a suspended one-match away supporters ban after England fans were heard singing sectarian chants during their Nations League victory over Spain last weekend.

Some of the 3,000 supporters who travelled to Madrid were heard singing 'f*** the Pope and the IRA' inside Madrid's Metropolitano Stadium on Sunday.

As a result, UEFA have fined the FA and banned away fans from attending one UEFA match for 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour'.

That said, the ban will only take effect if England supporters reoffend within the next two years.

It is a fortunate reprieve given the Three Lions' next away fixture is their Nations League quarter-final, the draw for which is on Friday.

Meanwhile, the FA have committed to identifying those involved and taking action - which could see football banning orders imposed.

In a statement to Daily Mail Sport, the FA said: 'We will not tolerate this unacceptable and deeply offensive chanting, and will work with the police who attend all England home and away matches to identify the perpetrators and take the necessary action.'

England fans land FA in hot water over 'f*** the Pope and the IRA' chant during Spain victory

England supporters have notoriously sung the anti-Catholic and loyalist chant. In 2024, the Irish police urged travelling fans to 'respect local culture' before their Nations League match against the Republic of Ireland.

Fans were also filmed in Milan city centre on the eve of the clash against Italy in 2022 singing the same incendiary chant - just one year after their European Championship final defeat to the Italians.

Meanwhile, then England boss Roy Hodgson and the FA were forced to condemn supporters after the inflammatory chant was heard throughout England's 3-1 friendly victory over Scotland at Celtic Park in 2014. Around 5,000 fans travelled to the devoutly Catholic club.

The issue is not limited to international football. In August, Daily Mail Sport revealed that Chelsea wrote to supporters after a section of their fans were heard singing the sectarian chant away at Fulham on the opening weekend of the Premier League season.

England boss Thomas Tuchel was asked about racism in his pre-Spain press conference.

'I never expect racism and the dressing room is the most anti-racist place on Earth and that's exactly how it works,' Tuchel said.

'I expect emotional and of course supporting fans from Spain for their national team. That's what I expect, but I don't expect racism nowhere.

'I'm shocked if it happens, and it should happen nowhere, and I'm the first one to stand up for these kind of values.

'My trust is that we have a friendly atmosphere, that we have an atmosphere who is clearly in favour of the Spanish team, and that football does what it does best: bring people together and not divide people.'

Sports.title: Premier League clubs vote 18-2 in favour of footing legal bill for top-flight chiefs if Man City's sponsors sue them for defamation... with City and Nottingham Forest voting against
Sports.content:
Premier League clubs have voted to protect the organisation's bigwigs from any individual legal action taken by Manchester City's sponsors.

Instead, the clubs - including City themselves - will foot any legal bills incurred by a potential corporate defamation suit.

Daily Mail Sport understands there was widespread support from clubs to insulate Premier League chief executive Richard Masters and the four other league directors.

The vote passed with 18 clubs in favour, and City and Nottingham Forest against.

It is understood Forest opted to vote that way as they felt they had not been given sufficient information or enough time to consider the proposal and its implications, as opposed to representing a show of support for City.

The matter was the first item on the agenda at the Premier League shareholders' meeting in the Savoy Hotel on Thursday and was addressed quickly with limited discussion.

Clubs had a paper for the proposed rule change before the meeting and there was significant support to extend the legal protection to individuals on the league's board.

This marks the first time since the Premier League’s inception that insurance arrangements for its board members have been reviewed.

Premier League clubs will foot the bill if Manchester City's sponsors sue for defamation

In September, City were found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules after a seven-year legal process.

An independent commission appointed by the Premier League found City inflated their revenues by £900million – disguising money from their Abu Dhabi ownership group as sponsorship revenue.

Etihad Airways, owned by the Abu Dhabi government, denied being ‘involved in improper commercial arrangements’ and said it was considering legal action in response to the verdict.

Meanwhile, another City sponsor, Etisalat - a telecommunications company - is also weighing up legal action.

City, though, maintain their innocence and are appealing the decision, which could see them relegated from the top flight.

Sports.title: Glazer family split over selling Man Utd after Mauricio Pochettino intervention
Sports.content:
Glazer family split over selling Man Utd after Mauricio Pochettino intervention

Manchester United's long-term future has once again come into focus amid claims that the Glazer family intervened in the club's recent search for a new head coach

View 2 Images Manchester United's ownership continues to attract scrutiny (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The Glazer family are once again said to be split over the future of Manchester United, with some siblings understood to be 'pushing each other' to sell more of the club.

‌



‌



United were acquired by the Glazers back in 2005 in a leveraged buyout which saw the Premier League giants loaded with debt. They have remained in situ since, though they did sell a stake of the club - and hand over sporting power - to the Ineos chief, Sir Jim Ratcliffe back in 2024.

‌



With United's fortunes nosediving, fresh scrutiny over the club's ownership has arrived, particularly in the wake of the poor start to the season which triggered another managerial change.

‌



Avram and Joel Glazer recommended Mauricio Pochettino as the coach to succeed Michael Carrick despite Ratcliffe having control of sporting operations at Old Trafford, though Bloomberg also reports that some members of the family have been pushing others to sell more of the club, which it's claimed they value at around $6billion (£4.5bn).

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



The report adds that some members of the family believed they had 'missed an opportunity to cash out' following news that a consortium led by Amazon's Jeff Bezos purchased a stake in Liverpool at the summer.

A potential takeover clause in that deal may see Liverpool valued above Manchester United for the first time at $7 billion (£5.3bn). Ratcliffe has a similar option to buy out the Glazers long-term which would cost in the region of £3bn.

‌



The Glazer's intervention in the search for a new manager comes at a time where United have made their worst start to a season for 40 years. Poor form under Carrick, sacked less than six months after being named permanent head coach, has seen the Red Devils slide into the Premier League relegation zone.

View 2 Images The Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe have both been criticised by Manchester United supporters (Image: James Gill - Danehouse, Getty Images)

‌



Though Carrick carried the can for results with the sack, the Manchester United Supporters Trust made it clear that the ownership are culpable for the club's malaise.

"The reason Manchester United fans have continued to support Michael Carrick in recent weeks is that they know that responsibility for United’s problems do not primarily rest with him or indeed his predecessors as manager, they said in a statement.

‌



"They lie with the ownership. The Glazers' debt-funded takeover continues to burden the club. When INEOS came in they promised sporting excellence, but yet with repeated changes in football leadership we have seen anything but.

"It is time for the owners to explain themselves and show some accountability."

Sports.title: Shakur Stevenson must take more risks if he wants the big offers to roll in after Zuffa exit
Sports.content:
Shakur Stevenson must take more risks if he wants the big offers to roll in after Zuffa exit

Shakur Stevenson will really discover his worth when purse bids for his mandatory WBO title defence against Raymond Muratella start to roll in after his brief Zuffa stint

View 2 Images Purse bids for Shakur Stevenson's mandatory WBO title defence will commence later this month (Image: Cris Esqueda/Golden Boy)

The economics of boxing are speaking truth to Shakur Stevenson. Failure to reach a deal to defend his WBO super lightweight title against mandatory challenger Raymond Muratella has sent the fight to purse bids.

‌



‌



Stevenson, who signed then split with Zuffa earlier this year without lacing a glove, appears to value himself differently to others. Zuffa could not make the numbers meet Stevenson’s expectations. Now he is about to learn his market worth to the big broadcasters in when purse bids are considered on the last day of the month.

‌



Stevenson is immensely talented. Having won bantamweight silver at the 2016 Olympics, he has progressed untroubled from featherweight to super lightweight world champion as a pro.

‌



He’s slick, but to the point of boredom. The majority of boxing fans want to be entertained. They admire and appreciate skill but need action.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources

He likes to compare himself to Terence Crawford and fighters of that ilk. The difference is, Crawford was exciting, and could fight when he had to. I don’t recall seeing Stevenson contest a riveting round. Talent is not enough. Being hard to hit is only half the bargain.

‌



Great defensive fighters like Floyd Mayweather Jnr, Roy Jones Jnr, Crawford, Pernell Whittaker, Sugar Ray Leonard, were to a greater or lesser degree hard to hit, but everyone of them came to the party when they had to.

Stevenson has not shown an ounce of their aggression in 25 fights. Unbeaten IBF lightweight champion Muratalla is coming up to super lightweight for the first time. He doesn’t have the same brand power as Stevenson’s last opponent, Teofimo Lopez. Stevenson does, but not as much as he thinks.

‌



Someone needs to remind Stevenson that the great boxers are not only technically blessed, they are forged in great fights.

View 2 Images Dana White's Zuffa lost Stevenson's services last month (Image: Getty)

‌



It matters to be remembered. And to be remembered fans must care who wins. This involves taking a risk in the ring, putting everything on the line.

Stevenson might argue that taking a risk is stupid if you can win another way. Plus it shortens your career. And he would be right. But if he wants to be considered an all-time great, he has to offer more. The guys that get the balance right are the ones that go down in history.

Article continues below

Stevenson certainly has the tools to be impactful. He just needs to step forward. He chooses not to. Fair enough, but don’t complain when the big offers do not pour in.

Follow Barry on X at @‌ClonesCyclone @mcguigan’s_Gym

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino dealt transfer blow as Man Utd target in new contract talks
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino dealt transfer blow as Man Utd target in new contract talks

Manchester United are expected to be active in January with defensive reinforcements on the agenda - but one transfer target has held contract talks with his current club

View 2 Images Calvin Bassey is a Manchester United transfer target (Image: Marc Atkins)

Fulham are attempting to prevent Manchester United from signing Calvin Bassey in January by tying the central defender down to a new contract.

‌



‌



Bassey, 26, has enjoyed a stellar start to the new Premier League campaign. Alongside his fine form, the Nigeria international has captained the side under Alvaro Arbeloa, who is eager to keep the former Ajax and Rangers man at Craven Cottage despite interest from Old Trafford.

‌



Reinforcements in defence are a necessity in the upcoming winter window for United, who have the joint-worst defensive record among Europe's top five leagues after shipping 30 goals already this term.

‌



Bassey has emerged as one potential option for the Red Devils and their new head coach, Mauricio Pochettino, ahead of January - but Fulham have been working on a new contract for the defender, per The Athletic.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



They have acted with Bassey now well inside the final year of his current deal, though Fulham do hold an option to extend those terms by a further 12 months. The report adds that Fulham have no intention of selling Bassey in January.

Bassey has made over 100 appearances for Fulham since joining them from Ajax in 2023 and his experience of the Premier League means he would represent an oven-ready player for Pochettino, who inherits a beleaguered team who fell into the relegation zone prior to the international break.

‌



United have other targets heading into the winter window including Jarrad Branthwaite, who they tried to sign back in the summer of 2024.

View 2 Images Mauricio Pochettino is expected to be backed in the winter transfer window (Image: JC Ruiz)

‌



It remains to be seen if Everton would entertain selling a player they rejected two bids for previously, the second of which reached the £50million mark.

Bassey's Fulham teammate, Antonee Robinson, is another player of interest ahead of the mid-season window with United short on left-back cover.

Article continues below

Diogo Dalot has been forced to deputise in the position with Luke Shaw unavailable and has struggled for form. Robinson again boasts extensive Premier League experience and, crucially, is a player known to Pochettino from the USMNT set-up.

Sports.title: Man Utd's eight January transfer targets rated and slated as two priorities emerge
Sports.content:
Man Utd's eight January transfer targets rated and slated as two priorities emerge

Manchester United and Mauricio Pochettino have to transform the club's early season fortune and may be forced to dip into the transfer market in January

View 3 Images Mauricio Pochettino has work to do (Image: Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty Images)

Manchester United have started a new era under Mauricio Pochettino and are a matter of weeks away from their new boss truly putting his stamp on the squad. The January transfer window awaits, with United already linked with fixing problem positions in defence and up front.

‌



‌



Target Lewis Hall is unlikely to be available at the turn of the year, so United will have to work smartly to secure the right deals during a notoriously difficult time to find a good deal. The coming months will also display how much sway the Argentine has over sporting director Jason Wilcox's plans.

‌



With United in 18th place, something needs to change. But are the right options available for the Red Devils to lurch them into European contention under Pochettino?

‌



Mirror Football takes a look at some of the players already linked with Old Trafford and rates how appropriate they would be.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



Jarrad Branthwaite

View 3 Images Manchester United have previously targeted Jarrad Branthwaite (Image: Mark Cosgrove/News Images/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The Everton defender has long been linked with Manchester United after the Red Devils attempted to land the Toffees star in 2024. Instead, United landed Leny Yoro and Matthijs de Ligt.

‌



The England international has once again established himself under David Moyes after struggling with injury in recent seasons.

Mirror verdict: Branthwaite would provide a solid option for United with plenty of Premier League experience. His progress could match well with the side should Pochettino be able to turn things around. However, he will demand an elite fee after Everton turned down a £50million offer more than two years ago, and his injury record is cause for concern in a backline that has seen a lot of injuries already. 7/10.

‌



Calvin Bassey

The Fulham central defender has impressed so far this season and has experience of playing a left-back during the early part of his career. The former Rangers and Ajax defender is known for his leadership, having captained the Cottagers on multiple occasions.

Mirror verdict: Could Bassey serve as an improvement on United's current option? Probably. Is the answer to helping United return to the top echelons? Probably not. He would be able to provide pace and physicality to a defence that has been required to sit deeper due to its limitations and would be able to instigate attacks driving from the back. 5/10.

‌



Nathan Collins

Brentford star Collins is another central defender who would bring leadership benefits, given his experience as captain of the Bees and the Republic of Ireland. The 25-year-old already has more than 150 Premier League appearances and would offer strong physical presence.

‌



Mirror verdict: Collins has not featured a great deal due to injury so far this season, and his ability to play a high line may provide Pochettino with some concern. The international is under contract until 2029 and may prove too costly for the benefit he would provide. 4/10.

Antonee Robinson

View 3 Images Mauricio Pochettino is familiar with Antonee Robinson (Image: Ronald Cortes/Getty Images)

‌



Another candidate from Fulham and an option who would be plug-and-play on the left side of defence. Pochettino is familiar with the 29-year-old from his time with the United States, and Robinson is under contract until the summer of 2028, meaning it could be an appropriate time for the Cottagers to cash in.

Mirror verdict: In some respects, it feels as though United may have missed the boat on Robinson. His signing would only provide a short-term option before requiring greater depth in the position once again. 6/10.

‌



Alejandre Balde

The Barcelona left-back has struggled for minutes so far this season, having fallen behind Joao Cancelo in the pecking order at Camp Nou. The 23-year-old Spaniard has no experience outside of La Liga, and Barca chief Deco has said he will not be on the move in January.

Mirror verdict: While Balde is far from a guaranteed success, perhaps he could offer an option on loan before United attempt to sign Lewis Hall from Newcastle in the summer. 5/10.

‌

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Folarin Balogun

The US forward has struggled for minutes at Monaco since his failed transfer to Everton on transfer deadline day. The 25-year-old remains keen to depart the principality and has thrived under Pochettino on the international stage.

Balogun might only have fleeting Premier League experience from his time at Arsenal but was a star of their youth setup before departing for Ligue 1. With Everton agreeing a £40m deal in the summer, there would be a degree of confidence that a move could be arranged for a smaller fee now.

‌



Mirror verdict: United might not be able to benefit from any Donald Trump interventions, but if they want to add to their forward depth prudently, Balogun may be a smart option if Pochettino also rates him. If United want their standout, star striker, a move for the forward comes with a great deal more risk, despite a more moderate fee than Benjamin Sesko's. 7/10.

Alex Freeman

Another American connection, Alex Freeman could provide a versatile option at right-back or in the centre of defence for Pochettino. Still just 22, there is plenty of room for Freeman to grow under Pochettino's tutelage, and he is also capable in a more advanced position.

‌



Mirror verdict: It's far from certain that Freeman fixes United's problem positions, though he may raise the floor on the club's right flank. Whether he is a sensible signing would all come down to how highly he is regarded by the new boss. 6/10.

Igor Matanovic

Igor Matanovic has started this season well with eight goals in 13 appearances for Freiburg. The Croatia international, 23, already has 17 caps for his home nation after bagging 15 goals in his debut season for the German side.

‌



Matanovic has reportedly been keen on a move to United, but has also been rated at £50m.

Mirror verdict: It would be an expensive swing for United to take a chance on Matanovic based simply on his recent form. 4/10.

Sports.title: Injured Luke Humphries winces in pain as he loses to rank outsider in Grand Slam of Darts
Sports.content:
Injured Luke Humphries winces in pain as he loses to rank outsider in Grand Slam of Darts

Luke Humphries has followed Luke Littler in crashing out of the tournament

View 2 Images Luke Humphries after missing a double to win the match (Image: Sky Sports)

An injured Luke Humphries crashed out of the Grand Slam of Darts after losing 10-9 to rank outsider Tom Sykes. The 2024 Grand Slam champion went into the match with a neck injury and fell 4-0 down, but rallied to force a decider.

‌



‌



Humphries had a dart to win it as he almost took out 128 before the world number 72 held his nerve to secure the biggest win of his career. It means the world numbers one and two have gone out on consecutive nights after world champion Luke Littler lost to Jermaine Wattimena on Wednesday.

‌



Humphries was hampered throughout by his injury, struggling to bend down at one point after dropping one of his arrows. Wayne Mardle said on Sky Sports commentary: "This afternoon, and as you can see, the way he bent down there, Luke Humphries had a humongous heat pad on his neck.

‌



"He was telling me that he had a trapped nerve and it's been released now by a specialist, but he's still struggling. So I don't know how he's going to cope, but when he dropped that dart, you see the way he bent down? There's limited movement."

Barry Hearn forced to respond after major backlash to Luke Littler Netflix show READ MORE :

Despite that, Cool Hand battled on and hauled himself back into the match, taking a 6-5 lead. Sykes then won the next three legs to go 8-5 up. At 9-7 down, Humphries won two in a row to force a decider, fitting for a match of such quality and drama.

Humphries carved out a chance to win it but missed it, and Sykes coolly mopped it up to set up a quarter-final against another big name - James Wade or Michael van Gerwen.

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

A disbelieving Sykes said: "It is unbelievable, honestly. Luke let me off a few times in the first bit. I set off really well, and I got into a 4-0 lead. When he got it back to 5-5, I thought, 'Here we go.' He started turning it on. But, yeah, I'm just buzzing to get it over the line in the end."

‌



On needing double 18 to win it, he added: "I was a bit nervous, but obviously I thought the game was over when I turned round and saw Luke hit the first triple 18 there, and then he hit the second one, and then he wired it.

"I was so cold on that last one. I just thought, 'Just hit it first dart, no messing about and get into it,' and I did.

‌



"It is mental, honestly, 15 years of hard work, and now I'm playing the best guys in the world every week. I'm riding a wave at the minute and I'll keep trying to ride it."

View 2 Images Luke Humphries looked in agony at times (Image: Sky Sports)

‌



Humphries referenced his injury on social media after the match. He wrote on X: Well done @TomSykes180, absolutely amazing performance!!

"So proud of the way I played tonight with what I've had to go through with injury the last 48 hours. Gave it my absolute all there. Wish everyone all the best for the rest of the tournament."

‌



Sykes is in his first year as a PDC Tour player, making his win over Humphries an even bigger shock than Wattimena's triumph over Littler 24 hours earlier. The 19-year-old was eyeing a third successive title in Wolverhampton, but succumbed to a 10-8 loss to the Dutchman.

After winning the first five major titles of the year, Littler looked unbeatable, but he has now lost his cloak of invincibility on the big stage.

Article continues below

The Nuke is not due to play again until the opening night of the World Championship on December 11, having failed to qualify for the Players Championships Finals in Minehead at the end of November.

Sports.title: 'I loved playing for Liverpool - but then everything changed and I had to leave'
Sports.content:
'I loved playing for Liverpool - but then everything changed and I had to leave'

Liverpool underwent a period of change as Xabi Alonso, Javier Mascherano and Fernando Torres left in succession

View 2 Images Fernando Torres was unhappy with the club's sales (Image: Michael Steele, Getty Images)

Fernando Torres has opened up about how 'everything changed' at Liverpool in the lead-up to his controversial switch to Chelsea. The former striker's deadline-day departure from Anfield to Stamford Bridge in 2011 left countless Reds fans devastated.

‌



‌



Torres joined the Blues in a £50million deal and went on to claim Champions League and Europa League glory, but he remains best remembered in the Premier League for his goalscoring exploits with the Reds. The Atletico Madrid prodigy sent shockwaves around the division when he chose to leave, but it appears it was an exit that was a long time in the making.

‌



Torres said on the Aldo Meets podcast. "It's hard to explain. Long story short, everything changed at Liverpool."

‌



The World Cup winner had 'felt at home' from day one with the Reds and was delighted to have signed for a club that consistently competed in Champions League finals. The bond between Liverpool's squad and supporters was also appealing, while he already had compatriots at Anfield in Xabi Alonso, Pepe Reina and Alvaro Arbeloa.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



His partnership with Steven Gerrard, 'the best player' he ever played alongside, and the management of Rafael Benitez had given Torres ample reason to feel optimistic. Yet as the Reds slumped to seventh place in 2009/10 and the Spanish manager left the club, uncertainty began to take hold in the striker's mind.

"They started to sell our best players," he said. "Xabi [Alonso] went to Real Madrid (in 2009) and Javier Mascherano to Barcelona (in 2010). Rafa had also left. It was like: 'What's going on here?'".

‌



"We had been close in the Premier League and Champions League. We were only one step away and just needed to add a couple of players to the squad. Instead, the ones coming in were not the best quality."

View 2 Images Fernando Torres of Liverpool celebrates scoring his team's third goal during the Barclays Premier League match between Wolverhampton Wanderers and Liverpool at Molineux

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

While the exodus of talent halted as Tom Hicks and George Gillett sought buyers, FSG's takeover failed to restore Torres' faith in the club's trajectory.

‌



The striker gained little comfort from John Henry when the incoming owner outlined a fresh transfer strategy. With the club prioritising youth development, Torres harboured doubts about his prospects of securing trophies at 27.

After discussions with sporting director Damien Comolli, the forward felt unwanted at Anfield. "The feeling I got was that he didn't really care if I was going to leave," Torres added.

‌



"He said: 'If we can find a replacement, you can go'. He didn't say: 'Let's make a new project, you need to stay, we're going to bring in this one and this one.'".

Torres maintains his switch to Chelsea was justified, though he retains some regret about his Anfield departure. He lifted the Champions League trophy with the Blues but felt remorseful about upsetting Liverpool supporters.

Article continues below

"Back then, for me it was all about winning trophies," he said. "But as you get older, you realise that's not the main thing. The connection you have with people is more important. Being happy and feeling that you're really part of something is more important."
