World.title: Can the Rohingya genocide verdict deliver justice?
World.content:
The ICJ has ruled against Myanmar, but safe return, citizenship and reparations remain far from guaranteed.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice did something it had never done in its 80-year history: It held a state responsible for committing genocide. By nine votes to six, the court found that Myanmar’s 2017 campaign against the Rohingya crossed the gravest threshold in international law.

That matters because Myanmar’s defence was never simply that nothing terrible happened. It argued that its “clearance operations” followed attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) and were, however brutal, fundamentally counterterrorism. Genocide requires more than proof of killing, rape or village destruction; it requires specific intent to destroy a protected group.

The court found that Myanmar’s government forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed widespread sexual violence, inflicted extreme violence on children and attacked people fleeing towards Bangladesh. Taking the evidence together, it concluded that the “only reasonable inference” was an intention to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.

That strips away the central evasion of the past decade. The ARSA attacks were real. So was armed conflict. But rebellion is not a legal alibi for genocide. Nor can the atrocities now be dismissed as excesses by rogue soldiers. This was a judgement about what Myanmar, as a state, did to a people.

The 9-6 split will inevitably be used by Myanmar to cast doubt on the ruling. But the judgement is final and binding. And by 10 votes to five, the court went further, ordering reparations, including safe, voluntary and dignified return, family reunification, restitution of property and compensation where restitution is impossible.



For Rohingya survivors, that is extraordinary vindication. Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the courtroom, called it “a great day for the Rohingya”. In Cox’s Bazar, refugees had been making an equally practical demand: They want to go home, but with rights, citizenship and dignity.

But here is the problem: You cannot eat a judgement. You cannot live inside one. You cannot rebuild a burned village with one or raise a child safely inside one.

The ICJ has no enforcement arm. Under Article 94(2) of the United Nations Charter, noncompliance can be taken to the UN Security Council (UNSC), where China or Russia could block action. That makes pressure outside the UNSC essential: Targeted sanctions, ASEAN diplomacy, the ICC investigation and Argentina’s universal-jurisdiction case, where arrest warrants have already been issued for 25 suspects.

Who governs the map has also changed. In 2017, Myanmar’s military dominated Rakhine. Today, the Arakan Army controls most of it, and UN investigators have documented forced recruitment, movement restrictions, arbitrary killings and other abuses against Rohingya under its rule.

Any serious return framework must therefore deal with whoever controls the ground. Bangladesh should tie cross-border trade, humanitarian access and political engagement with the Arakan Army to measurable Rohingya benchmarks: Freedom of movement, restoration of land, an end to forced recruitment, international monitoring and a pathway to citizenship. Dhaka should also press Myanmar’s authorities, ASEAN, China, India, Gulf states and Western governments to support a monitored return-and-reparations mechanism. For too long, ports, pipelines and trade corridors have been treated as “strategic” while the Rohingya remain in the humanitarian file.

Everyone wants something from Myanmar. The Rohingya should finally be part of the bill.

None of this matters if the camps fall apart before return becomes possible. About 95 percent of Rohingya refugees are moderately to highly vulnerable and rely almost entirely on humanitarian assistance. The UN’s scaled-down 2026 response plan seeks $710.5m, 26 percent less than the previous year’s appeal. In April, the World Food Programme reduced support for about two-thirds of refugees under a new tiered system; about 17 percent now receive only $7 per person per month.

Donors applauding the verdict should fund the wait as seriously as they praise the destination. The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, which backed The Gambia’s case, and Gulf donors have a particular responsibility. Western governments should restore cuts, while lenders and donors should support Bangladeshi host communities. Underfunded camps feed trafficking, exploitation and dangerous sea journeys towards Malaysia and Indonesia. A judgement that opens a path home is worth little if the people it was meant for cannot survive the wait.



Reparations now have legal force, not merely moral appeal. Property claims should be documented; land restored where possible; compensation paid where it cannot. Aid says: You are suffering, so we will help you survive. Reparations say: A wrong was done to you, and someone is obliged to repair it.

The verdict is enormous. The test now is simpler: Can the Rohingya go home as citizens, reclaim their land, receive compensation and raise their children somewhere other than a refugee camp?

The court has established the truth. Now justice has to bring it home.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Drone operator removes Man United training footage and issues apology
World.content:
The footage, filmed during new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session, was uploaded online.

A drone operator who filmed Manchester United’s ⁠training session ⁠this week has apologised for what he called a “total error of judgement” and removed the footage from ⁠his YouTube channel.

The footage, filmed at United’s Carrington training ground during new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session on ⁠Thursday, was uploaded online under the username “CC OVERVIEW”.

In a statement posted on his YouTube channel on Friday, the drone operator said that while the flight was legal under drone regulations, filming ‌the session had been “unethical”.

“My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time,” he said.

“I fully accept it was unethical on my part. I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players ⁠for my actions and sincerely hope those ⁠actions do not affect the outcome of any match.”

The operator added that he had wrongly assumed only warm-up activities would be visible and that ⁠the training session would be open to various media outlets.

He also said neither Liverpool ⁠nor any other football club had been ⁠involved in his decision to film at Carrington.

“The video has been removed from my channel,” he said.

Pochettino arrived from the US men’s national team this ‌week after United sacked Michael Carrick, and faces an immediate test with a trip to Liverpool on Sunday.

United are ‌languishing ‌18th in the league table after winning just one of their 10 games. Liverpool are fourth.

World.title: Russia unleashes retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges
World.content:
The attack follows Putin’s pledge of ‘painful’ response to Ukraine’s attack on symbolic Crimean bridge.

Russia launched a barrage of air attacks on Ukraine, killing eight people, as it targeted Kyiv’s bridges and infrastructure across the country.

The attacks overnight on Thursday into Friday hit vital transport bridges spanning the Dnipro River in the capital and knocked out power generation in several parts of Ukraine, officials said.

The missile and drone swarms came shortly after Russia’s President Vladimir Putin threatened retaliation for Ukraine’s targeting of a symbolic bridge linking his country with the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014.

Eight ⁠people – including six in Kyiv – were killed in the overnight attacks, and ⁠28 wounded, ‌Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said in a social media post.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said ballistic missiles had damaged the Podilskyi, Darnitskyi, and Southern bridges, requiring traffic restrictions across the Dnipro.

Buildings, transport and logistics infrastructure were hit in several districts of the city, the Kyiv City Military Administration said in a statement. Citywide electricity disruptions were also reported.

Elsewhere, Ukrainian sources reported that one person was killed as a strike hit a hospital in the Zaporizhia region. Nuclear ⁠power plants across the country were forced to reduce operations, causing outages in Kyiv and 10 regions, First Deputy ‌Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said.

Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on Friday that road and rail bridges in Kyiv used to transport weapons and military equipment to ⁠the battlefield were targeted. It added that its forces hit defence ⁠industry facilities as well as energy and transport infrastructure in several regions of Ukraine.

The large-scale attack came hours after Putin pledged a “painful” response to Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch Bridge earlier this week. The attack severed the key road link across the Kerch Strait.



“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin told reporters on Thursday in China, where he attended a summit with the Chinese and United States presidents. Putin said the roadside of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” and pledged to rebuild it.

Ukraine continued its efforts to target energy and military infrastructure overnight. Russia’s Defence Ministry reported that its forces had intercepted 310 Ukrainian drones.

A Ukrainian drone ⁠attack damaged an ⁠industrial facility in Russia’s western ‌region of Smolensk, Governor Vasily Anokhin said on the ⁠Telegram messaging app, ⁠without identifying ⁠the facility.

The commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned ⁠Systems Forces said on Friday that 40 Russian oil ⁠facilities and defence ⁠industry targets have been hit over the past 50 days.

Moscow-installed officials in occupied eastern Ukraine also reported three people had been killed during an attack.

‘Unacceptable’

The overnight hostilities illustrate the lack of progress in US-led efforts to mediate a ceasefire.

US envoy Jared Kushner said on Thursday that Russia is comfortable with Europe joining the negotiations, and also with the idea of security guarantees for post-war Ukraine that are modelled on NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

Early on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said cooperation between Ukraine, the US and Europe on negotiations is “becoming closer” and that he hoped the US would organise the first multilateral meeting involving the Europeans “as soon as possible”.

Russian ⁠Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said ⁠later that ⁠a visit by three European Union representatives to Russia ‌is “under consideration”.

However, he added that any form of Ukrainian membership of NATO is unacceptable to Moscow.

“[E]ven the notion of a formula for Ukraine’s quasi-membership of NATO, and the search for some sort of – in inverted commas – ‘creative ⁠solution’ in this area, is an option that is ⁠unacceptable to us. We discuss security guarantees first and foremost in terms of ensuring the security of our own country,” Ryabkov was quoted as saying by the Interfax news agency.

“As far as Ukraine is concerned, let ⁠them recognise the irrevocable nature of our demand ⁠that this state must not join NATO. When that happens, I think the issue of security guarantees can be discussed in one way or another,” Ryabkov was quoted as adding.

World.title: Kenya’s growing doping crisis overshadows legacy as athletics powerhouse
World.content:
Since 2017, more than 140 Kenyan athletes have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit, most of them distance runners.

Over decades, Kenya built a legacy of producing elite runners who dominated distance running. The recipe for success was simple: High-altitude training, a whole-foods diet, early nights, consistency.

But a quiet, underhanded addition over the past few years is threatening to tarnish its legacy and the dozens of global accolades that stemmed from it – doping.

The African nation’s latest doping scandal is perhaps the most shocking; Peres Jepchirchir, world and Olympic marathon champion, was handed a three-year ban on Thursday for testing positive for banned blood booster EPO.

The Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said Jepchirchir’s sample was taken before her Sydney Marathon victory in August, where she stormed to her fourth World Marathon Majors win after triumph in New York (2021), Boston (2022), and London (2024). She’s also a former half-marathon world record holder.

Jepchirchir, who admitted to breaching anti-doping rules, is arguably the most prominent and successful in a string of Kenyan athletes who have faced formal doping sanctions over the past decade. Since 2017, more than 140 Kenyan athletes have been suspended by AIU, most of them distance runners.

How has Kenyan athletics ended up at this point and what comes next? Al Jazeera Sport spoke to experts to find out.

Why has there been a rise in doping violations among Kenyan runners?

Rather than seeing it as a rise, the reality is that more athletes are being tested, caught, and publicised for doping violations, former Kenyan middle-distance runner Martin Keino told Al Jazeera.



“Testing has expanded, particularly out-of-competition testing, and the AIU now goes after suspicious patterns instead of waiting for a positive sample,” said Keino, a former pacer who helped set seven world records.

“The problem is real, but the visibility is new.”

What drives athletes to dope?

Financial insecurity, fear of decline in performance, and pressure to deliver are some of the biggest factors, Keino explained.

“Kenya produces a huge number of runners chasing a very small number of life-changing contracts. When one breakthrough can lift a whole family out of poverty, the pull to find an edge gets much stronger.

“Add weak local controls on banned substances, unqualified ‘coaches’ and agents who push for quick results, and doping can spread quietly.”

For Kenyan Olympic champion Wilfred Bungei, men’s 800m champion at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, the rise in doping violations hits closer to home.

Bungei is a relative veteran compared with contemporary Kenyan greats like Eliud Kipchoge, Sebastian Sawe and Faith Kipyegon, who have continued the legacy built by the likes of Martin’s father Kip Keino, one of Kenya’s first Olympic champions in the 1960s. He says doping violations by the likes of Jepchirchir and Ruth Chepngetich jeopardise the legitimacy of future victories while tarnishing the current legacy.

“For decades, Kenya has built its athletics on solid hard work from dedicated athletes. Now, some athletes are choosing the shortest way to make it big in athletics, by cheating,” Bungei said.

“I can only describe it as greed, selfishness and above all just plain stupidity to not understand that it’s not you the doper who is damaged but thousands of Kenyan athletes who built their careers on pure sweat and discipline.”

Caroline Mwanzia, an international sports lawyer practising in anti-doping, safeguarding, and sports governance, had a more straightforward view.

“For some athletes, it is because of intentionally wanting to gain an unfair advantage over other athletes competing,” she said.

“Others may have taken medicinal drugs without first obtaining a Therapeutic Use Exemption [TUE], but most athletes are simply being ignorant.”

Are athletes always at fault for doping violations?

This is where the lines get blurred on whether athletes or their support personnel are responsible for what goes into their bodies. Bungei insists that the responsibility “sits squarely on the athlete”.

“I don’t believe that an athlete with integrity would be encouraged by anyone to do what is wrong,” he said.



Keino held a similar sentiment. “Most elite athletes know the basics: The prohibited list, testing, whereabouts rules, the penalties. You can’t compete at World Marathon Major level and claim total ignorance of the rules.”

But knowing the rules is different from understanding every product, injection, supplement, or “recovery treatment” handed to you, Keino explained.

“Some athletes take things without really understanding the risks, the dosages, the detection windows, or who is supplying them. Others take banned substances knowingly and hide behind ignorance later.”

Per a 2016 investigation, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) found two Kenyan athletes who attempted to escape their sanctions by providing falsified medical records, one of which WADA termed the “culminating peak in an overall strategy of cover-up and concealment by the athlete”.

“That’s why education has to be practical. A seminar where someone reads out the WADA code isn’t enough,” Keino emphasised.

“Athletes need to hear it plainly: Never take an injection or unknown substance without checking it, keep records, ask questions, and walk away from any coach or agent who can’t explain what they’re giving you.”

WADA also concluded in its investigation that “athletes in Kenya are insufficiently educated on doping and/or wilfully blind as to the consequences of doping.”

Why do elite athletes risk doping?

Experience doesn’t make you immune to pressure, fear, or bad decisions, Keino explained.

“Established runners actually carry a different kind of pressure. They have a reputation to protect, a lifestyle to maintain, and people depending on them.

“An injury, a dip in form, or a few poor races can hit contracts, appearance fees, and sponsorship fast.”

Keino went on to explain that for veteran athletes like Jepchirchir and Chepngetich, doping is not to break into the elite circle but to stay on top longer, keep up with younger athletes, or bounce back from a setback.

“None of that excuses it – at that level, nobody can credibly say they don’t know what EPO is, how it works, or why it’s banned.”

Should Kenya be sanctioned by global bodies?

“Back in 2009 when a few doping cases had been reported, I advocated for the criminalisation of doping and people thought I was too harsh. Almost 20 years later, Kenya’s image is on the line,” said Bungei, who still believes the government should make doping a criminal offence in Kenya.

In September, Kenya signed the Anti-Doping Amendment Bill 2026 to align with WADA’s updated code, a decade after it was first signed into law after WADA declared Kenya non-compliant with global anti-doping rules and regulations.

“Better options [than sanctions] are stronger audits of Kenya’s anti-doping system, funding for testing and education, bans for repeat enablers, and conditions attached to hosting major events,” Keino said.

“Nairobi’s award of the 2029 World Athletics Championships should come with real accountability, not just prestige.”

World.title: Pakistan minister visits India for first time since 2025 war
World.content:
Islamabad and New Delhi insist the visit is strictly multilateral, despite hopes it could open a channel for contact.

Share Pakistan minister visits India for first time since 2025 war on social media

Islamabad, Pakistan — Pakistan’s climate change minister, Musadik Malik, arrived in New Delhi on Friday, becoming the first Pakistani federal minister to visit India since the neighbours fought a four-day war in May 2025.

Malik is attending the first Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, a three-day gathering that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is due to inaugurate on Friday evening. Malik is expected to address the forum on Saturday.

No bilateral meeting has been announced. Pakistan’s Foreign Office said on Thursday that its participation was “reflective of its contribution as an active SCO member State to promote dialogue, cooperation and understanding in line with ‘Shanghai Spirit’”.

It is the first such visit since then-Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari travelled to Goa in May 2023.

Both governments have framed these exchanges as routine SCO business.

With Pakistan due to host the bloc’s leaders next August, the question is how far contact confined to a multilateral forum can go — and whether this could set the stage for Modi to travel to Islamabad for the summit.

The choice of minister

Indian media, quoting diplomatic sources, reported that India’s invitation was for Pakistan’s minister for national heritage and culture, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi.

Neither government has confirmed this.

Pakistan’s Foreign Office said on November 6 only that it had received an invitation and would decide after consultations. Islamabad has not said why it sent Malik.



The Foreign Office said Malik would “share Pakistan’s perspective on the salience of dialogue among civilisations” and meet SCO member states on the sidelines.

Jauhar Saleem, president of the Islamabad-based Institute of Regional Studies (IRS) and a former foreign secretary, said the choice was Pakistan’s to make.

“There is no hard and fast rule about who represents a country at such fora, and it is the prerogative of the invited state to nominate the representative it considers most appropriate,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Civilisation is not only about heritage and culture; it is about how societies relate to their land, their rivers, and one another,” Saleem added.

Khurram Dastgir Khan, a former federal minister for foreign affairs and defence and senior leader of the governing Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), said the choice was deliberate.

Sending a minister of its own choosing “lets Pakistan take part as an SCO member without being seen to buy into India’s framing or showcase,” he told Al Jazeera.

He said it also signalled Pakistan’s aim “to be seen as a constructive host for the 2027 summit; thereby nudging the door open an inch for PM Modi’s participation”.

Pakistan took over the SCO’s rotating chairmanship on September 1 and will host the leaders’ summit in Islamabad in August 2027, the month both countries mark 80 years of independence.

New Delhi’s position

New Delhi has sought to keep the visit within a narrow SCO frame.

At an October 28 briefing, foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India had invited “all SCO members” “as per established practice”, along with dialogue partners and one observer.

Asked whether New Delhi was reviewing its Pakistan policy ahead of upcoming multilateral engagements, he said: “Post the Pahalgam attack, we have a Pakistan policy. That Pakistan policy remains in place; there has been no change.”

India blames Pakistan for the April 2025 attack in Pahalgam, in Indian-administered Kashmir, in which gunmen killed 26 civilians, setting the stage for the war that followed. Islamabad denies any involvement.

Sharat Sabharwal, India’s high commissioner to Pakistan from 2009 to 2013, said the invitation followed from India’s role as host.

“This is a meeting in the SCO framework, where India, as the organiser, has to invite all member countries. Therefore, at this juncture, there is no reason to look for any deeper meaning in this visit,” he told Al Jazeera.



Modi proposed the forum at last year’s SCO summit in Tianjin, China.

Irfan Nooruddin, a professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, said the initiative gave New Delhi a narrative of its own.

“If anything, it will be spun as further indication of India’s leading role in the region and its magnanimity in terms of including Pakistan in the dialogues,” he told Al Jazeera.

Rezaul Hasan Laskar, foreign affairs editor at The Hindustan Times newspaper in New Delhi, said there was little appetite at home for anything more.

“The government has maintained this is a multilateral engagement under the SCO framework, and that there will be no bilateral engagements with Pakistan till the issue of terrorism is addressed,” he told Al Jazeera. “There doesn’t appear to be widespread public backing for a fresh approach towards Pakistan.”

The SCO has been one of the few forums bringing the two countries together since they joined in 2017.

Bhutto-Zardari’s visit to Goa ended in public sparring. In his speech, he warned against “weaponising terrorism for diplomatic point scoring”, without naming India.

Jaishankar later described him to reporters as a “promoter, justifier and spokesperson of a terrorism industry”. The two did not hold a separate bilateral meeting.

Jaishankar’s subsequent visit to Islamabad in October 2024, for an SCO heads of government meeting, passed more quietly, with pleasantries but no talks.

In September this year, Alok Dimri, India’s SCO coordinator, spent three days in Islamabad and shook hands with Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar. He described the visit to reporters as “an annual rotational ritual of the SCO”.

Dastgir said such contact had done little to change the course of relations.

“The Indian External Affairs Minister’s October 2024 trip to Islamabad for SCO proved a dead-end, despite the hoopla. It did not prevent open hostilities in May 2025,” he said.

Salman Bashir, a former Pakistani high commissioner to India, was blunter. “SCO is an opportunity to maintain a semblance of civility. Don’t think that it is a pathway to normalcy,” he told Al Jazeera.

Frozen ties

Beyond the SCO calendar, nearly every bilateral link remains frozen.

India has held the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty “in abeyance” since the Pahalgam attack.

On August 31, a court of arbitration in The Hague ruled that India could not suspend the treaty unilaterally. New Delhi rejected the court’s jurisdiction.

In September, Indian and Pakistani naval vessels collided in the Arabian Sea, prompting India to summon Pakistan’s chargé d’affaires in protest. Neither country has had a high commissioner in the other’s capital since 2019.

Contact has continued below the official level.



Laskar pointed to “several Track 1.5 and Track 2 engagements right from a few months after the conflict in May last year,” referring to semi-official and unofficial meetings only partly involving government representation.

The road to Islamabad

Pakistan’s chairmanship will bring a series of tests before next August.

At its summit in Bishkek, the SCO named Lahore its tourism and cultural capital for 2026-27. During his visit, Dimri said he hoped to see the city.

The biggest test will be the leaders’ summit itself. Indian officials have told local media that New Delhi will decide its level of representation closer to the date.

Laskar said a breakthrough was hard to predict, but such a visit “could be the pathway to opening all sorts of possibilities”.

Dastgir said SCO meetings “can provide the pretext for bilateral communication, however rudimentary. Sidelines encounters need no announcement and no concession.”

Nooruddin did not rule out a visit by Modi.

“If there’s a single leader in India’s context who could do that, and get away with it, it is he. A sort of Nixon goes to China, if you would,” he said.

“But, again, so much will happen between now and next August that prognosticating so far into the future is pretty pointless. Let’s just say that it’s entirely possible that Modi goes but I wouldn’t bet on it.”

World.title: Russia’s day-long attack on Kyiv damages embassies
World.content:
NewsFeed Russia’s day-long attack on Kyiv damages embassies

Russia carried out a day-long aerial attack on Kyiv, damaging key bridges, European embassies, and a historic cathedral. Al Jazeera’s crew witnessed the barrage overhead.

World.title: El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term after constitution change
World.content:
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has officially launched a re-election campaign that critics say illustrates his bid to make El Salvador a one-party state.

Supporters gathered outside the Supreme Electoral Tribunal on Thursday as Bukele arrived to register his candidacy for the February elections.

The populist is widely expected to win the race thanks to the huge political support earned by his crackdown on El Salvador’s violent cartels.

However, the launch of the campaign comes after his party Nuevas Ideas used its supermajority in the country’s congress to remove term limits on the presidency and extend the length of terms from five to six years.

Critics accuse the president of consolidating power by removing checks and balances. The Bertelsmann Transformation Index and others accuse Bukele of creating a de facto one-party state.

The 45-year-old has made uprooting El Salvador’s cartels a core part of his presidency and political persona.

“In El Salvador there is total, complete open democracy,” Bukele told the crowd on Thursday. “We’re sending a message to the world that El Salvador will never return to the past.”

He has now begun exporting the model. Last month, he sent about 2,500 soldiers to Haiti after four Salvadoran members of a United Nations-backed force went missing. The deployment has been welcomed by gang-wracked Port-au-Prince.

However, many analysts question Bukele’s motives, accusing him of exploiting the crisis on the island nation to enhance his reputation.



“Bukele is running for a third consecutive term after packing the court, rewriting the constitution to his liking and jailing or forcing into exile those who dare criticise him,” Juan Pappier of Human Rights Watch said, according to The Associated Press news agency.

“The absolute concentration of power in his hands has been the defining feature of his administration.”

Last year, Nuevas Ideas used its supermajority in Congress to abolish second-round votes and bring forward national elections by two years, to February 2027.

World.title: US robbery suspects charged over alleged $22M train heist spree
World.content:
NewsFeed US robbery suspects charged over alleged $22M train heist spree

A suspected robbery crew who filmed themselves on an alleged $22M dollar spree breaking into trains is facing charges in the United States. Prosecutors say the stolen goods included millions of dollars worth of Nike sneakers and electronics.

World.title: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
World.content:
Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.

The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.

The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.

A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.

"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.

"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."

Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.

The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.

World.title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis
World.content:
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

World.title: Three Kyiv bridges hit during major Russian missile attack
World.content:
Russia has targeted bridges in Kyiv and killed eight during one of the largest air attacks of the war so far, days after Ukraine inflicted heavy damage on the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Two people were killed in Russian strikes on a railway station in the western city of Lviv.

Ballistic missiles hit three bridges over the Dnipro River, vital routes which people in Kyiv rely on to move around the city, with six deaths confirmed in the capital.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for Ukraine's strike on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.

The three Kyiv bridges targeted overnight - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - have been closed to traffic, adding to disruption created by retaliatory strikes on bridges earlier this week.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary".

World.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
World.content:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (Â£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

World.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
World.content:
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

World.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
World.content:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders â Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron â were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

World.title: Nigeria moves to end jail terms for attempted suicide
World.content:
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for those who survive.

The proposal seeks to shift Nigeria's approach from criminal punishment to treatment and rehabilitation.

It follows years of calls for reform from mental health professionals. A separate bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide has already passed its second reading in the Senate.

Under Nigeria's law, attempted suicide is a criminal offence with those convicted facing up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both.

The Senate bill also seeks to replace criminal penalties for attempted suicide with medical treatment, rehabilitation and support.

It was sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.

He also warned that families might conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma.

He stressed that the bill is not aimed at legalising or encouraging suicide attempts but rather protecting the survivors.

Tinubu's proposal has been welcomed by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who had previously suggested that people who survived suicide attempts should be sent to prison.

"We are saying that suicide is a crime for now. Therefore, if you attempt it, we will send you to prison," Akpabio had said.

However, after receiving the Tinubu's proposal, he sought to clarify his earlier remarks, saying they did not apply to people experiencing mental health conditions.

He added that punishing people whose actions were influenced by mental health conditions would be insensitive.

Tinubu's letter follows sustained calls from mental health professionals for the law to be changed.

At a parliamentary public hearing in May 2024, the then president of the Association of Psychiatrists of Nigeria, Professor Taiwo Obindo, urged lawmakers to remove criminal penalties for attempted suicide.

"Why do we, as a nation, then punish individuals who are ill and need medical attention rather than prosecution?" he asked.

Drawing on his experience as a psychiatrist, Obindo said most people who die by suicide have a history of mental illness.

Akpabio has referred the president's amendment bill to the relevant senate committee for further consideration.

Nigeria is among several African countries where attempted suicide remains a criminal offence.

Ghana decriminalised attempted suicide in 2023, while Kenya's High Court ruled in January 2025 that the law criminalising it was unconstitutional.

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

World.title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
World.content:
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.

The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.

In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.

Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".

Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.

In the same post, the president announced he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.

While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".

He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".

Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.

World.title: Arravo Team-2 wins FirstBank charity golf challenge
World.content:
Arravo Team-2 has won the 2026 FirstBank Corporate Golf Challenge for Charity, finishing top of the competition at the golf section of Ikoyi Club 1938, Lagos.

The quartet of Lynda Obieze, Sheun Olagoke, Ufuoma Oghoje and Uche Ubakanma recorded 95 stableford points to claim the title at the corporate competition, which formed part of activities marking the 65th FirstBank Lagos Amateur Open Golf Championship.

The team defeated defending champions Mactay Team-2, who finished with 78 points, to secure the title.

Arravo Group Chief Executive Officer, Ayo Adegboye, expressed delight at the victory and thanked FirstBank for sustaining the initiative, which brings corporate organisations together to raise funds for charity.

He said Arravo’s participation was driven by its commitment to social impact and its shared values with the bank, adding that the company had supported the competition for three years and would return for the next edition.

“We support FirstBank Lagos Open because we share in the values for which FirstBank is noted for. 65-years of unbroken sponsorship is no mean feat. “We congratulate [FirstBank] and promise to be back next year,” Mr Adegboye said.

He said the company’s involvement in the event also reflected its belief in charitable causes, describing giving back to society as an expression of faith.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“For me, the work of charity is also a work of faith, if you ask me. And if I have to go by my faith and my belief, it’s something I strongly believe in. So it’s something I’ll do over and over again,” he said.

Other finishers

Team Ration, comprising Olawale Olabintan, Adeola Banjoko, Olaide Okubanjo and Ademola Osindero, finished third with 78 points after losing to Mactay Team-2 on countback.

Mactay Team-1 came next with 78 points, also losing on countback, while Team FirstBank, represented by Tolulope Olugbemi, Olutayo Aderinto, Ibrahim Bello and Adeniran Oladele, finished fifth with 77 points.

Arravo Team-1 finished sixth, while JAGZ Nation placed seventh.

Meanwhile, Ismail Omamegbe, FirstBank’s Acting Group Head of Marketing and Corporate Communications, pledged the bank’s continued support for initiatives that positively impact lives.

The Corporate Golf Challenge for Charity is part of the 65th FirstBank Lagos Amateur Open Golf Championship, which runs from 16 to 22 November at Ikoyi Club 1938. The annual competition brings corporate organisations together for golf and charitable fundraising, and FirstBank pledged continued support for initiatives that benefit communities.

World.title: COP31: ‘Africa is not a laboratory’, campaigner warns over marine geoengineering
World.content:
Africa must not become a testing ground for geoengineering, a climate campaigner has warned, calling for fishing communities to have a say in decisions about ocean-based climate projects.

Kwami Kpondzo, who co-coordinates the Africa Working Group of the Hands Off Mother Earth (HOME) Alliance, gave the warning on the sidelines of the UN climate summit COP31 in Antalya, Turkey.

He said coastal communities must not be excluded from decisions on technologies that could affect their waters and livelihoods.

“Africa is not a lab; it is not a laboratory for geoengineering,” Mr Kpondzo told PREMIUM TIMES on Wednesday.

His warning comes as researchers study whether South Africa’s Saldanha Bay could host a trial of marine carbon dioxide removal and as delegates at COP31 disagree over the technology.

The first draft of the summit’s main decision, released on Monday, contains wording on carbon dioxide removal in general. Climate groups at the summit protested against marine geoengineering, PREMIUM TIMES reported.

Wording of that kind in the decision text would support more research into the methods, which Mr Kpondzo said was the wrong use of money.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the money should rather go to measures that improve conditions in affected communities.

“We want that money to be put for real solutions that communities are pushing for,” he said.

How marine carbon removal works

Marine carbon dioxide removal covers methods meant to make the ocean absorb and hold more carbon dioxide, such as adding alkaline materials to seawater or adding iron to grow phytoplankton, tiny organisms that take up carbon dioxide.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) says carbon removal is required to reach net zero but cannot substitute for deep emissions cuts. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) lists many uncertainties about the ocean-based methods effectiveness, cost and effects on people and ecosystems.

Mr Kpondzo said fishers in the Gulf of Guinea could face pollution, fewer fish and limits on where they can work, although he did not cite damage from any existing project.

He said coastal communities are told they will earn money from selling carbon but need to know the risks first.

“Awareness raising is very important for coastal communities this time around,” he said.

Researchers are studying Saldanha Bay, in South Africa’s Western Cape province, as a possible site for a pilot that would add alkaline material to seawater.

Caitlin Wale, the engineer whose company runs the project, said in an interview in October that a pilot would go ahead only after laboratory studies and contained experiments confirmed it was appropriate.

Sustained push against geoengineering

HOME Alliance says it will continue to collaborate with its 200 member network across over 45 countries to push back geoengineering efforts in Africa, especially through capacity building and sustained advocacy.

Mr Kpondzo said their “Don’t Geoengineer Africa” campaign is training community groups, civil society organisations and students in Ghana, Uganda, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Togo and Nigeria, where the Health of Mother Earth Foundation (HOMEF) leads the work.

The group is also advocating against solar radiation modification technologies, which aims to cool the planet by reflecting sunlight. African environment ministers rejected it in 2023 and in July 2025, saying it has no actual role in addressing climate change.

Mr Kpondzo also called for the removal of carbon markets from the climate talks, adding that emissions should be cut where they are produced.

“The only way to cut the emissions is to do it at the source, not from the technologies and not from the financialisation of nature,” he said.

World.title: Lampard delivers Onyeka’s injury update ahead of Crystal Palace clash
World.content:
Coventry City manager Frank Lampard has revealed that Super Eagles midfielder Frank Onyeka has returned to training but remains a doubt for Saturday’s Premier League meeting with Crystal Palace at the CBS Arena.

The Nigerian international suffered an injury setback shortly before the November international break, ruling him out of Nigeria’s double-header against Tanzania in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers.

Onyeka also missed Coventry City’s last two league fixtures against Sunderland and Everton, leaving Lampard without the midfielder during a crucial period of the campaign.

However, the 47-year-old has offered some encouragement ahead of the weekend encounter, confirming that the former Brentford player has resumed training with the squad.

Speaking during his pre-match press conference, Lampard remained cautious about the midfielder’s availability, suggesting that a final decision would depend on his fitness.

“He trained today so we’ll see,” the Coventry manager said when asked about Onyeka’s condition.

Onyeka battles to regain fitness after injury setback

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The midfielder’s return to training represents a positive development for Coventry, who will be keen to have his energy, physical presence and defensive qualities back in their midfield.

Onyeka initially joined the Sky Blues on loan from Brentford during the winter transfer window last season and quickly became an important figure in their push for promotion to the Premier League.

His contributions during the promotion campaign convinced the club to activate the purchase clause in his agreement, making his transfer permanent ahead of the current season.

The 28-year-old has since featured in eight matches across all competitions for Coventry, establishing himself as one of the options available to Lampard in midfield.

READ ALSO: GWFA to train walking football referees in Lagos

Coventry seek return to winning ways

Lampard will be hoping to welcome Onyeka back into contention as Coventry prepare to face Crystal Palace following the international break.

The Sky Blues will be looking to rediscover their winning form after their recent league outings against Sunderland and Everton, with Saturday’s fixture presenting another opportunity to strengthen their position in the Premier League.

However, with Onyeka only just returning to training, the Coventry manager must decide whether the Nigerian is ready to feature or requires additional time to regain full match fitness.

His availability will be a welcome boost for Lampard, particularly as Coventry look to get their campaign back on track.

World.title: COP31: Expert calls for united African front in climate negotiations
World.content:
An African development expert has warned that competing national interests and inadequate coordination among African countries could weaken the continent’s influence in global climate negotiations, particularly its push for climate finance and a fair transition away from fossil fuels.

Hannington Owegi, secretary-general of the Participatory Ecological Land Use Management (PELUM) Association Regional Secretariat, said African countries were struggling to translate their shared climate concerns into a sufficiently coordinated negotiating position.

In an interview with PREMIUM TIMES at the ongoing 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, Mr Owegi said differences in countries’ economic and energy priorities should not prevent them from identifying common interests and negotiating collectively.

“We tend to think that African diversity is a weakness. It is not. But within the African continent, we are fragmented. The negotiations are fragmented. We don’t seem to be agreeing,” he said.

He added that civil society organisations advocating climate action were also fragmented, making it difficult to build the collective pressure needed to influence negotiations.

Competing interests

African countries have repeatedly called for a just and equitable energy transition that recognises their development needs, including access to affordable electricity, industrialisation, employment and poverty reduction.

However, the continent’s energy and economic circumstances vary considerably.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Countries such as Nigeria, Angola and Mozambique have significant oil and gas interests, while others have different levels of dependence on fossil fuels and varying capacities to develop renewable energy.

For countries with substantial petroleum resources, moving away from fossil fuels raises questions about government revenue, foreign investment, employment and the future of their energy industries.

At the same time, many African countries face limited electricity access, high energy costs and inadequate infrastructure, making the choice of energy pathways a major development concern.

These differences complicate discussions about how quickly countries should move away from fossil fuels and what support they would require to do so.

Mr Owegi said competing priorities were weakening Africa’s negotiating strength, but noted that countries could still agree on common demands even where their national circumstances differed.

“Different priorities should not break us, but rather unite us,” he said.

He identified climate finance, agricultural production and productivity as areas around which African countries could develop a common negotiating strategy.

Mr Owegi, however, said he could not speak specifically to the motivations or negotiating priorities of individual oil-producing countries because his organisation did not work directly in those countries.

Instead, he suggested that regional economic communities should play a stronger role in helping countries coordinate their interests before international negotiations.

He said countries could first agree on shared priorities within their respective regional blocs and use those positions to develop a stronger continental approach.

Africa’s common negotiating demands

Despite the differences in national circumstances, African countries have an established negotiating structure through the African Group of Negotiators (AGN), which coordinates the continent’s positions in United Nations climate negotiations.

Ahead of COP31, the group developed an action matrix outlining priorities and responsibilities across areas including adaptation, climate finance, agriculture and just transition.

The group’s priorities reflect the continent’s longstanding argument that its development needs must be considered in global climate decisions, particularly because it contributes relatively little to greenhouse gas emissions but faces significant consequences from rising temperatures.

According to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA), the continent contributes less than four per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions but faces some of the heaviest climate impacts.

The commission estimates that Africa needs about $277 billion annually to implement its climate plans, but only about 11 per cent of that amount is currently met. It also says that just $3 to $4 out of every $100 in global climate finance reaches the continent.

These funding gaps have made climate finance one of Africa’s most important negotiating priorities.

At COP31, the AGN has continued to call for adequate, predictable and accessible funding, particularly grant-based and highly concessional finance, to support adaptation and the implementation of countries’ climate commitments.

On 18 November, the group’s chair, Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, reiterated that climate finance, adaptation and a fair, adequately financed just transition remained central to Africa’s negotiating demands.

The group has also argued that transition pathways must reflect the different development circumstances of African countries and should not compromise their legitimate aspirations for energy access and industrialisation.

However, Mr Owegi believes that agreeing on common priorities is only part of the challenge; African countries must also coordinate their approaches well enough to influence the outcome of negotiations.

Beyond fossil fuels

Mr Owegi also said Africa should approach the energy transition as a broader development process rather than a discussion focused exclusively on replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy.

He added that the transition should include changes in agricultural production, food systems and infrastructure, particularly because these sectors are closely connected to livelihoods and economic development across the continent.

“Energy transition should not be looked at from one pillar of fossil fuel,” he said.

He argued that treating energy, agriculture and infrastructure as separate issues could undermine efforts to achieve a transition that addresses the needs of African communities.

For him, a fair transition should consider how countries can improve agricultural productivity, expand access to electricity, develop infrastructure and create economic opportunities while responding to climate change.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has identified energy access, investment in clean energy infrastructure and the development of local energy industries as important considerations for Africa’s transition.

Mr Owegi said African countries should continue pressing for a just transition but move beyond repeated discussions towards concrete agreements and implementation.

He noted that the concept had featured in international climate discussions for decades, yet countries were still struggling to agree on how to translate it into action.

World.title: GWFA to train walking football referees in Lagos
World.content:
The Global Walking Football Alliance (GWFA) will hold a referee training workshop on Saturday in Lagos as the sport continues to expand its reach in Nigeria.

The workshop, scheduled for 21 November at the Eagle Club, Surulere, will be led by international referee and GWFA instructor, Ricky Weir, as organisers seek to improve officiating standards and develop more qualified referees for the growing sport.

The one-day programme will combine classroom instruction with practical sessions, including match observation, examination and individual officiating assessments.

According to the organisers, participants will begin with a classroom session on pre-match preparation and the Laws of the Game before observing four league matches officiated by international match officials.

Each match will be followed by a question-and-answer session, allowing trainees to examine refereeing decisions and discuss relevant interpretations of the rules.

After a break, participants will return for another classroom session on post-match review of the Laws of the Game before taking a theory examination.

The workshop will conclude with individual practical assessments, after which results will be announced and certificates presented to successful participants.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Walking football gains ground

The training comes amid growing interest in walking football, locally known as Waka Football, with the sport expanding beyond Lagos to other parts of Nigeria.

What began in Lagos with four teams has developed into the fourth season of the Lagos Walking Football League, which now attracts men’s, women’s and corporate participation.

READ ALSO: Mbah salutes Rangers on winning 9th Nigeria Premier Football League title

The Eagle Club pitch in Surulere has also emerged as a major hub for the sport in the country.

Beyond Lagos, walking football has spread to Abuja, Kano and Plateau State, which organisers identify as the fourth state to embrace the sport.

The increasing participation has heightened the need for trained officials capable of ensuring consistent application of the rules and maintaining standards as more teams and competitions emerge.

The GWFA workshop is expected to contribute to that process by equipping prospective referees with the theoretical knowledge and practical experience required to officiate walking football matches.

World.title: Simon Kolawole chronicles intrigues of 2023 presidential election in new book
World.content:
The much-anticipated book on the 2023 presidential election by Simon Kolawole, journalist and founder of TheCable newspaper, will go on sale on Monday, 23 November.

The book, titled, ‘Winning Formula: The Inside Story of Nigeria’s 2023 Presidential Election’, is an authoritative account of the controversial election “enriched by insider briefings, court filings and polling data, and told with the pace of a newsroom and the eye of a data analyst, according to Cable Books, the publishers.

“This is the definitive account of how Bola Tinubu outmanoeuvred Muhammadu Buhari, how Atiku Abubakar and Nyesom Wike destroyed each other’s presidential ambition, how Peter Obi and the Obidient movement became a phenomenon — and how the winning formula that decided it all was hiding in plain sight,” Simon Kolawole said.

In the 296-page book, Mr Kolawole explains the voting patterns that have determined every winner of the presidential election since 1999, the story behind the Muslim-Muslim ticket, and how Professor Yemi Osinbajo, Mr Buhari’s vice-president, lost out in the power game.

“This is a story of naivety, cat-and-mouse games, cold calculations — and subterfuge,” Simon Kolawole added.

The 2023 presidential election was the most contested and the most controversial in a generation: four candidates polling over a million votes each, a technology glitch that froze the country in real time—and a thrilling court battle that generated global headlines as three candidates lay claim to victory.

At the heart of ‘Winning Formula’, distributed nationwide by Rovingheights bookstore, is a fascinating argument: in the Fourth Republic, no candidate has reached the presidency without building a competitive coalition across at least two of Nigeria’s three largest voting blocs — the Hausa-Fulani, the Igbo and the Yoruba — as well as adding decisive support from a minority geopolitical zone.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Part political history, part electoral arithmetic and part behind-the-scenes narrative, ‘Winning Formula’ explains not only how the 2023 election was won, but why Nigeria’s deepest divisions can also compel the alliances that decide its presidency.

World.title: 2027 Politics Watch: From Atiku’s INEC audit demand to APGA’s Tinubu endorsement
World.content:
Atiku Abubakar, whose presidential nomination under the African Democratic Congress (ADC) was invalidated by a 5 November Federal High Court judgement that the party is appealing, asked the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) on Thursday to allow outside experts to examine its proposed checks on polling-unit results.

The request came ahead of a nationwide mock accreditation exercise scheduled for 28 November.

In Awka, Anambra State Governor Chukwuma Soludo handed the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA) flag to Vice-President Kashim Shettima, who received it on President Bola Tinubu’s behalf. The ceremony, at a joint APGA–APC rally, reaffirmed APGA’s support for the APC presidential ticket.

It came a day before Peter Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate, was due to hold a town hall in Onitsha, and amid a dispute over a billboard featuring Mr Obi.

Atiku asks who can clear a flagged result

In a statement reported by Nigerian Tribune, Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of Mr Atiku’s campaign council, said the former vice-president had written to the INEC chairman on behalf of the ADC and allied stakeholders.

Mr Atiku requested an independent audit of technology he described as artificial intelligence and intelligent document processing, which he said INEC planned to introduce into its result-verification process.

He wants independent cybersecurity experts, party technology representatives and civil society technologists to examine the system’s source code, training data and decision logs before the 28 November exercise.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He also asked INEC to publish the procedure for handling flagged result sheets, including who reviews discrepancies, how decisions are recorded, how parties are notified and how errors can be challenged.

He wants the commission to reaffirm the legal status of the physical Form EC8A and explain how conflicts between paper records and automated assessments would be resolved.

INEC has described part of its proposed process. Its ICT director, Lawrence Bayode, said presiding officers would use the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) to photograph the completed Form EC8A and then enter the figures electronically. The system would compare the two records and flag discrepancies before results are uploaded to the INEC Result Viewing portal (IReV).

Mr Bayode acknowledged that unclear handwriting could be misread, in which case the presiding officer could proceed after checking the flagged discrepancy.

The paper form, he said, remains the official polling-unit record. PREMIUM TIMES reported Mr Bayode’s explanation, which did not describe the proposed result checks as artificial intelligence.

Whether every proposed feature will be used during the 28 November mock exercise has not been established. INEC says the exercise will test accreditation and electronic result transmission across the country.

The ADC campaign council separately asked INEC on Wednesday to postpone the exercise, citing a letter that gave political parties until 18 November to submit the names of their agents. INEC’s response to Mr Atiku’s audit request could not be independently confirmed in the reporting reviewed.

Rival ADC camp asks INEC to remove candidates

INEC faced a separate demand from the ADC faction aligned with Nafiu Bala Gombe.

In a Thursday statement reported by Blueprint, Rufus Ikanmi, chairman of the faction’s Board of Trustees, urged the commission to enforce the 5 November Federal High Court judgement delivered by Justice Peter Lifu.

He demanded the removal of David Mark and Rauf Aregbesola from INEC’s leadership records and the delisting of candidates submitted under their executive. Mr Ikanmi maintained that the judgement remained binding because it had not been stayed, varied or set aside by a superior court.

The judgement invalidated the Mark-led leadership and decisions taken under it, including the process that produced Atiku’s presidential nomination.

The Mark-led ADC has appealed on 17 grounds. It also applied for a stay of execution at the Federal High Court and sought an injunction from the Court of Appeal preventing INEC from altering the party’s leadership and candidate records.

The stay application had not been heard as of 7 November. No order granting either application had been independently verified. PREMIUM TIMES reported the 17-ground appeal and the request to restrain INEC.

Mr Gombe also informed INEC on 16 November that he had resumed duty as national chairman.

INEC National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna told journalists on 7 November that the commission would study the certified true copy of the judgement before taking a position. He said INEC would obey any subsequent court order granting a stay or injunction.

The two camps are pressing INEC in opposite directions: one wants the trial court’s orders implemented, while the other wants the existing records preserved.

APGA hands over flag as Anambra explains billboard removal

The flag handover took place at the “SoluTinubu 2027” rally, held under the banner of “Progressives Working Together”.

It reaffirmed an earlier decision rather than creating a new alliance. Mr Soludo announced APGA’s adoption of Mr Tinubu in May 2025, during the president’s visit to Awka.

At APGA’s campaign launch on 6 November, he repeated that the party would field no presidential candidate and set a target of securing at least half of Anambra’s presidential votes for the incumbent.

The arrangement allows APGA to contest other seats under its own banner while supporting Mr Tinubu for president.

The rally coincided with controversy over a billboard carrying images of Mr Obi and Senator Victor Umeh, the NDC candidate for Anambra Central Senatorial District.

The state government confirmed removing the billboard but denied that the decision was politically motivated.

Information Commissioner Law Mefor said in a Thursday statement that Mr Umeh had paid his own signage fee but Mr Obi had not made the separate payment required.

Mr Mefor cited the Anambra State Signage Act, 2010, and said the same requirements would apply to candidates from other parties. The government explained its position in a statement on the billboard’s removal.

The state’s signage agency announced in May that presidential candidates would pay ₦50 million and senatorial candidates ₦20 million for campaign permits.

The government’s explanation did not identify the specific provision requiring a separate payment when two candidates share a billboard for which one has already paid. Whether the same requirement has been applied to comparable APC or APGA s also remains unclear.

Reports of violence at APC’s Kaduna flag-off as stadium dispute continues

Kaduna Governor Uba Sani led the state APC’s campaign flag-off at Ranchers Bees Stadium on Thursday, inaugurating its campaign council and presenting flags to candidates.

However, The Sun reported that men armed with cutlasses, knives and clubs stormed the stadium during the inauguration, hurled chairs, chased participants and smashed journalists’ equipment, citing eyewitnesses.

No police statement confirming the incident or casualty figure was identified in the sources reviewed.

The APC’s Kaduna campaign director-general, Ben Kure, described the flag-off as successful and said the party was prepared for a peaceful, issue-based campaign, according to Nigerian Tribune.

The venue was already in dispute. The ADC said it sought to use the stadium on 17 and 18 November, ahead of the APC’s 19 November event. It said a letter dated 12 November from the state Ministry of Local Government declined its request because the stadium was undergoing repairs.

ADC National Publicity Secretary Bolaji Abdullahi called that explanation ridiculous, noting that the APC had held its presidential campaign flag-off at the same stadium on 24 October.

The Kaduna State Government denied preventing the ADC from using the facility. Commissioner for Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs Sadiq Mamman Lagos said the government had issued no such directive.

Governor Sani’s press secretary, Ibraheem Musa, said the stadium was open to all political parties following a formal application.

He maintained that damage from the 24 October rally had been repaired within three days, according to Blueprint’s report on the government’s response.

On Tuesday, the Senate urged governors to stop denying opposition parties access to public facilities and called for action against candidates linked to electoral violence.

Reports differed on the scope of its recommendation to INEC. One Vanguard report said senators wanted candidates disqualified where their supporters were found responsible for instigating or participating in violence.

Another account described the proposed disqualification as applying to candidates found responsible through court convictions. The Senate’s resolution text was not available for verification.

The Arewa Consultative Forum (ACF) separately warned against emerging political violence, urged restraint and called on President Tinubu and state governors to treat political opponents fairly and provide unhindered access to public facilities.

Court throws out challenge to Bello’s Kogi ticket

At the Federal High Court in Abuja, Justice Inyang Ekwo ruled against Momoh Obaro, who had asked to be declared the winner of the APC’s 18 May senatorial primary in Kogi Central and recognised as the candidate instead of former Kogi Governor Yahaya Bello.

The judge held that Mr Obaro had not exhausted the party’s internal dispute-resolution process.

He also found that the primary election result sheets relied upon by Mr Obaro lacked signatures from the chairman and secretary of the committee that conducted the exercise.

The ruling, reported by PREMIUM TIMES, leaves Mr Bello’s nomination undisturbed in that suit.

A day earlier, Justice Ekwo ruled in favour of former Governor Gabriel Suswam in a separate APC nomination dispute in Benue North-East, affirming him as the winner of the primary and declaring unlawful his replacement by Senator Emmanuel Udende.

The court accepted results showing Mr Suswam received 131,083 votes against Mr Udende’s 1,364, according to PREMIUM TIMES’ report on the Benue judgement.

Presidency sets December milestone for CNG buses

The federal government signed an agreement with Chinese manufacturer Yutong in Lagos on Thursday for the supply and local assembly of compressed natural gas buses, according to The Eagle.

The arrangement falls under the Presidential Initiative on Compressed Natural Gas and Electric Vehicles and supports the National Affordable CNG Transit Programme.

Under the agreement announced by the Presidency, Yutong is expected to supply an initial 300 buses, with the first 100 due in Lagos by the end of December. Subsequent vehicles are planned for local assembly by YP Automobiles Bus Assembly at the former Leyland plant in Ibadan, Oyo State.

The Presidency put the intended fare reduction at approximately 40 per cent on participating routes, linking the initiative to Mr Tinubu’s 2027–2031 agenda.

That remains a government target, not a measured reduction in transport costs.

The government’s first deadline is the promised arrival of 100 buses in December. Whether commuters benefit will depend on where the vehicles operate, how fares are set and whether the projected reduction reaches passengers.

World.title: Tinubu celebrates Jonathan at 69
World.content:
​President Bola Tinubu has congratulated former President Goodluck Ebele Jonathan on his 69th birthday on 20 November.

​The president celebrated Mr Jonathan’s distinguished leadership and enduring contributions to Nigeria’s democratic development.

​President Tinubu described the former president as a patriot and statesman whose commitment to national unity, democratic governance, and Nigeria’s peaceful advancement remains an important part of the country’s political history.

​The president acknowledged the former leader’s years of dedicated service to the nation—first as deputy governor and governor of Bayelsa State, then as vice president, and ultimately as president and commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.
