World.title: ‎INEC releases 86,931 new PVCs for collection in Kogi
World.content:
FILE IMAGE

‎By Boluwaji Obahopo, Lokoja

‎‎The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) in Kogi State has announced the availability of 86,931 Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) for residents who participated in the second phase of the Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) exercise.

‎The State Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC) Dr. Shehu Wahab, made this known in a press statement made available to newsmen in Lokoja on Friday.

‎According to the commission, the second phase of the CVR exercise was conducted between January 5 and April 17, 2026.

‎‎INEC said, “The 86,931 PVCs produced for eligible registrants have been delivered to our offices across the 21 Local Government Areas of the state and are now ready for collection.”

‎‎The commission advised registrants to visit the INEC office in the Local Government Area where they completed their registration to collect their cards.

‎‎It said registrants are expected to come with their registration slips or printouts, or a valid means of identification where required.

‎‎INEC also clarified that PVCs from the first phase of the registration exercise are still available for collection.

‎‎”PVCs would not be issued through proxies, registrants must personally collect their cards. Collection is available at INEC LGA offices from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., Monday to Friday.”

‎The commission further directed registrants to check the status of their PVCs and locate their collection centres through its CVR portal, cvr.inecnigeria.org.

‎‎INEC urged all voters who participated in the second phase of the CVR exercise to collect their PVCs without delay, noting that the cards are essential for participation in future elections.

‎‎The commission said timely collection would help ensure that no eligible voter is disenfranchised.

‎‎Wahab expressed appreciation to registrants for their patience during the production, verification and distribution processes, assuring that the commission remained committed to ensuring that every eligible voter obtains a PVC and is able to exercise their democratic right.

World.title: ADC, NDC, PDP, others halt campaigns, sign common agreement Nov 30
World.content:
By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA: Member parties of the Coalition for Democracy, among them the African Democratic Congress ADC, the Nigeria Democratic Congress NDC and a faction of the Peoples Democratic Party PDP among others will suspend campaign activities nationwide on Monday, 30th November 2026, to attend the second summit of the coalition.

The decision was announced in a statement issued on Friday and signed by Salihu Moh. Lukman on behalf of the coalition parties.

According to him, concerned parties will sign a common agreement ahead of the January 16 presidential elections.

The summit had been scheduled for Monday, 23rd November 2026, but Linkman said member parties asked that it be rescheduled because their candidates and campaign teams are now deep into demanding programmes across the country.

“It is more important that every party, every presidential candidate and every national chairman is in the room than that the Summit holds on its original date,” the committee said.

The committee said the new date was agreed in consultation with key stakeholders to secure the widest possible participation. To make that commitment real, all member parties agreed to suspend campaign activities nationwide on the day, so that their leadership can attend in full.

“Parties competing hard for votes are prepared to stand down their campaigns for a day, together, because the defence of Nigeria’s democratic space is bigger than any one campaign,” it said.

According to the statement, the summit will finalise and sign the coalition’s common agreement and set the course for the work ahead of the 16 January 2027 elections.

The committee thanked member parties, delegates and partners for their understanding and regretted any inconvenience caused by the change. It said venue and accreditation details remain as communicated.

The coalition emerged from the G100 Opposition Summit held in Abuja on 31 August 2026. It is a multiparty platform pioneered by the ADC, the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), the NDC, the PDP, the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and the Social Democratic Party (SDP).

The statement said it was established to give practical expression to the resolutions of that summit, and is committed to defending Nigeria’s constitutional democracy, protecting political pluralism, and ensuring free, fair, credible and competitive elections.

It described the coalition as a framework for opposition parties to coordinate their efforts, safeguard democratic institutions, uphold the rule of law, and protect the fundamental rights of Nigerians to freely choose their leaders.

“We will walk into that room united, and walk out of it committed,” the committee said.

World.title: 2030: FG takes decisive action to end open defecation with Executive Order
World.content:
By Gabriel Ewepu

ABUJA – IN a renewed commitment, the Federal Government has unveiled a new Executive Order to accelerate Nigeria’s drive towards ending open defecation by 2030.

The unveiling of the Open Defecation Free Nigeria by 2030 and Other Related Matters Order, 2025 coincided with the commemoration of World Toilet Day and the seventh anniversary of the Clean Nigeria campaign in Abuja on Thursday.

Vice President Kashim Shettima, represented by the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Delivery and Coordination in the Office of the Vice President, Akubo Adegbe, described the Executive Order as a decisive step towards translating government commitments into measurable sanitation outcomes.

Shettima said the order marks a transition from fragmented interventions to stronger coordination, measurable results and sustainable national progress.

He called on state and local governments to strengthen accountability, increase sanitation financing and sustain community-led behavioural change

He disclosed that since the launch of the Clean Nigeria campaign in 2019, 185 of the country’s 774 local government areas have attained Open Defecation Free (ODF) status, while Jigawa and Katsina remain the only states certified as ODF nationwide.

While acknowledging the progress recorded, the Vice President warned that the country still had considerable ground to cover, urging states yet to achieve ODF status to establish monthly and quarterly targets and make their progress publicly available.

He also cautioned against a reversal of gains in communities already certified as open defecation-free, stressing the need for sustained monitoring and accountability to protect existing achievements.

According to him, Nigeria must prioritise sustainable financing, reliable data, stronger institutions, effective implementation and continuous behavioural change to achieve the 2030 target.

He also called on state and local governments to take ownership of the campaign by allocating adequate resources and strengthening sanitation institutions, while urging development partners, the private sector, traditional rulers, community leaders and civil society organisations to sustain their support.

Shettima, who chairs the Steering Committee of the Clean Nigeria Project, reaffirmed the Federal Government’s commitment to working with subnational governments, noting that the National Economic Council would also be deployed to advance and sustain the national sanitation agenda.

Linking the campaign to this year’s World Toilet Day theme, “Sanitation and Gender Equality,” the Vice President highlighted the disproportionate burden poor sanitation places on women and girls.

He noted that inadequate access to safe and private sanitation facilities undermines their health, security, dignity, education and participation in economic and social activities.

He called for inclusive policies and investments that address the sanitation needs of women, girls, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable populations.

Meanwhile, the Minister of Water Resources and Sanitation, Engr Joseph Utsev, in his speech said the Clean Nigeria campaign had evolved beyond public awareness and mobilisation into a national platform for policy coordination, institutional engagement, community participation and performance monitoring.

Utsev highlighted the revised Clean Nigeria Strategy 2025–2030, which is structured around six strategic pillars, as well as the newly introduced Clean Nigeria Real Time Monitoring and Information System designed to improve data management, track implementation and strengthen accountability.

Reflecting on the campaign’s seven-year journey, the minister identified five critical lessons, including the need to translate political commitment into adequate financing and practical action, prevent communities from relapsing into open defecation, strengthen community ownership, adopt a multi-sectoral approach and ensure that reliable data informs planning and resource allocation.

The Minister of Youth Development, Ayodele Olawande, said the ministry was contributing to the campaign through youth mobilisation and community advocacy, disclosing that more than 1,000 youth volunteers had been trained to promote sanitation awareness and behavioural change.

He said pilot interventions were ongoing in Bauchi, Kaduna, Benue, Ebonyi and Oyo states, adding that young people also had an important role to play in promoting gender-responsive sanitation.

Olawande specifically emphasised menstrual hygiene education, access to safe and private toilet facilities and the need to eliminate the stigma associated with menstruation.

Goodwill messages were also delivered by the former Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, Didi Esther Walson-Jack, alongside representatives of civil society organisations, professional bodies and development partners, who reaffirmed the importance of collective action in achieving Nigeria’s 2030 open defecation elimination target.

World.title: Good night Olufemi Ajasa, you were more than a friend
World.content:
Femi Ajasa

By Taiwo George

During the launch of the Converged Digital Newsroom of Media Trust Group, Alhaji Mohammed Idris, Minister of information and National Orientation, shared a personal story. While tracing the success story of the company, the Minister who was Special Guest at the occasion, narrated an encounter he had with Malam Kabir Yusuf, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Media Trust Group.

According to him, several decades ago, he and Media Trust Chairman had a sit-down session in Kaduna and Malam Yusuf told him about his dream of owning a successful media outfit, while he, the Minister, told Malam Kabiru of his own dream to be a Public Relations merchant. If there is anyone whom I shared my dream in this profession with, it was Olufemi. But because tomorrow is not promised to anyone, I unlike the Minister, would not have the opportunity to ever watch my late brother and colleague relieve a similar encounter in future. Kabi o osi!

Femi and I shared many things in common. We attended same institution, though while he was at the Communication School of the Lagos State University (LASU) in Anthony, I was at the main campus in Ojo. We got admitted the same year and graduated same year.

Our marital journey also has striking similarities. His wife and mine are both Mass Communicators. Our spouses were first colleagues before signing lifetime contract. While Femi met his wife at Uni, I met mine during the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) programme. At death, Femi was the Online Editor of Vanguard, I’m currently the Online Editor of Daily Trust. Both of us are not just proud sons of Lagos, but we share ancestral ties.

This is why it’s still quite difficult to come to terms with his sudden demise. A man of few words. He moved on whenever he made his point. Femi was never the one who would bore you with a conversation. Each time we spoke on phone, he went straight to the point. The few times the conversation dragged I said let me quickly make this final point, he would respond, “Oya na!”, and follow up with, “Take care!” whenever I summarized my point. Something unusual happened on the eve of his death. We usually compared notes on so many issues, particularly work. I came across an information which had to do with his workplace and forwarded same message to him via WhatsApp but it didn’t deliver. An online Editor being offline during that period?

I assumed he was in a place where network was bad, and would respond when he read the message until Monday morning when Victor Ogunyinka, our mutual friend, broke the news to me. I screamed and my wife who was coincidentally sleeping on the same couch Femi and his family sat when they attended the parlour party during my son’s third-year birthday, woke up. I told her what happened and she regained consciousness immediately. We went over a few memories with Femi and said prayers for the wife and kids he left behind.

Where do I start sharing the memories from? I remember when I was to relocate from Lagos to Abuja, Femi heard the news before I shared with him. Having moved to the capital city years before I did, I sought his advice on a number of issues, especially accommodation. He didn’t like the choice I eventually made but I convinced him. Weeks later when he hosted a get together for me and a few colleagues, he joked that I got there far behind schedule because of the distance but I protested saying it was because of work and we all laughed it over. On a journalists’ WhatsApp Forum where a link on his obituary was dropped, a colleague wrote, “What a fine man! God rest his soul.”

Talking about good looks, it’s common for people to command attraction in the early years of their youth but in the case of Femi, the charm improved as he aged. During the get together he organised for me upon relocation to Abuja, I almost didn’t recognize him. So cute and charming, I was like ’Abuja working well for you bro’, and he laughed asking which Ábuja? To prove that, he still didn’t lose his charm when Vanguard job took him back to Lagos.

Femi touched so many lives. He was always on the lookout for opportunities to make life better for colleagues. When he clocked 40 four years ago, one of his mentees told me we needed to find a way to celebrate him. He came up with the idea of surprise package which clicked and quickly we got Funsho, his wife, into the picture. Because the mentee was in Lagos, I was the one who coordinated things after which he got in touch with Funsho who the package was delivered to and she kept it till he returned from work. The next morning, Femi called, “Taiwoooooo!! You ehn! Thanks man! Thanks man.” The conversation ended.

Femi was a caring father who was involved in the lives of his children. As they made their way into the living room during the birthday, he watched them unlace their shoes and guided them to where they kept them. They also had chit chats that ended with smiles during the party. Not every father has such time in a busy era like this. Femi was a man who would praise you when the need arose and knock you if that’s what he felt you deserved. At a retreat organised three years ago, my boss asked me to get someone to review our brand, it was Femi who came through and he gave the team very practical and useful insights.

After the 2023 election, Femi called me saying, “Taiwooooo, superb coverage! You guys really tried. I followed the fantastic job your team did. Daily Trust was number two in terms of coverage.” To him a brand whose name I won’t deliberately mention (not Vanguard) was number one and he gave his reasons. Other times, Femi would argue Vanguard’s dominance of the digital terrain and irrespective of my point, he would say emphatically, ‘Vanguard is number one!” When my platform was the talk of town over a controversial story, Femi called and asked, “Taiwo, what did you guys do there? You want to set this country on fire? Take time o!”

The undeniable truth is that Femi loved his job and did it with passion. He gave his best to it and touched lives in the process. Every job has its challenges, but the aspect of the profession my late brother and I find ourselves in is no doubt demanding. It’s not a stroll in the park to manage the digital arm of a thriving newspaper. A decision taken within split seconds could ruin the brand’s hard-earned trust and you would be worse for it. The job is so jealous that at times, we cast headlines in the dream. I’ve lost the number of times an unexpected, unplanned activity disrupted a schedule planned for weeks or months.

As Online Editor, you have to stay alert to guide your team and ensure things go smoothly. A colleague shared a video of Femi with his laptop beside him on the hospital bed and I connected with that immediately. I’ve travelled that route before. I remember when I was trapped in the hospital for days but still couldn’t let go of my laptop. My older son fell ill so the mother rushed him to hospital and I joined them after work. As of the time I got there, my younger son had also started showing symptoms. The matron advised that he should be taken away immediately to prevent the situation from getting worse. The responsibility of taking care of him fell on me but as my wife walked out with my younger son, I signalled her to wait outside. I needed something from the car, my laptop.

Back to Femi, in that video, he said he was on drip and needed to rest before for a few hours before getting back to work. We’ve lost many colleagues recently. In August, it was Otunba Dotun Oladipo, who collapsed at work and gave up in the hospital. In September, it was Felix Onigbinde who also slipped into coma while on duty. Death is an inevitability for all mortals, that we know; but what about these untimely deaths? I think it’s high time we found a way to sort out work-life balance. Many questions racing through my mind over my friend’s demise.

Was it substandard treatment? Did he ignore warning signs? Was he too busy to take care of his health? Does this have spiritual undertone? What happened to Femi? We can’t question God. I never imagined not having Femi around in the next 30 years but such is life: here today, gone tomorrow. I’ve been following the drama trailing the death of gospel singer Olayemi Bayonle, better known as Toluwanisings, not knowing that death was lurking around the corner. Sleep well, my friend and brother. Ki Oluwa te e si afefe rere. Ishe owo re oni baje o. Your son will tell your story someday, good night.

World.title: The weekend reset that makes your new week easier
World.content:
By Josephine Agbonkhese

There is something about the weekend that makes us realise just how much we have been carrying throughout the week. After days of juggling work, family responsibilities and other commitments, the weekend offers an opportunity to slow down, catch our breath and put a few things in order.

Beyond sleeping in, watching our favourite shows or catching up with friends, the weekend is also a good time to prepare for the days ahead. A few simple activities can make the transition into a new week less stressful and more manageable.

Tidy up your space

You do not need an elaborate cleaning exercise. Start with the areas you use most. Clear the kitchen counter, arrange the living room, put away scattered clothes and organise your workspace. A tidy environment can make it easier to concentrate and settle into your daily activities. It also feels good to start Monday without a pile of unfinished chores staring back at you.

Plan your outfits ahead

Save yourself the morning rush by deciding what to wear before the week begins. Check your calendar, consider your appointments and put together outfits that suit your activities. Iron your clothes, arrange your shoes and accessories, and ensure everything is ready. If you have children, preparing their school uniforms can also save valuable time. It is an opportunity to rediscover pieces in your wardrobe and experiment with new combinations.

Prepare a few meals

After a long day at work, deciding what to cook can become another chore. A little meal preparation over the weekend can help. Wash and portion vegetables, prepare a stew or soup, cook basic ingredients or simply plan your meals for the week. You do not have to prepare everything in advance. Knowing what you intend to eat can save time, reduce food waste and discourage expensive last-minute purchases.

Take a break from your screen

If your weekdays involve computers, messages and endless social media scrolling, use part of the weekend to disconnect. Put your phone aside for a few hours. Read a book, take a walk, spend time with family or enjoy a quiet moment without feeling the need to document it online. Constant notifications can make it difficult to switch off mentally. Spending some time away from screens allows you to be more present and enjoy other activities.

Review your finances

A weekend reset is a good opportunity to review your spending. Check your account balance, look through recent transactions and consider the expenses coming up during the week. Set aside money for transportation, groceries, school needs and other commitments. A simple spending plan can help prevent unnecessary financial pressure. It is not about denying yourself life’s pleasures but about knowing what you have and how best to manage it.

Make time for yourself

Between work, family and social obligations, personal time can easily become an afterthought. Dedicate part of your weekend to something you genuinely enjoy. Visit a favourite restaurant, get your hair or nails done, exercise, listen to music, watch a movie or catch up with a friend. You could also spend an afternoon doing absolutely nothing. Remember, rest is not a reward you must earn after completing every task. It is essential to maintaining your well-being.

Write down your priorities for the week

Before Monday arrives, take a few minutes to think about what you need to accomplish. Write down your important tasks, appointments and deadlines. Identify the three things that deserve your attention first. Having a written plan gives you a clearer sense of direction and makes it easier to approach your responsibilities one step at a time. It also helps you distinguish between what is urgent and what can wait.

Get enough sleep

Proper rest is perhaps the most underrated part of a weekend reset. Staying up late to squeeze in another movie or finish unfinished chores can leave you struggling on Monday morning. Maintain a regular bedtime, reduce late-night screen time and create a comfortable sleeping environment.

World.title: Three children orphaned in acid horror
World.content:
*Three Lives Left in the Shadows of Domestic Violence and Sickle Cell Struggles, after murder and suicide

By Adeola Badru

For three children in Akufo, Ido Local Government Area of Oyo State, life has become a painful journey into uncertainty. In one devastating episode, they lost both parents—the two people they should have been able to depend on for love, protection, education and survival.

Their tragedy is particularly heartbreaking because two of the surviving children reportedly battle recurrent sickle cell crises, requiring regular medication and medical attention. At a time when they need parental care more than ever, they have, instead, been left to confront grief, illness, financial hardship and an uncertain future.

Their story is not merely about the death of two parents. It is about a family reportedly torn apart by years of domestic violence, a marriage allegedly marked by repeated abuse and three innocent children left to bear the consequences of circumstances beyond their control.

The incident reportedly followed years of domestic violence. The husband, identified as 49-year-old Mr Lekan Adedeji, allegedly poured acid on his wife, 44-year-old, before ingesting the same corrosive substance. Both subsequently died.

The couple had been married for more than 25 years, but what should have been a lifetime of companionship was, according to the woman’s family, characterised by repeated physical abuse and disagreements over childbearing, even after the health implications of their genetic compatibility became known.

Speaking with Vanguard, Morufat Ashake, the deceased woman’s younger sister, who has taken custody of the children, recounted the painful circumstances surrounding the marriage and the events preceding the fatal attack.

She explained that the couple were unaware of their genotype status when they married. It was only after their first three children began experiencing recurrent illnesses that they discovered the medical implications of their genetic compatibility.

According to Ashake, Zainab eventually gave birth to six children, three of whom died from complications associated with sickle cell disorder.

The surviving children are Rashida Adedeji, 20, who is SS; Folawe Adedeji, 17, who is AS; and Folahanmi Adedeji, six, who is also AS. Rashida and the youngest child reportedly experience recurrent health crises and require consistent medical attention.

But the family’s medical challenges were not the only difficulties Zainab allegedly endured. Ashake said her sister suffered years of physical abuse from her husband, who reportedly continued insisting on having more children despite knowing the potential health implications.

Eventually, Zainab reportedly found the courage to leave the matrimonial home, hoping to escape the violence. She had been away for about three months before the incident.

Although members of the family had previously intervened and persuaded her to return, Ashake said her sister had reached a point where she could no longer endure the situation.

Sadly, the decision that should have marked the beginning of a safer chapter in Zainab’s life did not prevent the tragedy that followed.

A school fees invitation that ended in horror

Ashake traced the circumstances surrounding the fatal encounter to December last year, when Lekan allegedly contacted his estranged wife under the pretext of giving her money for their second daughter’s West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE) fees.

Believing the invitation concerned their daughter’s education, Zainab reportedly visited the house with Folawe and her youngest son, Folahanmi.

According to her account, Lekan instructed Folawe to take her younger brother outside. The teenager remained in the compound, sweeping, when she suddenly heard her mother’s screams coming from inside the house.

Alarmed, she attempted to open the door but was allegedly prevented from entering by her father.

She alleged that Lekan subsequently poured acid over Zainab’s body and attempted to force her to drink the corrosive substance.

Ashake further disclosed that before ingesting the substance, Lekan allegedly handed his mobile phone and the money intended for the children’s school fees to another person.

Both victims required urgent medical attention. Despite efforts to save Zainab’s life, she eventually succumbed to her injuries on January 23. The family reportedly spent more than N4 million attempting to secure treatment for her.

For the children, the incident meant losing their mother in particularly traumatic circumstances and subsequently being left without their father.

An ageing grandmother, three children and an uncertain future

Their maternal grandmother, 62-year-old Titilayo Ayoola, corroborated Ashake’s account, describing her daughter’s marriage as one marked by years of suffering.

Ayoola now faces the enormous responsibility of caring for three grandchildren who have lost both parents, including two who reportedly require regular medical attention.

At an age when she should ordinarily be enjoying some rest, she must now worry about medication, hospital bills, school fees and the emotional wellbeing of children struggling to comprehend their loss.

Her concern reflects the difficult reality confronting the family. Love and determination may provide emotional support, but the children also need sustained financial assistance, medical care, educational support and psychological counselling.

For Rashida, the eldest, the pain is compounded by uncertainty about what lies ahead.

Folawe, 17, who reportedly witnessed the events preceding her mother’s death, also described the family’s predicament.

Her experience is particularly distressing. At an age when she should be concentrating on her education and dreams, she is having to process a traumatic experience involving the violent loss of her mother.

Their youngest sibling, six-year-old Folahanmi, must also grow up without the daily presence of either parent.

The family previously lived in a four-bedroom flat built by Lekan in Akufo. However, the house that once accommodated the family has become associated with the violent incident that brought their marriage to a tragic end.

A tragedy that demands society’s attention

Beyond the immediate grief of the Adedeji family, the incident raises troubling questions about domestic violence and the protection available to victims seeking to escape abusive relationships.

Marriage should never become a prison in which one partner lives in perpetual fear of the other. Neither should leaving an abusive relationship expose a victim to further danger.

The family’s account also underscores the importance of genotype awareness, responsible family planning and access to proper medical counselling.

For the three surviving children, however, these lessons come amid a reality far more painful than any public discussion can capture.

They need help to continue their education, manage their medical conditions and recover from the emotional trauma of losing both parents.

Their grandmother and maternal aunt have assumed responsibility, but they cannot shoulder the burden alone.

Perhaps the cruelest dimension of this tragedy is that three children who had no control over their parents’ decisions, disagreements or relationship must now live with the consequences.

A mother is gone. A father is gone. Three children remain, carrying grief, medical challenges and questions that may never have satisfactory answers.

They did not choose the home into which they were born. They did not choose the circumstances that shaped their childhood. And they certainly did not choose to become orphans.

Yet, they must now find the strength to survive, heal, remain healthy and dream again.

For them, the tragedy is not over. It has only entered another chapter—one in which society must decide whether to look away or extend a helping hand.

Vanguard News

World.title: Nigeria, Russia move to ease trade, strengthen customs cooperation
World.content:
By Providence Ayanfeoluwa

The Nigeria Customs Service, NCS and Federal Customs Service of Russia have signed a cooperation agreement aimed at strengthening bilateral trade facilitation, intelligence sharing and customs enforcement, while exploring mutual recognition of their Authorised Economic Operator, AEO programmes.

The service in a statement said the Agreement on Cooperation and Mutual Assistance in Customs Matters, CMAA provides a framework for collaboration in customs procedures, information exchange, financial integrity, border security and personnel capacity development.

Speaking, Comptroller-General of Customs, Adewale Adeniyi, who led the Nigerian delegation, described the agreement as a strategic instrument for safeguarding economic integrity, securing supply chains and strengthening trade governance.

He explained that the signing followed months of technical consultations, legal reviews and constructive engagements between both administrations.

Adeniyi explained that the NCS had accelerated its digital transformation through the adoption of electronic systems for customs declarations, payments and submission of supporting documents. According to him, the reforms demonstrate that revenue generation and trade facilitation can complement each other, in line with the World Customs Organisation’s SAFE Framework of Standards.

On the implementation of the agreement, the Customs boss identified cooperation between the two countries’ AEO programmes as a major priority.

He said both administrations would exchange experiences on their respective frameworks and operational procedures, with the long-term objective of achieving mutual recognition to facilitate the movement of cargo and reward compliant traders.

The two sides also explored arrangements for exchanging customs statistics and trade data to improve analysis of bilateral trade flows.

Adeniyi disclosed that Nigeria was participating in the World Customs Organisation’s data initiative. Russia’s Head of Customs, Valery Pikalyov, explained that his administration was authorised to collect and exchange customs statistics derived from declarations. Pikalyov expressed readiness to explore a dedicated data-sharing arrangement with Nigeria.

The agreement also provides for cooperation against customs offences, illicit financial flows, grey-market importations, tax evasion, counterfeit goods, narcotics and other prohibited or hazardous materials. It further establishes a framework for direct operational assistance, personnel training and the exchange of professional expertise between the two administrations.

World.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, November 20, 2026
World.content:
The Nigerian naira continued to face downward pressure against the United States dollar across both the official Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) and the parallel market on Friday, November 20, 2026, driven by tightening foreign exchange supply and rising end-of-year seasonal demand.

Official Market Performance

Real-time interbank spot tracking at the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market placed the US dollar at ₦1,352.54 during early morning trading on Friday, following an opening rate of ₦1,351.86 and an intraday peak of ₦1,355.31.

This early session trading follows Thursday’s official Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) volume-weighted benchmark, which saw the naira depreciate to a four-month low. According to official CBN data for the November 19 trading session, the NFEM weighted average rate settled at ₦1,376.58 per dollar, while the indicative closing rate rose to ₦1,388.00 per dollar from ₦1,379.99 recorded on Wednesday. Intraday interbank transactions on Thursday were conducted between a low of ₦1,370.00 and a high of ₦1,397.00 per dollar. Despite the depreciation, market liquidity improved significantly, with NFEM interbank turnover surging by 59.13 percent to $800.31 million across 184 deals, up from $502.88 million the previous day.

Parallel Market Rates

In the parallel market, commonly referred to as the black market, the local currency weakened further as Bureau de Change (BDC) operators and street dealers in Lagos and Abuja quoted the US dollar at a selling rate of up to ₦1,468 per dollar on Friday morning, following Thursday’s close between ₦1,461 and ₦1,468. Buying rates among informal currency dealers hovered between ₦1,445 and ₦1,458 depending on transaction volume and location.

With Thursday’s official closing benchmark at ₦1,388.00 and parallel market quotations reaching ₦1,468.00, the spread between the official and unofficial windows widened to ₦80.00 per dollar, compared to ₦70.01 recorded earlier in the week.

Market Drivers and Reserve Outlook

Since the end of October, when the naira closed at ₦1,346.00 in the official window and ₦1,373.00 in the parallel market, the currency has lost ₦42.00 and ₦95.00 in the respective segments. Meanwhile, Nigeria’s gross external reserves stood at $54.71 billion as of November 18, 2026, reflecting a moderation of $554 million from the October 27 peak of $55.26 billion.

Financial analysts note that the recent divergence between both windows is largely fueled by heightened festive import demand, corporate obligations, and reduced autonomous foreign exchange inflows rather than a structural depletion of the country’s external reserves.

World.title: Kano APC Crisis: Chieftain Seeks Tinubu, Yari’s Intervention
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

. Warns divisions could undermine party’s electoral chances

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

A chieftain of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Kano State, Aminu Shehu Sharada, has appealed to President Bola Tinubu and the Director-General of the party’s Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, to urgently intervene in the growing divisions within the state chapter ahead of the 2027 general election.

Sharada warned that the internal disagreements among party leaders and stakeholders could undermine the APC’s electoral prospects if left unresolved, urging the party’s national leadership to initiate immediate reconciliation efforts.

In a personally signed statement issued yesterday, titled, ‘Time for Unity, Dialogue and Responsible Leadership’, the APC chieftain cautioned against attempts to present a misleading picture of unity within the Kano chapter, insisting that the party was facing disagreements that required urgent attention.

“Anyone giving the impression that everything is fine within the Kano APC is not giving Mr President the full picture.

“There are disagreements and visible concerns among party leaders and stakeholders, and if they are not addressed early, they could have wider consequences for the party,” he said.

Sharada stressed that the immediate responsibility of all APC stakeholders in Kano was to build a united political platform capable of securing victory across all elective positions in the 2027 general election.

He listed the presidential, governorship, senatorial, House of Representatives and State House of Assembly elections as critical contests the party must approach with a common purpose and collective commitment.

According to him, the prevailing disagreements and confrontations within the party were unnecessary and could weaken its ability to mobilise supporters and effectively challenge its political opponents.

“This is not the time to take sides or deepen existing divisions. It is time for consultation, reconciliation and genuine political engagement because there is no justification for the continued disagreements, confrontations and arguments within our party in Kano State,” he stated.

He argued that the political challenges confronting the party were greater than the personal interests of individual leaders and stakeholders, adding that collective action remained the only sustainable path to restoring confidence and strengthening the APC’s electoral machinery in the state.

“The challenges before us are bigger than individual interests, and the only way forward is for our leaders and stakeholders to come together and resolve their differences in the interest of the party,” he said.

Against this backdrop, Sharada specifically appealed to Tinubu and Yari to give the situation in Kano special attention and facilitate a reconciliation process capable of addressing the grievances of aggrieved stakeholders.

“It is against this background that I am making a sincere and urgent appeal to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, His Excellency Abdulaziz Yari, to pay particular attention to the situation within the Kano State chapter of our party and facilitate a timely intervention,” he added.

The APC chieftain maintained that the party had a broad base of committed members and influential stakeholders whose political contributions would be essential to its success in 2027.

He, however, noted that harnessing the strength of the party’s membership would require purposeful leadership capable of bringing contending interests together, listening to genuine grievances and establishing a common political direction.

Sharada emphasised that dialogue, mutual understanding and responsible leadership should take precedence over personal rivalries, warning implicitly that allowing internal disagreements to persist could jeopardise the party’s collective ambitions in Kano.

World.title: PalmPay Takes Fraud Prevention Campaign to Lagos Streets, Warns Residents Against Financial Scams
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Residents of Lagos were engaged on common financial fraud tactics and ways to protect their banking information as PalmPay held its annual fraud awareness walk in the state to mark International Fraud Awareness Week.

The walk, in its third consecutive year, brought together representatives of the financial services sector and other stakeholders to educate the public on emerging fraud schemes and the importance of safeguarding personal financial information.

During the exercise, participants engaged residents on common methods used by fraudsters, including impersonation, phishing and attempts to obtain sensitive banking details such as one-time passwords (OTPs), personal identification numbers (PINs) and account passwords.

The initiative follows previous editions of the walk, including last year’s outing in Kano, as part of efforts to take fraud prevention education directly to communities.

Speaking during the exercise, Olorunfemi Hanson, Head of Marketing and Communications at PalmPay, said public education remained an important part of addressing financial fraud.

“Fraud tactics continue to evolve, making it important for consumers to understand how these schemes work and the steps they can take to protect themselves. Taking awareness directly to communities provides an opportunity to engage people, address misconceptions and reinforce basic security practices. Tackling financial fraud also requires collaboration among financial institutions, regulators, industry stakeholders and consumers,” he said.
