Addressing Parliament during the 2026 State of the Nation Address on Wednesday, Ruto said his administration had prioritised lowering the cost of essential goods and services while increasing earnings across key sectors of the economy.

“Our economic proposition was simple: Reduce the cost for families and increase the income from what they do,” he said.

On food prices, the President cited the government’s fertiliser subsidy programme, which has reduced the price of a 50-kilogramme bag of fertiliser from Sh7,500 in 2022 to Sh2,000 this year.

He said the government had distributed 38.5 million bags of subsidised fertiliser to farmers, contributing to an increase in maize production from 44.3 million bags in 2022 to 71 million bags last year.

Consequently, maize imports declined from 9.9 million bags to 3.3 million bags, while the average price of a two-kilogramme packet of sifted maize flour dropped from a high of Sh230 in September 2022 to Sh152 in September this year.

Ruto also highlighted gains in the tea, coffee, dairy and sugar industries, saying government interventions had helped improve production and increase farmers' earnings.

He said the Cherry Advance Revolving Fund had disbursed Sh15.07 billion to 684,000 coffee farmers, while tea export earnings increased from Sh163 billion in 2022 to Sh187 billion in 2025.

In the dairy sector, milk production rose from 4.5 billion litres to 5.52 billion litres, while average earnings for farmers increased from Sh32 to Sh60 per litre last month.

Sugar production, he added, increased by 60 per cent between January and October, with cane crushing rising by 57 per cent. The industry is projected to produce more than 900,000 tonnes by the end of the year, with Sh1.2 billion in bonuses expected to be paid to sugarcane farmers.

On healthcare, Ruto said the Social Health Authority (SHA) was designed to ease the financial burden of medical expenses on households through a shared health financing system.

In education, he said the government had employed 100,000 teachers and was preparing to recruit an additional 20,000 to address staffing shortages and reduce the burden on parents who pay teachers hired through Boards of Management.

He added that 23,000 classrooms had been constructed, while 1,600 laboratories were being built and equipped.

The President said the annual education allocation had increased from Sh521 billion in the 2022/23 financial year to Sh784 billion in the current financial year.

"These investments improve the quality of education while progressively reducing the need for Kenyans to finance education," he said.

On affordable housing, Ruto said more than 313,000 homes were at different stages of construction across the 47 counties, with over 1.37 million Kenyans registered on the Boma Yangu platform and more than 18,000 homes already allocated.

He said households could work towards homeownership through monthly payments starting at Sh4,000, which he argued would help ease the burden of rent.

The housing programme, according to the President, had also generated more than 1.1 million employment opportunities and reserved orders worth over Sh61 billion for Jua Kali artisans.

On employment, Ruto said 350,000 Kenyans had secured jobs through the digital economy programme, while another 707,000 had obtained employment abroad through international labour mobility initiatives.

He also cited the Hustler Fund, saying more than seven million Kenyans had established credit records through the programme, with cumulative borrowing reaching Sh94 billion.

Under the NYOTA programme, more than 133,000 young entrepreneurs had received training, mentorship and Sh50,000 each in start-up capital, he said.

The President further announced proposed tax measures aimed at increasing disposable incomes, including exempting workers earning Sh32,333 or less per month from Pay As You Earn (PAYE).

Other proposals include scrapping stamp duty on land transactions valued at Sh1 million or less and removing the 25 per cent import duty on mobile phones.

On pending bills, Ruto said the government had approved the settlement of 28,726 verified claims amounting to Sh27.8 billion, covering debts of Sh50 million and below dating back to 2005.

He added that Sh18 billion owed to public universities and another Sh16 billion owed to public and private hospitals under the former National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) had been approved for payment and were undergoing Treasury processing.

“These are not isolated interventions, but parts of one comprehensive undertaking,” Ruto said.

He maintained that the government's economic strategy was anchored on reducing household expenditure, increasing incomes and expanding opportunities for Kenyans.

World.title: After 22 years of waiting, woman welcomes quadruplet boys
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Samuel Langat speaks to journalists outside St Clare's Kaplong Mission hospital in Sotik Subcounty, Bomet county after his wife Lily Langat gave to quadruplets at the hospital. [Kiprono Kurgat, Standard]

After 22 years of waiting to become a mother, a woman has welcomed quadruplet boys in a rare and joyful birth that has brought immense happiness to her family.

Lily Langat delivered the quadruplets through a Caesarean section at St Clare’s Kaplong Mission Hospital in Sotik Sub-County on November 14, 2026.

The four boys arrived after more than two decades of waiting for a child in what the family described as a double blessing.

The 43-year-old mother could not hide her joy, saying the arrival of the four babies was an answer to years of prayer.

“I am very grateful to God for giving me four babies at once. This is a great blessing to my family. I thank the hospital staff for ensuring I got to see these bundles of joy,” she said.

“I have been praying and waiting upon God to give me double for the trouble. I have been childless for a long time, and God could not have given me a better gift than this,” she added.

She said she had been looking forward to the moment after doctors informed her early in the pregnancy that she could be carrying quadruplets.

Hospital staff celebrated the successful delivery, describing it as a rare occurrence at the facility.

A nurse who spoke with The Standard said the mother and her four newborns were in stable condition.

“We were delighted to deliver the babies. The mother faced some difficulties because of the combined weight of the four babies, but both she and the newborns are now stable,” she said.

The nurse said the babies had been placed in the nursery for observation and were doing well.

“This is a rare case in this hospital. We have had twins before, but this is different. None of the babies has developed complications so far, and we expect them to be discharged once they are fully stable,” she said.

She added that the mother was also recovering well and was expected to be discharged once doctors were satisfied with the condition of the newborns.

Lily's husband, Samuel Langat, appealed to well-wishers to support the family as they prepare to raise the four children.

“Raising four babies at once is no easy task. I am calling on well-wishers to lend a helping hand as we begin this extraordinary journey,” he said.

“Our four precious miracles have arrived safely, and while our hearts are overflowing with gratitude, the reality of caring for four newborns at once has brought challenges,” he added.

Naturally conceived quadruplets are extremely rare, although the likelihood varies depending on several factors, including maternal age and fertility treatment.

The birth marks a remarkable new beginning for the Langat family after 22 years of waiting for a child.

World.title: TSC picks Cheptumo Ayabei as new Chief Executive Officer
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Teachers Service Commission headquarters in Nairobi. [File, Standard]

The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) has picked Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer, making him the first person with a disability to head the commission.

Ayabei emerged top in interviews conducted on Monday, beating four other candidates, including the commission’s acting chief executive, Dr Evaleen Jesang Mitei, to become the country’s top teachers’ employer.

His selection ends a prolonged search for a substantive head of the commission, which has operated under acting leadership since the departure of former CEO Nancy Macharia in June 2025.

Ayabei, who hails from Baringo County, is currently TSC’s Director of Finance, having served at the commission for more than two decades. He joined the institution in 1999 as a Finance Officer before rising through the ranks to become Director of Finance in 2009.

His elevation marks a significant milestone for the representation of persons with disabilities in the country’s public institutions.

Ayabei was the first candidate to face the selection panel at 9am at the commission’s headquarters in Upper Hill, Nairobi. He was followed by Mitei at 10am, Robert Odette at 11am, Lawrence Ngai Kaburu at noon and Farah Abdi Saman at 1pm.

The five candidates were shortlisted from 124 applicants who responded to a fresh  issued on September 29. Applications closed on October 30.

Ayabei holds a Bachelor of Education degree in Mathematics and Economics from Kenyatta University and a Master’s degree in Finance and Banking from the University of Stirling in the United Kingdom. He is also a Certified Public Accountant.

Before joining TSC, he worked at the Ministry of Education between 1990 and 1999.

He takes over at a critical time for the commission, which oversees the employment, deployment, promotion and discipline of teachers across the country. He will inherit mounting pressure over teacher shortages, recruitment, promotions, transfers and the management of the teaching workforce.

The recruitment process had faced legal challenges, with a petition filed at the Employment and Labour Relations Court in Kisii seeking to halt the exercise.

The case, filed by Evans Morara Nyangongo under Cause E038 of 2026, challenged the fresh recruitment and raised questions about Mitei’s participation in the process while serving as acting CEO and seeking the substantive position.

Nyangongo sought to stop the commission from proceeding with the appointment until the issues raised in the petition were determined.

However, the court dismissed both the application and the suit, with no orders as to costs, clearing the way for the interviews.

In its defence, TSC maintained that the decision to advertise the position had been made collectively by the commission’s board and not by the acting CEO.

In a replying affidavit, TSC chairman Jamleck Muturi John maintained that Mitei had neither participated in the board’s deliberations on the recruitment nor influenced the process.

The fresh recruitment followed an earlier court decision that nullified the previous exercise over procedural irregularities, forcing the commission to restart the search for a substantive chief executive.

World.title: Thwake Dam project reaches 94pc completion
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Thwake Multipurpose Dam, which is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment.[File,Standard]

Thwake Dam is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment as residents seek a review of alleged construction-related damage claims.

Principal Secretary for Water and Sanitation Julius Korir told the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Blue Economy, Water and Irrigation that construction had reached 94.2 per cent.

The dam is being built at the confluence of the Athi and Thwake rivers along the Makueni-Kitui border. It is designed to provide water for domestic use, irrigation and electricity generation.

Martin Kimeu, a resident of Wote, said the project would improve access to water for farming in the region.

“Ukambani is fertile. Water has been the biggest impediment to the realization of our agricultural potential. Thwake Dam water is the clear solution to this,” he said.

Kimeu also defended the compensation process, saying he had followed the project since its inception and believed the exercise had been conducted properly.

Jacob Mwanzia, a resident of Madangi Village, said households in his area had been assessed and compensated. He argued that outstanding complaints should be addressed without delaying the project.

Mariam Mwikali, another resident, said assessments had been conducted on affected properties and residents given an opportunity to raise concerns.

However, some households have complained that construction-related blasting damaged their homes. Residents have reported cracks in walls, windows and foundations as well as dust, noise and ground vibrations.

In August 2026, residents from villages in Mavindini Ward, organised under the Thwake Dam Blasting-Affected Community Committee, sought an independent review by the African Development Bank (AfDB).

The residents alleged that some properties had been left out of assessments and compensation. They also sought access to assessment reports, photographs, measurements, valuation records and estimates for repairs or reconstruction.

A project official said the dam's safety department invited competitive bids for an independent assessment of properties potentially affected by blasting. Agile Consulting was selected to conduct the exercise.

The official said the consultant assessed 330 households within a two-kilometre radius of the construction site and submitted its report to the project implementation team. A large proportion of those assessed were satisfied with the exercise, the official added, without giving a breakdown.

Ben Mwongela, a director at Agile Consulting, said the assessment reviewed blasting records, vibration data and compliance with regulatory standards.

The exercise also involved documenting households, classifying structural defects and preparing bills of quantities and cost estimates for repairs or reconstruction, he said.

The AfDB conducted a field mission to the project between September 21 and 25, with its report published on October 21, 2026.

The bank's team, led by project task manager Nancy Ogal, met residents whose homes had been affected by blasting and identified outstanding health, safety, environmental and social issues, including homeowner grievances.

The bank called for timely compensation and continued monitoring of the project's environmental and social performance.

During a stakeholder engagement visit to Mavindini in October, Korir said the government had secured additional funding after the project experienced cash-flow constraints.

“When we ran short of cash, we engaged with our development partners, and they allocated additional funding, and this money will now go towards total completion of the project,” he said.

In June 2026, the AfDB approved additional financing of €68.39 million to support completion of the first phase, alongside funding from the Kenyan government.

The bank said the financing would support engineering refinements and safety works, including strengthening foundations, raising the dam and constructing two additional saddle dams.

The project has four phases. The first involves construction of the dam, while the subsequent phases cover hydropower generation, water supply and sanitation infrastructure, and irrigation.

The dam is approximately 80.5 metres high and has a planned storage capacity of 688 million cubic metres.

Once the water supply component is operational, the project is expected to provide 150,000 cubic metres of treated water daily to an estimated 1.3 million people in Makueni and Kitui counties and Konza Technopolis in Machakos County.

The irrigation scheme is designed to cover 40,000 hectares, equivalent to about 100,000 acres of agricultural land.

The project is also designed to generate 20 megawatts of hydropower.

The water supply, irrigation and hydropower components require infrastructure beyond the dam structure, including treatment and distribution networks and power generation facilities.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”

The report shows how widespread the abuse is. “Twenty-six percent of women age 15–49 have ever experienced technology-facilitated violence from any perpetrator,” the report says, and 21 per cent experienced it often or sometimes in the 12 months before the survey. Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced it at the hands of a current, most recent or previous partner.

The burden is not spread evenly, the report states that Nairobi City records the highest lifetime experience from any perpetrator at 33 per cent, followed by Murang’a and Baringo at 32 per cent each.

“For abuse by an intimate partner, Homa Bay 36 per cent and Baringo 35 per cent lead, while in the 12 months before the survey Trans Nzoia topped the list at 31 per cent. At the other end, Mandera and Wajir report just 3 per cent, a figure that may say as much about silence as about safety,” the report says

The picture is similar among young people. A 2024 rapid study by the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, working with the UNFPA and Women Economic Empowerment, found that nearly 90 per cent of young adults enrolled in three Nairobi tertiary institutions had witnessed TFGBV, and 39 per cent had experienced it personally.

Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced gender violence committed by a current, most recent or previous partner, and 22 per cent did so in the past year. When women were asked who was responsible, the answer was blunt. Current husbands or intimate partners accounted for 61 per cent of perpetrators, former partners for 22 per cent and strangers for just 13 per cent.

Women who have never been married or had a partner face a different threat. For them, the most common perpetrators are strangers at 45 per cent, online attackers at 23 per cent and friends or acquaintances at 20 per cent.

Warning signs

Control is the common thread. The report describes such behaviours by a male partner as “important early warning signs that may escalate into violence within a relationship.”

Sixty-one per cent of ever-partnered women say their current or most recent partner has shown at least one controlling behaviour, and 27 per cent report three or more. Half say he has been jealous or angry when they spoke to other men, and 36 per cent say he insists on knowing where they are at all times. Others describe partners who demand passwords or read messages without consent.

Age and marital status matter. Technology-based gender violence is lowest among girls aged 15–19 at 10 per cent and highest among women aged 20–24 at 37 per cent. Forty-one per cent of divorced, separated or widowed women have experienced it, compared with 27 per cent of married women and 19 per cent of the never married.

Yet the digital rights advocate Cherie Oyier, a programmes officer at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), says the low figures in some places should not be read as safety. Much of the abuse happens where nobody can see it.

“Closed applications, meaning like WhatsApp, those are the ones that most people, intimate partners will usually use,” she says. “Even as you are scrolling the internet to look for these instances, we may not be able to catch it. But it does not mean that it is not happening or that it is at a lower level.”

Culture also silences women. “Most women are told just endure, this is what marriage is about,” Oyier says. “Sometimes they don’t know, it’s so overt, like it doesn’t come out clearly that this is abuse. So most of the times, it is not reported.”

Online, abuse has been turned into entertainment. “It has become banter,” she says. “Even the people who are experiencing it have trivialised it. It’s now ingrained to you, like this is something that happens, you should expect it actually. If you post a picture, one of the things that you are thinking about is what kind of comments am I going to get.”

A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: Not so fast: Court slams brake on ARA over wealth forfeiture
World.content:
Felix Mecha Nyakundi could not provide a plausible explanation for how he amassed his wealth.

The Court of Appeal has ruled that the government cannot go after a person’s wealth without prior investigations to establish reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property constitutes proceeds of crime.

In a landmark judgment, Justices Patrick Kiage, Jamila Mohammed and Nduma Nderi said that although it does not require a person to be charged for a crime for the Asset Recovery Agency (ARA) to come knocking, it bears the responsibility to link the wealth or cash to a crime.

World.title: Urgent US warning in Kuwait to prepare for airspace closures
World.content:
The United States has issued an urgent US warning in Kuwait, calling on American citizens in the country to stay away from US-affiliated sites and facilities. The advisory also urges travelers to prepare for sudden flight cancellations and potential airspace closures amid escalating security tensions and recent attacks targeting American interests across the Gulf region.

In an updated security alert, the US Embassy in Kuwait advised Americans to exercise extreme caution and maintain a low profile. Citizens are encouraged to closely monitor official flight updates from Kuwait International Airport and major airlines in anticipation of widespread regional aviation disruptions that could occur with little or no advance notice.

Travel advisory and contingency plans

Alongside the US warning in Kuwait, the US State Department has maintained its Level 3 travel advisory for the country, which officially urges citizens to “reconsider travel” due to heightened security risks. Officials strongly recommended that anyone planning to travel to or from the Middle East prepare immediate contingency plans that do not rely solely on commercial air travel.

To stay informed as the situation evolves on the ground, the State Department is also urging all US citizens residing in or visiting the region to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP). Registering with STEP allows the embassy to send real-time emergency alerts directly to travelers and makes it easier to locate citizens during an urgent crisis.

World.title: Egypt repays $38.2 billion in external debt amid record foreign reserves
World.content:
Official data released by the Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) highlights a resilient external financial position over the past year, marked by all-time high foreign currency reserves and steady progress in meeting international debt obligations.

Debt service costs ease slightly

During the 2025/2026 fiscal year, Cairo paid out $38.2 billion to service its external debt—a $500 million reduction compared to the $38.7 billion spent the previous year.

Lower interest obligations drove the annual savings, with total repayments divided between $30.4 billion in principal installments and $7.8 billion in interest payments.

External debt stock and exchange rate factors

While annual servicing costs dipped, Egypt’s overall external debt stock edged up by 3.3 percent to reach $166.7 billion by the end of June 2026, representing 38.2 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

According to central bank figures, two main factors accounted for the increase:

New financing: Net external borrowing inflows rose by roughly $6.4 billion.

Currency valuation shifts: Fluctuations in the exchange rates of non-dollar borrowed currencies against the US dollar added approximately $900 million to the headline debt figure.

Record foreign currency reserves

Alongside its debt repayments, Egypt’s net international reserves climbed to an unprecedented $57.5 billion in October 2026, up by $152 million from September’s $57.35 billion.

The milestone underscores a sustained foreign currency turnaround, with reserves expanding by roughly $22 billion over the 32 months following the landmark Ras El-Hekma investment deal signed with the United Arab Emirates in February 2024.

World.title: Mohamed Salah signing sparked global buzz and boosted tourism: Trabzonspor President
World.content:
The arrival of Egyptian forward Mohamed Salah has transformed Trabzonspor’s commercial reach and breathed new life into the Turkish city’s economy, according to club president Ertuğrul Doğan.

Speaking to Turkish broadcaster TRT Spor, Doğan reflected on the massive wave of international media coverage—particularly in England—that followed the Egyptian national team captain’s move to the Turkish Super Lig side.

A commercial and tourism windfall

Doğan explained that landing marquee global stars has become a cornerstone of modern football marketing, noting that Salah’s arrival immediately propelled Trabzonspor onto the world stage. Since the transfer, the club’s matches have been broadcast across 50 countries, while jersey sales and season ticket purchases have shattered all-time club records.

Beyond the pitch and merchandise stands, the president emphasized that the signing delivered an unexpected economic lift to the Black Sea city of Trabzon itself by stimulating local tourism. Salah’s official unveiling alone drew an unprecedented crowd of more than 50,000 fans, creating what Doğan described as an electric, once-in-a-lifetime atmosphere.

Eyes on Richarlison next

Sharing behind-the-scenes details of the transfer, Doğan revealed that negotiations with Salah began remotely over Zoom during the summer break, eliminating the need for an in-person meeting before finalizing the agreement. He also noted that his son, Kory, accompanied him during the official contract signing.

Looking ahead, Doğan hinted that Trabzonspor is far from finished with its ambitious recruitment drive, confirming that the club’s board admires Tottenham Hotspur’s Brazilian striker Richarlison as a potential future target.

World.title: Egypt forecasts slight temperature rise nationwide on Friday
World.content:
The Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA) has released its weather forecast for Friday, noting a slight rise in temperatures across most of the country alongside morning mist.

Autumn weather will prevail during the day, feeling moderately warm across most regions and hot in southern Upper Egypt, before turning cool to cold overnight and in the early morning hours.

Expected weather phenomena

Meteorologists also noted a slight chance of scattered cloud cover stretching from the north down to Greater Cairo and the Suez Canal cities, which could bring light, non-disruptive drizzle to isolated areas.

The authority urged citizens to take all necessary precautions to minimize the impact of expected weather conditions and to continue monitoring official updates.

World.title: What’s causing all these outages? The internet is held together with shoestring and bubblegum
World.content:
The fragility of our online systems was on display this past week after back-to-back-to-back outages disrupted flights, global business and national security systems.

No one should be shocked: The internet is a loosely connected patchwork project reliant on some seriously outdated systems containing numerous vulnerabilities – many of which we are just discovering.

An apt xkcd cartoon visualizes “all modern digital infrastructure” as a giant Jenga-style tower supported by one, thin, vertical block with the label: “a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003.”

AI has given security researchers a vastly improved capability to find those weak supports and strengthen them. But bad actors have the same tools, and they’re scoping out ways to target weak structures and exploit them.

The race is on. AI is sending companies and the government into overdrive to keep adversaries out. But in the process, some companies appear to be pushing out security updates that weren’t ready for primetime.

Each of the mega-outages of the past week appears to have a different root cause. Forensics takes time, and the exact cause of each disruption isn’t yet known. Early indications seem to rule out a coordinated attack.

But they all appear to share a common vulnerability: The technologies supporting the internet just weren’t built for a world in which online systems are so interconnected and computers can find and exploit weaknesses faster than humans can.

“These events do not fill me with confidence about the resilience of our digital infrastructure,” said Matthew Green, member of the Johns Hopkins Information Security Institute.

Don’t be shocked if these outages keep happening.

The Titanic

One of those Jenga blocks is PHP, a programming language most people have probably never heard of – even though it powers 70% of the world’s websites. Researchers using AI agents this summer discovered a method to exploit a PHP vulnerability that could allow an attacker to read passwords, steal entire databases or take over websites.

It was patched last month. But the fact that a decades-old tool supporting nearly three-quarters of the websites held a major flaw underscores the problem the internet faces.

“We’re dependent on so many things we’ve never even heard of behind the scenes that keep society running,” said Stuart Madnick, an IT security professor at MIT. “In that regard, we’ve become tremendously vulnerable to things we don’t even know about until something goes wrong.”

That’s why another decent analogy for the state of today’s internet is the Titanic.

The ocean liner’s watertight bulkheads were unable to withstand a failure that exceeded the ship’s architects’ worst-case-scenario assumptions. Even the best-designed systems sometimes succumb to threats and problems that the designers couldn’t have imagined when they built them, noted Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and cofounder of QuSecure, a cryptography provider for the US government.

Now those threats include AI.

Agents can work faster and longer than humans, making them particularly useful at finding security holes by employing trial and error techniques. A yet-unproven but widely held theory from security experts about the reason for the recent string of outages is the rush to patch and beat bad actors to the punch. Those expedited updates may contain bugs themselves, causing system outages.

“Sometimes you do a patch, you push an upgrade in a system, it behaves abnormally, and it tips over, so to speak,” said Chris Krebs, former United States Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, in an interview with CNN’s Pamela Brown on Tuesday. “I think that’s a lot of what we’ve seen with Microsoft, maybe, and with the FAA last week.”

Meanwhile, autonomous AI agents are increasingly overwhelming networks with unprecedented traffic demands, noted Claire Le Goues, computer science professor at Carnegie Mellon University.

For example, Microsoft said its systems went down under the weight of a massive traffic load, and they failed to restore themselves because of a bug that was deployed during an update. The FAA’s initial assessment of a massive outage that led to a nationwide ground stop was that a router update sent out bad traffic, which then overwhelmed its networks. It’s not clear that AI was to blame for either outage, but those are the kinds of conditions that are increasingly prevalent across networks.

“AI may become the stress test that exposes weaknesses we’ve been living with for decades,” said Krauthamer.

What’s next?

The good news, perhaps, is these incidents appear thematically related but not part of some coordinated cyberattack by a foreign adversary. As my colleague John Miller notes, we can’t rule that out just yet, but these incidents don’t carry most of the hallmarks of a massive system intrusion.

The bad news, however, is that the lack of evidence of a cyberattack shouldn’t give us any comfort: If our systems are this vulnerable without a cyber intrusion, imagine what adversaries could do if they were trying to attack us.

“It means that even when our enemies are not trying to attack us, we can attack ourselves just because the systems are so complex and fragile,” said Richard Clarke, former US counterterrorism czar for the George H.W. Bush, Clinton and George W. Bush administrations, in an interview with CNN’s Michael Smerconish on Saturday.

So, while the events of the past week may not be surprising, they should be a wake-up call.

Some experts advocate for a massive, coordinated effort to harden our digital critical infrastructure.

“We are learning again and again that incremental fixes to our infrastructure are no longer sufficient to maintain the resilient systems we need in place,” Krauthamer said. “Our systems must evolve resilience in a way we’ve never faced in the past.”

But some are skeptical that will happen. These problems happen in spurts, rise in the public consciousness, then fade when the systems are restored.

“We’re not doing a good job learning about these things,” said Madnick, who has been teaching about IT security for five decades.

The lack of resource dedication to the underlying problem – ancient systems supporting modern threats – raises the vulnerability of an even more serious problem in the future.

“I keep saying the worst is yet to come,” said Madnick. “So far, I haven’t been proven wrong.”

World.title: Iran’s oil leverage is weakening. That could push it toward escalation
World.content:
Iran’s hold over the Strait of Hormuz is slipping, and experts warn that a cornered Tehran has tended to choose escalation over capitulation.

Oil is flowing again despite continued Iranian attacks on shipping in the waterway, eroding the leverage Tehran has wielded against the United States since the war began. Now, Iran may be looking for ways to break the stalemate as US President Donald Trump piles economic pressure on the Islamic Republic in the hope of forcing it to make concessions.

Iran rattled the global energy market at the outset of the conflict when it effectively shuttered the maritime chokepoint through which a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war. The price of oil surged globally, prompting some economists to warn of a worldwide recession should the closure continue.

American consumers were dealt higher prices at the gas pump, and spiraling energy costs were seen as a major factor in big Republican losses in the US midterm election this month. Trump himself acknowledged that the war was partly to blame for his party’s defeat.

A motorist pumps fuel at a gas station as US fuel prices begin to fall in Miami, Florida, on November 10. Joe Raedle/Getty Images

But a global recession never materialized. Oil exports from the region are now close to pre-war levels, and the global market may soon have more crude than it needs. For Iran, that’s a problem.

Iranian officials have nonetheless claimed victory, arguing that Tehran’s closure of the strait has already yielded major strategic gains. Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, made his country’s intention clear: “We want to impose a cost on the Americans that makes attacking Iran too expensive, and that serves as a deterrent.”

A diminishing threat

Experts say one of Iran’s main wartime strategies – exerting pressure on global energy markets – may now be losing its potency.

Danny Citrinowicz, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel, said that Tehran has long sought to “internationalize” the cost of war. But “if oil prices continue to fall despite Iranian attacks, an important part of that strategy becomes less effective,” he told CNN.

Oil prices have fallen sharply in recent weeks despite an escalation in Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iraqi tanker trucks load gasoline at the Baniyas oil terminal in Syria’s Tartus province on September 27. Moawia Atrash/picture-alliance/dpa/AP

The International Energy Agency attributes this to recovered Gulf exports, with oil supply expected to surpass demand in the fourth quarter for the first time since the outbreak of the Iran war in February.

“It certainly seems that Iran is either unwilling or unable to prevent the flow of crude oil at present,” David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at the consultancy firm Capital Economics, told CNN, adding that “navigability in the strait is still far short of pre-crisis norms.”

Ahria Roushanbakhti, head of the fuel desk at Axis Limited, the Middle East’s largest energy liquidity provider, said that while Iran may be losing some of its hold on the waterway, its ability to cause significant damage to energy infrastructure in the region remains worrying.

An emboldened Iran

Iran experts say that at this point in the conflict, Tehran is unlikely to dampen its demands but rather escalate its military operations to break the “neither war nor peace” stalemate with the US that is crippling Iran’s economy.

Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said that Tehran appears more confident than ever after Trump’s midterm setback, celebrating the Republican Party’s losses.

But oil prices dipped after the midterm results as fears eased that Trump would reignite the war and Tehran ramped up diplomacy with mediators.

“Markets appear to be increasingly assuming that a return to full-scale war is unlikely and that oil supplies will gradually recover,” Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN.

“But that assumption could change quickly if Iran decides to intensify the confrontation,” he said.

That may be unfolding, as Iran already appears to be looking at other options to pressure the US back to the negotiating table.

Added threats by the US may even force Iran into more proactive measures that would be costly for both sides, experts said.

Tehran’s options

The conflict has escalated rapidly in recent days after a period of relative calm. The region saw a series of back-and-forth attacks by Iran and allied Houthi rebels in Yemen on Gulf countries, as well as US attacks on Iranian territory around the strait.

Presented with the possibility of perceived capitulation or military escalation, Iran’s hardline regime has tended to choose the latter despite the cost, experts say.

“When it feels cornered, it may become more aggressive, not less,” Citrinowicz said.

Iranian women volunteers receive military training at a center for ordinary citizens at Azadi Square in Tehran, Iran, on November 10. Majid Asgaripour/Wana News Agency/Reuters

Iran may choose to increase pressure on tankers using the US-supported route in the Strait of Hormuz, said Azizi, of the International Crisis Group. It may also choose to disrupt ship-to-ship transfers of oil, or target Gulf infrastructure or alternative export routes that allow Gulf countries to bypass some Tehran’s restrictions in Hormuz, he said.

Tehran also appears to be lowering the threshold for retaliation. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Tuesday said it targeted American radars in Bahrain following unspecified “US drone violations of Iran’s airspace.” It has also warned Bahrain’s Sunni rulers against mistreatment of the majority Shiite population.

Iran has warned countries against allowing the US to use their territory to attack it. National security chief Rezaei said last week that “all military bases… from Western Asia to Europe, will be legitimate targets.”

“There will be no safe distance or safe haven for aggressors,” he warned, adding that “no base will remain immune.”

This shows that Iran may not only be looking to expand its scope of operations, but is now “signaling that even violations of its airspace could trigger attacks against American assets,” Azizi said.

Others believe there is not much else the Islamic Republic can do that can bring Washington to agree to a deal that works for Iran.

Parsi of the Quincy Institute said that further action by Iran will not make a difference. What could make a change, he said, is the one thing that Iranians are disinclined to do: give Trump a “symbolic” victory that is “ego-soothing and face-saving.”

The Iranians, he said, are more opposed to a symbolic loss than a substantive one, which only adds to the stalemate.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei speaks at a press conference in Tehran on November 15. Xinhua/Shutterstock

Meanwhile, a third US aircraft carrier strike group recently entered US Central Command’s area of responsibility, where it is expected to – at least temporarily – join ongoing operations that include enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports and escorting commercial ships willing to transit the strait.

Washington may be misjudging Iran’s breaking point, experts said.

Tehran’s latest operations fit into a “broader shift in Iranian military thinking toward more proactive deterrence,” Azizi said.

“If the leadership concludes that its leverage over Hormuz is weakening while the American blockade continues to impose economic costs, it may decide to go further, potentially even challenging US naval forces more directly,” he said.

This would be considerably riskier, he said “but Iran may see it as necessary to break the blockade rather than allow its position to deteriorate gradually.”

World.title: The Trump team’s messaging problems on tech outages, broken down
World.content:
Two weeks after the GOP’s shellacking in the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration is embroiled in a crisis that it has often made worse with its messaging.

A series of tech outages impacting air travel, banks, online communications and even a highly classified network used by the National Security Agency has Americans spooked — and often wondering what’s going on.

And the messaging from the administration has been so confusing — or, in some cases, largely absent — that it’s fed into the growing unease.

It’s gotten to the point where former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt on Tuesday took to pointing out when members of the administration actually get it right, in her estimation.

Former Trump Homeland Security spokeswoman Tricia McLaughlin added on X: “Americans aren’t stupid. We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.”

Here’s a look at how some of the main players — including some who could succeed Trump as the GOP presidential standard-bearer — have handled things.

Trump: The man who isn’t there

President Donald Trump is now telling Americans concerned about the tech outages to “relax.”

“Tell them to relax. Everything’s good. These are individual events,” the president told Fox News in an interview in China that aired Wednesday night.

Largely, his problem has been his absence — his lack of any public presence on the issue and his lack of reassurance in a scary time.

He said virtually nothing for two days about Friday’s rare and chaotic full ground stop at the nation’s airports, even as he posted repeatedly on social media about renovation projects like Washington’s public golf course. By Sunday, he posted blaming the Biden administration and asking Congress for more money to modernize the Federal Aviation Administration.

By Monday, he said he didn’t “take any responsibility” for the ground stop. He said he had been working in the Oval Office when it happened but had delegated the messaging to others.

“I didn’t think there was any reason for me to do (it),” Trump told reporters while departing the White House for Asia.

And his comments are making him look increasingly out of touch. Before telling Americans to relax about the tech outages, he effectively shrugged them off.

“It’s life,” Trump said after landing in the Philippines when asked whether he was concerned about the outages. “When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

One of the main lessons of the 2026 election was that voters saw Trump as unconcerned about their priorities. His response to these outages has been a case in point.

Trump has never been good at empathizing. But he doesn’t even seem to be trying.

Perhaps nobody has come in for criticism like Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Even MAGA-aligned conservative commentators have called him “a buffoon” and “unfit for office,” with Megyn Kelly saying she has “zero faith in this man.”

The reason has been a characteristically unsteady stream of messages, compounded with a highly questionable decision to fly to a college football game on Saturday, even as many Americans were still stranded. (Mullin has stressed that he’s required to fly in a government plane because of his job.)

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton speak with each other before the start of a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on Capitol Hill on November 18. Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

Mullin kicked things off Friday amid the ground stop by saying that he didn’t “want to say this is a crisis, but it is.” He then began Friday night’s press conference with a pretty tone-deaf joke about how it was Friday the 13th. (There are few people with less of a sense of humor than the stranded traveler.)

By Monday, he was offering speculation about what was happening with the tech outages based on “one guy that’s very smart with tech” but was “not Elon (Musk).” It was a performance more befitting of a TV pundit than the guy in charge of responding to the crisis.

But Mullin’s biggest optics problem was deciding to go to the Texas-LSU football game on Saturday, which was first reported Tuesday morning by the New York Post. When challenged about that decision Tuesday on CNBC, Mullin noted that the airspace at the time was “completely open” — although many people were still stranded — and said that even as he’s working hard, “we’ve still got to live our life at the same time.”

Talk about tone-deaf.

Mullin kept trying to explain at a congressional hearing Wednesday, telling the House Homeland Security Committee that canceling his travel plans would have looked like “distrust that we’re not even willing to fly.” But that sounds quite different from his initial explanation. And it seems a little too cute by half.

The thing is, to those familiar with Mullin’s TV appearances even before he became DHS secretary, he’s always had this in him. The former Oklahoma senator gets things wrong. He’s often off-message. It’s just that this is the first time it’s been front and center for the American public. And he compounded that with a Ted Cruz-level travel gaffe.

Duffy: A message even Republicans don’t want to hear

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s problem has been his choice of message — basically blaming the ground stop on a lack of FAA modernization funding from Congress.

The first problem is that he previously scoffed at this kind of blame-shifting. As CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski reports, after a 2023 ground stop under the Biden administration, Duffy suggested the problem was leadership rather than funding.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy walks through the US Capitol on his way to attend a Senate GOP luncheon on November 17. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

“They got billions of dollars, the FAA did, over Covid,” Duffy said on Fox News at the time. “And now they’re gonna come back and say, ‘We want even more money to fix this crisis that we weren’t able to handle when, you know, for what, three hours in the morning aircraft couldn’t, couldn’t fly.’”

The second is that while Duffy has been consistently asking for more money, he’s rubbed even Republicans the wrong way with his latest request.

After previously asking for $30 billion more for FAA modernization, he quickly jacked that up to $50 billion — but without saying why. Congressional Republicans have balked both at the implication that they were to blame for what happened Friday and at the idea that they should just shovel money on top of the $12.5 billion that Congress approved in the GOP’s spending and policy bill last year, when that hasn’t all been marked as spent yet.

Clayton: Some rare competence

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has increasingly been dispatched — including at Wednesday’s hearing — in an apparent effort to steady the ship.

During a Fox Business appearance Tuesday and at Wednesday’s hearing, he’s sought to underscore the administration’s conclusion that the tech outages aren’t due to some malign foreign actor.

“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Clayton said at the hearing. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”

It was pretty standard stuff from the administration, but it was delivered with the kind of confidence and authority that has been lacking elsewhere.

Leavitt on Tuesday praised the decision to dispatch Clayton — the implication being that he was an improvement on the others.

Rubio: Some rare empathy

Leavitt has also conspicuously praised Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who has stepped forward to offer the empathy and concern that Trump hasn’t.

Rubio acknowledged while in the Philippines this week that the outages highlight important questions about “vulnerabilities” in our technology. He also nodded to people being “nervous” and “anxious.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio prepares to speak to the media at the Solaire hotel in Paranaque, Metro Manila, Philippines, on Wednesday. Carlos Barria/Reuters

He added at another point: “We fully acknowledge that this is unsettling, to see these reports, day after day, of some technical failures. … We get it.”

“We take these things very seriously,” Rubio added. “Obviously, we’re always vigilant.”

Again, standard leader stuff. But it underscored the lack of similar comments from Trump.

Vance: Canceling his plans (unlike Trump)

Vice President JD Vance hasn’t said as much as other players, but he did make some pretty big news Wednesday by abruptly canceling his appearance at the New York Times’ DealBook Summit. The stated reason: He was asked to attend meetings in Washington amid the tech outages.

It’s unclear what (or who) specifically prompted the last-minute cancellation. Vance has clearly been trying to craft a brand somewhat independent of Trump. And Wednesday’s was an interesting move, given the president’s lack of public attention to the issue and that fact that some have questioned whether he should have canceled his own plans to travel to Asia.

Vance has also wandered into some trouble, though. After he echoed the party line of blaming the administration’s predecessors for the state of the nation’s air travel system, even Fox News’ Laura Ingraham balked.

“Well, you guys have been in charge the last two years,” Ingraham interjected, adding: “Why hasn’t it gotten fixed?”

The White House press secretary: Still conspicuously nonexistent

The entire episode has also underscored the strange lack of a replacement for Leavitt.

It’s been nearly three months since she left her job in late August. It’s also been almost a month since her initial replacement, Katie Zacharia, was fired after just five days.

These are moments when the administration could really use disciplined messengers fully devoted to briefing the media every day. But apparently they can’t find the right person — and those filling the void have struggled.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

World.title: UN top court finds Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against Rohingya minority
World.content:
Myanmar committed genocide against the country’s long-persecuted Rohingya minority, the United Nations’ top court found Thursday, an unprecedented ruling that survivors of the atrocities have waited almost a decade to hear.

The historic judgement marks the first time the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also known as the World Court, has held a state accountable for genocide in its 80-year history — and the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar.

The court’s decision – by nine votes to six – also comes at a time when the broader idea of international justice has come under fire from the Trump administration.

For the Rohingya, the ICJ’s judgment is a “turning point.”

“It is the difference between being told our history was a tragedy, and being told our history was a crime that must be answered for,” said Murshid Alam, who was just 12 years old when he was driven from his home in Myanmar’s Rakhine state.

Myanmar army members burn Rohingya houses in Mandru, Myanmar, on September 6, 2017. Yousuf Tushar/LightRocket/Getty Images

A Bangladeshi man helps Rohingya Muslim refugees to disembark from a boat on the Bangladeshi shoreline of the Naf river after crossing the border from Myanmar in Teknaf on September 30, 2017. Fred Dufour/AFP/Getty Images Rohingya women and children wait to get distributed meals at Moynarghona refugee settlement near Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, November 24, 2017. Susana Vera/Reuters

The ICJ’s rulings are final and binding, but the court – which hears disputes between states – doesn’t have the power to enforce its decisions. Its orders, however, are sent to the UN Security Council, which could decide to implement the court’s ruling through a resolution.

Between 2016 and 2017, the military in Buddhist-majority Myanmar targeted villages and towns home to Rohingya communities, looting, burning and slaughtering their inhabitants, and expelling hundreds of thousands from the country.

CNN reporting at the time documented harrowing stories from Rohingya who saw their family members raped or killed by soldiers, and in some case their Buddhist neighbors joining in the massacres. Photos showed streams of terrified people fleeing burning villages on foot or piling into overcrowded boats as they sought to reach neighboring Bangladesh and safety.

This case against Myanmar was brought in 2019 by The Gambia, a country thousands of miles from where the killings took place, in a world-first. The United States and Canada previously declared the atrocities as genocide.

After seven years of weighing evidence and hearing witness testimony, the ICJ found that the scale and nature of Myanmar’s atrocities “went well beyond what would be required to punish the population and are instead characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group,” presiding judge Iwasawa Yuji said during a nearly three-hour reading.

“The court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy” the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.

An aerial view shows the Rohingya refugee camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on November 17, 2026. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP/Getty Images

In its judgement, the court established the military “engaged in indiscriminate killings” and gave particular weight to the “widespread acts of sexual violence, and extreme acts of violence against children” as well as security forces’ attacks on “Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh.”

Myanmar had denied its “clearance operations” were intended to destroy the Rohingya population, and said the military was conducting legitimate counter-terrorism operations against a Rohingya insurgent group. The court rejected that defense, saying the Myanmar military did not distinguish between militants and civilians.

CNN has reached out to Myanmar’s military-backed government for comment on the ruling.

‘The world sees our suffering’

Murshid Alam was a child when he was forced out of his home in Myanmar’s Rakhine state by a hail of gunfire. In the chaos of the escape, he was shot in his ear — a “terrifying experience,” he told CNN. The wound has healed, but the “secondary trauma of losing my home and seeing my community destroyed” has not.

Alam was one of more than 740,000 Rohingya people who fled to Bangladesh to escape the massacres. The sprawling refugee camps that he came of age in have since become the world’s largest, hosting more than 1.2 million people.

“Our generation has grown up in displacement. We have known nothing but statelessness,” said Alam, 22, who now works to educate and advocate for young people in the Cox’s Bazar camps as founder of the Rohingya Youth Union.

The genocide ruling, he said, “tells us that the world sees our suffering and refuses to let it be erased.

Dawda Jallow, Minister of Justice of the Republic of Gambia. Phil Nijhuis/AFP/Getty Images

Following The Gambia’s successful application to bring the case, the ICJ allowed South Africa to bring a case against Israel over its war with Hamas in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. Israel denies the genocide charge.

That has led to concerns among some the court could come into collision with the Trump administration – already on a campaign to “dismantle” another institution, the International Criminal Court. Last month, its UN ambassador Mike Waltz accused the ICJ of trying to lower the threshold for a genocide verdict in the Myanmar case that he claimed could potentially be “weaponized” against American soldiers.

What next for the Rohingya?

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingya, including to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return to their place of residence and reunification of families,” and return all property lost or damaged. It also ordered Myanmar to ensure their future protection from discrimination and persecution.

It is unlikely Myanmar will adhere. The head of the Myanmar military during the massacres, Min Aung Hlaing is now the country’s leader after he overthrew the elected government – and has dismissed the Rohingya identity as “imaginary.” His military-backed government has shown little interest in allowing Rohingya to return.

Mohammed Shoaib, 7, who was shot on his chest before crossing the border from Myanmar in August, shows his injury outside a medical centre after seeing a doctor, at Kutupalong refugee camp near Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh November 5, 2017. Adnan Abidi/Reuters Armed Myanmar soldiers patrol a village in Maungdaw located in Rakhine State as security operation continue following attacks by armed militant Muslims in October 2016. AFP/Getty Images

What they would return to is another question. In the Rohingya homeland of Rakhine state, the military-backed government is not in control. An ethnic armed group called the Arakan Army controls the vast majority of the state, including areas that border Bangladesh, and has been accused of widespread abuses against civilians in its areas.

Meanwhile, the military has ramped up airstrikes across the state as part of its grinding civil war, dropping bombs on civilian markets and hospitals, in response to territorial losses.

Rohingya now living in the camps cannot work and face dire conditions, including trafficking, exploitation, meagre food rations, and a lack of basic education.

Alam, in the Bangladesh refugee camp, hoped the ruling could pave the way for a return to the home he fled as a young boy.

“The Rohingya do not want to live in refugee camps forever. We want to return to our homeland in Rakhine state with our rights, our citizenship, and our dignity fully restored,” he said.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

World.title: How a $54 Million Deal Nearly Handed Liberia’s Identity Registry to an Austrian Firm Without a Bid
World.content:
MONROVIA – Rick Scott got to the registration center in Red Light before dawn. He had left his job, paid the $5 fee and joined a line hundreds of people long. By evening, he went home with no ID card. It was his fourth try that week.

By Rodney D. Sieh

“I leave my job in the morning and come to find an identification card because it’s a government mandate,” the 54-year-old businessman told New Narratives earlier this year. “Some of us are not feeling well, but we are forced to come here.”



For Liberians outside Monrovia, it is worse. In many counties there is a single enrollment center. A resident of Foya can pay for transport to enroll, go home, then pay again to come back for the card.

The card is not optional. Under an April 2025 executive order, Liberians need it to bank, buy a SIM card, see a doctor, enroll in school and deal

with immigration. Many have been turned away from those services before they could even get one.

This is the problem the government said OeSD would fix. When President Joseph Nyuma Boakai sent the Legislature a $54.7 million concession to rebuild Liberia’s national identity system, it came with his approval. It also came with an operator already picked. Nobody had bid for the job.



Now a House joint committee has recommended that the deal be thrown out entirely. In a report dated Nov. 18, 2026, the Joint Committee on Investment and Concessions and on Ways, Means, Finance and Budget said it found “over 40 distinct defects” in the agreement between the government and OeSD International GmbH. The Austrian firm’s Vienna-registered contracting entity, the report says, has share capital of just 35,000 euros.

The committee said several of the defects were “statutory violations that occurred prior to execution.” Ratification by the Legislature, it said, could not cure them. Several sources familiar with the deal told FrontPageAfrica the President was badly misled by aides who pushed it.

One source, closed to the process to FPA on condition of anonymity that the deal “was going to take the NIR to the cleaners.” Among the most glaring items: a $19.82 million data center the country does not need, because LIBTELCO already has one.

The committee’s case against the agreement comes down to three things: there was no bidding, Liberians’ biometric data was left unprotected and the registry’s own legal mandate was signed away.

A deal sealed before the rules were followed

Liberia already has a national biometric platform. In April 2017, after an open tender among 19 firms, the government paid Techno Brain $5.9 million to build and maintain it. The National Identification Registry (NIR), the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation (NASSCORP) and the National Elections Commission (NEC) still use it.

The OeSD deal would have scrapped that system. The committee report and earlier reporting, including leaked procurement documents first published by FrontPageAfrica in August 2025, show how it took shape:

* Dec. 18, 2024: The government signs a non-binding memorandum of understanding with OeSD International GmbH.

* Feb. 9–14, 2025: Liberian officials travel to Austria on a due-diligence trip paid for by OeSD, the company they were supposed to be vetting.

* May 2025: The Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC) refuses a request to sole-source the contract.

* May 30, 2025: The NIR signs an undisclosed contract with OeSD anyway.

* June 23, 2025: The government suspends the issuance of national biometric ID cards.

* July 5, 2025: A presidential memo to a new steering committee chaired by National Security Advisor Samuel Kofi Woods says OeSD has already been selected and orders that the process be “upheld.

* July 7, 2025: Two days later, the PPCC formally rejects restricted bidding and orders open international competitive bidding and a formal concession plan. The committee says that order “was never followed.”

* April 30, 2026: The concession agreement is signed.

* July 15, 2026: The President approves it and sends it to the Legislature.

* Oct. 15, 2026: The House refers it to the joint committee, which holds hearings on Oct. 28, Nov. 4 and Nov. 11.

The July 2025 memo treated as settled a choice the procurement regulator was about to reject. Woods told The Liberian Investigator at the time that he had not advised the President on the ID contract.

NIR Executive Director Andrew Peters has defended the deal. In September, he told FrontPageAfrica that OeSD would finance about $54.7 million under a build-operate-transfer arrangement to ease the burden on a cash-strapped government. He said Liberian identity data would remain “a national asset under the authority and control of the Republic of Liberia.”

The committee’s reading of the contract is very different.

‘Shall be void’: no bidding, no certificate

The committee’s first and heaviest finding is that the deal was never competed. In its words, the agreement is “legally void.” Under Regulation 57(4) of the PPCC’s amended 2026 regulations, any concession procured without a Certificate of Concession “shall be void.” The committee said the OeSD agreement cites none.

The Executive also went around the PPCC’s July 2025 order for open international bidding. Instead, the deal was handled as an unsolicited proposal. Lawmakers said that route was closed on two counts:

* Regulation 69(9) bars unsolicited proposals when the government makes substantial financial contributions or when the service is contestable.

* Regulation 69(18) requires competitive bidding whenever rival proposals arrive before PPCC approval.

There were rival proposals. MWETANA and Dynamic Global Technologies came forward in September 2025, Lake Piso Solutions on Sept. 29, 2025, and MRT on April 3, 2026. Each submitted an expression of interest, an objection to sole-sourcing or an alternative proposal before the contract was signed.

The committee also found that no summary of the deal’s main terms was published two weeks before signing. Required stakeholder forums in the 15 county seats were never held.

Liberian tech firms: ‘Bad for Liberia’

Liberia’s own technology sector told lawmakers the same thing. Members of the Liberia Information Technology Consortium (LITCON) testified before the joint committee that the concession duplicated systems Liberia already has and was bad for the country.

Top of their list was the data center. The contract charges $19.82 million for a “Renewable License” data center. Yet the state-owned Liberia Telecommunications Corporation (LIBTELCO) already runs a Tier III facility where the system could be co-located, and the government is already obliged to provide Tier IV capacity. In other words, Liberia would pay nearly $20 million for something it already owns.

The committee reached the same conclusion. It also found that the deal would abandon the Techno Brain platform the NIR, NASSCORP and the NEC still use.

Local firms have been sounding the alarm for more than a year. In August 2025, eight Liberian-owned ICT companies wrote to National Security Advisor Woods.

They warned that the NIR was preparing to sole-source a foreign firm and that citizens’ biometric data could end up under foreign control, according to a report of the letter. Among the signers were MWETANA and DGT, two of the firms the committee says were later passed over. The companies noted that Liberia’s biometric ID system, launched in 2012, was built by Liberian experts. They asked that identity-document contracts be at least 75 percent Liberian-owned.

This week, PSI Liberia and its sister company, M Tosh Prints Media, demonstrated biometric equipment at the Capitol and questioned why qualified local firms were never given “an opportunity to compete.” Their representative, Varney Fahnbulleh, showed about $2 million worth of equipment and services, including 150 biometric enrollment kits. By

comparison, the concessionaire committed to 146 kits in its second year. He also said PPCC Executive Director Bodger Scott Johnson had told lawmakers that the President’s Jan. 30, 2026 letter did not ask for single-sourcing.

Who holds the keys to Liberians’ identities?

Every Liberian who enrolls hands over fingerprints and a photograph of their face. Unlike a password, those can never be changed. If they leak, they stay leaked for life. The NIR has said repeatedly that Liberians’ data would stay under Liberian control. The committee found nothing in the contract to guarantee it.

The agreement does not require that primary or backup data be hosted inside Liberia. It does not require hardware security modules, the devices that protect encryption keys. And it does not require the government to hold the root encryption keys to its own citizens’ biometric records.

Lawmakers said the contract allowed data to be transferred before the deal took effect. That breaks the 1,000-record limit on off-site data in Section 23(b) of the Data Protection Act. It also breaks electoral data laws, because the agencies whose data was involved had not consented.

The committee flagged three other risks:

* Base64 is not encryption. Biometric templates would be sent using Base64 encoding. That is a format for moving data, not a lock. Anyone who intercepts it can read it.

* ID by referral. Annex 2, Section 7.1 lets people enroll themselves by phone, including signing up “friends, family and colleagues.” That produces a “partially verified” National Identification Number (NIN) good for opening bank accounts and registering SIM cards before any fingerprints are taken. The committee called it an open door to “systemic identity fraud.”

* Paying twice for storage. The $19.82 million data center, flagged by LITCON, duplicates capacity Liberia already has.

A chapter on data

Protection that appeared in a January 2026 draft was deleted before the agreement was signed, the committee said. So were chapters on anti-corruption and state auditing.

Signing away the registry’s job

The third ground goes to what the NIR exists to do. Article 7.1 of the agreement gives OeSD the exclusive right to assign NINs. It also makes OeSD the only provider of ID cards and identity checks. Under Sections 3.1, 3.2(d) and 7.3 of the NIR Act of 2011, those powers belong to the NIR alone. The committee cited the Supreme Court’s Feb. 12, 2026 ruling in LAC v. LRA that a concession cannot override a statute.

Other clauses reached further:

A toll on daily life

Articles 7.3 and 12.1 would make paid OeSD verification mandatory for nearly every public and private service, from banking and SIM cards to permits and court business. The committee said that goes beyond the NIR Act, and that Executive Order 147 cannot legally expand it.

* Skipping the Legislature. Article 5.3 lets the two parties waive conditions precedent by mutual agreement. One of those conditions is legislative ratification. Lawmakers called the clause “ultra vires and unacceptable.”

* Liberia in a London courtroom. Article 31 sends disputes to UNCITRAL arbitration in London and waives Liberia’s sovereign immunity from enforcement. That would expose Liberian state assets abroad.

* Other agencies’ work. Appendix 4 lists work and residence permits among the concession’s requirements. Those belong to the Ministry of Labour and the Liberia Immigration Service.

* Few jobs for Liberians. The deal sets no measurable targets for Liberians in senior management or in the workforce over its 10-year life. It does not require any role for Liberian-owned IT firms.

* ⁠On money, the committee said it rebuilt the financial model from OeSD’s own Annex 5 tables. It found a lopsided structure that pushes costs and risks onto the Republic while guaranteeing the operator’s returns.

The document itself was a mess. The agreement was signed April 30, 2026, but Annexes 2 and 4 are dated May 4 and Annex 1 is dated May 5. The whole fee schedule and revenue split sit in those annexes. That leaves “no legal certainty that the economic terms were agreed upon at signing,” the committee said.

The text sent to lawmakers also contained duplicated pages, missing clauses from Article 3 and Article 12.2, broken cross-references and an unsigned template memorandum for Ecobank. It even got the NIR director’s name wrong, calling Andrew Peters “Peter Andrews.”

Back to the drawing board

The report was signed by members of both committees. They are led by Rep. Foday E. Fahnbulleh, chairman of Investment and Concessions, and Rep. P. Mike Jurry, chairman of Ways, Means, Finance and Budget. It now goes to the full House, which the committee urged to “reject and decline ratification” of the agreement “in its entirety.”

The committee also wants the House to give the Executive three directives:

1. Enforce the law. Restore the NIR’s statutory role as a service bureau, overseen by its Board of Registrars and the General Auditing Commission.

2. Bid it out. Follow the PPCC’s July 2025 order and the 2026 regulations. That means a valid Certificate of Concession, a value-for-money assessment, and weighing upgrades to the existing biometric system against competing bids.

3. Protect the data. Make any future vendor comply with the Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2026, the Cybercrime Act of 2025 and the mandates of the NEC, the Liberia Revenue Authority, the Liberia Immigration Service and the Ministry of Health.

FrontPageAfrica sent detailed questions to NIR Executive Director Andrew Peters about the committee’s findings. He had not responded by press time.

None of that helps Rick Scott, or the traveler from Foya. ID card issuance has been suspended since June 2025. New Narratives reported that the program also stalled over about $1.7 million the government owed Techno Brain. Fewer than 15 percent of the population holds an official ID card, according to Biometric Update.

The question lawmakers are now asking is not whether Liberia needs a modern ID system. It is who decided that one Austrian company, contracting through a 35,000-euro Vienna entity, should build it, and why nobody else was allowed to try.

World.title: Liberia: Attorney General Summoned Over IB Atlantic IV Release Order; Crew Still Held Past Deadline
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Justice Ministry’s failure to obey a court order to release the vessel IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members has turned into a direct confrontation with the judiciary.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Criminal Court “A” has summoned Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. Betty Lamin-Blamo to answer allegations of contempt.



Assigned Circuit Judge D. Onesimus Banwon issued a writ of summons ordering Lamin-Blamo to appear before the court at the Temple of Justice on Friday, Nov. 20, at 9 a.m. She must show cause why she should not be held in contempt for disobeying the court’s order to release the ship and its crew.

As of Thursday, when the writ was issued, the vessel and all seven crew members were still in state custody. The court’s deadline had passed at 4 p.m. Wednesday.

The summons puts the country’s chief legal officer before a judge to account for the government’s failure to obey a court order. It comes in a case that has dragged on for nearly three months without a full public explanation of what the vessel was doing or the legal grounds for holding it.

‘Show cause’



The writ, dated Nov. 19 and issued under the authority of the First Judicial Circuit, Montserrado County, is explicit. It orders the attorney general to explain why she should not be held in contempt for disobeying the release order.

Assistant Clerk of Court Gideon A. Eshun issued the summons to Montserrado County Sheriff H. C. Sulonich or his deputy for service. The court told the sheriff to report back to the clerk’s office on how the summons was served.
