The writ is not a finding of contempt. But it is a serious step. It requires the government’s top lawyer to answer personally for her ministry’s failure to comply.

It also raises a larger question: Can the government keep people and property in custody after a court has ordered their release, without going back to the court for permission?

Deadline passes, crew stays put

Judge Banwon had ordered the release of the IB Atlantic IV and its crew after their lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition challenging their detention. The ministry was given until 4 p.m. Wednesday to comply.

It did not. At about 5 p.m. Wednesday, FrontPageAfrica observed that the order had not been carried out. Lawyers for the seven crew members confirmed their clients were still being held.

By Thursday, nothing had changed. That left the court to take the extra step of summoning the attorney general.

Reached late Wednesday and asked why the release had not happened, Solicitor General Cllr. Abrahim Sillah gave no explanation.

“I will refer you to find out from the court, my brother,” Sillah told FrontPageAfrica.

His answer left the central question unaddressed: On what legal basis is the government still holding the ship and its crew after the court’s deadline expired?

Ministry ‘struggling’ for an explanation

Sources at the Justice Ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter, told FrontPageAfrica earlier that the ministry was struggling to come up with an explanation for the continued detention.

Part of the difficulty, the sources said, was the government’s own earlier public statements that it was investigating the vessel’s movements and how it came to be intercepted. No findings from that investigation have been made public. That left officials hard-pressed to justify holding the ship and crew in the face of a court order.

The sources said the ministry was considering releasing the vessel and crew early Thursday to comply with the order. That did not happen.

Lamin-Blamo is now expected to explain in court why the order was not obeyed on time, and to present whatever legal justification the government has for keeping the ship and crew in custody.

The ship that slipped away

The IB Atlantic IV is a 41-year-old, Comoros-flagged general cargo ship. It first drew attention this summer when it lingered off York Island in Tewor District, Grand Cape Mount County, alarming residents and fishermen.

Before that, the ship had already tried to get into Liberia. On July 13, a Liberian businessman, Kuiah, wrote to the Liberia Maritime Authority (LiMA) on behalf of a company called Madris Group of Companies Inc. He asked for docking rights and a dive team at the Freeport of Monrovia, describing the vessel as disabled and “in distress.” FrontPageAfrica later reported that Kuiah, a former deputy at Roberts International Airport who was dismissed, was the company’s sole owner. LiMA turned the request down. The ship was still in Sierra Leonean waters at the time and had not docked anywhere, yet it was already seeking a Liberian berth.

Once the vessel drifted onto the Liberian side of the maritime border, the order came to search and seize it. It kept moving. On Aug. 4, then-Armed Forces of Liberia Chief of Staff Maj. Gen. Davidson Forleh confirmed that security forces were in pursuit. He told FrontPageAfrica that the Coast Guard’s boats were not equipped to chase a ship far out to sea. With Nigerian help, the military tracked it off Rivercess County but could not board it.

Investigators also looked into reports that a smaller vessel had approached the IB Atlantic IV and tried to throw something aboard. The government said a Liberian fishing vessel had gone out to meet the ship, and the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority opened an inquiry.

The ship was finally seized by Ivorian authorities on Aug. 9. On Aug. 14, Information Minister Jerolinmek M. Piah confirmed the arrest and said Liberia was working with Côte d’Ivoire to bring it back. It returned under Liberian Coast Guard command on Aug. 27.

The chase unfolded amid a widening national drug-trafficking scandal, and speculation about contraband aboard ran high. But authorities have never publicly established that any narcotics were found on the vessel.

Its return was supposed to give the government a chance to investigate and give the public a full account. Instead, the ship and crew stayed in custody for nearly three months with no findings released. That drove the vessel’s management and crew to court.

Friday’s test

For the seven crew members, the case has meant months of uncertainty, held aboard a ship whose presence in Liberian waters is still unexplained.

The government is now being asked to answer for more than the vessel. It must also explain why it kept the ship and its crew in custody after a judge ordered them freed.

That answer is due Friday at 9 a.m., when Lamin-Blamo is expected to appear before Criminal Court “A” at the Temple of Justice.

World.title: Who Tried to Sell Liberia’s Identity?
World.content:
The $54.7 million national ID deal ignored the procurement regulator, shut out every competitor and stripped away the safeguards protecting Liberians’ biometric data. Rejecting it is not enough. The President must find out who tried to slip it past him, and hold them to account

A NATION’S IDENTITY is not a commodity. It is the record that says who belongs, who can vote, who can open a bank account, who can cross a border and come home. The National Identification Registry was created to keep that record in Liberian hands, under Liberian law.

THAT IS WHY the House joint committee’s report on the $54.7 million concession with OeSD International should alarm every Liberian. The committee found more than 40 defects in the agreement. Several, it said, were violations of the law committed before the deal was even signed. No vote of the Legislature can cure them.



STRIP AWAY THE technical language and the story is simple. In May 2025, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission refused a request to hand the contract to OeSD without competition. Then, on May 30, the NIR signed a contract with OeSD anyway. In July 2025, the PPCC ordered open international bidding and a formal concession plan. That order, the committee says, “was never followed.”

RIVAL FIRMS, INCLUDING Liberian ones, came forward. They were ignored. No Certificate of Concession was obtained, though the regulations say a concession without one “shall be void.” No summary of terms was published. No county consultations were held. Liberian officials even made their due-diligence trip to Austria at OeSD’s expense, vetting a company that was paying their way.

WHAT EMERGED WAS a contract that would have handed a private company the exclusive power to assign every Liberian’s national ID number. It would have made paid verification mandatory for banking, SIM cards, permits and the courts. It would have sent disputes to London and waived the Republic’s immunity over its assets abroad. It would have charged nearly $20 million for a data center Liberia does not need, when LIBTELCO already has one. And it would have done all this without requiring that Liberians’ fingerprints and faces be stored in Liberia, or that the government hold the keys to them.

THE CONTRACT EVEN contained a clause letting the parties waive legislative ratification. Chapters on data protection, anti-corruption and state auditing that appeared in a January 2026 draft were gone by the time it was signed.



THIS WAS NOT carelessness. Mistakes do not repeat themselves at every step, each time in the same direction. A process that ignores the regulator twice, shuts out every competitor and quietly deletes the safeguards is a process designed to avoid scrutiny.

PRESIDENT JOSEPH NYUMA Boakai approved this agreement and sent it to the Legislature in July. Sources tell this newspaper he was badly misled by those who brought it to him. We are prepared to believe that. A President cannot read every annex. He must rely on the people around him to tell him the truth.

BUT IF THE President was misled, then someone misled him. And the people who did so are still in place.

THE HOUSE SHOULD adopt the committee’s report and reject the deal in full. That is only the first step. Killing a bad contract does nothing to fix the process that produced it, or to stop the same people from trying again under a new name.

WE THEREFORE CALL on the President to act on three fronts.

FIRST, ORDER AN independent review of how this concession was put together. It should establish who decided to bypass the PPCC, who signed the May 2025 contract, who approved the OeSD-funded trip to Austria and who removed the safeguards from the January draft. The General Auditing Commission and the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission are equipped to do this work, and the findings should be made public.

SECOND, HOLD ACCOUNTABLE those responsible. Officials who knowingly ignored a binding order of the procurement regulator, or who put a deal before the President without telling him it had been rejected, should be suspended while the review runs. Where the review finds wrongdoing, they should be dismissed and, if the law was broken, prosecuted. A government that came to power promising to rescue Liberia from impunity cannot let this pass with a quiet withdrawal.

THIRD, START OVER, the right way. That means open international bidding, as the PPCC ordered more than a year ago. It means a real value-for-money test that weighs upgrading the systems Liberia already owns. It means fair room for Liberian technology firms. And it means firm guarantees, written into the contract, that Liberians’ biometric data stays in Liberia under Liberian control.

THE REGISTRY’S LEADERSHIP owes the public answers too. This newspaper has put detailed questions to the NIR. We are still waiting.

MEANWHILE, ID CARD issuance has been suspended since June 2025. Liberians still need the card to bank, register a SIM card and get basic services. They have waited long enough for a working system. They should not also be asked to pay for one built to dodge the rules.

THE HOUSE COMMITTEE has done its part. Now it is the President’s turn. He should find out who tried to slip this deal past him, and past the Liberian people, and make sure it never happens again

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Hails Diaspora Medical Mission, Welcomes 100-Surgery Annual Cardiac Care Plan
World.content:
MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has praised Hands International for its humanitarian medical intervention in Liberia, describing the organization’s contribution as a significant boost to the country’s healthcare delivery system.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The President made the remarks Wednesday, November 18, during an appreciation and farewell ceremony at the Executive Mansion, marking the conclusion of a seven-day free international medical and surgical mission conducted at the 14 Military Hospital.



The mission, which brought together more than 60 visiting medical professionals, provided free consultations, specialized treatments, and surgical interventions to thousands of Liberians.

According to the 14 Military Hospital, the team performed more than 46 surgical procedures without recording a single death, while providing services to over 1,800 patients and conducting more than 4,000 medical encounters.

President Boakai particularly commended members of the delegation, many of whom he described as “retired but not tired,” for returning to Liberia to use their professional expertise in service to humanity.

He also welcomed the organization’s plans to establish a sustainable cardiac care program in Liberia, with a target of performing 100 heart surgeries for children annually.



The President described the decision to return to Liberia and offer specialized medical services as more than an ordinary humanitarian intervention, saying it demonstrated genuine love and concern for fellow human beings.

“One thing you’re going to do when you leave here is that this community and the people you have met will now live in your mind,” President Boakai told the delegation.

He also renewed his appeal to Liberians in the diaspora to regard the country not simply as a place to visit occasionally but as their home, where they can invest their time, skills, and resources to support national development.

Cardiac Care Initiative

Meanwhile, Dr. Reynold S. Agard, President of Hands International and head of the visiting delegation, announced that the organization intends to work with local health authorities and cardiology specialists to establish a sustainable cardiac care program.

Dr. Agard said the decision followed concerning findings during the medical mission, which revealed cases of dangerously high blood pressure, untreated heart conditions, and other potentially life-threatening cardiovascular diseases.

He said the organization intends to strengthen Liberia’s local capacity to diagnose and treat heart conditions, particularly among children, drawing on lessons from its previous interventions in Nigeria.

The proposed target of 100 children’s heart surgeries annually could provide critical intervention for families facing limited access to specialized cardiac treatment.

However, the initiative would require sustained collaboration with local medical institutions, specialists, and health authorities to build the capacity needed to deliver the services.

Government Commends Intervention

Earlier, Minister of State for Presidential Affairs Samuel A. Stevquoah welcomed the delegation to the Executive Mansion and expressed the government’s appreciation for its contribution to Liberia’s healthcare sector.

“Liberia welcomes you and we thank you for your service to the Liberian people,” Stevquoah said.

President Boakai welcomed the organization’s plans to establish a sustainable cardiac care program in Liberia, with a target of performing 100 heart surgeries for children annually.

He described the mission’s contribution as impactful and deserving of national appreciation.

In special remarks, Defense Minister Cllr. Oswald Natu Tweh also expressed gratitude to the delegation, noting that the mission responded to President Boakai’s call for Liberians in the diaspora to return home and contribute their expertise to national development.

“Liberia has strengthened its defense in health, and the military is a force for good,” Tweh said.

He expressed pride that the 14 Military Hospital was selected to host the medical mission, which provided what he described as critically needed healthcare services.

Diaspora Connection

Mrs. Christine Neyor, who helped facilitate the mission through her longstanding relationship with Dr. Agard, her primary care physician, described the intervention as one of the largest medical missions ever undertaken in Liberia.

She said she and her husband, Hon. Christopher Neyor, leveraged their longstanding relationship with Dr. Agard to bring the team to Liberia and provide free medical services to residents.

Also speaking, Erasmus T. Williams, Head of the Diaspora Affairs Office at the Executive Mansion, praised Hands International for its contribution and expressed hope that the organization would return to Liberia in the near future.

Mission’s Impact

Providing an overview of the mission’s activities, Captain Dr. Augustine Kollie of the 14 Military Hospital said the visiting team operated in Liberia from November 8 to 14, 2026.

He reported that the team performed more than 46 surgical procedures with zero mortality, served over 1,800 patients, and recorded more than 4,000 medical encounters.

Hands International is a nonprofit humanitarian organization that provides healthcare assistance to underserved communities and promotes sustainable community transformation through partnerships and international collaboration.

As a symbolic gesture of appreciation, President Boakai presented Liberian seal lapel pins to members of the visiting delegation. Dr. Agard was also presented with traditional Liberian attire in recognition of his leadership and the organization’s humanitarian contribution.

World.title: Boakai Seeks Specialized Family Courts Across Liberia to Protect Children, Resolve Domestic Disputes
World.content:
The proposed legislation also seeks to amend relevant provisions of the Judiciary Law, the Civil Procedure Law, and the Domestic Relations Law, while providing for the establishment of a specialized Family Court in each county of the Republic.

MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has submitted a proposed legislation seeking to establish specialized Family Courts across Liberia to strengthen the protection of children and improve the resolution of family-related disputes.

By Obediah Johnson

The bill, titled the Family Court Act of Liberia, was submitted to the Liberian Senate on Thursday, November 19.



The proposed legislation also seeks to amend relevant provisions of the Judiciary Law, the Civil Procedure Law, and the Domestic Relations Law, while providing for the establishment of a specialized Family Court in each county of the Republic.

In a letter accompanying the submission, President Boakai said the proposed Act comprehensively outlines the court’s jurisdiction, powers, structure, and other related matters.

He said the legislation is intended to improve judicial efficiency by creating a specialized forum to handle civil and quasi-criminal family matters.

According to the President, establishing the courts would help reduce case backlogs in Circuit and Magisterial Courts while ensuring the timely adjudication of disputes.



The proposed law also places emphasis on child protection and family welfare, with the President highlighting the need to prioritize the best interests of children as provided under the Children’s Law of 2011.

It would establish legal mechanisms for handling matters involving child custody, guardianship, adoption, child protection, and rehabilitation.

Beyond judicial efficiency, President Boakai said the proposed legislation would promote social stability by addressing family disputes that have historically undermined community cohesion.

He noted that the specialized courts would provide holistic interventions integrating legal, social, and psychological support to help resolve family conflicts and promote unity and stability.

“The Act ensures constitutional compliance, aligning with Article 65 of the Constitution, which vests the Judiciary with authority to interpret laws and resolve disputes, while granting the Legislature the power to establish specialized courts,” the President stated.

Boakai described the proposed Family Court as a significant step toward modernizing Liberia’s judicial system, emphasizing that disputes affecting children and families require a more sensitive, efficient, and fair approach.

He said the establishment of the courts would strengthen the rule of law and advance social justice throughout the country.

“I respectfully request the Legislature to give due consideration to this Act and enact it into law in the interest of the Liberian people,” President Boakai stated.

Meanwhile, the proposed legislation has been forwarded to the Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights, Claims and Petition for legislative scrutiny.

World.title: Africa Surf Tour Returns to Liberia, Pays Tribute to Late Surfer Brahema Gross
World.content:
Liberia will host the continental surfing festival for the second time from December 10–13, 2026, bringing together surfers and sporting enthusiasts from across Africa and beyond for four days of competition, music, cultural exchange, and a tribute to late Liberian surfer Brahema Gross.

MONROVIA — Liberia is preparing to host the Annual Africa Surf Tour for the second time, with the four-day festival scheduled for December 10–13, 2026, at RLJ Resorts in Monrovia.

According to a press release issued by the organizers, the event will bring together surfers, sporting enthusiasts, international partners, and tourism stakeholders from across Africa and beyond to celebrate surfing, promote unity, and strengthen relationships within the African sporting community.



The tour returns to Liberia following its inaugural continental edition in Robertsport, Grand Cape Mount County, in 2024, which placed the country at the center of Africa’s emerging surfing movement.

This year’s event will move from the renowned surfing destination of Robertsport to the nation’s capital, Monrovia.

A major highlight of the gathering will be a tribute to the memory of Liberia’s own Brahema Gross, whose legacy the organizers say will be celebrated through the sport that connects people, cultures, and nations across the continent.

Oumar Seye, President of the Africa Surfing Confederation (ASC), expressed excitement about returning the continental event to Liberia, describing the country as an important part of African surfing history.



“Liberia holds a special place in the history of African surfing as the home of our first-ever Africa Surf Tour in 2024. Returning for our second time is an opportunity to strengthen the bonds within our African surfing family and celebrate what makes this sport so special,” Seye said.

He added that the gathering would also provide an opportunity to honor Gross and recognize the lasting relationships built through the sport.

“Africa is one surfing family, and Liberia is an important part of that family,” he stated.

Representative Naquetta Ricks, President of the Liberia Surfing Association, welcomed the return of the tour, describing it as another milestone for Liberia’s surfing community.

She said hosting the inaugural edition in Robertsport in 2024 was a historic moment for the country, while bringing the second edition to Monrovia would further showcase Liberia’s place in African surfing.

“This year’s tour is especially meaningful because we will be bringing the African surfing community together to pay tribute to our own Brahema Gross. His memory will live on through the sport that unites us,” Ricks said.

She invited African and international surfing communities to participate in the festival, celebrate their shared passion, and experience Liberia’s hospitality.

Beyond the sporting competition, the Annual Africa Surf Tour is expected to promote youth participation, cultural exchange, and stronger relationships among African surfing nations.

The organizers also see the event as an opportunity to showcase Liberia’s potential as a destination for sports and coastal tourism, citing its coastline, vibrant communities, and growing surfing culture.

The Liberia Surfing Association, in collaboration with the Africa Surfing Confederation, is inviting surfers, international partners, media institutions, tourism stakeholders, and members of the public to attend the gathering.

The four-day festival will run from December 10 to 13 at RLJ Resorts in Monrovia.

For media inquiries, the organizers listed Dr. Clarice Ford-Kulah of the Liberia Surfing Association as the contact person at 404 200 7789 via WhatsApp.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai to Take Seafarers’ Safety Fight to UN Security Council Amid Rising Maritime Threats
World.content:
MARSHALL, Margibi County — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has pledged to use Liberia’s upcoming Presidency of the United Nations Security Council to push for stronger international protection of seafarers caught in armed conflicts and other maritime security threats.

By Edwin G. Genoway, Jr.

Speaking Thursday at the Marshall High-Level Dialogue on Global Maritime Safety, Security and Welfare of Seafarers at the Liberia Maritime Training Institute in Marshall City, Margibi County, President Boakai said Liberia’s position on the Security Council presents an important opportunity to influence global discussions on maritime safety and international peace.



Liberia is expected to assume the rotating presidency of the UN Security Council on December 3, 2026, marking its return to the Council’s leadership for the first time in more than six decades.

The President disclosed that his government intends to use the opportunity to draw international attention to the dangers confronting civilian seafarers in conflict zones, including through a high-level open debate at the United Nations.

He stressed that seafarers are ordinary workers who transport goods across international waters and should never be treated as participants in armed conflicts.

“They sign on to deliver cargo, not to go to war,” President Boakai said.



He warned that armed conflicts, piracy, drug trafficking, illegal fishing, cyberattacks, and other criminal activities continue to threaten maritime transportation and the lives of people working at sea.

The President emphasized that seafarers, including cooks, engineers, deck officers, and captains, are civilians who deserve protection under international humanitarian law.

“When the sea is calm and safe, Liberia thrives. When it is troubled, our national security is threatened,” he said.

Liberia’s Maritime Responsibility

President Boakai also highlighted Liberia’s position as the world’s largest maritime registry by tonnage, with more than 300 million gross tons registered under its flag.

He said Liberia’s responsibility extends beyond the commercial benefits of operating one of the world’s largest ship registries to ensuring the safety and welfare of people working aboard vessels flying its flag.

“Our flag is not just a business. Every ship flying the Liberian flag carries our name and our pride. The people on board, in a real sense, are under our care,” he added.

He called for stronger international cooperation to facilitate medical evacuations, crew changes, and the safe return of seafarers stranded in conflict-affected areas.

The Liberian leader also underscored the need to strengthen the country’s Coast Guard, fisheries authority, maritime institutions, and justice system to improve its capacity to respond to maritime threats and prosecute criminals operating in its waters.

On regional security, Boakai called for closer cooperation among countries in the Gulf of Guinea, stressing that no single country can effectively secure the region’s maritime space alone.

He reaffirmed Liberia’s commitment to working with ECOWAS, neighboring countries, and international partners under the Yaoundé Code of Conduct.

Liberia Eyes High-Level UN Debate

Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti, who delivered the keynote address, described maritime security as critical to Liberia’s national interests and the stability of the global economy.

She noted that approximately 80 percent of global trade by volume is transported by sea, making the safety of shipping routes essential to the movement of food, fuel, medicine, and other basic commodities.

Nyanti warned that attacks on commercial vessels and disruptions along major shipping routes can increase the cost of goods and affect ordinary people, including those living far from coastal communities.

She identified piracy, armed robbery at sea, and illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing as major threats to national revenue, local markets, and food security.

The Foreign Minister further noted that nearly two million seafarers keep global supply chains moving but continue to face kidnapping, attacks, abandonment, and other dangers while performing their duties.

Drawing from her personal experience traveling by vessel between Aden and Djibouti, Nyanti recalled the security precautions taken aboard ships amid threats from Somali pirates, including briefings on safe rooms and citadels.

She disclosed that Liberia had launched a “Group of Friends” initiative with India in New York to promote international discussions on maritime security and shipping safety.

Nyanti also announced that Liberia intends to convene a high-level debate on maritime security at the UN Security Council on December 3, 2026, under President Boakai’s chairmanship.

She said Liberia would use its position to amplify the concerns of coastal and flag states while working with the International Maritime Organization and regional partners to strengthen maritime security.

UN Warns Maritime Insecurity Affects All Nations

The United Nations Resident Coordinator in Liberia, Christiane N. Umutoni, said maritime security should not be regarded as an issue affecting only countries with coastlines.

She explained that landlocked countries also depend on the sea because international trade, communication systems, energy supplies, and food security are closely connected to maritime activities.

“We are all maritime nations, whether we have a coastline or not, because we all depend on the sea,” Umutoni said.

She pointed to the importance of oceans in supporting global trade and hosting critical infrastructure, including undersea communication cables and gas pipelines.

Umutoni warned that piracy, human and narcotics trafficking, illegal fishing, cyber threats, and environmental crimes have consequences that extend far beyond coastal communities.

According to her, attacks on shipping routes, illegal fishing, and damage to undersea cables can disrupt the availability of medicine, internet services, fuel, and other essential supplies.

She reaffirmed the United Nations’ commitment to supporting Liberia in maritime governance, regional cooperation, security, peacebuilding, development, and environmental protection.

She identified the International Maritime Organization, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, the UN Development Programme, and other international institutions as important partners in addressing maritime challenges.

Umutoni also urged cadets at the Liberia Maritime Training Institute to recognize that their professional responsibilities extend beyond operating vessels, as they will play an important role in protecting the global maritime system.

Maritime Authority Raises Alarm Over Seafarers’ Safety

Earlier, Commissioner of the Liberia Maritime Authority, Cllr. Neto Zarzar Lighe, welcomed participants on behalf of the Authority and the Liberia Maritime Training Institute.

Lighe thanked the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for collaborating in organizing the dialogue, describing it as an important part of Liberia’s preparations for its upcoming presidency of the UN Security Council.

He emphasized that shipping remains central to the transportation of essential commodities, including fuel and rice, while seafarers constitute the human force behind the global maritime industry.

The Commissioner identified the Black Sea, Red Sea, Strait of Hormuz, and Gulf of Guinea as areas where armed conflicts, piracy, cyberattacks, and drug smuggling continue to expose seafarers to serious risks.

Citing reports from the Liberia Maritime Authority and the International Maritime Organization, Lighe said there had been approximately 100 attacks or attempted attacks on commercial vessels, resulting in the deaths of at least 25 seafarers.

He also referred to United Nations estimates indicating that approximately 6,000 seafarers were stranded in conflict regions.

“Beyond every number is a human being,” Lighe said.

He highlighted the human consequences of maritime insecurity, including families waiting anxiously for loved ones, children growing up while their fathers are away at sea, and young officers performing their duties under the constant threat of attacks.

Lighe stressed that seafarers did not create the conflicts threatening their lives and should not become forgotten victims of violence at sea.

He called for stronger international cooperation, noting that no single government or institution can effectively address the growing threats confronting the maritime industry.

The dialogue was held under the theme, “Enhancing Global Maritime Security and the Welfare of Seafarers for International Peace and Shared Prosperity in a Period of Heightened Insecurity.”

It also marked the inaugural celebration of Liberian Maritime Week, bringing together government officials, international partners, maritime professionals, and cadets to discuss strategies for improving maritime safety, security, and seafarers’ welfare.

In his closing remarks, President Boakai urged cadets to take their training seriously, assuring them that Liberia would continue to advocate for the safety and welfare of seafarers around the world.

He subsequently declared the Marshall High-Level Dialogue officially open.

World.title: Liberia Turns Commitment into Action as Steering Committee Adopts Landmark Resolutions for Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum
World.content:
L-R: Madam Hadja Mamaka Bility, Minister of State without Portfolio and Chairperson of the Steering Committee, President Joseph Boakai and co-chair Ambassador Aliou Mamadou Dia, UNDP Resident Representative.

Monrovia – Liberia has taken a major step forward in its journey from remembrance to reconciliation with the adoption of a set of landmark resolutions that lay the foundation for the establishment of the Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum.

The resolutions, adopted during the First Steering Committee Meeting held in Monrovia from 16-18 November 2026, transform a national vision into a concrete implementation roadmap and reaffirm Liberia’s determination to preserve its history, honor victims and survivors, and strengthen peace for future generations.

The outcomes of the meeting build on the vision articulated by Joseph Nyumah Boakai, President of Liberia, during the launch of the National Historical Recovery Initiative.



President Boakai stressed that the Museum must place victims and survivors at the center of the national healing process and serve as a space where Liberia confronts its history honestly while building a more peaceful future. The resolutions adopted in Monrovia translate that vision into concrete actions and institutional commitments.

“This Museum must not simply tell the story of our past; it must help shape the future we seek. The experiences of victims and survivors must guide this process, ensuring that remembrance becomes a bridge to healing, reconciliation and lasting peace,” the Liberian Leader stressed.

Convened under the leadership of Hon. Hadja Mamaka Bility, Minister of State without Portfolio and Chairperson of the Steering Committee, and co-chaired by Ambassador Aliou Mamadou Dia, UNDP Resident Representative, the meeting brought together government institutions, civil society organizations, victims and survivors, women’s and youth groups, traditional and religious leaders, development partners and international experts committed to advancing one of Liberia’s most significant nation-building initiatives.

Following three days of deliberations, the Steering Committee endorsed the Project Charter as the foundational framework for implementation, formally confirmed the institution’s name as the Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum, adopted a Performance Measurement Baseline Plan through December 2027, approved a comprehensive budget framework, and endorsed a 90-day action plan to accelerate implementation. These resolutions establish the governance, accountability and operational mechanisms required to move the initiative from concept to reality.



A significant outcome was the formal establishment of five Technical Working Groups responsible for the Museum’s core pillars, including historical narrative development, archives and memorialization, governance and legal frameworks, architecture and design, and education, reconciliation and public engagement.

Together, these groups will ensure that the Museum reflects Liberia’s diverse histories and provides an inclusive platform for preserving memory and promoting dialogue.

Addressing the meeting, Hon. Hadja Mamaka Bility described the resolutions as a turning point in Liberia’s effort to preserve its historical legacy and advance reconciliation.

“What we have achieved here is more than the adoption of resolutions. We have laid the foundation for a national institution that will safeguard our history, honor the dignity of victims and survivors, and help future generations understand the cost of conflict and the value of peace.”

The Steering Committee also endorsed a resource mobilization and financing strategy requiring contributions from government, the United Nations system, bilateral and multilateral partners, foundations, the private sector and the Liberian diaspora.

The collective financing framework reflects broad national and international support for the initiative and a shared recognition of its importance to Liberia’s long-term peacebuilding efforts.

For Aliou Mamadou Dia, UNDP Resident Representative and Co-Chair of the Steering Committee, the resolutions demonstrate Liberia’s determination to transform memory into a force for national renewal.

“A memorial museum is not only about remembering the past. It is about ensuring that the lessons of history guide future generations. Through these resolutions, Liberia is creating a platform where truth, education, dialogue and reconciliation can come together to strengthen peace and national unity.”

The meeting further endorsed an international technical cooperation framework involving Rwanda, South Africa, the University of South Africa (UNISA) and UNDP, enabling Liberia to benefit from global experiences in memorialization, reconciliation and institutional development.

The Committee also directed the Secretariat to conclude cooperation arrangements and establish mechanisms for knowledge exchange and technical support.

The resolutions adopted at the close of the meeting capture a shared conviction that the Museum must be more than a physical structure. It must become a living institution that preserves collective memory, encourages reflection, promotes civic education and fosters dialogue across generations.

It also reaffirms that women, youth, persons with disabilities, traditional leaders and marginalized communities must have meaningful roles in shaping the Museum’s development and future programming.

Ultimately, the resolutions adopted by the Steering Committee represent more than administrative decisions. They are a declaration of national intent. They signal Liberia’s commitment to confronting its history with honesty, honoring those affected by conflict with dignity, and creating a lasting institution that transforms remembrance into reconciliation, learning into understanding, and memory into a foundation for enduring peace.

As Liberia embarks on the implementation phase of this historic initiative, the message emerging from Monrovia is clear: the country is not merely preserving its past; it is investing in a future built on truth, healing, inclusion and hope.

World.title: Chipepo hails Zesco team effort after Arrows win
World.content:
Zesco United coach Mwenya Chipepo has praised his players for their team effort following Thursday’s 2-1 win over Red Arrows as the Super Division campaign gets tense.

The victory was Zesco’s second home win of the transitional campaign and an important result in Stream B of the Super League.

Chipepo said overcoming Arrows was not easy, given their pedigree.

“We are very happy to beat the Red Arrows. Beating Red Arrows is not easy,” Chipepo said.

“They are playing in the group stage of the CAF Confederation Cup; they have experienced players and a good coach.”

“We are very happy to pick three points. Every player is putting in effort,” he said.

The match was also a farewell for Captain Lindo Mkhonta, who is leaving the club after joining in 2023.

Mkhonta was given a guard of honour before kick-off, in recognition of four years of service to the Ndola-based side.

It proved to be a fitting send-off for the captain, as Zesco secured maximum points.

“We are going to miss such a leader. He has done well for the club,” Chipepo said.

“He is respectful and disciplined. We pray to have another player of such a caliber,” he said.

World.title: Kangwa confident Chipolopolo will qualify for AFCON
World.content:
Chipolopolo vice-captain Kings Kangwa has expressed confidence that Zambia will qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, AFCON, despite a difficult qualifying campaign.

Zambia’s hopes suffered a setback after a 1-1 draw against Burundi away in Bujumbura on Tuesday, on match-day four.

Coach George Lwandamina’s team has now collected five points from a possible 12, after one win, two draws and one defeat.

Zambia has dropped from second to third place in Group I after Togo beat Algeria 3-0 later on Tuesday night.

Algeria tops Group I with seven points, followed by Togo on six, Zambia on five and Burundi on three. The top two teams will qualify for the 2027 AFCON to be hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

Zambia has two matches remaining – at home against Algeria and away to Togo between 22 and 30 March 2027.

Kangwa, who missed Zambia’s first three qualifying games due to suspension before returning against Burundi, said the team will give everything to qualify.

*“It is always an honour to represent my country. Hard one to take from Tuesday’s game, but we keep pushing. We have two important games remaining and we will give everything we have, fight until the end and do our very best to secure our place at AFCON 2027. Thank you for the support.”

Kangwa also saluted Zambia captain Fashion Sakala, who announced his international retirement after the match against Burundi.

Sakala announced his retirement on Facebook, describing captaining Chipolopolo as among the proudest moments of his life.

Kangwa said: “Thank you, our captain, Fashion Sakala, for your leadership and everything you’ve given to the national team. It’s been a privilege sharing the pitch with you, Mafasho!”

Meanwhile, Zambia striker Albert Kangwanda said Chipolopolo will fight hard to qualify.

He said: “I am always proud to don the national team colours. With two more games, we will fight with everything in us to qualify and make the nation proud.”

World.title: Hichilema Reshapes IDC Board, Names Four New Directors And Drops Three
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has appointed four new members to the board of the Industrial Development Corporation (IDC) and terminated the appointments of three others, reshaping the leadership of the State’s main investment and holding company.

The new members are Ms Helen Mutinta Samatebele, Ms Inutu Zaloumis, Mr Basil Nundwe and Mr Chintu Mulendema. Leaving the board are Mr Windu Matoka, Ms Beatrice Nkanza and Mr Edson Hamakowa.

The changes were announced in a statement issued by State House Chief Communications Specialist Clayson Hamasaka, who said the Head of State had thanked the outgoing members for their work at the corporation.

“President Hichilema thanks the outgoing members of the board for their service and contribution to the Industrial Development Corporation Limited and wishes them well in their future endeavours,” Mr Hamasaka said.

The President also congratulated the incoming directors. He urged them to discharge their responsibilities with diligence, integrity and commitment, in the best interests of the people of Zambia.

The appointments carry particular weight because of how the corporation is governed. Under the IDC’s structure, the sitting President chairs the board of directors, which also includes Cabinet ministers, public servants, private sector members and the Group Chief Executive Officer.

The four new directors therefore join a board that Mr Hichilema himself leads. The board oversees a company wholly owned by Government that holds majority or minority stakes in State-owned enterprises and investee companies across the economy.

The IDC is mandated to drive industrialisation and job creation by building new industries, lowering investment risk and co-investing with private-sector partners to diversify the economy.

Its operations span energy and infrastructure, mining, agriculture and forestry, manufacturing, telecommunications, transport, health, tourism, real estate and financial services.

The new board takes office in a week when the corporation set out the scale of the task facing some of its companies. Appearing before the Parliamentary Committee on Economic Affairs, IDC Acting Chief Executive Officer Raphael Chipoma said Zambia Railways Limited (ZRL) required US$1.7 billion for comprehensive rehabilitation and modernisation, against K553 million allocated in the 2027 national budget.

Mr Chipoma told the committee that ZESCO had been allocated K1.1 billion for capitalisation, while the proposed Development Finance Institution had received K400 million in the same budget. He commended Government for supporting State-owned enterprises but stressed the need for adequate capitalisation for them to fulfil their mandates.

The corporation’s reach also extends into health, where it is a partner, with the Ministry of Health and the American College of Surgeons, in the local kidney transplant programme at the University Teaching Hospital (UTH).

The Head of State’s message to the incoming directors was the same one he gave the outgoing members on their way out: service to the corporation and to the country.

The four new members now take their seats on the board, alongside President Hichilema as chairperson, the Cabinet ministers, the public servants and the Group CEO.

World.title: Forensic Analyst Links Sampa To Facebook Page In ECZ Fake Polling Station Case
World.content:
A digital forensics expert has told the Lusaka Magistrate’s Court that former Matero Member of Parliament Mr Miles Sampa was responsible for a Facebook page that published allegations that the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) had set up an illegal polling station in Chawama Constituency.

Mr Jeff Sitali, manager for digital forensics at the Zambia Cyber Security Agency, gave the evidence before Lusaka Resident Magistrate Webster Milumbe during the continued trial of Mr Sampa, who is facing one count of transmitting unsolicited or deceptive communication.

The charge stems from a social media post published on January 15, 2026. The post alleged that the ECZ had opened a fake polling station on Ring Road in Lusaka and that a Government minister was transporting voters to the facility.

Mr Sitali told the court that he received instructions on January 20, 2026, five days after the post appeared, to conduct data extraction, preservation and analysis on a Facebook page linked to the former lawmaker.

He said the original links provided in the request initially yielded no information. That forced him to go directly to the Facebook page cited in the investigation and work from the page itself.

The witness told the magistrate that he examined the page’s profile details, transparency records and administrative information. His examination established that the page had undergone Meta verification and had been created on October 16, 2012.

Mr Sitali said he then identified posts on the page that corresponded to the dates under investigation, placing the material within the period covered by the charge.

He told the court that although some of the wording in the posts differed, they carried similar allegations. These were that the ECZ had set up an illegal polling station in Chawama and that a minister was transporting voters there.

The forensics manager said screenshots of the posts were taken and preserved before a forensic report on his findings was compiled.

His evidence goes to the central question in the case: who controlled the page that carried the allegations against the electoral body. By tying the verified page and its posts to Mr Sampa, the State is seeking to establish that the former Matero lawmaker was behind the publication.

Mr Sampa has yet to test the evidence. The defence will get its first chance to challenge the analyst’s methods and conclusions under cross-examination.

Magistrate Milumbe adjourned the matter to December 3, 2026, when Mr Sitali is due to return to the witness box for cross-examination.

World.title: More Than K7 Billion Paid To FRA Maize Suppliers, Government Says Balance Is Coming
World.content:
Government has paid more than K7 billion to farmers who supplied maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) during the 2026 crop marketing season. Chief Government Spokesperson Elvis Nkandu assured those still waiting that every outstanding payment will be settled.

Mr Nkandu, who is also Minister of Information and Media, said payments were being processed on a first-come, first-served basis after Parliament approved a K19.9 billion supplementary budget. Of that amount, K14.7 billion was set aside for money owed to farmers.

The payment exercise began on November 13. The Minister said Government remained committed to completing it within the 10 to 15 days announced by President Hakainde Hichilema, and he urged farmers still awaiting their money to remain patient.

The update came when the Government spokesperson appeared on the Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation (ZNBC) Government Forum programme. He used the platform to call on citizens, including the media, to rally behind the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He said Government was shifting its focus from economic stabilisation to accelerated growth through the five-year agenda, which is anchored on increased production. Expanding the country’s gross domestic product (GDP), he said, would translate into improved social welfare, jobs, reduced poverty and better livelihoods for citizens.

He said Government had spent three years restructuring the country’s debt after the 2021 general election, creating the fiscal space to concentrate on economic expansion. Despite the challenges of that period, Government had continued paying retirees and recruiting public service workers.

Mr Nkandu set out the thinking behind the new phase. “After stabilisation, we are now saying, let us grow,” he said. “If we did what we did on the stabilisation part, then we can do even more on the growth part.”

The agenda sets measurable production targets of 10 million metric tonnes of maize, 11,000 megawatts of electricity and annual copper output of three million metric tonnes. The 2025/2026 season has already produced a record maize harvest of 4.94 million tonnes.

The Information Minister said reaching the maize target would create a substantial surplus for export, given that domestic consumption stood below four million metric tonnes. Higher electricity generation, he said, would support industrial growth and employment creation.

He said the production drive was about the country standing on its own feet. “This time around, we would want to be as independent as we can, and you can only be independent when you are able to produce what you can consume and also export more for the growth of your economy,” Mr Nkandu said.

He urged the media to counter misinformation by giving citizens accurate information about Government programmes and policies.

Separately, the Minister met the Zambia Media Women’s Association (ZAMWA) executive committee, led by chairperson Ms Monica Mayuni. He pledged Government’s commitment to addressing poor salaries, delayed payments, job insecurity, gender discrimination, online harassment and limited leadership opportunities in the industry.

He said Government would engage media owners, journalists and other stakeholders to improve working conditions, and pledged to champion a minimum wage for journalists, particularly those in the private media.

On safety, he was direct. “No journalist, male or female, should be harassed, threatened or attacked for doing their work. That is unacceptable,” Mr Nkandu said, urging ZAMWA to document cases of harassment and report them to the relevant authorities.

Ms Mayuni called for improved remuneration, professional training, international exposure and more women in media leadership.

For maize farmers still waiting, Government’s position is unchanged. Payments continue in the order claims were received, funded by the K14.7 billion approved by Parliament, within the window set by President Hichilema.

World.title: Brilliant but broke: what is Government’s plan for the children left out of HELSB?
World.content:
Every year, thousands of Zambian children work hard, pass their Grade 12, get admitted to UNZA, CBU, Mulungushi, Mukuba, Chalimbana and other public universities, and then they hit a wall.

Not because they failed. Not because they are not brilliant. But because they are poor, and the Higher Education Loans and Scholarships Board (HELSB) has no money for them.

Government loves to announce how many loans it has awarded. It rarely announces how many it has left behind. Let us look at Government’s own numbers.

The numbers Government does not want you to see

At UNZA for 2025/2026, HELSB received 5,798 applications. Of those, 4,929 (85%) met the eligibility criteria. They were poor enough, brilliant enough, young enough, and had the right documents. But only 3,926 were awarded loans.

That means 1,003 fully eligible students at UNZA alone were left out. One thousand and three children who did everything right, and were told: sorry, there is no money for you.

At Chalimbana University, it was worse. HELSB received 1,687 applications. 1,469 were eligible. Only 492 were awarded. That means 977 eligible students, two out of every three, were abandoned.

At Kwame Nkrumah and Mukuba combined, 1,270 were awarded. At Levy Mwanawasa Medical University, 452 were awarded out of 533 applications. At Palabana, 186 out of 239.

In total, HELSB says it awarded 16,273 new student loans in 2025, supporting 45,091 beneficiaries. That sounds big, until HELSB’s own Chief Executive, Dr John Machayi, admitted the truth in Livingstone in October 2026: approximately 45.3% of student financing requests went unmet in the previous academic year due to budgetary constraints.

Almost half. Almost half of our children who asked for help were turned away.

Eligible, but left to suffer

We must be clear about what ‘eligible but not awarded’ means. It does not mean the child failed. It means the child passed, the child is vulnerable, the child qualifies, but Government’s pot is empty. So what happens to that child?

She goes home to a village in Kaputa with an admission letter she cannot use. He defers for a year, then another year, then gives up and starts pushing a wheelbarrow in Lusaka.

A brilliant girl who could have been a doctor becomes a maid. A brilliant boy who could have been an engineer becomes a call boy at a bus station. This is how Zambia kills its own future, quietly, one rejected loan at a time.

And for those who do get a loan, the pain does not end. They are given only 25%, 50%, 75% or 100% of tuition, depending on how vulnerable HELSB judges them to be.

If you get 25%, where does a poor family find the other 75%? If you get 50%, where does a widow find the other half? Government calls this ‘support’. For many families, it is still a death sentence for their child’s dream.

The cruel rules that lock children out

Even before the money runs out, the rules themselves lock out thousands. If you finished Grade 12 before 2020 or 2021, you are out, even if you were looking after your sick mother. If you are over 26, you are out, even if poverty delayed your schooling.

If you made one mistake on your documents, if your scan was unclear, if you missed one parent’s NRC, you are out. If you already got a loan at another university, you are out.

These are not rules for helping the vulnerable. These are rules for finding reasons to say NO.

And what about the children who never even apply because they know they cannot afford the internet to apply online, or cannot get a guarantor, or cannot get to Lusaka to appeal? They are invisible in the statistics, but they are real.

My questions to Government

I am not writing this to insult HELSB staff. They are working with what they have. I am writing to ask Government, the people who control the budget, direct questions.

1. What is your plan for the 1,003 eligible students left out at UNZA, and the 977 left out at Chalimbana, and the thousands more across Zambia?

Do you have a supplementary budget? A second intake? A CDF bursary guarantee? Or are you just going to let them stay home?

2. When will you increase funding from K1.8 billion to match the real demand?

Government disbursements grew from K558 million in 2021 to K1.8 billion in 2025, and the loan portfolio is now past K10 billion. That is progress, but it is not enough when 45.3% are still unmet. Why is education still getting only 13.4% of the budget when you claim it is a priority?

3. What about the brilliant child who gets 25% or 50% and cannot find the rest?

Will you top them up? Will you allow universities to let them learn as they pay? Or will you watch them drop out in second year?

4. What about scholarships, not just loans?

A loan is a debt. A poor child should not have to start adult life in debt at 15% compound interest, with deductions chasing them even when they have no job. Where are the full government scholarships for orphans, for children with disabilities, for top performers from rural schools?

5. What about CDF?

Government boasts about Constituency Development Fund bursaries. But in many constituencies, CDF bursaries are late, politicised, or too small. Can you publish, constituency by constituency, how many students CDF actually helped, and how much they got?

We cannot afford to waste brilliance

Zambia is a poor country, but we are not poor in talent. Our talent is in those villages, in those compounds, in those crowded classrooms where a child studies by candlelight and still gets 6 points.

When we deny that child a loan, we are not saving money. We are losing a doctor, a teacher, an engineer, a nurse, a scientist. We are losing the very people who could lift Zambia out of poverty.

I am calling on Government to:

Publish the full national picture (how many applied, how many were eligible, how many were awarded, and how many were left out) for every university. Create an emergency fund for all eligible-but-not-awarded students. Move from loans to full scholarships for the extremely vulnerable. Reform HELSB’s harsh age and sitting-year rules. Scrap the 15% compound interest that turns help into bondage.

Our children did their part. They passed. They got admitted. They applied. Now Government must do its part.

What is your plan for them?

By H.E. Ms Saboi Imboela

President, National Democratic Congress (NDC)

19 November 2026

World.title: Non-compliance of labour laws worries Kalomo DC
World.content:
Kalomo District Commissioner, Joshua Sikaduli, has expressed concern of non-compliance of the stipulated labour laws by some white commercial farmers in the area.

Mr Sikaduli notes that some farm workers have been subjected to work in un-environmentally friendly places, placing them in several hazardous situations.

Speaking during a radio special programme on Namwianga radio, Mr Sikaduli says most farm workers in Kalomo are forced to work without protective gear, poor sanitation and being offered low wages alongside matters of child labour and prodded the District Labour Department to serious look into the matter to safeguard the human rights of those affected.

“I have received reports of poor wages, no protective gear and ill treatment of workers from these commercial farmers and am directing the labour department to intensify inspections in these farms and ensure that labour laws are followed,” Mr Sikaduli said.

Among the most complaints by farm workers include low wages, long working hours and transport allowances, health safety, indiscriminate dismissals, and other statutory obligations such as contributing to social security schemes.

The minimum wage for domestic workers under the employment code Act no. 3 of 2019 and Statutory Instrument no. 49 of 2023 which took effect on January 1, 2024 is pegged at K1,300.00 per month; broken down as K1,100.00 as a wage and K200.00 as transport allowance, if not provided by the employer.

Nevertheless, a separate snap check among several farm workers in nearby farms revealed that workers were getting below 1,300.00 per month depending on their scope of work and job roles in the farmsteads.

And District Labour Officer, Samson Shapola, said every worker is entitled to K57.00 per every working day but laments that most farm workers are illiterate to fully understand their statutory obligations hence the friction between the employees and employers in the farmsteads.

World.title: Avic International agrees to partially open Sakanya Border
World.content:
Avic International, the contractor working on the Ndola-Sakania- Mufulira road has agreed to the request by the government to partially open the border facility so that truckers can utilise the truck park area.

Speaking after inspecting the road, Minister of Infrastructure and Urban Development, Collins Nzovu, was concerned with the congestion of trucks headed to Sakania Border noting that it poses both public and health risks such as cholera.

Mr Nnzovu emphasised that partially opening the Border will decongest the Ndola-Sakanya road and provide proper sanitary facilities for truck drivers.

The Minister noted that as talks to find lasting solutions on ways of decongesting the roads with the neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo, there is need to park in an area where there are proper sanitation facilities.

He described the quick completion of the Border post as a matter of an emergency to assist the drivers.

“As a matter of emergency, we are asking Avic International to accelerate the completion of that infrastructure so that we help our truckers with proper toilets and shower rooms,” he noted.

The contractor, AVIC International, has since agreed to the request, on condition that the Road Development Agency (RDA) inspects the area.

Avic International Deputy Project Manager, Jack Huang, revealed that the truck parking lot can accommodate about 300 trucks and provides refreshment facilities for drivers.

He noted that the truck park which is at about 95 percent completion will be officially handed over before the end of December this year.

Earlier, during the inspection of the Ndola-Sakanya-Mufulira road, the Road Development Agency (RDA) Director and Chief Executive Officer said that the defects on the road were quickly rectified and the project is on course.

Mr Chuma highlighted that the Agency is closely monitoring the project through an expert to ensure that it meets the standards.
