World.title: Africa: Africa's Just Transition Ambitions Face Hurdles At COP31
World.content:
Antalya, TÃ¼rkiye — Valepi Banda still remembers the day she lost dozens of chickens in June last year in Zambia's capital, Lusaka, after the heating system failed due to power cuts.

The southern African nation was experiencing load-shedding schedules lasting eight hours a day, and the 22-year-old poultry farmer had no backup power.

Zambia, which relies on hydropower plants, was struggling after consecutive droughts caused low water levels in Lake Kariba, its largest, triggering a power crisis.

"We created a timetable for load shedding, but they never followed it. It made me sluggish," Banda, a student at a university in Zambia, told IPS at the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.



"I was raising some chickens in the backyard. And because broilers need heating every time, most of the chickens died."

Banda has since stopped rearing chickens and is now keeping goats.

"I stopped chicken farming because it was too risky, and I had no buffer," she said.

Countries like Zambia that generate about 90% of their electricity from renewables are banking on the Belém Action Mechanism (BAM), an UNFCCC framework created at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, to support workers, communities, and countries shifting toward low-carbon economies.

For Zambia and Kenya, the challenge involves not only shutting down coal-fired power plants but also expanding renewables and building electricity infrastructure to provide access to affordable electricity for poor communities.

They also want fossil-dependent countries to shift away from dirty fuels because it is their vulnerable communities who suffer from extreme weather events like floods and droughts.

Parties at COP31 in the resort of the Mediterranean country are negotiating about BAM's operational and governance details.

Activists demand a Just Transition Mechanism at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey. Credit: Farai Shawn Matiashe/IPS

Deadlock

Developing countries want a new institution to coordinate global "just transition" efforts as nations shift away from fossil fuels as agreed at COP30 in Belém.

But developed countries are opposing this proposal, insisting that the UNFCCC coordinate the just transition.

Brandon Wu, director of policy and campaigns at ActionAid USA, said that there is no progress on the just transition.

"This is frustrating because that is what they agreed to last year. Certainly, they are worried that it will require resourcing," he said.

"They are afraid that a powerful just transition mechanism will require some financing."

Nona Chai of the Just Transition Alliance, a network of environmental justice groups and local unions tackling polluting extractive industries that harm communities and workers, said the European Union, United Kingdom and Japan are trying to weaken the Just Transition Mechanism and are running away from their responsibility to fund Global South countries.

"That is not acceptable because the whole reason civil society proposed the BAM in the first place is that existing resources are insufficient for a just transition," she said.

"It is sad. It is shameful. It should not be happening. They are reversing course on all the progress that was made on the Belem-Antalya Mechanism at COP 30 last year. It was a historic win for our movements."

Global South Demands Finance, Technical Support for Shifting From Fossil Fuels

Wu said they want a Just Transition Mechanism that provides support for developing nations.

"Whether it is technical support or capacity building. It does not all have to be just money. Money is part of it, but a lot of it is technical support and capacity building for how we design just transition plans, how we plan for changes in the economy so that we are not leaving workers behind," he said.

Chai said that the funding must come as grants to ensure that Global South countries avoid being trapped in debt.

"We need a mechanism that will actually promote grant-based, non-debt-creating funding for Global South countries and affected groups," she said.

Developing nations have often resorted to debt to fund renewable energy projects, adaptation and other mitigation projects. This has left many countries in debt distress.

In 2022, public debt in Africa reached USD 1.8 trillion, according to the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD).

For Banda, she wants a Just Transition Mechanism that can help her country expand renewables to complement hydro power plants exposed to droughts.

"We are looking at how best we can supplement our electricity generation because we are a country that depends on hydroelectricity. And because of the repeated effects of climate change and the drought, we have seen a decrease in the amount that we generate," she said.

Power crisis affects small businesses, and just transition will help them access affordable clean energy, Banda said.

Close 

Africa possesses world-class solar, wind, and hydropower potential, alongside critical minerals needed for clean technologies.

It contains 60% of the world's best solar resources, yet accounts for only about 1% of installed solar PV, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

But about 600 million people lack electricity access, with half of them living in three countries, namely Nigeria, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo, according to the IEA.

Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for roughly 85% of the global population lacking electricity.

Nearly a billion people in Sub-Saharan Africa lack access to modern and clean cooking solutions.

Banda said that on a policy level, the government is trying to diversify its energy mix, but a lack of funding is a setback.

Authorities expect water levels to drop again this year in Lake Kariba, shared between Zimbabwe and Zambia, because of the anticipated El Niño.

"I am already anxious. It is triggering. I do not know how bad it will be," she said.

IPS UN Bureau Report

World.title: Africa: 22 African Countries Face Debt Distress, 14 At High Risk - AfDB
World.content:
The African Development Bank (AfDB) has disclosed that 14 African countries were at high risk of debt distress as of July 2026, while eight others were already in debt distress, highlighting the growing pressure of public borrowing on the continent's economies.

The bank warned that rising debt-service obligations were increasingly constraining governments' fiscal space, limiting their capacity to fund essential services and development priorities.

The disclosure was contained in AfDB's November 2026 report, Africa's Macroeconomic Performance and Outlook, which examined the continent's public debt situation and growing vulnerabilities.

According to the report, the growing reliance of African governments on external commercial and domestic borrowing has driven up debt-service costs and heightened vulnerabilities.



It noted that about $87 billion left the continent in interest costs between 2022 and 2024, equivalent to 19 per cent of total debt-service payments, while interest payments on external debt alone accounted for 6.3 per cent of government revenue in 2024.

The report also disclosed that the share of government revenue allocated to external debt service rose from 23.7 per cent in 2017 to 31 per cent in 2024, reflecting the increasing burden of servicing foreign obligations.

It said the high cost of debt was diverting resources from essential spending on health, education and infrastructure, adding that between 2021 and 2023, 25 of the 51 African countries with available data spent more on interest payments than on healthcare.

The bank identified the changing composition of public debt as another source of vulnerability, noting that African countries were increasingly moving away from concessional financing towards non-Paris Club creditors and non-concessional sources, including Eurobonds, commercial bank loans and syndicated facilities.

It added that several countries had also turned to domestic borrowing in response to growing spending pressures, weak domestic revenue mobilisation and declining access to international financing.

Despite the mounting risks, the AfDB projected that Africa's public debt-to-GDP ratio would decline from an average of 62.6 per cent in 2025 to 60.7 per cent by 2030.

However, it cautioned that the outlook remained vulnerable to weaker economic growth, further increases in interest rates and renewed fiscal profligacy, particularly in commercial borrowing.

The bank called for stronger debt management, more productive use of borrowed funds and timely debt relief for countries already in distress.

It disclosed that six African countries had restructured their debt since 2020 to rebuild fiscal space and secure relief, but said progress under the G20 Common Framework had generally been slow.

World.title: South Africa: Betting Turnover Rises to R1.4-Trillion
World.content:
After paying out winnings, operators kept R84.5-billion

South Africa's betting turnover reached R1.4-trillion in the 2025/26 financial year, according to the National Gambling Board (NGB). That is more than 57 times the R24.5-billion wagered in 2013/14.

Betting includes wagers on sports, horse racing, fixed-odds events and other contingencies through licensed bookmakers and totalizators. The market is dominated by two big names - Betway and Hollywoodbets.



Betting overtook casinos in turnover in 2021/22 and has grown rapidly since. Casino turnover, by comparison, has barely changed over the past 12 years. It rose from R251-billion in 2013/14 to R280-billion in 2025/26, an increase of about 12% before inflation.

This year, casino turnover actually dropped compared with last year, while betting continued to rise rapidly.

Total turnover across all gambling sectors reached R1.76-trillion in 2025/26, up from R1.5-trillion the previous year. This includes every rand wagered, including winnings that are bet again, sometimes repeatedly.

After paying out winnings, operators were left with R84.5-billion in 2025/26, up from R74.5-billion the previous year. Of this, R62.2-billion was from betting alone.

To put it into perspective - gamblers lost R84.5-billion in 2025/26. That same year, the state spent R88-billion on child support grants for almost 13 million children.

Legal loophole

Online casinos in South Africa often say that "all games are fixed-odds betting events". This matters because licensed online betting is generally permitted in South Africa, but online interactive casino gambling is not.

Betting means wagering on an uncertain outcome in the real world, such as a match or a horse race. Licensed bookmakers may take these bets online. Interactive gambling means casino games played online, such as slots, roulette and blackjack. Section 11 of the National Gambling Act bans it. The loophole is that some bookmakers present casino games (for example livestreamed roulette) as fixed-odds "bets" on an outcome.

In October 2025, the Supreme Court of Appeal ruled that bookmakers licensed in Gauteng cannot offer fixed-odds bets on casino games under the Gauteng Gambling Act. But the ruling is specific to Gauteng legislation. It does not apply to other provinces such as the Western Cape, where such bets are currently allowed.

Gambling companies spent about R2.6-billion on advertising in the 12 months to March 2025, according to figures reported by Moneyweb. Hollywoodbets alone spent over R775-million.

In July, World Sports Betting took a cash-prize promotion into a preschool classroom at Cornwall Hill College in Pretoria. After the video caused outrage, the company apologised and withdrew from the campaign.

Betting companies also sponsor or partner with the country's biggest sports teams and events, including the PSL's Betway Premiership, Bafana Bafana, Kaizer Chiefs, Orlando Pirates, the Proteas, the Springboks and the Netball Proteas.

Celebrities who advertise online gambling contribute to this growing societal problem. They make an activity that should, at best, be done prudently seem normal, even glamorous. Eben and Anlia Etzebeth, Cassper Nyovest, Siphiwe Tshabalala, Jimmy Tau, Phumudzo Manenzhe, Herschelle Gibbs and JamJam are among the famous people who shill for an industry that is a threat to health and financial well-being.

Since 2022, the UK has banned sports, TV and social media personalities from advertising gambling. The ban is aimed at protecting under-18s and "other vulnerable groups".

Calling for help?

Meanwhile, the National Responsible Gambling Programme's helpline handled 1,263,470 calls in 2025/26, up 25% from 1,013,626 in 2024/25. In 2023/24, it received just 140,263 calls.

But the increase does not necessarily mean that more gamblers were seeking help for gambling problems.

Close 

According to the NGB, most of the calls came from people trying to reach betting operators about customer-service matters, including account and withdrawal queries. The NGB automatically redirected most of these calls.

GroundUp called the helpline to see how this works. The first prompt is to "press 1 for betting account queries". Pressing 1 leads to a second menu, which asks which gambling operator the caller needs help with. The caller is then redirected to that operator's call centre.

Of the 83,541 calls recorded in the helpline's case-management system in 2025/26, 77% were classified as wrong numbers. These were people who did not press 1, and instead went to an operator from the helpline. Only 5,443 calls were classified as treatment-related.

The NGB said the large volume of unrelated calls increased operating costs, affected staff productivity and could lead to staff fatigue. It said the growing number of calls could be due to the greater visibility of the helpline number in betting-company advertising.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 20, 2026
World.content:
Dozens Missing After Migrant Boat Capsizes Off Senegal

Search operations are continuing off Senegal's Atlantic coast after a boat carrying an estimated 50 to 100 migrants capsized near Yenne, south of Dakar. Four bodies have been recovered, while dozens remain missing. The latest tragedy comes less than two weeks after another shipwreck killed at least 39 people. Senegalese President Diomaye Faye has called for an investigation into the factors driving irregular migration. The International Organisation for Migration estimates that at least 454 people have died or gone missing along the West African coast this year. Survivors told authorities that the boat was carrying about 100 people, including five women. The Senegalese navy also reported rescuing more than 1,400 people during operations on Monday and Tuesday, highlighting the scale of irregular migration along the Atlantic route.

Two in Five African Children Exposed to Conflict

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Around 260 million children in Africa lived within 50 kilometres of armed conflict in 2025, representing two in five children on the continent, according to a new Save the Children report. The figure marks a nearly 20% increase from 2024, with Africa accounting for 44% of children living near conflict worldwide. The figure grew to a record 589 million globally, or nearly one in four children. The report said the UN documented 38,967 grave violations against children in armed conflict in 2025. This included more than 14,000 children killed or seriously injured, and 5,128 abducted children. Around 86% of verified sexual violence cases against children occurred in African conflict zones, with increases recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Sudan. Meanwhile, attacks on schools and hospitals rose for the fifth consecutive year, while verified incidents of humanitarian aid being blocked climbed to 8,322. Save the Children has called on warring parties to allow safe humanitarian access and urged governments to hold those responsible for violations against children accountable.

US Consortium Wins $60bn Kenya Mining Project

A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, which is estimated to contain more than $60 billion worth of critical minerals, including niobium. The consortium plans to establish mineral processing and refining facilities in Kenya to ensure the country retains more economic benefits. The project has sparked concerns among local communities about possible environmental damage and threats to ancestral heritage. Two rival bidders are also reportedly preparing to challenge the tender outcome. The project is part of Washington's efforts to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce its reliance on China, which dominates global mineral processing. Frontier Minerals must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet regulatory requirements before development can proceed.

Somalia Orders UAE Ambassador to Leave Within 72 Hours

Somalia has ordered the United Arab Emirates' ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and recalled its own ambassador from Abu Dhabi for consultations, escalating diplomatic tensions between the two countries. Mogadishu accused the UAE of interfering in its internal affairs through unauthorised military arrangements, support for armed groups and agreements with regional administrations over strategic ports. The dispute reflects growing tensions over sovereignty and regional influence in the Horn of Africa. Somalia's government has also demanded that all foreign dealings with the country go through the federal government. The latest developments follow Mogadishu's decision to annul agreements with the UAE in January 2026 on security cooperation, defense and port-related arrangements.

Zimbabwe Prioritises Security Ministries in 2027 Budget

Zimbabwe's security-related ministries have been allocated a combined ZWG59.5 billion in the 2027 national budget presented by Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube. The allocations include ZWG23.4 billion for Defence, ZWG20.5 billion for Home Affairs and ZWG15.6 billion for the Office of the President and Cabinet. The budget has raised questions about government spending priorities, particularly as agriculture, food security and climate resilience face growing pressure from a looming El Niño-induced drought. Youth empowerment received ZWG1.6 billion, while the budget projects a ZWG3.2 billion deficit. Meanwhile, the Health Ministry was allocated ZWG33.7 billion and Primary and Secondary Education received ZWG46.8 billion. Concerns remain that the money earmarked will not necessarily mean improved services since government ministries have often been allocated much less than their approved budget.

Rights Group Demands Criminal Probe Into South Africa's R218m Arms Exports to Myanmar

The Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC) has called for a criminal investigation into South Africa's authorisation and export of more than R218 million worth of arms and military equipment to Myanmar between 2017 and 2021. The call follows an International Court of Justice ruling finding that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority. SALC wants the National Prosecuting Authority and the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation to investigate the National Conventional Arms Control Committee and others involved in approving the exports. South Africa's government has welcomed the ruling, saying it will assess its implications for international law and ongoing cases under the Genocide Convention. The exports included transceivers, communication equipment and rangefinders. The permits were later set aside by the High Court in Pretoria in July 2024 after a case brought by SALC. The organisation argues that authorities must investigate the entire chain of responsibility, from the manufacturers and permit approvals to the contracts and eventual exports.

Close 

Somaliland Rejects Somalia's Claim of Authority Over Its Foreign Affairs

Somaliland has rejected Somalia's claims to jurisdiction over its foreign affairs, insisting that it has complete control over its territory and international relations. In a statement, Somaliland's Foreign Ministry said its diplomatic engagements, economic partnerships and strategic agreements do not require approval from Mogadishu. The response comes amid growing tensions between the two administrations over sovereignty and Somalia's efforts to challenge Somaliland's dealings with international partners. Somaliland says it re-asserted its independence in 1991 and will continue to seek international cooperation. The ministry said that when Somaliland and Somalia united in 1960, they never ratified the union by any mutual legal act, and that secession did not create Somaliland statehood but restored it. It also reaffirmed its commitment to protecting its territorial integrity while pursuing partnerships it considers beneficial to its economy and regional stability.

World.title: South Africa: Rights Group Calls for Criminal Probe Into SA Arms Sales to Genocide-Linked Myanmar
World.content:
Taung Paw camp in Myebon, Myanmar, is cut off from any access to the outside world.

South Africa's arms sales to Myanmar between 2017 and 2021 face renewed scrutiny after the International Court of Justice found the military government committed genocide.

The Southern Africa Litigation Centre (Salc) has called on the National Prosecuting Authority and the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation to open a criminal investigation into South Africa's authorisation and export of arms to Myanmar between 2017 and 2021.

This should include investigating the National Conventional Arms Control Committee (NCACC), comprising Cabinet ministers and senior officials, which officially authorised the sale of the SA arms to Myanmar, a Salc statement made clear.

The litigation centre issued the call in the light of the judgment of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday, 19 November, that the Myanmar military government had committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in Myanmar and had violated the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.

Salc said the ICJ judgment - the court's first verdict of genocide - was historic and its impact on the genocide case South Africa has brought against Israel at the court could be lasting, "as it clarifies both the law and the standard of evidence that applies to states' obligations under the Genocide Convention".

"The judgment speaks directly to questions that could be relevant for South Africa's case," said Atilla Kisla, international justice cluster...

World.title: Somalia: Somaliland Rejects Somalia's Claim of Authority Over Its Foreign Relations
World.content:
Hargeisa — Somaliland rejected Somalia's claims of jurisdiction over its affairs on Thursday, accusing Mogadishu of trying to speak on its behalf and saying its diplomatic engagements, economic partnerships and strategic arrangements require no approval from Somalia.

"The Republic of Somaliland rejects the Somalian Government's claims of jurisdiction over its sovereign affairs," the government said. "Somaliland exercises exclusive authority over its territory and foreign relations."

In a press release issued in Hargeisa, Somaliland's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said the dispute followed a series of moves by Somalia's government concerning Somaliland's dealings abroad.



"The Government of the Republic of Somaliland takes note of a series of recent actions by the Somalian Government purporting to speak for or constrain Somaliland's external relations," the ministry said.

"These actions carry no authority over Somaliland's sovereign decisions and constitute an unwarranted attempt to interfere in matters beyond Mogadishu's jurisdiction."

The ministry pointed to Somaliland's independence from Britain on June 26, 1960, five days before the former Italian-administered territory gained independence and the two territories united. It argued that the union was never duly ratified through a mutually agreed and legally binding Act of Union and that Somaliland's original sovereignty therefore remained intact.

"On 18 May 1991, Somaliland restored the exercise of its sovereign authority within the internationally established boundaries inherited at independence, consistent with the African principle of uti possidetis juris," the ministry said. "Somaliland's position is therefore one of restored statehood, not secession."

The ministry said Somaliland's national interests guide its foreign policy and that its relationships with international partners are based on mutual respect and shared interests.

"Its diplomatic engagements, economic partnerships, and strategic arrangements are founded on mutual respect and shared interests and are not subject to authorization or consent from Mogadishu," the ministry said.

"The Government of the Republic of Somaliland underscores that unilateral claims of jurisdiction, regardless of their form, neither confer authority over Somaliland's external affairs nor diminish its right to pursue independent international partnerships."

The ministry said Somaliland would continue to pursue international cooperation while safeguarding its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

"The Republic of Somaliland remains steadfast in safeguarding its sovereignty and territorial integrity while advancing mutually beneficial international cooperation and contributing to regional peace, stability, and prosperity," it said.

World.title: Africa: Africa Accounts for Half of World's Children Living in Conflict Zones, NGO Warns
World.content:
Children walk at a camp for displaced persons in Port Sudan, which is hosting families who fled violence across the country, including Darfur and Kordofan regions.

Around 260 million children in Africa were living close to armed conflict in 2025 - amounting to two in five, a larger proportion than ever previously recorded, the charity Save the Children said in a report on Thursday. Worldwide, nearly one in four children lived near fighting.

The number of children living in conflict zones in Africa rose by nearly 20 percent from 2024 to 2025, when the continent accounted for 44 percent of the global total.

Around one in eight lived in conflict zones in 2010, compared with around two in five in 2025 - roughly the same share as in the Middle East.



Meanwhile, the global count climbed from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025, the highest since records began in 1990. It covers children who lived within 50 kilometres of at least one conflict incident in their country that year.

"These record-high figures are a stark reminder that conflict is devastating the daily lives, education, health and future prospects of hundreds of millions of children," said Gudrun Ostby, a research professor at the Peace Research Institute Oslo, which produced the report.

Rising heat puts Africa's mothers and children in danger

Abductions and sexual violence

The UN verified 38,967 grave violations against children in armed conflict in 2025, the second-highest annual total since monitoring began in 2005. More than half took place in the occupied Palestinian territory, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Nigeria.

More than 14,000 children were killed or seriously injured and 5,128 were abducted. Attacks on schools and hospitals rose for a fifth year in a row, to 2,930.

Sexual violence against children is widely underreported, Save the Children said.

Around 86 percent of the cases verified in 2025 were in African conflict zones. From 2024 to 2025, cases rose from 358 to 592 in the DRC, and from 74 to 193 in Sudan.

In the eastern DRC, violence forced a 17-year-old girl and her family from their home. When they returned months later, armed men broke in, shot her brother dead and raped her.

"We had fled the war, but it came knocking at our door again," the girl said in testimony published by Save the Children. The morning after the attack, neighbours helped her reach a health centre, where she received emergency medical care and ongoing psychological and social support.

Sexual violence surges in Mozambique's Cabo Delgado as war grinds on

Barriers to aid

Blocking aid was the fastest-growing violation tracked in the report, with verified incidents rising from 509 in 2015 to 8,322 in 2025 - nearly one an hour on average. More than 70 percent of the 2025 cases involved Palestinian children.

Close 

Denial of aid accounted for more than one in five verified violations that year, second in number only to the killing and maiming of children.

"We're seeing aid weaponised, attacked and deliberately disrupted," said Inger Ashing, chief executive of Save the Children International.

Warring parties should let humanitarian relief reach civilians safely and governments need to hold those responsible for violations against children to account, the NGO said.

(with newswires)

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Contained Ebola With Preparation, Not Luck. Africa Needs More of the Same
World.content:
A participant in the eastern DR Congo receives a vaccine as part of a trial to tackle the Ebola Bundibugyo virus.

Nairobi — Last week, on 11 November, Kenya discharged its last Ebola patient, just 37 days after the country recorded the first-ever case of the virus in its territory. If no new cases emerge over the next six weeks, Kenya will be officially declared Ebola free on 23 December. So far, zero community transmission has been recorded in the country.

That's an outcome that Kenya can be proud of, and it's not just a case of good luck. In June - shortly after the Ebola outbreak had been declared in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, but months before Kenya saw its first case - Kenya's National Public Health Institute (KNPHI) invited a Ugandan epidemiologist to teach some 200 Kenyan health workers the importance of investigating every health alert and looking into every unexplained death.

Using simple digital tools to both support and elevate local expertise is a quick, cost effective way to ensure that communities - and nations - stand robust in the face of outbreaks

And when Kenya's first case was declared on October 6, KNPHI sprang into action, running twice-weekly virtual training sessions for frontline health workers and surveillance officers across the country. The Ugandan experiences, particularly on contact tracing, became essential here, helping Kenyan public health officials break the chain of transmission.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

That kind of response - both nimble and far-reaching - is precisely what's needed to contain an outbreak of a disease like Ebola. KNPHI was able to move fast and reach so many people thanks to virtual networks that were set up before the outbreak reached Kenya. Africa needs more investment in these kinds of networks, which my organization, Project ECHO, supports - not just in the middle of a crisis, but before the next emergency hits.

One reason that virtual networks are so powerful is that they elevate the voices of community members, which are our strongest shields against future outbreaks. Local health workers, officials, faith leaders, civil society groups, and trusted volunteers are often able to spot unusual health events before formal systems do.

Engaging with community leaders also allows us to combine global expertise with essential local context. As we've seen with Ebola, a failure to respect local traditions regarding burial practices, for example, has proven to be a serious challenge in containing the disease's spread.

Embedding medical best practice with established and respected members of the local community - who understand the cultural context, and can work through it - can help us guard against such challenges.

Investing in virtual networks permanently strengthens local health capacity, which is ultimately our strongest protection against future outbreaks. Recent funding cuts to the WHO and other global health programs have undercut health staffing in many communities, making such networks more essential than ever.

Networks that include community health workers can also be used to spread knowledge and information to communities between outbreaks - which is just as essential as emergency response.

In Senegal, for example, the Institut Pasteur runs virtual training sessions on hemorrhagic and viral diseases that are reaching healthcare workers in communities across francophone West Africa and beyond.

And in Zambia, where the government has embraced virtual learning networks for more than a decade, regional and local information hubs are actively connecting frontline health workers with national and international expertise in real time, accelerating the sharing of evolving guidance, supporting mentorship, and creating peer networks that reduce professional isolation.

Even in conflict zones these digital networks have proved remarkably resilient. Since 2023, Sudan has been torn apart by civil war, genocide and gender-based violence. But an international digital network, built in close collaboration with local partners, has enabled global experts to train Sudanese health workers on how to treat victims of rape and other violence.

Some of the sessions have been facilitated through Telegram to accommodate the limited Internet bandwidth. Sometimes, the sessions take place late at night, when the connection is stronger.

The cases of Senegal, Zambia and Sudan show what's possible when technology is used to serve local leadership. As we respond to the ongoing Ebola outbreak - and as we prepare for future crises - we must apply these lessons at scale.

Close 

We will always need high-level expertise and cutting-edge medicine. But we cannot let our investments in those areas distract us from investing in the networks that reach the communities on the frontlines, and that allow for cultural considerations to be taken into account. Using simple digital tools to both support and elevate local expertise is a quick, cost effective way to ensure that communities - and nations - stand robust in the face of outbreaks.

Existing virtual networks gave KNPHI the digital infrastructure it needed to move quickly in response to Kenya's first Ebola case, broadcasting essential information to frontline health workers and surveillance officers across the country in a matter of days. Africa needs more of these virtual networks to reach communities across the continent - to protect the communities themselves, and to protect us all.

Dr. Caroline Kisia is Africa Director of Project ECHO.

World.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test – and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position – breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty, and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

World.title: Popular video game GTA VI drives fears of dangerous copycat stunts for young players, former cop warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The highly anticipated release of "Grand Theft Auto VI," or "GTA VI," is reigniting concerns about the potential dangers of violent video games, with a law enforcement expert warning parents to pay attention to how younger players distinguish virtual crime from real-life consequences.

Released on Thursday, GTA VI is the sixth installment in game developer Rockstar Games' crime-adventure franchise. Following a male and female duo through high-stakes checkpoints, the game throws players into a world fueled by gunfire, street races, and luxury car heists.

The game's release is bringing about renewed fears to the real-world behavior and crime that has followed previous releases.

'GTA VI' PROMOTIONAL BLITZ HITS CHINA, A COUNTRY WHERE THE GAME ISN'T EVEN APPROVED FOR SALE

Fox News Digital spoke with former police captain Joshua Schirard, who said previous installments of the franchise have been linked to instances of young people attempting to imitate criminal activity depicted in the games.

"This is not unprecedented," Schirard said, pointing to incidents dating back to the release of Grand Theft Auto IV, back in 2008.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"We actually saw real crime. We saw some teenagers arrested for robberies, for burglaries right after the release, directly citing that they were imitating the things that they were doing in the game."

Concerns resurfaced following the release of Grand Theft Auto V, when young people allegedly attempted dangerous stunts inspired by the game, including subway surfing.

INSIDE THE TEEN TAKEOVERS THREATENING TO EXPLODE THIS SUMMER AS CITIES REMAIN ON EDGE: 'VERY WORRIED'

In July 2025, four teens were arrested for surfing a subway train in New York City. The NYPD previously told Fox News Digital that there were 200 reported "apprehensions" for subway surfing incidents from November 2023 through July 2025.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Schirard also pointed to several young adults who were arrested for impersonating police officers, saying they directly cited the video game as their inspiration.

"Once again directly citing under their own volition that they are imitating things from the game, so obviously these do have an effect on what we see in real life," he said.

Still, Schirard cautioned against assuming that children who play violent video games will inevitably engage in criminal behavior.

YOUR KID’S GAMING HABIT COULD BE BUILDING A FUTURE CAREER, NEW SURVEY SHOWS

He said there is no clear evidence of a widespread increase in crime corresponding with the release of previous installments.

"Just because your kid is into these games and likes playing video games doesn't mean that they are going to go and carry out crime," Schirard said.

TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS

Instead, he emphasized the importance of parental involvement and making sure children understand the difference between fictional gameplay and real-world actions.

"Do they understand that distinction? Do they understand the difference between fiction and real life and the consequences that really come with some of those actions that they're gonna take part in in the game," he said.

CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS

Rather than simply banning conversations about the game, Schirard encourages parents to take an active interest in what their children are playing.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"It's probably a really fun game. It's a great opportunity to kind of share in your kid's passions. Go in there, play it with them, watch them, ask them how they're doing and what they're doing," he said. "This is a really good conversation to have and a real way to kind of breach into that subject."

CREEPY 'CAT IN THE HAT' TREND TARGETS SCHOOLS AS COSTUMED FIGURE ALLEGEDLY CHASES TEEN GIRL

He also uses the GTA release to remind parents of dangers posed by social media trends, which can encourage children to recreate dangerous stunts for the sake of "going viral."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Schirard said parents should be particularly mindful of viral challenges circulating on platforms such as TikTok.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"There's far less data to support that they're going to go out and carry out these very, very complex bank robberies that are going on in this video game, but a lot of data to support that they are going to want to go out and do the door kicker challenge that they saw all around TikTok," he said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

"Those are the areas where we really need to be focused."

SEND US A TIP

As excitement builds around GTA VI, Schirard's message to parents is not necessarily to panic over the game itself, but to remain engaged, understand what their children are consuming and address the potential consequences of bringing fictional scenarios into the real world.

World.title: 'Food Babe' declares war on the 'holiday death aisle' ahead of Thanksgiving
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As Thanksgiving approaches, food activist Vani Hari is targeting the processed ingredients lurking in holiday favorites — and offering a different way to celebrate in her new cookbook.

For most Americans, the colorful displays of cookies, candy and seasonal treats greeting shoppers at the supermarket signal that the holidays have arrived.

For food activist Vani Hari, better known as the "Food Babe," they're something she considers far more sinister: the "holiday death aisle."

7 COSTCO THANKSGIVING FOOD DEALS AND STEALS THAT SHOPPERS CAN'T MISS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON

She's warning families to take a closer look at what's on their holiday tables.

"I don't think you need to celebrate the holidays with poison," Hari told Fox News Digital. "You can celebrate the holiday with good, real food."

The outspoken food activist is taking on America's holiday eating habits in her new cookbook, "Food Babe Feast: More Than 100 Real Food Recipes for Every Celebration," released earlier this month.

Her target isn't just Halloween candy or Christmas cookies. It's an entire food industry she accuses of exploiting nostalgia and convincing Americans that unhealthy indulgences are harmless because they happen only once a year.

8 COMMON FOOD PRESERVATIVES LINKED TO HIGHER RISK OF HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE AND HEART DISEASE

"The holiday death aisle is the front of the store — every grocery store, no matter what holiday season it is — where they take over the store with brightly colored treats and concoctions and a lot of different ultra-processed foods that are marketed for that holiday," Hari said.

"But I'm telling you, it's not just once a year. It is every month in the grocery store that something's changing."

The Washington, D.C.-based National Grocers Association (NGA) pushed back on that characterization.

"Seasonal displays are a longstanding retail tradition that help shoppers celebrate holidays and special occasions, but they represent just one part of what local supermarkets offer," an NGA spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

AMERICANS WHO 'SCREW UP' THEIR EATING SHOULD USE A SIMPLE FIX, SAYS STANFORD SCIENTIST

"From fresh produce and locally sourced foods to nutritious options and seasonal favorites, independent grocers provide families with a broad selection of products year-round, while maintaining their everyday focus on delivering quality, value and choice to the communities they serve."

Hari argues that even traditional Thanksgiving staples can contain controversial additives, pointing to packaged stuffing, canned cranberry sauce and ingredients commonly used in green bean casserole.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Washington, D.C.-based National Grocers Association for comment.

Among the substances that Hari urges consumers to avoid are preservatives butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) and butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT), artificial food dyes and other additives.

RFK JR TAKES MAHA TO THE KITCHEN WITH HHS COOKING SERIES PROMOTING HEALTHY MEALS FOR UNDER $5

Her warnings come as federal regulators are taking a fresh look at certain food chemicals. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced reassessments of BHA and BHT in 2026, although those reviews do not establish that foods containing the additives are poisonous or unsafe at permitted levels.

Hari, however, sees the issue as part of a much bigger problem: a steady stream of heavily processed foods marketed around holidays, birthday parties and other celebrations.

"You can have cupcakes, but you need to know what's in them."

Her answer is to recreate familiar favorites with ingredients she considers healthier.

CLICK HERE TO 

Instead of canned cranberry sauce sweetened with high-fructose corn syrup, she offers a homemade version sweetened with pineapple. Her cookbook also includes homemade pumpkin spice lattes, peppermint mochas and festive desserts.

But for all her criticism of processed food, Hari insists she isn't trying to take the joy out of holiday eating.

"You can have cupcakes, but you need to know what's in them," she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

One of the book's most personal recipes is a decadent Christmas chocolate roll passed down from her late mother-in-law, whose namesake granddaughter appears in the cookbook.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

It's a reminder that holiday food is as much about family memories as it is about ingredients, according to Hari.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Americans, she said, shouldn't have to choose between the two.

World.title: Elon Musk's space giant cozies up to Dem power brokers as party vows to put his empire under siege
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Elon Musk’s SpaceX has hired a team of veteran Washington lobbyists with Democratic connections as the party prepares to take control of Congress and intensify scrutiny of his business empire.

Democratic lawmakers have signaled plans to investigate several aspects of Musk’s business dealings and government relationships, including allegations that SpaceX improperly restricted Ukraine’s satellite communications, whether the Pentagon has become overly dependent on the company and potential conflicts of interest stemming from Musk’s relationship with the Trump administration.

Against that backdrop, newly released public records show SpaceX has retained five veteran lobbyists from Mehlman Consulting, a bipartisan D.C.-based government affairs firm, several of whom have deep ties to Democratic lawmakers and former administrations.

SpaceX, with a market capitalization of nearly $2 trillion, is home to Musk's holdings in aerospace engineering, artificial intelligence, telecommunications and space transportation. If Democrats successfully knock it down a peg, the resulting loss in value could send shockwaves throughout the economy.

DEMOCRATS SET SIGHTS ON ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER MIDTERM WINS, BUT PRITZKER DRAWS A SURPRISING LINE

Musk has worked to publicly distance himself from the right wing since the GOP's poor midterm performance, recently stating that he’s "not MAGA" at a New York Times summit.

"I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much. Or maybe it would have been much worse without that," he said at the event. "I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that."

HOW ELON MUSK GOT BACK IN TRUMP'S ORBIT AFTER NUCLEAR FALLOUT, INSIDERS REVEAL: 'WATER UNDER THE BRIDGE'

Musk isn’t the first tech leader to throw money to Democratic operatives, seemingly to prepare for the incoming congressional majority. Palantir, another frequent target of Democratic criticism, has also retained lobbyists with ties to the party.

"I think at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money and they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability," Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former Biden administration official, told NPR of Palantir’s hirings.

WHY CORPORATE AMERICA NEEDS ONE PLAYBOOK FOR A DIVIDED WASHINGTON AFTER NOVEMBER

Technology stocks took a sharp hit in the days after Democrats won their stunning midterm victory, with AI infrastructure and data-center companies among the hardest hit as investors weighed the prospect of tighter regulation.

The throng of lobbyists adds to Musk’s already large arsenal of paid influencers, which includes Republicans and Democrats at the state and federal levels.

Musk’s new agents include the former deputy chief of staff to Sen. Maria Cantwell, who is slated to take over the powerful Commerce Committee in January; a former aide to Vice President Al Gore and a host of other one-time high-ranking Democratic staffers. The effective date of registration listed on the lobbying records was Oct. 1, around the time many were predicting Democrats would win control of Congress.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

SpaceX and Mehlman Consulting did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

World.title: ‘Austin Powers’ star Mike Myers seems to think liberal Hollywood is just ‘groovy’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

On Veterans Day, Nov. 11, Variety posted a quick interview with actor Mike Myers on X that has over 600,000 views and counting. At the outset, I should state that I have long been a fan of Myers. Partially because of his demonstrated talent and partially because of my Scottish and Canadian roots.

Now, the reason the Variety post is getting so much attention is because Myers hints that he may make Austin Powers a bit more political. During the interview, Variety asked Myers if the forthcoming film featuring Powers would "reflect" the current political climate.

Myers – with tongue seemingly firmly in cheek – answered in part: "I can neither confirm nor deny the existence or nonexistence of such a commentary. I mean the world has happened. But it's a much happier world, Austin's world, so it's been a lot of fun. I'm really enjoying it."

ROB LOWE CALLS OUT HOLLYWOOD DOUBLE STANDARD AFTER FESTIVALS REJECT BEN SHAPIRO-WRITTEN FILM

Some took note of Myers' answer regarding "the world has happened but it’s a much happier world" was given just a week after the Democrats crushed Trump and the Republican Party on Nov. 3. Myers then seemed to add weight to that observation by adding: "But I have to say, in the last few weeks, I think fear has had it, and love is on the way back."

The reporter from Variety then pushed Myers on that answer. "The wave of happiness, the blue wave?" Myers faltered for a second seemingly recognizing the need for political diplomacy before confirming which side of the political divide he inhabits.

DAVID SPADE AND DANA CARVEY CALL OUT HOLLYWOOD FOR FOCUSING TOO MUCH ON RACE AND GENDER

"No, well, it’s not — regardless of left or right, though I am a lefty, I’m Canadian, I’m a progressive, always have been," Myers said. "I just think we’re sick of fear, and we want more love."

To Myers I would ask: What "fear" are you sick of and what "fear" do you think "has had it?" Care to elaborate?

HOLLYWOOD PRODUCER BEHIND 'APOLLO 13' REJECTS POLITICS IN HIS MOVIES, SEEKS TO UNITE AUDIENCES

I would then tell Myers that I – like the vast majority of citizens in the United States, Canada and around the world – come from the "working-class," "blue-collar," life-is-a-daily-struggle side of the financial divide. And I, like most from that world, begrudge Myers none of his success, enormous wealth and the entrenched-elite bubble it allows him to reside within.

All we ask of Myers is that he remember that life is very, very hard for most people. And when they can afford to go to a movie or pay for one via a streaming service, they simply want to be entertained. They want and need an entertainment vehicle which will help to decompress their constantly troubled minds. The last thing they want is to go to a movie and have entrenched elites from Hollywood – many who barely finished high school – lecture them, speak down to them or outright insult them and their beliefs and faith.

DEAN CAIN SAYS HOLLYWOOD'S WOKE ERA IS ENDING: 'WE'LL LOOK BACK AND SAY THAT WAS STUPID'

Sadly, that has not been the case for well over the last decade. The "Marvel Cinematic Universe," the "Star Wars" franchise and multiple other films have continually and increasingly overloaded their "entertainment" with "woke" narratives and identity politics-driven characters. A strategy which has collectively cost those studios billions of dollars.

I would then ask Myers if he truly understands how that is possible. The correct answer being that over the course of the last five-plus decades, those with the ability to hire in Hollywood have systematically discriminated against Republicans, conservatives and people of faith.

LIBERAL FACULTY STILL HUGELY OUTNUMBER CONSERVATIVES IN HIGHER EDUCATION: REPORT

Myers proclaims: "I am a lefty … I’m a progressive voter, always have been."Honestly, good for him. He should – and must – be able to identify with a political or ideological doctrine which makes the most sense to him. Just as he should be able to shout it out.

That said, my next question to Myers would be: Do you honestly think Republican-leaning or conservative actors in Hollywood have the luxury – and the right – to shout out, "I am a righty … I’m a conservative voter, always have been," without fear of serious repercussions to their careers and very livelihoods? Has that fear "had it," Mr. Myers?

Some took note of Myers' answer regarding "the world has happened but it’s a much happier world" was given just a week after the Democrats crushed Trump and the Republican Party on Nov. 3.

And, to extrapolate upon that, I have long maintained that over the course of that same five decades-plus, the left has secured a vicelike grip on what I call the "five major megaphones" of our nation. Those being: the media, academia, entertainment, science and medicine.

Do you think that at Yale University, where over 95% of the faculty supports the Democratic Party, that a conservative professor or student can shout out: "I am a righty … I’m a conservative voter, always have been," without fearing for their jobs or chance to graduate? The same question applies to the media, science and medicine.

Going back to the interview with Variety, Myers would do well to read the comments. The very idea of him politicizing Austin Powers has outraged most.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Understanding that, I have a suggestion for Myers. He should have Austin Powers jump into his 1999 Volkswagen New Beetle time machine and go back at least five decades to fight the multiple "Dr. Evils" blatantly discriminating against those in the film industry who dare to have contrary beliefs.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Once that critical mission is accomplished, Myers can have "Austin Powers" transport right back into the Hollywood of 2026 where studios no longer insult at least half their audiences but simply entertain with the understanding that life is incredibly difficult for almost all on earth.

World.title: Trump will face reporters after historic Xi-Putin talks as war questions linger
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump is set to face reporters Friday after wrapping up a historic visit to China that brought him together with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for unprecedented three-way talks.

The leaders struck a warm diplomatic tone despite lingering questions over the war in Ukraine, nuclear arms negotiations and tensions in the Middle East — as well as stalled trade negotiations between the U.S. and China.

The summit in Shenzhen marked the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, bringing Trump face-to-face with two of America's chief geopolitical adversaries. Washington has spent years arming Ukraine in its war against Russia, while the Pentagon has long identified China as its primary "pacing challenge" in the Indo-Pacific.

Trump's scheduled press conference at noon on Friday will offer an opportunity to elaborate on what the meetings accomplished and whether the diplomatic discussions will lead to concrete agreements.

CHINA BLOCKS BLOOMBERG REPORTER FROM TRUMP-PUTIN-XI MEETING OVER QUESTION TO TRUMP

The gathering between the three world powers produced a joint declaration pledging dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, maintaining stable energy supplies and reforming the United Nations, but stopped short of announcing major breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran.

President Trump described his trip as "Great and Highly Consequential" in a Truth Social post announcing that he will hold a press conference at the White House midday on Friday.

Trump last appeared in the briefing room on Nov. 9, 2026, with UFC CEO Dana White after the president joked about offering him the press secretary job. On Nov. 13, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy held a White House briefing regarding the FAA nationwide ground stop.

The president has not had a press secretary since Katie Zacharia's few-day stint last month in the role succeeding Karoline Leavitt. Zacharia held one briefing on Oct. 13, 2026, but was removed from the job after widespread backlash regarding her ability to serve in the role and her claims to be an attorney.

Throughout the China visit, Trump emphasized his personal relationships with Xi and Putin, praising the Chinese leader for an elaborate welcome that included a military flyover and referring to both presidents as friends.

"President Xi and I have formed an outstanding personal relationship," Trump said during their bilateral meeting Thursday. "Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it."

Trump also told Xi that their friendship had grown closer over the years and predicted the two countries would avoid major problems as long as they remained in power.

During a separate meeting with Putin, Trump greeted the Russian leader by calling him "my friend," despite the lack of a breakthrough in his longstanding efforts to negotiate an end to Russia's war in Ukraine.

The president later expressed optimism about those efforts, saying he had spent much of his bilateral meeting with Putin discussing the conflict.

"I think things are happening," Trump said during the trilateral meeting. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war."

Putin also acknowledged that Ukraine had been a focus of his separate discussions with Xi and Trump, but the three leaders' joint declaration made no mention of the conflict or any new peace initiative.

The summit also put nuclear arms control back in the spotlight months after the expiration of New START, the last remaining treaty limiting U.S. and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.

Trump argued that the three countries were uniquely positioned to reduce the world's nuclear stockpiles, while acknowledging the difficulty of persuading nuclear powers to give up their weapons.

"Once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them," Trump said.

TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL

The leaders ultimately agreed to pursue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation, but announced no binding arms reductions or timetable for negotiations.

Trump also pointed to potential cooperation with China on Iran, asserting that Washington and Beijing shared an interest in preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon and keeping energy flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.

"Both the United States and China have an interest in ensuring that energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, and that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon," Trump said during his meeting with Xi.

"We both feel that very strongly on both points," he added.

The remarks were notable given China's economic ties to Tehran, including its purchases of Iranian oil, which have provided an important source of revenue for the Iranian government despite Western sanctions.

Beijing's commercial relationship with Iran has complicated U.S. efforts to isolate Tehran, although Trump's remarks did not establish whether China had agreed to change its oil purchases or take additional steps to pressure Iran over its nuclear program.

Trade was another focus of Trump's meeting with Xi, with the president touting what he described as progress toward a more balanced economic relationship and signaling that he would seek additional purchases of American agricultural products.

Under what Trump called the "30-for-30" deal, he said the two countries had agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion in trade.

"Our farmers have done very well, and I'll be asking you to do some more for our farmers," Trump said, adding that China had an "insatiable appetite" for American products.

The discussions came as Washington and Beijing continued to navigate disagreements over tariffs, rare earth minerals and access to advanced technology.

Trump also used the APEC summit to declare the United States the world leader in "superintelligence," making the assertion in Shenzhen, one of China's major technology hubs, as the two countries compete for dominance in artificial intelligence.

But the most consequential diplomatic development remained the historic trilateral meeting, which Trump described as an opportunity for the three powers to pursue cooperation despite their disagreements.

"We are really making history," Trump said.

World.title: Medicare for All sounds free. But wait until you see your huge tax bill
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Imagine a politician knocking on your front door with the greatest financial offer in American history.

No more health insurance premiums. No more deductibles. No more copayments. And everybody gets healthcare courtesy of Uncle Sam.

Sounds fantastic, doesn't it?

EL-SAYED ADMITS FREE HEALTHCARE MEANS PAYING 'A LITTLE BIT MORE IN TAXES' REGARDLESS OF INCOME

There's just one tiny problem.

Your doctor isn't working for free. Your hospital isn't operating for free. And the government doesn't have a magical money tree growing behind the White House.

Welcome to Medicare for All, where the healthcare might be free at the doctor's office, but the bill eventually shows up somewhere else.

Usually in your paycheck.

DSA LEADER DISMISSES $49T COST ESTIMATE FOR SOCIALIST POLICIES AS A 'MADE-UP NUMBER'

The $30 trillion elephant in the room

Let's start with some numbers.

LET SOCIALISTS ROB FROM THE RICH 100% AND YOU STILL WON’T BE ABLE TO PAY THE BILLS

The Congressional Budget Office has modeled single-payer healthcare systems that would increase federal healthcare spending by approximately $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion annually by 2030.

That's potentially $30 trillion over a decade at the upper end of that annual range. For perspective, America's entire federal government collected roughly $5.4 trillion in revenue in fiscal 2026.

$50 TRILLION IN DEBT IS NOT A DISTANT THREAT. AMERICA IS SPEEDING TOWARDS IT

Think about that.

We're talking about adding a massive new federal financing responsibility to a government already carrying more than $40 trillion in debt.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY'

Supporters correctly point out that Americans would no longer pay many private insurance premiums and out-of-pocket costs. But eliminating your insurance premium doesn't eliminate the underlying medical bill. It just changes who sends you the invoice.

Congratulations! Your premium is now a tax

THE DSA’S DANGEROUS FINE PRINT. THEY'RE COMING FOR MILLIONAIRES (AND YOU)

The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget examined what financing approximately $30 trillion in additional federal spending over 10 years might require.

The Congressional Budget Office has modeled single-payer healthcare systems that would increase federal healthcare spending by approximately $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion annually by 2030.

One illustrative option was a 32% payroll tax. Another was a 25% income surtax.

DEPROGRAMMED: A 'KIND OFFER' OF DEATH SENT THIS COUPLE RUNNING FROM UNIVERSAL HEALTH CARE

Those aren't official Medicare for All proposals. They're examples of the scale of taxation potentially required if either tax were used alone. And here's where the political sales pitch gets interesting.

A family might save thousands in premiums and deductibles but pay substantially more in taxes.

Another family could come out ahead. The result depends on income, healthcare needs and the financing structure.

You can't determine whether Medicare for All saves your family money until somebody tells you exactly how they're paying for it.

Your insurance card doesn't create another doctor

Here's another inconvenient detail.

If millions more Americans can obtain medical services without worrying about bills, demand for care could increase. That's potentially good for people who currently go without treatment.

But who's providing all those additional appointments? We already have shortages of healthcare professionals in many communities.

Expanding coverage without expanding medical capacity can create longer waits for some services. And if Washington attempts to control spending by reducing reimbursements, hospitals and physicians face another challenge.

You can promise everybody a doctor's appointment. You can't legislate another 100,000 doctors into existence overnight.

What happens to the insurance you already have?

Nearly half of Americans are expected to receive employer-sponsored health coverage in 2026. A comprehensive Medicare for All proposal would fundamentally replace that system.

Some Americans would welcome the change. Others might lose coverage arrangements, provider networks or benefits they currently prefer. Employers would face major adjustments, too.

We're talking about adding a massive new federal financing responsibility to a government already carrying more than $40 trillion in debt.

And don't forget that Medicare itself isn't free today. Beneficiaries commonly pay Part B premiums, face deductibles and often purchase supplemental coverage.

A proposed Medicare for All system with no premiums or deductibles would actually be more generous in important respects than traditional Medicare.

That generosity comes with a price tag.

The government can't repeal economics

Here's what bothers me most about the Medicare for All debate.

Politicians talk about healthcare as though the primary challenge is deciding who deserves coverage. The harder financial question is how America delivers affordable, high-quality care without bankrupting families, overwhelming taxpayers or destabilizing hospitals.

The United States spent approximately $5.3 trillion on healthcare in 2024.

We absolutely need to address prices, administrative waste, prescription drug costs and access to medical care.

A single-payer system might reduce some of those expenses. But the savings aren't guaranteed, and neither is a painless transition.

The real question isn't whether Americans deserve healthcare. Of course, they do. It's whether Washington can finance and administer an enormously expanded system without creating a different set of financial problems.

Because there's one financial lesson every American should understand. When a politician tells you something costing trillions of dollars will be free, don't ask where to sign up.

Ask where they're hiding the bill.

World.title: FBI arrests Georgia man accused of sending cryptocurrency to ISIS-linked individuals and groups
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Georgia man is facing federal charges after allegedly sending more than $26,000 to individuals and groups affiliated with ISIS, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced.

Younes Moustafa Younes, 34, of Lavonia, Georgia, was charged with one count of international money laundering and one count of destruction of evidence, according to the DOJ.

Younes was arrested Nov. 18 and made his initial appearance Thursday in federal court.

Federal prosecutors allege Younes altered and destroyed evidence leading up to his arrest. During a search of his apartment, FBI agents discovered three cellphones submerged in an unknown solution, including one that had been smashed and another with its identification number removed, according to the criminal complaint.

FBI ARRESTS 3 MEN WHO ALLEGEDLY PLEDGED ALLEGIANCE TO ISIS, FUNDED DRONE ATTACKS TARGETING US TROOPS OVERSEAS

Investigators also found shredded documents submerged in an unknown solution inside a bathtub.

According to the complaint, Younes sent approximately $16,807 through cryptocurrency transactions between December 2025 and June 2026, using multiple phone numbers and accounts allegedly intended to conceal his identity.

Investigators say at least some of the funds were intended to support ISIS operations in Syria.

Prosecutors also allege that Younes sent approximately $9,206 through 11 cryptocurrency transactions between December 2021 and April 2022, using an alias to conceal his involvement.

NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS

The FBI first identified Younes in 2020 after he allegedly accessed ISIS propaganda online, according to the complaint.

During an interview with law enforcement, Younes acknowledged viewing the material but denied supporting extremist ideologies.

Prosecutors allege he later became increasingly radicalized, expressing support for ISIS and other terrorist figures through encrypted communications.

If convicted, Younes faces up to 20 years in federal prison on each charge, according to the Justice Department.

The international money laundering charge also carries a potential fine of up to $500,000, while the destruction of evidence charge carries a potential fine of up to $250,000.
