World.title: Senate passes bill simplifying permitting rules to build in America, sending it to House
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday night to pass a sweeping bill to simplify and overhaul permitting rules for energy and infrastructure projects.

The bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, was crafted by an unusual coalition of Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va.; Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

The legislation would revise and speed up environmental reviews with tighter deadlines; accelerate electricity transmission; restrict the power of federal agencies to revoke existing permits; and reduce chokepoints for approving and completing projects.

To conservatives, it’s about cutting government bureaucracy.

“For far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty,” Capito said.

For liberals, it’s an opportunity to make it easier to build long-sought projects, including clean energy, and address high costs.

“Democrats are focused on lowering energy costs, reducing emissions, and stopping data centers’ free ride,” Whitehouse said. “Americans will start to get some relief quickly if this bill passes.”

In an attempt to alleviate Americans’ concerns about data centers, the bill would require “new data centers of 20 megawatts or more to pay the full incremental cost of the infrastructure built to serve them,” according to the Bipartisan Policy Center.

The legislation sparked opposition from some environmental groups and Native American tribal organizations, which objected to easing reviews and consultation rules that can be used to protect their interests. The bulk of the opposition in the Senate came from Democrats.

Still, the willingness to simplify permitting rules represents a philosophical shift for the Democrats who endorsed it. Part of the reason is that liberal policy experts recognized that existing laws hinder their own goals.

“This removes a lot of the obstacles that hamstrung [Joe] Biden’s climate investments,” said Adam Jentleson, a former Senate Democratic aide and founder of the research group Searchlight Institute. “A big part of the Inflation Reduction Act — a lot of the projects couldn’t break ground because of all the red tape.”

The bill still needs approval from the House, where Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., expressed optimism that Congress will send a bill to President Donald Trump’s desk.

“Well, we want to see a bill pass both chambers,” Scalise said when asked if the House will take up the Senate version of the legislation. “Obviously, the details matter. ... Hopefully, they pass a good bill back, and if not, we’ll work out those differences. But we want to get a bill to the president’s desk, and that’s still got a great chance to happen.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said the clearest path to making a law is for the House to take the Senate’s measure and pass it, noting that it has been through extensive debate.

“It has been litigated now for months. Continues to be,” Thune told reporters. “Everything gets more complicated over here procedurally, and if it were to go over there and then come back over here, I can’t predict what happens. So hopefully there’ll be the critical mass there to move it. ... It’s been through the full monty when it comes to the legislating process.”

World.title: Justice Department seeks dismissal of its lawsuit in Alaska Senate race
World.content:
The Trump administration on Thursday asked an appeals court to toss a civil suit it filed last month in Alaska that sought to take the extraordinary step of blocking certification of a state-run election unless the incumbent Senate Republican emerged victorious.

Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ended up winning the race this week.

The lawsuit, filed by the Justice Department in October, followed President Donald Trump’s repeated claims that the inclusion of candidate Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot, alongside Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, was a stunt to “defraud” voters.

Dan J. Sullivan and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, R-Alaska. AP; Getty

In its filing Thursday, the Justice Department asked the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to declare the lawsuit moot, citing Peltola’s victory.

“The United States brought this lawsuit to ensure that the State and its officers fulfill Alaska’s obligation to protect the integrity of its election,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward wrote in the filing.

He added that the government “therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means” of examining whether votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan were intended to be cast for the incumbent.

The ability to prove voters miscast their ballots was seen by many as an insurmountable hurdle when the lawsuit was initially filed.

Before the Trump administration filed its lawsuit, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that Dan J. Sullivan was eligible to remain on the ballot.

On Nov. 1, a federal judge in Alaska rejected the administration’s plea to separate and preserve certain ballots in the Senate election, following a request from the Republican-led state government that the judge permanently dismiss the “meritless lawsuit.”

Trump insisted in the weeks leading up to the election that the two Sullivan candidates would confuse voters and said that he was the one who encouraged the lawsuit.

“I’m the one that said do it,” he told reporters during his midterm blitz in October.

Days after the administration filed its lawsuit, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to jump into the race. Peltola has denied any wrongdoing.

Trump argued that Peltola should be prosecuted over the allegations, saying on Oct. 28, “This is voter fraud at the highest level,” and that Peltola “should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted, and so should the fake Dan Sullivan.”

Peltola won Alaska’s Senate race with an outright majority, meaning the state did not have to use its ranked choice tabulation process to determine a winner. As a result, the votes cast for either Sullivan did not affect the outcome.

Alaska is not the only place where the Trump administration tried to intervene in the election process, which is conducted by state officials under U.S. law.

In California, the DOJ demanded state officials set aside roughly 20,000 ballots that it alleged were sent to noncitizens. California officials argued that the list of alleged noncitizens provided by the DOJ was outdated and included legitimate voters.

The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s efforts a day before the election, and the Justice Department moved to dismiss its lawsuit later that week.

World.title: White House national cyber director is leaving the administration after series of tech outages
World.content:
White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is leaving the Trump administration, a White House official confirmed Thursday, in the wake of tech outages that hit both the private and public sectors.

Cairncross will be replaced by Kirsten A. Davies, who currently serves as the chief information officer at the Defense Department, a source close to the White House told NBC News.

Davies will serve in an acting capacity, the source said. The position requires Senate confirmation.

Axios was first to report the personnel changes.

Cairncross has served as head of the Office of the National Cyber Director since August 2025. The office oversees all government cybersecurity policy and strategy.

National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross speaks at Semafor's "Silicon Valley and The World" conference in Menlo Park, California, on Monday. Godofredo A. Vasquez / AFP via Getty

He has been directly involved with the White House’s deliberations over AI policy, including after Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick directed Anthropic to take down its two most powerful AI systems over the summer due to national security concerns.

Cairncross is leaving his post after a series of tech outages affected both private companies and government agencies over the past week. Administration officials as well as Democratic members of Congress have said the outages do not appear to be the result of cyberattacks, though some have suggested AI may have played a role.

The White House, when reached for comment Thursday night, did not provide details about the staffing changes.

Cairncross’ previous White House roles include senior adviser to the White House chief of staff during Trump’s first term.

During the 2016 election cycle, he was the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer. He worked for the RNC again during the 2024 cycle, serving as then-chief operating officer Chris LaCivita’s deputy.

Davies posted on X about her new position.

“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected. Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future,” she wrote. “Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future.”

The source close to the White House said Davies will strengthen the president’s cybersecurity team, which includes Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser.

World.title: Walmart stocks up on inflation-weary shoppers ahead of the holidays
World.content:
Walmart isn’t just adding inventory for the holiday shopping season; it’s also racking up more customers looking for discounts as inflation maintains its grip on the U.S. economy.

The retail giant on Thursday said it gained market share and raised its sales outlook for the third time this year as bargain hunters across income levels hit stores and fill their online shopping carts.

“Looking ahead, we expect a strong holiday season,” CEO John Furner said on an earnings call with analysts Thursday.

Walmart, which is generally considered a barometer for the U.S. economy, has long been a go-to store for consumers seeking discounts. Rising prices have pushed many consumers to rethink where they shop, and Walmart has benefited from more higher-income shoppers. As it draws more affluent customers, the company has launched a fashion-forward women’s apparel brand and expanded its e-commerce and advertising businesses.

Walmart isn’t alone in gaining momentum with thrifty shoppers ahead of the holidays. Rivals Target and Costco are also seeing customers respond to their value offerings, both posting sales increases and Target raising its outlook.

The results illustrate the resilience of American consumers, who keep spending even while grocery and gas prices rise and paycheck growth lags the pace of inflation.

“In spite of that, consumers are finding ways to get what they need for their families,” Matthew Shay, president of the National Retail Federation, told NBC News on Wednesday.

Still, it’s shaping up to be a strong holiday season, and not just for Walmart. The National Retail Federation forecasts that sales in November and December will top $1 trillion in the U.S. for the first time. But that doesn’t necessarily mean consumers are buying more items; rather, they’re paying a higher price at checkout.

This season, Walmart said it lowered the price of 7,700 items by the end of the third quarter while expanding deals on groceries. The company said it will also offer a Thanksgiving meal basket for 10 at $3.50 per person, including turkey, Stove Top stuffing, mashed potatoes and other staples.

Walmart also raked in more revenue from its membership fees, which surged 17% in the quarter. The company announced a bundled deal that includes memberships to Walmart+ and its warehouse-club subsidiary Sam’s Club, as well as perks including free access to streaming platforms and gas savings.

While shoppers seem to be sold on Walmart heading into the holidays, Wall Street was a bit more cautious. The company’s stock slipped about 1% to $126 a share amid a broader market sell-off Thursday, even as quarterly revenue and profit surpassed investors’ expectations.

Goldman Sachs analysts said they still rated Walmart’s stock a “buy,” projecting it’ll hit $132 a share.

Nonetheless, they also flagged risks to the company’s outlook, including the potential for an economic slowdown and more intense price competition from its big-box and online rivals.

World.title: El Niño strikes again, breaking rain records in San Francisco and along Florida’s Atlantic coast
World.content:
As storms pound both coasts on Wednesday and Thursday, a strong El Niño is once again rearing its head, breaking rainfall records and causing coastal flooding in California and Florida.

Downtown San Francisco set a new record for daily rainfall Wednesday, at 2.64 inches. The previous record was 2.24 inches on Nov. 18, 1918.

“Yesterday completely smashed those records,” said Anamaria Navarette, a National Weather Service meteorologist in the agency’s San Francisco Bay Area office. “El Niño certainly is playing a part in the event.”

Two waterspouts — a rotating, tornado-like column of moisture over the sea — formed in the San Francisco Bay on Wednesday, and another near Santa Cruz, to the south. Gusty winds downed trees and power lines, while rain soaked burn scars from past wildfires, prompting flash flood warnings.

World.title: Can Democrats force an end to the Iran war when they take Congress?
World.content:
Washington — For months, Democrats have made ending the Iran war a core part of their pitch to midterm voters, promising that if they win control of Congress, they'll push President Trump to end an unpopular conflict that they blame for price increases.

Now, with Democrats set to take decisive majorities in the House and Senate next year, some members want to use the power of the purse to pressure the Trump administration to wind down the war, using must-pass bills as leverage. Exactly when — and how — they plan to act are less clear.

Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut told CBS News before the election that she would support "cutting off the funds for the Iran war." DeLauro is set to chair the powerful House Appropriations Committee, which has the ability to block funding.

"If they want money, they have to get congressional approval," DeLauro said.

The first pressure point could arrive in a matter of weeks, before Democrats take control of Congress. Lawmakers face a Dec. 11 deadline to extend funding for most federal agencies and prevent a government shutdown. Several Democrats have argued the party should block any stopgap bill that doesn't restrict funding for the Iran war.

But some top House Democrats who will control key committees next year are backing away from that approach, warning it could lead to a shutdown.

DeLauro is part of government funding negotiations and favors a short-term extension until February if full-year appropriations measures are not passed by the deadline. She indicated that she is against using a continuing resolution as leverage.

"I think that the American people would like to see us end the war," she told reporters Wednesday. "I also believe that the American people may not believe that shutting the government down ends the war."

In a statement to CBS News on Thursday, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York said he would oppose a continuing resolution "if I believed shutting down government helped us actually achieve that."

"But I believe it would only shut down parts of government that Americans rely on," said Meeks, who is the incoming chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

The party's House and Senate leaders — Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Chuck Schumer — support ending the Iran war but have not specified what their approach will be, including whether they're open to attaching language to a stopgap funding bill.

Jeffries said Tuesday the House and Senate appropriations committees are in "active conversation" about how to fund the government.

"I don't want to get out ahead of that process," he told reporters at a news conference. "What is clear is that the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran needs to end. It should end today."

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who is challenging Schumer for majority leader, has argued the party should use the Dec. 11 deadline to force restrictions on the Iran war.

Van Hollen said in a statement last week that any funding deal "must include language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran." It was cosigned by Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and more moderate Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado.

Some Democrats also plan to offer amendments to any government funding deal to block war funding until the conflict is authorized by Congress, including Bennet, Duckworth, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Schumer-allied Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York.

Senate Democrats discussed how to proceed during a closed-door lunch meeting on Tuesday. Van Hollen told reporters they "had a very good discussion," but there was "no final decision."

Reps. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona and Ro Khanna of California said they would also vote against any funding package that "does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations in Iran."

What could Democrats do next year?

After Democrats formally take control of the House and Senate in January, they could have several opportunities to attach Iran war-related language to must-pass legislation, in addition to voting on standalone bills and resolutions to restrict the war.

Lawmakers will likely need to extend government funding again, and they will need to raise the debt limit at some point next year. The appropriations process for the 2028 fiscal year and the annual National Defense Authorization Act are two other possible points of leverage.

Schumer told reporters earlier this month that "we are going to end the war," and said, "the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people."

Still, blocking the president from taking military action in Iran could be a challenging task.

"It is a complicated thing to force the president to stop using military force, and does require an alignment of political opportunity, savvy legislating, coordination that just is going to take time and political capital to implement," said Scott R. Anderson, a former State Department attorney and Brookings Institution senior fellow.

Mr. Trump has vowed to use his veto power liberally. Democrats would need support from several Senate Republicans and dozens of House Republicans to override his veto.

Beyond that, Mr. Trump and other presidents have claimed sweeping authority to direct the military. The president did not seek congressional authorization for the Iran war. Instead, he told lawmakers shortly after the war began that he "acted pursuant to my constitutional authority as Commander in Chief," in a notice issued under the War Powers Resolution, which requires the president to notify Congress of military hostilities within 48 hours.

That 1973 law also limits hostilities to 60 days — with an extra 30-day grace period to withdraw troops — unless lawmakers pass an authorization for use of military force, and it allows Congress to pass resolutions directing the president to terminate hostilities before then.

House and Senate Democrats have used that law to vote to terminate hostilities several times this year, drawing support from some moderate or anti-interventionist Republicans. One war powers resolution cleared both chambers in June. But the Trump administration has brushed off those votes, arguing the War Powers Resolution is unconstitutional. On Thursday, the Senate blocked another House-passed resolution, losing Republican support for reining in Mr. Trump on Iran.

Jeffries said Tuesday that House Democrats are discussing whether to force more votes on war powers resolutions this year.

"It's something that's under discussion right now, and we'll take a look at vehicles that we have available to us," he said. "But it certainly is the case that early on in the new Congress, we're going to aggressively move to end the reckless Republican war of choice in Iran."

Later in the day, during an interview at the Atlantic Summit in Washington, Jeffries indicated that Democrats would vote next year on a resolution "that has the force of the law."

The resolution that cleared the House and Senate in June was passed under a procedure that did not require the president's signature.

Jeffries said the goal is to send a war powers resolution to Mr. Trump's desk, essentially daring him to veto it. The war remains deeply unpopular with Americans.

"There's nothing more powerful than putting that bill on the president's desk," Jeffries said.

Meeks told CBS News that starting in January, "I will introduce a War Powers Resolution, support legislation that cuts off funding for this war, and require the administration to take diplomacy seriously by sending real diplomats, not the president's golf buddy and son in law."

Other Democrats have backed using funding bills as leverage. Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia said in one recent interview that if the Trump administration doesn't follow already-passed war powers resolutions, "our only choice is to use the appropriations process to forbid funding for war operations, unless the president gets the legally required authorization by Congress."

Asked about Democrats' plans, a White House official told CBS News: "As President Trump and Secretary Rubio stated, our economic pressure campaign is devastating Iran to such an extent that the President does not have any need to conduct major combat operations."

"The Democrats continue to prove that have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to baselessly obstruct the President's agenda," the official said.

What could restrictions on the Iran war look like?

There is some history of Congress constraining the president's ability to make war. In 1973, the House and Senate overwhelmingly passed legislation blocking the government from using funds for hostilities in Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. Then-President Richard Nixon signed it into law.

Anderson told CBS News that if lawmakers want to force an end to the Iran war, they could pass legislation that either prohibits hostilities with Iran outright or bars the president from using federal funds to pay for the war, or both.

"You need some sort of affirmative bar to block the president from acting," he said. "Even then, there's kind of a question of, 'Does the president listen? How enforceable is it?'"

Another open question: What specific military actions Democrats might try to ban.

The U.S. has not conducted large-scale offensive operations against Iran in recent months, but the conflict has remained at a simmer. The two countries have exchanged occasional strikes — typically after the U.S. military alleges imminent threats from Iran — and the U.S. has enforced a blockade on Iranian ports and escorted oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Anderson says Congress could try to bar the Trump administration from resuming offensive bombings, and the blockade on Iran could also be restricted. Defensive operations are likely to be exempted, though the bill would need to be worded carefully.

In the past, Anderson notes, presidents have argued the Constitution inherently gives them the power to carry out operations to defend U.S. nationals, regardless of any legislative complications — an argument President Gerald Ford used to evacuate Saigon and order some other operations around the tail end of the Vietnam War.

"If you do an absolute funding cutoff, what do you do when you have U.S. vessels traversing the Strait of Hormuz and they do get shot at by Iranians, or American sailors get captured?" he said.

Democrats have yet to publicly lay out a plan for how they plan to counter the administration if it defies Congress on ending the war. If Democrats believe the administration isn't complying with its obligations, the House or Senate could sue, but the outcome could be hard to predict.

Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the incoming chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, has argued that impeaching Mr. Trump over the war should be an option.

"How are we going to stop him? What law are we going to pass when he chooses not to obey the law?" Smith said in an interview with CNN last month, prior to the election.

Smith told The New Republic earlier this month that even if Democrats forbid any funding for the war, "the legal language and the loopholes — the ways that Trump can sort of jump out of it — those will all continue to be challenges."

"We are headed into uncharted territory here," Smith said.

Anderson said he believes Democrats are serious about passing restrictions on the Iran war, but it could take multiple attempts and plenty of "political fighting and legal maneuvering."

"People do need to be patient," Anderson said. "There is this expectation that Democrats won and the Iran war will end tomorrow. That is not what is going to happen."

World.title: Meet Anthropic's 7 co-founders, now worth about $20 billion each
World.content:
Anthropic's seven co-founders are in for a massive payday.

Each of Anthropic's co-founders is now worth about $20 billion, based on their stock holdings and the initial price of its record-setting initial stock offering. Their individual wealth, at least on paper, will put them in the same ranks as Rupert Murdoch and his family, worth a combined $20 billion, and famed inventor James Dyson, who is worth $19.9 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Anthropic, the AI developer behind the popular Claude chatbot, started trading shortly before noon on Thursday on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT." Its shares were priced at $83 each, well above the targeted range of $70 to $78 apiece, suggesting strong investor demand.

That came to pass as its price quickly surged above $115 once trading began. Shares later lost some of their early gains and wound up at $97.17 — still 17.1% higher.

The IPO was the largest in U.S. history, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion public offering in June.

The IPO also turned many Anthropic employees into instant millionaires. The typical worker at the company could be worth more than $40 million after the initial stock sale, CNBC reported, citing regulatory filings and investors.

Here's what to know about the seven Anthropic founders.

Dario Amodei: $19.7 billion

CEO Dario Amodei, 43, co-founded Anthropic in 2021 after working at OpenAI, its chief rival in the race to dominate the artificial intelligence space. He has said he was prompted to launch Anthropic because he wanted to build an AI model aligned with broader human goals, such as advancing scientific knowledge.

His 237.3 million Class A shares are worth about $19.7 billion, based on the $83 per-share price reserved for Anthropic insiders and early investors.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco's Mission District with his sister, Daniela, another co-founder set to realize billions in wealth. Their father was a leather craftsman, while their mother managed public library renovations, according to the New York Times.

Amodei, who earned a Ph.D. in biophysics from Princeton and a bachelor's degree from Stanford, also completed a postdoctoral fellowship at Stanford's medical school, and also worked at Google Brain, the search giant's AI research lab.

Daniela Amodei: $19.8 billion

Daniela Amodei, 39, co-founded Anthropic with her brother after also working at OpenAI, where she held positions including vice president of safety and policy.

Her 238 million shares will be worth about $19.8 billion, based on the $83 per-share IPO price.

Amodei, who holds a bachelor's degree in English literature from the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Stanford University's business school that she hadn't planned to focus on AI. "I really think of myself as a generalist," she said.

She told Stanford that she and her brother decided to leave OpenAI to form Anthropic based on their values.

"We were running towards something versus running away from something. We had this vision in our heads of wanting to create an organization where the values that matter to us around safety and around responsibility were at the forefront of what we were doing," she said.

Tom Brown: $20 billion

Tom Brown, 39, another of the seven co-founders of Anthropic, serves as the company's chief compute officer.

His 240.8 million shares are valued at $20 billion, based on the $83 per-share IPO price.

Before co-founding Anthropic, Brown led the engineering of GPT-3 at OpenAI, according to his company bio. He has a master's degree from MIT, where he majored in computer science with a focus on how it applied to cognitive science.

Jack Clark: $19.8 billion

Clark, 37, co-founded Anthropic with Dario and Daniela Amodei, and now serves as the head of the Anthropic Institute, which the company describes as a think tank focused on researching the societal implications of AI.

Clark's 242.3 million shares are worth about $19.8 billion.

Clark served as policy director of OpenAI before co-founding Anthropic, and is a former tech journalist who covered supercomputers, neural networks and advanced technology for publications including BusinessWeek.

Jared Kaplan: $19.8 billion

Kaplan, 42, serves as Anthropic's chief science officer and is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University, where he has taught courses on the foundations of deep learning, according to his company bio.

His 239 million shares are worth $19.8 billion, based on the IPO price.

Kaplan, who has a Ph.D. in physics from Harvard University and a bachelor's degree in physics and math from Stanford, spent the first 15 years of his career in academia as a theoretical physicist, according to Anthropic. He was also "instrumental in building GPT-3 and Codex at OpenAI," his bio states.

Sam McCandlish: $19.9 billion

McCandlish, 36, is Anthropic's chief architect, focusing on large-scale AI model training, leading pretraining and research productivity, according to his company bio.

His 240 million shares are worth about $19.9 billion, based on the IPO price.

Before co-founding Anthropic, he led a team at OpenAI, where he focused on the science and scaling of machine learning. He has a Ph.D. in theoretical physics from Stanford University and a bachelor's degree in math and physics from Brandeis University.

Christopher Olah: $19.9 billion

Olah, who is in his early 30s, is the interpretability research lead at Anthropic. Olah previously led interpretability research at OpenAI, according to his company bio.

His 239.5 million shares are worth about $19.9 billion, based on the IPO price.

World.title: Photos, videos show devastating South Florida flooding
World.content:
South Florida communities are reeling in the aftermath of widespread flooding that forced evacuations and school closures this week.

Rain lashed coastal areas east of Orlando, dumping as much as eight inches there by early Thursday afternoon. In the city of Palm Bay, near Cape Canaveral, officials announced a mix of mandatory and voluntary evacuations for different neighborhoods and offered to transport residents away from their homes by boat.

A stop sign stands in a flooded street in Cocoa, Florida, on Nov. 19, 2026. Cyndy Paulin via AP

Parts of Florida's Broward County, which includes Fort Lauderdale and the nearby coastal city of Hollywood, received more than 17 inches of rain, and up to a foot of rain fell in other areas. Photos and video footage show neighborhoods inundated, with residential properties and vehicles partially submerged in water.

CBS News Miami reported that floodwaters were receding across South Florida late on Thursday. But heavy rains and flash flooding were expected to continued through Friday as the storms moved north, possibly toward the Carolinas and the mid-Atlantic into the weekend, the National Weather Service said.

Fort Lauderdale Fire Rescue shared multiple videos to social media that captured its crew members either driving or wading on foot through knee-high waters. In several of them, rescuers were seen collecting debris and approaching vehicles that had become stranded on flooded roads.

FLFR High Water Teams are out assisting folks who need help in the flooding. pic.twitter.com/VXkqSrlgce — Fort Lauderdale Fire Rescue (@FLFR411) November 18, 2026

One video, shared by X user Sruly Meyer, showed floodwaters rushing over a Hollywood street where his Uber was driving. The water appeared to create small waves that lapped against tree trunks and inched up the surrounding driveways.

"Insane flooding. Uber to airport," Meyer captioned the video.

Insane flooding. Uber to airport. Stirling off 67th in Hollywood. pic.twitter.com/Fayxd6jNDW — Sruly Meyer (@SrulySaysStuff) November 18, 2026

Law enforcement officers conducted rescues in particularly hard-hit locations. Officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said they rescued more than 70 residents, in addition to 20 or 30 pets, from a flooded Hollywood apartment complex on Wednesday, CBS Miami reported.

The officers used high-profile vehicles to navigate deep floodwaters and help residents evacuate, including one resident who posted on Instagram about being trapped inside the complex as water levels began to rise.

Law enforcement officers from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission help evacuate a cat from a flooded neighborhood in Hollywood, Florida, on Nov. 18, 2026. Joe Raedle / Getty Images

No injuries or deaths have been reported in connection with the torrential rain or flooding, but officials and local residents told CBS Miami a number of families "lost everything."

Knee-deep floodwaters were reported inside some people's homes and ground-level apartments.

Floodwaters inundate the area around a home in Hollywood, Florida, on Nov. 18, 2026. Joe Raedle / Getty Images

People walk their bikes along a flooded street on Nov. 18, 2026, in Hollywood, Florida. Joe Raedle / Getty Images

Multiple school buildings and at least one medical facility also flooded on Wednesday, with Broward County Public Schools reporting waters had breached classrooms inside schools in Hollywood as well as the nearby town of Davie.

One hospital also reported a breach, leading it to temporarily suspend visitations. The rain also caused the roof of a synagogue to collapse.

Capt. Jeff Carroll, a law enforcement officer from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, is pictured asking a resident of Hollywood, Florida, if they need help evacuating on Nov. 18, 2026. Joe Raedle / Getty Images

Broward County officials activated a countywide state of emergency as conditions worsened.

Some motorists were forced to abandon their cars as flooding made roads impassable and caused the vehicles to stall, Broward County officials said at a news conference to announce school closures.

Pounding rain also flooded on- and off-ramps leading to and from one Florida interstate highway, and a section of the state's turnpike filled with water.

World.title: Beloved hippo Fiona dies days after swallowing hat
World.content:
Fiona the hippo, who survived being born prematurely almost a decade ago, and whose story captured hearts around the world, has died, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced Thursday.

"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a news release. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."

Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, had ingested a knit hat that ended up in her enclosure by accident last week, the zoo said, and despite the team's efforts to get it out of her system, "it was ultimately too much to overcome."

A Cincinnati Zoo spokesperson confirmed to CBS News that the hat Fiona swallowed had been tossed in the air by a zoo visitor, then catapulted it into the enclosure by a ceiling fan.

Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, eats her specialty birthday cake to celebrate turning 3 on Jan. 23, 2020. John Minchillo/AP

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said. "She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many."

Before Fiona's death, veterinarians closely monitored her health, turning to an unconventional method to try to help her pass the blockage by borrowing a vibration plate from a horse farm. They had Fiona stand on the device several times a day, hoping the vibrations would help move the material through her digestive system.

Fiona would have been 10 years old this January. Her birth in 2017 drew the attention of millions on social media after she was born prematurely, weighing just 29 pounds, far below the typical 55–120 pounds for a newborn Nile hippo. Fiona was the first Nile hippo born at the zoo in 75 years.

Fiona with a zookeeper in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden on Jan. 10, 2018. John Minchillo / AP

To support baby Fiona, zoo staffers worked around the clock to care for her, including bottle-feeding her and helping her learn to swim.

In August 2022, Fiona's little brother, Fritz, was born at the Cincinnati Zoo.

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine called Fiona "a true icon" of the zoo, saying in a social media post that she "captured the hearts of Ohioans and those around the world, bringing joy to millions."

"Fiona was a symbol of perseverance and joy in Cincinnati," Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval wrote on X. "She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world. Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."

The Cincinnati Bengals even paid tribute to Fiona, saying: "Rest in peace, Fiona. The queen of the Queen City."

World.title: 14 arrested for SoCal train heist ring; nearly $23 million stolen
World.content:
More than a dozen people were arrested on federal charges Thursday for allegedly stealing nearly $23 million in goods, including Nike sneakers and power tools, as part of a Southern California train heist ring.

"This marks the largest property crime bust in LAPD railroad industry history," said Los Angeles Police Department Chief Jim McDonnell during a news conference after the arrests were announced. "This is much more than modern-day train robbery. ... It was a highly coordinated criminal operation that disrupted our nation's supply chain. When it happens, businesses are left without products to sell, and customers may face delays and higher prices."

In a news release from the U.S. Department of Justice, prosecutors said the 14 suspects stole the products from more than three dozen trains in places like Pico Rivera and Fullerton, and sold them on the black market.

According to the DOJ's release, charges against the suspects include conspiracy, theft of interstate railroad cargo and possession or receipt of stolen interstate railroad cargo, and violence against railroad carriers.

Prosecutors allege that from February 2024 to August 2026, the suspects targeted "high-value trains traveling through Southern California" carrying Nike sneakers and other products, intending to steal the products and resell them on the black market.

The alleged leader, Nathan Angel, directed other members to rent or use trucks and vans to reach railroad tracks, where they would board the trains.

"Nathan Angel and other co-conspirators predetermined locations along the tracks to disable the trains," the release said, adding that they would cut the air hoses of the trains, forcing them to come to emergency stops, where the alleged burglars would then take the cargo and load it into the trucks and vans. It was then taken to what the DOJ called stash houses, including the residences of three of the suspects.

According to the DOJ's release, suspects would send photos of the stolen products to potential buyers, including people working at a business identified in the documents as "Company 1," a sneaker and streetwear resale company headquartered in Los Angeles.

"The scale of the theft is staggering. We have charged a crew of 14 in a scheme to steal more than $22.5 million in cargo from at least three dozen freight trains in Southern California," said U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli in a statement. "We will prosecute the people who raid these trains and those who knowingly turn stolen cargo into cash."

Essayli also shared a video of the alleged suspects using power tools to cut into the back of a storage container on a moving train.

"It's always easier when they post their own stuff on their own social media," said LAPD Deputy Chief Alan Hamilton during the news conference. "I will say that in this investigation, we utilized different technologies, technological resources. We have some of the best players in the game on this team; I'm very proud of the work that they've done."

Prosecutors say two suspects, identified as Fredy Marquina and Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez, sold thousands of pairs of stolen Nikes and other products to Company 1 for more than $1.08 million between May and October 2025.

The suspects include:

Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East LA

Daniel "Rayo" Angel, 38, of East LA

Rodolfo Angel, also known as "Rudy" or "Flaco," 23, of East LA

Jose "Joe" Luis Angel, 23, of East LA

Donta "Dret" Hedgeman, 27, of East LA

Fernando Alexis Alvarado Villegas, 27, of South LA

Daniel Garcia, 36, of East LA

Carlos "JD" Robert Estrada, 28, of Whittier

Angel "Fluffy" Sanchez, 24, of Commerce

Ruben "Bubu" Mario Banuelos, 26, of East LA

Fredy Marquina, 25, of downtown LA's Westlake neighborhood

Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez, 23, of South LA's Vermont Square neighborhood

Jorge Angel Aguilar Espinoza, 36, of East LA

Ricardo Mares, 32, of LA's Florence-Firestone area

If convicted as charged, the defendants all face a maximum sentence of five years in federal prison for the conspiracy charges, up to 10 years for each count of theft, and a maximum sentence of life in federal prison for each violence against railroad cars charge.

The investigation was conducted by personnel from Homeland Security Investigations, the LAPD's Commercial Crimes Bureau, the Union Pacific Railroad Police Department and the California Highway Patrol's Cargo Theft Interdiction Program.

World.title: Senate passes bipartisan permitting bill designed to boost energy projects
World.content:
Washington — The Senate approved a long-sought bipartisan permitting reform bill on Thursday, following a major breakthrough on legislation that aims to cut costs by ramping up the speed of infrastructure and energy projects.

In a 62 to 33 vote, the upper chamber passed the measure on a bipartisan basis. The bill now heads to the House. President Trump has expressed support for the deal.

Fifteen members of the Democratic caucus voted yes, along with virtually all Republicans. Thirty-one Democrats voted no, largely raising concerns that the bill would weaken environmental protections and lead to more fossil fuel projects. Republican Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Josh Hawley of Missouri also voted no.

The vote follows years of on-and-off negotiations over how to speed up major infrastructure projects by streamlining the complicated permitting processes that can snag projects for years — an issue that has drawn more attention amid rising energy prices.

"This bill is years in the making," Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday.

Supporters say the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, will make it easier to build both renewable energy and fossil fuel projects, along with the high-tension power lines that support them. Negotiators announced a breakthrough on the legislation in September, touting a "historic, bipartisan agreement to reform America's federal environmental review and permitting processes."

"This is a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects, certainly without giving up any of the strong protections for our environment," Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia said at the time.

Capito said the agreement represented "something that's become increasingly rare in Washington — Republicans and Democrats, sitting down, identifying a problem, and in this case a problem that has festered for at least a decade and more that impacts all Americans, and for us to sit down and work together to solve it." She said the American people "sent us here to do big things."

"This is a big thing," Capito said. "It's monumental, and it's legacy-setting."

GOP Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming, who worked alongside Capito on permitting reform efforts for years, stressed the need for the legislation in a floor speech this week, saying, "If we want life to be more affordable in America, we need to make it more affordable to build in America, but also more convenient — more efficient."

The Wyoming Republican said, "In America today, it takes too long, and it costs too much to build," putting the blame on Washington for slowing things down, as projects are put in the "regulatory penalty box — waiting to act, waiting to build, workers sitting on the sidelines."

Barrasso lauded the bill for streamlining environmental and judicial reviews and limiting lawsuits, calling them common-sense reforms. He argued that the legislation represented a "responsible path" for producing more energy and protecting the environment, saying, "We can do both."

But some progressives have balked at the legislation, arguing it could erode environmental protections and doubting Mr. Trump will allow renewable projects to be built. While the bill does have the backing of some renewable energy leaders and developers, it also faced opposition from environmental groups.

Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon cited concerns about how it will affect states' rights to protect clean water and air, its implications for fossil fuel over renewable energy sources and how it could make it easier to build and power new data centers, along with its impact on the deficit. Sen. Ron Wyden, also of Oregon, opposed the bill as well, and sought a vote on an amendment to ban data centers on public lands.

The two senators have also expressed concern about how the bill could impact tribal rights.

"Embedded in this bill is a fundamental question about the direction we go regarding our responsibilities to this planet," Merkley said ahead of the vote Thursday.

Merkley acknowledged the bill could "turn the faucet potentially on" for renewable energy, but he said he's concerned Mr. Trump will continue to block wind energy projects. He argued that by allowing more natural gas and other fossil fuel projects, it will "open another floodgate for carbon that we won't ever be able to reverse."

After its passage in the Senate, the bill faces an uncertain future in the House, where opposition on multiple fronts has thrown into question whether the bill can make it through the lower chamber before year's end.

While some House Republicans have cited changes to the bill's provisions on transmission related to grid reliability, some House Democrats have also stressed that they would like to see the legislation altered. Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking member on the House Natural Resources Committee, has raised doubts about the bill. In one all-caps X post, he argued the Trump administration could use the bill to approve fossil fuel projects while continuing to slow-walk renewable energy projects.

A spokesperson for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said earlier this month that he "supports the need for permitting reform," but argued the Senate's legislation "falls short in several areas."

"Leader Jeffries will not rubber-stamp legislation that emerges from the Senate without more constructive involvement with our caucus as we fight to make life more affordable for the American people," the spokesperson said.

Some opponents have also suggested that Democrats could have more leverage to negotiate next year, when the party takes control of the House and Senate. Mr. Trump will ultimately need to sign any bill. But others believe the push is only possible with a GOP governing trifecta at the helm.

Thune told reporters on Thursday that he didn't know whether the House would be able to pass the bill as is, or need to make changes, noting that it's "been litigated now for months."

"The best way to get anything done around here is for them to pick up the bill and pass it," Thune said. "If it were to go over there and then come back over here, I mean, I don't know what I can't predict what happens. So hopefully there'll be the critical mass there to move it. I don't know what else you can add to it or detract from it. I think it's been through the full monty when it comes to the legislating process."

World.title: Army delays detonation in Iowa that could send toxic dust into Illinois
World.content:
The U.S. Army has delayed plans to detonate unstable explosives at a munition plant in Iowa, after elected leaders and environmental groups raised concerns about the risks of a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles that could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.

The dust plume is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces.

The detonation was originally scheduled for noon CT Friday, Nov. 20, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, a small community of 360 people, four hours west of Chicago, near the Mississippi River. However, on Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced the explosion would be delayed until Monday.

"Public safety is the Army's top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow's controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23. This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," Telle wrote in a post on X.

The Army plans two controlled detonations involving 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in military ammunition since World War I. The Associated Press reported the material totals about 5 tons. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the material has deteriorated during storage, allowing lead azide to recrystallize and become increasingly sensitive to friction and shock.

"In March of this year, the Army uncovered degrading Lead Azide housed in bunkers at the installation and immediately began communicating with stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed," Telle wrote in a post on X. "In coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency, experts, and the local community, it was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area. Public communication is essential to public trust. Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information."

In a statement after the Army postponed the detonation, U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) wrote on X, "The American people deserved better than this."

"This whole operation was poorly planned and poorly communicated. Families were abruptly told to avoid the area, unsure if they would return to broken homes and whether their air and water could be at risk due to toxic lead exposure. This was unacceptable and a failure of leadership of epic proportions," Duckworth wrote. "Moving forward, I will continue to demand answers about how we even got to this point and accountability to make sure the Army never allows unsafe conditions to get this dire again."

U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) called on the Army to hold a community town hall meeting on Saturday to answer questions from the public before proceeding with the demonstration on Monday.

Thursday afternoon, two environmental groups filed a lawsuit in the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to block the detonation. Earthjustice, a nonprofit public interest environmental law organization, filed the suit on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter. They are challenging the validity of the emergency permit granted by the EPA.

"We were very concerned about the very short notice that people in Iowa had to prepare," said Kerri Johannsen, senior director of policy and programs with the Iowa Environmental Council. "We also have not seen the evidence that the EPA used to determine that this was the best course of action, in terms of safety and health."

Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, noted in a news release that the EPA itself says there is no safe level of exposure to lead.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal," Schmidt said.

Iowans protested and some made plans to fortify their homes or leave the state.

"I called my daughter and said, 'I'm coming to Chicago,'" said Pam Munce, who lives in Burlington.

Garrett Anthony, who also lives in Burlington, said he plans to put a tarp over his air conditioner.

"And I'm going to try and seal up windows as best I can," he said.

The barrels had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command. A routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati said.

The Army said moving or transporting the material now poses an unacceptable risk of accidentally detonating it, potentially even killing the explosives technicians handling it. After evaluating alternative disposal methods, military officials determined that detonating the explosives in place was the safest available option. Barati said the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather. "We're really concerned that it will detonate on its own," Barai said.

The Army describes such operations near populated communities as highly uncommon, it told CBS News Chicago.

"A team of experts from around the nation got together to figure out what the best and safest disposal method was, and they determined that the safest method would be to detonate it in place," Barati said.

The Army says it is taking several steps to limit the amount of lead-containing dust released during the explosions, including earthworks, soil wetting and air monitoring. According to the AP, the barrels are surrounded by concrete and buried under soil, with sand barriers stacked two stories high around them. Barati said the soil will be sprayed with water and the air misted to try to keep the majority of the lead on Army property. EPA's permit also requires environmental monitoring at the installation and off-site locations, along with post-detonation sampling and cleanup measures.

With the detonation delayed until Monday, the winds are expected to be different than Friday, meaning that plume of lead dust could impact a completely different group of people as it moves in a different direction.

Residents urged to evacuate as explosions could shatter windows

The planned detonations are powerful enough that the Army is warning of possible damage to nearby buildings, including shattered windows. Residents in Middletown's City Park neighborhood are being asked to temporarily evacuate their homes from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday. Residents who can't leave should stay inside with windows and doors closed, officials said.

In its Nov. 15 public advisory, the Army says residents should expect loud explosions, ground vibrations and a visible dust plume. Temporary accommodations will be available at the Armed Forces Reserve Center in Middletown.

Elected officials urged Army and EPA to delay planned detonation

A group of Democratic and Republican elected officials from Illinois and Iowa had urged the Pentagon and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to delay the planned detonation and seek safer alternatives.

"While we understand the urgent need to address these volatile materials, their detonation has the potential to spread lead contamination in and around the region. We call on you to consider delaying this detonation until there is an opportunity to explore safer alternatives," they wrote to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and U.S. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. "Iowa and Illinois residents understandably are concerned about the potential health impacts of the scheduled detonation."

The elected officials who signed the letter include:

U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois)

U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)

U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Illinois)

U.S. Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois)

U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (R-Illinois)

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker

U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Illinois)

U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa)

They also raised concerns about communication with the public before the detonation.

"Our offices have received reports of poor communication from the Army and EPA about the detonation plans and anticipated monitoring after the detonation. In addition, there are significant concerns about appropriate Army and EPA oversight of this contractor-operated facility, the site of which remains on a Superfund list. We urge you to examine the contractor's handling of this and other hazardous material to prevent any future issues," they wrote.

Toxic lead dust could travel miles downwind

Following the initial blast, airborne toxic dust becomes the main concern. According to the Army's published plume forecasts and public safety advisory, the explosions are expected to release particles containing lead into the atmosphere.

The preliminary maps show a potential airborne plume stretching northward across eastern Iowa, the Mississippi River, and potentially into far northwest Illinois. The Army notified communities as far as 100 miles away Sunday, the AP reported, and thousands of people live along the plume's projected track.

In addition to airborne dust, toxic dust particles are expected to settle on surfaces. That raises concerns about possible lead contamination on agricultural land, residential properties, playground equipment and other outdoor surfaces.

A plume of dust containing toxic lead particles is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois Friday, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces. National Weather Service

Actual exposure levels and the extent of any contamination will depend on the amount of lead released, atmospheric conditions and how much material settles out of the plume.

Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade naturally over time. Once deposited, it can persist in soil for decades and may be transported through erosion or runoff into waterways.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that no safe blood lead level has been identified in children. Even relatively low levels of lead in the blood have been linked to learning difficulties, developmental delays and behavioral problems. Lead exposure is also especially dangerous to pregnant women.

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa's Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, told the AP it is encouraging that the Army and EPA are working to minimize the dust, but it's still unknown how much will end up in the air and on surfaces. He said he is particularly concerned about toddlers who put everything in their mouths. Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters, told the AP that high doses over a short period can cause lead poisoning and make people feel sick.

The Army's forecasts do not establish that harmful exposure will occur at every location within the projected plume. The Army says extensive modeling predicted that lead particle levels in the air may be elevated but still well below the level at which the EPA would require protective action, according to the AP. Environmental sampling will be needed to determine where lead was deposited and at what concentrations.

Weather conditions will determine where the plume travels

Wind direction, speed and vertical motion in the atmosphere will play critical roles in determining the plume's eventual path. Officials expect the dust to linger for no more than an hour, depending on wind speed, according to the AP.

Current forecast guidance suggests gusty southerly winds of 20 to 30 miles per hour Friday will carry the plume northward through eastern Iowa, keeping it well west of the Chicago metropolitan area. Communities closer to the Mississippi River and the Illinois border could be more relevant to potential downwind exposure. The exact path remains subject to change as the detonation approaches.

Under the EPA's emergency permit, the operation cannot proceed if certain unfavorable weather conditions are forecast, including surface winds below 1 mph or above 15 mph, strong winds aloft, thunderstorms, precipitation or temperature inversions. There is no word yet on whether Friday's gusty winds could cancel the detonation.

The Army is required to update its plume forecasts six hours before the operation, and hourly thereafter until the detonations are completed.

Army promises environmental monitoring and cleanup

The permit requires soil and surface-wipe sampling to begin within 24 hours in accessible public and consenting private areas where modeled lead-dust deposition meets a specified threshold. The Army must also submit environmental findings and proposed remediation plans to EPA.

For residents potentially affected by dust deposition, the Army recommends wet-cleaning surfaces that people frequently touch, including outdoor toys, playground equipment, patio furniture and windowsills. However, questions remain about the extent of contamination that could occur beyond the ammunition plant, the effectiveness of cleanup efforts and how residents will know whether their properties are safe.

This photo provided by the U.S. Army shows the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on May 14, 2024. (Shawn Eldridge/U.S. Army via AP) Shawn Eldridge

EPA issues emergency permit for detonation

On Nov. 13, the EPA issued an emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide at a location not authorized for the activity under the facility's existing hazardous-waste permit. In its Nov. 16 public notice, EPA said the emergency authorization was necessary to address an imminent threat to public safety posed by the unstable explosives.

The detonation is being regulated under the federal Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA, which governs the treatment, storage and disposal of hazardous waste. However, federal emergency-permitting provisions allow greater flexibility than ordinary permitting procedures. Under 40 CFR § 270.61, applicable environmental requirements must be incorporated into emergency permits to the extent possible and consistent with the emergency situation.

The emergency permit issued for Middletown includes specific environmental safeguards and incorporates applicable federal hazardous-waste regulations. It remains unclear whether EPA modified or omitted any requirements that would ordinarily apply to this operation because of its emergency designation.

The EPA's authorization does not mean the detonation will produce no environmental contamination.

CBS News Chicago has sought additional information about the EPA's environmental risk assessment and the standards that would trigger cleanup of affected properties.

The Illinois Department of Public Health referred CBS News Chicago's questions about potential health impacts back to the EPA. Environmental and public health officials in Illinois have urged the military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state after the detonations, the AP reported.

Iowa Health and Human Services told CBS News Chicago it was made aware of the planned detonation only very recently and is coordinating with other state agencies as they assess and respond to the public health concerns. The agency said the Army released two maps showing possible exposure but did not say what conditions the modeling included.

Community concerns grow ahead of detonation

Some residents and environmental advocates are questioning whether the planned detonation has received sufficient independent scrutiny. Protest organizers have called for greater transparency, independent environmental review and assurances that any contamination resulting from the explosions will be properly addressed.

U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek was among those calling for the detonation to be delayed, arguing the public needs a better understanding of the potential health impacts, the AP reported.

Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of the degraded lead azide, after the plant paused operations for a review and the material was discovered, the AP reported. The Army previously held a public open house on Oct. 15, where military officials discussed the safety operation and answered residents' questions.

Some schools in the region canceled classes Friday before the detonation was delayed, including in Danville, a few miles from the plant. Superintendent Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but the uncertainties made closing "the most responsible decision." He wrote that he is not suggesting the detonation will create unsafe conditions: "The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon," the AP reported.

In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles northeast of the plant, city officials learned of their potential exposure Sunday, when the Army's map put the town in the center of the dust exposure area, the AP reported. The school district announced Tuesday it will close Friday with no events or sports practices, and the public library will also close. The local fire department plans to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles. City officials said the EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample air, soil and water during and after the detonation, and the city plans to do its own testing.

"The biggest issue we're having is the lack of information," Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker told the AP. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds' office said it was first briefed on the public advisory Monday.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture advised bringing animals, bales of hay and water indoors. Staff at the Iowa State University Extension office in Des Moines County fielded calls Thursday from residents "deathly afraid" for their animals and vegetable gardens, staff member Morgan Hoenig told the AP. "We ran out of soil test kits yesterday," she said.

The Army recommends that those within the projected exposure area consider avoiding outdoor activities, remaining indoors with windows closed and setting ventilation systems to recirculate air until officials announce that the exposure period has ended.

The latest official plume forecasts, public advisories and safety instructions are available on the U.S. Army's Iowa Army Ammunition Plant information page.
