World.title: DOJ moves to dismiss lawsuit over Alaska Senate race
World.content:
The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, ending a much-criticized gambit by the president to prevent one of his political rivals from taking office.

The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that the second Sullivan's candidacy is legal and that he could be on the ballot. Earlier this month, a federal judge in Alaska threw out the Trump administration's lawsuit.

Attorneys for the state, which is currently controlled by Republicans, also objected to the administration's move, calling it legally "meritless" and filing papers to help get the initial case dismissed. The administration moved Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.

In their filing, Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court's dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway. They said the court "should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground."

"The United States therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means of 'determin[ing] whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan,'" Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward wrote in the filing.

That decision comes after Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats' 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in its midterm blowout. Peltola won by more votes than were taken by the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan.

In a statement responding to the filing, Peltola said it was time to move on: "Now that the election is over and the voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in, I'm eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans."

Messages from The Associated Press seeking comment were also left with Sen. Sullivan's campaign and the Alaska Department of Law.

The Department of Justice filed the lawsuit at President Trump's direction, saying that a Peltola win should not be certified until an investigation can determine if voters were confused. The administration never explained how such an investigation could take place given the secrecy of the ballot.

The case was filed before The New York Times reported on texts and other documents that appeared to show Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting the retired schoolteacher from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg. He was listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot, with no party preference, to distinguish him from the senator, who was identified as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan has long insisted he ran on his own and Peltola has denied any involvement, saying she was "not interested in tricking voters."

Mr. Trump also has demanded that Peltola be prosecuted for the scheme, and federal investigators swarmed into Alaska before Election Day. Tricks involving decoy candidates such as the second Sullivan have been a staple of U.S. politics for decades, and Mr. Trump's allies have also used them, though occasionally the schemes do lead to criminal charges.

Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy also ordered an investigation into Peltola's campaign after The Times report came out and, prior to Election Day, the DOJ's top prosecutor in Alaska called the reporting "troubling."

It was at least the second time since the Nov. 3 election that the Department of Justice has acted to dismiss one of its high-profile lawsuits interfering in states' handling of their elections.

Just days after the election that saw Democrats flip control of Congress and peel off big wins in races for governor and state legislatures, the Justice Department moved to drop a lawsuit seeking to prevent California officials from counting roughly 20,000 ballots. The Trump administration alleged the ballots belonged to suspected noncitizens, but election officials questioned the validity of the data and said the government's list contained many U.S. citizens.

World.title: How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
World.content:
How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain

toggle caption i Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images

For the last year, Will Ragland and a team of researchers at the Center for American Progress — a left-leaning think tank in Washington, D.C. — have dedicated themselves to counting how much money President Trump and his family have made in his second term.

So far, they put the total at nearly $3 billion. More than 2 billion dollars of the earnings come from cryptocurrency ventures.

"You could probably combine all of the past presidents' income made during their time in office," Ragland says. "And it wouldn't come close to what we're seeing here."

This unprecedented profit could soon become a major political problem for the president.

After campaigning heavily on an anti-corruption message that resonated with voters, Democrats are promising to make holding Trump and his administration accountable a critical plank of their oversight agenda when they take over both the Senate and the House next year.

Sponsor Message

From Sen. Elizabeth Warren from Massachusetts to Rep. Robert Garcia from California, prominent Democrats are vowing to hold oversight hearings and hold President Trump and his administration accountable.

"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," Rep. Garcia warned in a letter after the midterms this month warning Trump, his family and his administration to preserve records.

Here's a guide to how Trump made his crypto wealth.

Trump's meme coin

Shortly before his inauguration in early 2025, Trump and now-First Lady Melania Trump each launched their own meme coins — or cryptocurrencies based on Internet memes, cartoon characters, or even jokes.

Trump made over $600 million from the meme coin called $TRUMP, according to the president's own disclosures.

In an effort to drum up demand for the coin, Trump also held two galas for the top holders of $TRUMP. The president promised the closest access to himself to those who invested the most in the coin.

A third gala is scheduled for Sunday at his golf course in Virginia.

Many of the guests for the first event last year were likely to have been foreign, according to media reports. The second dinner, held this year, attracted considerably less interest, though participants also described a significant presence of people from abroad.

Sponsor Message

For Ragland and other anti-corruption activists, the dinners raise significant concerns about potential conflicts of interest.

"This is a way for foreign investors, foreign countries in some instances, to try and get as much influence as they can and use that as leverage for deals that they want to make that are helpful to them," Ragland says.

Already, top Democrats including Rep. Jamie Raskin from Maryland have launched investigations — and the galas are likely to become an aspect of their oversight into Trump's crypto ventures next year.

A White House spokesperson warned Democrats against pursuing "sham investigations" when contacted by NPR about the Democrats' oversight plans.

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," Lauren Bis said in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

A crypto deal with a U.A.E. firm

But the biggest source of Trump's wealth over his second term comes from a crypto venture called World Liberty Financial, which the president's family helped launch even before Trump won the 2024 presidential election.

Working with Steve Witkoff — whom Trump would later appoint as U.S. envoy for the Middle East — as well as Witkoff's son Zack Witkoff, the Trump family started World Liberty Financial late in 2024.

The venture revolves around a type of cryptocurrency called stablecoin (here's an NPR explainer). Zach Witkoff now serves as the CEO of World Liberty Financial.

Just days before Trump's inauguration, World Liberty received a $500 million investment in exchange for 49% of the company.

The buyer? A firm linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family who serves as the kingdom's national security adviser. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

Sponsor Message

The investment was an extraordinary show of faith in a young company that was striving to get a foothold in the crypto sector.

Months later, the U.A.E. earned a substantial concession: The U.S. eased export restrictions, allowing the shipment of about 500,000 of the most advanced American AI chips to the kingdom. The shipment was critical in the U.A.E's ambition to build big AI data clusters and become an AI power.

Democrats have seized on the timing, although President Trump has denied any quid pro quo. In a recent interview with CBS' 60 Minutes, the president said he does not keep track of how much money he makes from his business ventures.

"I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make – I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know," Trump told 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat.

But Will Ragland and his team have tallied up the earnings linked to World Liberty Financial and its stablecoin business: The total, they say, is over $1.7 billion.

World Liberty Financial declined to comment.

toggle caption i Vahid Salemi/AP

Another major deal for Trump's crypto venture

Another key deal with World Liberty Financial helped boost the profile of the company's cryptocurrency — and the Trump family's profits.

Using $2 billion of World Liberty Financial's stablecoin, a separate firm — also led by Sheikh Tahnoon — bought a small stake in a top crypto exchange called Binance last year.

The deal instantly elevated World Liberty Financial's stablecoin into one of the biggest in the market.

Months later, Changpeng Zhao — the convicted founder of Binance who no longer runs the crypto exchange — was pardoned by President Trump. CZ, as he's widely known, still has the biggest stake in Binance and weighs in publicly, including when the exchange got hacked earlier this month.

Meanwhile, the relationship between Binance and World Liberty deepened. Binance actively promoted World Liberty Financial's stablecoin to its customers, further elevating the market valuation of the cryptocurrency to $5 billion, according to The New York Times.

Sponsor Message

While the relationship has come under scrutiny, Binance has strongly defended the acceptance of World Liberty's cryptocurrency as having been done on its own merits.

"Any suggestion that Binance did anything to support World Liberty Financial or USD1 to gain political favour or influence a legal outcome is false," a spokesperson told NPR in an email, referring to World Liberty's stablecoin. A representative for CZ declined to comment.

But transparency advocates are suspicious — and so are top Democrats. In a widely quoted social message, Rep. Robert Garcia posted a social media message for the Trump family and his administration: "Lawyer up."

World.title: New York City unveils a bold plan to move its jails off Rikers Island
World.content:
New York City unveils a bold plan to move its jails off Rikers Island

toggle caption i Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR

New York City officials on Friday unveiled their plan to close the troubled jail complex on Rikers Island, the city's main pre-trial detention center, which has been plagued with reports of abuse and neglect for decades.

"It is long past time to close what's been a moral stain on our city," Mayor Zohran Mamdani told NPR. "We cannot simply accept the old approaches to public safety just because they've always been done that way."

Rikers, which sits on a former garbage dump in the East River, has long been infamous for its dismal conditions – including crumbling infrastructure. Inmates have accused guards of excessive force, sexual assault and high rates of violence in multiple lawsuits.

Sponsor Message

Last year, a federal judge called the amount of violence at Rikers an "unconstitutional danger" for both the people held there and the staff.

Since 2022, more than 50 people have died in the custody of the New York City Department of Correction. Almost all had been held at Rikers. People have been found unresponsive. They have died by suicide and been beaten to death. Federal court records say Rikers is "significantly more violent" than comparable jails.

But now, city officials say they finally have momentum to close the jail for good, and the newly released plan details how they intend to do that.

toggle caption i Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR

The plan — which takes on both the conditions inside the jails and the size of the population behind bars — is ambitious. It seeks to transform how the city government thinks about crime prevention and safety overall, says Insha Rahman, president of the Vera Institute of Justice, a criminal justice reform nonprofit.

"If New York City can do this at scale, which it will, it is encouragement for places like LA, like Chicago, like Philadelphia, like Houston to do the same," Rahman says.

A goal set by the city years ago

In 2019, the New York City Council approved a plan to close Rikers by 2027, and to build in its place four smaller jails in Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and the Bronx.

Sponsor Message

Rikers is on an island between Queens and the Bronx, out of sight for many New Yorkers. The borough-based jails will be closer to the courts and to public transit, making it easier for families , lawyers and service providers to visit people inside the facilities.

Since 2019, not a lot of progress has been made toward closing Rikers. City officials acknowledge they won't make the 2027 deadline. But Mamdani says the city is in a new moment.

"We're not the first administration to talk about this. We also know that the last administration had no interest in advancing this," Mamdani told NPR. "And we are also confident that we can be the first administration to deliver on it."

toggle caption i Michael Appleton/Mayoral Photography Office

Earlier this year, he appointed a "Close Rikers Czar" dedicated to closing the jail and reducing the jail population. The mayor also appointed Stanley Richards as commissioner of the DOC, the first formerly incarcerated person to lead the department.

Mamdani says his administration has already taken concrete steps: The city revived plans for a housing initiative for New Yorkers released from jail with medical needs, for instance, and it opened a therapeutic housing unit at a public hospital in Manhattan.

'Human dignity at the center of incarceration'

Last year, a federal judge stripped the city of its authority over Rikers. Operations are now controlled by a remediation manager, who released his own initial plan earlier this year for bringing the jail system into legal compliance, independent of the city's plan.

Aspects of that plan took inspiration from carceral systems in Europe, a growing trend among correctional leaders across the U.S. The remediation manager, Nicholas Deml, traveled with Commissioner Richards to Germany earlier this year on a trip organized by the Vera Institute. There, they observed the country's prisons and jails, which are often regarded as an international model.

toggle caption i Lena Mucha

"While German correctional systems are not directly transferable to New York, they reflect a fundamentally different orientation — one that places human dignity at the center of incarceration," Deml wrote in his plan.

Sponsor Message

Last month, the Vera Institute took a second group of New Yorkers to Germany to see how jails can look when they're done right, including the Moabit jail in Berlin. Each member of that group had a part to play in reimagining New York City's criminal justice system: a prosecutor, a judge, a city councilmember, the chief who supervises officers at Rikers, among others.

At first glance, the group observed, Moabit looked like a lot of jails in the U.S., but key differences emerged on closer inspection. The jail was quiet. The cells had windows to the outside. In some of them, a door inside connected it to the adjacent cell.

"Some people are afraid of the first night here, and sometimes it really helps just to open the door to have someone to talk to," Katharina Spanaus, a staff member at Moabit, told the group.

There were also televisions in the cells to calm people down, and in the hallway, a vending machine selling cigarettes.

"I'll never forget the cigarette vending machine," says Christopher Watler, who was recently appointed chair of the New York City Board of Correction, which oversees the city's jail system.

toggle caption i Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR

What struck him wasn't really the cigarettes, but what the gesture communicates about treating people as human, Watler says.

It also showed him how far New York City has to go.

Just a week earlier, he sat at his first board meeting in New York, where he heard stories that evoked a different image. At the start, the board listened to anonymous phone calls from people held at Rikers.

The callers voiced concerns: A woman reported black mold. A man said he was denied his medications. Another pleaded for a less violent environment.

"New York City's a great city. Our jail system isn't great," Watler says. "It's a broken thing. But how do you repair broken things?"

Sponsor Message

'The sum of all the efforts will help'

The four new jails won't be fully completed for another six years. Each facility will have more access to natural light and fresh air, and more space for recreation, vocational training and education.

Together, the new jails will hold about 2,000 fewer people than the approximately 6,600 people Rikers holds now.

The city's plan invests more than $250 million across the next several years in efforts to reduce the number of people in jail, for instance, by expanding alternatives to incarceration like diversion programs and electronic monitoring.

toggle caption i Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR

It also aims to keep people from committing crimes, by expanding services like supportive housing and mental health treatment.

Another way to lower a jail's population is to shorten how long people stay there. The average length of stay of people in New York City DOC custody was nearly twice as long in 2025 as it was in 2015, according to the policy journal Vital City.

The vast majority of people at Rikers are awaiting trial, and many of their cases take longer to process than national standards dictate. Nearly a quarter have been in jail for more than a year.

Judge Joseph Zayas, chief administrative judge of the New York State Unified Court System, told NPR there are many factors that can lengthen a jail stay, including processing evidence during discovery and administering mental health assessments, for instance.

toggle caption i Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR

"The only way to solve this backlog problem is to hit each of these things. The sum of all of the efforts will help," Zayas says.

The city is planning a task force dedicated to speeding up court cases, but the forces affecting that are outside city hall's control. Judges act independently from the mayor, as do district attorneys. City officials say they are investing in those relationships.

'If you are wrong, then you have crowded jails'

Some people, including those with deep knowledge of Rikers, are concerned with what happens if the city doesn't lower the jail population enough.

Sponsor Message

Vincent Schiraldi, who was DOC commissioner under Mayor Bill de Blasio, says he can understand that.

"It's really hard to have the guts to forecast lower incarceration numbers. Because if you are wrong, then you have crowded jails and you're in trouble," says Schiraldi, who now runs a philanthropic fund to close Rikers.

Other cities have dramatically reduced their jail populations. After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, New Orleans reduced its jail population by more than two thirds in the decade after.

Schiraldi pointed out that aside from an increase during the pandemic, crime rates have trended downward for decades.

toggle caption i Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR

If crime increases again, Schiraldi says, "Then we deal with it. What is the scenario by which the government spends billions of dollars just in case?"

But Elizabeth Glazer, who led the Office of Criminal Justice under de Blasio, told NPR she hopes the mayor will be pragmatic when it comes to having contingency plans – including the possibility of building again on Rikers Island.

She says it is possible to shrink the jail population, but it's not going to be easy.

"It requires relentless attention, coordination and organization around a common goal to get it done," says Glazer, who is also the founder of Vital City. "Even if you hit that number, the question is, can that be sustained for the decades when all you have is that capacity?"

Still, for some people the city's plan is a crucial opportunity, after years of inaction have left thousands of people held at the jail under inhumane conditions.

toggle caption i Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

"We wait for these perfect plans, and for all the reasons we know, including funding, those perfect plans never come to pass. And so what do we do? We do nothing," says Tina Luongo, who leads the criminal defense practice at the Legal Aid Society, which brought the class action lawsuit that resulted in the remediation manager's appointment.

Sponsor Message

Changing the culture at Rikers

Officials caution the new jails alone won't solve the systemic problems at Rikers.

Over the last decade, the federal government has documented a "culture of violence" among the guards. In 2023, more than 700 women sued the city alleging they'd been raped or sexually abused by staff at Rikers, according to a Gothamist investigation .

"People talk about culture change and that's really just a euphemism for the extraordinary brutality and violence that has plagued Rikers," Glazer says. "If you're going to move the very same system into the new buildings, you're going to move the problem of violence as well."

In their report, city officials outline plans for more training and mentoring for staff, tighter oversight, and more programming for people in jail.

Commissioner Richards told NPR he wants to see the jail's culture transform and become more like what he saw in Germany, where human dignity is non-negotiable for everyone. That includes staff, who Richards says have been demonized.

toggle caption i Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR

"Part of the work that I'm doing is showing value and appreciation to our staff. So they begin to expand their capacity to show that same value and humanity to the people who come to us," Richards says.

But he didn't offer specifics on what exactly will change. That may be in part because he has a more immediate focus: safety and security.

The plan set forth by Deml, the remediation manager, starts with the most basic correctional functions, including protocols for securing doors. Richards, who was incarcerated at Rikers himself 40 years ago, says they need to start somewhere.

"Everybody wants something to happen by tomorrow. And we are in a moment of urgency. But it takes time to turn," he says.

The larger goal remains the same: for the failures of Rikers to not be carried into the next generation of New York City jails.

World.title: The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties
World.content:
The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties

toggle caption i Stefan Rousseau/Pool PA via AP

BRUSSELS — A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.

Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.

Sponsor Message

Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world's biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.

"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained," he said this week.

Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.

toggle caption i Alberto Pezzali/AP

Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be "a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security."

Burnham pitched the package of agreements expected to be signed Friday as a way of "cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people."

He said "a closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe."

Sponsor Message

The deals are set to include an agreement for up to 100,000 young adults from Britain to live and work in EU countries for up to three years, and the same number of Europeans to come to the U.K.

There will also be an emissions trading agreement and a deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products that will make things cheaper and easier for British exporters to Europe. Burnham says the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain's economy.

To get the deals, the U.K. must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines Britain's independence.

"I'm afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again," Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told the BBC. He said "it's perfectly clear that this very, very soon becomes a debate about: do we rejoin or do we stay out?"

The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.'s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.

"Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential," Costa said ahead of the meeting. "By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond."

Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country's intentions.

Ireland's ambassador in London, Sonja Hyland, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, "there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant." If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must "make a clear decision as to what it wants."

World.title: Why the U.S. air traffic control system still relies on an 'antique' network
World.content:
Why the U.S. air traffic control system still relies on an 'antique' network

toggle caption i William Liang/AP

Rossana D'Antonio was at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, just about to board a plane back to Los Angeles, when the Federal Aviation Administration declared a nationwide ground stop.

D'Antonio's flight was canceled last Friday, along with thousands of others. She was lucky, and got a seat on a flight Saturday morning.

"By then, of course, the hotels were all booked. And so I spent the night at JFK," she said with a rueful laugh.

D'Antonio is not just a frequent flier. She also is the president-elect of the American Society of Civil Engineers. So her mind went right to infrastructure.

Sponsor Message

"The very first thing I thought of was, 'We told you so,'" D'Antonio told NPR. "We are reliant on a system that was considered to be state of the art back in the 1980s. This is common knowledge. We've known about it, and we simply haven't acted swiftly enough."

Last week's nationwide ground stop was an unwelcome reminder that the U.S.' air traffic control system runs on antiquated technology.

"We have a patchwork, archaic federal telephone network," the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, Bryan Bedford, said Thursday at Honeywell Aerospace's American Aviation Leadership Summit in Washington. "Which is why we gotta get off [of] it as fast as humanly possible, while maintaining safety."

toggle caption i Cliff Owen/AP

The FAA is still unsure exactly what caused the telecommunications meltdown that led to the nationwide ground stop, just the second since 9/11. But the agency says it started with work to install a router at a remote facility in Arkansas -- part of an ongoing effort to replace outdated copper wiring with modern fiber-optic cables.

No one disputes that the old equipment is a problem, or that updates now underway should have happened a long time ago. So why is the world's busiest and most complex airspace still running on network technology from the 1980s?

Sponsor Message

Former FAA and DOT officials say the answer starts with decades of underfunding.

"At its core, it's a money problem," Michael Huerta, a former FAA administrator during the Obama administration, said in an interview last year. "The FAA has been asked to do more with less."

toggle caption i Charles Rex Arbogast/AP

The agency has tried to invest in new technology. But at the same time, Huerta said, the older systems must stay running to keep planes in the air 365 days a year, 24 hours a day.

The older networks are fragile, and expensive to maintain because they're obsolete, former FAA officials say. And it's challenging to connect them with modern equipment designed to run on fiber-optic networks.

"This should have been taken on earlier," said William Voss, a former FAA executive involved in previous modernization efforts back in the 1990s. "It's effectively been eating all the money up trying to run this antique store in the biggest air traffic system in the world."

The FAA got an influx of money last year when Congress allocated $12.5 billion to upgrade the air traffic control system. But Voss warned the task is complicated and daunting.

"There's not a lot of people that have done that in one big leap," he said.

toggle caption i ELAINE THOMPSON/ASSOCIATED PRESS/AP

Voss worries the Trump administration is moving too quickly, without allowing enough time for planning and coordination. And he wonders why the failed network upgrade that crippled the nation's airspace was scheduled during a busy Friday afternoon.

"I can't imagine why you do that unless you are just under tremendous schedule pressure," Voss said.

The timing also seems questionable to Dave Spero. He's the national president of Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, the union that represents technicians at the FAA.

"No, I wouldn't do that on a Friday afternoon," he said. "To be safe, I would probably want to schedule it on a midnight shift."

Sponsor Message

The Government Accountability Office also raised concerns about the speed of modernization work. In a report published in September, the GAO said the administration has been accelerating the timeline of modernization work already underway -- including the telecommunications network that failed on Friday.

"They are basically buying speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and the potential for disruptions in the national airspace," said Kevin Walsh, the director of the GAO's Information Technology and Cybersecurity team, who was the lead on the report.

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

The GAO report also noted the first phase of the FAA's modernization effort includes more than 11,000 distinct projects with no integrated master plan.

"While that may work, it increases the risk of outages, especially when dealing with these older systems, which are prone to failure," Walsh said.

But the Trump administration defends its approach.

"Some of you will say I'm moving too fast. Some of you say, I'm moving too slow. Um, maybe I'm Goldilocks and I'm going just right here," said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy after meeting Republican Senators at the Capitol on Tuesday. "But I'll just tell you, the longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes."

toggle caption i Jacquelyn Martin/AP

There's another reason, experts say, the Trump administration might want to move quickly.

After decades of air traffic control modernization attempts that took longer and delivered less than promised, the FAA wants to show Congress that it's serious this time, said Eric Soskin, a former inspector general at the Department of Transportation.

"That's a powerful signal to say, hey, we're going to get it done. We are going to carry out this important effort," Soskin said.

The FAA still has a lot of modernization work left to do, with the potential for more disruptions ahead, other former agency leaders warned.

"I don't expect another major US shutdown. The FAA is going to avoid that at all costs," said Michael O'Donnell, a former senior executive at the agency.

Sponsor Message

"We'll get some disruptions, but I don't think it'll be anything like we saw on Friday night … I'd be really shocked and surprised, and a little worried, if that happened again."

World.title: Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days
World.content:
Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.

D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.

Sponsor Message

Chutkan's new five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.

"The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement.

The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.

That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.

In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

"This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered.

Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.

Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location, saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.

Sponsor Message

In court filings and a recently unveiled website, the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security. Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.

In a declaration this week, Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR on Thursday that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has pursued with vigor in his second term. Some of them, like the White House ballroom and Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, are well underway. Others, like the Kennedy Center closure and East Potomac golf course redevelopment, are held up by various legal challenges.

Democrats have said they will use their forthcoming majority in Congress to push back on Trump's construction agenda, including by blocking federal funding. But experts say the fate of many of these projects will ultimately be up to the court.

'Time is of the essence' at East Potomac

Trump's dream of redeveloping a municipal D.C. golf course into a championship-level venue is also temporarily on hold, despite his repeated social media pronouncements that the park would close and work would begin on Nov. 15.

Another D.C. district judge, Ana Reyes, intervened Saturday to order the administration to keep East Potomac Park open for two weeks, on the eve of its indefinite closure.

Sponsor Message

But the golf course itself is currently unstaffed, since its operator lease expired on Sunday. That hasn't stopped locals from showing up and teeing off, finding creative ways to mark the holes after the flagsticks were removed from the course.

Reyes has ordered both parties to weigh in on whether she has the authority to order the government to keep the golf course open.

On Wednesday, the Trump administration officially appealed Reyes' restraining order as it had promised. That order is currently set to expire on Nov. 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving.

Noting that timing, the plaintiffs in the case — local golfers and historic preservationists — have asked Reyes to extend her order by another two weeks, until Dec. 12, while she considers the underlying legal issues and decides whether to issue a longer preliminary injunction.

The government, on the other hand, said "the court already has everything it needs to promptly consider a motion for preliminary injunction" and has proposed a schedule that would enable her to issue a final ruling by Nov. 28.

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

In the meantime, the administration took another step forward in the federal review process on Thursday. The Interior Department presented its plan for the golf course to the Commission of Fine Arts, one of two federal agencies which would need to approve the project.

Commission Secretary Thomas Luebke said some 700 members of the public submitted comments ahead of the meeting, all but three in opposition to the golf course proposal.

The biggest concerns had to do with making the park less accessible to golfers of all levels, as well as cyclists, runners and picnickers who use the park's perimeter loop, which would be eliminated. There were other concerns about the impact of major road races — like the Marine Corps Marathon — that use that road, the loss of historic cherry trees and the cost of the project (the Interior Department said deferred maintenance alone would cost $43 million but did not specify how much the renovations would cost).

Sponsor Message

Over a dozen other people spoke out in the room, sharing their personal experiences with the park, raising questions about gaps in the presentation and urging the commission to defer or outright reject any plan that does not leave the perimeter loop intact.

Commissioners — all of whom were appointed by Trump — did not have the quorum needed to vote on preliminary approval. Several offered praise for the idea of beautifying the space and overhauling the golf course, but questioned whether this plan is the best way to do it.

Vice Chair Rodney Mims Cook, Jr., a Trump ally, said there seems to be enough space in the park to accommodate the aspects that people care about, like preserving the historic mini-golf course. His comments prompted applause from many of the people who had crowded into the meeting room.

Cook asked the Interior Department to bring alternative designs to its next meeting, in late January. The administration has said it plans to present the same proposal to the National Capital Planning Commission at its meeting in early December.

Administration officials said in Thursday's meeting, as they have in previous court hearings, that their plan is not yet finalized. Judge Reyes, however, is not convinced and accused the administration of already taking steps to carry it out, like cutting down hundreds of trees.

Plaintiffs in the case argue the administration has violated federal environmental law by splitting the project into smaller parts, like the tree removal, to bypass necessary reviews. And they say the administration skipped required legal steps in its rush to close off most of the park, which Reyes seemed to agree with in her order.

"In its haste to meet an arbitrary deadline, the Government has likely violated at least the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act," she wrote.

Sponsor Message

Trump has repeatedly described the East Potomac golf course as decrepit and dangerous, and challenged Reyes' authority over the project. Over the weekend, he reiterated that Reyes was appointed by President Biden and slammed her decision as "highly destructive and political."

"Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost!"

Government lawyers asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case in mid-October, accusing her of bias and hostility. She denied that request on legal grounds. Tensions between Reyes and the administration have dominated this case so far, with the judge ordering a misconduct inquiry into whether government officials and lawyers misled the court about its plans for the park.

Government lawyers have pushed back, telling the court Thursday that such an inquiry is "not necessary."

World.title: The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
World.content:
The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife

toggle caption i Richard Drury/Getty Images

Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.

She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."

Sponsor Message

It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)

As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?

David and Nina's Four L's

When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:

Love. "You gotta love each other."

Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me, and she still has her."

Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.

Sponsor Message

Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.

toggle caption i Kerry Thompson/NPR

The Magic Six

I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn . She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection , where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.

Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?

The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six .

Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.

Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.

Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.

Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.

Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.

Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.

Sponsor Message

State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.

Listen. Don't Fix.

Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.

"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.

Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."

It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.

Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.

Find Your Rhythm

Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?

Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order. Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.

Sponsor Message

As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."

So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."

World.title: 'Bigger than Barack Obama's election': Scholars reflect on Mississippi Senate race
World.content:
'Bigger than Barack Obama's election': Scholars reflect on Mississippi Senate race

Scott Colom is now this Southern state's first Black U.S. senator in nearly 150 years. Scholars and Mississippi natives Eddie Glaude and Kiese Laymon discuss the historic significance of his victory.

Transcript

TONYA MOSLEY, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Tonya Mosley. In the final weeks of Mississippi's Senate race, Democrat Scott Colom showed up outside a Donald Trump rally for his opponent and started talking to voters waiting to get in. He spent more than a year traveling across Mississippi, trying to convince people he could win, and last week, he did. Three years earlier, his opponent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, had blocked Colom's nomination to become a federal judge. Now he's headed to Washington to take her seat in the Senate.

But there's a much longer history behind the victory. Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian, descended from an enslaved woman. He's now the state's first Black U.S. senator in nearly a hundred and fifty years. It's a remarkable moment in a state where Black political power was once built, then violently dismantled in the years after Reconstruction. During the Great Migration, generations of Black Americans, including my family, fled Mississippi to escape Jim Crow and racial terror. Others, like Colom's family, stayed and fought for change.

My guests today are two sons of Mississippi who have spent their lives examining the place they call home. Eddie Glaude is a professor of African American studies at Princeton University and grew up in Moss Point, a small town on the state's Gulf Coast. Writer Kiese Laymon grew up in the state's capital of Jackson. He's the author of the memoir "Heavy" and a professor of creative writing at Rice University. Kiese and Eddie, welcome to FRESH AIR.

EDDIE GLAUDE: Thanks for having us.

KIESE LAYMON: Good to be here with y'all. Thank you.

MOSLEY: Well, Eddie, I want to start with you. When Colom won, you talked about being that little boy growing up in Moss Point, who never could have imagined a moment like this. And now we are here. And I'm actually just wondering, at what point in this race did you start to believe that it was possible?

GLAUDE: When the state of Mississippi hinted that it was about to redistrict, that they were going to engage in that project of gerrymandering that Donald Trump called for, there were these marches all throughout the South, and they were organized under the banner, All Roads Lead to the South. And Derrick Johnson gave me a call. He's the president and CEO of the NAACP, and I think in addition to that, he is the former president of the Mississippi chapter of the NAACP.

So he gave me a call and asked me to come down to Jackson to participate in the march there. And I did. And I was overwhelmed. I saw the organizing. I saw the infrastructure. I saw young people and older folk. And one of the things I did not hear was just this kind of nostalgic longing for the movement of the mid-20th century. What I heard instead and saw was organizing. They were counting. They were doing the math, Tonya. How many people do we need to turn out in DeSoto? How many people do we need to turn out in Holmes, in Jackson County, you know, in Hinds?

And what was so fascinating is that I knew then - and I was on stage with Congressman Bennie Thompson and Scott Colom. And I heard Scott speak, and I believed at that moment that he had a chance. You know, he's a political athlete, that's clear. But what was clearer to me was that these folks were ready. They were coming after us, and they were about to see the full weight and power of Black voters in Mississippi. They were going to undermine the math that was informing the redistricting effort. So I looked at Scott, and I looked at him closely, and I listened and, you know, I felt that Mississippi charm, and I said...

LAYMON: (Laughter).

GLAUDE: ...OK. All right. We about to shock the world up in here.

MOSLEY: Kiese, how would you describe the mobilization, what it looked like on the ground there that maybe the national audience didn't really see? We just kind of - we know about the win and that there was a great mobilization.

LAYMON: I think that's a great question. You know, one of the things I think with this particular mobilization, unlike what we saw with Espy, and this goes to...

MOSLEY: And Espy - just to describe who Espy - Mike Espy...

LAYMON: Mike Espy...

MOSLEY: ...Actually ran against Hyde-Smith...

LAYMON: Yeah.

MOSLEY: ...Several years ago.

LAYMON: Right, ran against Cindy Hyde-Smith a few years ago. I worked hard on that campaign. I was living in Oxford at the time. I remember one morning, and Espy's - I don't want to say this person's name, but Espy's primary donor knocked on my door, sat on my porch. And the thing he was trying to, like, get me to understand was that we have to get Mike to let his hands go. That's what he kept saying. We have to let Mike let his hands go.

Now, Mike Espy, I think we need to understand - this is important for what Scott Colom did - was seen as a traditional, clean, electable Democrat, meaning that the people who put Mike Espy forward did not think he would offend many Republicans. What I loved about what Scott was doing this year was Scott, I think, took off that cloak of what some people call political respectability in terms of the look. And that was part of the galvanization. And so when I realized that Scott could win was when I saw, obviously, the commercial, the pick-a-protein commercial. Now, for me, I thought, Scott - my mother is a political scientist. She said, Kiese, I think Scott's going to have the votes. But in Mississippi, having the votes doesn't mean you're going to win.

And when I saw that pick another protein commercial, I thought that he had the cultural force to stop the Republican Party from doing what a lot of us assumed the Republican Party would do if it was too close. So for me on the ground, I saw a different kind of candidate, followed by different kinds of potential voters. And what I love about this moment is that those people, like my mother, who grew up in a political Mississippi that was very close, very contained, you had to bring your best visual self to every situation. They walked with those young sisters and brothers in hoodies, you know, with earrings all over their faces. It was not just, like, an intergenerational march. It was an intercultural march and an intercultural election. And I just feel like that is some of what I don't hear much of the national media talking about.

MOSLEY: Also it's just so interesting, you know, Colom didn't have much money from the National Democratic Party. And this particular political ad that you're talking about is just one of the creative ways that they were able to reach voters. And I actually want to play the one that you're talking about, where essentially the background of this ad is that his opponent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, during an interview, suggested that people struggling with the rising price of beef could simply choose another protein. And here is how Colom's campaign responded. Let's listen.

(SOUNDBITE OF AD)

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: The price of beef continuing to go up.

CINDY HYDE-SMITH: You know, you have so many proteins to choose from.

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR #1: (As MS Voter) Pick another protein? [Expletive] I'd rather pick another senator instead.

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR #2: (As MS Voter) Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I'd rather pick another senator.

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR #3: (As MS Voter) Pick another protein? What the F?

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR #4: (As MS Voter) Pick another senator instead.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

MOSLEY: That's a political ad...

LAYMON: It's great.

MOSLEY: ...For now Senator-elect Scott Colom. And, Kiese, you said that when you saw that commercial, you knew that he'd win. I want to know from you, Eddie. I mean, beyond the humor, he's actually talking about something really real - the cost of living in one of the poorest states in the country. How much of this victory do you think was about the way he spoke to people, and how much was it about actually what he's saying, you know?

GLAUDE: It's a combination of both, I think. You know, what was so brilliant about the ad is that you can see and hear - right? - the cultural residences. It's quintessentially Mississippi. It's Mississippi concentrated.

LAYMON: (Laughter).

GLAUDE: And what you hear is that it cuts across racial boundaries. So the rhythm of the speech that you heard, the white man who, you know, who drew out...

MOSLEY: Right.

GLAUDE: ...You know, the expletive. You know, the white woman who asked in a very shrill kind of way, what the? You know, that - and the rhythm of it is everybody in Mississippi knows that's how you cuss, right? So...

LAYMON: (Laughter).

MOSLEY: You, like, really draw it out, huh? Yeah.

GLAUDE: Right. I mean, so it sounded familiar. But the thing is that on top of that performance was the substantive issue. Cindy Hyde-Smith had been absent. She hasn't been representing the state. And so here she is, in this very kind of crude and callous way, saying, let them eat cake, too, right? Having her Marie Antoinette moment on television in some ways.

And so they were able to bring these two things together, the kind of cultural resonances that Kiese was talking about and then connect it with the substantive critique of Hyde-Smith that she wasn't representing the state. She wasn't addressing the fundamental material conditions of Mississippians, no matter what side of town they live on, no matter what color their skin. And so it was a kind of wonderful distillation of both of those elements.

LAYMON: And can I just say one more thing about that, just hopping off what Eddie said? The wonder to me also, just as, like, a person who creates, you know, words and word culture, is that they made Scott the subject and the viewer. So the wonder of that is like, yes, the beginning, we see this young, white man cussing the way white boys in Mississippi cuss. We see the older sister in the beginning eating catfish, talking the way all my aunties cuss. We see the older white woman at the end, at the grocery store, trying to get something that's not affordable. And then we see Scott doing what? Watching as we watched, laughing as we laughed and saying pick another senator instead.

So that move - right? - he starts to embody the viewer. And I don't care what political persuasion you are. Every viewer had Scott Colom's response to that, which is to laugh. So it's smart and it's genius. But it also does something that I think most word sort of assemblages can't, which is take the subject, and then the subject becomes the viewer. So the point of view shifts. And we start to look at this ad through Scott, or Scott starts to look at this ad through us. I just think it was like the most impactful political ad of my life by far.

MOSLEY: Let's take a short break. If you're just joining us, my guests are Princeton scholar Eddie Glaude and Rice University Professor Kiese Laymon. We'll be right back after a short break. This is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF JULIAN LAGE GROUP'S "IOWA TAKEN")

MOSLEY: This is FRESH AIR. And today I am talking with Eddie Glaude and Kiese Laymon about Scott Colom's historic Senate election win in Mississippi.

I want to break down something a little bit. I just want us to get a deeper understanding of Cindy Hyde-Smith just for a brief moment, especially through the context of the last few years. I don't know how much radical intervention we can expect from a senator, but I expect Scott Colom, while keeping himself and his family safe, to also keep all children of Mississippi safe by all means necessary or to attempt to. And I think that will lead to this being not just the first, but the first of a real, sustained movement for love, progress and connectivity in Mississippi.

GLAUDE: Yeah. Yeah, that's it. You know, I pray that he doesn't fall for the siren song of Washington, D.C.

MOSLEY: Oh.

LAYMON: Yeah. Yeah.

GLAUDE: You know, Washington, D.C., offers, you know, all sorts of temptations about the nature of power, about what it means to be the first and the like. I hope he takes that gift of Mississippi that orients us in a certain sort of way to the world. I hope he brings it to Washington, D.C., and he lets all of them see it for what it is and all of its power. I know that's being abstract, but that has everything to do with, I think, the power of what it means to be from this place. That's the first thing.

The second thing, I think, you know, politicians inevitably disappoint. I learned that early on. But I want to see what Cassandra Welchlin and Rukia Lumumba and...

LAYMON: Yeah.

GLAUDE: ...Sister Lambright-Haynes and all of those organizers on the ground who made this possible - I want to see what they do in holding Scott Colom accountable. I can't wait to continue to see what they do, and how Scott plays this role in that effort.

LAYMON: Yes. I agree with Eddie. I mean, I hope - and if there's any moment where Democrats could learn that you must follow the people, it is this moment. And I hope that the Democrats - you follow the people by funding the people but also being open to the people's visions. And I have absolute trust in that group of people that helped Scott get elected. I have no doubt in my mind that their vision for Mississippi is the vision for Mississippi and actually the vision for this nation and the world. Whether the Democratic Party sees that or not is something else. But...

GLAUDE: (Laughter).

LAYMON: ...It's right there. It's right there for you.

MOSLEY: Kiese Laymon and Eddie Glaude, thank you so much for this conversation.

GLAUDE: Thank you.

LAYMON: Thank you so much for giving us space.

MOSLEY: Eddie Glaude is a professor of African American Studies at Princeton University and the author of several books, including "Begin Again" and "America, U.S.A." Kiese Laymon is a professor of English and creative writing at Rice University and the author of the acclaimed memoir, "Heavy." His new memoir, "Good, God: A Creation Story," will be published this spring.

(SOUNDBITE OF DEEP BLUE ORGAN TRIO'S "YOU HAVEN'T DONE NOTHIN'")

MOSLEY: If you'd like to catch up on interviews you've missed, like our conversation with LeVar Burton about his new memoir or Lynn Novick about her new documentary on crime and punishment in America, check out our podcast. You'll find lots of FRESH AIR interviews. You can also watch some of our interviews on our YouTube page, thisisfreshair.

FRESH AIR's executive producer is Sam Briger. Our technical director and engineer is Audrey Bentham. Our interviews and reviews are produced and edited by Phyllis Myers, Roberta Shorrock, Ann Marie Baldonado, Lauren Krenzel, Therese Madden, Monique Nazareth, Susan Nyakundi, Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez-Wisler. Our digital media producer is Molly Seavy-Nesper. Thea Chaloner directed today's show. With Terry Gross, I'm Tonya Mosley.

World.title: Why some Americans are stockpiling for a 90-day power outage
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The number of Americans stockpiling bottled water, non-perishable food and other emergency supplies has spiked over the past few weeks, a trend that has only accelerated in the wake of a series of high-profile tech outages.

The jump in purchases has triggered questions to the highest levels of the administration, with both U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance trying to assure Americans there's no need for doomsday prepping.

"Tell them to relax, everything's good," Trump said in a Thursday interview with Fox News. "I'll let you know if there's a problem."

"A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water,” Vance told Fox News earlier this week. “My answer to that is no."

The evidence of stockpiling is far and wide, including U.S. media reports of recent spikes in sales of emergency supplies at stores in California, Ohio and Oklahoma.

Walmart customers were stocking up on more propane, bottled water and camping gear than usual earlier ​this month, a company spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday.

WATCH | Amid reports of panic buying, U.S. officials try to calm fears over tech outages: Trump officials grilled over tech outages that have Americans on edge | Duration closed caption 2:29 Top U.S. national security officials faced tough questions from lawmakers Thursday over a series of tech outages and disruptions affecting airports, banks and Microsoft services that have rattled the American public and raised concerns about panic buying.

Survival Frog, an online U.S. retailer specializing in emergency supplies, says its sales volume shot up 450 per cent in the three weeks since Oct. 27, with new customers accounting for the bulk of the increase, Axios reported on Thursday.

Since late October, Costco's U.S. sales data showed an increase in purchases of "rice, canned goods, water, paper products, generators, batteries and similar items seemingly in response to a variety of concerns on social media," a company executive told Bloomberg this week.

Stockpiling predates tech outages

Web searches for "emergency supplies" are up 300 per cent in the past month compared with the same time period last year, according to Google Trends.

The start of the stockpiling began several weeks before the recent string of tech failures.

It traces back to misleading TikTok and Facebook posts that followed a directive from Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth.

Originally announced in late September, the Pentagon initiative dubbed FORTRESS America (Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability) includes a plan for every major U.S. military installation to have the capability to generate its own electricity.

The start of the stockpiling began several weeks before the recent string of tech failures. It traces back to misleading TikTok and Facebook posts that followed a directive from Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. (Leonardo Fernandez Viloria/Reuters)

"So bases remain lit, aircraft fly, and command centers stay online even if the civilian grid is taken down by cyberattack or sabotage," said the Pentagon news release on Hegseth's announcement.

On Oct. 25, Fox News reported more details of Hegseth's directive, including a specific nugget about a 90-day time frame.

U.S. bases prep for 90 days without power

"The Pentagon is preparing U.S. military bases to keep operating for at least 90 days without outside support as it prepares for the possibility of a major war that could cripple power grids, disrupt supply chains and threaten critical infrastructure on American soil," said the report.

Within days of that story, Google searches for "90 day power outage" spiked by 5,000 per cent and retailers saw jumps in customers buying emergency supplies.

Videos quickly mushroomed on TikTok and YouTube twisting the content of the Fox News story, either suggesting that the U.S. government was warning people to prepare for a 90-day blackout or that the government was itself preparing for a 90-day blackout.

By mid-November, multiple TikTok videos falsely claimed a 90-day power outage would hit the U.S. on Nov. 17, the fact-checking website PolitiFact reported.

The government of Germany renewed its recommendation for stockpiling at least a three-day supply of such basics as bottled water and non-perishable ready-to-eat food. The photo shows items in an emergency kit from German humanitarian aid organization Malteser Hilfsdienst. (Thilo Schmuelgen/Reuters)

Some events that actually happened likely did little to the quell the paranoia.

A cyberattack raised temperatures in hundreds of supermarket freezers across France in mid-October, spoiling tens of millions of euros worth of food. French authorities blamed Iran-backed hackers.

The U.K. government launched an official "Be Ready" campaign in October, urging the British people to prepare to be self-sufficient for 72 hours in the event of an emergency.

Then just two weeks later, the European Commission unveiled new emergency preparedness guidelines.

And then came the cascade of outages that shut down Microsoft services, stranded hundreds of thousands of U.S. air passengers, blocked customers at some U.S. banks from doing transactions online and put the National Security Agency's classified communications network offline all in the space of six days.

Mehdi Hossain, an associate professor of marketing at the University of Rhode Island, has researched the panic buying that defined the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Luggage at San Diego International Airport, three days after the ground-stop order that led to the cancellation of some 20,000 flights across the U.S. (Gregory Bull/The Associated Press)

Hossain says uncertainty over how the pandemic would unfold meant that people had no reference point for how they should prepare, while the high levels of anxiety over the potential seriousness of the threat triggered stockpiling that at times became irrational.

"What was really happening under the hood is the thought that, 'OK, if I don't prepare for this reality, and I suffer and my family suffers because of my lack of preparedness, I am going to regret it,'" Hossain told CBC News.

He says some similar psychology appears to have been at work in recent weeks, fuelled by those false reports on social media.

"It's a snowball kind of effect," Hossain said. "That fake news, when it validates with your fear, you start trusting it more than probably you should, and you start acting on it."

World.title: A Montrealer died in Istanbul. Authorities blame food poisoning but what we found suggests something else
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, a healthy 24-year-old Montrealer, died suddenly in Istanbul on June 17, 2025.

A Turkish autopsy report concluded the cause of death was food poisoning.

But for her family, that doesn't add up.

A joint investigation into Deveaux-Cattino's death by Enquête and the fifth estate revealed a different poison at work and 12 similar deaths.

The recent medical school graduate had decided to celebrate by taking a trip with a few of her closest friends.

"She'd never been to Turkey," said her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. "She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country."

The group hit the tourist trail and its highlights, including the requisite balloon ride in Cappadocia.

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino had never been to Turkey before her trip in 2025, says her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. ‘She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country.’ (Radio-Caanda)

With only two days to go, Bérengère and one of her friends headed for Istanbul, a city she'd longed to visit.

Watch the full documentary, "The Invisble Killer," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m .

They checked into Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel and went straight out to explore. They soaked up the sights and street food, then settled down for a proper meal, a chicken casserole followed by Turkish tea and baklava.

The next morning, they woke violently ill.

Laurie recalls the final days

The details of those final days come from Laurie, the woman who travelled to Istanbul with Bérengère. What happened on that trip left her traumatized and we've agreed to protect her identity and not use her real name.

She said that within minutes of waking, Bérengère was throwing up.

"Then I started feeling unwell," Laurie said, "and suddenly we were taking turns running to the bathroom to vomit until we realized that whatever it was, it wasn't just going to pass."

They called the front desk and an ambulance took them to hospital.

‘My sister is younger than me,’ said Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino, right. ‘I’d never imagined a life without her.’ (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)

'Things aren't going well'

That same day, across the ocean in Montreal, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino saw her screen light up: Laurie was FaceTiming her.

"I thought: 'This isn't normal. Something's off. This is going to be bad news,'" said Deveaux-Cattino. "She says 'Élo, we're in the hospital in Istanbul, and things aren't going well. I've been told to contact the family.'"

Deveaux-Cattino and her father, Henri Cattino, scrambled to find flights to Istanbul. While waiting for their connection in Paris, Deveaux-Cattino called the embassy.

"I said: 'Please, can you tell me if my sister has died?'" said Deveaux-Cattino. ”And she said: 'I'm very sorry, Éléonore, but your sister is dead.'"

Three days into their trip to Istanbul in November 2025, the Böcek family from Hamburg fell ill. Five days later, all four family members were dead, poisoned by phosphine gas. (@ismailsaymaz/X)

The Böcek family

The Deveaux-Cattinos repatriated Bérengère's body and asked the Quebec coroner's office to examine it. They buried their daughter and sister without confirmation of the cause of death.

As they waited for answers from Turkey, the family speculated about what else could explain Bérengère's death: Organ trafficking? Alcohol poisoning? Medical malpractice?

Then, in November, as we were investigating, a diplomatic source texted with a tip that pointed to an entirely different explanation.

"A family of four has just died in Istanbul. Watch this report."

The Böceks, a Turkish-German family from Hamburg, were visiting Istanbul. Their hotel was blocks from where Bérengère and Laurie stayed. All four fell ill and died within days of each other.

Investigators initially suspected food poisoning there, too. But within days, authorities concluded that another poison had been at work: aluminum phosphide, a highly toxic agricultural pesticide used to kill rodents and insects.

The 'bomb'

Exterminators call aluminum phosphide "the bomb." It is used in pellet form. Once the pellets are exposed to air, they release phosphine gas. Exterminators say that when placed in a sealed room, the gas kills every living, breathing thing within 72 hours. In Turkey, it's illegal to use in urban areas.

But, like all big cities, Istanbul has a bedbug problem.

WATCH | An exterminator explains treatments to kill bedbugs: Safe extermination of bedbugs | Duration 1:26 Istanbul exterminator Birkan Cihan explains the difference between legal and lethal treatments to kill bedbugs.

Exterminator Birkan Cihan said he can barely keep up with calls from desperate home and hotel owners. Some ask whether he treats bedbugs with "gas." He doesn't.

"We tell them their neighbours could die from it, and that they could, too. But they say: 'We have no choice, it's the only thing that works,'" Cihan said

The phosphine gas these pellets emit is so potent and volatile that it can spread through a building, even if the area being treated is sealed.

In the case of the Böcek family, fumigation in the neighbouring room was determined to be what killed all four of them.

Investigations by Enquête and the fifth estate have found similar cases. In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand.

In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand. (Submitted by Bélanger family)

'That doesn't make any sense'

Just before Christmas 2025, the Deveaux-Cattinos received the autopsy report from Turkey. It concluded that food poisoning caused Bérengère's death. Unconvinced, they handed the report to the Quebec coroner's office.

"The coroner here ran some tests, and she couldn't confirm that food poisoning was the cause of death because, usually, there are signs of intestinal irritation," Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino said. "There were none in my sister's case."

We showed the Turkish autopsy report to another Quebec pathologist. Although not authorized to speak publicly, he also questioned the autopsy's conclusions.

"Two young, healthy women who end up in the hospital with food poisoning — OK, I'll buy that. But to die of it so quickly, without any signs of bloody diarrhea or other complications, that doesn't make any sense."

Turkish freelance journalist Ayse Adanali covered the story of the death of the Böcek family in Istanbul in 2025. (Radio-Canada)

Women and children

In Turkey, we started working with Ayse Adanali, a freelance Turkish journalist who'd covered the Böcek story.

Together, we documented nearly 30 cases of phosphine poisoning, including a dozen deaths, since 2023 in Turkey.
