Some were tourists, like the two Dutch teenagers found dead by their father in their Istanbul hotel room in August 2025. But most of the victims were Turkish, like Karan Yazıcı, a three-year-old boy poisoned in Istanbul in April 2025 following a fumigation in the neighbouring apartment.

The majority of the victims are women and children. Members of the same family were often poisoned together. While some survived, others died. In most cases, food poisoning was initially blamed for making them sick.

'This is not food poisoning'

Şebnem Korur Fincancı is a human rights activist, professor emeritus and leading forensic pathologist in Turkey.

She's studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas.

Turkish forensic pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı has studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas. (Radio-Canada)

She'd never heard about Bérengère; her death had not been covered by Turkish media.

"This is not food poisoning," she said after reading the Turkish autopsy report.

"I don't think that this is food poisoning because there is no story of diarrhea, only throwing up."

She added that the timing of Bérengère's decline suggests food poisoning couldn't be the culprit.

"Rather, it is the pesticide poisoning."

Fincancı sees one undeniable detail in this report, a finding common to all victims of phosphine gas poisoning she's examined: something called metabolic acidosis, which increases the levels of acidity in the body.

"There is the metabolic acidosis, which also indicates the pesticide intoxication," she said. 'It is one of the main findings of these kinds of cases."

She believes there could be more cases of phosphine poisoning than currently reported.

"With all these misdiagnoses, we have to consider the situation."

Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and her friend, Laurie, stayed at the Seven Days Hotel in Istanbul. (Radio-Canada)

150 bites

We scoured hundreds of Google and Tripadvisor reviews for the Seven Days Hotel to see if they'd had a bedbug problem around the time of Bérengère and Laurie's stay.

One stood out: A tourist claiming he'd been bitten 150 times during his stay in June 2025.

We tracked him down. He confirmed he stayed in Room 107, the room next door to where the two women stayed 10 days later.

The windows in those two rooms open onto each other.

That left one critical question: Had Room 107 been treated after his stay? And, if so, with what?

We contacted hotel manager Bahattin Demir. He remembered Bérengère and Laurie and had gone to the hospital after they'd been admitted.

We told him about the tourist in Room 107 and asked him whether extermination work in that room could have killed Bérengère.

"I don't think so, because if it was that product, I'm sure that, you know, everybody would have this problem," he said.

Inside Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel where Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and Laurie stayed. (Radio-Canada)

He said exterminators spray the rooms in the hotel monthly. He offered to contact them and find out what product they use, but then wrote back, referring us to them for more details.

The extermination company is called Wolves.

A contact called them for us. We're protecting her identity because undercover work can lead to jail time in Turkey.

Posing as an Air BnB owner in Istanbul's Fatih district, she claimed to be struggling with bedbugs.

The employee was cautious on the phone.

He didn't name the product specifically, but his detailed description is similar to how aluminum phosphide is used.

"For 72 hours, nobody goes in, the doors are locked and nothing living enters."

We called Wolves for an interview. The employee who answered the phone was not authorized to speak, but denied using aluminum phosphide.

Neither the hospital that treated Bérengère nor the Forensic Medical Centre where her autopsy was performed replied to our inquiries.

The tourism police similarly declined our interview request.

Going over notes Laurie had shared, we noticed she and Bérengère had left the window open the first night. But the next evening, to avoid being woken by the call to prayer, they closed it and turned on the air conditioning. And that was the night they got sick.

We asked pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı whether phosphine gas residue could build up in air conditioners.

"Of course," she said.

WATCH | Honouring her sister's memory: A life without her | Duration 0:52 Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants her sister, Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, to be remembered.

'Those who are gone'

The Böceks' case went to trial in June 2026. The defendants were charged with criminal negligence causing the deaths of this family of four. The ruling came down within days. The owners of the extermination company were found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in prison. The hotel owner and employees received 12 to 13 years.

While awaiting the verdict, the paternal grandfather, Yilmaz Böcek, commented that even the stiffest penalty could never bring back his children and grandchildren.

"Those who are gone never come back."

Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants Bérengère to be remembered.

"My sister is younger than me. I'd never imagined a life without her. We used to be two against the world … now I'm all alone," she said.

"But I'm stubborn. And since she can no longer speak, I'll speak for her. I'll never let her go."

In the summer of 2026, the government of Canada added a new entry to its travel advisory for Turkey, alerting travellers to "cases of poisoning linked to the use of chemical pesticides in tourist accommodations in Istanbul."

After this story first aired on Oct. 15, 2026, Turkish consular officials contacted us, confirming the investigation into Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino's death in Istanbul remains open.

World.title: Large AI companies 'desperate for compute' are crowding out Canadian startups at home
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ottawa's new budget promises to help Canadian AI companies access processing power on home soil — something that's been a challenge as smaller startups struggle to compete with tech giants for increasingly scarce computing resources.

The federal government is promising 500 megawatts of "sovereign AI compute" to help expand domestic computing capacity using financial tools such as backstops and offtake agreements to encourage private investment, but questions remain about when that capacity will become available and how companies will be able to access it.

For Al Vigier, CEO of Vancouver-based AI company Caseway, accessing computing capacity in Canada is critical to serving his customers.

Caseway develops AI and automation tools primarily for the court system, and also works with law firms and the defence sector. Many of its clients require their information to remain in Canada.

"Most of our clients, the courts, the defence, the Canadian military, they require sovereign AI, which basically means that they don't want their data to leave Canada. They want their data to be governed by Canadian law and they want to enter into agreements with Canadian companies," he said.

But that option doesn't exist in Canada at the moment, Vigier added, so certain Caseway customers won't use the company's AI offerings. For other clients who are more flexible with where their data lands, Caseway has to turn to the U.S. or elsewhere for computing power.

Al Vigier is the CEO of Caseway, a Vancouver-based AI company that builds automation for enterprises and government. (Submitted by Al Vigier)

Canada, like many other countries, relies heavily on U.S. technology companies for cloud services, including remote computing and data storage offered by tech giants such as Amazon and Microsoft.

That dependence raises concerns about data sovereignty, since U.S. laws can give American intelligence and law-enforcement agencies access to information held by technology providers under certain circumstances.

Vigier said the federal government's commitment is exciting because it could help address those concerns. But while he'd like to offer sovereign computing services to clients immediately, he's worried about how the policy will be implemented and when the capacity will become available.

Canadian computing power in high demand

Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto who helped launch Canada's sovereign AI compute strategy , said major technology companies such as Meta, Google and OpenAI are "desperate for compute."

As AI models become more powerful and more people use them, he said "the demand just skyrockets."

For Canadian startups looking to use AI on a larger scale, "it can be hard to secure these contracts because these big hyperscalers can come in and just buy up all the use for five to 10 years into the future," Mullin said.

"And if you're ... a project developer for a data centre, you'd say, 'Oh, it's very easy. I'll just sign one contract with a big, huge company and I've sold all my compute. I don't have to worry about kind of smaller contracts and selling to smaller Canadian firms.'"

The scale of investment by major technology companies is already evident in Canada.

Earlier this year, Meta announced plans to build its first Canadian data centre , a massive one-gigawatt project northeast of Edmonton. Once completed, it is expected to be among the country's largest data centres and the first hyperscale data centre in Alberta.

In October, U.S. AI company Anthropic announced it had signed a long-term lease for the first 95-megawatt phase of a data centre project in Nova Scotia. Canadian clean energy company EverWind Fuels will build and own the facility, while Anthropic will lease the capacity for at least 20 years.

WATCH | Telus to build new AI data centre in B.C. under federal sovereign AI initiative: Government partners with Telus on building sovereign AI infrastructure | Duration closed caption 1:26 Telus will build a new AI data centre in B.C., under the federal Enabling Large-Scale Sovereign AI Data Centres initiative, Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Evan Solomon announced on Monday. The project ‘reflects the kind of ambitious infrastructure that we need as a country,’ Solomon said.

Ramping up efforts for sovereign AI

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) says it is working to bring the capacity online "as quickly as possible," but has not provided a firm timeline.

"The government is engaging with a number of proponents on potential projects across Canada that could significantly expand domestic AI compute capacity," a spokesperson said in an emailed statement to CBC News. "These projects are at different stages of development and commercial discussions are ongoing, and it would be premature to confirm specific timelines, projects or locations."

ISED said pricing and access arrangements have not yet been decided, although the government expects companies using the capacity to pay market-based rates.

The commitment is part of a broader federal strategy to support sovereign AI. In October, Ottawa also announced it would invest up to $1.6 billion in Toronto-based AI company Cohere.

LISTEN | The Cohere story part one: Carney's $1.6B bet: Front Burner 31:44 The Cohere story part one: Carney's $1.6B bet

500 megawatts could be a 'drop in the bucket'

Clay Swerdelian, CEO of Calgary-based Verano.AI, said he'd welcome the opportunity to keep his company's computing operations in Canada, provided the price was right.

Verano.AI primarily supports the energy sector, using AI-powered tools to automate work related to regulatory matters.

Swerdelian says the company has developed their own AI agents and models to handle tasks involving confidential information, including enterprise data and methane emissions data that clients wouldn't want to share with external AI services.

Clay Swerdelian is the CEO of Verano.AI based in Calgary which primarily supports the energy sector with AI-powered automation of workflow on regulatory matters. (Submitted by Clay Swerdelian)

Swerdelian says he expects Canada to experience a "massive boom" when it comes to companies looking for computing power, partly driven by the recent U.S. midterm election results.

"A lot of the red states are now blue states and a lot of the blue states won't allow data centres, so they're shifting to Canada," he said.

"And the place to be is Alberta for the most part, because the gas and all the land that we have and the infrastructure and everything is kind of built out already other than, of course, the data centres themselves."

Given that growing demand, Swerdelian says Ottawa's proposed 500 megawatts of computing capacity could be a "drop in the bucket."

And with no firm timeline for when that capacity will become available, Mullin said Canadian startups may have little choice but to continue relying on computing services outside the country.

"These firms could try and just buy compute back from hyperscalers, and in many cases that may be south of the border and that just makes us more vulnerable as a country," he said.

"That means things like all that data is crossing the international border subject to U.S. law. It means we don't control these assets, they could be taken away, they can be repurposed for something else and that just makes us overall more dependent."

World.title: They finally had their dream food truck. Then it was repossessed
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

While Maylin Rodriguez prepares lunch service in Oxford, N.S., she worries about how her family will repay a loan for a food truck it no longer has.

Rodriguez and her family had run their business, LeoMay Fusion, out of the food truck for about a year in rural Nova Scotia before RCMP officers showed up in mid-October and they learned a previous lender was repossessing the second-hand vehicle.

"We were like, this can't be happening. We paid for this truck. We think that we did things properly. They just let us know that the person who sold it to us had no right to sell the truck,” she said.

“We were devastated. Still in this disbelief.”

Rodriguez and her husband, son and daughter-in-law now serve customers out of the canteen in the community’s arena. They are open seven days a week, trying to repay the approximately $65,000 they borrowed to buy the truck, outfit it and get the business up and running.

The family travelled to Quebec to buy the truck and then operated for about a year after upgrading it. (LeoMay Food Truck/Facebook)

But they say their sales at the canteen are less than 10 per cent of what they earned serving dishes inspired by their Cuban and Venezuelan roots at events around the region.

They bought the food truck in Quebec after connecting with a seller on Facebook Marketplace. From the start, they said, it didn’t operate as promised and they had to upgrade the water system and deep fryer.

The family, who came to Canada in the past decade, said they had a steep learning curve — from figuring out how to do the accounting and taxes to sourcing the food and cooking quality meals quickly. They did plenty of research and asked other businesses for advice, said Leonardo Illas Jr., Rodriguez’s son.

"At first it was just a dream, then working toward getting things going, then suddenly you're there and it's fantastic but it's definitely challenging,” he said.

The family that operates LeoMay Fusion took their food truck to events across Nova Scotia and to other parts of the Maritimes. (Submitted by LeoMay Fusion)

It was a dream that ended abruptly when they learned there was a lien against the truck in Quebec. It wasn’t caught when they registered the vehicle in Nova Scotia.

Now the family wants to warn others to take precautions when buying second-hand goods.

Up to purchaser to search for liens

Lenders and some companies, like garages, can place liens on a vehicle, allowing them to repossess it if debts go unpaid. Liens can also be applied to mobile homes, boats, off-road vehicles and tractors.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre said in a statement it’s important for buyers to do due diligence, including verifying a seller’s information, confirming ownership and checking for outstanding liens or financial claims.

Rodriguez said they took their bill of sale to the Société de l'assurance automobile du Québec, which handles vehicle registration in Quebec, and were told they could proceed with registering it in Nova Scotia. She said no one mentioned checking for liens there or when they registered it.

The Nova Scotia Registry of Motor Vehicles requires a certificate signed from a past owner, but it is not responsible for checking for liens, a spokesperson told CBC News.

There is a site that for a fee searches for liens across the territories and Atlantic Canada using a vehicle’s identification number (VIN). Quebec and other provinces have separate systems.

Leonardo Illas Jr., left, says his father Leo Illas Sr., right, has been applying to jobs. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)

Dealerships are responsible for checking for liens before they sell used vehicles, but the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada warns that the rules around whether private sellers must disclose liens vary by province. It advises people to check for liens themselves through online personal property searches.

Rodriguez said her family didn’t know the right questions to ask and learned too late about the importance of checking for liens.

“What about new Canadians, newcomers, young people that don't know and they want to … [be] entrepreneurs? It would be great if they can have some guidance,” said Rodriguez.

“We come here, we learn English, we learn new rules, but we can't learn [it] all. And I think the institutions should offer as much information as they can so we can be prepared."

Considering legal action

Rodriguez said they’ve shared all the documentation they have with police in Longueuil, Que. The force said it is reviewing the incident and there have been no criminal charges.

RCMP in Nova Scotia declined to comment as they are not the lead agency. Their only involvement was being there as a safety precaution when the truck was repossessed, and a spokesperson said lenders often ask for their presence.

Meanwhile, the family is still on the hook for the money they borrowed. They said they’ve consulted a lawyer in Quebec but don’t know if they can afford to take any legal action.

The Cumberland branch of the Community Business Development Corporation, which issued their loan, said in a statement that they “recognize the difficult circumstances facing the business owners,” but declined to comment on the case.

Maylin Rodriguez, who is originally from Cuba, hopes lenders and other organizations consider that newcomers don't always know the right questions to ask when starting businesses. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)

The LeoMay Fusion team had hoped to operate the canteen and food truck concurrently this winter. Instead, they had to cancel commitments to community groups, who they thanked for being understanding.

“We served large events. We had the whole season scheduled, so we were counting on that revenue. But then [we] changed to here,” Rodriguez said at the canteen.

“We've seen a significant drop in our earnings, which is understandable because it's a small town.”

'Heartbreaking to hear what happened'

Ongoing repairs at the Oxford rink mean there is currently no ice surface, resulting in slower days at the canteen. The family said they’ve been grateful for the support of loyal customers like Emme Bidwell, who stopped in on Monday, picking up a chicken and pork rice bowl.

“It’s one of my favourite meals,” Bidwell said. "It's just heartbreaking to hear what happened. But anything we can do to support our local small restaurants."

LeoMay Fusion has a takeout window in the arena in Oxford, N.S. (Elizabeth McMillan/CBC)

Illas already works a second job. His father is looking for one.

“It's been a lot — having to apply for jobs, having to deal with lawyers, having to deal with the police … cancelling events,” said Illas.

Rodriguez said she understands they may never get their money back, and hopes lenders and other organizations consider their story and ways to better support other newcomers.

“Of course we want justice for our family. We would like to recover what we lost," she said.

"But if we can prevent someone else, another family, newcomer, new Canadian, someone trying to build a business, to go through the same pain that we're going [through], then speaking publicly is worth it,” added Rodriguez.

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Canadian investment dollars are one of the villains in Spain's election fight over housing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At a Madrid apartment complex just outside the city's centre, red maple leaves hang upside down in windows along with defiant posters urging Canadian investment money to get out of their neighbourhood.

"They are pushing us out of our houses," said Rafael Cuadrado, who has lived in the complex for 20 years.

The main target of the residents' wrath is Toronto-based Brookfield Corporation.

A sign on a window of a Madrid apartment accuses Toronto-based Brookfield of treating tenants unfairly. In a statement to CBC News, Brookfield said it complies with all 'applicable Spanish tenancy legislation, including statutory tenant protections and extension requirements.' (Jason Ho/CBC)

One of Canada's premier financial and investment institutions, Brookfield owns 900 units in Cuadrado's residential complex, along with approximately 4,100 others around the Spanish capital.

Cuadrado and other residents accuse Brookfield of planning to let their leases expire and then flip their homes for market prices that few here can afford. He says several of his neighbours have already received notices from Brookfield's management company informing them their tenancies will not be extended.

CBC News has seen one letter sent to a tenant who was told their expiring lease would not be renewed and they would have to turn over the keys to their apartment.

It's not illegal, but the residents say it's unfair.

"Our daughter came here when she was two years old. This is our first house ... so this is our life," Cuadrado told CBC News in his living room.

Many of the residents are long-time tenants who moved into the buildings when they used to be part of Madrid's public housing stock. Most pay rents well below the current market rate, as a succession of lease extensions and government-mandated rent caps have kept their outlay relatively low.

Raphael Cuadrado lives in a Madrid apartment complex owned by Brookfield, one of Canada's top investment firms. He and other residents fear the company plans to flip their units when their leases expire. (Jason Ho/CBC)

Cuadrado says he pays 930 euros a month for his 800-square-foot, three-bedroom apartment. The unit would likely fetch about 1,500 euros on the open market.

"Why do we have to leave our house because there is a big investment company coming from abroad to get a profit [from] us?" he said. "No way."

WATCH | Clashes in Spain as thousands protest nation's housing crisis: Clashes in Spain as millions protest nation's housing crisis | Duration closed caption 2:13 Spain saw widespread disruption Wednesday, including clashes with police in Barcelona, as millions protested the country's housing crisis. The demonstrations come one month after the death of an 87-year-old pensioner who had been evicted from her home.

'Vulture funds'

Anger over housing in Spain has hit a breaking point.

The eviction of Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal in late September, after the 87-year-old woman was unable to pay a hefty rent increase, sent protesters into the streets. Authorities evicted her on the back of a stretcher and she died in hospital a few weeks later.

Her eviction prompted Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call an election for Nov. 29, with housing the central issue.

Spain's public unions, which allied with the tenants, are casting money from institutional investors, such as pension plans, as one of the primary villains. And some of them are Canadian.

"'Vulture funds' are what they call them," said Alicia Del Rio, who is with Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid (Madrid Tenants Union), one of the country's most prominent advocates for renters.

Del Rio blames a succession of cash-strapped Spanish governments for laying out the welcome mat for foreign investors, who she says have in turn treated Spanish residential properties as a commodity to be flipped, with little regard for the people living in them.

Alicia Del Rio is with Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid, Spain's most prominent tenants union. (Jason Ho/CBC)

"[The government] gave the message, 'Welcome to Spain, this is going to be your paradise.'"

Canadian owners

Canadian retirement funds and investment firms are designed to seek out safe returns — wherever they can find them. And Spain is seen as an attractive place to grow that money.

Along with Brookfield, Canada Pension Plan Investments has a roughly 900-million-euro portfolio ($1.4 billion Cdn) in the Spanish housing sector, although it's focused on student housing rather than residential homes. It owns approximately 13,000 dorm-type beds across Spain and Portugal, concentrated in cities with large universities.

In a statement to CBC News, CPP said its investments help "expand the overall supply of housing available to students without removing existing homes from the conventional residential market."

HOOPP — Health Care of the Ontario Pension Plan — owns approximately 700 million euros ($1.1 billion Cdn) worth of Spanish properties, including 27 residential buildings and 2,300 Madrid homes.

The Spanish tenant unions haven't raised any specific concerns about HOOPP's activities or its properties.

Whether foreign investment firms are cornering the country's housing market has become one of Spain's most fiercely debated issues.

Numbers from the Bank of Spain say institutional investors control only a tiny share — roughly two per cent — of the country's total housing stock.

The tenant unions, however, say the fact that many of those properties used to be public, non-market housing for middle- or lower-income families matters far more than their share of the national total.

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez appears at a campaign rally in Palma de Mallorca on Nov. 14, ahead of the Nov. 29 general election. (Francisco Ubilla/Reuters)

They also claim that the concentration of apartments in central areas of cities gives companies like Brookfield outsized power to drive up rents across entire neighbourhoods.

Brookfield used to be chaired by Prime Minister Mark Carney, but he had left the company more than a year before it bought the Spanish homes in March 2026 from U.S. private equity giant Blackstone.

Blackstone held the buildings for 13 years. Residents claim Brookfield's intention is to sell the apartments once their existing leases finish.

Residents of the Madrid building told CBC News that when Brookfield eventually puts their apartments on the open market, they believe they could fetch upward of 600,000 euros apiece — a price few of them can pay.

"It is a constant anguish that is affecting our mental health," said Yutzy Fany Vargas Jimenez, who has lived in the complex for 20 years.

Engaging residents

In a statement to CBC News, Brookfield says any allegation that it is forcing people out of their homes is false.

"We comply with all applicable tenancy laws and tenant protections, and allegations that we terminate rental contracts in breach of these protections are inaccurate," said the statement.

None of the residents that CBC News spoke to had suggested Brookfield had cut short an existing lease. Rather, their concerns were about what will happen when their current tenancy contracts expire.

"We are working closely with our local operating partner, to engage with residents and address their concerns, while continuing to invest in the maintenance and quality of these homes and providing opportunities for residents who wish to become homeowners," the Brookfield statement continued.

The company didn't explicitly address whether it plans to terminate leases when current contracts expire, as the residents claim. However, the company did say it will review individual tenancy matters on a case-by-case basis.

Residents of a Madrid apartment complex say Brookfield intends to force them out of their homes when their leases expire. The company told CBC News that all of its rental arrangements in Spain 'reflect the applicable Spanish legal framework, including statutory requirements governing lease duration.' (Jason Ho/CBC)

Election issue

The cost of housing has become a central issue in Spain's upcoming election, although the roots of the problem can be traced back almost two decades.

Sara Herrero, an associate professor and MBA director at the EAE business school in Madrid, says after the 2008 global financial crisis, Spain was broke and its government turned to private capital to bail it out.

"The situation was really horrible," Herrero recalled, as governments and municipalities were forced to unload real estate they had on their balance sheets.

She said at the time, international funds were among the only buyers willing to inject billions of euros into the Spanish economy, helping banks clean up their toxic debt.

"What if they didn't come? What would have happened with these many residential houses if these supposed 'vulture funds' didn't come to Spain?" she said.

"They were doing a legal thing."

Sara Herrero is vice-dean of academic planning and financial management at EAE Madrid, one of Spain's top business schools. (Jason Ho/CBC)

Soaring prices

But recently, property values in the country have soared, rising 34 per cent in the past five years.

"The problem is the basic economic problem of supply and demand," Herrero said. "It's the perfect storm of low salaries, high population growth and high taxes."

The Bank of Spain also estimates upward of 300,000 homes have been converted to short-term tourism rentals, further displacing long-term tenants.

The left-wing government of Prime Minister Sanchez is trying to harness the housing anger to help with his re-election bid — even though the price hikes have all happened under his watch.

People in Madrid take part in a 24-hour nationwide general strike on Nov. 11 demanding wages that allow access to what demonstrators say is decent housing. (Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters)

Sanchez even appeared to give tacit support to the unions leading the general strike, as he passed tenant-friendly decrees that would likely be reversed if he fails to get re-elected.

His opponents on the political right, the People's Party and the far-right VOX, accused Sanchez of creating the crisis by passing legislation that made it hard for landlords to stay profitable, thereby discouraging new supply.

The latest opinion polls in Spain continue to favour a right-of-centre coalition taking power after Nov. 29, although they also indicate Sanchez's party has shown some recent momentum.

Tenant Raphael Cuadrado says he has repeatedly written to the Canadian Embassy in Madrid, hoping someone there can help residents who are worried about their future.

So far, he says he has not received a reply.

"This is day-by-day fighting, and this is not a life," he said.

In a statement to CBC News, Global Affairs Canada said any questions about Brookfield and its activities in Spain should be directed at the company.

World.title: Ever buy more than you mean to when shopping online? This could be why
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ever buy more than you mean to online? It could be by design.

CBC's Marketplace tracked popular online shopping sites Amazon, Shein, Temu and Walmart, revealing the tactics companies use which can influence your behaviour.

Can you trust every sale countdown timer? How about that inventory counter? Not necessarily.

They can be part of what experts call "dark patterns," a type of design on a website or app that can steer you into a decision that might not be in your best interest, and something that can be found across the internet .

"What's spooky about it is that people don't even know it's happening, and so their choices as shoppers are being guided invisibly," said Ryan Fritsch, an advocate for protecting consumers in the digital marketplace and a lawyer for the Law Commission of Ontario.

Ryan Fritsch, lawyer for the Law Commission of Ontario, says dark patterns 'try and trick consumers into making choices that may not be in their interest.' (Will Arnold/CBC)

Marketplace put it to the test in a series of spot checks, tracking sites and apps each week for about a month, and found several pressure tactics. Here’s what to be aware of the next time you're shopping online.

False urgency

The team saw a pair of leggings on Amazon with a stock counter that said only one left, so they bought what appeared to be the last pair. But eight minutes later, they were able to buy a second pair.

A message from Amazon saying we recently ordered what they said was the last pair of leggings, before we ordered a second pair. (CBC)

That second pair shipped a few days later than the first, but Fritsch said, "I think that if they're telling you there's only one left, that should be an honest statement. Otherwise, they are deceiving consumers. It's unfair."

Amazon’s stock count said these leggings were the last pair, but Asha Tomlinson and Ryan Fritsch show two pairs of leggings. (CBC)

Similarly, the Marketplace team saw coupons on Shein with a 24-hour countdown timer. But when the time ran out, the sale simply started over again.

"It's creating a false sense of urgency," said Jacquelyn Burkell, a professor in the faculty of information and media studies at the Western University in London, Ont.

"They're playing you, right?" said Fritsch. "The consumer is being induced to make an impulsive purchase that may not be in their best interest when other, better options might be available to them."

Pre-selected options

Another tactic is pre-selected options, which can also work against a consumer’s best interests. When buying the leggings on Amazon, Marketplace noticed the company had pre-selected slightly faster paid shipping for $7.98 as the default — even though free shipping was an option.

Fritsch said a busy shopper might not even notice.

Paid delivery was a pre-selected option on Amazon Canada, even though free delivery was available. (CBC)

Visual interference

Something else experts say to watch for are bright colours that can draw your eye and lead you into a decision. During checkout, both Walmart and Amazon used bright colours to attract attention to signing up for their membership programs, while the option to decline was on a white background.

A pop-up message on Amazon promoting their membership with a yellow button saying 'Start 30-day FREE trial.' (CBC)

Burkell said "a big bright yellow thing is going to be more evident to you" and "when it attracts attention…you're more likely to act."

Shoppers who Marketplace spoke with at the CBC Broadcast Centre in Toronto agreed.

Trisha Arocena said she’s seen this on Amazon before and "it makes the decision almost easier for you. So you're prompted to go ahead and click."

Ritu Gill said if she’s in a rush, "Your eyes do follow … the bright blue button. 'Let me just click yes, yes, yes, get through this and make the purchase.'"

A pop-up message on Walmart Canada promoting their membership with a blue button saying 'Confirm Plan.' (CBC)

In a statement, a spokesperson for Walmart Canada said the company's goal is to provide customers with a transparent and easy-to-navigate online shopping experience. They said the membership offer is optional and clearly presents consumers with "both the membership option and the option to close the offer and continue with their checkout."

The statement added that Walmart is "committed to complying with applicable laws and regulations."

An Amazon spokesperson said in an email that they "work hard to offer customers a transparent and trustworthy shopping experience."

"When Amazon displays how many units of an item are left in stock, that information reflects inventory on hand and ready to ship with a specific delivery estimate. The Amazon.ca store complies with all applicable Canadian laws, including consumer protection, competition and privacy laws."

Nagging

After the Marketplace team left items in the shopping cart on Temu, the company immediately emailed saying "Action required" and "Complete checkout" with a price drop. Temu continued to email and text about the cart multiple times in the following days.

This type of dark pattern, called nagging, can wear people down, says Burkell.

"Eventually people are just going to give in and say, 'Oh fine, I'll buy it.'"

It’s a tactic that works, says Arocena.

"If it was on my cart, chances are I was somewhat ready to check out … so that price drop ultimately convinces me to move forward with the purchase."

Gamification

Another design tactic to watch for: games on shopping sites that can keep consumers locked in to the site.

While browsing on Shein, the Marketplace team spotted an animated promotion that offered the chance to grab three free items: an iPhone Duo, an iPhone Max and a pair of AirPods Max. The chance to win didn’t come until about a week later but the prizes were first come, first serve and the stock was limited to one of each.

Fritsch says the game keeps consumers in the habit of visiting the site and "captured as a customer."

In an email, a Shein spokesperson said the company "is committed to complying with applicable laws and regulations in the markets where we operate." They added that they provide a transparent shopping experience and regularly review features on their platform as well as identify opportunities to improve customers’ shopping experience.

Confirmation shaming

On a "spin to win" game on Temu, the Marketplace team got a $350 credit. Although the game said they were just one step away from claiming it, they didn’t manage to get the credit, despite making multiple purchases.

When the Marketplace team left the app, a message said "Cancel your account rewards?" The options were "Stay and withdraw" or "I don't want cash."

Fritsch says that language is called confirmation shaming, which manipulates a consumer's emotions.

"The idea here is that a consumer has made a choice and they want to exercise that choice. And then at the last step, the vendor says, ‘Whoa, whoa, whoa, are you sure you wanna do this? You're walking away from all this potential money.'"

A message on Temu’s app that appeared when trying to leave a game saying 'I don’t want cash.' (CBC)

A Temu spokesperson said in a statement that "the interactive elements in our app are intended to make shopping more engaging and give users opportunities to unlock additional discounts. Users have a choice: they can shop without playing games, close a game and return to shopping, and turn off game-related notifications in the app’s settings."

In response to the repeated notifications, the company said users can unsubscribe from texts and email promotions. They added that they "listen to customer feedback ... and continue to refine platform features."

Possible solution?

In the European Union, lawmakers are making a push to specifically ban dark patterns through their Digital Services Act.

Marketplace checked out some of the same shopping sites using a VPN set to Sweden and found some differences. For example, on Amazon, free shipping was the pre-selected option, rather than paid shipping. Temu didn’t send emails after items were left in the cart. And coupons on Shein actually seemed to expire. (Walmart does not operate in Europe.)

"This is precisely what our services are monitoring," said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson on digital tech sovereignty for the European Commission. He said the differences between the North American and European shopping experiences on these sites show that the approach in the EU is working.

Even so, the European Commission wants to strengthen consumer protection further through the Digital Fairness Act .

"We need to reach that level where the Wild West is completely over in the online world, where platforms operate in a regulated environment, just like shops do in real life," said Regnier.

World.title: Canada looks to break Starlink's grip on Arctic military communications
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Dominion Dynamics, an Ottawa-based defence technology company, has struck a deal with Canadian satellite giant Telesat, an agreement that opens the door to the development of a homegrown alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink.

The $2.2-million partnership announced Thursday is part of a broader push to give the Canadian military greater control over the technology it relies upon to defend the Arctic.

The deal will see the two companies develop rugged, portable satellite antennas capable of connecting soldiers and uncrewed military aircraft to Telesat's planned Lightspeed constellation of low-Earth-orbit satellites.

Securing the agreement is good news for Telesat, which faces a separate, but critical debt maturity issue. Roughly $3.1 billion in debt related to the company's legacy satellite business is expected to come due between December 2026 and October 2027.

WATCH | More about Starlink and Telesat: Carney wants Canada to move away from Elon Musk’s Starlink. Can it? | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 7:54 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada will ‘diversify away’ from Elon Musk’s Starlink as it looks to reduce its reliance on U.S. technology. But with Canadian alternative Telesat Lightspeed still years away from full service, how difficult will that be?

Creditors have given Telesat management until Jan. 18, 2027, to reorganize the legacy end of the business, which is separate from the low-Earth satellite group that has signed with Dominion.

The project with Dominion, which includes financial support from the National Research Council, is intended to give Canadian troops a secure communications network that is not dependent on an American commercial provider.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has warned about the dangers of becoming dependent on a single technology provider whose decisions can have profound consequences for national sovereignty.

Eliot Pence, founder and chief executive of Dominion Dynamics, said the experience in Ukraine has demonstrated why Canada needs alternatives.

"Obviously, we've seen Starlink be shut off in Ukraine," Pence said. "What we're really building here is in addition to that [communications] structure."

The technology being developed would allow military units and autonomous aircraft to communicate directly through the Canadian-controlled Telesat network.

Pence described the concept as something similar to Starlink's portable satellite terminals, but designed specifically for military operations in Canada's harsh northern environment.

"Think of it as a Starlink Mini, but a Telesat Dominion Mini," he said. "It's a sovereign comms link designed specifically for the Arctic" with military specifications.

Starlink difficult to avoid

The partnership does not mean, however, that Canada is about to abandon Starlink.

Pence suggested that the American company's enormous satellite constellation makes it difficult to avoid entirely.

"It'll have to have some interoperability with Starlink because the proliferation of their satellites is just so much more," he said.

He said the goal, instead, is to ensure Canadian commanders have alternatives should one communications network become unavailable, unreliable or politically problematic.

Dominion's existing communications technology is designed to manage multiple networks, allowing military systems to switch between them when necessary.

The company intends to develop two prototype terminals: a lightweight version that soldiers can carry into the field and a larger model for autonomous aircraft and other uncrewed military systems.

Both would be designed to withstand extreme cold and operate in remote locations with limited infrastructure.

The Canadian military is the intended first customer, although no defence procurement contract has been announced.

Dominion says the technology could eventually be used by Canadian Rangers, the Coast Guard, RCMP and emergency responders operating in the North.

There is, however, a significant hurdle.

WATCH | More about Dominion Dynamics: AI drone warfare is here. Should Canada buy in? | Duration closed caption 6:05 Governments are spending billions on the autonomous arms race — should Canada join in? For The National, CBC’s Jennifer Yoon examines the future of AI-powered military weapons, what it means for international humanitarian law and where Canada fits in.

Telesat must first get its Lightspeed constellation into orbit and operational. The company currently expects to begin commercial service at high latitudes around the end of March 2028.

The Telesat agreement is one of several partnerships Dominion has announced this week as it attempts to establish itself as a major Canadian player in the rapidly expanding market for autonomous military aircraft.

On Friday, the company said, in addition to working on the Telesat receiver, Dominion has recruited the satellite-maker and a series of other Canadian firms to work on Scout, its uncrewed combat aircraft.

The other companies supporting the development of Scout include Thales Canada, Top Aces, ITPS Canada, PV Labs, SRC Can, Altitude Aerospace, Groupe DCM, HSB Solutions, North Aircraft Industries and RAMPF Composite Solutions.

Also on Tuesday, the company announced a collaboration with Pratt & Whitney Canada to provide the propulsion system for Dominion Scout, an uncrewed combat aircraft being designed to operate alongside conventional fighter jets.

Scout is intended to fly long distances over the Arctic, conduct surveillance and potentially carry out strikes against hostile targets.

The aircraft will be built around a Canadian-manufactured PW300-series engine.

Pence said securing an engine supplier was a critical milestone for a project still in development.

"You don't really have a plane until you have a propulsion system," he said.

World.title: Russian attacks on Kyiv kill 3, cripple bridges and cut power
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Russia launched missiles and drones across Kyiv overnight that killed three people, injured nine others and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure, local authorities said Friday.

The attacks came hours after President Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate against Ukraine for three aerial attacks this week on the vital Kerch Bridge, which links occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland.

"We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that," Putin told reporters Thursday in China, where he attended a summit with the Chinese and U.S. presidents. Putin said the road side of the bridge had been "seriously damaged" and vowed to rebuild.

The Kyiv City Military Administration said the attack struck four districts of the capital. The attack caused widespread electricity disruptions. Energy provider DTEK said parts of the Pecherskyi, Solomianskyi, Holosiivskyi, Dniprovskyi and Darnytskyi districts were without power following the strikes.

Non-residential buildings were damaged in the Obolonskyi and Holosiivskyi districts, while transport and logistics infrastructure was hit in the Podilskyi and Darnytskyi districts, it said in a statement.

WATCH | Why does Ukraine keep hitting Russia's prized Kerch Bridge? : Why does Ukraine keep hitting Russia's prized Kerch Bridge? | Duration 2:17 Ukraine just carried out its most damaging attack ever on Russia's prized Kerch Bridge, which connects occupied Crimea with mainland Russia. CBC’s Briar Stewart explains why the 19-kilometre bridge has been a top target for Ukraine ever since the early days Russia's full-scale invasion.

Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a ballistic missile attack damaged the Podilskyi Bridge, forcing authorities to close traffic from the right bank to the left bank of the Dnipro River. The Darnitskyi Bridge was also damaged, he said.

A further strike hit the Southern Bridge, where traffic remains restricted. Only vehicles weighing up to 10 tons traveling from the left bank to the right bank, and public transport weighing up to 18 tons, are being permitted, he said.

Klitschko urged residents to avoid traveling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary. He asked businesses and institutions to arrange remote working wherever possible.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: How Do We Address Violence When It Comes from a Fellow Activist?
World.content:
Photo: Urci Dream/CC

If we want to transform power relations, that transformation must also take place among ourselves.

By Brisa Bucardo (Confidencial)

HAVANA TIMES – Throughout my life, I have learned to speak out against gender-based violence, political violence, abuse of power, and racist violence. My involvement with feminism has also led me to examine what I have learned and recognize how much of the machismo we challenge remains present in the ways we think and relate to one another.

However, I find it curious that when certain behaviors come from other women, something changes in the way I react. I begin looking for explanations, thinking about the violence that woman may have experienced, about the patterns we have all internalized. And sometimes, while trying to understand her, I end up not knowing how to set boundaries against what is hurting me, especially when we share the same spaces.

It is clear to me that machismo is also reproduced among women. It can appear in competition, discrediting others, controlling relationships, or the habit of turning women against one another. Recognizing its structural roots is important but understanding them does not mean overlooking these behaviors. Having experienced violence does not prevent us from perpetrating it, nor does our history of activism place us above the principles we defend.

Reflecting on this, I have come to realize that reacting to violence committed by another woman makes me feel as though I am betraying something fundamental to my own feminism. It sounds contradictory, but I am not the only one who experiences this. I know that setting boundaries should not make me feel guilty, but it does.

During my journey into forced exile, I experienced an attempted kidnapping. During that improvised escape, we trusted someone because he was an opponent of the dictatorship I was fleeing. Another person who helped me get out of that situation told me something I will never forget: “I thought that because he was an opposition activist, he was a good person.” I am not comparing that experience to situations that may arise within an organization, but I do remember what I learned then. Sharing a cause does not guarantee sharing ethical principles.

In exile, trust takes on particular importance. Many of us arrive after losing our homelands, routines, and loved ones, carrying wounds that did not begin with exile. Finding fellow women with whom we can connect helps us rebuild a sense of belonging. That is why, when trust is violated, the consequences can extend beyond a personal relationship and affect how we experience spaces we once considered our own.

There are ways of exercising power that do not require open threats. They can appear through constant interference in other people’s decisions, attempts to control relationships, or efforts to influence how people perceive one another. Sometimes an insinuation, a distorted account, or a seemingly well-intentioned expression of concern is enough to plant doubts. We do not always recognize these dynamics because we tend to look for violence in its more obvious forms.

Part of the political culture we challenge remains present in our own practices. We come from contexts where power struggles, silence, disparagement, and personal loyalties have shaped sociopolitical relationships. And sometimes we carry those same patterns into spaces that are supposed to operate horizontally. Disagreements are no longer discussed openly, competing accounts circulate in private conversations, and factions form. What seems to matter more is how many people support a position rather than what actually happened. I am not talking about organizing to denounce violence and demand justice, but about turning differences and tensions into struggles for influence.

I am particularly concerned when emotional bonds end up becoming political capital. When closeness seems to imply an obligation to support certain positions, when disagreeing or standing beside someone who is being mistreated by a person close to us is interpreted as disloyalty. We can know a fellow activist for years and still be unaware of how she treats other people. Affection should not replace our ethical judgment, nor should hearing one side of a story first prevent us from thinking for ourselves.

It is also important to recognize that we have the power to stop some of these practices, even when they come from someone we love. On one occasion, I listened to the account of someone very close to me and, rather than accepting it as the only truth, I also tried to approach the other person, without intending to take sides. Over time, as I observed certain attitudes and learned more about the situation, I realized that things were very different from how they had been described to me. The person initially portrayed as responsible for the conflict was actually being discredited and mistreated.

That experience led me to question a relationship I had valued until then, not because of a personal disagreement, but because I began to recognize behaviors I could no longer justify. It also made me think about how often, out of affection or loyalty, we may end up supporting practices that harm other women without even stopping to question them. Sometimes we also have a responsibility to break with those dynamics, even when doing so means reassessing our own relationships.

We talk a great deal about care within feminist movements, but what does it mean to care without reproducing power relations? Concern for another woman does not give us authority over her life, her relationships, or how she chooses to participate. Nor does commitment to a cause give us the right to interfere in everything. If we defend women’s autonomy, that commitment must be reflected in our everyday relationships.

In Central America, feminists have been subjected to attacks, hatred, and deeply sexist attempts to discredit us. That hostility has also influenced how we handle internal contradictions. I understand the fear that any criticism might be used to undermine our struggles. But how often have we ended up applying the saying that “dirty laundry should be washed at home”? And what happens when, even within that home, we cannot find the conditions to speak openly?

I worry that protecting an image of unity may become more important than examining our own practices. Silence should not become the price of defending a cause.

Not every disagreement constitutes violence, nor can we attribute intentions to others that we do not know. But we should not need an obvious act of aggression to question specific behaviors. Sometimes their consequences can be seen in the distrust they seek to generate, the relationships they damage, or the freedom that others feel they have lost.

When a situation involves women with whom we share affection and struggles, speaking out about what is happening can come at a cost. We wonder how others will react, what versions of events will circulate, or whether we will be able to continue participating without discomfort. Even without an explicit prohibition, we begin weighing our words and decisions. And those who listen also bear responsibility for what they repeat and the conclusions they draw.

We can care about a fellow activist while questioning her behavior, support her without endorsing everything she does, or distance ourselves without launching a campaign against her. No relationship should demand loyalties that take precedence over our principles.

And here another question arises for me. Why do we assume that every situation must end in reconciliation? Is it always necessary to sit face-to-face with someone who has hurt us to demonstrate political maturity? Some conversations make it possible to acknowledge mistakes and repair relationships, but insisting on such an encounter can be retraumatizing if a woman feels she must agree to it in order to maintain her place within a group.

After a breach of trust or an experience of violence, it is not always possible to return to normal. Some encounters create tension, conversations in which we carefully measure every word, and spaces that no longer feel comfortable. Coexistence cannot be built on an obligation to pretend that nothing happened.

I also think about the women who eventually withdraw. Some stop attending meetings, making proposals, or taking on responsibilities, not because they have stopped believing in a cause, but because staying has become exhausting. From the outside, those absences may be mistaken for a lack of interest. How many fellow activists have we lost without asking ourselves what conditions made it difficult for them to continue?

Perhaps part of my feminist learning process involves accepting this contradiction and no longer thinking that questioning a fellow activist means abandoning my convictions. I also feel the need to bring into the open issues that we often avoid discussing publicly for fear that doing so will be interpreted as a lack of unity. But what good is defending our unity if maintaining it requires us to give up questioning ourselves?

I believe we need to develop collective ways of addressing these situations without depending on personal affinities or on who holds the most influence within a group. This means listening without automatically accepting one version of events, recognizing power imbalances, setting boundaries against practices that discredit others, and creating conditions in which women can speak about what they are experiencing without fear of losing their place.

It also means understanding that not every situation can be resolved through reconciliation, and that distancing ourselves from someone should not prevent us from continuing to share a common struggle.

This is not about demanding perfect relationships or pretending that our organizations are free of contradictions. It is about accepting the political responsibility to examine them and act when we identify harmful practices.

If we want to transform power relations, that transformation must also take place among ourselves. And perhaps a more genuine way of building unity is to stop confusing it with always agreeing and instead ground it in our ability to question ourselves, acknowledge responsibility, and ensure that no fellow activist has to choose between her dignity and her political participation.

First published in Spanish by Confidencial and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.
