Zimbabwe has also bought drought insurance from the African Risk Capacity, a continental risk pool, for a US$3.4 million premium. After the 2023/24 drought the same scheme paid US$31.8 million, which helped more than 508,000 vulnerable households.

Not everyone sees the growth reaching people. Caston Matewu, a legislator for Marondera, a town east of Harare, said after the speech that “the people who are benefiting from this growth are those who are already rich”, and he questioned whether ministries would receive their full allocations.

Parliament now debates the proposals before they become law. The local-buying framework is due by 31 March 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Zimbabwe’s 2027 budget add new taxes?

No. The finance minister ruled out new taxes, though Parliament must still approve the proposals.

Who gains most from the changes?

Wage earners, phone and electric-vehicle buyers and anyone sending money electronically pay less. Large buyers face a new duty to source locally.

Will Zimbabwe’s lithium exports change?

Officials have set January 2027 as the end date for concentrate exports. Foreign mine owners will watch whether the budget’s raw-mineral language alters that plan.

World.title: New Book Details How Tinubu Won Nigeria
World.content:
A new book by journalist Simon Kolawole tells the inside story of Tinubu’s 2023 win and argues that Nigerian presidents win by uniting voting blocs.

Aso Rock, the granite hill beside the presidential complex in Abuja. File photo. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

NIGERIA · POLITICS

A new book promises an inside account of how Bola Tinubu won Nigeria’s 2023 presidential election. Winning Formula: The Inside Story of Nigeria’s 2023 Presidential Election, by the journalist Simon Kolawole, goes on sale on Monday 23 November 2026.

Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country and a major oil producer, so the way its presidents win matters to investors and to the large Nigerian diaspora in the United States. The book arrives as the country looks ahead to its next presidential vote.

Key Facts The country Nigeria, Africa’s most populous nation, is led by President Bola Tinubu, elected in 2023.

What happened Cable Books, a Nigerian publisher, puts Winning Formula on sale on Monday 23 November 2026.

The author Simon Kolawole, a Nigerian journalist, wrote the 296-page account of the 2023 presidential race.

The argument The book argues winners since 1999 united two of the three biggest voting blocs.

Prediction markets Polymarket (a prediction market) gives Tinubu 70% to win the next presidential vote (5:17 a.m. ET).

A new book by journalist Simon Kolawole tells the inside story of Tinubu’s 2023 win and argues that Nigerian presidents win by uniting voting blocs.

What the Book Claims

Cable Books, the publisher, calls the 296-page work an authoritative account “enriched by insider briefings, court filings and polling data.” Kolawole calls it “a story of naivety, cat-and-mouse games, cold calculations” and subterfuge.

He says it explains how Tinubu outmanoeuvred the then president, Muhammadu Buhari, and how Atiku Abubakar, the opposition People’s Democratic Party candidate, and Nyesom Wike, then governor of Rivers State, damaged each other’s ambitions. It also covers how Peter Obi, the Labour Party candidate, and his Obidient movement of young supporters became a phenomenon, and how Yemi Osinbajo, Buhari’s vice president, lost out.

The book also tells the story behind the Muslim-Muslim ticket, in which Tinubu chose a fellow Muslim, Kashim Shettima, as his running mate. That choice broke with Nigerian custom, which has usually balanced a Muslim and a Christian on the top two lines.

The Voting Pattern It Describes

The central argument is that since the return to civilian rule in 1999, no candidate has reached the presidency without a competitive coalition across at least two of the three largest voting blocs. Those are the Hausa-Fulani, the Igbo and the Yoruba, Nigeria’s three largest ethnic groups, plus decisive support from a minority region.

Kolawole says this “winning formula” was “hiding in plain sight” in 2023. Nigeria’s constitution adds a second test, since a winner needs the most votes and at least one quarter of the vote in at least two thirds of the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

What the Official Record Shows

Mahmood Yakubu, then chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), declared Tinubu the winner in Abuja at 4:10 a.m. on Wednesday 1 March 2023. Tinubu had 8,794,726 votes, ahead of Atiku with 6,984,520 and Obi with 6,101,533.

Atiku and Obi challenged the result, and on Thursday 26 October 2023 the Supreme Court, in a ruling by seven judges led by Justice John Okoro, dismissed both appeals. It affirmed the 6 September 2023 decision of the Presidential Election Petition Court.

For more context, read our guide to the 2027 election race and our report on how the election chief admits a trust gap. Both show what is at stake before 2027.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a prediction market platform, traders gave Tinubu a 70% chance of winning the next Nigerian presidential election as of 5:17 a.m. ET (10:17 UTC) on Friday 20 November 2026. Peter Obi stood at 24% and Atiku Abubakar at 5%, with about US$161,000 traded on the market.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Why It Matters

Tinubu’s 8,794,726 votes were about 37% of the 24,025,940 valid votes counted, so a majority of voters backed someone else. That is why the coalition arithmetic in the book, and not a single large bloc, is the real story of Nigerian presidential politics.

A book by a veteran editor will not change the next vote, but it gives readers a map of how deals were struck last time. The checkpoints to watch are the book’s release on 23 November 2026 and the reactions of the people it names.

What It Means for You

If you hold Nigerian bonds or shares through US funds, the next presidential vote is the largest political event on your calendar. A clear account of how the last one was won helps you judge which alliances could decide the next.

Readers in the Nigerian diaspora can order the book through Rovingheights, the bookstore chain that the publisher says will distribute it nationwide. Travellers need not change plans, since the book carries no rule or policy.

What Is Not Known

We have not read the book, and the claims about its content are the publisher’s and the author’s own description. We found no public reply from the people it names by Friday 20 November 2026.

The price and the export edition have not been announced in the publisher’s statement. It is also not known whether the book discloses new documents or relies on earlier public records.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is Winning Formula by Simon Kolawole?

It is a 296-page book on Nigeria’s 2023 presidential election, published by Cable Books. It goes on sale on Monday 23 November 2026.

Who Won Nigeria’s 2023 Presidential Election?

Bola Tinubu, who received 8,794,726 votes according to the election commission. Atiku Abubakar had 6,984,520 and Peter Obi 6,101,533.

Did the Courts Uphold the 2023 Result?

Yes. On 26 October 2023 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeals of Atiku and Obi.

What Is the Muslim-Muslim Ticket?

It was the 2023 pairing of Tinubu and his running mate Kashim Shettima, who are both Muslim. Nigerian tickets have usually balanced a Muslim and a Christian.

World.title: Panama’s Rubén Blades Backs Vamos Movement
World.content:
Singer Rubén Blades says Panama needs a new way of running the state, and he is putting his name behind the Vamos coalition.

File photo, January 2013. From left, the musicians Danilo Pérez, Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter and Rubén Blades, as named on Commons. (Photo: US Embassy Panama, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

PANAMA · POLITICS

Rubén Blades, Panama’s best-known salsa singer and a former tourism minister, said on Thursday 19 November 2026 that he stands “100%” behind the Vamos coalition. It is the clearest public backing yet from one of the country’s most recognisable voices, ahead of the general election due in 2029.

Vamos is a movement of independent politicians that won seats and local offices in 2024 and now wants to register as a political party. For US readers, the story shows how the country that hosts the Panama Canal, a key route for US trade, is debating its own political future.

Key Facts The country Panama, home of the Panama Canal, is led by President José Raúl Mulino.

What happened Singer Rubén Blades said on 19 November 2026 he is “100%” behind the Vamos coalition.

The group Vamos (“Let’s Go”), independents’ coalition, began forming a party on 25 September 2026.

His warning Blades says nothing changes while government runs on patronage, meaning favours for loyalty.

What Blades Said

Blades said he made his commitment in 2024 to the young members of Vamos, and he repeated it this week. “I am with them 100%,” he said, adding that he will help “in every way I can.”

He named Juan Diego Vásquez, a former lawmaker who is expected to be its president, and Gabriel Silva, another member of the team he supports. He added that he hopes to be in Panama in 2028 to explain why the country needs “a different paradigm” (a different way of running things).

Blades said change will come from young people, while older Panamanians can help with experience. He said Vásquez, Silva and others now working in Vamos give Panama “an opportunity to change things.”

Why He Targets Patronage

Asked how he rates President Mulino’s government, Blades did not praise or attack a policy. He said nothing will change until the administrative model based on clientelismo (patronage, where jobs and favours reward political loyalty) changes.

He called that his view of Panama’s core problem and said he has written and said it “a thousand times.” He also said the state is borrowing to pay debt, and that tax revenue and foreign investment have fallen, claims that are his own and that we have not checked against official data.

What Vamos Is

In plain English, Vamos grew out of the 2024 elections, when independents running under its banner won office. They include members of the National Assembly (Panama’s parliament), mayors and local representatives.

On 25 September 2026 the coalition filed its papers with Panama’s Electoral Tribunal, the body that runs elections, to begin turning itself into a party. It must still win the tribunal’s recognition before it can compete as one.

Our report on the delayed election law overhaul covers the proposed changes to the rules for independents and new parties. A second report covers how Mulino vetoed part of the electoral districts bill for the 2029 election.

What It Means for You

If you invest in Panama or use its canal, nothing in Blades’s comments changes a rule, a tariff or a toll. They matter as a signal of how much support independent politicians can gather before 2029.

Fans should know that Blades has said publicly that his 2026 and 2027 concerts could be his last, and that he wants to spend more time in Panama. Readers can follow who holds power in our Latin America Power Map, which ranks Panama and its neighbours.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Blades plans to run for office himself, because his statements describe support and not a candidacy. It is also unknown whether Vamos will meet the support the Electoral Tribunal requires to be recognised as a party.

The government has not answered his criticism of its debt and investment record. His figures on revenue and foreign investment remain his assessment until official data are compared.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who Is Rubén Blades?

He is a Panamanian salsa singer, songwriter and actor, and a former tourism minister. He has campaigned for political change in Panama for decades.

What Is the Vamos Coalition?

Vamos is a coalition of independent politicians that won office in Panama in 2024. On 25 September 2026 it filed papers with the Electoral Tribunal to become a political party.

Is Rubén Blades Running for Office?

He did not say so in this interview, and described his role as helping Vamos “in every way I can.” He said he hopes to be in Panama in 2028.

When Is Panama’s Next General Election?

The next general election is due in 2029. Parties in formation must register with the Electoral Tribunal before then.

World.title: Mr Price Sales Jump 42% After Europe Deal
World.content:
Mr Price's takeover of NKD lifted sales by more than 40%, but earnings per share grew only 2%. The company says financing costs weighed on profit and expects trading to stay hard.

File photo. The towers of Sandton, Johannesburg's main business district, South Africa. Photo: Andres de Wet, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Retail: South Africa

Mr Price Group, the clothing and homeware chain listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), said on Friday 20 November 2026 that retail sales jumped 41.8% to R25.3 billion (about US$1.45 billion) in the six months to 26 September. Nearly all of that growth comes from NKD, a European discount retailer it bought this year.

Profit per share barely moved. Headline earnings per share, South Africa’s standard measure that strips out one-off items, rose only 2.0% to 523.0 cents (about US$0.30).

Mr Price agreed in December 2025 to buy NKD, which runs discount shops in seven European markets, and the deal took effect on 31 March 2026. This is therefore the first half-year to include NKD’s trading, and NKD ended it with 2,162 shops after opening 44 and closing 36.

Before the deal, Mr Price earned its money in Africa. Its African sales rose 3.1% to R18.4 billion (about US$1.05 billion), but sales in comparable shops, a measure that leaves out newly opened stores, were flat.

That points to a business growing mainly by adding shops, not by selling more through the old ones. Last year the interim dividend rose 6.5% to 323.2 cents, so the pace of growth in shareholder payouts has slowed to 2.0% this year.

The group now runs 5,410 shops, of which 3,248 are in Africa. NKD’s 2,162 shops make up about 40% of the total.

Basic earnings per share, which include one-off items, rose just 0.2% to 513.6 cents (about US$0.29). Diluted headline earnings per share, which allow for extra shares that could be issued, rose 2.2% to 508.6 cents.

NKD earned an operating profit of R526 million (about US$30 million) on its R6.9 billion (about US$395 million) of sales, an operating margin of 7.5%, the company said. Group operating profit rose 30.7% to R2.8 billion (about US$160 million), well behind the rise in sales.

Africa supplied R2.2 billion (about US$126 million) of that profit, up 5.9%. The company’s results announcement says that, as anticipated, financing costs weighed on earnings growth, and it lists R32.3 million (about US$1.85 million) of one-off costs for refinancing NKD’s German debt.

Mr Price gave a cautious outlook. It said trading conditions are “likely to remain challenging for the remainder of the financial year” and described the backdrop in Africa and Europe as one of “persistent volatility and heightened unpredictability”.

The announcement also says the group is managing supply-chain pressure, including at the port of Durban, during the key festive trading period. It adds that NKD’s earnings are weighted towards the first half of the financial year.

Cash from operations was R4.8 billion (about US$275 million) and net debt, borrowings minus cash, stood at R7.7 billion (about US$440 million). The company’s own figures show a business funding a large acquisition while still paying out about 63% of profit as dividends.

Shareholders receive an interim dividend of 329.5 cents a share (about US$0.19), up 2.0%. Shares bought up to Tuesday 8 December 2026 carry the payout, which is paid on Monday 14 December 2026.

For investors who follow South African stocks, the result shows how a takeover can lift sales far faster than profit per share. Mr Price shares trade in Johannesburg under the ticker MRP.

Readers who want more on the local market can follow our South Africa coverage and our earlier report on Naspers and Prosus shares. Rand figures in this article are converted at R17.48 to the US dollar, the market rate on 20 November 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is NKD?

NKD is a European discount retailer of clothing and homeware that Mr Price now owns. The group counts its results from the date the deal took effect.

Why did profit per share rise less than sales?

Sales now include a whole new business, while profit per share depends on what is left after costs and the share count. The company says financing costs, including the debt taken on for the NKD deal, weighed on earnings growth.

Where does Mr Price trade?

Mr Price Group is listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange under the ticker MRP. Its dividend is paid in South African rand.

World.title: De Beers CEO Acquires 10 Anglo Shares
World.content:
A small purchase through a staff share plan by the head of De Beers is, in our reading, no signal about the sale. The sale of the diamond business is still unsigned.

File photo, 2016. The Letšeng diamond mine plant and camp at night at Letšeng-la-Terae in Lesotho's Mokhotlong district. (Photo: Lschefa, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Companies: South Africa

Al Cook, chief executive of the diamond company De Beers, acquired 10 shares in its parent, the London-listed miner Anglo American, on 16 November 2026. They were worth £372.20 (about US$488), half of them added by the company, and Anglo disclosed the deal two days later in a notice about a staff share plan, which in our reading is no signal.

The filing belongs to a monthly employee share plan, and it matters mainly as a reminder of a bigger story. Anglo is trying to sell its 85% stake in De Beers, and African governments are lining up for a share.

Anglo published the notice on 18 November on the London Stock Exchange’s regulatory news service, under the heading “Director/PDMR Shareholding”. PDMR stands for person discharging managerial responsibility, a senior manager whose dealings in company shares must be disclosed under UK market abuse rules.

Cook’s shares were Partnership Shares (bought by the employee) and Matching Shares (added by the company) under Anglo’s Share Incentive Plan, a plan the notice calls an HMRC-approved all-employee share plan; HMRC is the UK tax authority. The notice says staff buy shares through monthly salary deductions and the company allots an equal number of Matching Shares.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Ghana's central bank cuts its rate to 11%” Get the brief

Cook was not the only name on the list. The same notice covered Anglo chief executive Duncan Wanblad, finance chief John Heasley and five other senior managers, who each received 8 shares at the same price on 16 November.

One of them, Alison Atkinson, who runs projects and development, exercised 1,110 options at £16.70 (about US$21.88) each under Sharesave, a savings-linked option plan, and kept the shares on 17 November, on top of her 8 plan shares. An earlier notice of 16 October 2026 reported the same kind of plan purchase, made on 14 October.

The notice lists the Cook purchase under an all-employee plan, so it is not an open-market trade that investors might read for confidence. At about US$488 (at 1.31 dollars per pound, the 20 November rate from the market-data provider RT), it is in our judgement too small to say anything about his view of the sale.

File photo, April 2019. A road in Gaborone’s business district. Botswana, whose capital this is, owns 15% of De Beers. (Photo: Jota @ BRAZIL, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

The real story is the sale itself. Anglo has said it will sell its 85% of De Beers, while Botswana owns the other 15% and holds a right of first refusal, which lets it match a buyer’s offer.

On Monday 9 November 2026, Botswana’s President Duma Boko told parliament that his country will double its holding to 30% and become the largest shareholder. Anglo said the same day that it is “encouraged by the progress we have made to date”.

Anglo added that it continues to work with Botswana’s government, other governments and the Global Diamond Consortium “towards agreeing binding transaction documents”. The consortium is an investor group led by Gareth Penny, a former De Beers chief executive, and a Botswana official said in July 2026 that Anglo had chosen it as buyer.

On Friday 13 November 2026, a spokesperson for Angola’s mines ministry said that Angola seeks a 10% holding. A 10% stake for Namibia has also been reported, but it is unconfirmed.

No price has been confirmed. Nothing is signed, and neither the signing date nor the final stakes are known.

For American readers, the link is the jewellery counter. De Beers is one of the best-known names in diamond jewellery in our view, so who owns it, and how much say African governments gain, can affect supply and pricing to US buyers and retailers.

Anglo has its primary listing in London and another in Johannesburg, among other listings. Readers who follow the group can find more in South Africa news.

Until a binding agreement appears, the 10-share purchase stays what the notice says it is, a small transaction inside a staff plan. The next real signal would be the signed documents that Anglo says it is working towards.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the purchase suggest Cook expects the sale to go ahead?

No. The notice lists the purchase under an all-employee share plan, so in our judgement it carries no information about the sale.

What is a PDMR notice?

It is a disclosure that UK market abuse rules require when a senior manager deals in company shares. It lets investors see such dealings, however small.

Who will own De Beers after the sale?

That is not decided. Botswana says it will become the largest shareholder if the deal closes, but Anglo has not signed binding documents and the final stakes are unconfirmed.

GUYANA · SPORT

Three primary schools from three corners of Guyana meet at the National Stadium in Providence, near the capital Georgetown, on Friday 20 November 2026 to decide a national cricket title. Play starts at 9:00 a.m. local time (8:00 a.m. Eastern), and the public can walk in free.

Skeldon Primary comes from Upper Corentyne in Berbice, a county in Guyana’s east. Regma Primary comes from Upper Demerara, and St. Lawrence Primary comes from East Bank Essequibo, in Essequibo county in the west.

How the Day Works

The three finalists meet in competitive matches on the day, and only one school can take the national title. The detailed match format was not part of the announcement.

The organisers call the day the finals and closing ceremony, and they have invited families, students and cricket fans. Entry is completely free.

The Defending Champion

St. Lawrence Primary won last year’s final on Saturday 15 November 2025, beating Massiah Primary from Upper Corentyne in Berbice. Supply Primary from East Bank Demerara was the third finalist.

That final was moved indoors to the National Gymnasium in Georgetown because the rainy season arrived early. The awards went to St. Lawrence’s Tianna Steele as best batter and tournament most valuable player, Susanie Turnail of Massiah as best bowler and Avidesh Pitam of Massiah as best fielder.

Why It Matters

The programme began in Guyana in 2023 and is aimed at children aged 7 to 11, according to Cricket West Indies. Bissoondyal Singh leads the Guyana Cricket Board, the national governing body, and sits on the board of Cricket West Indies.

Last year Steven Jacobs, a minister within Guyana’s Ministry of Culture, Youth and Sport, challenged the partners to go beyond 75 schools and 1,500 pupils. This year’s field of more than 100 schools goes past the school part of that target.

Ronald Williams, secretary of the Guyana Cricket Board, said the partnership between Cricket West Indies and Republic Bank will give young cricketers a pathway. Los Angeles will stage six-team men’s and women’s T20 tournaments from 12 to 29 July 2028.

What It Means for You

If you plan to be in Georgetown, the final is a free morning out and a chance to see schoolchildren play at an international-standard ground. Arrive early and carry rain protection, because last year’s final had to move indoors.

For American cricket fans and parents, the programme shows how a bank-funded school scheme can build the sport from the ground up. Republic Bank says the programme belongs to its ‘Power to Make a Difference’ social investment effort.

What Is Not Known

The result is not known, because play only starts on Friday morning. Prize details, captains’ names and any broadcast plan were not part of the organisers’ announcements for the final.

It is unclear whether weather will force a move indoors again. The number of girls among this year’s players has not been published.

World.title: Costa Rica Ranks Among the 10 Safest Countries to Visit in 2027
World.content:
Costa Rica is the only Central American country named among the 10 safest destinations for travelers in 2027, according to the Risk Map 2027 released by Swedish risk-management firm Safeture and travel intelligence company Riskline. The annual map rates every country on Riskline’s five-level scale of Low, Moderate, Medium, High and Extreme. It weighs security, crime, health and environmental risks, and access to medical care.

Costa Rica appears on the list of standout safe countries alongside Bhutan, Canada, Chile, Denmark, Iceland, New Zealand, Singapore, Slovenia and Switzerland. Riskline’s analysts chose those countries from every region of the world. The list is not ranked. Within Central America, Costa Rica, Belize and El Salvador share the region’s lowest risk rating. Panama and Nicaragua are rated Medium. Guatemala and Honduras are in the High category.

El Salvador’s rating is one of the biggest changes on the 2027 map. The country moved from Medium to Moderate, making it one of only six countries worldwide whose risk level improved over the past 12 months. The others were the Maldives, Bangladesh, Cameroon, Mozambique and Nepal.

That puts El Salvador in the same tier as Germany, Finland and Cyprus, which all slipped from Low to Moderate this year. Honduras is the region’s most prominent concern on the map. San Pedro Sula, its second-largest city, is one of the 10 least safe cities in the world, alongside Kabul, Port-au-Prince, Bamako, Goma, Guayaquil, Port Moresby, Quetta, Sana’a and Tehran.

Fifteen countries moved to a higher risk level this year. Most of them are in the Middle East, where Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates jumped from Moderate to High. Saudi Arabia and Jordan rose from Medium to High, and Iran moved up to Extreme. Closer to home, Cuba rose from Moderate to Medium.

The 10 least safe countries on the 2027 map are Colombia, Haiti, Iran, Myanmar, Niger, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Yemen, and the West Bank and Gaza. “This year’s map shows how quickly the risk picture can change,” said Jonas Brorson, chief marketing officer at Safeture.

The two companies say the map gives a broad picture and does not replace a full risk assessment. Ratings can also vary a lot within a single country. A separate 2027 assessment by security firm Global Guardian also placed Costa Rica and Panama among Central America’s most stable destinations. That report identified Guatemala and Nicaragua as the region’s most serious concerns.

Costa Rica’s place on the safest list comes as the country continues to deal with drug-related violence, which has kept homicides near record levels in recent years. Most of that violence is concentrated in specific urban and coastal areas and involves criminal groups, not visitors.

The full Risk Map 2027 can be downloaded free at safeture.com/riskmaps.

World.title: Costa Rica Hit by 3.6 Million Malware Attempts as Hackers Shift to Targeted Attacks
World.content:
Costa Rica had about 3.6 million attempted malware infections between September 2025 and September 2026, according to the latest Latin America threat landscape report from cybersecurity company Kaspersky. That is the second-highest figure among the five Central American and Caribbean countries in the report. The Dominican Republic led with 4.2 million, followed by Costa Rica, Guatemala with 3.4 million, Panama with 3.3 million and El Salvador with 1.2 million.

Kaspersky’s previous annual report, which covered a slightly different period, put Costa Rica at 3.9 million attempts. Across Latin America, Kaspersky said it blocked 592 million malware infection attempts over the 12 months, an 18% drop from the year before. Brazil and Mexico accounted for the largest totals, with 330 million and 102 million respectively.

The company cautioned that the decline does not mean the region is safer. Rather than relying mainly on mass campaigns built to infect as many devices as possible, attackers are increasingly concentrating on specific targets, particularly government agencies and large industries.

Government institutions accounted for 27.3% of blocked malware attempts across Latin America, followed by process manufacturing at 12.5%, retail and wholesale trade at 11.5% and healthcare at 8.3%. The report does not break those shares down by country. Costa Rica knows what a targeted attack on the state can cost. In 2022, the Conti ransomware group crippled Finance Ministry systems and other public institutions, prompting the government to declare a national emergency.

The figures reflect detections among users of Kaspersky’s own products, so they point to trends rather than the total number of attacks in each country. Among the most common threats the report identified are pirated programs and unauthorized license activation tools. These downloads often ask users to switch off their antivirus first, which gives malicious software an easy way in.

Once installed, spyware bundled with pirated software can harvest passwords and other confidential data, exposing individuals and organizations to fraud or extortion. Adware is another frequent problem. Although it is mostly associated with unwanted ads and browser redirects, some programs can also steer users toward fraudulent websites and more serious threats.

Fabio Assolini, Kaspersky’s lead security researcher, said many people in the region still put their digital security at risk to get paid software for free, and that criminals exploit that demand by hiding highly malicious files inside copies of expensive programs. Assolini said the overall drop in detections reflects a change in strategy, as attackers move away from simple mass-distributed malware toward professional operations capable of causing greater financial and operational damage to governments and major industries.

Kaspersky recommends a zero-tolerance approach to pirated software, downloading programs only from developers’ websites or official app stores, installing security updates promptly, and using reliable security software at home and at work. The regional decline may look encouraging, but the report suggests the more important question is no longer how many attacks are occurring, but how much damage a single successful one can cause.

World.title: Costa Rica Is Latin America’s Priciest Place to Retire as the Dollar Hits a Record Low
World.content:
Costa Rica is regularly ranked among the best places in the world to retire, but one analysis of cost-of-living data found it is also the most expensive country in Latin America in which to retire comfortably. A record-low dollar is widening that gap for retirees whose income arrives in U.S. currency.

The analysis, published in September by Bloomberg Línea using NetCredit and Numbeo data compiled by Visual Capitalist, estimated that $556,000 in savings is needed to retire comfortably in Costa Rica. That placed the country 16th worldwide and first in Latin America, ahead of Uruguay at $451,000 and Mexico at $356,000.

The same analysis put the U.S. figure at about $738,000, meaning Costa Rica still costs roughly a quarter less than retiring at home. Its estimates assume nearly 15 years of retirement and exclude taxes and health care costs, and the authors noted that results can vary significantly by city, housing and lifestyle.

Costa Rica’s standing in lifestyle rankings remains high. International Living’s 2026 Global Retirement Index placed it third with a score of 87.6, behind Greece and Panama, and ranked it first in the index’s climate category. A separate index by Global Citizen Solutions ranked Costa Rica’s Pensionado visa fourth in the world.

The exchange rate is now eroding the cost advantage those rankings rely on. The dollar closed at 444.85 colones on Nov. 18 in the central bank’s Monex market, the lowest level since the platform began operating in November 2006. It started 2026 at 497.07 colones, a decline of 10.5%, and analysts expect further declines before year-end.

For a retiree living on a $1,000 monthly pension, the minimum income required for Pensionado residency, the difference shows up every month. At January’s rate, $1,000 converted to about 497,000 colones; at Wednesday’s rate, it brings about 445,000, roughly 52,000 colones less each month, or about $117 at current rates. Banks also pay less than the Monex average when they buy dollars from customers.

International Living’s index estimated monthly living expenses in Costa Rica at about $1,500 for a single person to roughly $4,000 for a couple seeking a comfortable lifestyle. The Bloomberg Línea analysis cited high housing costs, prices for some foods, transport, electricity, imported goods and exchange-rate risk as factors behind Costa Rica’s higher requirement.

The pressure on the dollar is seasonal and expected to continue, as the high tourist season, year-end aguinaldo bonuses and tax payments increase the supply of dollars in the country. International Living’s next index is expected in the coming weeks; the 2026 edition was released in December 2025.

World.title: Court File Alleges Diablo-Linked Group Tortured US Surfer Kurt Van Dyke for His PINs
World.content:
The men who killed American surfer Kurt Van Dyke in February allegedly belonged to a group linked to Alejandro Arias Monge, the alleged drug trafficker known as “Diablo,” according to the court file in the case. The file also alleges that Van Dyke was bound and tortured to force him to reveal the PINs for his bank cards.

Van Dyke, 66, was found dead on Feb. 14 in Hone Creek, near Cahuita on Costa Rica’s southern Caribbean coast. A Santa Cruz, California, native known in surfing circles as “King,” he had run Hotel Puerto Viejo for decades. His killing was first reported as a robbery.

Two suspects are in custody. A 31-year-old woman surnamed Arroyo Ramírez, who had a long relationship with Van Dyke, and a man surnamed Gutiérrez Víctor were detained on Nov. 12. On Nov. 15, the Talamanca Criminal Court ordered both held for six months of pretrial detention while prosecutors investigate them for aggravated homicide.

Neither has been charged or convicted, and both are presumed innocent. The allegations described below come from the prosecution’s case file and have not been tested in court.

According to the file, the plan took shape on the morning of Feb. 14. Arroyo Ramírez allegedly persuaded Van Dyke to come to her home in Hone Creek under false pretenses. Prosecutors allege that once he was there, she sent WhatsApp messages telling the others he was unprotected and how to get in.

The file states that the attackers entered, immobilized Van Dyke and tied his hands and feet. They then allegedly tortured him and inflicted stab wounds as they tried to obtain his bank PINs. Prosecutors attribute the killing to a structured group acting together to seize his assets and take his life.

A neighbor called 911 at 10:35 a.m. to report that armed men had broken in, restrained both people inside and stolen the woman’s car and phone, according to the file. Security cameras recorded Van Dyke calling for help at about 10 a.m. Investigators found no sign of forced entry.

The medical-legal report concluded that Van Dyke died of asphyxia caused by compression of the neck, with a fractured hyoid bone, and that he had been tortured. He was found under a bed with his hands and feet bound, a sheet around his head and multiple stab wounds. Investigators allege that the woman staged the robbery and reported her own vehicle stolen to conceal her role.

The car was later recovered in good condition, and investigators determined that her account did not match the evidence. The file also describes alleged threats in the months before the killing. On Jan. 4, Arroyo Ramírez allegedly demanded $1,500 from Van Dyke and threatened to send people from Diablo’s group to harm another former partner of his and their son.

Arias Monge was captured on July 24 in San Bernardino de Sarapiquí at the end of an operation authorities named Némesis, and he is being held at La Reforma prison. Reports on the file have not said whether he is a suspect in the Van Dyke case. Investigations into his network have already reached a police officer and two Pococí judges.

The case is being handled under file 26-000171-0829-PE by the organized crime unit of the Limón Prosecutor’s Office, under the supervision of the deputy prosecutor’s office for money laundering. The OIJ is still looking for two more men believed to have taken part in the attack.

Anyone with information can contact the OIJ’s confidential line at 800-8000-645.

World.title: El Niño Could Thin Out Costa Rica’s Winter Humpback Whale Season
World.content:
Humpback whales from the North Pacific are about to begin arriving off Costa Rica’s Pacific coast, but this season opens under one of the strongest El Niño events in decades. Researchers and tour operators across the region are warning that warmer water could mean fewer whales or a later arrival.

Costa Rica is one of the few places visited by two separate humpback populations. According to the International Whaling Commission, whales that feed off the northwestern coast of the United States travel to Costa Rica’s tropical Pacific waters from December to March to mate, give birth and nurse their calves. A southern population that feeds near the Antarctic Peninsula and southern Chile visits from July to mid-November.

The southern season that just ended had already raised concerns. In August, guides with Priscilla Tours in the Golfo Dulce reported fewer humpbacks than in past years. One guide described a morning when only one of roughly 30 to 40 boats saw a whale and said it had happened twice this season.

A captain with more than 12 years of experience said the whales now spend longer periods farther out rather than staying inside the gulf, and linked the change to warmer water. The guides also reported partial or total bleaching on some corals.

Their observations are anecdotal, and no figures quantifying a decline have been published. A McGill University-led study, which used satellite tracking data from 2009 to 2016 on 42 humpbacks tagged off Costa Rica, Panama and Ecuador, found that the whales combine local conditions such as sea temperature and food availability with long-term memory of their Antarctic feeding grounds to time their migration.

According to one account of the findings, the whales began leaving earlier in years when sea surface temperatures peaked early, particularly El Niño years, and in Costa Rica warmer water coincided with lower chlorophyll and earlier departures. That account noted the study does not prove warming caused this year’s reported drop in sightings.

The northern whales face their own pressures. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates a better than 79% chance that El Niño will remain strong to very strong through the January to March 2027 period. A recent University of Hawaii study of North Pacific humpbacks during the 2014 to 2016 marine heat wave found that whales facing food shortages cut their activity to save energy. That helped them survive but did not sustain early-stage pregnancies.

Similar concerns are coming from Mexico. Astrid Frisch Jordán, head of the whale conservation group ECOBAC in Bahía de Banderas, said early this month that the high sea temperatures would probably reduce the number of whales or delay their arrival, adding that warm water usually means fewer whales. The season there is expected to begin in the first half of December.

The main viewing areas remain the southern Pacific coast, including Dominical, Uvita, Bahía Drake, Isla del Caño and the Golfo Dulce, along with Manuel Antonio, Quepos, Jacó and parts of the Gulf of Nicoya in the central Pacific, and the Golfo de Papagayo, Tamarindo, El Coco and Sámara in the north.

Under rules from SINAC and the Environment Ministry, boats must keep at least 200 meters (656 feet) from the whales and carry a whale-watching permit. Whether this season follows the pattern seen in warm years should become clear in the coming weeks, as the first northern whales reach Costa Rican waters.

World.title: Don’t Drink This Bottled Water, Costa Rica’s Health Ministry Warns
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Ministry of Health is warning the public not to buy or drink NIMBU purified water from lot 27/08/26. Laboratory tests found coliform bacteria at levels far above what is allowed in drinking water. Check the label before you open a bottle. The affected lot is printed as 27/08/26 and carries sanitary registration number AS-CR-21-08146. The water is made by Eliviana S.A. for Alpemusa S.A.

Tests by the Laboratory of Pharmaceutical Analysis and Advisory found total coliforms above 1,600 MPN per 100 milliliters (3.4 fluid ounces). The permitted maximum is less than 1.1, which puts the sample more than a thousand times over the limit. Coliforms are the bacteria labs use to judge whether water is safe to drink. When they show up, the water may also carry other germs that can make you sick. The lab also identified Rhizobium radiobacter, a bacterium normally found in soil.

The problem came to light after a consumer reported dark particles floating in a bottle from a different lot of the same product, dated 28/05/2025. The ministry says its findings show contamination in at least two lots. If you have bottles from either lot, don’t drink them. The ministry’s warning centers on lot 27/08/26, but some reports describe it as covering the brand as a whole, so the safest choice until the investigation ends is to avoid NIMBU water entirely.

If you already drank it and feel unwell, see a doctor rather than treating yourself at home. The ministry lists gastrointestinal symptoms, fever and general malaise as the signs to watch for. No formal recall has been announced, which means bottles from the affected lot may still be on store shelves. You can report any bottles you find, or any illness you suspect is linked to the product, through the Ministry of Health’s official channels.

The warning comes as Costa Rica heads into an El Niño dry season in which the national water utility has already asked households to cut water use. The ministry said it will keep investigating to determine how far the contamination reaches.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Top Prosecutor May Face Lawmakers Over Slain Journalist’s Threat Complaints
World.content:
Costa Rica’s ruling party wants the top prosecutor and its acting chief of judicial police to explain to lawmakers how they handled the threat complaints filed by journalist Camilo Rodríguez before he was shot dead on Monday. Nogui Acosta Jaén, head of the Pueblo Soberano caucus, announced in the Legislative Assembly that his party will file a motion in the Special Permanent Commission on Security and Drug Trafficking.

The motion seeks to summon Attorney General Carlo Díaz Sánchez, Deputy Prosecutor Mauricio Boraschi Hernández and acting Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) Director Michael Soto Rojas. The summons is not yet approved. The motion must be filed and voted in the commission, where it was expected to be taken up on Thursday. The ruling caucus holds five of the commission’s nine seats.

Acosta said the inquiry should examine how the justice system processed Rodríguez’s complaints and how people who speak out on social media can be protected. He also pointed to one of the journalist’s videos in which, according to Acosta, Rodríguez suggested that the person threatening him had links to the attorney general. Acosta did not present evidence to support that claim, and the Public Ministry has not responded to it publicly.

Opposition lawmaker Claudia Dobles of the Coalición Agenda Ciudadana said she supported calling the judicial officials but questioned why the motion leaves out Public Security Minister Gerald Campos Valverde. The motion comes two days after the ruling caucus approved, by 29 votes to 21, a separate motion demanding the resignations of Díaz and Ombudswoman Angie Cruickshank over their inspection of the new maximum-security prison. Opposition lawmakers criticized the timing of that vote.

On Wednesday, the Public Ministry announced that Díaz will personally lead a specialized team of organized crime prosecutors and prosecutors from Heredia to direct the murder investigation alongside the OIJ. Díaz said the decision reflected the seriousness of the case and that the team would act with rigor and technical precision.

Rodríguez, 50, was killed on the afternoon of Nov. 16 on Route 32 in San Miguel de Santo Domingo, Heredia, as he was returning to San José from Guápiles. According to preliminary reports from authorities, two men on a motorcycle pulled up beside his vehicle, fired repeatedly and fled.

Vladimir Muñoz, acting deputy director of the OIJ, said the attackers had information about the journalist’s vehicle and took advantage of it being stopped in traffic. Investigators are trying to establish whether other people followed Rodríguez and alerted the gunmen, a line the OIJ first raised earlier this week.

Agents searched Rodríguez’s apartment overnight Monday into Tuesday and seized four cellphones, a hard drive, other electronic devices and documents for forensic analysis, according to the Public Ministry and OIJ. No arrests had been announced as of Thursday morning, and authorities have not confirmed a motive.

Prosecutors have said that one of the main lines of investigation concerns Rodríguez’s public allegations about links between organized crime, drug trafficking and political parties. Investigators have not ruled out other motives, including business disputes. Rodríguez had reported multiple threats against him before his death. Díaz has said the journalist was referred to the Public Ministry’s victim and witness protection office but declined the protection measures offered, which are voluntary.

Hundreds of people attended his funeral Mass on Wednesday afternoon at the Cathedral of Nuestra Señora del Carmen in Cartago, where mourners greeted the casket with applause and calls for justice. Bishop Mario Quirós of Cartago asked for comfort for the family and for a more just society.

His mother, Sara Chaverri, called for justice and for the country to act against crime. His brother Andrés Rodríguez thanked the public and said the institutional response must go beyond catching the gunmen and lead to changes that address the violence. Burial followed at the General Cemetery of Cartago.

The killing has drawn condemnation from the government, judicial authorities, the United Nations, Reporters Without Borders, the U.S. Embassy and a joint statement from the European Union, Canada, the United Kingdom and Switzerland, which called it an attack on freedom of expression and of the press.

Rodríguez is the third journalist shot dead in Costa Rica in a quarter century, after radio host Parmenio Medina in 2001 and Ivannia Mora in 2003. How quickly investigators identify both the gunmen and whoever ordered the killing is likely to shape public confidence in the country’s justice system for years to come.

World.title: Why Costa Ricans Head for Puriscal When the Rains Stop
World.content:
Ask a Costa Rican where to go on a Sunday in late November and there is a good chance the answer will be Puriscal. The city sits in the hills about an hour west of San José, close enough for a day trip and far enough to feel like the countryside most Ticos remember from childhood. For a few weeks between the end of the rains and Christmas, everything that makes the place worth the drive arrives at once.

Puriscal has never needed a beach or a volcano to draw visitors. What it offers is simpler: winding ridge roads, long views across the Central Valley, small farms, butcher shops with wood fires going and a pace of life that the capital lost long ago. This is the season when all of that is at its best.

The first reason is the weather. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) forecast the dry season to settle over the Central Valley during the second week of November, and in Puriscal the change is easy to feel. Afternoon downpours give way to blue skies, and the trade winds that Costa Ricans call the Christmas winds begin to blow across the ridges.

Those winds matter here more than in most places. They clear the haze, cool the air and open up views that stay hidden behind cloud for much of the rainy season. On a clear December morning a visitor can stand on a ridge above Santiago de Puriscal and see the valley on one side and the hills falling away toward the Pacific on the other.

The timing also flatters the land. The rainy season has left the hills green, though in a drier-than-normal El Niño year the pastures may start turning gold sooner than usual. Back roads that turn to mud in the wet months are dry and passable again, which opens routes through villages that many visitors never reach.

The second reason is pork. Puriscal is known across the country as the home of the chicharrón, and families here have been raising pigs and curing meat for generations. People drive out from San José every weekend of the year for a plate of fried pork with yuca, tortillas and a squeeze of lime, but in the weeks before Christmas the habit becomes a pilgrimage.

The reason is the Feria del Chicharrón, the fair that has filled the center of Santiago de Puriscal in the early weeks of December for more than two decades. Vendors start frying before the morning mist has lifted, and by midday the smell of pork and woodsmoke has spread across the town. Past editions have added live music, craft stalls, carnival rides and a horse parade to the food.

The crowds are real and the fair has drawn more than 6,000 visitors to the canton in a single week, a large number for a town of this size. Last year it opened on the last weekend of November and ran through Dec. 8, and anyone planning a trip this year should check the dates with the organizers before setting out.

The calendar does the rest since the aguinaldo, the extra month of salary that Costa Rican workers receive at the end of the year, lands in December, and the school year ends around the same time. Families have a little more money and a lot more free time, and a drive to Puriscal costs far less than a weekend at the coast.

Pork is also the meat of the Costa Rican Christmas. It goes into the tamales that families make together in December and onto the table as roast leg on Christmas Eve. Plenty of visitors leave Puriscal with a cooler in the trunk, stocked by the same butchers their parents bought from.

There is more to do than eat. The canton lies where the dry forest of the Pacific slope meets the wetter forest of the highlands, and that mix draws birdwatchers, who find the trails easier going once the rains stop. Others come for the old tobacco country, the roadside stands selling fruit and local produce or simply the drive itself.

What Puriscal offers in these weeks is a version of Costa Rica that many people assume has disappeared. It has clean air, green hills, good food cooked over a fire and neighbors who still greet strangers in the street. Costa Ricans have always known where to find it, and this is the time of year they go.

World.title: Orange Walk construction worker Noe Perez charged with murder of Henry Nunez
World.content:
Orange Walk construction worker Noe Perez charged with murder of Henry Nunez

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have arrested and charged Noe Perez, 39, a construction worker from Orange Walk Town, with the murder of Henry Javier Nunez.

Nunez, 32, was found dead on a sugar road in Chan Pine Ridge Village on Tuesday, November 17. He had suffered multiple stab wounds, and his body was partially burned.

As Breaking Belize News previously reported, Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith said investigators believe Nunez was fatally stabbed during a fight with a man he knew. Police had detained two people in connection with the case.

The police update announcing the charge did not specify a motive or say what became of the other person detained.

World.title: BREAKING: Four (4) persons killed and one seriously injured in accident between a passenger bus and a SUV on the George Price Highway in the Cayo District
World.content:
BREAKING: Four (4) persons killed and one seriously injured in accident between a passenger bus and a SUV on the George Price Highway in the Cayo District

By Jose Luis Cruz: Earlier tonight Breaking Belize News (BBN) reported that a serious traffic accident had occurred on the bridge that forms the border between Unitedville and Georgeville in the Cayo District.

Reports from the scene of the accident is that four (4) persons lost their life and a fifth is seriously injured.

The SUV and the passenger bus were traveling in opposite direction when the head on collision occurred right on the bridge on the George Price Highway. The bridge is commonly referred to as the Lucio Chief bridge by residents of the Cayo area.

The four (4) individuals who lost their life were all occupants of the SUV.

The fifth person that was injured was rushed to the hospital for emergency treatment.

World.title: International News: Heavy fighting erupts in Haiti as security forces launch major operation against gangs
World.content:
International News: Heavy fighting erupts in Haiti as security forces launch major operation against gangs

By Zoila Palma: Heavy fighting erupted in Haiti today as the country’s armed forces and police launched an aggressive security operation to regain control of Martissant, a strategic corridor connecting the capital, Port-au-Prince, to the country’s western and southern regions.

The operation marks the first major attempt in five years to remove powerful gangs that have maintained control of the area, AP reports.

Haiti’s National Police reported that at least 34 suspected gang members were killed during clashes involving police officers and a task force that includes personnel from Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL Erik Prince.

Local media reported heavy gunfire and explosions from explosive drones as armored vehicles moved through Martissant. The area is located along Route 2, a major transportation link that previously carried thousands of commuters and shipments daily. Since gangs seized control in 2021, movement through the corridor has been severely restricted, with armed groups reportedly charging motorists tolls and opening fire on vehicles attempting to pass. The disruption has also affected the delivery of goods and humanitarian assistance, forcing residents and aid workers to rely on dangerous alternative routes.

The violence in Martissant dates back to June 2021, when rival gangs attacked each other, setting homes on fire, killing residents and destroying businesses before taking control of the local police station.

A United Nations report estimated that the clashes displaced at least 19,000 people and affected approximately 800,000 others. Subsequent reports documented the displacement of more than one million people and the relocation of hundreds of public and private institutions. Meanwhile, a UN-backed gang suppression force has intensified operations in several areas, including Tabarre and the Artibonite region, targeting gang strongholds and clearing roads, schools and other facilities previously controlled by armed groups.

El Salvador has also deployed approximately 2,500 troops to Haiti following an October 18 attack in which four Salvadoran personnel went missing.

Acting on orders from President Nayib Bukele, Salvadoran forces have targeted the residences of two powerful Haitian gang leaders, Jeff and Lanmò San Jou, although neither leader was killed.

Thousands of Haitians reportedly took to the streets this week in support of Bukele’s intervention, while security experts have raised concerns about unilateral military operations and civilian casualties linked to explosive drone attacks.

World.title: Cabinet extends Garifuna Settlement Day wishes, urges caution on the roads
World.content:
Cabinet extends Garifuna Settlement Day wishes, urges caution on the roads

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Cabinet has extended warm wishes to all Belizeans as the country celebrates Garifuna Settlement Day today, November 19.

In a release issued from Belmopan, Cabinet said the day honours the rich history, resilience and cultural contributions of the Garifuna people to Belize.

It said the national observance recognises the traditions, music, language and heritage that continue to enrich Belize’s cultural identity.

With activities taking place across the country, Cabinet also issued a reminder to motorists.

Drivers are urged to exercise caution, remain attentive, observe speed limits and make responsible choices on the road.

Cabinet wished everyone a joyful and safe Garifuna Settlement Day.

World.title: International News: APEC Summit overshadowed by big-power politics
World.content:
International News: APEC Summit overshadowed by big-power politics

By Zoila Palma: Chinese President Xi Jinping has called on Asia-Pacific economies to strengthen cooperation in trade and technology development as leaders gathered in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on Thursday.

However, discussions on economic cooperation and open trade were overshadowed by growing geopolitical tensions and a rare trilateral meeting involving Xi, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, AP reports.

Addressing leaders from the 21 APEC economies, Xi urged countries to prioritize shared interests and maintain openness in trade and technological development.

“APEC members are like passengers riding the same boat,” Xi said, calling on members to work together, support one another and strengthen economic ties amid global challenges.

The summit featured traditional diplomatic engagements, including bilateral meetings, a gala dinner and a group photograph, while showcasing China’s technological advancements through artificial intelligence and robotics.

Trump, meanwhile, highlighted the strength of the U.S. economy, claimed his administration had attracted trillions of dollars in investments and said he expected to secure additional trade agreements. He also pledged to oppose what he described as “globalist” efforts to regulate artificial intelligence.

Technology competition between the United States and China remained a major concern, particularly Washington’s restrictions on China’s access to advanced computer chips used in artificial intelligence.

The United States recently tightened controls on remote access to advanced AI technology, a move experts say closed a significant loophole that had allowed China access to billions of dollars’ worth of advanced Nvidia chips.

Chinese leaders have emphasized the need for fair access to AI technology and cooperation on cybersecurity, financial stability and economic growth.

World.title: Xunantunich open but ferry limited to pedestrians; ATM and Nohoch Che’en under review
World.content:
Xunantunich open but ferry limited to pedestrians; ATM and Nohoch Che’en under review

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Institute of Archaeology says the Xunantunich Archaeological Reserve is open today, Thursday, November 19, but the ferry is operating as a pedestrian crossing only.

Visitors will not be able to take vehicles across the Mopan River and should be prepared to walk up to the site from the crossing.

In a notice issued at 6:00am, the Institute also advised that the Actun Tunichil Muknal (ATM) Cave and the Nohoch Che’en Archaeological Reserve are experiencing elevated river levels.

Its team is monitoring both sites and was expected to issue a further update within about an hour to confirm whether they will open to visitors today.

All other archaeological reserves across the country are open for visitation.

The Institute of Archaeology, a branch of the National Institute of Culture and History (NICH), says it will continue to monitor conditions and provide updates as needed.

Tour operators and visitors with bookings for ATM or Nohoch Che’en are advised to confirm the status of the sites before travelling.

World.title: 2027 could bring record heat, higher fuel costs and tougher economic pressure for Belize
World.content:
2027 could bring record heat, higher fuel costs and tougher economic pressure for Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Economist has released a preview of its annual forecast, The World Ahead 2027, and several of its themes have direct implications for Belize.

The publication expects 2027 to be the hottest year on record, driven by a “super El Niño,” with more droughts, heatwaves and extreme weather.

For Belize, that points to pressure on farmers, water supplies and hydro power generation, at a time when the country is already leaning more on expensive diesel to keep the lights on.

The outlook also anticipates continued fallout from the Iran conflict, including disrupted energy flows and tight fertiliser supplies. Belize imports its fuel and much of its farm inputs, so higher global prices feed quickly into electricity bills, transport and the cost of food.

The Economist warns as well that government borrowing costs are rising across wealthy countries. Higher global interest rates matter for Belize, which carries a public debt of about BZ$4.65 billion.

Taiwan is another theme. The publication describes the next two years as dangerous for the island, given China’s military ambitions and Taiwan’s 2028 elections. Belize is one of the few countries that maintains diplomatic relations with Taiwan, a partnership of 37 years that brings significant development support.

On energy, the outlook argues that renewables offer countries a way out of volatile global fuel markets. That is relevant to Belize’s ongoing debate over electricity costs and energy security.

The full edition of The World Ahead 2027 is being published today by The Economist.

World.title: Belize gets sunshine for Garifuna Settlement Day with just a few showers
World.content:
Belize gets sunshine for Garifuna Settlement Day with just a few showers

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The weather is cooperating for the 19th.

According to the Met Service, today will be sunny with cloudy spells, and tonight will be partly cloudy. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated for most of the country.

There is a medium chance of a few more showers offshore this morning, inland this afternoon and over the south tonight. Those celebrating in Dangriga, Hopkins, Seine Bight, Punta Gorda and other southern communities may want to keep an umbrella close this evening.

Daytime highs will reach 87°F on the coast, 90°F inland and 76°F in the hills.

At sea, winds are from the northwest at 5 to 10 knots, becoming northeast. Seas are slight, with waves of 1 to 3 feet.

The outlook for Friday and Friday night is for generally fair weather with isolated showers or thunderstorms. A few are possible inland on Friday afternoon.

Today’s tides include a low at 11:56am and a high at 5:55pm, followed by a low at 12:37am and a high at 6:33am on Friday.

The sun rose at 5:59am and sets at 5:16pm. The moon rises at 1:33pm and sets at 1:58am Friday.

World.title: Audit fallout
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness delivers the keynote address during the official opening of the Trelawny Adult Care Residential Facility in Falmouth on Thursday. (Photo: JIS)

PRIME Minister Dr Andrew Holness has charged that some of the findings in the latest auditor general (AuG) report on the management of Hurricane Melissa donations by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) should not have been included, as they raised concerns that could have been cleared up with readily available information.

At the same time he reiterated plans for a revamp of ODPEM, transitioning it into a national resilience organisation.

Speaking at the official opening of Trelawny Adult Care Residential Facility (formely infirmary) on Thursday, Holness said the Government had already started addressing structural and operational gaps within the agency, with the findings contained in the auditor general report further underscoring areas in need of continued strengthening.

He pointed out that the Government had commissioned an independent review of ODPEM in 2024, with the findings received in 2025.

Holness noted that the review highlighted several challenges, with recommendations for changes to the agency’s leadership, staff upgrades, system improvements, and a clearer mandate.

“We will move swiftly to address the issues at ODPEM, including the staffing issues, and appoint permanent leadership, and restructure it. So, we are well advanced in what we need to do to restructure ODPEM, and those things will probably move with a little bit more speed now,” declared Holness as he argued that some of the matters raised in the October report were of serious concern, but that others could have been clarified before being presented as findings.

“The report, in some instances — some of the points that have been itemised — are of great concern, as I have said, but some of them are easily explained, and probably should not have been a part of the report. For example, the report of 200 houses donated by the Government of China, only 30-plus can be accounted for.

“That is absolutely something that should never have been in a report, because you can easily see where they are. There are reports even before, where Minister [Robert] Montague and [a] Member of Parliament [in] Westmoreland toured facilities where some of the houses were stored, and so it is there. The ODPEM has come out and they have clarified that they have [been] handed over to the Ministry of Economic Growth and [Infrastructure Development], that has the duty to build the platforms,” said Holness.

The Auditor General’s Hurricane Melissa Relief Initiative Audit: Compliance Audit Report on Management and Distribution of In-Kind Donations, which was tabled in Parliament on Tuesday, listed 200 prefabricated houses, valued at approximately $139.1 million, among 1,332 fixed assets donated to the Government for response to the October 2025 Category 5 storm which devastated sections of the island.

The audit found that ODPEM had not provided receipt forms for the houses and had not entered the internationally donated assets in its inventory records or fixed asset register.

The auditors also reported that they had verified the existence of 31 prefabricated houses. The report did not conclude that the remaining houses had been stolen or were missing; rather, it identified gaps in the documentation and records needed to account for the donated assets.

Despite his belief that some things should not have been in the report, Holness also defended the role of the auditor general.

“The auditor general is an important part of our democracy that it is able to do this. There are other countries that don’t have this, but this is an important part. The society, however, has to develop the understanding of what the reports mean before drawing conclusions,” said Holness.

The prime minister also addressed concerns about relief supplies that had spoilt, describing the matter as one of inventory management and agreed with the auditor general that there is a need to ensure that older goods are distributed before newer supplies.

During a physical inspection of Warehouse 3 on June 18, the auditor general’s team found 359 boxes of crackers past their best-before dates, as well as insects on the packaging of some consumable items. The report noted that the other items inspected were within their usable dates.

The audit further found that ODPEM had not maintained adequate store records to allow auditors to compare the physical stock with the quantities received and distributed. It also noted that rice remained in storage about three months after an infestation of weevils had been reported.

Holness said the circumstances surrounding donated goods, including their expiry dates, should be considered before conclusions are drawn.

“Normally your first in is your first out, and you have to have a process to look at the date of expiration that comes in on some of the items that you have, so you try to either dispose of them, or send them out. It is a complicated issue… I won’t go any further than to say that when you are dealing with donated items, the expiration dates are sometimes close to the use date. So you have to bear that in mind when you make your conclusions on that finding,” he argued.

Holness also addressed ODPEM’s use of donated funds to pay Customs clearance fees for relief goods, acknowledging that the spending did not follow the instructions given for how the money should be used.

The auditor general found that ODPEM spent approximately $45.1 million from its Donation Account on brokerage and related clearance fees, as well as warehouse rental and utility expenses. Of that amount, $32.97 million was used to clear goods intended for private organisations.

The donated funds had been approved to support the Government-Directed Roof Repair and Semi-permanent Housing Solution Programme under the broader Shelter Recovery Programme.

ODPEM acknowledged in its response to the audit that the brokerage fees fell outside the approved expenditure, but said the payments were considered necessary to prevent delays in releasing relief consignments.

Holness said the decision was made at the executive level of ODPEM and was not a decision made by the Government’s executive leadership.

“But I suspect they may be thinking that, if they didn’t pay, they wouldn’t get the goods, or if they didn’t pay, the goods would stay on the wharf, generating more fees that the Government would have to pay,” added Holness.

World.title: Sandals South Coast reopens under US$250-million ‘Sandals 2.0’ upgrade
World.content:
The entrance to be revamped Sandals South Coast showing the heart-shaped porte-cochère lobby. (Photo: Anthony Lewis)

WHITEHOUSE, Westmoreland — Just over a year after taking a direct hit from Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, the reimagined Sandals South Coast officially reopened its doors on Thursday with Executive Chairman Adam Stewart declaring the property’s rapid transformation a triumph of Jamaican resilience and teamwork.

According to Stewart, Sandals Resorts International (SRI) has invested no less than US$250 million across three of its hurricane-damaged Jamaican properties — Sandals South Coast, Sandals Montego Bay, and the rebranded Sandals Caribbean Cay (formerly Sandals Royal Caribbean) — to usher in a new era for the brand.

“My dad taught us, never waste a good crisis,” declared Stewart, referring to the philosophy of his late father and Sandals founder, Gordon “Butch” Stewart.

“We have spent no less than a quarter-billion US dollars taking Sandals from what it was to what we now call Sandals 2.0: New restaurants, new pools, new architecture, new designs, new features, new amenities. So, you know, we have a message to our competition: While you are trying to get back to baseline, catch us if you can,” added Stewart.

Stewart was addressing the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the rehabilitated resort in Westmoreland. The hotel, which sustained severe damage during the Category 5 storm, was rehabilitated by a combined team of Jamaican and American architects, engineers, and hospitality workers over a compressed 10-month period and welcomed its first guests of 448 on Wednesday,

The remaining two badly damaged properties are slated to reopen on December 18, 2026.

Stewart praised the scale and speed of the rehabilitation effort at the 380-room property located in Whitehouse.

“What the team of Sandals demonstrated here was nothing short of a miracle. Two-plus years of work compressed into 10 months. We worked with American and Jamaican architects until the coffee couldn’t help them any more,” Stewart told the gathering.

The ceremony drew bipartisan representation from political leadership, tourism officials and stakeholders and Stewart commended the country’s political maturity in the aftermath of Melissa.

“Jamaica as a country, even on both sides of the political divide, it is amazing the maturity, it is amazing the advancement that we have made as a country, how we can talk about complex things and how we can find solutions to make sure that love for country is never far away from our performance and what it is that we’re doing,” Stewart stated.

He revealed that during the recovery period, Sandals kept its team members on payroll with full benefits and 50 per cent of their gratuities. The hotel also hosted and housed team members who were stranded in their communities.

Stewart pointed out that during the COVID-19 pandemic in Jamaica (2020-2021) and in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, the hotel housed and fed essential personnel — including members of the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF), Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), air traffic controllers, embassies, non-governmental organisations, and the staff and contractors of Jamaica Public Service (JPS), which occupied a third of the resort — free of cost.

He also recounted the harrowing hours during and after Melissa when for hours Sandals executives lost contact with the property until former General Manager O’Brian Heron — now president of the Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) and SRI’s newly promoted head of operations — managed to send a WhatsApp message.

Stewart highlighted Heron’s heroism during the height of the storm where he risked his life to ensure the security of his team members.

Meanwhile state minister in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright lauded SRI for its 45-year contribution to Jamaica’s economy, workforce, and global brand.

Seiveright described the home-grown hospitality giant as an “economic powerhouse” and “one of the greatest entrepreneurial success stories this region has ever, ever produced.”

Highlighting the resort chain’s vast footprint, Seiveright noted that Sandals employs approximately 20,000 people across the Caribbean, including more than 7,000 in Jamaica.

Sandals South Coast employs between 900 and 1,000 workers — primarily from surrounding communities — making it one of Westmoreland and western Jamaica’s largest private-sector employers.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security Dr Horace Chang hailed the reopening of Sandals South Coast as a defining symbol of national resilience.

According to Chang, Jamaica’s tourism sector and its security apparatus are emerging stronger a year after the historic storm made landfall in Westmoreland.

“Melissa wrote a chapter about what we lost, today, Sandals South Coast writes the next chapter about what we rebuilt,” declared Chang.

“Let’s say Jamaica is open. Jamaica is safe. Jamaica is back. Sandals are back, leading the way,” added Chang.

World.title: Ras-I comes into his own with Kingman Live
World.content:
Ras-I to host Kingman Live on December

For years Ras-I has been steadily building his place in reggae music, carving out an identity through introspective songwriting, conscious lyrics, and a willingness to draw from his own lived experiences. The artiste is now preparing to embrace a new chapter in his journey, one that will see him step into the spotlight as the headliner of his own live production.

Dubbed Kingman Live, the event represents more than another performance opportunity for the rising reggae sensation. It is the culmination of years of artistic development, a growing connection with audiences, and the determination of a team that has been working to bring the vision to life.

Originally conceptualised for 2023, Kingman Live had to be put on hold when the pieces failed to fall into place. Rather than force the production, the artiste and his team opted to reassess their plans and wait for a more opportune moment.

In the intervening years, the artiste has continued to build momentum, with the release of his album and a succession of singles helping to expand his reach.

“The album, the momentum from singles release and everything, we started to gain a lot more traction and then corporate came on board, and that was very instrumental because we know how challenging it is to produce live events. It nuh cheap at all. So my team and I — Apryl included — decided that now was the right time. Di people dem ready for Kingman Live and we ago give it to dem,” he said.

That reference to Apryl McIntosh carries particular weight. McIntosh, Ras-I’s manager, passed away recently. Her death left a significant void in both his professional and personal life. Her contribution to the development of Kingman Live makes her absence especially poignant.

“Kingman Live wouldn’t be happening at all without Apryl, and so, of course, we have to honour her memory in a special way. We will definitely want to have a tribute section to her,” he shared.

The loss has also forced Ras-I to confront grief while navigating the demands of an industry that rarely pauses. He admits that he is still processing McIntosh’s passing, taking each day as it comes and accepting that healing does not follow a predictable pattern.

“Everybody have dem own way of grieving, mine is day by day. Every day is different; some days you’re up, other days you’re not. Some days the emotions high,” he said.

Music has naturally become one of his anchors during this period. Whether listening to other artistes, revisiting his own catalogue, or simply allowing himself to be immersed in sound, he finds comfort in music. His faith also provides reassurance, while activities such as playing football offer an opportunity to disrupt negative thought patterns.

“Through the Almighty, I just gwaan hold it and know say this too shall pass. I just always try to break the cycle, do something that mash up the negative momentum… play ball,” he explained.

That ability to draw from life’s difficult moments is also reflected in his approach to songwriting. Rather than relying solely on imagined scenarios, Ras-I uses his experiences as the foundation for his music, allowing his artistic expression to evolve alongside his personal growth.
