He views each new experience as an opportunity to create, particularly as he continues to navigate the demands and rewards of a developing career.

“I just write about my experiences daily. As you grow in the industry, there are fresh experiences, so every time I break a new barrier, there’s new material,” he said.

It is an approach that has informed both his album and the collaborations featured on the project, with the artiste explaining that many of the songs were born out of similar moments of personal and professional progression.

And while the emotional demands of the past months have presented their own challenges, his attention remains firmly fixed on delivering a memorable experience when Kingman Live takes place.

He said preparations are progressing well, despite the need to bring additional personnel on board following McIntosh’s passing. He is confident in the new additions to the team and says the musicians and artistes involved are equally prepared to deliver.

“The band is ready, I am ready, and all the artistes on board are ready — the ones announced and the ones not on the flyers, because we have a whole heap of special guests passing through,” he revealed.

For audiences, he promises an evening centred on the kind of live musical connection that has become increasingly important to him.

Rather than an elaborate spectacle designed around social media moments, Ras-I wants to recapture the uncomplicated enjoyment of attending a show, discovering music, and connecting with artistes in real time.

“People should just expect good vibes. Remember when we used to go show and just ‘fuljoy’ the music, the live entertainment, that’s what it will be like,” he said.

He sees the production as an opportunity to introduce audiences to artistes they may not necessarily know beyond a handful of songs, giving them the chance to experience their music in a more intimate and meaningful setting.

For him, that is part of a wider conversation about the importance of live entertainment in Jamaica’s musical landscape.

“Kingman Live is my way of saying we need more live events, because we have a lot of music and you can only experience it the right way through in-person vibes — not through a phone screen from a 30-second video, but the real feeling, drum and bass with conscious lyrics,” he said.

It is perhaps an appropriate reflection of where Ras-I finds himself at this stage of his career. Having spent years developing his craft and gradually building an audience, he is now taking greater ownership of the spaces in which his music can be experienced.

There is still much to navigate, both personally and professionally, but Kingman Live offers a tangible reminder of how far he has come.

And, as he prepares to take centre stage, the moment is as much about celebrating that growth as it is about acknowledging the people and experiences that helped bring him there.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: BARITA SEEKS $9.3B IN FRESH FUNDING
World.content:
BARITA Investments Limited is returning to the public bond market with plans to raise up to $9.3 billion through a combination of Jamaican- and US-dollar-denominated securities, as the investment company seeks to strengthen its balance sheet and secure funding for new investment products.

In a prospectus published on Tuesday, Barita outlined a three-tranche bond offer comprising two US-dollar instruments and one Jamaican-dollar instrument, with interest rates ranging from 7.25 per cent to 10.50 per cent and repayment periods of two to five years.

The company is seeking to raise US$10 million in each of the two US-dollar tranches, with the option to increase each to US$15 million if demand permits. The Jamaican-dollar tranche targets $3 billion, with provision to increase the amount to $4.5 billion.

Investors in the first tranche will earn annual interest of 7.25 per cent over two years, while the second tranche offers 10.50 per cent over three years. The third tranche carries an interest rate of 8.25 per cent over five years.

Barita intends to use the proceeds to strengthen its capital base, improve liquidity and support the development and introduction of new investment products as it works to diversify its earnings.

“Continued emphasis on disciplined risk management, recurring income generation and balance sheet resilience, alongside selective participation in emerging investment and capital market opportunities, should support Barita’s competitiveness and long-term earnings growth,” the company stated in its prospectus.

Although Barita outlined the broad purposes of the fundraising, it did not specify how much would be allocated to each activity. Transaction costs associated with the offer are expected to remain below $200 million.

“We will strengthen liquidity and diversify our funding sources. With policy rates higher in Jamaica and the United States, we will manage the maturity and repricing of assets and liabilities and adjust funding terms where appropriate to protect net interest margins,” said Barita chairman Mark Myers in the company’s fourth quarter report ending September 30.

The bond offer also enters a market recently buoyed by Scotiabank Caribbean Holdings Limited’s $63.50-billion acquisition of the remaining minority shares in Scotia Group Jamaica Limited (SGJ), a transaction that has returned a substantial amount of capital to investors and potentially created fresh demand for investment securities.

Barita has been actively deploying capital into different opportunities over the last year. This included the acquisition of Barita Fund Managers Limited (formerly JN Fund Managers Limited) in January for $3.81 billion. The acquisition expanded Barita’s assets under management by at least $52 billion and contributed $789.5 million to Barita’s net operating income (NOI) and $60.2 million to net profit.

Barita also acquired Key Homes Limited from MJR Real Estate Holdings Limited in December 2025 as it brings some of its real estate plans to its balance sheet. The consideration for this deal was a series of debentures over five years valued at US$111.53 million ($17.63 billion). Key Homes owns a 101 acre property known as Windsor Estates in St Ann. This acquisition contributed $897 million in fair value gains to Barita’s NOI and increased its investment property balance to $20.23 billion.

The investment firm reported a 136 per cent increase in its net operating income from $8.70 billion to $20.47 billion for its financial year ending September 30. The bulk of this improved earning capacity was attributed to $13.27 billion in gains on its investment activities. Accordingly, Barita raked in $4.68 billion in realised gains and $8.59 billion in unrealised gains, with $7.09 billion arising in the fourth quarter.

Although revenue generation improved during the year, operating expenses doubled from $4.64 billion to $10.78 billion, which included $2.38 billion in credit loss provisions for amounts in doubt. There was also a sevenfold increase in the loss from its associate during the year.

Despite the higher costs, Barita’s profit before tax grew 126 per cent to $8.85 billion while net profit doubled from $3.01 billion to $6.03 billion. These figures are unaudited and subject to final review in the upcoming audited financial statements by newly appointed auditor PwC.

“We are tightening control of technology, administrative and transformation spending, simplifying processes and using targeted automation to lower the cost of serving clients. This work goes hand in hand with modernising our systems and improving digital service. Our aim is to improve operating leverage so that more of our revenue growth translates into earnings,” Myers explained on the 2027 objectives.

Barita’s balance sheet moved by 32 per cent to $196.17 billion, reflecting the benefits of its Barita Fund Managers and Key Homes acquisitions. The investment firm’s pledged assets reached $116.28 billion as it continued to grow its repurchase agreement (repo) book with its clients.

Equity increased by four per cent to $36.59 billion as Barita recorded unrealised losses on some investments and proposed a $3.25 billion dividend to be paid on November 30.

The investment firm is working to develop some of the real estate properties under its alternative investment portfolio. Three of the sites held by MJR Real Estate are in active pre-development, with demolition work completed former Ice Factory on Harbour Street and former Eden Gardens property on Lady Musgrave Road. MJR Real Estate is owned by the Barita Real Estate Unit Trust.

“Over time, we expect completed developments to broaden the portfolio’s sources of return through proceeds from sales and recurring income from leasing and operations, complementing the Group’s securities and asset management businesses,” Myers noted.

This is the company’s second public bond offer following its June 2025 bond listing where it raised $4.74 billion and US$20 million from investors. Tranche I and tranche III from that listing are scheduled to mature in June 2027, with US$10.22 million and $1.37 billion payable to investors, respectively.

Barita intends to apply to list the different tranches on the JSE’s Bond Markets. Barita currently has five securities listed on the JSE Bond Market and two securities on the JSE USD Bond Market.

Investors seeking to purchase tranches I or III must subscribe to a minimum of US$1,500 and apply in multiples of US$100 for higher amounts. The tranche II offer requires a minimum of $50,000 and increments in multiples of $1,000 for higher amounts. Applications can be made on Barita’s Boss website or through selling agents such as Jamaica Money Market Brokers Limited (JMMB), Barita Fund Managers, Proven Wealth Limited or VM Wealth Management Limited. The offer opens on November 25 and is scheduled to close by December 29.

World.title: ITALIAN JOB
World.content:
Jamaican winger Jamone Lyle (centre) dribbles away from Canada’s Eloi Breton (right) and Ulrich Zamble during the Concacaf Under-17 qualifiers encounter between Jamaica and Canada in Costa Rica on February 11, 2026. Lyle is one of Jamaica’s top players at the FIFA Under-17 World Cup, where they will play Italy today at 10:00 am in their opening match. (Photo: JFF Media)

Jamaica’s Under-17 Reggae Boyz will begin their FIFA Under-17 World Cup campaign against European champions Italy on Friday at 10 am, and Jamaica Football Federation President Michael Ricketts is confident that the team is adequately prepared and has urged Jamaicans to rally behind the youngsters.

Jamaica, appearing in its third Under-17 FIFA World Cup and first in 15 years since they last competed in 2011 in Mexico, are paired in Group E with Italy, Ivory Coast and Uzbekistan.

The Jamaicans will be hoping to make a positive start against the Italians before facing Uzbekistan on November 23 and Ivory Coast on November 26.

Despite acknowledging the difficulty of the assignment, Ricketts is confident that the team is adequately prepared and has urged Jamaicans to rally behind the youngsters.

“We will open our World Cup campaign against Italy and obviously, this is going to be a tough encounter. In fact, I think we are in a very tough group. But the important thing is that we are here and we are going to represent ourselves and our country well,” Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer.

“I think they are mentally and physically well prepared. We’re just hoping that they will execute on the field tomorrow and we’ll get a good result,” he added.

Jamaica qualified for the tournament after winning all three of their Concacaf group matches, with forward Jahmarie Nolan playing a significant role, scoring four goals and providing two assists.

The likes of Jamone Lyle, who like Nolan recently made his senior debut, as well as Tyrique Robinson, Dwayne Burger, Justin Hayles, Nathaniel McCarthy, Jaeshawn Edwards, Kelvin D Brown, and Kelvin O Brown, should carry the fight for Jamaica.

The team’s qualification represents another milestone for Jamaica’s youth football programme, particularly following the Under-15 team’s appearance at the World Cup just a month ago, as the federation tries to qualify all its teams.

“Being to a World Cup is no ordinary achievement and we must express our gratitude to all the key stakeholders, who would have contributed to the success of our youth programmes. Just a month ago, our Under-15s were at the World Cup and they also did so very well,” Ricketts said.

The Under-15 World Cup and Festival was open to all 211 FIFA member associations and did not require qualification.

Meanwhile, the JFF president also credited the federation’s technical staff, which is supported by FIFA, for contributing to the development of the country’s youth programmes.

“I must express my gratitude to the coaches, the technical staff, administrative staff and all those who have contributed to the growth and development of our youth programmes. Our TDS programme, which of course is supported by FIFA, has done so very well and that probably would have been the framework that would have contributed so significantly to our youth programmes,” he added.

Jamaica’s history at the Under-17 World Cup has been mixed.

Their first appearance came in 1999 in New Zealand, where they lost all three group matches without scoring a goal.

They returned to the competition in 2011 in Mexico, where they recorded their first point with a 1-1 draw against France. Zhelano Barnes scored Jamaica’s first goal at the tournament.

Now, 15 years later, the Young Reggae Boyz have another opportunity to improve on that record and make a lasting impression on the global stage.

Ricketts is calling on Jamaicans at home and abroad to give the team their full support as they embark on the latest chapter in the country’s football history.

“I want all of Jamaica to rally around our youngsters and, of course, give them as much support as you can as we embark on another historic exercise,” he said.

World.title: Business set to ‘pickup’ for CAR Jamaica
World.content:
Carwyn Brown, sales executive, CAR Jamaica, with the all-new Musso Grand pickup. (Photo: Rory Daley)

CAR Jamaica launched its newest model, the all-new KGM Musso Grand, on Friday, November 13, at their Lady Musgrave Road showroom.

“The Musso is one of the best-selling pickups on its side of the world, and we know for sure it will do well here in Jamaica because we have a great extensive pickup culture here in Jamaica,” Mellisa Bailey, general manager, CAR Jamaica, told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

The Musso is a long-time name for fans of the Ssangyong brand, now KG Mobility. Originally an SUV, the Musso had a dual cab pickup version called the Musso Sport Utility Truck, or Musso Sports. For 2027, it’s a traditional body-on-frame four-door pickup only.

Powered by a 2.2-litre four-cylinder turbo diesel, it drives a six-speed automatic transmission with part-time four-wheel drive, and has all the technology, safety, and convenience features expected in a modern pickup.

Making the Musso unique is its two trim levels. The standard Musso is a small, shorter vehicle, with a 122-inch wheelbase and a full body length of 203-inches.

In Musso Grand trim, the vehicle gains 4.4-inches of wheelbase and 12 inches in body length, the large majority of which is in the rear tray for more cargo space. The Musso can handle a payload up to approximately 2,400lb and tow up to approximately 7,700lb.

“The Musso is perfect for a work-life balance,” explained Carwyn Brown, sales executive, CAR Jamaica.

Brown expects the Musso to appeal to lifestyle pickup buyers and expand the company’s reach into the commercial vehicle segment.

Both the Musso and Musso Grand are available with a six-year warranty and several service packages.

The third brand CAR Jamaica is set to represent was finally revealed by Bailey at the Musso launch.

“Car Jamaica is definitely expanding. We are excited to bring a full electric option, Xpeng, out of China. The launch for that is coming soon,” she said.

World.title: BOJ rate hikes raise mortgage payment fears
World.content:
At a time when Jamaicans are already struggling with punishing cost of living, homeowners carrying hefty mortgages are expressing fresh concerns following two consecutive policy interest rate hikes by the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ).

It has raised fears among them that monthly mortgage payments could climb further and place additional financial pressure on their already stretched pockets.

The BOJ raised its benchmark policy rate on September 29 by 50 basis points from 5.5 per cent to 6.0 per cent – the bank’s first rate increase since November 2022 – and again on Thursday to 6.5 per cent, a decision the central bank said was taken in the context of “an upside risk that inflation could remain above the target range until late 2027”.

READ: BOJ increases policy rate to 6.5% as inflation pressures persist

Jamaica’s annual inflation rate eased to 8.2 per cent in October from 8.6 per cent in September, but remained above the Bank of Jamaica’s target.

The policy rate is what the BOJ pays deposit-taking institutions on balances held at the central bank, and serves as a benchmark for borrowing costs.

One woman, who is in her eighth year of mortgage payments, said she is apprehensive, maintaining that her budget cannot handle any more pressure.

“You budget for a certain amount that your mortgage rate will be, and you don’t know what percentage it’s going to be increased by and when they do it, they’re not going to give you a grace period or anything,” she said.

The mortgager reflected on the 2022 rate hike, and the subsequent cycle of five cuts that brought it down from seven per cent.

“A [few] years ago, when the interest rate went up, our mortgage went up and so did the home insurance, and then when the BOJ reduced the rates, the mortgage went down,” she explained.

With the interest rates up again, she said she is “of course” worried.

“Because right now, I am maxed out; I don’t have any extras. Nothing working with…I’m maxed out. If it increases, I don’t know what I would do. I [would] just hope that eventually it’s going to decrease again.”

There are some Jamaicans, however, who say their mortgages have not decreased since that 2022 spike, as some commercial banks were slow to reduce their lending rates, prompting calls for a reduction from lobby groups including the Private Sector Organisation of Jamaica (PSOJ), Jamaica Manufacturers and Exporters Association (JMEA) and Jamaica Chamber of Commerce.

One male mortgager said the 2022 increase added a huge chunk to his payment that he is still grappling with.

“By itself, it added $28,000 to my monthly payments. What’s worse is that mere days after being informed about the interest rate increase, I was informed that the peril insurance rate has been increased as well, resulting in another increase in my monthly payment,” he explained.

That was four years ago, and unlike some, he says, he has not gotten any relief. Now with the BOJ increasing rates again, the possibility of additional hikes is distressing.

“I am very apprehensive about the possibility of another increase, because I simply cannot afford it. I am paying approximately $40,000 more in monthly mortgage payments in just four years, when my salary hasn’t budged. Considering all the other increases in cost of living, the struggle is real,” he lamented.

One female mortgager who borrowed directly from the National Housing Trust and is about halfway through paying off a 25-year mortgage said her relief at not necessarily being subject to an increase because of the interest rate hike is immense.

“I am terribly relieved because since that time there have been adjustments based on policy changes so the mortgage I started out with is not the mortgage I now pay,” she explained, adding, “I am very relieved, and I am still thinking and trying to find a way to exit the agreement before the 25 years because…I really look at it now, and I don’t want to be trapped that long.”

Another male mortgager, who is nearing retirement age and has around $8 million left to pay on his own mortgage, was less concerned about any potential increases.

“I think, yeah, there are people who legitimately would want to worry about these things. I really don’t. I have the mortgage already, I have to pay it. The only thing I could maybe try to do is shop around for another entity, financial company that might offer me a better rate. But that’s a lot of hassle,” he said.

Realtor and CEO & Qualifying Director for Easton Douglas Consultants Ltd, Kari Douglas explained that it was unlikely that the increase would drastically affect the housing market locally, maintaining that there are factors in purchasing a home that carry more weight than the current interest rate.

However, she did have advice for potential homeowners.

“A rate increase raises the cost of borrowing, so buyers should test their budget, confirm whether their rate is fixed or variable, and buy only what they can comfortably carry if rates move again. Take the time to get a proper valuation so you’re paying a price that the market supports and borrowing against real value,” she urged.

Douglas said prospective purchasers should also shop around and compare the rates, fees and terms of different banks, building societies, and credit unions to ensure the lowest possible rates.

World.title: ‘I will not be baited into a one-sided apology’, says Burchell
World.content:
Nekeisha Burchell

KINGSTON, Jamaica—Member of Parliament (MP) for St James Southern, Nekeisha Burchell, has stated that she will not be baited into a one-sided apology over statements she directed at the MP for St Andrew West Rural, Juliet Cuthbert-Flynn, during a tense sitting of the House of Representatives on November 17.

Burchell, while responding to an off-mic quip from Cuthbert-Flynn about her ability to adequately prepare for parliamentary debates, said “mi go a gud, gud school enuh. Mi neva run fi a living”.

Cuthbert-Flynn, a four-time Olympian and minister of state in the ministry of national security and peace, and other Government MPs were incensed by the remark. The member for St Catherine East Central, Alando Terrelonge, rose on a point of order to demand that Burchell withdraw the statement. He accused Burchell of disrespecting athletes. She eventually withdrew the remark after she was ordered to do so by deputy speaker of the House, Heroy Clarke.

The next morning, the dispute erupted into a below-the-belt war of words when Cuthbert-Flynn posted on social media that she was “proud to have earned my living on my feet”.

Burchell has come under pressure to apologise to both Cuthbert-Flynn and Jamaican athletes in general.

But, in a video posted to social media on Thursday, she indicated that there will be no such apology even while stating that, “I have tremendous respect for Jamaica’s athletes, and the discipline and sacrifice behind their achievements”.

Burchell said she has since spoken with athletes, adding that, “I’ve taken the time to speak with managers and leaders in the sporting fraternity and generally they understood this was a personal retort directed at Juliet, not an attack on athletes as a group”. She said if there’s any athlete who took offence, “no disrespect was intended”.

Describing Cuthbert-Flynn as chief heckler, Burchell said she has observed since entering the Parliament, that Government members “throw stones and hide their hands. When somebody responds, they present themselves as the victims and demand one-sided apologies”.

She accused the Government of using its parliamentary majority to condemn the response “while ignoring the attacks that provoked it – kind of how they deal with Beenie Man”, she said. “I was baited into a retort, but I will not be baited into a one-sided apology that pretends the provocation never happened”.

Burchell insisted that there cannot be one standard of respect for the majority and another for the minority. She has declared that she will not be bullied into silence.

The first-term MP who represents the opposition People’s National Party has often locked horns with Government members. She began her video by expressing regret for “allowing myself to be drawn out in Parliament this week, and I shouldn’t have”. She outlined her educational and professional achievements before entering representational politics, moving from Mt Alvernia High School to the University of the West Indies, to the London School of Economics.

“I built a career running campaigns across the Caribbean and working in different countries, just making a name for myself.

“So imagine standing in Parliament trying to make a contribution, and somebody across the floor is repeatedly questioning your education, your ability, and tell you that you didn’t even write your own speech? Me, who has been writing speeches for presidents, prime ministers and business leaders for nearly two decades,” Burchell said.

“And she just wouldn’t stop, the remarks kept coming, getting more personal and insulting, while I’m on my feet trying to concentrate,” she added.

Responding to Cuthbert-Flynn’s comment that she made her accomplishments on her feet, Burchell said, “I understood exactly what she’s saying; she was suggesting that while she worked for her achievements, I somehow slept my way to mine. Burchell said it’s the same sexual insinuations she has had to endure since entering representational politics, from both males and females.

World.title: ‘Staff deserve answers’ on Commission cyberattack, union says
World.content:
The lack of internal communication is “unacceptable,” he wrote in the email, titled “Staff deserve answers now.”

“It’s simply inconceivable that news outlets around the world are covering the incident while staff are still waiting for their first direct update from the Commission,” he wrote, adding that current and retired colleagues have written to R&D with concerns.

The union has several thousand members, Sebastiani said in a comment.

Some staff told R&D that managers denied a cyberattack had taken place and said the incident was a routine technical issue, Sebastiani wrote in the email.

The lack of communication is especially grave because internal HR systems are affected, meaning sensitive personal data may be at risk, the union representative wrote. He called for the Commission to immediately explain the incident to all staff, including information about what data was affected, and to carry out an independent review.

The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor, the internal EU data watchdog, a spokesperson for the regulator said.

The Commission did not immediately respond to a request about the union email. Spokesperson Thomas Regnier said on Thursday that the Commission took “the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign,” adding that individual systems were targeted and that “in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned.”

World.title: Brussels to link UK-EU summit package to tuition fee demands
World.content:
“The Council agrees that adoption of the Council Decisions on signing of the ETS, SPS and YES agreements will not precede the conclusion of the negotiations on the supplementing Agreement providing for equal treatment on tuition fees,” a draft of the statement seen by POLITICO says.

The statement is expected to be formally adopted on Friday morning by written procedure, an EU diplomat said.

A second EU diplomat said: “You can see this as a clear signal from Brussels that this is a package deal.” But they added that there was a “political commitment” to get fees over the line: “We just need to work out the details — and that’s not happening today.”

While there is no binding clause in today’s summit agreement linking the trade and youth experience deals with the tuition fee cut, the separate statement drawn up by the EU council effectively says the EU could block their implementation through its own processes if talks on fees do not conclude.

Asked about the link between the four deals, an EU official said: “What we have agreed is that we will complete this in six months. I think this is an important element. So let’s hope that everything can go ahead.”

However, the official insisted: “We don’t take anyone hostage here.”

World.title: Germany says investors ready to spend €25B to buy TikTok Europe
World.content:
A teenager holds her smartphone displaying the logo of Chinese social network Tik Tok in Brussels on July 7, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

Germany and Austria floated the initiative earlier this week, citing concerns about the Chinese-owned company’s influence on European democracy.

BRUSSELS — The German government has found investors interested in investing as much as €25 billion to buy the majority of TikTok's EU operations, Berlin's culture minister Wolfram Weimer told reporters on Friday.

"We have spoken to a lot of investors already," he said. "It's a pan-European initiative and we think that they are able to invest around about 25 billion euros in that kind of business. And TikTok Europe should be open to sell 75% to 80% of the shares."

Germany and Austria floated the Trump-style initiative earlier this week, citing concerns about TikTok's influence on European democracy. TikTok said there was "zero merit" to the proposal.

World.title: Emmanuel Macron hosts Kamala Harris at Elysée
World.content:
The French leader is hosting the former vice president in a “private capacity,” the Elysée said.

PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron will host former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris at the Elysée Palace on Friday, according to his office.

Macron is meeting Harris in “a private capacity for a brief courtesy meeting in the presence of her husband, as he sometimes does at the request of certain former leaders,” the Elysée said in a statement.

The face-to-face comes shortly after the Democrats’ emphatic victory in U.S. midterm elections and as strains grow between Paris and Washington over peace talks on the war in Ukraine. Macron and U.S. President Donald Trump, who defeated Harris in the 2024 presidential election, have had a hot-and-cold relationship in recent years.

World.title: Russia hits 3 Kyiv bridges in major attack, while Poland reports airspace violation
World.content:
Frightened birds fly against the backdrop of a contrail left by an air-defence missile intercepting a jet-powered drone during an aerial attack on Kyiv on November 18, 2026. | Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images

The overnight strikes, which killed at least five people across Ukraine, came hours after Vladimir Putin vowed a painful response to Ukraine’s attacks on the Crimean bridge.

Russia launched a massive missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight, killing at least five people and damaging three of Kyiv’s main bridges across the Dnipro River — while Poland reported a violation of its airspace.

The strikes came hours after U.S. President Donald Trump called into a meeting of Ukraine’s European allies from Air Force One and said Russian President Vladimir Putin was serious about peace negotiations.

In Kyiv, three people were killed and about 15 were injured, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Ballistic missiles damaged the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi crossing and the Darnytskyi bridge and hit the Southern Bridge again, prompting Klitschko to urge residents not to drive into the city and employers to let staff work from home. “The enemy’s missile attack on Kyiv is ongoing,” he added.

World.content:
Pattinson will star as Bond, although as the EU is funding the project, we have been forced to cast Ursula von der Leyen as his boss, M.

Budgetary constraints mean that instead of swanky cocktail bars and high-rolling casinos, late-night scenes will be filmed inside the Hairy Canary pub and at Maison Antoine friterie.

World.title: UK ‘playing catch up’ with Nordic countries on crisis preparations, says minister
World.content:
Jarvis pointed out a national risk register that highlights widespread power outages, the loss of drinking water and terrorist and state threats as among the most significant risks to the U.K. He added: “If you look at the things that I’ve said in Parliament on the record [and] the conversations that we’re having nationally about the nature of the world that we are living in, I think there is a lot of conversation about the different threats that we face.”

He added: “There is a bit of balance to be struck because we absolutely don’t want to alarm the public — but we do want the public to be alert, we want the public to be prepared.”

Jarvis downplayed concerns that some in the U.K. government felt after Cabinet ministers joked about their personal stockpiles — including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, who said hers would include “mascara, concealer, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, some baked beans and a tin of custard.”

“As the security minister, there are lots of things that I worry about at any one time. That isn’t one of them,” he said. “I think it’s quite helpful in terms of promoting the conversation. I think it’s quite helpful in terms of focusing people’s minds about what they would do in their own households.

“That’s the essence of this campaign. It’s about making sure that there is that resilience in households … so I’m entirely relaxed that people are having a conversation about Sauvignon Blanc or whatever it might be.”

Jarvis said he had “obviously followed my own guidance” when building his own home stockpile, including a radio and torch, and had not added any special treats beyond the checklist. He does, however, have a ready supply of eggs at home. “I’ve always found it incredibly relaxing to keep chickens, not least when you have a reasonably busy and demanding job,” he said. “There’s something very peaceful about them.”

World.title: Papal progress: Vatican Museums explore a century of Popemobiles
World.content:
There once was a pope who could tell his driver when to accelerate, when to slow down and even when to return to the Vatican, simply by pressing a button. Another, by contrast, had a car turned into an open-top vehicle so that he could be seen more clearly by the crowd. And then there was John Paul II, who had a barber's chair adapted as a papal seat, so that he could greet the faithful.

 

The cars of popes tell a story that goes far beyond engines, bodywork and comfort. They reveal the character of the pontiffs, the way they choose to be among people and, above all, how communication of the papacy has changed - from the solemnity of limousines to the search for direct contact with the faithful, and the growing need to protect those who travel under the spotlight.

This is the journey traced by the exhibition "A century of Popemobiles", that's now on at the Vatican Museums (source in Italian). Eight historic Mercedes-Benz cars retrace almost 100 years of papal mobility. They are accompanied by a Benz Patent-Motorwagen from 1886, considered the first car in history, and a new Mercedes-Benz S-Class, broadening the view of how the automobile has evolved.

Sandro Barbagallo, curator of the Vatican Museums historical collections says each vehicle has its own story: "The message is very simple: papal mobility exists so that the pope can draw close to everyone, all over the world. The use of cars is not just about moving the Pontiff around within Vatican City".

We have seen this too in the most recent images of apostolic journeys: the Pope crossing cities and, from the moment after he steps off the plane, being able to make himself visible, bless people and ensure there is direct contact with the people of God. Sandro Barbagallo Curator of the historical collections of the Vatican Museums

A story in which each pontiff has, in one way or another, left his mark, including by choosing how he wished to be transported.

Pius XI, the Pope who fell in love with his car

The relationship between Mercedes-Benz and the Vatican officially begins in 1930, when Pius XI receives a Nürburg 460 (W 08), a large limousine donated by the German car manufacturer. It is the first Mercedes regularly used by a pope.

Mercedes-Benz Nürburg 460 (W 08). Donated to Pope Pius XI on 23 May 1930 Directorate of Museums and Cultural Heritage

Achille Ratti, elected in 1922, was a man of culture, a scholar and lover of the mountains, with a past as a mountaineer and explorer. A Pontiff accustomed to looking far ahead, who did not shun the innovations of his time. The car also became a tool for leaving the Vatican, after the long period of the so-called imprisonment of the popes, which began with the end of the Papal States in 1870.

The Nürburg 460 is far from a standard official car: the interior is customised with a single seat for the pope, upholstered in fine silk brocade, selected woods, metallic detailing and a decorated ceiling. A kind of travelling sitting room, designed to underline the prestige of the papal figure.

But it is not just a question of luxury. Some papal cars from that era had a 'backseat driver' function panel, allowing the pope to instruct the chauffeur using buttons labelled "Forward", "Slow", "Right" and "Return to the Vatican". A sort of remote control before its time.

John XXIII, the "good Pope" who opens the windows

The pope's public presence also changed with John XXIII. Angelo Roncalli, a.ka. the "good Pope", had an informal style, a cheerful manner and a natural ability to relate to people. His pontificate, shaped by the Second Vatican Council, led the Church into a period of greater dialogue and openness.

The cars began to follow this transformation as well. In 1960, the Mercedes 300 d Landaulet (W 189) arrived, with rear windows that can be completely removed to allow the pope to be seen more easily and better greet people during public outings.

The features are already those of a vehicle built around the needs of the most important passenger: an electrically adjustable central seat, controls for the air conditioning and communications within easy reach, automatic steps to make it easier to get in and out of the vehicle.

Mercedes seems to have understood that the pope's car must not only take him to his destination: it must also allow him to meet people along the way.

Paul VI, the travelling Pope who invents the papamobile

If there is one pontiff who turned travel into a fundamental part of papal communication, it is Paul VI. Giovanni Battista Montini is the first modern pope to travel by plane and to make a series of international apostolic journeys, reaching places never before visited by a pontiff.

In 1964 he flew to the Holy Land, then to India in 1965, and in the following years to other continents. His mission was to reach the faithful in Rome and beyond by going to their countries to meet people and let them see him up close.

His Mercedes 600 Pullman Landaulet (W 100) from 1965 has a roof that opens at the rear specifically so that the pontiff can greet the crowds.

Mercedes-Benz 600 Pullman Landaulet - Donated to Pope Paul VI in September 1965 Fanuel Morelli

In 1967, a Mercedes 300 SEL Pullman (W 109) also arrives, another of the cars that mark the evolution of papal automobiles.

But the birth of the modern papamobile is above all linked to a practical need. As Barbagallo explains, "up until Paul VI, and then also with John Paul I, who as we all know had a very brief pontificate, the Pope went to audiences and even entered the Paul VI Audience Hall on a sedia gestatoria".

Paul VI, who found himself celebrating the Jubilee of 1975, was the first to realise that with the sedia gestatoria he could no longer make circuits around St Peter's Square, so he arranged for an open-top car to be purchased Sandro Barbagallo Curator of the historical collections of the Vatican Museums

That first vehicle was still a production car made available to the Pontiff. But it marked a decisive change: the Pope no longer simply had to be transported, he could now cross the square and be seen by all the pilgrims.

To grasp the difference between the traditional papal saloons and the papamobiles, Barbagallo retraces the evolution of these vehicles: "The way they have developed has constantly highlighted, on the one hand, the Pope's comfort, on the other his security, and on yet another the fact that the Pope can be seen. In saloons, that is the black cars, the Pope is only seen by those on his side of the vehicle, whereas in a papamobile he can be seen equally from the right, the left, the front or the back. That, of course, is what creates the difference between the two means of transport".

John Paul II, the Pope of the crowds and the barber's chair

With John Paul II, the popemobile became an icon. Karol Wojtyła was a pope with a strong physical presence, used to direct contact, long international journeys and vast crowds. Before becoming Pope he was an actor, poet, sports enthusiast and lover of the mountains. It is no surprise that he was not especially drawn to the idea of remaining seated in a closed limousine.

From the beginning he refused to use the traditional sedia gestatoria, the ceremonial chair on which popes were carried during ceremonies. He preferred a motor vehicle that allowed him to move around and greet people freely.

This is where one of the most curious episodes in the history of popemobiles comes in: for some of the first open vehicles a swivelling barber's chair was adapted, mounted on a metal base. A decidedly unusual seat for the head of the Catholic Church, but practical in allowing him to turn and greet the crowd from every side.

The Mercedes that fixed the image of the modern popemobile in the public imagination arrived in 1980, for John Paul II's trip to Germany. It is a 230 G (W 460), based on the G-Class, with a raised seat and a large transparent dome at the rear. The Pope can be seen from every side while remaining protected from the weather.

Mercedes-Benz 230 G (W 460). Pope John Paul II aboard the Vatican's first papamobile, 1980 Directorate of Museums and Cultural Heritage

On 13 May 1981, however, the attempted assassination in St Peter's Square changed everything. From that moment the pope's safety became a central concern and the popemobiles were gradually fitted with bullet-proof protection.

As Barbagallo recalls, "that first popemobile was, of course, a standard production car given for the Pope's use; it had no comforts and no particular safety features. But from then on there was an evolution that, sadly, is also closely linked to the attack in St Peter's Square on John Paul II, after which heavily armoured popemobiles began to be used, as they still are today".

The G-Class became one of the most recognisable models of his pontificate. In 1997, a long-wheelbase Mercedes S 500 Landaulet (series 140) also joined the fleet, with a hydraulically operated rear soft top and a large seat for the pope.

In 2002 the Mercedes ML 430 "Popemobile" (W 163) was added to the history of papal vehicles, another off-roader adapted to the pontiff's needs.

Benedict XVI, technology and the search for protection

With Benedict XVI the style changes again. Joseph Ratzinger, a theologian and intellectual, has a more reserved approach than his predecessor's stage presence, but maintains the tradition of close encounters with the faithful.

In 2012, the Mercedes ML 500 "Popemobile" (W 166) arrives, with larger glass surfaces to improve visibility and reduce the sense of separation between the pope and the people.

It is a popemobile that attempts to reconcile two needs that have become inseparable: protection and proximity. The pontiff must be visible, but must also be able to travel in safety.

A car that is more than just a car

Today, the popemobile is far more than a means of transport. As Leo XIV made clear at the inauguration of the exhibition, it has become a means of bringing the pontiff closer to people.

And there is a curious detail that illustrates how special the relationship with these vehicles is: the Pope's seat is unlike any other. Designed for him alone, every detail, from the position of the seat to the heated support bar, is suited to his needs.

Een the way a pope chooses to travel can say a great deal about how he chooses to be in the world.

The exhibition at the Vatican Museums, set up in the glass pavilion of the Giardino Quadrato, will remain open until 28 January 2027.

The papal vehicles on display

· Mercedes-Benz Nürburg 460 (W 08), 1930

· Mercedes-Benz 300 d Landaulet (W 189), 1960

· Mercedes-Benz 600 Pullman Landaulet (W 100), 1965

· Mercedes-Benz 300 SEL Pullman (W 109), 1967

· Mercedes-Benz 230 G (W 460), 1980

· Mercedes-Benz S 500 long-wheelbase Landaulet (series 140), 1997

· Mercedes-Benz ML 430 "Papamobile" (W 163), 2002

· Mercedes-Benz ML 500 "Papamobile" (W 166), 2012

Two other vehicles broaden the historical perspective of the exhibition: a Benz Patent-Motorwagen from 1886 and a new Mercedes-Benz S-Class.

World.title: World is being ‘held hostage by oil mafia’: How one tiny country is putting its foot down at COP31
World.content:
It’s crunch time as COP31 enters its final day of discussions, following a lacklustre draft deal that sparked heavy backlash.

 

The annual UN climate summit, which is being held in Antalya, Türkiye, may overrun into the weekend amid growing divisions.

Yesterday (19 November), co-host Australia unveiled a slimmed-down draft deal that removed all mentions of fossil fuels – the leading driver of climate change – despite growing momentum to publish an exit strategy.

It signals a repeat of the COP30 summit in Belém last year, where the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) was erased from the final deal following resistance from fossil-fuel exporting countries.

Panama threatens to block final COP31 deal

COP agreements require consensus from all parties – that’s almost 200 nations – which means progress is often slow and incremental.

However, Panama appears to be putting its foot down, threatening to block any final deal that doesn’t deliver on a cap of oil production alongside a strident defence of science.

In a letter to COP31 hosts, Panama’s environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro said his country would “not join any consensus, and will formally object in the closing plenaries, to the adoption of any decision that does not lead to an outcome satisfactory” to its principles and values.

Navarro added that Panama would “not lend its name” to “complacent or ineffective language” in the final pact.

Earlier this week, the politician argued that the world is being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and that nations are “in love with its kidnappers”.

We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good. Juan Carlos Navarro Panama’s environment minister

“They torture us for our own good, they destroy our planet for our own good. They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, unlimited, boundless love. And we are so stupid that we fall for it.”

TAFF roadmaps gain appeal outside of the UN remit

Nations agreed at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels, but language around energy sources is highly contested at the yearly talks.

However, following the first TAFF conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, which took place in April, several countries have established their own exit strategy – with Europe leading the way.

Before COP31, France, Germany and the Netherlands published national roadmaps to get away from coal, oil and gas.

On 11 November, two days into the talks, Finland affirmed its commitment to TAFF.

Almost a week later (17 November), Denmark, Portugal, Luxembourg and Spain announced their own national plans.

While “you can always wish and fight” for TAFF to be anchored in the cover decision, “this is not for us the ultimate benchmark for success,” German Environment Ministry State Secretary Heike Henn told reporters on Monday (16 November), ahead of the draft’s publication. “The success is in doing, in a growing coalition,” she said.

What will COP31 actually decide?

Experts have criticised the erasure of fossil fuels from the latest draft deal, warning that the talks risk becoming a “ghost COP”.

"The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here,” Mohamed Adow, founder and director of climate think tank Power Shift Africa said on Thursday, 19 November.

“After the progress made in 2023 at COP28 in Dubai where fossil fuels were mentioned for the first time, there is now no mention of the f-word at all.

“COP31 has been muzzled on the most important threat causing the climate crisis.”

Inga Fritzen Buan from environmental group WWF told news agency AFP that some major fossil energy producers are attempting to “undermine” everything related to emissions cuts and the energy transition.

“With this draft, they’re succeeding,” Buan added. “This is not a mere disagreement over the placement of a comma.”

Electrification takes centre stage

The latest text included a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35 per cent by 2035 – a key initiative of Türkiye.

However, concern remains that the draft deal does not explicitly require that extra electricity be powered by clean energy rather than coal or gas.

“We are going to fight for clean electrification” met by renewables and nuclear energy, French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut told reporters.

Some countries rejected calls to ramp up carbon capture, utilisation and storage technology, which critics see as an expensive distraction from cutting pollution.

The draft also proposes further discussions toward “tripling” finance for climate adaptation measures by 2035, but drops a $120 billion (approximately €109 billion) goal being sought by developing nations.

Rich nations have long resisted calls to increase support for countries struggling to adapt to climate change, citing budget constraints and insisting that big emerging economies such as China also contribute.

The draft deal also contains a recognition of the “best-available science” and a reference to the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), a key battleground at COP31.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 20th, 2026 – Midday
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Portugal national public sector strike over pay disrupts key services
World.content:
Public administration workers are staging a nationwide strike this Friday.

 

In Lisbon, the coordinator of the Frente Comum said this morning that the protest has been seeing strong participation since overnight and that the first effects can already be felt in areas such as health, education and rubbish collection.

In some of these services, such as hospitals, only minimum services are being provided. On the figures for education, Sebastião Santana said, quoted by the Lusa news agency, that "data are still being collected" but "many schools are closed across the country".

Also in the morning, the secretary general of FENPROF, José Feliciano Costa, said there was a "significant number of schools on strike", particularly in Greater Lisbon. "Today teachers will join the public sector strike also because they see their careers being devalued," the union leader told Lusa.

In health, more specifically in hospitals, Joana Bordalo e Sá, vice president of the National Federation of Doctors (FNAM), said that "minimum services are being rigorously complied with", with the greatest constraints affecting consultations and scheduled surgeries.

"This is a strike for patients and for the National Health Service. Ana Paula Martins [health minister] knows the chaos that is going on in healthcare and does nothing to solve it," she told reporters this morning.

The protest was called by the Frente Comum, affiliated to the CGTP, to demand better wages to keep up with inflation and cope with the cost of living. The union front is calling for a pay rise of no less than 15%, with a minimum increase of 150 euros for everyone, and is also advocating raising the basic pay in the public administration to 1,150 euros, with effect from 1 January.

Unions want to influence budget debate

In an interview with RTP, the coordinator of the Frente Comum accused the government of having no real will to negotiate.

"We are at the fourth round of negotiations and the government insists on not moving from its starting point," said Sebastião Santana, who cited the executive's proposal to increase the meal allowance as an example.

"The government proposed an increase of 15 cents compared with the first proposal it presented for the meal allowance, which is ridiculous." The union organisation is demanding a 13 euro increase in this area, stressing that the government's proposal would raise the current amount to 6.45%, falling far short of workers' demands who, according to Sebastião Santa, have some of the lowest wages in Europe and have been losing purchasing power "for more than a decade and a half".

The union leader also explained that the choice of date for the protest is intended to influence the budget debate.

"The strike is on the 20th and not on the 25th in order to influence the discussion of the State Budget," he said.

World.title: Former French PM de Villepin launches presidential bid, as centrists and conservatives slide in polls
World.content:
Former conservative French Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin announced his presidential bid on Friday, as he decried the country's "decaying" political and social climate.

 

In an apparent reference to the hard-left France Unbowed and far-right National Rally party, he called out the rise of "radical forces", while accusing French President Emmanuel Macron of "paving the way" to their ascension.

He later clarified that he did not place the France Unbowed party and the National Rally on the same level, calling out the

He stressed the vital need to address France's economic situation, as it grapples with one of the highest levels of public debt in the eurozone. De Villepin pledged to bring this debt below 3% of GDP, while backing increased taxes on the ultra-wealthy.

On Europe, he decried the bloc's absence on the international scene, while also stating that France struggles to make its voice heard within the union. De Villepin said he supports the creation of a European security council for the bloc's major powers — France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Poland.

The 73-year old is the third candidate to announce his presidential bid in November alone, after former French judoka heavyweight Teddy Riner and hard-right leader of the Reconquêtes Eric Zemmour.

His candidacy comes as France's centrists and conservatives — including centrist Gabriel Attal, alongside conservatives Édouard Philippe and Bruno Retailleau — have been struggling to gain ground, according to the latest polls.

This is also a result of a fractured political landscape, as the left-wing and right-wing bloc were left weakened by Macron's election in 2017, on a centrist programme with his party En Marche.

The race remains dominated by the far-right National Rally party and the hard left France Unbowed party. Their respective candidates, Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon are respectively polling around 32–36% and 17-19.5%, according to an Ifop-Fiducial survey published on 18 November.

As the central and conservative political bloc struggles to unite, the prospect of a possible primary to select a joint candidate has become a hotly contested issue, with candidates such as former prime minister Édouard Philippe refusing to take part.

Disagreements have also centred over how broad the possible primary should be in terms of including candidates on the right, given that the objective is to rally as many possible votes from conservatives — but also centrists.

World.title: Brussels puts military fuel needs at heart of new oil security strategy
World.content:
The European Commission wants EU governments to look beyond emergency oil stockpiles to secure enough diesel, jet fuel and other oil products to keep essential services and military operations running during a prolonged crisis, according to a draft document seen by Euronews.

 

More than half of EU countries (61.54%) reported trouble ensuring sufficient fuel access when armed forces move across the continent in a 2025 Commission impact assessment, posing a major hurdle for the bloc's plans for military readiness by 2030.

With Russia's war against Ukraine at its border and a series of hybrid attacks sweeping the continent over the past weeks, Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius recently warned that the EU needs to prepare for a substantial increase in military fuel consumption during a conflict.

He noted that in the event of a war outbreak, NATO could need to move and sustain 100,000 troops during the first ten days of a crisis, stressing the importance of diesel and jet fuel for military operations.

The EU's new approach to energy security deems it crucial to place oil supplies within the EU's wider defence and strategy preparedness agenda to "prevent or minimise risks" on a range of measures.

According to the draft document, which lays out an overhaul of the Commission's oil security rules, national governments would need to assess how much emergency fuel they hold and whether their refineries, ports, pipelines and distribution networks could withstand major disruptions.

"Inadequacy between the evolution of consumption, including military demand, and the evolution of the fuel supply chain, including along military mobility corridors," reads the paper, referring to assessments expected by EU governments.

AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi Danish military forces participate in an exercise with hundreds of troops from several European NATO members in Kangerlussuaq, Greenland, Wednesday, Sept. 17, 2025.

Under the draft rules, EU countries would have to factor military demand into their national risk assessments, including the possibility of sudden increases in fuel requirements and simultaneous pressure from civilian and military consumers.

A recent NATO energy security study found that the EU's ability to fuel its armed forces could be undermined by a shrinking refinery industry, growing dependence on foreign suppliers and insufficient jet fuel reserves.

"Jet fuel is precisely the product on which NATO Europe is structurally short. It is also the fuel most likely to retain (or even grow) its demand to 2050, and the product with the least amount of stock cover at 49 days," reads the study.

NATO's study noted that Europe imports between 27% and 30% of its jet fuel from outside the region, leaving it exposed to foreign suppliers.

Dependence is also highly concentrated — 36% of external imports come from one supplier, while three countries account for 65% of all external supplies.

Assessing refinery's capacity

While EU governments are pursuing industrial decarbonisation, strategically important refining capacity is disappearing, raising the question of whether the bloc's refinery industry is becoming a national security liability.

Despite the efforts to accelerate the energy transition, the new energy security framework puts considerable attention on refineries — an industry sector in decline across Europe over the past nearly two decades.

"We need to counter this trend and ensure that we have adequate and flexible refining capacity in Europe. Today and for the future. This is not just a matter of economic competitiveness. It is also a matter of security," the Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said after a dialogue on refineries alongside Defense Commissioner Kubilius.

Even if EU countries have access to crude oil alone, they need sufficient capacity to turn it into the diesel, gasoline and jet fuel required by transport, industry and defence.

According to the draft document, national authorities would have to identify their refineries, assess their production capacity and report major closures, expansions and planned investments.

Brussels also expects capitals to examine the consequences of losing critical infrastructure and becoming overly dependent on a limited number of foreign suppliers.

The document suggests the Commission is asking governments to consider whether allowing domestic refining capacity to disappear could create a strategic vulnerability that can't easily be repaired if a crisis hits.

The draft would also require EU capitals to map their dependence on individual suppliers, including the countries from which they import crude oil, diesel, gasoline and jet fuel.

The goal is to assess how these dependencies could evolve over the next five years and what would happen if a major supplier suddenly stopped deliveries.

EU countries could face greater scrutiny over their emergency preparedness.

The draft document suggests that capitals would need to prepare national risk assessments and preparedness and response plans covering physical attacks, cyber threats, extreme weather, ownership of critical infrastructure and prolonged disruptions affecting several supply routes.

Collision course with clean transition

Environmental campaigners have argued that reviving refineries across the EU could slow down the bloc's goal to cut CO2 emissions at a time when a series of climate policies are being diluted.

The softening of the EU's carbon market and the CO2 emissions car rules, alongside the delay in implementing methane rules, raises questions over whether Brussels will reach its 2040 climate target to ultimately become carbon neutral by 2050.

Despite seeking to boost electrification and reduce oil consumption, Brussels recognises that armed forces will continue to need reliable supplies of diesel and jet fuel, including during sudden increases in military demand.

The Commission is expected to unveil its proposal to revise oil security supply rules on 2 December.

World.title: How eight European countries are tackling the housing crisis
World.content:
House prices have surged by almost 70% in the EU since 2015, and rents have climbed by 25%, far outstripping income growth, according to the bloc's statistics office, Eurostat.

 

Costs have risen the most in Portugal, followed by the Netherlands.

Rising housing costs have helped fuel a wave of protests across Europe. Housing rights groups and trade unions from France, the UK, Belgium, Spain, Italy, Portugal and Greece have called for three days of coordinated action from Friday, 20 November. They are demanding that governments guarantee the right to housing and bring down housing, food and energy costs.

Governments across Europe have announced measures ranging from rent caps and tighter rules on short-term lets to plans to build more affordable homes, as rising prices and a shortage of homes squeeze renters and buyers.

Here is a look at the measures being taken to ease the burden.

Spain

The eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her lifelong home in September sparked a national uproar that led parliament to pass new laws restricting evictions and property speculation.

But lawmakers rejected the automatic renewal of tenancy agreements, a main demand of protesters, and the conservative Popular Party, which leads in opinion polls, has vowed to repeal the measures if it takes power after the 29 November general election.

The left-wing government had already passed a law in 2023 calling for more social housing and rent controls in regions where the housing crisis was most acute.

But the measures have been applied only sporadically so far.

Barcelona, one of the most visited cities in Europe, has pledged to get more flats on the market by not renewing the roughly 10,000 permits for tourist rentals on Airbnb and other sites.

Portugal

The centre-right government of Prime Minister Luís Montenegro has focused on tax measures to encourage owners to put their homes or flats on the rental market.

He has also raised taxes on property purchases by non-residents.

But in September, lawmakers approved a rental market overhaul that makes it easier and quicker to evict tenants who do not pay their rent, sparking a wave of protests.

The Netherlands

The government of one of Europe's most densely populated countries set rent caps for many privately owned homes.

But many owners preferred to sell instead, leaving fewer homes available to rent, while rents for properties outside the cap continued to rise.

Earlier this year, the government announced new measures aimed at speeding up housing construction while guaranteeing that two-thirds of the new homes would be kept affordable for buyers and renters.

France

Since 2023, the centrist government has promised a "supply shock" with measures to encourage the construction of new homes and get more homes onto the rental market, including by easing environmental rules.

One bill currently under discussion in parliament would relax rules forcing owners to improve poorly insulated homes before they can be rented out.

The far right wants the insulation rules scrapped altogether.

The bill would also streamline the rules on home construction and provide bigger tax breaks to private landlords.

Germany

A lack of affordable rental properties in Germany has led to a revival in housing cooperatives, member-owned associations that offer an alternative to both renting and ownership.

Residents buy shares in the cooperative, which owns and manages the housing, and pay fees for their flats, helping to keep costs down and protect tenants from speculation.

Cooperatives now manage around 10% of Germany's rental stock.

Since 2010, rents on new leases have been capped in regions where housing markets are tightest, which has reined in prices but led to a decline in new home construction.

The left-wing party Die Linke made Berlin's housing crisis a rallying cry in recent local elections, promising to expropriate tens of thousands of flats owned by corporate landlords, a move the central government is trying to block.

Britain

The Labour government wants to increase supply by creating 300,000 social homes while also providing financial help for first-time buyers.

It has also banned no-fault evictions and limited rent increases to once a year.

But high interest rates, along with tax and regulatory burdens, continue to limit the construction of new homes needed to ease the chronic shortage.

Italy

Protests have led the government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to lower taxes on rental income, a move aimed at encouraging more owners to put homes and flats on the market.

It plans to make around 100,000 more homes available over the next 10 years, either by renovating existing social housing or building new homes, while simplifying regulatory procedures.

Greece

Authorities have focused on limiting the surge in short-term rentals in one of Europe's top tourist destinations, in particular in Athens and Thessaloniki.

The government has also reined in its "golden visa" programme for foreigners who buy property, which critics say has taken homes off the market for Greeks.

Subsidies provide lower-interest mortgages for first-time buyers, and public funds are also available for owners who commit to long-term rentals after renovating their properties.

World.title: Bhutan: Traditional wood painting shapes the kingdom's architecture
World.content:
With a fine brush and hand-mixed colours, traditional painter Karma Wangchuk brings plain timber to life through elaborate dragons and ornate motifs, practising Shing Tshon, a centuries-old wood-painting craft that gives Bhutanese architecture its signature vibrancy. From private homes and monasteries to public buildings and footbridges, these colourful designs, frequently woven with Buddhist prayers and sacred symbolism, are an ever-present sight across the Himalayan kingdom.

 

Protected by government building codes that champion traditional styles, Shing Tshon is deeply rooted in Bhutan’s national identity. To keep the craft thriving alongside rapid modernisation, the National Institute for Zorig Chusum in Thimphu instructs young trainees in all 13 traditional arts and crafts, ensuring that the country’s distinctive painted woodwork remains visible on new builds as well as ancient monuments.

World.title: Podcast: Living on the breadline, France's 35-hour week and a divisive tax
World.content:
The French government's decision to raise the minimum wage has failed to satisfy protesters struggling to make ends meet amid the cost-of-living crisis. Also, did the introduction of the 35-hour working week actually help reduce unemployment? The evidence is mixed. And a look at the history of France's second-largest tax, the CSG, and why it's dividing politicians.

Advertising

French unions and workers have been protesting over the rising cost of living and wages that are failing to keep up with inflation. In response, the government has agreed to increase the minimum wage, known as the Smic, by 1.6 percent – putting an extra €24 a month into the pockets of the lowest earners. But the measure has failed to satisfy unions and public sector workers, who took to the streets again this week for a day of strike action. We hear what it's like to live on the breadline and the arguments for raising public sector wages. (Listen @0')

France introduced the 35-hour working week in 2000, aiming to reduce high unemployment by spreading work among more people. After five years of research, labour economist Elio Nimier-David has found that the reform failed to achieve its intended goals, while the question of how much people should work continues to divide politicians today. (Listen @19'20'')

The CSG, or general social contribution, was introduced in 1990 and is now France's second-largest tax after VAT, raising billions of euros to fund the country's social security system. But its broad reach and proportional rate have made it a political target, as presidential candidates debate how to ease the cost-of-living crisis and put more money back into people's pockets. (Listen @15'10'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.
