World.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
World.content:
German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how?

Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.

In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.

Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."

The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.

Can crisis reinvent the car again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German auto industry faces restructuring

Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.

Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot."

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Berger agreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation."

In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

In Germany, Mercedes has three assembly plants and seven facilities that manufacture drivetrains and components Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

Unions dig in amid fight for survival

Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.

Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.

Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.

"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.

China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.

Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

Mercedes plans more than 40 model launches by next year — a growing share will be built outside Germany Image: Joan Cros/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?'

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security."

PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.

"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.

With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.

"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.

Production remains resilient despite decline

Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).

IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000."

Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.

Analysts call for faster reform

For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany."

"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

World.title: Ukraine updates: Kyiv targeted by missile strikes, bridges hit
World.content:
Ukrainian officials said that the death toll has risen to at least 8 following an overnight Russian aerial bombardment.

Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said six of the eight people killed were ‌in Kyiv. Two deaths were also reported at a railway station in the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.

Ukraine's Air Force said Russia had launched 84 cruise missiles in the attack, adding that almost all of them were destroyed.

An unspecified number of ballistic missiles and more than 400 attack drones were also reported to have been destroyed.

World.title: COP31: UN Climate summit enters final phase with no deal in sight
World.content:
Skip next section COP summit poised to be extended with no deal imminent

Calls to 'make polluters pay' are still not being heeded Image: Yasin Akgul/AFP

Delegations from nearly 200 countries have been meeting in the Turkish resort city of Antalya since November 9 to negotiate ways to tackle global warming and provide financial aid to the world's poorest and most vulnerable nations to climate change.

But, as in previous years, countries remain sharply divided, and consensus has proven elusive.

Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, nations pledged to move away from fossil fuels, although no target or timeline was ever set.

Oil- and gas-producing countries have strongly resisted attempts to bring that particular issue back to the negotiating table.

Last year's COP30 summit in Brazil concluded with no mention of fossil fuels, prompting some nations to pursue the fight outside of the UN's sphere.

This year's summit is being held against the backdrop of rising living costs and the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has sent shockwaves through global energy markets and sent prices soaring.

Those challenges have taken the focus away from long-standing issues like rising global temperatures and increasingly frequent and extreme weather disasters, which have been exacerbated by this year's record-breaking El Nino.

In an initial draft deal earlier in the week, the phaseout of fossil fuels was included.

Australia's climate minister, who is steering the talks, predicted 'intense consultations' that would last all day and into the night Image: Yasin Akgul/AFP

But a new draft declaration released on Thursday night by Australia, which is co-hosting the summit, omits any mention of gas, oil and coal, widely recognized as the main drivers of climate change.

The omission is a "black mark," France's Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said.

Climate activists have also slammed what they call a "glaring regression."

"You cannot solve a fossil fuel crisis by pretending we don't need to phase out fossil fuels," said Harjeet Singh, convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign.

The director of Power Shift Africa, Mohamed Adow, also condemned the slimmed-down draft text, which he said had "gone backwards."

Despite the current differences, Australia's Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, said, "We will be consulting and negotiating until it is very clear to us that we have a consensus."

World.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
World.content:
According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.

Why is Lufthansa cutting 1,000 jobs?

This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).

VW on the brink To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful."

"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said.

At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.

How else is Lufthansa planning to save money?

The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.

Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.

The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

World.title: Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?
World.content:
From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.

"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.

"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."

Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.

"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.

"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.

Shoulda, woulda, coulda: Is it too late to bring temperatures under control?

The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

As permafrost melts, it releases carbon dioxide which adds to the greenhouse gas effect that continues to warm the planet Image: MAXIM SHEMETOV/REUTERS

A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.

Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."

He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.

Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

Solar energy has experienced record growth for years Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.

But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.

The countries pushing for a fossil fuel phaseout

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.

A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.

So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.

COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."

France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.



Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."

Every fraction of a degree matters

Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.

It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.

And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

Each fraction of a degree of warming will bring with it escalating climate extremes so it's still all to play for, say scientists Image: Apu Gomes/AFP

Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.

Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.

"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she said. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess."

World.title: India: Pakistani minister visits Delhi for SCO forum amid frozen ties
World.content:
11/20/2026 November 20, 2026 Rahul Gandhi says India has become a 'side player' in world affairs, BJP hits back

Rahul Gandhi was addressing students and faculty at the University of Chicago, a day after a similar interaction at Columbia University Image: ANI News/IMAGO

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi told students at the University of Chicago that India has become a "side player" in global affairs, prompting Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to respond sharply.

"India, by its size, naturally has a global voice and India should be actively involved in global conversations. But frankly, India has become a side player," Gandhi said in his interaction with students and faculty at the university, citing neighbor Pakistan's role in US-Iran talks.

He also questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi's reliance on personal ties with leaders like Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin: "Friendship is not the point. Who gives a damn about friendship? Do you really think that geopolitics is going to work because the guy is your friend?"

Gandhi was on a two-day visit to the US Image: ANI News/IMAGO

When asked by a Pakistani participant about relations between the neighbors, Gandhi said talks could begin if Pakistan stopped backing terrorism. "And it is impossible for us to accept our innocent people being murdered and having a conversation with Pakistan," he said.

Reiterating allegations about electoral rolls, he also ruled out an opposition election boycott: "If we were to say that we are not going to participate in elections, Indian democracy would end that very instant."

BJP spokesperson CR Kesavan took to social media to write, "Rahul Gandhi, the LoP [Leader of Opposition], sounds like an eager cheerleader and a shameless propagandist for Pakistan and his reckless remarks expose how clueless Rahul Gandhi is about global geopolitics."

World.title: China's Xi praises 'turnaround' in relationship with Australia
World.content:
The leaders of Australia and China have held talks on sidelines of APEC summit. Australian PM Anthony Albanese is also slated to meet Chinese Premier Li Qiang.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks on Friday, following which Xi hailed a "comprehensive turnaround" in the ties between two nations and Albanese said his country was engaging "constructively" with Beijing.

The leaders met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Forum (APEC) summit in China's Shenzhen.

What did Xi say to Albanese?

Xi pointed out to Albanese that they had met four times since the latter became Australia's Prime Minister in 2022.

"I think it is fair to say that together we have brought about a comprehensive ​turnaround in China-Australia relations," the Chinese President said.

Xi also called for enhancing cooperation in agriculture, ​energy, the ‌green economy and artificial intelligence, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.

Why is China important for Australia?

China is Australia's top trading partner.

The relations between the two countries hit rock bottom under Canberra's former centre-right coalition government, which had called for an independent inquiry into the origins of the coronavirus.

An angry China retaliated by imposing import curbs worth $13 billion (€12.2 billion) on Australian timber, coal, barley, lobsters and wine.

Since Albanese's centre-left Labor party came to power, China has lifted most of its blocks on Australian exports.

But friction in ties has surfaced occasionally on issues such as China conducting a missile test in the South Pacific and Australia tightening a foreign investment screening in the critical minerals sector.

"It is important that Australia continue to engage in a constructive way with China, manage our differences, but not be defined by them," Albanese told the media on Friday.

"What happens in China does matter for Australia," he added.

Iron ore, a pressure point

Albanese is expected to travel to Beijing and meet China's Premier Li Qiang later on Friday.

On Monday, Australia, which is the world's biggest producer of iron ore, called out China's "manipulation" of trade in the commodity over Beijing's formation of a central buying body to purchase ‌ore on behalf of its steelmakers.

A single buyer has increased bargaining power in negotiations with sellers.

Albanese and Li will attend a business roundtable comprising of senior executives from Australian mining giants Rio Tinto and BHP and ​Chinese company executives.

World.title: Germany news: Merz joins German-Ukrainian business forum
World.content:
11/20/2026 November 20, 2026 Germany's electricity exports rise

Germany's electricity exports rose in the first three quarters of this year, according to official data released on Friday.

According to the energy association BDEW, Germany has been a net importer of electricity since 2023.

The neighbouring countries Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands, were the most important buyers of German electricity in the first nine months of 2026.

Together, they bought about half of all German electricity exports.

The volume of German electricity exported rose by 25.5% compared with the same period last year, to 48.8 terawatt-hours, while its value increased by 51.3% to €4.3 billion ($4.7 billion).



Electricity imports into Germany fell by 13.3% in volume, but at 49.2 terawatt-hours they remained slightly above exports.

While imported electricity cost an average of €116 per megawatt-hour, 39% more than a year earlier, exported electricity from Germany averaged only €87 per megawatt-hour, some 20.6% more than a year earlier.

With a high share of renewable energy sources, wind and solar, Germany tends to offer electricity when supply is high and prices are low, but in times of shortage it has to pay higher prices for imported electricity.

World.title: Feijóo se lanza al ataque ante un Sánchez que evita el cuerpo a cuerpo
World.content:
En el único cara a cara de la campaña, el candidato popular enmienda la totalidad de la gestión del Gobierno y cuestiona una y otra vez la decencia de su rival, que opta por un tono pausado y minimiza el choque directo

Alberto Núñez Feijóo fue en tromba contra Pedro Sánchez, no solo con una enmienda a la totalidad de sus ocho años de gestión, sino cuestionando una y otra vez tanto la competencia como la integridad y decencia del presidente. Ante las descargas de Feijóo, siempre en tono acusatorio, el candidato socialista evitó el choque, adoptando una actitud por momentos autocrítica, respondiendo a los duros golpes de su adversario con cierta mesura. Es la síntesis del primer —y único— cara a cara entre los dos principales aspirantes a la presidencia, que tuvo lugar este jueves. Aunque primero en las encuestas y favorito para llegar a La Moncloa, Feijóo renunció al papel de solemnidad presidencial y se lanzó a degüello contra Sánchez, que, aunque necesitado de remontada, optó por minimizar el cuerpo a cuerpo y centrarse en la defensa de su gestión. A diferencia del debate de 2023, no se exasperó ante su adversario.

El debate empezó tras unos largos prolegómenos bajo el escrutinio de las cámaras, donde se evidenció la frialdad que reina entre Sánchez y Feijóo. No en vano, llevan sin reunirse a solas desde marzo de 2025. Mientras se preparaban, apenas se miraban. No había comenzado el cara a cara y ya había dejado un mensaje: los líderes de los dos principales partidos de la cuarta economía del euro no tienen ni esa mínima relación suficiente para decirse las cuatro vaguedades propias de una incómoda charla de ascensor.

00:16 Feijóo acusa a Sánchez de "ponerse a bailar a las 48 horas" tras los funerales en Urda El candidato del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, antes del cara a cara electoral. Foto: Juanjo Martín (EFE)

En el minuto de apertura, Feijóo ya hizo una declaración de intenciones, con un diagnóstico catastrofista de toda la gestión del Gobierno, de Ceuta a los accidentes ferroviarios pasando por el apagón, con el máximo énfasis en la corrupción, incluidas menciones al hermano y la esposa del presidente. Tras dar por buena la descripción que el expresident catalán Carles Puigdemont acaba de hacer sobre Sánchez —“cínico”, “con ambición desmedida”, repasó—, Feijóo remató con una especie de desagravio a Mariano Rajoy, al que en 2015 Sánchez dijo en un cara a cara que España necesitaba “un presidente decente”, y no él. Justo eso es lo que le dijo a Sánchez en su primer minuto el líder del PP, que empezó a mil revoluciones. Fue la primera vez de las muchas en que lo llamó indecente.

Sánchez no entró al trapo. Al contrario, su primer minuto estuvo en su mayoría dedicado a la autocrítica. “Mi Gobierno no ha sido perfecto”, afirmó el líder socialista, que admitió que había “confiado en gente que no debía” y que no había arreglado el problema de la vivienda. ¿Sobre su hermano, sobre su esposa, sobre Puigdemont? Ni una palabra.

03:44 Sánchez y Feijóo sobre vivienda con Maricarmen presente Un grupo de personas sigue el debate entre Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo. Foto: ÁLVARO GARCÍA

En el bloque de vivienda, Feijóo volvió a demostrar que tenía más ganas de guerra que Sánchez. Mencionó —sin estar relacionado con la vivienda— a Jésica, la “amiga” del encarcelado José Luis Ábalos. El socialista siguió sin entrar al trapo. Ese modo zen iba a ser su tónica de la noche. Se centró en defender su gestión de vivienda, reprochando al líder del PP que no aplicase la ley estatal y no aceptase que el mercado necesita una “regulación”. Sin hacer sangre. Es más, se mostraba “medio de acuerdo” con Feijóo, al que le concedió que había que construir más. Pero el candidato del PP no iba por ese camino. Interrumpía a Sánchez y le reprochaba que no hubiera hecho todo lo que decía que había que hacer en sus ocho años, negándole cualquier mérito. Al final, Sánchez sí saltó.

—Mucho trabajo le va a dar a los verificadores —soltó el presidente, una manera elegante de decir que Feijóo estaba incurriendo en falsedades.

Quedaron claras dos posiciones sobre vivienda. Sánchez se centra en la necesidad de “regulación”. Feijóo, en lo contrario. Los dos coincidieron en que hay que construir más. En cuanto a actitud, el candidato popular seguía mucho más beligerante. Y lo estaría toda la noche.

Interrupciones una y otra vez

La economía es un tema en el que el Gobierno se siente cómodo, encadenando récords de empleo y revalidando año tras año su condición de líder en crecimiento de la UE. Feijóo no hizo tampoco ahí la menor concesión. “Precios, impuestos y corrupción”, resumió la situación Feijóo, que recalcó que mientras la “bolsa de la compra” ha subido un 43%, los salarios no lo habían hecho tanto. “Ha sableado a los españoles a impuestos” y “ha triturado la clase media” fueron dos de sus frases.

El guion se repetía. El contraste de tonos era llamativo. El de Sánchez era dos grados más bajo que el de Feijóo, al que no le recogía el guante. Era como si los dos fueran por caminos tan distintos que no llegaban ni a chocar, aunque las direcciones fueran las contrarias.

Sánchez se quejaba con aire paciente de las frecuentes interrupciones de Feijóo, a lo que este oponía que solo estaba intentando “dialogar”. No había acuerdo en nada. Si el candidato socialista destacaba que la UE había dado una “muy buena noticia” con la mejora de las previsiones de crecimiento, Feijóo replicaba que también José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero —al que le pilló la mayor recesión en un siglo— presumía de datos económicos. Casi en cada intervención, Feijóo hacía un cuestionamiento de la “decencia” y la “honestidad” del Gobierno y su jefe. Sánchez evitaba una y otra vez el choque. Sí salió a la ofensiva al presionar a Feijóo para que aclarase si iba a subir el salario mínimo. El candidato popular concedió que sí, pero que lo importante era “subir el salario medio” y rebajar impuestos, un ingrediente omnipresente en su discurso.

02:33 Sánchez y Feijóo se acusan mutuamente por los casos de corrupción Los candidatos del PSOE y el PP a las elecciones generales en el plató del debate en la Academia de Televisión. Foto: ÁLVARO GARCÍA

Afloró entonces por primera vez el nombre de Santiago Abascal, líder de Vox. Lo trajo a colación Sánchez, que le recordó a Feijóo que tanto su familia política como la de “su socio”, Abascal, se oponen a bajadas de impuestos a las grandes fortunas transnacionales. El candidato popular no respondió a la alusión al dirigente ultraderechista. Golpeó a Sánchez en uno de sus puntos débiles, al recordarle que no ha aprobado presupuestos en toda la legislatura. Y afirmó, en un discurso antiimpuestos de creciente peso en la derecha, que en el país “cada vez se paga más y se recibe menos”.

El candidato popular no concedía nada a Sánchez. Si este destacaba que la deuda pública había bajado en relación con el PIB, Feijóo afirmaba que en términos brutos había crecido. Una y otra vez, el líder del PP seguía interrumpiendo. Hasta tal punto lo hacía que se acabó quedando sin tiempo antes de acabar el bloque, como le tuvo que recordar la moderadora del debate, la periodista María Casado, presidenta de la Academia de la Televisión, institución organizadora.

Las pensiones y los bailes

Tras una pausa publicitaria, Sánchez cambió el paso y salió más a la ofensiva en el bloque de políticas sociales, acusando a Feijóo y a Abascal —segunda mención— de meter “miedo” sobre las pensiones, de recortar en sanidad, de estar dispuestos a elevar el gasto en defensa al 5% a costa de más erosión de los servicios públicos y de sembrar dudas sobre las cuentas españolas.

El líder del PP, que seguía interrumpiendo, mantuvo su registro. Incluso lo endureció. Aludió a las “prostitutas pagadas con dinero público” y afeó a Sánchez que, tras el funeral por las víctimas de Urda, se pusiera “a bailar” en un mitin. De nuevo, en vez de revolverse, Sánchez pidió perdón a las víctimas de los accidentes de Adamuz y Urda, “un dolor que me llevaré conmigo”, dijo.

—¿Y se pone a bailar a las 48 horas? —reaccionó Feijóo, que dejó pasar algunas de las preguntas que Sánchez le hizo sobre sus planes. Pero no sobre las pensiones. Ahí sí quiso dejar claro que no tenía intención de recortar. Él mismo dio el dato que lo explica: hay más de 9 millones de pensionistas. Y las generaciones mayores son las que menos se abstienen. Pese a la insistencia de Feijóo, Sánchez no quería dejar de hablar de pensiones y de posibles recortes si gobierna la derecha. Y le insistió en que Ester Muñoz, portavoz parlamentaria del PP, había dicho que el sistema “va a petar”.

“Dos rombos” por la corrupción

Si en cada bloque Feijóo mencionaba la corrupción, más aún —claro— en el dedicado a la corrupción. Incluso dijo que las televisiones deberían poner “dos rombos”, porque iba a hablar de las “guarradas” que hizo el Gobierno. Tras volver a hablar de “prostitutas”, un recurso frecuente de Feijóo —“montaban ustedes orgías en la pandemia”, dijo—, le soltó a Sánchez que “quizás deba responder ante los tribunales” en el futuro y lo acusó de haber adelantado las elecciones para huir de los escándalos.

El presidente volvió a pedir perdón, para después afirmar que no iba a “aceptar lecciones” del partido “más corrupto de España”. Cuando añadió que su Gobierno era “uno de los más limpios” de la historia democrática, Feijóo saltó:

—¿Qué me dice usted?

Otra vez, la misma dinámica. Ante los ataques de máxima contundencia de Feijóo, presentando a Sánchez como un indecente, el candidato socialista respondía con suavidad. “Ustedes han delinquido mucho, señor Sánchez”, le llegó a soltar Feijóo. Y tampoco ahí el presidente del Gobierno salió de su modo calmado. “Ay, señor Feijóo”, soltó en una ocasión con una risa. Estaba claro. Sánchez no iba a endurecer ni el tono ni el rostro, dijera lo que dijera su adversario. ¿Una prueba de que no quería ir al barro? No le mencionó la archiconocida foto con Marcial Dorado. Eso sí, lo acusó de “difamar” a su hermano. Y en varias ocasiones le dijo que no aceptaba “lecciones” del PP. “No más Ábalos, no más Santos Cerdán”, le replicó Feijóo.

Aborto y eutanasia

Tras el choque sobre corrupción, Sánchez acusó a Feijóo de querer recortar el derecho al aborto y derogar la ley de eutanasia, opción que el propio candidato del PP ha reconocido en público. El líder popular se esperaba el ataque por ese flanco, porque tenía una frase preparada: “La muerte digna hay que respetarla, pero la vida digna hay que promoverla”. ¿Entonces, la va a derogar?, insistió Sánchez. “Voy a modificarla”, respondió. Esta vez no habló de derogar. El candidato socialista, que también había reprochado a Feijóo que el PP y Vox vayan a quitar las ayudas al cine según su ideología en Castilla y León, quiso seguir percutiendo con el aborto y la eutanasia. Pero Feijóo se había quedado sin tiempo para responder. Así que Sánchez cerró sin réplica el intercambio. “Esto no es limpio”, protestaba el candidato del PP.

Álvaro García Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo se saludan en el plató de la Academia de Televisión antes del inicio del debate cara a cara. Manu Fernandez (AP) El plató, con los candidatos ya presentes, minutos antes del debate. ÁLVARO GARCÍA Sánchez y Feijóo charlan con el realizador del debate Jesús Lozano este jueves en los momentos previos al cara a cara. Juanjo Martín (EFE) Los dos candidatos entran en el plató acompañados de María Casado, presentadora del debate organizado por la Academia de TV. Álvaro García Alberto Núñez Feijóo, candidato del PP, llega al cara a cara este jueves en en la Academia de TV. Alvaro Garcia Pedro Sánchez, candidato del PSOE, llega al cara a cara este jueves en en la Academia de TV. Álvaro García

En política internacional, Sánchez reivindicó las posiciones de su Gobierno en Ucrania, Gaza e Irán, un “faro” —dijo— en contraste con la “internacional ultraderechista”. Si Donald Trump o Javier Milei no son “lo que queremos para el mundo, no los queramos” tampoco para España, dijo, equiparando a Feijóo con estos líderes extranjeros. Feijóo tenía claro de qué país quería hablar: Marruecos. Como en todos los demás bloques, fue a degüello contra Sánchez, del que sugirió que estaba al servicio del país vecino. “Echo de menos que usted diga que no depende de Rabat”, afirmó Feijóo, para quien en Ceuta se ha producido una “invasión”. También en inmigración el choque fue ruidoso, con Feijóo en unas posiciones y un vocabulario muy próximos a los de Vox. “Su gobierno es un chollo para las mafias”, dijo el candidato popular.

En el último minuto, el reservado a pedir el voto, Feijóo volvió a su leit motiv de la noche: poner la decencia de Sánchez en cuestión. “Yo no bailo en los mítines, pero tampoco robo, ni miento”, dijo en alusión a Sánchez. No fue sorprendente a esas alturas que este no le respondiera. El candidato del PSOE dedicó su minuto a pedir a la gente votar contra la derecha y sus “tecnooligarcas” para preservar un gobierno que es “ejemplo de dignidad en el mundo” y de “avance”. Frente al “quien pueda hacer que haga” de José María Aznar, Sánchez ofreció una alternativa: “Quien pueda votar, que vote”.

World.title: ¿Quién ha ganado el duelo? Los analistas de EL PAÍS dan por vencedor a Feijóo sobre Sánchez
World.content:
Máriam Martínez-Bascuñán: “La victoria de los dos rombos”

Un debate no se gana igual cuando se llega con ventaja, y solo hay que conservarla, que cuando hay que remontar. Por eso, lo ocurrido esta noche tiene que medirse con la vara que cada uno traía; Feijóo no se podía equivocar, y Sánchez tenía que conseguir que algo cambiara.



Medido así, Feijóo ha salido con lo que venía a buscar, aunque cuesta llamar victoria a una noche en la que quien aspira a gobernar, interrumpiendo con una agresividad que no necesitaba quien solo tiene que conservar su ventaja, ha advertido de que su propio relato necesitaba dos rombos, ha convertido el bloque de vivienda en un repaso de las relaciones de Ábalos y ha llevado al plató al portero de un puticlub. Mientras tanto, un Sánchez demasiado pendiente de no repetir 2023, encontraba tarde su debate y ofreció una versión más sobria de sí mismo sin acabar de resolver esa disyuntiva que recorre el espinazo de la política española: ¿Entrará la extrema derecha en La Moncloa por primera vez en nuestra democracia? “Señor Feijóo, déjeme terminar” fue su frase más repetida. No es un buen lema. Sánchez no quiso bajar al barro, pero quedan 10 días de barro, y solo después sabremos si la marea de ultraderecha anega o no La Moncloa.

World.title: Silencios, “guarradas” y “estoy dialogando”: cinco momentos televisivos del cara a cara entre Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo
World.content:
Era el único cara a cara de la campaña electoral de 2026. Pedro Sánchez, presidente y candidato del PSOE, contra Alberto Núñez Feijóo, candidato del PP. Fue también un debate que no dio grandes momentos televisivos. Todo estuvo contenido y manteniendo el tono en el que había salido a enfrentarse cada uno. No había debate porque no debatían.

No hubo papeles, objetos, adoquines, erratas como “es una afirmación ruiz” ni nada que diera espectacularidad como en debates de anteriores legislaturas, sino que fue un debate sobrio, sentados y alejado del tono de una campaña electoral que se está lidiando en otro tono, el de los videopodcast y los programas de entretenimiento. Sánchez, de hecho, ha debatido más estos días con Carlos Franganillo y con Susanna Griso, que con Núñez Feijóo este jueves. Estos fueron los momentos televisivos en los que sí destacó:

El silencio incómodo antes del debate

Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo, antes del 'Cara a cara'. Academia de Televisión (EFE)

El debate empezó en la previa al debate. Después del apretón de manos cordial y sin mirarse, las cámaras siguieron grabando a los candidatos, primero divagando por el plató y después sentados en sus sillas. Así permaneció 10 largos minutos, una eternidad de silencio para la televisión, mientras los analistas de las distintas cadenas trataban de fijarse en cada detalle. Sin mirarse ni un momento, Sánchez y Feijóo pasaban los apuntes en un incómodo plano cenital que dejaba ver la coronilla de ambos. La nota de prensa de la Academia de Televisión no explicaba que el piloto rojo siguiera grabando tanto tiempo. Era un hecho atípico, y los analistas y periodistas respondían en directo que los partidos tampoco lo esperaban. Unos 10 minutos antes de empezar el cara a cara, la señal paró. Alguien se dio cuenta de que en televisión, todo será mirado con lupa.

De “me permite terminar” a “estoy dialogando”





00:57 Feijóo y Sánchez se interrumpen mutuamente durante el debate: "No me dejas hablar" Vídeo: Academia de Televisión

“Estamos dialogando” de Feijóo y “no me deja hablar” de Sánchez fueron frases repetidas en el debate una y otra vez. Empezó en la vivienda con un Sánchez que aseguro que “estaba medio de acuerdo” con su rival" y cuando este le cortó por la construcción de viviendas, le apuntó: “Yo le he escuchado ¿Puedo continuar?" y “No puedo hablar”. Feijóo respondía una y otra vez que estaba tratando de dialogar mientras se soltaban datos el uno y el otro. “Mucho trabajo le va a dar a los verificadores”, decía Sánchez sin mover su expresión. “Sí, encantado”, le respondía con sarcasmo Feijóo.

“Los verificadores van a tener trabajo con usted”, respondía más tarde el del PP a los datos del contrario. Y así siguió en las medidas económicas, mientras Sánchez hablaba a los telespectadores mirando a la cámara, y Feijóo arremetía contra Sánchez directamente, arrojándose datos contrapuestos. Y otra vez: “No me deja terminar”, y “Estamos dialogando”. “Yo le he escuchado” y “Usted ha venido a dar su discurso”. Las estrategias de ambos estaban claras y no encajaban.

Sánchez y las disculpas

01:34 Sánchez pide perdón a las víctimas de Adamuz y Urda y Feijóo le acusa de "ponerse a bailar a las 48 horas" Vídeo: Academia de Televisión

En el bloque de política social, Alberto Núñez Feijóo afeó las víctimas de los accidentes de AVE de la legislatura y pidió al presidente unas disculpas, recordándole que no fue al funeral: “Aproveche para pedir disculpas”. Sánchez no dudó en hacerlo, en uno de los momentos más reales entre discursos ya construidos: “Me ha dicho que si pido perdón a las familias de las víctimas y por supuesto que lo pido. Es un dolor que me llevaré conmigo. Me hago cargo. Es lo que tiene que hacer un Gobierno: Estar con las víctimas y decir la verdad, algo que ustedes no han hecho en crisis como el metro de Valencia, con el Yak-42 ni la señora Ayuso con las muertes en la residencia en la pandemia”.

Los dos rombos y las “guarradas”

En el bloque sobre corrupción, Feijóo pidió que si hubiera niños viendo el debate que pusieran dos rombos en la pantalla: “Su Gobierno ha hecho todo tipo de guarradas”. El candidato del PP habló de que el PSOE “montaban orgías en la pandemia” y que contrataba “prostitutas con dinero público”. Sánchez dijo, sin embargo, que el suyo era “uno de los Gobiernos más limpios de la democracia” y comenzó a dar la lista también de todos los imputados del PP. Como en el resto del cara a cara, no hubo respuestas ni interpelaciones entre ellos, dijese lo que se dijese, nada rompía el bloque.

Los tacones de María Casado como ejemplo del cansancio electoral

00:42 María Casado termina el cara a cara con los zapatos sobre el atril Vídeo: Academia de Televisión

Una de las últimas imágenes vistas desde el plató del Cara a cara de La Academia de la Televisión fueron los tacones de la moderadora, María Casado (casi ausente en el debate), sobre la mesa tras la ardua jornada, mientras los equipos de asesores hablaban con los políticos. Era la mejor muestra del cansancio tras esta larga campaña electoral.

World.title: ‘El mal padre’: otra de tensiones entre un padre y sus hijos. Y está bien
World.content:
Es probable que se deba a la casualidad, pero hay épocas en el cine en las que se repiten obsesivamente los mismos temas. Y no se debe a eso tan lógico de que los modelos fueran apabullantes éxitos comerciales y se pretenda exprimir hasta la sobredosis las ubres de la venturosa vaca. No, se trata de un cine personal, ese al que denominan de autor y se supone que sus creadores se sienten absolutamente implicados con las problemáticas historias que cuentan. Que aborden el mismo tema es legítimo. Lo deseable sería que, aplicando distintos estilos, hicieran con esa temática películas poderosas, veraces, emocionantes.

Y por supuesto que el español Rodrigo Sorogoyen y el noruego Joachim Trier tuvieron derecho a poseer la misma idea argumental para rodar El ser querido y Valor sentimental, la de dos consagrados directores de cine que le ofrecen a sus hijas protagonizar sus próximas películas. Y que ambas señoras se hayan sentido abandonadas por ellos, que existan cuentas sentimentales que saldar. Pero vuelvo a encontrarme poco después con El mal padre, que continúa escarbando en los viejos traumas que pueden estallar en el reencuentro de hijos con ese padre que casi siempre estuvo ausente, por el que no se sintieron ni comprendidos ni ayudados.

Aquí los hijos son tres, fruto de su primer matrimonio. Y más tarde se añadirá su hermanastra, chica woke que vive en Estados Unidos y la única que no tiene atormentada su existencia. El padre reclama la presencia de sus cachorros, para pasar la Navidad en la vieja casa junto al mar y explicarles los motivos de su insólita petición. Está hecho polvo. La demencia, el alzhéimer y otros desastres físicos y mentales le van a convertir en un vegetal antes de que le llegue la ansiada muerte. Pero no les llora. Su lengua es viperina, cínica y procaz. También compleja y sincera. Tampoco les pide perdón porque ellos lo hayan sentido muy lejos. Es un intelectual empeñado en legar su obra maestra antes de largarse. Y confiesa lo que ha constituido el motor de su vida: “Leer, follar y viajar”. Ellos, por supuesto, no están incluidos en su amado mapa existencial.

Eduard Fernández, en 'El mal padre'. Cedida per Caramel / ACN

Y resulta que sus hijos, nada espectaculares al lado de su volcánico padre, están a la deriva interna, son grises, nada atractivos. Uno vive obsesionado e inseguro ante su próxima paternidad, su hermana destila permanente amargura sin pausas y sin prisas y no logra sus sueños de quedarse embarazada, y el otro, el más tierno, se dedica con infinito ánimo a un patético teatro experimental y siempre financiado por su padre. Y me ocurre con todas estas historias protagonizadas por padres egocéntricos e hijos sufridores que ninguno de sus personajes me cae bien. Independientemente de que tanto Javier Bardem en El ser querido como Eduard Fernández en El mal padre desempeñen un trabajo magnético, profundo, abarrotado de personalidad y talento en personajes con ciertas luces y bastantes sombras.

Más información Lea aquí las críticas de cine

Estoy interesado en El mal padre de principio a fin. Es una película con reconocible clima, bien escrita, interpretada y dirigida. El autor es Roberto Bueso. Mi problema es que me siento lejos de ellos. Hay una larga secuencia filmando una cena entre los hijos, el padre y los viejos amigos de este que está modélicamente descrita, pero en la que nadie me resulta simpático. Y alguno de ellos puede inspirarte piedad por la nube de frustración permanente que está instalada en su vida, pero no me gustaría nada compartir esa mesa. Hablo de gustos personales, no cinematográficos. Lo segundo funciona.

World.title: David Verdaguer, actor: “Un problema del periodismo y de la interpretación es que hay egos por medio todo el rato”
World.content:
De abril de 2015 a mayo de 2016, el antiguo corresponsal en Asia de El mundo, David Jiménez, dirigió el diario en el que había empezado como becario con 23 años. De aquella agridulce experiencia, de esos 13 meses que, según Jiménez, sufrió presiones del Gobierno de Mariano Rajoy, de las empresas y bancos más importantes del Ibex 35 y del mismo presidente de Unidad Editorial, la dueña del periódico, nació su novela El director, la base de un guion de Michel Gaztambide y Alejandro Hernández que Dani de la Orden ha llevado al cine en la película homónima. El director se estrena este viernes y David Verdaguer (Malgrat de Mar, Barcelona, 43 años) da vida a Jiménez.

Jiménez es el único personaje con su nombre real en pantalla. El resto, personas y empresas, se han rebautizado para no tener problemas legales, y del libro se ha eliminado bastante trama periodística “para centrar más el argumento en la parte de thriller”, apunta el mismo Verdaguer, quien confirma que varios medios de comunicación han rechazado hacer entrevistas al equipo o realizar críticas del filme. Algunos personajes, como el reportero de investigación al que da vida Guillermo Toledo, contaminado por las cloacas del Estado, levantan ampollas.

¿Hay tanto ego en la interpretación como en el periodismo? A priori, parecería que sí. Verdaguer ríe: “Para mí, son dos oficios muy bonitos, y coinciden en que son vocacionales. Y es cierto, un problema de ambas profesiones es que hay egos por medio todo el rato, ¿no? Eso es jodido, os entiendo muchísimo a los periodistas. Bueno, por eso y por más cosas”. De sí mismo, el ganador de dos premios Goya —como secundario por Estiu 1993 y como protagonista por Saben aquell— confiesa que tiene ego, “como cualquier ser humano”, aunque controlado.

David Verdaguer y Alberto San Juan, en 'El director'.

Siguiendo con los egos, el David Jiménez de cine, como el del libro, se maneja entre el afán naif de quien quiere cambiar a mejor el periódico en el que trabaja y su jactancia de que es el único llamado a semejante labor. Su alter ego subraya esa dicotomía: “Hay una parte del personaje muy idealista y otra de ‘yo podré cambiar lo que no ha cambiado nadie’. Está muy justificado: él era un reportero de guerra, que iba a su bola y daba las explicaciones justas. Y cuando se mete en la maquinaria de un gran periódico, la cosa cambia. Ahí me agarré para interpretar al personaje. Si yo tengo una compañía de teatro alternativo, las cosas más o menos funcionan, ¿no? Pero cuando entro a dirigir un teatro nacional, surgen las complicaciones. En todo caso, entiendo a su segundo, que le dice que no será el periódico soñado y que hay que hacer concesiones, pero que se puede hacer periodismo; entiendo al presidente de la editora [encarnado por Alberto San Juan]. Hay una parte más romántica e idealizada del oficio y otra más práctica. Es que yo también soy padre, y como actor he hecho películas increíbles cuando he podido elegir y he hecho truños. Y seguiré haciendo truños porque es un oficio. La vida es así”.

Asegura Verdaguer que hay todavía más similitudes entre el periodismo y la interpretación: “Sé que compartimos ansiedad, porque creo que los periodistas tenéis una noche de estreno cada día. Cada jornada es nueva para vosotros. Y cada día os jugáis, entre comillas, la carrera, como, también entre comillas, un actor cuando sube al escenario. Me parece una locura de estrés. Como actor, quieres que salga la mejor función, pero no siempre pasa. Como en el periodismo, ¿no?”. Aunque, al final, habrá una representación como habrá un periódico. “Eso es verdad. Y a la vez, una putada. Porque es lo que buscan los que ponen el dinero. Cada vez se ensaya menos, cada vez bajan más los presupuestos. Se escudan en el ‘Siempre sale’. Tócate los cojones”.

David Verdaguer, retratado en Barcelona. Carles Ribas

En El director, a Verdaguer, cuando aceptó el proyecto, le preocupó la verosimilitud. “Nos ayudó muchísimo Jiménez. Fue todos los días al rodaje. Nos corregía el lenguaje y las interacciones en la redacción para que lo rodado fuera real. Me ayudó y a la vez me acojonó. Aunque ya había vivido algo igual, porque en el rodaje de Saben aquell [el biopic de Eugenio, el humorista], el hijo de Eugenio estuvo presente todas las jornadas”. Eso sí, mientras que el actor imitó a Eugenio en el físico y en su gesto, en esta ocasión, Verdaguer aparece tal y como es. “Además, Dani quería que hablase rápido, porque David lo hace de manera muy lenta. Soy un actor más físico de lo que parece, nada del método, y por eso me agobio mucho con cambiar de aspecto. Y sé que parece una chorrada decir eso, pero me aprendo muy bien el texto. Lo necesito. Bueno, pues nunca había aprendido tanto diálogo como en El director. Ni lo había recitado tan rápido”.

Verdaguer no ha parado de trabajar, compaginando cine y teatro: sigue de gira “en bares de Barcelona” con el cabaret musical Dos señoros, junto al pianista Óscar Machancos. Ha dado vida a multitud de personajes, y alguno, como el de Uno para todos, similar al de El director: en aquel caso, un profesor sustituto llega a un pueblo que no conoce e intenta mejorar el día a día de su clase de sexto de primaria. “Ay, no me había dado cuenta. Es cierto, solo que allí tenía más pelo y era más guapo. Viendo mi carrera, he hecho muchos señores que llegan a sitios [risas]”.

David Verdaguer y Guillermo Toledo, en 'El director'.

La película llega a los cines en plena campaña electoral; este estreno se ha adelantado —estaba agendado para diciembre— para lanzarse este viernes a nueve días de las elecciones. “Aunque creo que todo el cine es político, porque toda película cuenta algo y tiene un punto de vista, en España hacemos pocos thrillers políticos, donde se hable sobre políticos, como El reino, donde entiendas y veas lo que ellos dicen, creen, en los que se retrate cómo presionan. Una pena”, reflexiona el actor.

Y cuestionado sobre la situación actual, se desboca: “Soy un pesimista vitalista. Es decir, yo a veces soy un poco pesimista, pero no doy por culo a nadie. El humor me ha salvado bastante. Quiero creer en la gente, no solo porque de eso depende el futuro de mi hija, que es mejor que yo en muchas cosas. Quiero pensar que la gente no es tonta del todo, que irá a votar. No sé cómo acabará esto. Es como si yo tengo goteras en casa, me cae la mierda en la cocina ¡y culpo al vecino de abajo! No lo puedo entender. Me parece tan mezquino como facilón. La mierda viene de otro lado. Me estoy metiendo en un jardín... En fin, confío en que los votantes tengan empatía”.

World.title: Students walk out against conscription and defence spending
World.content:
High school and university students nationwide will walk out of their classrooms at 1pm on Friday in a National Peace Protest against conscription and increasing defence spending, part of an international action day also taking place in 24 other countries including Germany, England and France.

“In our opinion, money is being taken away from care, education and housing to go to defence,” National Student Union (LSVb) chairwoman Evy Kras told RTL news. “At the same time, they want us to enlist. Young people feel betrayed and say: so far and no further. We want to be invested in us.”

She says these political spending choices are at the expense of young people, and that campaigns by the defence ministry paint an unrealistic picture of war. “They pretend it’s all very adventurous and flashy, but fighting in a war is not flashy.”

The LSVb, together with research and activist group Stop Wapenhandel, published a report earlier this week saying that defence spends €260 million annually on recruitment campaigns at schools and online. Meanwhile, they say, students have trouble making ends meet.

In at least 16 Dutch cities and dozens of schools, students will leave their classrooms at 1pm, fighting for an “affordable future”. In Amsterdam, students will gather at the Stopera, while in Utrecht, they’ll head to the Domplein and in Groningen to the Broerplein.

The Dutch group Stop the War Fever, which is organising the walkout, says on its website that the government refuses to work towards peace yet “pumps billions into weapons and war.”

Conscription

The group is asking to do away with conscription, move defence out of education and invest in the future of young people instead of weapons of war.

Currently, both men and women in the Netherlands aged between 17 and 45 must register for conscription, but since 1997, there has been no obligation to serve.

But the government is preparing legislation for a selective military conscription system that could be employed if it’s deemed necessary for security reasons.

Junior minister Derk Boswijk said in March that he couldn’t rule out the deployment of young people in the coming years.

“Many young people see it coming, now that the war is near at hand on the European continent,” student Camiel Breet told RTL News. “We want to fight against the cabinet’s plans.”

“This is the first post-Cold War generation that is both the generation of misfortune and grows up with the threat of war,” Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam professor of social change and conflict Jacquelien van Stekelenburg told RTL News. “A basic sense of peace is no longer self-evident for them.”

World.title: Tata Steel goes on trial accused of deliberate air pollution
World.content:
The criminal case against Tata Steel over alleged deliberate air pollution around its IJmuiden plant began at Amsterdam district court on Friday.

The public prosecution service (OM) accuses Tata Steel IJmuiden of intentionally and unlawfully releasing harmful substances into the air. The complainants say they suffer serious health problems and worry about local children, with soot accumulating in local playgrounds, broadcaster NOS reported. The public health institute RIVM has recorded above-average lung cancer rates in the area.

The case began in 2021, when lawyer Bénédicte Ficq filed a complaint on behalf of people living near the plant. Prosecutors opened an investigation the following year and announced in July that they would take the company to court. They are still considering whether individual managers can be held personally liable.

The case focuses on the plant’s coke-making ovens, where coal is heated at very high temperatures without oxygen to produce coke, a material used to make steel. If the coal is not heated for long enough, it remains partly unfinished (called raw coke) and can release harmful gases into the air and spread soot into the environment.

Tata says it is technically unavoidable that a batch is sometimes not heated for long enough. Prosecutors suspect the company accepts these incidents and deliberately does not report them. In July, Tata called the allegations “essentially unjust”.

Ficq told NOS it was “a tremendously important day” and said the emissions incidents were “foreseeable and avoidable”. She wants executives, including chairman Hans van den Berg, to be prosecuted as well.

€2bn subsidy at steak

The criminal case also affects a €2 billion state support package for Tata’s switch to greener steel. The cabinet said in July that it could pull out of the deal if the investigation raised “serious concerns”. According to NOS, talks have now been extended to March, and the trial is unlikely to be over by then.

World.title: Jetten “won’t be intimidated” by Russian threats and embassy hit
World.content:
Prime minister Rob Jetten has said he will not take “too seriously” a Russian warning that employees of Dutch arms maker Destinus could become legitimate military targets, and said the Netherlands would “not be intimidated” after its embassy in Kyiv was damaged in a Russian attack.

His comments came as Russian president Vladimir Putin vowed revenge for the Crimea bridge attack, in which Destinus says its missiles were used. On Thursday afternoon, the Dutch embassy was damaged during a Russian drone attack on Kyiv. Russia then launched a mass missile attack overnight, killing at least five people in Kyiv and Lviv, according to the Kyiv Independent.

No Dutch embassy staff were hurt and the damage caused to the building was likely indirect, Ukrainian air defence sources told broadcaster NOS. Nevertheless, foreign minister Tom Berendsen has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident.

“Further escalation”

The Russian embassy in the Netherlands released a statement on Thursday evening saying : “it is becoming increasingly difficult to regard the Netherlands as a mere bystander. Through its actions, The Hague is consistently deepening its involvement in the conflict, contributing to its prolongation and further escalation.”

This comes after the admission by Destinus that it was “proudly” involved in striking the Crimea bridge on Tuesday, and revelations in a subsequent investigation by the NRC that showed company personnel had allegedly been actively aiding drone fights on the battlefield with Russia, some of which appeared to be reckless.

The Russian embassy noted these details and pointed to civilian deaths caused by Ukrainian drones, and said that under international law, civilians who take a direct part in hostilities “become legitimate targets”. It also questioned whether the Dutch government was aware of the company’s activities, and demanded “clear explanations”.

The embassy’s claim that at least 40 staff went to Ukraine appears to misread the NRC report, which said it interviewed more than 40 people for the investigation.

❗️Important Statement by the 🇷🇺 Embassy of Russia in the Netherlands. Have 🇳🇱Dutch defense industry workers become combatants in Ukraine? Read the full text here:

https://t.co/uNtv0SQ070 https://t.co/Rbl4XQjUq6 — Russian Embassy in NL🇷🇺🇳🇱 (@rusembassynl) November 19, 2026

Jetten responds

Moscow is using the revelations to cover up its own setbacks in the war in Ukraine, Jetten said on Thursday evening during a summit of Ukraine’s allies in Berlin. “If they want to start down that road, we have plenty to say about it too,” he said, referring to Russia’s invasion and the many war crimes it is accused of.

Destinus chief executive Mikhail Kokorich, a former Russian national and Putin opponent, told NRC that staff had launched and operated test drones against Russian drones, but under the direction of Ukrainian soldiers. The company says it does not carry out military operations and only provides technical support under its contracts.

The defence ministry said that using a weapons system against a party to an armed conflict counts as direct participation in hostilities, but giving general instruction on how a system works does not. Civilians who take part directly lose their protection under the laws of war and can be prosecuted.

Defence minister Dilan Yeşilgöz declined to comment on the revelations. The Netherlands helps Ukraine in line with international humanitarian law, “and unfortunately we say nothing about anything else,” she told BNR at an arms fair in Rotterdam on Thursday. It is “much better” to test weapons in an exercise scenario than on a battlefield, she said.

MPs want answers

Defence experts told Nieuwsuur that Yeşilgöz should talk to the company and possibly order an inquiry into its role. That would include a June 2023 test near Kharkiv in which Destinus drones were aimed at targets near the Russian city of Voronezh. A drone hit a home in Voronezh that morning, injuring three people, but NRC could not establish whether it was a Destinus drone.

MPs from coalition and opposition parties have raised concerns. D66’s Mpanzu Bamenga called the report “worrying”, PRO’s Wimar Bolhuis wants explanations about export licences and drone testing, and Volt’s Laurens Dassen has called for an investigation. A senator from PvdD has also tabled written questions, according to NRC.

Foreign trade minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma said Dutch export controls are “very careful”, but that the cabinet has not yet been able to verify everything in the report.

The Dutch state is one of Destinus’ biggest customers. In June the cabinet agreed to pay €250 million for 700 Ruta cruise missiles for Ukraine, a package it first described as drones. After the Crimean bridge strike, which Destinus posted pictures of and said its Ruta missiles were used, Putin ruled out a partial ceasefire and promised a “much more painful” response.

World.title: Over 20,000 new homes completed, government still behind target
World.content:
Builders completed 18,100 new homes in the Netherlands between July and September, about 3,200 more than in the same period last year, according to figures from national statistics office CBS.

Completions were also up 1,600 compared to the second quarter. Counting conversions of offices and other buildings into homes, as well as demolitions and homes lost to renovation, the housing stock grew by 20,300 homes.

The number of building permits issued for new homes dropped sharply to 16,600, after an unusually high 48,900 in the second quarter. Almost 30,000 of those were issued in June alone. CBS said this was because local authorities rushed to register permits before new rules on grid congestion came into force.

As a result, the number of homes that have permits but have not yet been built fell by 1,400 to around 257,000. CBS said more homes have been given permits than have been built in recent years.

The value of permitted housing construction was €3 billion in the quarter, 19% lower than a year earlier.

Construction firms’ turnover rose 5.7% year on year, the third quarterly rise in a row. But 163 construction firms went bankrupt in the quarter, 30 more than in the previous three months.

The cabinet wants 100,000 homes to be added each year to tackle the housing shortage. That works out at 25,000 a quarter, around 5,000 more than were added between July and September.

World.title: Dutch embassy hit in Kyiv as Putin vows Crimea bridge revenge
World.content:
The Dutch embassy in Kyiv was hit during drone strikes on Thursday afternoon, damaging the building and surrounding area, though no one was reported harmed. Shortly thereafter, Russian president Putin pledged to respond to recent attacks on the Crimean bridge, which the Netherlands was involved in.

“Fortunately our colleagues are unharmed, though there is minor damage to the building,” Dutch foreign minister Tom Berendsen said. He said the ministry was looking into exactly what had happened and that its priority now was the wellbeing of its staff.

The Kyiv Independent reported that the projectile was a Russian drone which crashed close to the embassy, damaging cars and a security post and shattering windows in the building, during an hours-long attack on the capital. The site said it was not clear whether the drone had been aimed at the area around the embassy or had been shot down.

Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said Russian attacks on Kyiv had once again damaged a diplomatic mission, broadcaster NOS reported. Ukrainian media also reported Russian drone attacks throughout the day, with air raid sirens sounding several times in the capital.

Crimean bridge attack

The strike comes two days after a Ukrainian attack on the Kerch bridge to Crimea, which Dutch arms maker Destinus publicly said it had been involved in. Destinus said seven of its Ruta missiles had hit the bridge and that it was “proud to support the Ukrainian army”.

On Wednesday, Russia’s embassy in The Hague said Moscow had been informed of Dutch involvement and asked whether The Hague was “openly taking part in the conflict”.

Berendsen told MPs that Russian embassies were being used to spread the Kremlin’s narrative. “They want to drive a wedge between us, so we have to see it through that lens,” he said.

In April, Russia’s defence ministry put a Destinus factory on a list of potential targets, which former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev said should be taken “literally”, NOS and other outlets reported.

Staff in Ukraine

On Thursday morning, NRC reported that Destinus employees had personally shot down Russian drones in Ukraine and helped the Ukrainian army launch attacks towards Russia.

The defence ministry told the paper that using a weapon system against a party in an armed conflict counts as direct participation in hostilities.

Destinus denies carrying out military operations and says it only provided technical support. Defence minister Dilan Yeşilgöz has declined to comment on NRC’s findings.

Experts told NOS that by going public, Destinus could increase the risk of Russian sabotage or cyberattacks against it. “We know that Russia has gone after companies like this in Europe,” missile expert Fabian Hoffmann said. Defence analyst Patrick Bolder said the company was already on a Russian list of targets “and would not easily come off it”.

World.title: Prostate cancer surgeries improving: fewer men left incontinent
World.content:
The share of men who end up incontinent after having a prostate tumour removed has roughly halved over the past few years, broadcaster NOS reports.

Until 2020, about 30% of patients in the Netherlands who got the operation were left incontinent afterwards. Between 2022 and 2024 that fell to 14%, according to insurers’ data analysed by the quality registry Dutch Prostate Audit.

Prostate cancer is the most common cancer among men in the Netherlands. Just over 16,000 men were diagnosed with it last year, and it killed 3,334 in 2024, according to CBS figures.

There has been a huge gap in outcomes between the hospitals that do the surgeries, which has also narrowed a lot in recent years.

A PhD study looking at operations between 2016 to 2020 found that one hospital had a 19% rate of causing incontinence by the operation and another 85%. Now the differences go from about 10% to 25% at most.

“That was hard to face, and it forced urologists in the Netherlands to work together more on improving things,” Rik Somford, a urologist at the Canisius-Wilhelmina hospital in Nijmegen who chairs the working group behind the push, told NOS.

Patients still can’t see how individual hospitals perform, and people want more transparency. Next year hospitals will start publishing some results, including complications within 90 days, whether the cancer was fully removed and whether patients are still incontinent a year later.

World.title: UN court in The Hague rules Myanmar committed genocide
World.content:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority. It is the first time the UN’s highest court has found a state responsible for committing genocide.

Reading the judgment at the Peace Palace, court president Yuji Iwasawa said the court was “fully convinced” that Myanmar’s security forces had acted with the intent to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya population during a military crackdown in 2017.

The court found that soldiers killed thousands of Rohingya civilians (around 10,000, according to the evidence), committed widespread sexual violence and violence against children, and attacked people as they fled to neighbouring Bangladesh. More than 730,000 Rohingya crossed the border.

The case was brought in 2019 by The Gambia, with the backing of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Netherlands and Canada said in 2020 that they would intervene in support.

Myanmar has always denied genocide. It says the operation targeted Rohingya militants who had attacked police posts.

The ICJ settles disputes between states and is separate from the International Criminal Court (ICC), which is also in The Hague and prosecutes individuals. Its rulings are final and cannot be appealed, but the court has no way of enforcing them.

The ruling could also affect South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, which is still before the court, the Volkskrant reported. The judges said other motives, such as fighting an insurgency, do not rule out genocidal intent. But they kept the bar high: genocide has to be the only reasonable conclusion from the evidence as a whole.

World.title: 1,100 new poplars to save historic tree-lined Maas riverbanks
World.content:
Some 1,100 new poplars are being planted along the river Maas to preserve the rows of trees that have lined both banks for almost a century, broadcaster NOS reported.

The trees, which stand 110 metres apart between Boxmeer and Geertruidenberg, were once used by skippers to navigate river. They are known as beacon trees (bakenbomen) and have become a defining part of the river landscape.

Many of the original trees are reaching the end of their lives, and for years dead trees were not replaced. Only 700 are left. The replanting will bring the total to 1,800 over the coming years.

The national government, the provinces of Noord Brabant, Gelderland, and Limburg, and 14 local authorities along the river are putting €4.6 million into the project.

They signed the agreement on national tree day (Boomfeestdag) and have committed to paying for maintenance for the next 100 years. North Brabant will coordinate the work. A network of volunteers and civic groups is also involved.

The new trees are black poplars, which the provinces describe as native to the Maas valley and good for biodiversity and nature restoration.

Two Russian missiles and what is likely to have been a jet-powered drone struck Poland last night during large-scale attacks on Ukraine, the defence minister has confirmed. On Friday morning, an image published by Polish media outlet Wirtualna Polska showed a crater in the ground with a fire burning in the middle of it. The website reported that the object landed in a field in the village of Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland, around 60 kilometres from the Ukrainian border. It struck a few hundred metres from a building, but no injuries were reported. 🔴Tu spadł niezidentyfikowany obiekt. Mamy zdjęcie Niezidentyfikowany obiekt spadł w piątek rano na pole w miejscowości Nowy Lipowiec w powiecie biłgorajskim. Stało się to kilkaset metrów od zabudowań. Nikomu nic się nie stało. Mamy zdjęcie z tego miejsca… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) November 20, 2026 At a press conference later on Friday morning, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the object that had struck in Nowy Lipowiec was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile (the same type as one that entered Polish airspace and exploded in eastern Poland in July this year). The defence minister also revealed that another missile had fallen in the town of Rudnik nad Sanem and what is likely to be a jet-powered drone had struck in the village of Mołodycz. Both of those locations are also in southeastern Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border. He added that there were no reports of injuries or any damage to critical infrastructure as a result of the incidents in Poland, which he said had taken place during “one of the largest Russian attacks on Ukraine since the beginning of the full-scale war”. Kosiniak-Kamysz also suggested that the fact that these incidents had taken place now was “no coincidence in my opinion”, given that military exercises of the Coalition of the Willing – a group of countries supporting Ukraine – are taking place in Poland not far from where the missiles and drone struck. Previously, during the early hours of Friday, operational command of Poland’s armed forces reported that they had “activated the necessary forces in response to Russia’s strikes on targets in Ukraine”. Such communiques have become common in recent months, as Poland has had to scramble its forces in response to Russia’s increasing strikes on targets in western Ukraine, including a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw that was hit by a jet-powered drone in September this year. Just before 8 a.m. local time, Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed that there had been a violation of Polish airspace and that the relevant emergency and security services were at the scene. Later on Friday morning, Tusk met with his ministers responsible for security as well as representatives of the armed forces and security services to discuss the situation. In recent months, the Polish government has warned of intelligence suggesting the likelihood of “provocations” by Russia, including airspace and border violations. In September this year, a Russian helicopter briefly crossed the border from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Earlier this month, Poland claimed to have foiled some kind of ground operation around the border with Kaliningrad. Polish Prime Minister @donaldtusk claims that "individuals with flashlights" were observed at the Russian border last night. "We very quickly mobilised the appropriate forces and resources there, and managed to prevent a provocation," he added https://t.co/kD5OmpNagf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2026 In September 2025, around 20 Russian drones crossed Poland’s eastern borders in an unprecedented violation that prompted Poland to trigger NATO’s Article 4. Back in November 2022, during the early stages of Russia’s war in Ukraine, two people died in Poland after a missile crossed the Ukrainian border and struck the ground. It later transpired to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile fired in response to Russian attacks.
