Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK, has fined Allegro, one of Europe’s largest e-commerce platforms, 55 million zloty (€12.3 million) for misleading consumers over a campaign that promised to plant trees in exchange for collecting parcels through its delivery service. The case is one of a series of investigations into so-called “greenwashing” launched by the authority against companies operating in Poland. UOKiK found that two of the Polish e-commerce group’s practices relating to the tree-planting initiative had infringed consumers’ interests. The first involved promotional claims suggesting that collecting 10 parcels through Allegro’s delivery service would result in a tree being planted. In practice, however, Allegro calculated the number of trees to be planted using forecasts prepared the previous year, rather than linking plantings to individual consumers’ parcel collections. This meant that decisions on the number of trees had already been made before customers collected their parcels. 🌳 Greenwashing ma swoją cenę! Blisko 55 mln zł kary dla Allegro – ekologiczne obietnice miały zachęcać do odbioru paczek, ale rzeczywistość nie była tak zielona. Milionów deklarowanych drzew nigdy nie posadzono. ❌ Ekościema nie może się opłacać 🔎https://t.co/yPQznKz0H1 pic.twitter.com/UDcWXWq3LI — UOKiK (@UOKiKgovPL) November 18, 2026 The second breach concerned the conditions attached to the campaign, which Allegro failed to communicate clearly to consumers. According to UOKiK, Allegro’s promotional messages could have led customers to believe that collecting 10 parcels through their delivery was sufficient to trigger tree planting. In fact, customers had to do it within a single calendar year and, from January 2024, submit a dedication for the tree within a specified period. Without a dedication, collecting the required number of parcels did not result in a tree being planted or assigned to the customer. UOKiK also found that the option to submit a dedication was unavailable for extended periods. Between March and November 2024, the feature was disabled for a total of 264 days, the watchdog said. The prolonged interruptions could have led customers to forget about the requirement or abandon their attempts to submit a dedication, meaning they would not receive the promised tree. UOKiK imposed a fine of 29.9 million zloty for the first practice and 24.9 million zloty for the second. Its decision can still be appealed in court by Allegro, which has not yet commented on the decision. “Green claims must be truthful, specific and verifiable; otherwise, they may mislead consumers and constitute an example of greenwashing,” said UOKiK president Tomasz Chróstny. “If a consumer hears, ‘collect 10 parcels, and we will plant a tree,’ they have the right to interpret that literally,” Chróstny said, adding that “several million [trees] – more than half of the total number claimed by Allegro – were never planted at all”. When announcing its decision, UOKiK noted that, according to a 2025 consumer survey conducted by the European Union, 43% of Poles said that the environmental impact of a product or service influenced their choices. The Allegro case forms part of a broader crackdown on suspected greenwashing by companies operating in Poland. Alongside Allegro, UOKiK has brought charges against delivery companies DHL, DPD and InPost, mobility firm Bolt, retailers Tchibo and Zara, and cosmetics firm L’Oréal Polska. Poland has signed memorandums with four of its neighbouring countries – Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania – pledging to strengthen regional cooperation on natural gas supplies and the security of infrastructure. The initiative comes amid Poland’s efforts to use its liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity and transmission links to establish itself as a regional energy hub, helping its neighbours, especially landlocked countries to the south, diversify supplies and reduce their reliance on Russia. The two memorandums of understanding were signed in Warsaw during a ministerial meeting at the Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation (P-TEC), co-organised by the US Department of Energy, Poland’s energy ministry and the Global Energy Centre run by the Atlantic Council. Rozpoczęliśmy 7. edycję Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation (P-TEC) – jednego z kluczowych forów współpracy energetycznej Stanów Zjednoczonych oraz krajów Europy Środkowo-Wschodniej. ⚡️ W Warszawie spotkali się przedstawiciele rządu Stanów Zjednoczonych, państw… pic.twitter.com/7t8kLluubF — GAZ-SYSTEM (@GAZ_SYSTEM) November 18, 2026 One of them, signed by Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic – who collectively form the Visegrad Group – establishes a framework for closer collaboration between their gas transmission system operators and more effective use of existing infrastructure. In late 2022, for example, a new gas interconnector opened between Poland and Slovakia. However, since then, the pipeline has seen very little use, as Bratislava has continued to rely on Russian gas supplies. Hungary has also remained reliant on Russian gas. By contrast, Poland quickly phased out its imports of Russian energy after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It now receives most of its gas via a pipeline that runs from Norway through Denmark and through LNG that arrives by sea, sourced mainly from the US and Qatar. From autumn 2027, the EU will ban its member states from importing Russian gas. In September, Hungary’s energy minister said that his country will be ready to meet that deadline. Slovakia, however, is challenging the import ban at the European Court of Justice. As part of the new memorandum signed this week, the four Visegrad countries will assess the impact of phasing out Russian supplies on regional energy security. The second memorandum, signed between Poland’s Gaz-System and Lithuania’s Amber Grid and KN Energies – which operate gas and LNG infrastructure in the two countries – focuses on strengthening the resilience and security of energy infrastructure around the Baltic Sea. It provides for closer coordination between the companies, including information-sharing on threats and incidents, joint risk assessments, exchanges of expertise on infrastructure protection and crisis response, and joint training sessions and exercises. “The LNG terminals in Poland and Lithuania serve as critical supply hubs for…Central and Eastern Europe, significantly enhancing energy security and bolstering regional resilience,” said Sławomir Hinc, CEO of Gaz-System. But that “security depends on the resilience of every link in the chain”, added his counterpart at Amber Grid, Nemunas Biknius. “This regional agreement will enable us to strengthen that chain in a structured and coordinated way.” Poland has declared its ambition to become a hub for supplying gas to the CEE region, including Ukraine, in particular by expanding imports of LNG from the United States. In addition to its existing LNG terminal in Świnoujście, which opened a decade ago, it is planning to build two further floating storage and regasification units that will be located in the Bay of Gdańsk. The first of those, under construction in South Korea, is due to open in 2028. Last year, a record amount of natural gas was traded in Poland, surpassing the levels seen before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the energy crisis that followed. Among those arrested were some who had used AI to produce content depicting the abuse of minors. Around 170 searches took place, with prosecutors seizing a total of 1,096 electronic devices. Initial analysis indicates that almost 2.8 million files containing child sex abuse material were contained on them, said the National Prosecutor’s Office, which oversaw the operation. Those detained are all men, ranging in age from 18 to 73, and include a teacher and a doctor. All were Polish citizens apart from one Ukrainian and one Belarusian. Prosecutors have already charged 94 of the suspects with producing, possessing and/or disseminating materials related to the sexual exploitation of minors. Thirty-one of the suspects have been placed in pretrial detention. “Among those detained were people who used AI technology to produce materials depicting the sexual abuse of minors,” wrote the National Prosecutor’s Office. One suspect is also accused of taking photographs and videos of himself and children naked at a public swimming pool. In May this year, prosecutors announced the results of a similar operation against child pornography, which, by coincidence, also resulted in 123 people being detained. World.title: Polish Supreme Court rejects government’s position on Constitutional Tribunal
World.content: Why are you seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s rule-of-law crisis has taken another twist, after the Supreme Court (SN) issued a resolution effectively opposing the government’s position towards another top court, the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), and endorsing that of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. The SN found that TK rulings are only valid if issued by judges the president has sworn in and that they take effect even if the government refuses to publish them. Nawrocki has refused to swear in five TK judges, while the government has refused to publish 85 previous TK rulings. However, the government’s justice minister argues that the new SN resolution is itself invalid because it was issued by judges who were appointed unlawfully. Połączone izby Sądu Najwyższego o wyrokach Trybunału Konstytucyjnego jako podstawie wznowienia postępowaniahttps://t.co/DzgL6aDTGK pic.twitter.com/GpiGbWMvNn — Sąd Najwyższy (@SN_RP_) November 18, 2026 On Wednesday, the SN issued a resolution in response to questions over the validity of rulings issued by the TK. It found, among other things, that a valid TK ruling can only be issued by a panel of judges who, after being elected to the tribunal by parliament, have “taken an oath before the president, that is, in his presence”. Those latter words relate to a key dispute that has arisen around the TK. The government’s majority in parliament has this year chosen eight new TK judges, who would now form the majority on the 15-seat tribunal. However, Nawrocki has refused to receive the oath of five of those judges, citing concerns over the method of their appointment or their qualifications. Those five judges have instead arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies before a notary and then forwarded their oaths to the presidential chancellery. They and the government argue that this meets the requirement for them to take up their seats. However, Nawrocki and the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former government, reject that position and say that the judges cannot take up their seats on the court until the president receives their oath in person. The Supreme Court has now effectively endorsed their stance. Meanwhile, the SN also addressed another contentious issue. Since March 2024, the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – has refused to publish any of the 85 TK rulings issued in that time. That is because, under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, three judges were unlawfully appointed to the TK. The current government argues that TK rulings only take force when published in the official Journal of Laws. Indeed, so did the former PiS government when, in 2016, it refused to publish TK rulings that contradicted its judicial policies. However, the SN has now deemed that valid TK rulings enter force even if not published. “In a situation where the body responsible for publishing TK rulings fails to fulfil this obligation…these abuses by the executive power cannot affect the universally binding force of TK rulings,” said SN judge Aleksander Stępkowski, quoted by the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna daily. However, the validity of the SN’s resolution is itself contested as it was issued by judges whose own status is questioned. That is because they were appointed to the court through the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS) after it was overhauled by PiS in a manner that brought it under political control and rendered it invalid, according to Polish and European court rulings. The current government has generally rejected decisions issued by such “neo-judges”, as it calls them. And that position was reiterated on Thursday by justice minister Waldemar Żurek, who wrote that “the neo-judges in the Supreme Court have adopted a so-called resolution”. “Any decision issued with the participation of even one person appointed through the politicised National Council of the Judiciary after 2017 is a non-existent judgement,” he added. Neosędziowie w Sądzie Najwyższym podjęli nibyuchwałę połączonych trzech izb (III CZP 41/26), uznając, że nieopublikowane rozstrzygnięcia Trybunału Konstytucyjnego mają moc powszechnie obowiązującą, a za wyrok TK można uznać tylko taki wydany przez osoby, które złożyły ślubowanie… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 18, 2026 The SN’s resolution comes as the TK itself is embroiled in a crisis. At the end of October, the eight new TK judges chosen by parliament this year took control of the tribunal and announced that its chief justice, Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties. Święczkowski, supported by Nawrocki and the SN’s chief justice, Zbigniew Kapiński (also a “neo-judge”), has rejected that move as an illegal “coup d’état” and claims he is still in charge of the tribunal. However, police have prevented him from entering the building. On Wednesday, just as the SN was issuing its resolution, the eight government-backed TK judges announced that they had lifted Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution at the request of Żurek. World.title: Disputed Polish constitutional court announces chief justice stripped of immunity to face charges
World.content: Why are you seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government-backed judges who recently took control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) have announced that the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has been stripped of legal immunity in order to face criminal charges. Święczkowski, who was appointed to the TK under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, has condemned their takeover as an illegal “coup d’état” and says that any decisions issued by them have no validity. In a further development, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) announced yesterday that it has rejected a request by Święczkowski for an emergency order to suspend all proceedings against him at the TK. Trybunał Konstytucyjny zdecydował. Prokuratura może teraz stawiać zarzuty. Nikt nie stoi ponad prawem.https://t.co/trIEqa8Mh1 — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 18, 2026 A statement published on Wednesday evening on the tribunal’s website announced that motions from the prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, to strip Swięczkowski and the deputy head of the court, Bartłomiej Sochański, of immunity had been approved. The decision was made by the group of eight judges who dramatically took control of the TK on 30 October as riot police held back protesters outside. All of them were chosen by the government’s parliamentary majority this year, but opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of them. After taking over the tribunal, they declared that Święczkowski and Sochański had been suspended for their failure to properly fulfil their duties. They also launched internal disciplinary proceedings against the pair, with hearings in those cases due to take place later this week. Separately, Żurek, who serves as justice minister in addition to being prosecutor general, filed multiple requests to the TK for Święczkowski and Sochański to be stripped of their immunity in order to face criminal charges. Most of those were approved today. Among the alleged crimes prosecutors wish to charge Święczkowski with are abuse of power and failure to fulfil duties for his refusal to allow five judges chosen by parliament this year to take up their seats on the court. Sochański is accused of the same offences. Święczkowski has argued that he cannot admit those judges because, under Polish law, they are obliged to first swear an “oath before the president” and have not done so. Prosecutors also allege that Święczkowski used violence against those five judges to physically prevent them from entering the judges’ chambers at the TK. The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary” But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026 Further allegations against Święczkowski relate to his time serving as national prosecutor under the former PiS government. Prosecutors say that he abused his powers by making unauthorised use of material gathered from surveillance. They also accuse him of abusing his power by “maliciously” reassigning prosecutors to different locations as a form of punishment, despite there being no legal basis for doing so. However, although the TK today approved the lifting of Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunities, it did not consent to them being arrested and held in pretrial detention. It also rejected two additional requests from Żurek to lift Święczkowski’s immunity for other alleged crimes. The TK found the motions contained “formal deficiencies”. Skierowałem do Trybunału Konstytucyjnego kolejny, szósty już wniosek o uchylenie immunitetu Bogdanowi Święczkowskiemu, dołączając go do pięciu wniosków przekazanych w piątek. Dzisiejsza sprawa dotyczy zakupu systemu szpiegowskiego Hermes w czasie, gdy pełnił funkcję Prokuratora… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026 Święczkowski immediately rejected today’s decisions, saying that they had no legal validity. He describes the eight judges who have taken control as “usurpers”. However, on Tuesday, Święczkowski suffered another setback in his struggle to retain control over the TK after the European Court of Human Rights announced that it had rejected a request from him and Sochański for an interim measure ordering that all proceedings against them be suspended. The ECHR found that “the applicants had failed to demonstrate an imminent risk of irreparable harm to the core of their rights”. The decision stands in contrast to one made in May this year by the ECHR, when it ordered that the five judges Nawrocki has refused to swear in be admitted to the TK. Święczkowski ignored that order, arguing that the ECHR did not have the authority to issue it. European Court rejects request for interim measure in case concerning Constitutional Court of Poland. 🔗 https://t.co/I15bGXeeKF — ECHR CEDH (@ECHR_CEDH) November 17, 2026 Święczkowski has received backing from some other Polish institutions. President Nawrocki continues to recognise Święczkowski as the chief justice of the TK and has condemned the government-backed judges’ takeover of the court. The chief justice of the Supreme Court (a separate body from the TK), Zbigniew Kapiński, has also sided with Święczkowski and Nawrocki. Speaking to broadcaster RMF on Wednesday morning, Kapiński said that any decisions made by the eight judges who have taken over the TK “have no legal force”. Kapiński’s own status has also been subject to dispute. He was appointed to the Supreme Court under the PiS government through a judicial body overhauled in a manner that rendered it illegitimate, according to various European and Polish court rulings. On Monday, the central bank, whose governor is a longstanding associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, announced that it was suspending all outgoing payments from the TK’s bank accounts due to uncertainty over who holds legitimate control over the court. Poland’s central bank has frozen outgoing transfers from the bank accounts of the Constitutional Tribunal, citing conflicting claims over who has the authority to manage the court following a takeover by a group of judges backed by the government https://t.co/ZYkzoneojO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 17, 2026 The recent dramatic events at the TK follow a decade-long crisis around the Polish judiciary, triggered by the contested judicial reforms and appointments made by the former PiS government and PiS-aligned former President Andrzej Duda. The current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk that came to power in 2023 – has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK due to the presence of unlawfully appointed judges. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. The eight judges it has appointed now have a majority on the 15-person court, although five of them have not been sworn in by Nawrocki. The remaining seven judges, including Święczkowski and Sochański, were appointed when PiS was in power. World.title: New Kraków mayor withdraws from metro plans and seeks to shrink clean transport zone
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The administration of Kraków’s new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, has signalled that the city will withdraw from plans to build a metro system and will seek to shrink the size of the recently introduced Clean Transport Zone, which imposes additional costs on older, more polluting cars. “We won’t, like the previous administrations, make any promises regarding the metro,” deputy mayor Karol Wałachowski told local news service LoveKrakow. “We’re withdrawing from this project until central [government] or European funding becomes available.” The draft municipal budget for next year presented by Gibała allocates no funds towards preparation work for the metro, notes LoveKrakow. Instead, the new administration wants to establish seven new tram routes. For decades, Kraków has discussed the possibility of building a metro system, which would be just the second in Poland after Warsaw’s. In 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the idea. However, only in 2024 did the then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, who came to office that year, announce plans to build a metro. The city unveiled the planned route in 2025 and then, in July this year, it launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. Kraków has announced a €43 million tender for pre-design work on a planned new metro system, which would be only the second in Poland. The plans include a feasibility study, environmental report and assessment of the impact on existing buildings https://t.co/mB24RcVY96 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 But the idea now looks set to be abandoned after Miszalski was dismissed in a recall referendum earlier this year and Gibała was elected last month to replace him. While Gibała has often said that he would, in theory, like Kraków to have a metro system akin to Warsaw’s, he has argued that it would be impossible to build without significant funds from the European Union or Polish government. During this year’s election campaign, Gibała told news service Wirtualna Polska that he wanted to “honestly tell Kraków residents that, regardless of whether [Monika] Piątkowska [his opponent] or I win, there won’t be a metro anytime soon. We won’t build it without government funding”. Gibała said that, if elected, he would ask the government for a written guarantee of funding. “In my opinion, they won’t [give one], and the metro issue will die. I won’t spend millions more zloty on more expert teams and analyses [to prepare for the metro].” The issue has become tied up in national politics. Gibała is an independent while Piątkowska, his defeated rival, was from Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO) party. LoveKrakow reports, based on sources, that, if Tusk loses power at next year’s parliamentary elections, a new national government may be more willing to provide funds for the metro project. In one of his first announcements since being elected, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of the annual LGBT+ equality march. He argues that the event has become too "partisan" https://t.co/SS2EbRy6Ob — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 This week’s announcement of withdrawal from the metro plans was criticised by one of Miszalski’s former deputy mayors, Stanisław Mazur, who told Radio Kraków that the project should have been seen as “an investment that would significantly support the development of Kraków’s economy”. Two former rectors of Kraków’s AGH University, Antoni Tajduś and Tadeusz Słomka, also told LoveKrakow that it was vital to continue with the preparatory work for the metro system because otherwise, if funding does become available, the city would not be ready to implement the project. Separately, Gibała’s new administration has also presented draft plans to reduce the size of Kraków’s Clean Transport Zone, which was introduced at the start of this year and levies additional costs on drivers of old, more polluting cars. The project has long caused controversy. It was initially meant to go into force in 2024, but was blocked by a court ruling. There have also been legal challenges to the measures finally introduced this year. Many local politicians and officials have argued that the zone unfairly burdens drivers from outside Kraków who need to enter the city, in particular people with lower incomes, who are more likely to drive older cars and are hit harder by the new costs. A court has rejected an attempt to overturn the Clean Transport Zone that was introduced at the start of this year in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, and which places restrictions on driving older, more polluting cars https://t.co/NoAKsDgUus — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2026 During his election campaign, Gibała said that he wanted to reduce the size of the Clean Transport Zone, so that it covered only the city centre rather than the whole city. He also pledged to put any final decision about the zone to a public referendum. This week, another of his deputy mayors, Jan Hoffman, confirmed that city hall had presented draft plans to reduce the size of the zone. However, he noted that any change would have to be approved by the city council and also suggested that any final decision should be made in a referendum. Those plans were criticised by Kraków Smog Alarm, an NGO that fights for cleaner air. They said that reducing the scope of the Clean Transport Zone would harm residents’ health and result in tens of millions of zloty in fees being lost to the city budget. World.title: Polish government seeks to introduce maximum gas prices for consumers
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s government has announced plans to introduce a maximum price for natural gas to protect households from the continued impact of the US and Israel’s attacks on Iran earlier this year. The measure would be funded by a new special levy on certain energy companies. To enter into force, the bill must still be approved by parliament, where the government has a majority, and signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record amount of legislation. Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk noted that gas prices have been at elevated levels due to the ongoing crisis around the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East, which is normally a major conduit for both oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG). Tusk pointed out that the European gas benchmark price recently surpassed €100 per megawatt-hour (MWh), which was its highest level in four years. The figure has since fallen to around €85/MWh, though that is still more than double the level in January and February, before the US and Israel attacked Iran. Such costs are “unacceptable for any Polish family”, said the prime minister. “We can’t allow people to suffer because of decisions made abroad… about war in the Middle East. We don’t want Polish families to pay for it.” The government therefore wants to introduce a maximum price of 197.29 zloty (€44.15) per MWh (which is the level of the current state-regulated gas tariff) for the whole of 2027. The energy ministry estimates that this will save households that use gas for heating up to 1,863 zloty over the year. As well as individual households and housing cooperatives, the maximum price will also apply to entities providing important public services, such as schools, nurseries, hospitals and shelters. Companies selling gas to such consumers will then receive compensation from the state to cover the difference if the maximum price is below what the level of gas tariffs would normally be at that time. The costs of this compensation “will be largely covered by a new monthly gas levy” charged to “energy companies holding licences to trade natural gas with foreign countries and selling high-methane natural gas on the domestic market”, says the government. The levy would amount to 10% of net revenues from domestic sales of high-methane natural gas in 2027. Companies holding capacity rights amounting to less than 10% of the total capacity at entry points to Poland’s gas-transmission system would be exempt. While the legislation is unlikely to face obstacles in parliament, it remains unknown what Nawrocki’s position will be. The president has previously pushed for the government to lower energy prices. However, he also blocked a windfall tax on energy companies to subsidise fuel-price cuts, before eventually relenting. President @NawrockiKn has backed down and signed into law the government's proposed windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits, which he had previously blocked. In response, the government has reintroduced measures to lower prices at petrol stations https://t.co/icGEST8NAo — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 Earlier this year, analysis by Allianz, the world’s largest insurance company, found that Poland was among a group of 11 countries “most at risk” from a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Poland has become a growing consumer of gas in recent years. As the country has moved away from its traditional reliance on coal, gas has increasingly been used for both electricity generation and home heating. Last year, gas accounted for a record 13.2% of electricity production, up from just 2.7% in 2015. The latest figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that in 2024 almost 21% of households use gas for heating, up from 10% in 2015. Gas consumption reached its highest ever level in Poland this week – breaking a record set in 2021 – amid freezing winter temperatures and as the fuel continues to play a bigger role in the country's energy mix https://t.co/2wEWLPCV9l — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 10, 2026 The majority of gas consumed in Poland is imported – around 82% last year, according to the energy ministry. Around 43% of imports arrive in the form of LNG, delivered to a terminal at Świnoujście on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast. Last year, most of that LNG came from the United States (accounting for 30.7% of Poland’s total gas imports) and Qatar (11.2%). However, LNG exports from Qatar have been severely impacted by the difficulties around the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this month, Polish state energy giant Orlen exercised its right to terminate one of its two long-term LNG contracts with QatarEnergy, citing “the ongoing force majeure”. However, Orlen insisted that the decision “does not affect the security of gas supplies”. Most of Poland’s remaining gas imports come via the Baltic Pipe, which opened in 2022 and brings gas from Norway via Denmark. World.title: Michelin Guide Adds Four New Starred Restaurants in the Czech Republic
World.content:
The Michelin Guide has expanded its selection in the Czech Republic, awarding stars to four new restaurants.

The latest edition brings the country’s total to 13 Michelin-starred establishments, while 27 restaurants have received the Bib Gourmand distinction for good food at reasonable prices.

The new selection was announced at a gala ceremony, marking the second year of the Michelin Guide’s official presence in the Czech Republic.



All nine restaurants recognised in the inaugural edition have retained their distinctions, while four newcomers have joined the list.

Among the new one-star recipients is Zlatá Praha, located on the rooftop of the Fairmont Golden Prague hotel. The restaurant continues the tradition of the former establishment at the same location, previously housed in the InterContinental Hotel.

Another newcomer is Reason, a restaurant on the top floor of the Masaryčka building in central Prague. Designed by Zaha Hadid Architects and developed by Penta, the building offers panoramic views of the city. The restaurant is led by chef Jan Horák.

The third new addition is Taro, a contemporary Vietnamese restaurant inside the Dunaj Palace on Národní třída. The restaurant was founded by brothers Khanh Ta and Giang Ta.

The fourth newcomer is Salabka, a fine-dining restaurant in Prague’s Troja district. The establishment combines a restaurant with its own winery, distillery and accommodation. Its kitchen is led by chef Petr Kunc.

Papilio retains its two Michelin stars

The Czech Republic’s only two-Michelin-star restaurant remains Papilio, led by chef Jan Knedla. Located in Vysoký Újezd, near Beroun, the restaurant focuses on seasonal ingredients sourced from local farms and a contemporary interpretation of Czech cuisine. Knedla’s cooking also draws on memories of his childhood.

Several other restaurants retained their one-star distinctions, including Field, led by Radek Kašpárek, and Entrée in Olomouc, run by Přemek Forejt, known to Czech television audiences from MasterChef.

The selection also includes Essens, located in Hlohovec in the Lednice-Valtice area and headed by chef Otto Vašák, as well as La Villa in Zlín.

Last year’s edition brought particular attention to restaurants outside Prague, a development that also surprised Michelin inspectors. In the capital, the previous selection included Field, Štangl, Levitate, La Degustation Bohême Bourgeoise and Casa De Carli.

A total of 27 Czech restaurants received the award this year, including 11 new additions.

World.title: GTA VI Launch Week Comes With Special Food Menus Across Prague
World.content:
With Grand Theft Auto VI arriving on November 19, Bolt Food has teamed up with Prague restaurants to offer exclusive gaming menus, discounts and a competition to win PlayStation 5 consoles and copies of the game.

After years of anticipation and two delays, Grand Theft Auto VI finally arrives on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S on Thursday, November 19. For many players, the launch is likely to mean long gaming sessions and late nights. In Prague, there will also be plenty of food options to go with them.



From November 9 to 22, Bolt Food is running a special Gaming Campaign, bringing together local restaurants that have created menus inspired by the new game. The selection includes burgers, pizzas, sushi, chicken dishes and larger sharing meals, available exclusively through the delivery platform.

The campaign also includes discounts on selected offers and a competition featuring PlayStation 5 consoles and copies of GTA VI.

Win a PlayStation 5 or GTA VI

Bolt Food is giving away three PlayStation 5 consoles and 36 copies of Grand Theft Auto VI as part of the campaign.

To enter, customers need to order one of the participating gaming menus or place an order worth at least CZK 350 from a participating restaurant. Each qualifying order automatically counts as one entry, with no additional registration required.

Some orders may also include surprise gifts from Niceboy.

The competition runs in Prague until November 22. Full terms and conditions are available through Bolt Food’s Czech Instagram account, @boltfood_cz.

What Prague Restaurants Are Offering

Several restaurants have put together special dishes and combinations for the campaign. Here are some of the options available through Bolt Food.

Burgers and Comfort Food

Hoxton Burgers – Chorizo Smash

The burger restaurant has prepared a special smash burger featuring chorizo.

Želva – Trevor Burger

A substantial combination of a 170-gram beef patty, double cheddar, bacon chutney, blue cheese, maple syrup, crispy onions, jalapeños and chipotle mayonnaise, finished with a poutine topping.

Master Burger – Sunrise Burger

Beef, cheddar, bacon and a fried egg make up this burger, which takes inspiration from a classic breakfast combination.

Amici – Gaming Pizza and Burger Menus

Customers can choose between special gaming-themed pizza and burger menus.

Pizza for Sharing

Three Prague pizzerias have also joined the campaign with exclusive combinations.

Davinci offers three options: Street Hustler, Five Star Chase and Million Dollar Slice.

Presto Italiano has created three pizzas named after GTA-inspired characters: Jason’s Pizza, with chicken, pepperoni, bacon and red onion; Lucia’s Pizza, featuring pepperoni, bacon, chilli and Parmesan; and Raul’s Pizza, with a cream base, chicken, bacon, Gorgonzola and garlic.

Caruso is serving a Gaming Pizza topped with ham, bacon, spicy salami, smoked scamorza and onion.

Sushi and Japanese Food

Sushi fans can choose from several campaign-specific options.

Doebikokota – Respect +

The combination includes Philadelphia Classic rolls, crispy chicken gyoza and Coca-Cola.

Aurum Sushi has introduced three gaming options: Hot Pursuit, The Big Score and Wanted.

Imperial Sushi is offering several dishes, including Geisha Roll, Salmon & Tuna Snack, Office Snack, Baked Chicken on Iceberg Roll and Baked Chicken Tamago Roll.

Hasu Sushi – Hasu Gaming Challenge Set**

The special 18-piece set includes salmon nigiri, salmon maki and Sunshine Roll.

Chicken and Wraps

For those looking for something easy to eat during a gaming session, two restaurants are offering chicken-based options.

Chickin has introduced the GTA Power Griller and GTA Quesadilla, both available in double-bacon versions.

Louisiana Chicken is serving the Six Stars Sandwich, featuring crispy chicken strips with bacon-chilli sauce, tomato and iceberg lettuce, as well as the Wanted Wrap, which combines chicken nuggets with the same sauce.

Wraps, Kebabs and Sharing Combos

Other participating restaurants have opted for larger combinations and meals designed for different group sizes.

Burrito Loco – Crunchy Wrap Gaming Menu

The menu includes a drink and a choice of churros with chocolate dip or chips and salsa.

Mahir Kebab offers three combinations: Solo Mission, Duo Heist and Full Crew Combo, with portions designed for one, two or three people.

Matoka – I’m The Gamer Set

A special menu created for the campaign.

Something for the End of the Night

For those looking for a more substantial meal or something sweet, two more restaurants have joined the line-up.

Lasagneria – Spicy Lasagna and Oreo Tiramisu Combo

The main course combines Italian salsiccia sausage, chilli, béchamel and Grana Padano. Dessert comes in the form of Oreo tiramisu with mascarpone cream and espresso.

Na Květnici – Jason Duval Menu

A special menu named after one of the two main characters in GTA VI.

How to Order

All campaign menus are available through the Bolt Food app. Customers can browse the participating restaurants, select their preferred dishes and order directly for delivery.

The Gaming Campaign runs until November 22, meaning the special menus will only be available for a limited period.

Whether you’re planning a gaming night with friends or simply looking for something different to order this week, Prague’s restaurant line-up has plenty of options.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 – Dates, Locations and Opening Hours
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas market season will begin on November 20, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru.

The main markets in the city centre will follow on November 28, when the Christmas tree in Old Town Square will also be illuminated for the first time.

Markets and Advent events will take place across the Czech capital, from the historic centre to neighbourhoods such as Vinohrady, Smíchov and Karlín. While some will close on Christmas Eve, others will remain open until January 6, 2027.



Prague Christmas Markets 2026 – Full Schedule

Náměstí Míru | Nov 20 – Dec 24 |

Náměstí Republiky | Nov 25 – Dec 24 |

Tylovo náměstí | Nov 26 – Dec 24 |

Anděl, Smíchov | Nov 27 – Dec 31 |

Mariánské náměstí | Nov 27 – Jan 6 |

Old Town | Nov 28 – Jan 6 |

Wenceslas Square | Nov 28 – Jan 6 |

Jiří z Poděbrad Square | Nov 28 – Dec 23 |

Karlínske náměstí | Dec 6 |

When Will the Christmas Tree in Prague Be Lit?

The Christmas tree in Old Town Square will be illuminated for the first time on Saturday, November 28, marking the opening of Prague’s main Christmas market.

According to organiser Taiko, the tree will be installed on November 23 and 24. This year’s Norway spruce comes from Šimonovice in the Liberec Region. It is approximately 60 years old, stands 23 metres tall and has a trunk circumference of more than two metres.

After the Christmas season, apprentices from Jarov Secondary Vocational School will process its wood into products for social organisations in Prague.

Where to Find the Main Christmas Markets

Old Town Square

November 28, 2026 – January 6, 2027

Daily, 10:00–22:00

Prague’s largest Christmas market will feature wooden stalls selling decorations, handicrafts, gifts and traditional seasonal food. The Christmas tree and its lighting ceremony will once again be the main attraction.

Wenceslas Square

November 28, 2026 – January 6, 2027

Daily, 10:00–22:00

Located a short walk from Old Town Square, the market will offer Christmas decorations, gifts, handicrafts and refreshments.

Náměstí Míru

November 20 – December 24, 2026

Daily, 10:00–20:00

The first Christmas market of the season will open around the Church of St Ludmila. Stalls will sell Advent wreaths, candles, decorations, sweets and seasonal refreshments.

Anděl

November 27 – December 31, 2026

Daily, 8:00–20:00

The market in Smíchov’s pedestrian zone will remain open until New Year’s Eve, making it one of the few locations operating after Christmas.

Other Christmas Events in Prague

Several additional events will take place during Advent.

– Bavarian-Czech Advent Market: November 27–29 at Chotek Palace, with regional food, nativity scenes, woodcarving demonstrations and workshops.

– Christmas Craft Markets: December 5–6 at Výstaviště Praha, featuring around 150 artisans. Admission is free.

– Lemarket: December 11–13 at Galerie Mánes, showcasing Czech designers, independent brands, fashion and handmade gifts.

– New Town Advent: December 13 at the New Town Hall, with craft stalls, workshops, performances and free admission.

World.title: Chinese National Circus to Make Czech Debut in February 2027
World.content:
The National Circus of China will perform in the Czech Republic for the first time in February 2027, bringing its production ZENSATION: Grandmasters of Balance to Prague, Brno and Ostrava.

The show combines traditional Chinese acrobatics with contemporary stage production, drawing on an artistic tradition that dates back more than 2,000 years.



Titled ZENSATION: Grandmasters of Balance, the production brings together some of the circus’s best-known acts in a programme featuring performers trained at China’s leading circus academies.

Many have spent most of their lives mastering acrobatic disciplines, with years of intensive training behind the precision and control required for each performance.

The programme is designed as a retrospective of the Chinese circus, revisiting celebrated routines that have received awards at international festivals and attracted audiences around the world.

Rather than relying on elaborate visual effects, the production puts the emphasis on the performers themselves, highlighting balance, coordination, physical strength and precision.

Its approach combines established acrobatic techniques with a contemporary presentation, placing the human body and its capabilities at the centre of the show.

The production is directed by Raoul Schoregge, artistic director of the Chinese National Circus in Europe. Under his direction, the show brings together highlights from the circus’s long history in a format intended to appeal to both established fans of acrobatics and audiences encountering the tradition for the first time.

The February 2027 tour will visit three cities:

– Ostrava – February 2027

– Brno – February 2027

– Prague – February 2027

Tickets are available here.

World.title: Could You Crack the Case? English-Language Detective Game Comes to Prague
World.content:
On November 29, The Globe Bookstore & Café will host The Edenmoor Case, an interactive detective game that challenges teams to solve a fictional crime by examining evidence, questioning witnesses and putting their theories to the test.

Set in 1928 in the fictional town of Edenmoor, Louisiana, the game invites participants to step into the role of investigators.

Armed with an initial case file, players must uncover what happened, determine who can be trusted and build a convincing case before their time runs out.



Unlike traditional escape rooms, The Edenmoor Case does not rely on elaborate physical sets or theatrical performances. Instead, teams gather around a table and conduct their investigation through a digital platform, accessible from a laptop, tablet or smartphone.

The platform allows players to explore different locations, question witnesses, examine documents and uncover new leads. But the information they encounter is not always straightforward. Witness accounts may contradict one another, seemingly important details can lead nowhere, and a single overlooked clue could change the direction of an investigation.

Much of the experience unfolds through discussion between team members. Players compare their findings, challenge one another’s assumptions and decide which leads are worth pursuing.

With limited time and multiple possible interpretations of the evidence, reaching a shared conclusion becomes part of the challenge.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Edenmoor Case | Detective Game Prague (@edenmoor.case)

The game also introduces a competitive element. Several teams investigate the same crime simultaneously, working with identical evidence and under the same two-hour time limit. Each team must submit its conclusions, with the challenge focusing on the strength of the investigation rather than simply who finishes first.

Designed for groups of two to eight people, the English-language experience offers an alternative to traditional group activities in Prague. Friends, couples and colleagues can take part together, while individual participants are also welcome to register.

The next session takes place on Sunday, November 29, at The Globe Bookstore & Café, Pštrossova 6, Prague 1. Doors open at 4:00 PM, and the investigation begins at 5:00 PM.

Tickets cost 300 CZK per person in advance or 330 CZK at the door.

Registration and further information are available at www.edenmoor.eu/prague. Updates and a closer look at the game can also be found on Instagram at @edenmoor.case.

For private group bookings and enquiries, contact [email protected].

World.title: Samosas, Biryanis and Tandoori: Three Reasons to Visit Ekant in Prague
World.content:
Karlovo náměstí is not usually the first place people think of when planning a dinner out in Prague.

It is central, but it lacks the restaurant scene of neighbourhoods such as Vinohrady or Karlín. There are plenty of reasons to pass through, but perhaps fewer to stay for dinner.

Ekant Indian Restaurant is one of them.



The restaurant serves a broad menu of North Indian dishes, from curries and tandoori specialities to biryanis, samosas and freshly baked naan.

If there are two things worth ordering, they are the samosas and the biryanis. The latter are a particularly good alternative to the usual curry-and-rice combination, while the samosas make an easy choice to start a meal.

The menu also covers chicken, lamb and seafood dishes, alongside a sizeable vegetarian selection. Vegan options are available, too, and the restaurant can accommodate certain dietary requirements on request.

There is plenty of choice, whether you are visiting for a quick lunch, a relaxed dinner or a meal with friends. The restaurant has a casual dining room, with table service, takeaway and delivery available.

World.title: Need a Plumber or Electrician in Prague? This App Can Help
World.content:
Finding a reliable plumber, electrician, cleaner or handyman can be time-consuming, particularly for foreigners living in the Czech Republic who may not know where to look or whom to contact.

A Czech platform called Helplii aims to make the process easier by bringing customers and local service providers together through a single online marketplace.



Instead of searching through multiple websites, social media groups or personal recommendations, users can describe the job they need done and post a request through the Helplii app. Local professionals can then respond with offers, allowing customers to compare prices, availability and reviews before deciding whom to hire.

The process is designed to cover everything in one place. Once an offer has been accepted, customers can communicate directly with the provider through the app, share details and photos, and arrange the work. Payments are also handled through the platform.

Helplii covers a wide range of everyday services, including plumbing, electrical work, home repairs, cleaning, furniture assembly, gardening, moving assistance and pet sitting.

The platform also lists services such as IT support, accounting, tutoring, photography and translation.

According to the company, its marketplace currently covers more than 25 service categories and 16 cities and towns across the Czech Republic.

The platform focuses primarily on freelancers and small businesses, although larger service companies can also register. To offer services in the Czech Republic, providers must have a registered business identification number (IČO).

Helplii also includes several features intended to make transactions more transparent. Providers submit their own prices, customers can review ratings and feedback from previous jobs, and communication takes place within the app. Phone numbers remain hidden until an offer is accepted.

For service providers, the platform offers another way to find customers without having to rely entirely on advertising or personal contacts. They can receive requests matching their skills and availability, submit their prices and build a reputation through customer reviews.

Helplii is available for both iOS and Android devices.

World.title: West Ham Star Tomáš Souček Launches English Autobiography in Prague
World.content:
Tomáš Souček has presented the English edition of his autobiography at the British Embassy in Prague, with the book set to reach UK readers ahead of Christmas.

British Ambassador Matt Field welcomed the West Ham United midfielder to Thunovský Palace on Monday, November 16, for the launch. The event marked the next step for the autobiography, which was first published in the Czech Republic a year ago.

The English edition will be titled Tomáš Souček – My Story and will initially be available through West Ham’s official fan shop. Souček said the decision to translate the book had been made from the beginning, with the aim of making it accessible to supporters in England.



“I’m living a second life in England. My children are growing up there, and I feel right at home. That’s why I’m so happy we can bring this book to West Ham fans. I have an incredible connection with them, and they deserve it,” Souček said to Prague Morning.

The launch also featured an unusual alternative to the traditional champagne toast. Instead of pouring sparkling wine over the book, Souček and Field blew bubbles above its cover, referencing West Ham’s pre-match tradition and the club anthem I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles.

“In England, seeing a bubble blower means seeing West Ham. Besides, I’m not really a fan of being doused in alcohol. Bubbles are a much better fit for this book,” Souček said.

Field, meanwhile, recalled watching the Czech midfielder lift the UEFA Europa Conference League trophy in Prague in 2023.

“I’ve been a fan ever since. I know he’s scored more goals in the Premier League than any other Czech footballer. But apparently, that wasn’t enough for him, so he decided to write a book, too. As a diplomat, I can only hope he doesn’t decide to try his hand at my job as well. That would start to look like a hat-trick,” the ambassador joked.

The autobiography was written by Souček together with football journalists David Čermák and Jan Palička. It covers both his professional career and personal life, including his struggles with insomnia and depression at different stages of his football journey.

The English edition includes an additional chapter covering West Ham’s relegation season, the disappointing World Cup campaign in the United States and Souček’s return to football after a serious ankle injury.

World.title: Heavy rain and possible snow showers on the way to Hungary as temperatures plunge
World.content:
Hungary is in for a dramatic change in weather over the coming days, with another spell of widespread rain expected this weekend, followed by a sharp drop in temperatures and even possible snow showers early next week. Forecasters are also warning of freezing nights, with temperatures approaching -10°C in some frost-prone areas.

According to the Hungarian Meteorological Service (HungaroMet), a brief period of calmer weather on Friday will give way to a cold front on Saturday, followed by another low-pressure system bringing further widespread rainfall from Sunday afternoon.

Friday brings a brief break from the rain

Friday is expected to be relatively calm, with sunny spells returning to several parts of the country. Cloud cover will vary throughout the day, but significant rainfall is not forecast.

Temperatures will remain relatively mild for November, reaching around 9–15°C during the afternoon, although fresh to strong westerly winds may make it feel cooler.

Cold front and heavy rain to hit over the weekend

A cold front will move into Hungary from the northwest on Saturday, bringing scattered rain and showers. North-westerly winds will strengthen in several areas, while daytime temperatures are expected to range between 8 and 13°C.

Another low-pressure system will approach from the southwest on Sunday afternoon, bringing rainfall to almost the entire country. The heaviest precipitation is expected in southern Hungary, where more than 20 mm of rain could fall by Monday morning.

Some areas along the north-western and northern borders may receive considerably less rain, and a few locations could escape it altogether.

If you missed it: Will Hungary have a white Christmas in 2026? Here is what to expect this winter

Rain could turn into snow early next week

Temperatures will gradually fall as colder air moves into the country. The change could be significant enough for precipitation to turn mixed, with sleet and even snow showers possible in the first days of next week.

According to HungaroMet, rain could turn into snowfall in some parts of Hungary on Monday morning, before the precipitation gradually clears. Showers on Monday and Tuesday are also increasingly likely to fall as snow rather than rain.

The meteorological service has not yet specified exactly which regions are most likely to see snowfall.

Freezing nights and much colder days ahead

The start of next week will bring a much colder spell, with daytime highs expected to reach just 1–6°C across Hungary. Even in the south, temperatures may struggle to exceed 5°C, while northern areas could see readings only slightly above freezing.

Nights will become increasingly cold, with frost expected across almost the entire country. Temperatures in frost-prone areas, particularly northern valleys and the Homokhátság region, could drop close to -10°C.

Residents should therefore prepare for a sharp change from the relatively mild conditions expected on Friday, as winter-like weather arrives in Hungary early next week.

World.title: Serbian student movement leader “can’t wait” to work with Péter Magyar on cross-border corruption investigations
World.content:
Jovo Bakić, parliamentary leader of Serbia’s election-winning Student List, has said he “can’t wait” to establish close working ties with Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and jointly investigate alleged criminal activity on both sides of the border.

Former professor became a prominent critic of Vučić’s party

Speaking on independent Serbian television channel KTV on Wednesday evening, 18 November, Bakić said he hoped to work closely with “our friend Péter Magyar” to expose crime and those responsible for it in both countries. He added that the prospect would not please several Serbian politicians. “We have already made contact, but naturally we will have to wait until our new government is formed,” Bakić said.

Bakić was previously a sociology professor at the University of Belgrade and has supported the student movement against the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), led by former president Aleksandar Vučić, since its emergence. He became one of the movement’s most outspoken figures, repeatedly accusing the former ruling party of links to organised crime, as reported by Telex.

Preparations have already begun, but the real work must wait

In one of his best-known remarks, he described the SNS not as a political opponent but as a breeding ground for organised criminal activity. According to reports, the authorities have already begun pursuing alleged wrongdoing following the 25 October election, with more than 90 people reportedly having been detained in the two weeks after the vote on suspicion of corruption, abuse of office and money laundering.

Bakić’s proposed cooperation with Magyar, however, will have to wait for the formation of Serbia’s new government. The incoming administration has up to 90 days after the parliamentary session to secure approval.

Student List holds a parliamentary majority

The new Serbian parliament has been struggling to complete its inaugural session, now in its third day, amid lengthy speeches and breaks by the SNS, which has moved into opposition. The election of a new parliamentary speaker was expected on Thursday, 19 November.

Serbia currently has no president. According to the reports, the new speaker will temporarily perform presidential duties until a successor is inaugurated following the presidential election scheduled for 27 December.

Stay up-to-date: Viktor Orbán’s brother invoked family ties to seek visa help from ambassador, email reveals

How does the Serbian parliament look like?

The 250-seat parliament is dominated by the Student List, which secured 140 seats, while the United Serbia bloc associated with Vučić won 103. The remaining seven seats went to five minority lists, including two for the Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians.

With 126 votes required to form a government, the Student List has enough seats to govern without support from other parties. Its majority could give Bakić and his allies the parliamentary backing needed to pursue their promised anti-corruption agenda — and potentially develop the cross-border cooperation he has proposed with Magyar.

World.title: Official: Here’s how much minimum wage will be in Hungary in 2027
World.content:
Hungary’s minimum wage and guaranteed minimum wage for skilled workers will both increase from January 2027 after the government, employers and trade unions reached an agreement on next year’s pay rises. The new rates will mean higher gross salaries for the country’s lowest-paid workers, with planned tax relief expected to boost their take-home pay even further.

The agreement was announced by the Ministry of Social and Family Affairs following a meeting of the Permanent Consultation Forum of the Competitive Sector and the Government (VKF) on 19 November. The parties are expected to sign the agreement next week.

How much will the minimum wage increase?

Under the agreement, Hungary’s gross monthly minimum wage will rise by 7.5%, from its current level to HUF 347,000 (approximately EUR 930).

The guaranteed minimum wage, which applies to jobs requiring at least secondary-level qualifications or vocational training, will increase by 6.1% to HUF 396,000 (approximately EUR 1,060) per month.

The government says that, when combined with the planned tax credit, the increases could result in considerably higher net salaries for employees who are not eligible for other personal income tax allowances.

For these workers, the net minimum wage could rise by 17.2%, or almost HUF 37,000 per month. Those earning the guaranteed minimum wage could see their take-home pay increase by 13.3%, equivalent to around HUF 33,000 monthly.

The government argues that the arrangement strikes a balance between improving employees’ incomes and ensuring that businesses, particularly those in a more vulnerable financial position, can afford the higher wage costs.

Employers warn that businesses must be able to afford the increases

The agreement followed negotiations between the government, employers and employee representatives. According to the Ministry of Social and Family Affairs, the parties initially held significantly different positions but managed to reach a compromise after detailed discussions.

The National Association of Employers and Manufacturers (MGYOSZ) described the deal as a significant commitment on the part of employers, warning that improving economic conditions would be necessary to implement it without major difficulties.

“The parties could agree on the scale of the wage increase, but its funding cannot be decided at the negotiating table. Businesses have to generate the necessary resources on the market,” said Ákos Kalmár, a member of the MGYOSZ presidency.

The organisation also noted that different considerations influenced the two wage rates. When setting the minimum wage, negotiators had to consider both the economic capacity of businesses and the financial situation of the lowest-paid employees. For the guaranteed minimum wage, employers’ ability to bear additional costs and labour market conditions carried greater weight.

The final stage of negotiations reportedly involved lengthy and heated discussions over the guaranteed minimum wage. Employers and employee representatives also proposed a general 5% wage increase for the competitive sector.

Further wage negotiations planned for 2027

The government said the previous three-year wage agreement had been reviewed in light of changing macroeconomic conditions, with social partners involved in the process.

The parties also plan to work together next year on a medium-term, formula-based agreement. Its aim would be to ensure that nominal wage increases reflect the country’s economic performance while remaining fair to employees.

World.title: Poland to represent Hungary in Ukraine peace talks, foreign minister says during Budapest visit
World.content:
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has said Poland is prepared to represent the wider Central European region, including Hungary, in negotiations on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine. He made the remarks during a visit to Budapest on Thursday, 19 November, where he met Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán.

The two ministers discussed the war in Ukraine, regional security, energy cooperation and transport links between their countries. Sikorski also laid a wreath at the statue of Polish-Hungarian general Józef Bem.

Sikorski warns Russia could use peace talks to divide the West

Speaking about possible negotiations, Sikorski warned that Russia could use the process to drive a wedge between Western countries and weaken NATO. In his view, Moscow has shown little willingness to agree to a ceasefire.

He also expressed hope that US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping could put pressure on Vladimir Putin to end the war. However, he criticised the international attention given to Russia through high-level US-China-Russia engagement, arguing that it could give the Kremlin a misleading sense of importance.

Sikorski described Russia as an economic dwarf compared with the European Union and said European countries should recognise their collective influence.

Photo: MTI

Hungary, meanwhile, reiterated that it would not allow weapons shipments to Ukraine to pass through its territory. Budapest said it supported putting pressure on Russia through sanctions and condemned attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.

The ministers also discussed the situation of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine’s Transcarpathian region. Sikorski welcomed progress in Budapest’s talks with Kyiv on minority rights.

Hungary seeks access to Poland’s LNG infrastructure

Energy security was another key topic. Hungary is interested in accessing liquefied natural gas (LNG) through Poland’s terminal, although such cooperation would require the necessary infrastructure and agreements between the companies involved.

The ministers also discussed improving railway and other transport connections, as well as cooperation within the Visegrád Group (V4) and efforts to counter hybrid threats. Bilateral trade currently stands at around EUR 15 billion.

Photo: MTI

Budapest and Warsaw seek to rebuild relations

Sikorski’s visit was his first to Budapest in 12 years and came amid efforts by the new Hungarian government to restore closer relations with Poland. Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s first foreign trip after taking office was to Warsaw, signalling a change in Hungary’s regional diplomatic priorities.

The two countries are also preparing for the next presidential summit, scheduled for 2027, which will mark the 20th annual meeting of the Hungarian and Polish presidents.

Anita Orbán highlighted the importance of strengthening historical ties and practical cooperation. Sikorski, for his part, pointed to Poland’s economic development since the end of communism, saying the country’s economy had grown roughly 1,400 per cent and around 4.5 million Poles had returned from abroad.

Relations between the two countries had deteriorated under the previous Hungarian administration, particularly over Budapest’s approach to Russia and its close contacts with Moscow. Tensions were also fuelled by Hungary’s decision to grant asylum to Polish politicians Marcin Romanowski and Zbigniew Ziobro. Their asylum status was withdrawn in July 2026, and both subsequently left Hungary.

World.title: Budapest’s City Park Ice Rink celebrates 100 years with season opening this Friday
World.content:
Budapest’s City Park Ice Rink, Városligeti Műjégpálya, kicks off its 2026/2027 winter season this Friday, 20th November, marking an unusual milestone. Exactly 100 years ago to the day, workers switched on the first artificial cooling system beneath the lake, transforming how the Hungarian capital spent its winters. For expats, international students, and visitors in town this week, Friday night offers a rare chance to skate on a genuine piece of local history.

Author: Tselmeg Khosbayar

A century of artificial ice beside Vajdahunyad Castle

People have been skating in City Park since January 1870, when the Pest Skating Association first opened the lake to the public. Back then, skaters were completely at the mercy of the weather, if the water did not freeze solid, the season simply did not happen. That changed on 20th November 1926 with the installation of underground cooling pipes, making Budapest one of the earliest cities in Europe to run an outdoor artificial rink and guaranteeing a reliable winter season.

A century later, the City Park Ice Rink Budapest spans more than 12,000 square metres, ranking among Europe’s largest open-air rinks. Framed by the Neo-Baroque Skating Hall and the towers of Vajdahunyad Castle, it remains a winter fixture for locals and newcomers alike.

What to expect at Friday’s centenary opening

To mark the 100-year anniversary, gates open on Friday, 20th November from 5:00 PM to 9:00 PM. Organisers have lined up live music, figure-skating and ice-sport demonstrations, and family-friendly anniversary activities throughout the evening. Because the rink sits completely outdoors, final opening times always depend on weather conditions and last-minute ice preparation. Anyone heading over on Friday should check the official website (mujegpalya.hu) or the rink’s Facebook and Instagram pages beforehand for confirmed ticket releases and session hours.

Practical tips for first-time visitors

Getting to the rink at Olof Palme sétány 5, right behind Heroes’ Square, takes only a few minutes from central Budapest. Hop on the historic yellow M1 metro line from Deák Ferenc tér or Oktogon to Hősök tere, and walk two minutes across the square. Buying tickets online in advance is strongly recommended, especially for Friday nights and weekends when queues at the ticket window build up quickly. Keep in mind that daily skating is divided into morning (9:00 AM–1:00 PM) and afternoon/evening (5:00 PM–9:00 PM) sessions, with a break in between to resurface the ice.

Because the rink is wide open to the winter air, temperatures drop noticeably once the sun sets. Dress in warm layers, bring gloves both for warmth and to protect your hands if you take a tumble, and pack thick socks if you plan to rent skates at the entrance (you will need a valid ID or a small cash deposit). For quieter ice and room to practice, go on a weekday morning; for floodlights, music, and a livelier crowd, aim for Friday or Saturday evening.

Student discounts and on-site facilities

International students living in Budapest can take advantage of reduced entry prices by showing a valid student ID at the ticket desk. Inside the main Skating Hall, visitors have access to heated changing rooms, a guarded cloakroom for shoes and backpacks, and warm lounge areas to thaw out between laps.

Once open, the City Park Ice Rink Budapest typically stays active until late February, weather permitting. Paired with a hot drink from the on-site café or an evening soak at the neighbouring Széchenyi Thermal Bath, it remains one of the best ways to spend a winter day in the Hungarian capital.

World.title: Hungary lifts veto on Ukraine’s progress towards EU membership
World.content:
Hungary has withdrawn its objection to Ukraine and Moldova opening the final two negotiating clusters in their European Union accession processes, removing a significant obstacle to their membership bids.

Hungary lifts block on Ukraine’s EU plans

EU diplomats told the Kyiv Independent on 18 November that Budapest had dropped its opposition to the remaining steps needed to advance the two candidate countries’ negotiations. Hungary had previously withheld the final approval without publicly providing a formal explanation.

The decision concerns the clusters covering agriculture and the green agenda, the last two of six groups of policy areas to be opened in the accession process.

Further EU approval is still required

Hungary’s change of position does not mean the two clusters will open immediately. Ambassadors representing all 27 EU member states must first agree on a common position, followed by approval from national ministers. Only after these steps can an intergovernmental conference formally declare the clusters open.

All six clusters are currently expected to be opened by December. The focus will then shift increasingly towards the rule of law and anti-corruption requirements. Both Ukraine and Moldova must formally meet a series of interim benchmarks covering these areas before individual elements of their accession negotiations can be considered complete.

The European Commission’s annual enlargement assessments suggest that Moldova has largely completed the necessary work. EU and national diplomats reportedly expect the Commission to circulate a report confirming Chisinau’s progress during the week beginning 23 November.

Ukraine still faces additional challenges, particularly in implementing rule-of-law reforms. However, a joint EU-Ukraine task force has been established to accelerate the process. One EU diplomat told the Kyiv Independent that the cooperation could triple the pace of Ukraine’s progress.

Ukraine faces a longer reform process

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos and Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys have expressed hope that Ukraine will complete the required reforms by the end of Lithuania’s presidency of the Council of the EU in June 2027.

The political background to Hungary’s reversal remains subject to interpretation. The previous government of Viktor Orbán consistently adopted a critical position towards Ukraine’s EU ambitions. According to EU diplomats cited by the Kyiv Independent, the new Hungarian administration was also keen to avoid appearing too accommodating towards Kyiv.

The withdrawal of the objection therefore represents an important breakthrough for both Ukraine and Moldova, but it does not guarantee their eventual membership.

Opening the final negotiating clusters is only another stage in a lengthy process. Both countries will still need to demonstrate progress on democratic standards, the rule of law, anti-corruption measures and the adoption of EU legislation before accession talks can be concluded.
