World.title: Hungarian expert helps Montenegro move closer to EU membership, foreign minister says
World.content:
Hungary has sent an integration expert to Montenegro to work directly with the country’s government on its European Union accession process, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has announced. During talks in Budapest on Thursday, she and Montenegrin Deputy Prime Minister Filip Ivanović discussed how Hungary could help the Balkan country conclude its accession negotiations this year and become a full EU member in 2028.

Hungary provides practical support for Montenegro’s EU ambitions

In a Facebook post following their meeting, Orbán said Hungary was providing more than political backing for Montenegro’s EU ambitions. Hungarian integration experts have been sent to every Western Balkan country, with one now working directly alongside the Montenegrin government on its accession process.

The Foreign Ministry has also appointed a dedicated official to deal with Western Balkan affairs, aiming to make Hungary’s support for the region’s European integration more effective.

Orbán stressed that Montenegro had made significant progress over the past two decades and fulfilled most of the conditions required for EU membership.

She also highlighted the longstanding ties between the two countries. Hungary was among the first states to recognise Montenegro’s independence in 2006 and opened its embassy in Podgorica that same year. The two countries are celebrating the 20th anniversary of their diplomatic relations in 2026.

Hungarian companies also play an important role in the Montenegrin economy, while an increasing number of Hungarians are choosing the Balkan country as a holiday destination.

Filip Ivanović and Anita Orbán. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Anita

Hungary promises to push for faster EU enlargement

According to Orbán, Montenegro’s EU membership would send an important message to the entire Western Balkans: countries that meet the necessary conditions should have a place in the European Union.

She added that enlargement would strengthen both regional stability and Europe’s security.

The Hungarian foreign minister also congratulated Montenegro on the expected closure of two additional EU accession negotiating chapters in Brussels on Thursday, marking another step towards membership.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar has likewise pledged strong Hungarian support for Western Balkan enlargement. Speaking at a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin last week, he said Hungary maintained good relations with every Western Balkan country, without exception.

“Serbia and the Western Balkans can count on us,” Magyar said, adding that he would strongly advocate in Brussels for accelerating the region’s EU accession process.

Montenegro is currently among the frontrunners in the Western Balkans’ EU integration process, with 2028 identified as its target year for full membership.

World.title: Viktor Orbán’s brother invoked family ties to seek visa help from ambassador, email reveals
World.content:
Áron Orbán, the younger brother of former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, explicitly identified himself as the prime minister’s brother when asking Hungary’s ambassador to Iraq for help arranging visas for 16 people in 2023. The email, recently made public by György Velkey, Parliamentary State Secretary at the Foreign Ministry, adds to growing scrutiny of the former prime minister’s brother, who was arrested last week on suspicion of human trafficking and influence peddling.

“Áron Orbán (Prime Minister’s brother)” – the email to the Iraqi ambassador

The email, dated 21 August 2023, was addressed to Attila Tar, Hungary’s ambassador to Baghdad at the time. In it, Áron Orbán asked for assistance in arranging visa appointments for 16 people, adding that his local business partner was ready to receive them and put them to work. He also suggested that three more groups might follow.

“Could I kindly ask for a little help with suggesting appointments for the 16 people in the attachment?” he wrote, thanking the ambassador in advance.

According to the attached document, Orbán was seeking short-stay Schengen C visas for all 16 applicants through the Hungarian embassy in Iraq.

A C-type visa allows its holder to stay in the Schengen Area for up to 90 days. Such visas are generally issued for tourism, business trips and other short-term purposes.

However, Velkey questioned the way the request was presented, pointing out that the email referred to the visas as tourist visas despite mentioning that the applicants were expected to start working for a local partner.

Most notably, the email was signed “Áron Orbán (Prime Minister’s brother)”.

Further revelations about the former prime minister’s brother

Velkey has published several documents in recent days concerning Áron Orbán’s business activities and alleged access to Hungarian diplomatic services.

Earlier, he revealed a September 2023 letter in which the former prime minister’s brother offered cooperation to then Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó and recommended a new chief adviser, who also managed his investment portfolio. In July 2023, Orbán had also requested a personal meeting with Eszter Gyarmati, then the Foreign Ministry’s administrative state secretary, regarding a proposed strategic partnership covering education, IT and security technology services.

Another email published by Velkey reportedly showed that the Foreign Ministry had instructed its diplomatic missions in Vietnam to give special attention to two companies linked to Áron Orbán: Multi Shoot Zrt. and HR Capital Kft. The instructions also called for priority appointments, with the only explanation being that this was a “senior management expectation” of the ministry.

Viktor Orbán’s office previously described the allegations surrounding the emails as an attempt at defamation. It insisted that personal or family connections could not be used to influence government decisions during the previous administration. It also said that authorities had always taken the necessary steps whenever concerns arose over visa or residence permit applications, including those connected to the former prime minister’s brother and the Vietnamese visa cases.

Áron Orbán arrested on suspicion of human trafficking

On 11 November, a court ordered Áron Orbán and his partner to be held in pre-trial detention for one month. They are suspected of helping Vietnamese nationals travel to Western Europe through Hungary over several months in 2024.

According to investigators, the suspects allegedly assisted with visa applications at Hungarian diplomatic missions and charged recruitment fees per person, subsequently sharing the proceeds. Authorities believe that more than 100 Vietnamese citizens may have benefited from the scheme.

The National Office for Asset Recovery and Protection (NVVH) suspects Áron Orbán of influence peddling, while the National Bureau of Investigation suspects him and his associates of human smuggling committed commercially and as part of a criminal organisation. These remain allegations, and the investigation is ongoing.

Áron Orbán in a police vehicle after being detained. Photo: MTI

Telex investigation first exposed the visa business

Telex first investigated Áron Orbán’s business associates and alleged visa-related activities in 2025, publishing an extensive investigation into the network and its operations.

The investigation followed the leak of an audio recording in October 2024, in which Áron Orbán could be heard discussing visa-related matters with Dávid Héjj, an associate of Viktor Orbán working at the Prime Minister’s Cabinet Office.

The recording suggested that Áron Orbán and his associates had an interest in arranging visas, while some of their applications were reportedly being blocked by the authorities.

World.title: Former Ally of Albania’s PM Rama Denounces Ruling Party’s Governance
World.content:
Then Foreign Minister Elisa Spiropali at a press conference in Tirana, February 2026. Photo: EPA/MALTON DIBRA.

Former Foreign Minister Elisa Spiropali, once a close ally of Prime Minister Edi Rama, spoke out publicly against her own Socialist Party in a TV interview on Thursday evening after she was reportedly dismissed from all party structures at the Socialists’ general assembly on November 14.

“I joined the Socialist Party, as a reformist force to change Albania; but what is the value of that today?” Spiropali, who was also speaker of the Albanian parliament between 2024 and 2025, said in the interview with Top Channel TV.

The Socialist Party came to power in 2013 and Spiropal was a key figure until March this year, when she refused to follow Rama’s line on the scandal around Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Infrastructure Belinda Balluku, who was charged with interfering with public procurements and corruption.

The Special Anti-Corruption Prosecution called on parliament to remove Balluku’s immunity to allow for her arrest.

Reportedly, one day before the parliamentary vote on Balluku’s immunity, Rama ordered his MPs to vote against the prosecution’s request. However, Spiropali did not participate in the vote.

In the interview with Top Channel’s ‘Top Story’ programme, Spiropali described the Ballaku incident as “the worst example of governance by our political force”, and said the now-ousted minister was “the latest victim of a model that must change”.

“This is what I believed when I chose not to go to parliament to vote on the immunity issue,” she said.

Interviewer Grida Duma asked Spiropali how Ballaku could represent the “worst example” and also be a victim.

Spiropali responded: “At a time when power becomes so personalised that all filters and internal checks within a political force vanish, and it is now abundantly clear that political courage has disappeared, that there is no longer any willingness to raise issues for discussion within party forums, and that no one confronts significant matters concerning governance or the Socialist Party, then, inevitably, a pattern emerges defined by phone calls, text messages, arbitrary personal choices and grave errors.”

Spiropali claimed that Balluku still maintains some power within the party because all its internal democratic mechanisms have failed.

She declared: “We can no longer continue with people in political forums who are using the Socialist Party as a shield for their own personal predicaments. The Socialist Party is not a bunker where they can hide.”

Asked if she had personally come under political pressure, she said: “From morning till night.” Asked by whom, she replied: “By Belinda Balluku and the institutions of this state.”

Balluku has not responded publicly to these allegations. She has however denied wrongdoing in the corruption case. Rama has made no comment on Spiropali’s interview so far.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czechs, Slovaks Mark Velvet Revolution but Both Find Unity Elusive
World.content:
Russian drones hit close to Hungarian border; Orban used taxpayer money for sport trips

The war in Ukraine is getting closer to Hungary’s borders. On Tuesday, Russian drones struck Transcarpathia, Ukraine’s westernmost region – only 30 kilometres from the Hungarian border – and home to a significant Hungarian ethnic minority. While no casualties have been reported, the attacks caused infrastructure damage, and one of the drones exploded near the railway station in Mukachevo. In response, PM Peter Magyar announced the suspension of railway traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for two days. The attack was immediately seized on by the opposition Fidesz party, which accused the Tisza government of adopting Brussels’ “pro-war politics” and putting the security of the Hungarian minority at risk. “Peter Magyar’s government has abandoned its pro-peace policy and chosen to support the war instead of neutrality. This policy poses a threat to Hungary,” Fidesz wrote in a statement. The Hungarian government condemned the attack. Foreign Minister Anita Orban warned that “this is not the first air attack on Transcarpathia, and unfortunately, it will certainly not be the last,” expressing solidarity with the Ukrainian people. Russia also targeted Transcarpathia in 2025, but attacks on the region have been rare. Meanwhile, Russia’s ambassador to Hungary complained, in an interview with Demokrata, a Fidesz-aligned publication, about what he described as unfriendly steps taken by Hungarian diplomacy, including the expulsion of 10 Russian diplomats. He nevertheless expressed hope for mutually beneficial relations, saying that their future would depend on the Magyar government. He also issued a not-so-subtle warning about potential serious financial and legal consequences should the Hungarian government terminate its contract with Rosatom to construct the Paks II nuclear power plant. The project has been under review for several months.

This week it emerged that the Foreign Ministry under the previous government spent more than 280 million forints (about 760,000 euros) on sport-related trips for Orban and his retinue over the past decade, 444.hu reported. The revelations show that the former prime minister, a devoted football fan, financed most of his trips using taxpayers’ money via the Foreign Ministry’s budget. The report by 444.hu, based on data obtained by the publication through a lawsuit, found that the largest chunk, 180 million forints, was spent on accommodation, followed by transport at 79 million forints, airport VIP lounge services at 8.3 million forints, and miscellaneous expenses – taxis, parking, restaurant bills etc – another 10.3 million forints. These figures do not include trips made using a military aircraft or private jets, meaning the total public cost could be considerably higher. The most expensive trip was to Qatar in December 2022, where Orban attended the World Cup semi-final and final. Those two events cost taxpayers 131 million forints, of which 126 million went on accommodation. The second most expensive jaunt was to the 2016 Rio Olympics, costing 70.7 million forints, including 32 million for accommodation, flights, restaurant bills, sightseeing and other expenses. Other trips also raised questions about the use of public funds. Orban’s October 2017 visit to Switzerland for a World Cup qualifier cost nearly 2.5 million forints, including 1.3 million for a single night at the luxury Les Trois Rois hotel in Basel. Orban also attended Hungary’s World Cup qualifier against Ireland in 2025. Government offices and the Hungarian Football Federation had issued contradicting information about who paid for that trip, but the newly obtained records make clear that taxpayers covered the 14 million forints outlay. A subsequent trip to Portugal cost a further 7.9 million forints. The investigation into the football-related trips and their costs is part of a series by 444.hu about lavish spending habits of Orban and government delegations.

World.title: Russian Despatch: Without Vucic, Moscow Faces a Very Different Balkans
World.content:
November has turned into a month of frenetic diplomatic activity for Russia.

Moscow has not only resumed trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington on the settlement of its war against Ukraine, but also managed to expand the agenda to cover how the new security architecture of the whole of Europe should look after the end of hostilities.

And on Thursday, the leaders of Russia, the United States and China held an unprecedented trilateral meeting during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen, China.

There are serious doubts that any of the above undertakings will produce tangible results, but their optics have largely overshadowed a major setback Moscow suffered in the Balkans - the fall of Serbia’s Aleksandar Vucic, widely seen as a rare European ally for Russia.

World.title: Bitter Land: Croatia’s Unfinished Search for its Wartime Mass Graves
World.content:
Dzuro spent just short of 10 years investigating mass graves in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo.

It was in Kosovo that he first came to understand the toll it was taking on his mental health.

“I was in charge of the programme in Kosovo the first year, the first six months, when we exhumed 2,800 bodies,” he said.

One day, he experienced a flash of anger during a conversation between his mother and mother-in-law about a broken washing machine.

“People are dying there,” he said. “We are exhuming bodies from the graves every day, and we are talking about a stupid broken washing machine here. And at the time my wife just took me aside and said: ‘Vlad, what you’re doing is not normal.’”

“A ‘normal’ situation is a broken washing machine. Your work is not normal. Exhuming dead bodies every day is not normal,” Dzuro recalled his wife telling him. “For the first time, I understood that it actually does affect me – this type of work. I’m changing my behaviour because of the gap between what I considered important and what was important to ‘normal’ people – those who don’t do the kind of work I do.”

Dzuro eventually moved to a job at UN headquarters in New York. He has no regrets, though.

“I always look at it from the perspective of the victims’ families,” he told BIRN. “They wanted their loved ones back alive. And if they couldn’t be alive, then at least to have their bodies – to be able to bury them.”

Asked about the cooperation of Croatian authorities, Dzuro said the ICTY initially experienced some resistance, but that changed when they saw the results. He singled out Ivan Grujic, who spent more than two decades leading a team at the Veterans’ Ministry responsible for locating thousands of war missing. Grujic, a colonel, retired in 2016.

“Whatever we needed from Grujic – and he said he would provide it – we could count on him,” Dzuro said.

Contacted by BIRN, Grujic said that records existed for all the mass grave sites.

“The data exists, the GPS coordinates exist; the police and the State Attorney’s Office have access to this information, and everyone has the official records containing these details,” he said.

“It is possible to resolve a significant number of additional cases, though some victims will likely never be found – either because their bodies were destroyed or because they were carried away by the water,” Grujic said, referring to bodies tossed into the Danube or Drava rivers. He said that searches had also been conducted in Serbia.

“We brought back from Serbia the remains of approximately 200 to 300 individuals who were discovered there.”

Nevertheless, Grujic questioned the figure of 1,725 still missing, noting that a large number of exhumed bodies had yet to be formally identified.

“Some of these are ethnic Serbs,” he said.

‘I’m sorry I didn’t find them’

World.title: Scandal Topples US Envoy, But Greece’s Pivot to Pricey American Gas Continues
World.content:
In 2021, the year before the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia was still the European Union’s biggest single supplier of natural gas, even after years of diversification efforts following the Crimea annexation.

That year, Russia accounted for roughly 40 per cent of EU imports of pipeline gas; by 2025, that figure had dropped to some six per cent. Over the same period, according to EU data, LNG imports from the US tripled, making the bloc the world’s largest importer of LNG. US LNG accounted for almost 58 per cent of total imports.

Days after Guilfoyle took up her post in Athens at the beginning of November last year, Greece and the US signed a series of energy agreements.

Among them, the Greek company Atlantic SEE LNG Trade S.A., a joint venture between Aktor and Greek public gas corporation DEPA Commercial S.M.S.A., signed a deal with the US-based energy company Venture Global for the supply LNG in the amount of at least 0.5 million tonnes per annum over a period of 20 years, starting in 2030. The deal provided the option of an expanded purchase commitment up to approximately 1.5 million tonnes per annum.

Greek officials say the collaboration on the VGC is a project of “national importance”, but Roussos said that while Europe sheds its dependence on Russia, it risks falling into a new form of dependence: on American natural gas, which “is much more expensive than any competing natural gas, whether it’s Algerian, Iranian, Qatari, or Azeri”.

According to the Ohio-based Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, IIEFA, Greece “has been consistently paying the highest price for US LNG among EU Member States”.

In 2025, it said, Greece paid an average price of 38.7 euros per megawatt-hour, 12 per cent more than the average paid by EU countries.

The IEEFA forecasts that the US will become the largest supplier of natural gas to Europe and the EU in 2026, “while by 2028 it may cover 80 per cent of EU LNG imports”.

On average, however, “American LNG is the most expensive for European buyers”.

In an October op-ed in Kathimerini, Constantinos Filis, director of the Athens-based Institute of Global Affairs, IGA, and an Associate Professor at the American College of Greece, wrote: “The US, taking advantage of the EU’s inability to find suppliers capable of matching Russia in terms of volume, offered, at a higher cost, but in abundant supply, LNG to meet EU needs”.

“Furthermore, the decision to utilise the Vertical Corridor provided the project with the necessary momentum it had been seeking, given that European authorities were hesitant toward any plan that did not contribute to the green transition,” Filis wrote.

Andreas Stergiou, Professor of International Relations and European Relations in the Department of Economics at the University of Thessaly, told BIRN/Solomon: “What the US wants is first to sell energy and secondly to limit Russia’s geopolitical influence.”

Or as an official at Aktor put it, speaking on condition of anonymity: “Whoever controls energy, controls the world.”

‘Very uncompetitive’

World.title: ‘Dignity’ Promised as Serbia’s Parliament Elects New Speaker From Student List
World.content:
Aleksandar Cupic, an MP from the Student List, was elected Speaker of Serbia’s National Assembly on Thursday as the power handover continued following last month’s momentous elections in Serbia.

Members of the Student List applauded Cupic, whilst the majority of the now opposition United Serbia parliamentary group, led by former President Aleksandar Vucic of the Serbian Progressive Party, was absent.

Of the 239 MPs who took part in the vote, 97 voted for Stojan Radenovic, while 140 voted for Cupic.

In his first address as Speaker, Cupic spoke of his honour on taking the post.

“I call on all of you to do everything in our power to restore dignity to the country’s highest legislative body and state institution through lawful means, while also respecting the dignity of every individual MP,” he said.

Hew added that voters who had elected them expect all of them to be mindful of every word spoken in the chamber. “That is why dialogue and tolerance must become the foundation of the political culture of each and every one of us,” he said.

He added that parliament would foster constructive criticism and oversight, citing Voltaire’s words that “to cease criticism is to be dead”, and stressing that scrutiny makes public officials more serious and accountable.

“I promise all of you, as well as all the citizens of this country, that in this role, as in everything I have done in my life, I will be strict and fair. Strict with myself and fair to you,” he added.

Cupic addressed the earlier physical attack on the MP Lidija Vukicevic, calling it “irresponsible and inappropriate”, adding that the Student List also condemned it. Vukicevic, a member of the United Serbia parliamentary group, was doused with yoghurt as she entered parliament on Tuesday.

The next steps for parliament include electing deputy speakers and other parliamentary officials, while the country moves towards forming a new government, which must be elected within 90 days of parliament’s constitution.

Cupic is an assistant professor at the University of Belgrade’s Faculty of Transport and Traffic Engineering, where he has worked for more than two decades. Alongside his academic career, he is an organic farmer, growing fruit and vegetables with his wife on their family farm in Sopot, near Belgrade.

A father of six, Cupic entered politics through his involvement in the student-led movement and was nominated for the post of Speaker by the Student List. He has openly supported the student-led movement since the university blockades began in late-2024. He gained wider public attention after hosting hundreds of students on his property during their protest march to the city of Kragujevac.

On Tuesday, after 14 years, six parliamentary elections and an equal number of terms of parliament in which Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party and its coalition partners held a majority of seats, the new legislature was constituted.

New MPs that day confirmed their mandates and formed parliamentary groups, with Jovo Bakic appointed leader of the Student List group and Aleksandar Vucic heading the United Serbia group, which mostly consists of Serbian Progressive Party MPs. Their respective deputies are Aleksandra Stimac and Milenko Jovanov.

World.title: Media Capture: How Turkey Wrote the Manual on Building an Authoritarian State
World.content:
Television went first because it reaches the most people. The next targets are YouTube channels, independent streamers and social media, which have become a sanctuary for unemployed and exiled journalists.

The tools are already in place. Since 2019, the broadcasting regulator, RTUK, has had the power to demand licences for online broadcasting. Those who refuse can be blocked.

The 2022 Disinformation Law, which the ruling party promised would never be used against news media, has been used against journalists ever since. There have been access bans and bandwidth throttling at moments of political crisis. Global platforms, always ready to compromise rather than lose the Turkish market, have done the rest.

My forecast is a media landscape split in three: a loyal media machine that reaches every living room and says only what the government wants; a lively but fragile critical media, on YouTube and in exile, living on viewer donations and platform ads, that mostly reaches those who already disagree with the government; and, between these blocs, millions of voters who will hear only one side of the story.

That middle ground is the real target. Closing Halk TV and Sozcu TV was not only about silencing journalists. It was about making sure undecided voters never hear the other side.

The timing is no accident. The government wants to rush the country, with aggressive haste, toward the next election, with voices of opposition stifled and no free media.

When that day comes, it will have two options. It can accept a democratic change of power, or it can go down in history as the government that ended free elections in Turkey.

People outside Turkey often ask why Turks are not filling the streets. The answer is not indifference. When Imamoglu was arrested in 2025, hundreds of thousands protested. Nearly 2,000 people were detained, university students were put on trial and journalists covering the protests were arrested. People learned the price.

Fear is only part of it. Families are exhausted by years of high inflation, and many are simply trying to get to the end of the month. The opposition, whose own party has been handed to a trustee, is fighting for survival rather than leading a movement.

Each new seizure is news for a day before it becomes the new normal. That is how media capture works: not through one big shock, but through a series of smaller ones, none of them big enough on its own to start a revolt.

Ankara is not afraid of Brussels

World.title: Serbian Anti-Corruption Agency Files Criminal Complaint Against Belgrade Mayor
World.content:
Belgrade mayor Aleksandar Sapic. Photo: www.beograd.rs.

Serbia’s Anti-Corruption Agency has told BIRN that it has filed a criminal complaint to prosecutors about Belgrade Mayor Aleksandar Sapic, following a review of his assets and income, which the Agency launched back in 2018 and ended in January this year.

“During the extraordinary verification procedure, the Agency obtained data from public authorities and legal entities holding data relevant to the verification. After obtaining and analysing the collected documentation, the conditions were met for submitting a report/complaint, which the Agency filed with the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade,” the Agency stated.

The Agency did not specify which irregularities were established, or which assets and income the complaint relates to.

It said the proceedings before the prosecutor’s office had been classified as secret. Because of this, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office also declined to provide details about the proceedings.

The Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade is handling a number of other high-profile cases, such as the disputed nocturnal demolitions in the Savamala district of Belgrade and the fatal 2023 shootout in Banjska in Kosovo. None of them has yet reached a conclusion.

The office recently came under scrutiny, after a commission established by Serbia’s Supreme Public Prosecution Office said it had committed irregularities in handling several high-profile cases, adding that the report had been forwarded to the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office for the start of criminal proceedings. Following this, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office said it “rejected the allegations”.

Mayor Sapic’s assets first drew public attention in 2023, when BIRN and the Serbian news weekly Vreme published an investigation into his villa in Trieste, Italy. Data obtained by BIRN and Vreme showed that in May 2018, while President of the Municipality of New Belgrade, Sapic had bought the estate for 820,000 euros.

The property extends over almost 400 square metres and includes 13 rooms, a garage, part of a forest and an access road. However, in his asset declaration, submitted to the Agency in January 2019, the only new property listed was a 150-square-metre flat.

After the article was published, Sapic denied having tried to conceal the property, claiming he had reported it to the Agency along with the purchase contract. Sapic later claimed the assets declaration which listed only a 150-square-metre flat, had been filled in by his secretary and he had merely signed it.

In March 2023, Sapic filed two lawsuits against BIRN and sought 12 million dinars [102,000 euros] in damages, claiming that his honour and reputation had been harmed and that he had suffered mental anguish because of the published articles.

BIRN described these proceedings as SLAPP lawsuits, strategic lawsuits against public participation, which put journalists and media outlets under legal and financial pressure for reporting on matters of public interest.

Court proceedings in these lawsuits has continued into 2026.

World.title: European prosecutors charge individual in 213.7M euro fraud probe into rail modernisation in Bulgaria
World.content:
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Bulgaria has filed an indictment in the Sofia City Court against one suspect, following an investigation into a project for the modernisation of the Bulgarian railway infrastructure, EPPO said on November 19.

The project, which concerns parts of the railway section between Sofia and Plovdiv, is worth more than 213.7 million euro in EU financing.

The contract for the execution of the project was awarded to a consortium formed by three companies.

The accused is the legal representative of a company participating in the consortium.

According to the investigation, through the manager of the consortium, he submitted false information to the National Company Railway Infrastructure (NRIC) regarding the company he represented to illegally obtain EU funds.

His conduct enabled the consortium to be eligible to and to be awarded in 2019 the EU-funded grant agreement amounting to 213 714 235.14 euro.

Between 2019 and 2024, a total of 68 213 186.03 euro was paid out by the NRIC to the consortium, co-financed by the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) and the national budget.

In particular, the accused used the manager of the consortium, who had no knowledge of the relevant criminal circumstances, to declare that the company was not subject to insolvency proceedings. In reality, based on the evidence, it was declared insolvent already in 2012.

The investigation was supported by Bulgaria’s Interior Ministry National Police General Directorate and the State Agency for National Security.

Numerous searches and seizures were carried out throughout the investigation across various locations in Bulgaria, including company headquarters and private residences. Documents concerning the tender procedure and its implementation were also seized.

The initial crime report was submitted by OLAF, which also conducted a complementary investigation, EPPO said.

(Archive photo: NRIC)

World.title: Arrests in Bulgaria, the Netherlands and Poland in probe into multimillion euro VAT fraud
World.content:
At the request of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Munich, three suspects were arrested this week in an investigation into a multimillion VAT fraud, EPPO said on November 19.

The arrests took place in Bulgaria, the Netherlands, and Poland. Searches and seizures were also carried out in those countries.

The criminal organisation under investigation is suspected of operating a cross-border VAT carousel fraud – a complex criminal scheme that takes advantage of EU rules on cross-border transactions between its member states, as these are exempt from value-added tax.

It is understood that they sold AirPods via companies and missing traders based in Germany and Bulgaria.

The activities of these suspects alone may have caused an estimated tax loss of 23 million euro in Germany.

With the support of national authorities from Bulgaria, Germany, the Netherlands and Poland, searches were carried out at the premises of the suspects and companies under investigation.

These investigative measures are part of investigation Midas , targeting a transnational criminal organisation behind a 195 million euro VAT fraud scheme involving the sale of smartphones, small electronic devices and protective face masks.

(Archive photo: Interior Ministry)

World.title: EC opens two new infringement cases against Bulgaria
World.content:
The European Commission said on July 8 that it opened two new infringement cases against Bulgaria for failing to correctly transpose EU rules on deforestation and non-cash payments fraud.

In its latest infringements package, the EC said that it sent a letter of formal notice, the first stage in the infringement process, after Bulgaria failed to correctly implement the directive on non-cash payments fraud, which defines criminal offences and sanctions regarding fraud and counterfeiting of non-cash means of payment.

The Commission also found Bulgaria in breach of the EU Deforestation Regulation, which aims to ensure that key goods placed on the EU market do not contribute to deforestation and forest degradation, requiring member states to designate competent authorities responsible for implementing and enforcing the rules. Bulgaria did so for all commodities covered by the regulation, except rubber, the EC said.

Separately, the Commission also said that it was advancing an existing case by issuing a reasoned opinion, the second stage in the infringement process.

In that case, Bulgaria is accused of failing to correctly transpose the rules of the Seasonal Workers Directive, which outlines rules for the admission of third-country seasonal workers to the EU to meet seasonal labour demand.

(Entrance to the Berlaymont building, headquarters of the European Commission. Photo: EU Audiovisual Service)

World.title: FDI in Bulgaria in January-September 2026 was 3.96B euro
World.content:
Foreign direct investment in Bulgaria in the first nine months of the year stood at 3.96 billion euro, the equivalent of 3.1 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), statistics from the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) showed on November 19.

In January-September 2025, FDI was 2.38 billion euro, but the BNB originally reported 1.91 billion euro, which was revised upward later.

Investment in equity, including in the real estate sector, was 96.5 million euro (compared to an outflow of 10.5 million euro in January-September 2025) and the BNB figures showed 3.73 billion euro in re-invested earnings (compared to 3.33 billion euro for the first nine months of last year.)

Net receipts from real estate investments by foreign companies recorded an outflow of 11.1 million euro, compared to an outflow of 21.2 million euro in January-September 2025.

The central bank data showed 130.9 million euro in investment inflows as debt instruments, recorded as the change in the net liabilities of Bulgarian companies towards their foreign investor owners, compared to outflows of 935.3 million euro in the first nine months of 2025. Such financial flows include financial loans, suppliers’ credits and debt securities, BNB said.

By country, the largest direct investment in Bulgaria in the first three quarters of 2026 came from Greece (515.3 million euro), Luxembourg (487.1 million euro) and Switzerland (464.9 million euro). Notable net outflows were recorded towards the United States (-104.1 million euro) and Kazakhstan (-12.3 million euro).

According to preliminary figures, Bulgarian investment abroad increased by 406.8 million euro in January-September, compared to 379.2 million euro in the same period of last year, BNB said.

(Photo: Miroslav Sárička/freeimages.com)

World.title: Eric Rubin, former US ambassador to Bulgaria and former American Foreign Service Association president, dies at 65
World.content:
Eric Rubin, who was US ambassador to Bulgaria from 2016 to 2019 and subsequently served as president of the American Foreign Service Association (AFSA) died on November 17 at the age of 65.

“We extend our deepest condolences to Eric’s wife Nicole, daughters Liana and Rachel, his extended family, loved ones, friends, and the many colleagues whose lives were enriched by his kindness, wisdom, and unwavering sense of purpose,” AFSA said.

“We hope they find comfort in knowing that Eric’s legacy of service, integrity, and advocacy will endure. He will be deeply missed,” the association said.

At a ceremony on June 10 2019, Bulgaria’s highest state honour, the Stara Planina first degree, was conferred on Rubin for his contribution to the development of Bulgarian-US relations.

Before becoming US ambassador in Sofia , Rubin served as deputy assistant secretary in the Bureau of European and Eurasian Affairs, a position he held from 2011 to August 2015.

He was deputy chief of mission at the US embassy in Moscow, Russia from 2008 to 2011, executive assistant to the under secretary of state for political affairs from 2006 to 2008, and director of the office of policy and coordination from 2004 to 2006.

Before that, he was consul general and principal officer at the US consulate-general in Chiang Mai, Thailand from 2001 to 2004, resident associate and risk fellow at the Institute for the Study of Diplomacy at Georgetown University from 1999 to 2000, and special assistant to the under secretary of state for political affairs from 1998 to 1999.

He also served as assistant White House press secretary for foreign affairs and National Security Council director for public affairs from 1997 to 1998, special assistant to the Assistant Secretary of State for European Affairs from 1996 to 1997, and deputy political counsellor at the US embassy in Kyiv, Ukraine from 1994 to 1996. Rubin had a BA from Yale University.

World.title: US Senate foreign relations committee approves Holder’s appointment as ambassador to Bulgaria
World.content:
In a 13 – 8 vote on November 18, the US Senate foreign relations committee approved Trump nominee Douglas Holder becoming ambassador to Bulgaria

The post of US ambassador to Bulgaria has been vacant since Kenneth Merten’s resignation in January 2025.

Holder, born in the state of Georgia in 1966, attended Middle Tennessee State University, where he got a degree in political science.

He moved to Florida in 1997.

Holder’s Linkedin entry shows him as president of Doug Holder Real Estate Services from August 2005 to present and a partner in the Legis Group, a lobbying firm, from January 2017 to present.

He was a member of the Florida House of Representatives from 2006 to 2014, when term limits meant that he could not continue in office. Holder was a candidate for the Florida Senate in 2018 but lost in the Republican primary.

He is a lifetime member of the National Rifle Association.

On June 1 2026, Holder was nominated by Donald Trump to be the US ambassador to Bulgaria.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Parliament approves 155mm artillery, IRIS-T ground-based air defence systems deals
World.content:
Bulgaria’s Parliament voted on November 19 to approve a 696 million euro deal to acquire Caesar 155mm artillery from France, and ratified an agreement with Germany on the joint acquisition of IRIS-T SLM ground-based air defence systems.

The deal on the Caesars will see Bulgaria acquire 57 of the 155mm howitzers and additional components for them.

Financing will be done through the EU’s SAFE instrument and with funds from the budget of the Ministry of Defence.

Delivery of the equipment and weapons is planned to be completed by December 31 2030.

The investment expenditure project “Development of artillery support capabilities through the acquisition of 155 mm howitzers”, submitted by the Cabinet, was adopted with 158 votes in favour, no votes against and 19 abstentions.

It was supported by 124 MPs from Progressive Bulgaria, three from GERB-UDF, 12 from the Movement for Rights and Freedoms, 10 from We Continue the Change, and nine from Vuzrazhdane. Nineteen GERB-UDF MPs abstained.

GERB-UDF MP Hristo Gadzhev said that his parliamentary group had refrained from supporting the bill because of the increase in expenses.

Gadzhev said that the loan agreement on the deal which was ratified by Parliament was for 650 million euro. “Thirty-five million euro is no small difference,” he said.

“We cannot support it and will abstain, not for any other reason, but without having all this information about what it costs and how the prices were formed, we cannot vote for 280 million euro on good terms,” he said.

Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told the House: “In reality, these are the unforeseen costs that are added to the contract”.

“This does not mean that these financial resources will be spent. Why are there no details listed on what, how and why it is acquired? Well, because this is money for an investment expense, not a specific contract,” Stoyanov said.

“What I want to tell you is that before we sign each accompanying contract, we send it to the European Commission for review and only then do we take a position on a specific accompanying contract,” he said.

Democratic Bulgaria did not participate in the vote.

“We support the modernisation of the Bulgarian army, however, there are some feelings that there are some companies that are behind deals like this,” Democratic Bulgaria MP Ivailo Mirchev said.

“Things seem to be going well, and then the higher price is explained in another way. Now we are looking at these howitzers, in recent years several European countries have acquired such, the prices are much lower,” he said.

Parliament ratified in two readings in one sitting a Program Agreement between the Ministries of Defence of Germany and Bulgaria for the joint purchase of IRIS-T SLM systems under the Memorandum of Understanding on the Joint Purchase of Ground-Based Air Defence Systems within the Framework of the European Sky Shield Initiative.

A total of 179 MPs voted in favour, with none against. Ten Vuzrazhdane MPs abstained.

The ratification of the Program Agreement is in connection with the subsequent conclusion of a supply contract for the purpose of implementing the second stage of the project “Acquisition of Anti-Aircraft Missile Systems”, namely the joint acquisition of an additional five IRIS-T SLM anti-aircraft missile systems under the SAFE instrument, the Cabinet said in an explanatory memorandum.

Through the program agreement and supplement to the supply contract with Diehl Defence, the project for the acquisition of IRIS-T SLM air defence systems will be implemented to enhance the capabilities of the Air Force in accordance with the requirements of the security environment, it said.

(Photo of the Caesar: US Army)

World.title: Bulgarian prosecutors charge 11 over participation in ‘Ku Klux Klan’ far-right racist organisation in Plovdiv
World.content:
The Plovdiv District Prosecutor’s Office said on November 18 that it was charging 11 individuals, including four minors, with participation in a far-right racist organiation in Plovdiv calling itself the “Ku Klux Klan”.

The statement said that a 32-year-old individual has been charged with leading the “Ku Klux Klan organisation – Plovdiv Division”, with 10 members, from January 2025 to November 16 2026.

The organisation aimed to preach and incite discrimination, violence and hatred based on race, skin colour, origin, nationality, ethnicity and sexual orientation through speech, print, electronic information systems and otherwise, a crime under the Criminal Code.

The Plovdiv District Prosecutor’s Office is also charging 10 identified members of the organisation – men, including four minors aged 16 and 17, with participation in the same structure.

The statement said that on November 17, a joint special operation was carried out in the city of Plovdiv by the Interior Ministry and State Agency for National Security under the leadership of the Plovdiv District Prosecutor’s Office.

During searches and seizures in the city of Plovdiv and the town of Rakovski, at 14 addresses – homes and adjacent buildings inhabited by members of the structure, and in two motor vehicles, various material evidence was found – books, notebooks, badges, clothes with specific symbolism, telephones, masks, swastikas and other items proving affiliation with the far-right racist organisation.

The flag of the Plovdiv structure was also found at one of the addresses.

It was established that its members gathered from January 2025 to November 26 in various public places in the city of Plovdiv, including in restaurants.

The accused alleged leader was detained for a period of up to 72 hours by order of the supervising prosecutor.

The existence and activities of the organization became known during the investigation into the murder of 37-year-old Georgi Kuzev on Mladeshki Hulm in the city of Plovdiv on August 4 2026, the statement said.

Kuzev was murdered by a group of youths who adhered to extremist views.

The Ku Klux Klan is a US white supremacist group founded in 1865. In the 19th and 20th centuries, members were linked to extreme racist violence.

World.title: Foreign Workers Must Learn Croatian in 2027, But is That Really Integration?
World.content:
November the 20th, 2026 – Foreign workers must learn Croatian and be able to prove at least a basic level of it in 2027, but is that really integration into society? According to the law, it is, but according to experts, it’s far from enough.

You move from India, Bangladesh or Nepal to Croatia, an agency gets you a job, you learn about thirty basic phrases of its language, and according to the law, that’s enough to be considered “integrated.” Davor Kovacevic reports for Glas Slavonije that this is precisely what will be required of foreign workers in Croatia starting in 2027, as they will have to prove knowledge of the Croatian language at the A1.1 level in order to extend their residence and work permits.

However, is a basic knowledge of a few dozen words really the same as integration into society? According to Ivan Balabanić, a senior research associate at the Institute for Migration Research, the answer is a clear “no,” and the data his institute collects shows that Croatia has only scratched the surface of a problem that will become increasingly complex.

there are more barriers than language

When it comes to the biggest obstacles in the daily lives of foreign workers, Balabanić avoids singling out just one. Language barriers, inadequate housing, violations of labor rights, difficult access to healthcare, and social isolation, he says, are all intertwined, yet the common denominator of most of these problems is a lack of information. Croatia, he admits, is gradually responding to the new situation through regulations, though it remains an open question how much of it the administration manages to implement in practice. Stricter criteria for employers, for example, were meant to regulate the market, but they simultaneously increased the administrative burden, causing some workers to wait months for permit extensions.

The healthcare system is a particular problem, according to a November 2025 Institute survey conducted among 429 foreign workers from Asia and Africa in Zagreb and Zagreb County, only 28.7 percent of respondents have a chosen general practitioner, which seriously hampers regular healthcare. Language remains an obstacle even when workers try to find information on their own, as official institutional websites are often available exclusively in Croatian. Because of this, many find themselves in what Balabanić calls an information vacuum, in which the main, and sometimes only, source of information becomes their employer or employment agency. “A series of very practical questions, from whether an employer can hold onto their passport, to whether they are entitled to unemployment benefits, to whom to contact if their rights are violated—remain without a reliable answer for a large number of workers. What Croatia lacks today is not primarily regulations. It lacks a system that will enable a foreign worker to actually exercise the rights they have,” he pointed out.

acceptance from a society that was, until very recently, extremely homogenous

Balabanić views the obligation to pass the A1.1 exam simultaneously as an integration measure and an administrative condition, though he emphasised that its purpose should primarily be integration.

“Knowing the language of the country in which a person lives and works is one of the first prerequisites for starting to feel like part of society. Still, such a low level of language proficiency does not in itself solve the issues of foreign workers’ legal security or their ability to navigate Croatian administration. Integration does not begin with a language course, but at the moment when a foreign worker knows their rights and can genuinely exercise them,” Balabanić stated. Precisely for this reason, until a worker masters Croatian, information regarding residence, work, the healthcare system, and the protection of rights must be available to them in a language they understand, and, Balabanić stresses, in one central place rather than scattered across a series of different institutions. Alongside economic integration, which in Croatia today mostly boils down to the relationship between worker and employer, the social dimension is equally important. Foreign workers need to become familiar with the norms and values of the society they are entering, while the local population must also accept that Croatia is becoming more culturally diverse.

Just how weak that readiness currently is was shown by a November 2025 survey by the Institute for Migration Research conducted on a sample of 1,000 respondents: only 2.4 percent of citizens would accept a foreign worker as a friend, 5.7 percent as a neighbour, and only a negligible number of respondents as a family member.

“That is why I would say Croatia is still in the very early stages of integrating foreign workers. Language is an important first step, but without legal security, accessible information, social contacts, and the readiness of the local population to accept new fellow citizens, we cannot speak of a serious integration policy,” Balabanić stated. When it comes to financing integration, Balabanić clearly points out that the state should bear the largest share of the costs.

a(nother) financial burden for employers

The Croatian Chamber of Economy (HGK) pointed out that integrating a foreign worker places a serious financial burden on the employer. Through its own program “Welcome to Croatia,” HGK has so far included more than 400 foreign workers from 15 Croatian companies, while users of Croatian Employment Service (HZZ) vouchers for language learning are employed by 1,602 employers. According to HGK estimates, accommodation provided by the employer alone costs between 3,000 and 3,600 euros annually per worker, a language course costs between 300 and 500 euros, and administrative costs, such as residence and work permits, medical exams, and plane tickets, climb into the hundreds of euros. The new legal obligation will further increase costs, as the law stipulates that the cost of the standardised A1.1 exam is borne specifically by the employer.

taking responsibility

“The logic is simple: foreign workers come to Croatia primarily due to the needs of the domestic labour market and labour shortages in certain sectors. If the state creates a system that encourages the arrival of foreign workers, then it must also take on the largest share of responsibility for their integration,” he is clear.

This, he emphasised, doesn’t mean the responsibility must rest exclusively with the state. Local self-government plays an important role because integration happens within specific communities—the needs of workers in Istria are not the same as those in Lika or Zagreb. Employers bear their share of responsibility within the work environment, though Balabanić warns it would be wrong to shift the entire burden onto them, as they already bear significant hiring costs. The least burden, he believes, should be shifted onto the workers themselves, although they too have an obligation to actively participate in integration by learning the language and respecting the laws. It is precisely here that Balabanić sees a real danger of integration becoming something the state formally demands from a foreign worker without providing them the tools to actually fulfill that requirement.

“It wouldn’t be logical for Croatia to actively attract foreign workers because its economy needs them, and then declare their integration to be exclusively their personal problem,” he said. Particularly vulnerable, he warns, are workers facing overlapping adverse circumstances, those who went into debt just to reach Croatia through long chains of intermediaries, making it harder for them to refuse poor working conditions, as well as those employed by an employer upon whom they depend for their salary, accommodation, and information about their own rights.

the issue of language

Interestingly, employers themselves, according to an HGK survey on a sample of 572 companies, recognise the importance of language, with as many as 80 percent of respondents believing that learning Croatian would contribute most to easier integration of local and foreign workers in a shared work environment. However, HGK states that employers’ responsibility in practice already goes beyond merely paying for an exam. “It includes quality onboarding, mentorship support, and, where applicable, ensuring the adequacy of accommodation,” HGK stated. The Chamber believes that integration must remain a shared responsibility among institutions, employers, and workers.

World.title: Bjelovar Plans Extension of Brezovac Airport Following Wellovar Complex Completion
World.content:
November the 20th, 2026 – Bjelovar is planning the extension of the Brezovac Airport following the completion of the Wellovar complex. The desire is to attract more visitors to the newly opened facility.

The airport in the Bjelovar settlement of Brezovac could accommodate smaller passenger aircraft in the future, and its development opens up interesting opportunities for Bjelovar’s tourism. Ivan Karacony reports for Bjelovar Live that this is particularly relevant now given that the Wellovar geothermal complex in Veliko Korenovo is now completed and is just a few kilometres from the existing runway.

In its draft budget for 2027, the City of Bjelovar foresees the continued preparation of the airport expansion project, including a new runway and additional facilities. If realised, this project would expand the airport’s current sports purpose and enable the reception of smaller aircraft with a capacity of three to 10 passengers.

With the opening of Wellovar, a large geothermal sports and recreation complex featuring 10 indoor and outdoor pools, Bjelovar gained an attraction that, alongside the logical idea we might call “Operation Airport”—could draw additional visitors from Croatia and abroad. At least those who wish to reach their tourist destinations by plane and shorten their travel time. Of course, this does not involve large passenger airliners and regular commercial routes, but rather smaller private and business aircraft that could use the expanded airport in the future. In this context, the proximity of the Brezovac airport, located approximately 1.9 kilometres as the crow flies from Wellovar, and between 3.5 and four kilometres from the heart of Bjelovar, is particularly intriguing.

This opens up the possibility for the future airport to take on a specific tourism role alongside its sports function. The option of arriving via smaller private and business planes could be an added advantage for Wellovar visitors, as well as for business guests and other tourists coming to Bjelovar.

bjelovar’s more tourism-oriented future

This conclusion is backed by the official explanation of the city budget. The City of Bjelovar lists proximity to the city center, the planned Zagreb–Virovitica expressway, and Terme Bjelovar, Wellovar, as key advantages of the future airport expansion. The explanation highlights the potential for connecting air and road transport with tourist facilities, as well as introducing a passenger program for smaller aircraft. In other words, linking the airport and Wellovar stands out as one of the most interesting possibilities for Bjelovar’s future tourism development, although a concrete program for such a connection has not yet been presented. Thus, everything is still at the idea stage, albeit a good idea.

a newer runway for smaller passenger aircraft

The existing airport in Brezovac is currently used for sport aviation, and its infrastructure consists of a runway as well as business and auxiliary facilities used by the Bjelovar Aeroclub (Zrakoplovni klub Bjelovar). The planned expansion includes building a new runway and additional facilities to broaden airport activities. Clearly, this is a plan, or rather, an idea, to create conditions for accommodating smaller passenger planes, giving the airport new value and a new purpose.

For the Brezovac Airport expansion project, 33,000 euros were planned in the 2026 city budget for preparing project documentation, including the conceptual design, preliminary project, and environmental protection and parceling studies. Furthermore, according to the City of Bjelovar’s draft budget, another 33,000 euros are planned for the “Brezovac Airport” project in 2027. The projection for 2028 is 50,000 euros, while a significantly higher amount, 200,000 euros, is foreseen for 2029. When all is said and done, the sum of planned and projected amounts from 2026 to 2029 reaches 316,000 euros. It should be emphasised that this figure does not represent the total estimated cost of expanding the airport, but rather the funds listed in the budget documentation for that period. Additionally, this does not mean that all the stated money has already been spent or that all projected amounts will ultimately be realised.

Whether Brezovac will become an airport for smaller passenger planes in the future remains to be seen. However, given the proximity of Wellovar and the growth of the tourist offer, such infrastructure could gain new value far beyond its previous role in sport aviation. If Bjelovar already has a tourist attraction that might make someone want to arrive by plane, it is only logical to consider where that plane could actually land.

World.title: Dubrovnik Wins Global Model of Sustainable Tourism Award
World.content:
November the 20th, 2026 – After many years being the unfortunate poster child of mass tourism and “overtourism”, Dubrovnik has managed to turn things around so successfully that it has won the Global Model of Sustainable Tourism award.

The City of Dubrovnik is the recipient of the international “Global Model of Sustainable Tourism Award,” which was presented to it during the 21st annual session of the Global Forum on Human Settlements. Dubrovniknet reports that the ceremony was held on November the 13th in Antalya, Turkey, at the time of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31).

This is an international recognition that acknowledges cities and initiatives whose approach contributes to sustainable development, responsible tourism management, and the preservation of natural and cultural heritage. This year’s Forum gathered more than 300 representatives from over 50 countries worldwide, and among the award winners were cities and projects from China, Malaysia, the United Arab Emirates, Colombia, Croatia, and other countries.

The Mayor of the City of Dubrovnik, Mato Franković, addressed the ceremony participants via video message, thanking the Global Forum for this valuable international recognition, which confirmed Dubrovnik’s long-standing commitment to developing a more sustainable and responsible tourism model.

Mayor Franković emphasised that since 2017, through the “Respect the City” initiative, the City of Dubrovnik has been systematically working to establish a balance between tourism development, the protection of the UNESCO World Heritage area, the preservation of natural and cultural heritage, and the quality of life of its residents. Through responsible destination management, data-driven decision-making, the application of innovations, and investments in sustainable mobility and green infrastructure, Dubrovnik demonstrates how tourism can be a driver of positive change for the benefit of the local community and the environment.

“We believe that the future of tourism is not in attracting an ever-increasing number of visitors at any cost, but in creating a sustainable balance that brings benefits to everyone. This award is a great honor for us, as well as additional motivation to continue being an example and sharing our experiences with cities around the world,” the mayor stated.

This year’s Global Forum on Human Settlements was held under the theme “Resilient Cities, Just Transition: Empowering Climate Action Implementation,” with a special emphasis on the role of cities in confronting climate change, strengthening the resilience of urban environments, and implementing concrete sustainable development measures.

As a reminder, last year at the 20th Global Forum on Human Settlements, held in Geneva, the “Global Model of Sustainable Tourism” award was also won by the Lokrum Reserve Public Institution, for a management model that successfully harmonises tourism activities with the protection of natural and cultural heritage and the preservation of biodiversity.

World.title: Iberia to Reduce Flights from Zagreb Airport in 2027
World.content:
November the 20th, 2026 – The Spanish airline Iberia is set to reduce the number of flights it operates from Zagreb Airport in 2027.

The Spanish airline Iberia will significantly reduce the number of flights between Zagreb and Madrid during the summer season of 2027. As Index reports, according to the current schedule, the company will operate for a shorter period than this year, with fewer weekly departures, and Zagreb Airport could lose almost 38,000 available seats. As originally reported by the portal Croatian Aviation, Iberia has withdrawn from sale all flights planned from the end of March to the beginning of June 2027. Instead of starting in March, the first flight to Zagreb is now scheduled only for the 3rd of June.

a significant reduction in august 2027

At the beginning of June, Iberia will have only two return flights per week, and three in the middle of the month. In June this year the company operated five return flights per week on the same route. The reduction will continue in July, when four to five return flights per week are planned, instead of this year’s eight. The biggest difference will be in August. While this year Iberia operated nine return flights per week between Zagreb and Madrid, next year it plans only five. That is a reduction of approximately 44 percent.

flights will stop operating almost one month earlier

According to the current schedule, Iberia will operate its last flight of the season on 12 September 2027. This year, the company flew the route until 11 October, which means that next year the season will end almost a month earlier. Croatian Aviation estimates that due to the reduced number of flights and the shorter season, Zagreb will lose more than 100 Iberia return flights and almost 38,000 available seats in both directions. This is a comparison of offered capacity, not the number of already sold tickets or passengers left without transport.

The reduction in Iberia’s flights comes after Austrian Airlines decided to cancel the Vienna–Zagreb route, and British Airways withdrew from sale its flights between Zagreb and London Heathrow for summer 2027. Qatar Airways has also reduced the planned number of flights between Zagreb and Doha.

zagreb airport still has a huge amount of international connections

Nevertheless, Zagreb will not be left without a direct connection to Madrid, as Croatia Airlines also operates on that route and this year introduced flights to the Spanish capital for the first time during part of the winter schedule as well. As for London, Ryanair has actually increased its flights from Zagreb to London Stansted, and Croatia Airlines will also continue operating their own flights connecting the cities.

Croatian Aviation recalls that Zagreb Airport increased fees for airlines this spring, at a time when airlines are facing rising fuel prices due to the war in the Middle East. However, it must be said that there is currently no confirmation that Iberia reduced the number of flights precisely because of the increase in airport fees.

The announced schedule for summer 2027 can still change, and at the moment Iberia still plans to operate between Zagreb and Madrid from the 3rd of June to the 12th of September.

World.title: New Routes and More Flights to Croatia in Winter Schedule
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – New routes and more flights are on the cards for Croatia as part of the winter flight schedule.

Croatian airports are going to be connected by regular routes to 26 markets during the winter flight schedule, which is one more than last winter. Poslovni reports that there will be 35 airlines operating in total, or three more than before. 77 percent of operations are directed abroad with 110 unique routes, representing an increase of three routes, the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) has revealed.

HTZ collected the flight data for the winter schedule from Croatia’s airports in October. They add that the data shows positive trends continuing in the development of Croatia’s air connectivity with international markets.

“Continuous improvement of air connectivity is one of the important prerequisites for developing year-round tourism and strengthening Croatia’s international competitiveness. It is encouraging that even during the winter we see the arrival of new airlines, the introduction of new international routes, and an increase in the number of flights on a series of existing connections,” commented HTZ Director Kristjan Staničić, emphasizing the importance of connecting Croatia with new markets.

The HTZ highlights international routes such as Air China’s Zagreb – Bucharest – Beijing service, which continues to operate during the winter following its launch in September, as well as Ryanair’s Zagreb – Warsaw (Modlin) route, which will operate twice a week throughout the entire winter. British Airways will launch its Dubrovnik – London flights at the beginning of March 2027.

World.title: Vukovar: After 35 Years, a Mother Finds Her Son’s Remains
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – The siege of Vukovar and the subsequent massacre took place over three decades ago now, but after 35 long years, a mother has finally found her son’s remains.

For 35 long and painful years, the Bataković family didn’t know where Zlatko was. Index reports that they waited for an answer about his fate without a grave on which to place flowers and without the chance to properly say goodbye. After three and a half decades of uncertainty, his remains have finally been found, reports HRT. “When they told me, I felt such relief. Mum will finally get to light a candle at her son’s grave instead of in front of Our Lady,” said his brother Branko.

a quiet young man who grew up on the banks of the danube

Zlatko Bataković was 26 years old when he disappeared in wartime Vukovar. His older brother Branko remembers him as Džala, a quiet and peaceful young man who loved the Danube more than anything. “He would often come back from fishing without any fish. I would ask him: ‘So Zlatko, what do you even do there for 20 hours?’ He would reply: ‘Nothing, I just look at the water, it relaxes me.’ He would go to the Danube like that, sit and it would calm him. I couldn’t understand how someone could lose a whole day just looking at the water,” Branko recalls.

joining the national guard

Soon the time came when he could no longer sit peacefully by the river. In June 1991 Zlatko, together with three other young men from Mikluševci, enlisted in the Croatian National Guard. He had already made the decision and only came to tell his brother he was leaving. “It was the 10th of June 1991 when he told me: ‘Bajo, I’m joining the Guard.’ I asked him why, and he answered: ‘Bajo, better me than you, you’ve got two children, I have to go.’ Even then I didn’t understand it, but he left,” Branko revealed.

their final meeting

His brother last saw him in August, when he came to congratulate them on their wedding anniversary and birthday. That day Vukovar was being bombed and they came to pick Zlatko up. He started towards the vehicle but returned once more to his mother. “He came out. He was wearing a chain with a pendant that said Zlatko – we had bought it for him for his eighteenth birthday. He said to me: ‘I’m going now, I’ll give you all the money. Put it in the passport.’ I told him: ‘I won’t.’ And he answered: ‘You have to, you have to take it.’ He hugged me and kissed me,” his mother Veruška Bataković remembers.

She couldn’t know that she was seeing him for the last time ever. The war was becoming ever more brutal. Croatian defenders on positions around Vukovar were trying to stop the enemy forces. “I remember him telling me: ‘Nothing will come of this. They’ll just keep it as a buffer zone so there won’t be a conflict.’ We never even dreamed that something like this would happen,” says fellow fighter Zdenko Biki.

years turned into decades…

According to witness statements, Zlatko was captured at Ristić’s farm and taken in the direction of Negoslavci. There, his brother Branko says, he was recognised by a man who knew the family, but that did not save his life. “He told him: ‘I know you, you’re Veruška’s son. Why are you here? I’ll let you go home now.’ He took him to the back yard, fired a burst into his back and killed him,” Branko says. The years passed and every new piece of information raised hope. They searched for him among the living, on lists of prisoners and in the stories of returnees. They believed even in things that seemed impossible to others. “We even had information that the Serbs had taken them to the mines in Aleksinac to work. Mum used to dream that Zlatko was alive, that he was working in a mine in Serbia, that he had lost his memory and that he had a wife and two children,” Branko says.

zlatko was finally found, three and a half long decades later

Zlatko’s remains were found two years ago at Petrovačka dola. Branko asked Minister Tomo Medved for only one thing – that the news of the discovery not be published before he personally told his mother. He spent two days gathering the strength for that conversation. “Mum is always watching the TV. The news came at around five and I arrived at four. I called all the children to come in. She was surprised and happy. And then I hugged her and told her. That scream… it cannot be described,” Branko recalls.

For 35 years Veruška had no grave she could go to. In front of the image of Our Lady in the courtyard she lit candles, prayed and waited for the son she had last hugged in August 1991. Now she finally knows where her beloved son is. On his grave reads the name she had spoken in her prayers for decades. Behind the letters remains a life cut short at the age of 26 and a mother who waited decades for an answer. Now that she has received it, she still asks the same question.

“Why him of all people? Zlatko, you shouldn’t have gone. But we couldn’t stop him. That was his fate from birth and that’s that,” concluded Veruška Bataković.

World.title: Croatian Rest Stops Ranked Among the Best in Europe
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – Croatian rest stops have ranked among the best in Europe, coming 7th out of the 23 analysed countries.

A major analysis of rest stops across Europe was recently carried out, with Poland ranking the absolute best, and Sicily the worst. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that numerous areas of road user interest were looked into, whether it’s refuelling, using the toilet or just grabbing a coffee, rest areas are among the key elements of any motorway and travel plan.

Czechvignette.cz, an independent intermediary for the sale of Czech vignettes, conducted a study on the best and worst rest areas across Europe. It ranked as many as 5,363 rest areas along motorways in 26 European countries, based on more than seven million Google ratings and over 300,000 user reviews. The analysis covered petrol stations, classic rest areas and locations that offer both fuel and food. Countries were ranked according to the rating of a typical rest area, that is, the median rating of all ranked rest areas in the country. Only 23 countries with at least 10 ranked rest areas made the list. Finland (8), Ireland (9) and Luxembourg (8) did not have a sufficient number of rest areas.

croatia is positioned among europe’s best

According to the data, Croatia ranks 7th out of 23 countries based on the rating of a typical rest area, with a score of 4.21. It sits just behind Slovenia (4.24) and ahead of Hungary (4.15). Also in the top 10 are Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Romania, Austria, Czechia and Norway.

Toilets are the biggest source of complaints (23 percent), followed by staff and service (14 percent) and prices (10 percent). The highest-rated rest area on Croatian motorways is Krka – West on the A1 motorway in the southbound direction near Skradin, with a score of 4.62. The lowest-rated is Modruš – South on the A1 in the eastbound direction near Josipdol, with 3.82 stars. A typical Croatian rest area has a rating of 4.21 stars, which is the median score of the 90 ranked locations. Of the top 10, eight offer a full range of services. The remaining two (both Krka rest areas) have catering facilities.

Half of the 10 lowest-rated rest areas are located on the A3 motorway, while five of the 10 highest-rated are on the A1. According to the analysis, Karlovac County has three rest areas among the top 10 and two among the bottom 10.

neighbouring italy ranks exceptionally poorly

Looking at Europe as a whole, MOP Rudnik Zachód on Poland’s S19 expressway (near Kraśnik) is the highest-rated, with an average score of 4.72 stars. Poland can boast six of the ten highest-rated rest areas in Europe overall; Bulgaria has two, while Spain and Romania each have one. Returning to the top country on the list, a typical Polish rest area is rated 4.3 stars — the highest average among the 23 countries — while Belgium is at the very bottom with an average of 3.78, just behind Italy (3.79).

When looking at specific locations, the analysis shows that Area di parcheggio Costa Gaia Nord, a rest area on Sicily’s A29 motorway near Alcamo, is the lowest-rated in Europe, with an average score of 2.15 stars. France has as many as six of the ten lowest-rated rest areas. Toilets are the biggest source of complaints across Europe, they account for 23 percent of all written review complaints. Staff and service follow with 14 percent, and prices with 10 percent. Safety, parking, and fuel/EV charging each make up approximately four to six percent of complaints.

World.title: British Airways Cancels Zagreb-London Route as Ryanair Dominates
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – British Airways is cancelling its long-standing Zagreb-London route as Ryanair dominates the route from the Croatian capital to Stansted.

The famous British national carrier British Airways has decided to cancel its route between London and Zagreb. This significantly changes the flight offering between the capitals of Croatia and the United Kingdom, according to the portal Croatian Aviation.

British Airways, one of Europe’s largest airlines, is discontinuing the route that connected London Heathrow Airport with Zagreb. Index reports that for many years, this service was part of British Airways’ network and provided a direct link between the two cities, as well as onward connections to international destinations via the London hub. Last winter the airline made the route seasonal and did not operate it from the end of October until the end of March. Although the same arrangement had been announced for this year, flights have now been withdrawn from sale for next summer as well.

ryanair dominates the route – and it’s much cheaper

The market for flights between Zagreb and London has become highly competitive in recent years. Ryanair currently operates on this route, connecting Zagreb with Stansted Airport, while Croatia Airlines maintains a service to Heathrow. Ryanair’s entry has significantly affected market dynamics, especially in the segment of passengers for whom ticket price is the most important factor. Heathrow Airport continues to play a key role for business travellers and those continuing their journeys to other continents via London.

With the withdrawal of British Airways, Zagreb Airport is losing yet another major European carrier. The question arises whether the remaining airlines will be able to compensate for the capacity previously provided by British Airways. This is particularly relevant for direct flights to Heathrow, given that the airport is heavily congested and has no free slots available.

The departure of British Airways is an additional loss for Zagreb Airport, from which Austrian Airlines will also permanently withdraw in the near future
