World.title: Estonia plans accessible treetop trail in rare flying squirrel habitat
World.content:
Estonia's State Forest Management Center (RMK) plans to build a unique, wheelchair-accessible treetop nature and study trail in the Alutaguse National Park in Ida-Viru County.

Set between the Kauksi campsite and visitor center, the elevated route will replace stairs with gentle ramps so visitors with mobility issues can explore the forest canopy.

RMK Innovation Projects Manager Ulvar Kaubi said the structure is designed as a calm educational trail for a wide audience rather than an adventure course, allowing visitors to experience the forest from the height of the treetops.

"The central principle is accessibility. RMK wants the trail to be navigable by wheelchair and for the solution to take into account visitors' various special needs," Kaubi said, adding that RMK has already consulted the Estonian Chamber of Disabled People on the design.

Under current plans, the climb will use suitably graded walkways and rest platforms rather than stairs, opening up canopy views to people unable to use standard hiking trails and observation towers.

Treetop trail in Anykščiai, Lithuania, similar to the one planned for Alutaguse (though this will not have a viewing tower as here). Source: Screenshot from the visitbaltics.net website.

The trail's exact architectural design, height and length will be determined through an upcoming design competition. Kauksi was chosen after RMK, Enterprise Estonia (EIS) and Environmental Board (Keskkonnaamet) specialists evaluated 17 candidate sites nationwide, selecting it for its proximity to existing trails, the visitor center and the soon-to-be-renovated Kauksi recreation and camping area.

Rather than spanning the entire coastal forest between the campsite and visitor center, the elevated walkway will supplement the existing footpath so visitors can ascend smoothly into the canopy. Seating, observation points, information boards and interactive exhibits are planned along the route, while keeping foot traffic on a fixed path will protect forest-floor vegetation from trampling.

The RMK says it hopes the landmark will encourage longer stays in the Alutaguse area and boost business for local accommodation, catering and guiding providers.

In September, the government approved an expansion of the Alutaguse National Park of 24,749 hectares, to reach 69,768 hectares. This was done to link protected habitats together more effectively.

The park is Estonia's sole habitat for the critically endangered Siberian flying squirrel (Pteromys volans, pictured), a nocturnal glider that depends on continuous old-growth canopy cover to move between nest trees.

World.title: Estonia to close land border with Russia from December 1
World.content:
The Estonian government has decided to suspend border crossings with Russia for six months starting December 1 following a series of attacks from Russia that show no signs of abating.

Border crossings will be suspended at all Estonian-Russian road border checkpoints: Narva-1, Narva-2, Koidula, Luhamaa and Saatse. After six months, the government will assess whether the restrictions, imposed to protect national security and maintain public order, need to be adjusted.

"The overall picture is that Russia's hostile activities are showing no signs of abating," Prime Minister Kristen Michal said after Friday's government press conference. He added that there is no widespread naive optimism in Europe that Vladimir Putin has changed his stance.

Russia has also carried out various attacks against Estonia. Security agencies have recorded more than 10 such attacks over the years. "Estonia is acting firmly and calmly," Michal said.

Estonia has recently faced several attacks from Russia in quick succession, the latest again targeting the defense industry, with no signs of the attacks letting up. The government has decided to suspend border crossings between Estonia and Russia starting at 7 a.m. on December 1. The decision will be reviewed after six months.

In the coming weeks, the government will discuss measures to mitigate the impact of the border closure on residents of southeastern Estonia and Ida-Viru County.

Michal noted that Russia will continue its efforts to influence Estonia. Russia is developing various narratives aimed at influencing the upcoming Riigikogu elections.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna on Monday summoned Russia's chargé d'affaires to express Estonia's strong condemnation of the attempted arson attack carried out against defense industry company Threod Systems.

Tsahkna said Friday that Russia bears responsibility for the border closure. The decision is not linked to the latest attempted act of sabotage. Russia has carried out numerous attacks against both Estonia and Europe more broadly and these attacks have become increasingly severe.

The Estonian-Russian border runs through Lake Peipus. Border crossing points are highlighted on the map. Source: Helen Wright/ERR/OSM

World.title: Auditor general: Estonian state must sort out existing tasks before taking on new ones
World.content:
The state should first focus on fulfilling its existing responsibilities and resolving current problems rather than continually taking on new obligations, Auditor General Janar Holm said on ETV's "Esimene stuudio" talk show.

You've completed your annual report and delivered a lengthy speech to the Riigikogu. If we were to describe the tone in terms of colors, it was mostly shades of gray and black. What happened to the National Audit Office's optimism and sunshine?

I wouldn't say the optimism and sunshine have disappeared. We also highlight things that are going well, but the National Audit Office's job isn't just to talk about what's going well. It's primarily to draw attention to the problems we face and that need to be resolved. That's what we're allocated money in the state budget to do.

A few quotes: "The state is unable to set priorities," "Budget discipline is falling apart," "The state doesn't have a sufficiently clear picture of its future obligations." Have these problems grown over time or do you also see solutions?

The problems have remained relatively similar in recent years. If we look across Europe, Estonia is no different in this respect. We're in a relatively similar position to other countries. Our leaders know what the problems are, but they're difficult to solve because society has become polarized and the challenges are extremely complex. This isn't just an Estonian problem. It's the same across Europe.

One of the key instruments of management and governance is money and when it comes to money, you say the state lacks a comprehensive overview of how much of its funding for future years has already been committed. Why doesn't the Estonian state, or the Ministry of Finance, have this under control?

This is indeed one of the problems we highlighted. As we know, there is occasionally a need to make longer-term commitments and the law allows for this. Up to 50 percent of the current year's expenditures can be carried over into future budgets. When we asked how much spending we'd already committed to future years, knowing that we're facing a deficit, it turned out that nobody knew.

The Ministry of Finance doesn't know and neither do the other ministries, although some claimed they did. When we asked for the actual documentation, unfortunately it turned out that they didn't have it. We could eventually find ourselves in a situation where future governments and the Riigikogu are bound by decisions being made today. Their only role would be to find the money to cover those expenditures, and that's not how things should work.

It's one thing when you buy or plan something, but commitments can also be made in other ways. Your office's latest report says that unless European Union policy changes, Estonia could face a bill of up to €1 billion for failing to meet its climate obligations. That would be a staggering blow.

Absolutely. Just yesterday, we published an audit concerning the achievement of environmental targets in land use. There are indeed certain risks that we could end up having to pay out of our own pockets in the future. How much exactly, we don't know. That will become clear in the future. Time will tell.

And again, there are those people who say they warned us back then that we couldn't take on these obligations because they were beyond the state's means. Yet we agreed to them. Our government gave its consent. We said yes in Brussels. How is all this possible?

That's how these things happen. It's quite complicated and I understand the people who go to Europe to negotiate these terms. But we have to stand up for Estonia's interests and insist on clarity. I think quite a few countries, not just Estonia, are currently struggling to meet this particular target.

Thinking back to this audit, the saddest thing is realizing how many of these so-called solutions depend on methodology. A great deal can be decided without ever leaving your desk, including whether we're meeting the targets or not. The biggest problem with this issue is really the uncertainty. If we won't know until 2032 whether we've fulfilled our commitment for 2030, then we can't manage the process.

But who will be held accountable if it turns out that the amount is €1 billion, half a billion or some other sum? Who bears that responsibility?

In this audit, we've clearly outlined in an appendix how the decision-making process unfolded and who participated in it. That's where the responsibility lies. But the main question is always whether we actually knew what we were deciding or whether, as so often happens, we simply let things slide.

Continuing with the bigger budget picture: When you talk to politicians, they say it's all because of the major war between Ukraine and Russia, the war launched by Russia. Can an aggressive neighboring country be an excuse for the disorder in our budget accounting?

I think the war taking place next door has certainly played a major role in the fact that we're running a deficit. A lot of it also stems from the fact that we've only recently emerged from the COVID-19 crisis, during which we spent quite a lot of money. What's happening now has undoubtedly had an impact, but there are also areas where we can look at what we're doing ourselves and see what we could do better. We certainly can't blame everything on that alone.

Janar Holm. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

We've talked about defense spending before. This fall's biggest buzzword has undoubtedly been Datasel and the infamous artillery shell affair. Are you aware of any developments in this case or do we once again have to trust that all parties are acting in good faith and that the matter will simply be resolved?

I think the media have done a very good job of taking over the auditing from us. They've kept a close eye on the matter since we left off in September and I think things are pretty much exactly as they appear to the public right now. The matter is being investigated and various parliamentary committees are also looking into it.

One area the media may be paying less attention to, but which the National Audit Office is monitoring, is the audit of the Defense Forces' entire inventory. How are things going there? Because even in your speech to the Riigikogu, you specifically addressed the argument that, in difficult and urgent times, the Defense Forces shouldn't be counting socks but boots. Yet even those essential items haven't been properly accounted for.

Yes, the Defense Forces is currently working on this issue and we have quite good communication with the current defense minister. The government discusses the situation every month. Looking ahead, we'll probably be delivering a fairly similar message next year, because the problems have continued this year. We'll simply try to highlight what has improved.

There is a genuine effort underway to improve inventory records so that the financial accounts can also be corrected. But I'm afraid the problems will probably persist next year. We'll try to highlight whatever positive developments there have been.

And you're still not demanding that every cartridge and sock be counted. You're interested in much more expensive items, such as weapons systems, their components, communications equipment, fire-control devices and camouflage equipment. Yet even in those areas, the Defense Forces can't adequately account for these items.

Yes, and that's why I included those examples in my speech. At one point, I was quite concerned that people were trying to trivialize the issue by reducing it to cartridges and socks when we were actually dealing with serious weapons systems, specialized weaponry and other important equipment. There's room for improvement and I think perhaps by this time next year, the situation will be a little better.

But has the chaos that prevailed in defense procurement now been brought under control? Unsigned contracts, documentation errors and sometimes not even knowing when particular goods will arrive or what will be delivered. Have these problems started to be resolved?

We'll be able to say next year. This report covered the previous year and, as you know, a new director took over at the Estonian Center for Defense Investments at the beginning of the year. I also had quite a lot of contact with him early in the year.

My impression is that he's working to improve oversight of contract implementation because there really was something of a chaotic situation there too. It was quite difficult to establish exactly what had been received, what complied with the contracts and what didn't. We'll see next year. It's hard to say, but we have to hope for the best.

Looking at how Estonia is governed from your desk at the National Audit Office, how well is our country being run?

Every time I've spoken with a colleague from another country and then thought about Estonia, I'd say that, by comparison, I'm still proud to be Estonian. It always depends on what you're comparing us with. Our job is to highlight the problems that need to be resolved and the areas where we could do even better. And there are still plenty of areas where we could do better.

The question against this backdrop is how thoroughly different impacts are considered when decisions are made in our country. How well are we doing at that?

I get the feeling that we sometimes approach things the way they do in our literary classic "Kevade" (Oskar Luts' "Spring" —ed.): If you can't do the whole arithmetic problem, do half of it.

Sometimes, when preparing reforms and plans for governing the country, we do something similar. A great many costs and consequences only become apparent once implementation is underway. There are plenty of examples of this.

But if we do the wrong half, that's a problem, isn't it?

We really should do both halves. For a reform to succeed and changes to be successful, we need to know what the costs will be. It's absolutely essential that, whenever we launch an initiative, we understand right from the outset what it's going to cost.

Tomorrow (Friday — ed.), the government will begin discussing the closure of Estonia's eastern border. What does the impact assessment for closing the eastern border look like?

I can't say. The government will be briefed tomorrow on exactly what that would entail.

Isn't that impact assessment already available in the government's meeting information system?

I haven't had a chance to check. I imagine it probably is, if the meeting is tomorrow.

The president says a country shouldn't be governed on the basis of emotions. Do you agree with her?

That applies not just to the border but to every issue. We can't make decisions in the heat of emotion. We have to make rational decisions.

Could the decision to close the eastern border be overly emotional?

I can't say. I can't read the minds of government ministers. I hope the impact assessments have been carried out and that a wise decision will be made.

Let's also talk about development plans because you say there are quite a lot of them. Have you tried to count how many development plans the Estonian state has adopted?

There are fewer than there used to be. Work has been done to reduce their number, but there are still far too many for them to be taken seriously. Take the healthcare sector, for example, where there are 16 development plans in addition to the central public health development plan, with another seven being prepared.

There are people constantly drafting these plans and getting paid for it. Outside experts are brought in and paid, stakeholders are involved, brainstorming sessions are held and then it all gets put down on paper?

The work goes on.

How much does all this cost?

The work goes on constantly and it costs money. But the biggest cost is the decisions that aren't being made. Plans are good, but failing to make decisions comes at a cost.

I wouldn't even consider the cost of the consultation process or the people involved to be the main expense. It's the fact that things keep getting postponed. In certain sectors, development plans have simply provided an opportunity to put off making decisions.

Auditor General Janar Holm. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Are we actually trying to implement these plans or is the problem that all the energy, manpower and money go into drafting them and when it comes time for implementation, there are no officials assigned to the task and no funding?

I'm not sure that implementing every development plan is even the intention from the outset. Sometimes the aim may be more about calming people down and giving them hope because when there's no money, hope doesn't cost anything.

So basically, they're just pretending to do something?

Well, putting together a development plan is real work and it takes real time. But we should measure it by the results it produces.

I do want to stress, though, that this criticism doesn't mean Estonia shouldn't engage in development planning. Quite the opposite. There are positive examples too.

Take the defense sector where various development documents also serve as a basis for choosing between investment options. There are other examples as well. But we're talking about situations where, despite a development plan having been drawn up, nothing actually happens.

In the healthcare sector, we've been asking about various issues for several years and we're told that the one thing standing between us and success is just one more development plan. We come back later, the plan is finished, but success still hasn't arrived.

Let me give you another example from a different sector. About a year ago, an energy sector development plan was adopted. A couple of months later, Elering announced a new €1 billion procurement for gas-fired power plants that wasn't included in the plan. How is that possible? Could the fact that we're facing an electricity shortage really have come as a surprise to Elering?

Even before the new energy sector development plan was adopted, there was already an energy sector development plan and that wasn't being followed either.

I think the process of drawing up the new plan was positive in the sense that it took certain things off the table. There was also agreement on what wouldn't be done. But indeed, as this example shows, those decisions don't necessarily follow directly from the development plan.

But what would happen in Estonia if we agreed that we weren't going to draw up a single development plan ever again?

I don't think we should set that as a goal. We should continue to draw up credible development plans. We should still agree on where we want to get to, what we need to do to get there and how much it will cost. But we need to take the process seriously. And as I said, fortunately, there are examples of this being done well.

Let's take the healthcare sector, which you've also cited as an example. Your latest report says that healthcare capacity is falling increasingly behind demand for treatment and that reform plans exceed the ability to implement changes. Help us translate that into plain language. From a patient's perspective, doesn't it simply mean things are going to get worse?

Patients have an enormous selection of development plans to choose from, but indeed, that doesn't translate into better access to treatment.

What's the problem? If you look at each development plan individually, everything seems fine. But when you put them all together and consider what it would take to implement them, you have to think about the people needed, the money and the IT solutions. It's simply not possible to do all of that at once. Choices have to be made and those choices are difficult.

We have elections coming up soon and I imagine that although the party platforms haven't been published yet, all the parties will probably promise to shorten waiting lists for treatment and make healthcare even better. Some may be more candid about bringing private money into the system, although voters probably won't understand exactly what that means. But you already know that none of this will save the day or solve the problem, don't you?

Yes, that's right. There are no easy solutions to be found anywhere. But we have to start somewhere.

I also don't want to suggest that nothing is being done. Just yesterday, for example, the health minister defended a bill at its first reading that addressed issues involving family doctors, including provisions for situations where no family doctor is available, as we know is sometimes the case.

The opposition says she was solving her own problem?

Well, yes, that other issue added a certain twist to the matter, but the bill does genuinely address the problem of the large number of people on substitute patient lists.

But still, looking at this from the politicians' perspective: They promise things will get better, officials work toward making things better and then you come along and say they've only gotten halfway there. What should be done?

The first thing is that we should make a serious effort to finish what we've started.

First, we need to distinguish the basic functions that the state must fulfill. That includes healthcare, education and even public transportation. We should resolve the problems we've already left unaddressed. The worst thing we could do now is take on piles of new initiatives while leaving existing problems unresolved.

Part of the problem with these development plans is that they read like a description of paradise, but the cost of maintaining that paradise has to fit somewhere into the budget and the state budget strategy.

We're already struggling enormously to meet our existing obligations. Take special care services, for example. According to the ministry's own calculations, there's a €200 million funding shortfall.

And while we're talking about money here, we're also in a situation where we don't have enough people. One of the biggest problems in healthcare is that you can decide through the state budget strategy to provide more money, but you can't train a doctor in six months the way you can train a trolleybus driver. It takes much longer.

Auditor General Janar Holm. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

There are two solutions: Either provide more money, although we both understand that's very difficult, because judging by society's reaction to various tax increases, a large part of the population doesn't agree with that. The other option is simply to do less. How much thought is being given in Estonian politics and government today to the idea of actually doing less?

The problem is that taking things away is painful. It's much easier to add something new alongside what's already there. And that's how the state keeps getting bigger and bigger, with new functions being added while the old ones remain in place.

There have been cuts in the state budget, of course, both genuine cuts and cases where initial ambitions have simply been scaled back.

As a rule, people are simply told to do the same work with less money. That doesn't really solve the problem, though. It just creates more hardship.

Sometimes giving less money can also be a solution because it forces resources to be used more efficiently. But I think Estonia's problem right now is that the state has too many responsibilities.

If we were to say today that we're cutting the number of government officials by 20 percent, but all their responsibilities remained, life wouldn't get any better as a result.

So even when we're talking about reducing the number of officials, we should be honest about what we're going to do less of.

On Tuesday, I interviewed the President on Vikerraadio. She spoke at length about having the courage to make decisions, including unpopular ones. Does that courage exist in the public sector, among officials and politicians?

As I said at the beginning, I think there's an understanding that we can't go on like this.

When I referred to Europe, take France and Spain, for example. Everyone knows things can't continue this way, with expenditures constantly increasing. But try making those decisions when society is so polarized. It's really difficult.

Yes, I think having that courage means there may not be much chance of getting into a governing coalition after the next election. But decisions still have to be made.

With politicians, it's particularly understandable before elections that they want to be popular. So it follows that officials should help keep things on track and bring everyone back to reality. But thinking back over your own career — you've been a government official for a few years more than a quarter of a century — was there more courage when you started?

I think there was more courage, yes, and I also think society was more receptive to change.

There's a bit more anxiety now and I think a great many people agree that cuts are necessary. But it's a bit of a "not in my backyard" situation. People agree that cuts can be made, just not when they affect them personally.

A great many of the areas where substantial cuts could be made affect a great many people. So it's a catch-22. People want cuts, but at the same time, they don't.

Although we're constantly told that the state is short of money, your annual report once again raises the SmartCap case. How is it possible that the state borrows several billion euros while almost a quarter of a billion euros is just sitting in a checking account — or perhaps it's no longer there today? How is that possible?

At the beginning of the year, that was indeed the situation. The state was borrowing money with one hand and handing it over to investment funds with the other where it simply sat earning what was essentially deposit interest.

As the finance minister has said, this is regrettable and it's a problem.

Work is now underway to resolve the issue and I think that if things are done properly — meaning money is allocated when the time is right — the savings could be quite substantial.

World.title: Opposition parties demand Karmen Joller resign or face no-confidence vote
World.content:
Opposition parties Isamaa and the Social Democrats (SDE) have demanded Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller (Reform) resign over an alleged patient-list conflict of interest.

Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu warned Friday that if Joller does not step down over the weekend, his party will seek the 51 Riigikogu signatures needed to launch a no-confidence motion next week.

The calls follow a statement earlier Friday from the Estonian Medical Association declaring Joller had broken the law and was unfit for office after keeping her 1,745-patient family doctor list via a locum past the statutory one-year limit. Joller also submitted a bill to parliament that would extend that limit.

"The public has learned that Karmen Joller broke the law while in ministerial office in a matter involving her personal interest," Reinsalu wrote on social media, noting enforcement falls to the Estonian Health Insurance Fund (Tervisekassa), whose supervisory board Joller chairs.

Reinsalu accused Joller of initiating a bill to retroactively legalize the breach, calling it "a unique intertwining of conflicts of interest" that violates government ethics guidelines. If she refuses to quit, he added, Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) must dismiss her.

SDE chair Lauri Läänemets also urged Joller to take political responsibility and resign, saying the association's statement had deepened a trust crisis alongside unresolved funding shortages in special care and healthcare.

"The minister of social affairs must stand up for people's health and well-being," Läänemets said in a press release. "Since the special care funding crisis remains unresolved, access to medical care is worsening, and trust in the minister has been seriously damaged, Karmen Joller must resign."

Riigikogu Social Affairs Committee member Tanel Kiik (SDE) noted around 2,200 people with special needs have been waiting — some for years — for essential care services, while healthcare unions turned to the public conciliator after collective bargaining talks collapsed over budget cuts.

Joller, who became minister in March last year, moved to surrender her patient list only after the breach became public, shortly after submitting a bill allowing ministers who are family doctors to keep their practices covered throughout their term.

The Prosecutor's Office confirmed this week that exceeding the one-year substitution cap violates health regulations, though it is not a criminal offense.

Joller, a doctor who joined Reform in 2022 and rose to prominence during the Covid pandemic, maintains she receives no financial benefit from the list and ended her employment contract with the medical center holding it before taking office.

World.title: Gallery: Exhibition dedicated to Tallinn's iconic 'sprat tin view' opens at Seaplane Harbor
World.content:
On Thursday, the Estonian Maritime Museum and the Port of Tallinn opened the exhibition "Harbors of Tallinn" at the Seaplane Harbor, showcasing more than 40 works by Estonian artists depicting the Old Town skyline, ships, the sea and Tallinn's harbors.

Curator Tiit Pruuli believes maritime themes are a natural part of Estonian art.

"Estonia is a maritime nation. Nearly all of our great artists have explored maritime subjects, and many of them have also depicted the Port of Tallinn. This exhibition presents a selection of those works," he said.

According to the curator, artists' favorite motifs in Estonia's capital are the Old Town and the seashore with its harbors.

"These two have been so closely connected throughout the centuries that it is difficult to imagine one without the other," Pruuli added.

"The Tallinn Old Town skyline together with its harbors, popularly known as the 'sprat tin view,' is a landmark for us in the same way that Manhattan's skyscrapers are for New York, the mosque domes rising above the Bosporus are for Istanbul, or the Opera House and Harbor Bridge are for Sydney."

More than 40 works are on display, covering nearly a century of Estonian art, from 19th-century Baltic German painting to the 1980s. The exhibition includes works by Karl Burman, Richard Uutmaa, Jüri Arrak, Ando Keskküla and Jaan Elken, among others.

More than half of the works come from Tiit Pruuli's private collection. The remaining pieces are from the private collections of the Jõeleht family, David Pärnamets, Sven Pertens and Olav Osolin, as well as the collections of the Art Museum of Estonia, the Estonian Maritime Museum and the Tartu Art Museum.

According to Estonian Maritime Museum Director Urmas Dresen, the new exhibition is a natural continuation of the museum's own exhibition, "The Call of the Sea."

"With that exhibition, we introduced artworks from our own collections and the history contained within them. It was a tribute to the artists who answered the sea's call with brushstrokes," Dresen said. "In the new exhibition, the artist takes center stage: their style, their perspective and the way the Port of Tallinn has found its place in Estonian art over time," he added.

The exhibition will remain open through February 28.

World.title: Kaia Vask: People in Estonia hardworking and underpaid
World.content:
Estonia's minimum wage has the lowest purchasing power in the European Union. Higher wages could help companies retain employees and encourage employers to look for ways to improve work organization, writes Kaia Vask.

Imagine payday. The money arrives in your bank account, but every euro has already been spoken for. Rent, heating, electricity, food and fuel can consume most of your wages. You go to work every day and do your job well. You do not live beyond your means, yet your income is not enough to support your family until the next payday. Is this really all that honest work gets you in Estonia?

As of April 1 this year, the minimum wage for a full-time employee is €946 per month. That is the gross wage, from which taxes and other deductions are taken, leaving a considerably smaller amount in the employee's bank account. Meanwhile, consumer prices in October were up 4.2 percent compared with a year earlier, with housing and transportation becoming particularly expensive.

These are expenses that cannot be put off while waiting for better times. In Estonia's climate, it is impossible to get by without a roof over your head for most of the year and transportation costs are unavoidable for many people. According to Statistics Estonia, as many as four in 10 people were already commuting to work in another municipality three years ago.

Estonia's minimum wage has the lowest purchasing power in Europe

The purchasing power of Estonia's minimum wage is the lowest in the European Union (EU). According to Eurostat's July comparison, it ranks below all 22 EU member states that have a national minimum wage. In other words, minimum wage workers in Estonia can afford fewer goods and services than their counterparts in any of those countries.

Estonians are active in the labor market. Last year, the employment rate among women was the highest in the EU, while the rate among men was above average. So we do not have a problem with people's willingness to work, but rather with how much they are paid for their work. In a country that values work, having a full-time job should not mean constantly worrying about how to make ends meet until the next payday.

I am particularly concerned about the situation facing young people. Imagine a young person who has found a full-time job and wants to move out of their parents' home. They browse apartment rental listings, add up the security deposit, the first month's rent and other expenses and realize they simply cannot afford to live on their own.

Having a job should give young people the opportunity to become independent and make plans for the future. When a large share of their wages goes toward rent, food and commuting, there is little left to cover unexpected expenses or save for the future. Postponing independent living may therefore not be a matter of choice for young people, but a necessity.

In some families, parents can support their adult children while they study. In others, this is not possible because the parents' own income barely covers everyday expenses. As a result, two equally capable and hardworking young people may face very different opportunities from the very beginning of their independent lives.

The Eurostudent survey published this year shows that, for many university students in Estonia, working alongside their studies remains a matter of making ends meet. The proportion of students who could not pursue higher education without working has increased. While working during their studies provides valuable work experience, it also leaves students with less time to study.

In Estonia, young people are entitled to the same national minimum wage as other employees. This is an important principle that must be preserved. Pay should not depend on an employee's age.

Employers' concerns understandable, while rising salaries would benefit everyone

I also understand employers' concerns. Wage increases can raise business costs and require more careful decision-making, while smaller companies in particular may find it difficult to adapt quickly to changes. However, the future of Estonian business cannot depend on how long people can manage to get by on low wages.

"Available evidence provides no basis for treating job losses as an inevitable consequence of increasing the national minimum wage."

Estonia's experience so far does not support the claim that raising the minimum wage inevitably leads to job losses. A study by the University of Tartu's Center for Applied Social Sciences (RAKE) found that the impact of previous minimum wage increases on employment was largely statistically insignificant or even positive. This does not mean that raising wages is always risk-free, but the available evidence provides no basis for treating job losses as an inevitable consequence of increasing the national minimum wage.

The relationship between wage growth and productivity works both ways. Higher wages can help companies retain employees and encourage employers to look for ways to improve work organization, develop employees' skills and invest in new technology. None of this happens automatically, however. It requires decisions and investments by businesses, as well as government support to help smaller companies adapt to changes.

Higher wages also stimulate the economy. When lower-income workers have more money left after payday, they can spend more on goods and services. Some of that money then flows back to our businesses. Everyone benefits.

Trade unions expect employers to present a concrete proposal for the national minimum wage on November 23 that fairly reflects employees' contributions. This would provide an opportunity to reach an agreement and introduce the new minimum wage on the usual date, January 1, 2027.

This year, the €946 minimum wage did not take effect until April 1. This meant lost earnings for employees and lower tax revenue for the state budget. Because such delays harm both workers and public finances, this must not happen again in 2027.

The negotiations will also determine whether low-wage workers and their families can look to the future with a little more confidence next year and whether young people will be able to earn enough to move out of their parents' homes or reduce their working hours and devote more attention to their studies.

World.title: PÖFF and Odessa Film Festival to present the Free World Award
World.content:
The Odesa International Film Festival and the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) will begin presenting the Free World Award, recognizing films that explore themes of freedom, human dignity and human rights.

The establishment of the award is part of a memorandum of cooperation between PÖFF and the Ukrainian State Film Agency, signed Thursday by festival director Tiina Lokk and Andri Ossipov. The memorandum is valid for three years. The cooperation aims to increase the international visibility of Ukrainian cinema and strengthen ties between filmmakers from Ukraine, Estonia and other countries.

According to Lokk, the award demonstrates the humanity of the Ukrainian people. "When you are able to recognize and support others who are also fighting against injustice, even in such difficult circumstances, it speaks to dignity and a profound capacity for empathy," she said.

The inaugural award will go to Kurdish director Halkawt Mustafa for his film "No Paradise if You Are Killed by a Woman." The film tells the story of a Kurdish female sniper fighting against the Islamic State group in Iraq. Iraq has also submitted the film for Oscar consideration and it is screening in PÖFF's Best of Festivals program.

The award includes a bird-shaped sculpture symbolizing freedom. The sculpture is made from metal melted down from remnants of weapons and ammunition used in the war in Ukraine. The award will be presented at PÖFF's closing ceremony on November 20.

World.title: Martin Herem: An information operation built on sabotage
World.content:
Russia's attacks against Estonian defense industry companies are unlikely to intimidate either the companies themselves or society as a whole. However, the real impact and benefit may lie in the chain of events that follows, and that may have been exactly what the GRU intended to achieve, writes Martin Herem.

Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, carried out an attack against an Estonian defense industry company. Unsuccessfully. In essence, for the second time since August.

One might assume this was the result of carelessness or incompetence. The excellent work of the security services of several countries certainly deserves recognition. While this can generally be viewed as a failure, events of recent days have made me question that assessment. I now consider the results far more successful than they initially appeared.

No major material damage was caused. Apparently, none was caused in the previous incident either. These attacks are unlikely to frighten companies or society as a whole, but their impact and value may lie in the processes they set in motion afterward. That may have been precisely what the GRU was aiming for.

The first "result" is something we will inevitably create ourselves if we close border crossings with Russia. Regardless of the economic costs involved, such a decision would generate extensive debate and criticism among politicians and within society, as well as abroad. Government institutions would be forced into action, explaining processes and objectives with little practical benefit. Providing explanations may accomplish very little, but it certainly creates a workload.

"We simply failed to see the true objective behind the smoke from the arson attack."

In addition, debates would emerge around issues such as whether the border should have been closed long ago, whether the Latvian border should also be closed, whether this outcome was predictable, whether some people should still be allowed to cross for particular reasons, whether decisions are being driven by emotion rather than rational calculation, and so on.

As a result, people who should be focusing on genuinely important work will spend the coming days and weeks explaining, reporting, gathering facts and debunking misinformation. Countless unproductive work hours will be consumed. Important matters will be delayed.

Because the sabotage operation was carried out so poorly and our countermeasures were so effective, some people will naturally ask who was really behind it and what the actual objective was.

If that question arises in the mind of someone who already holds negative views toward the authorities, it becomes more likely that the "real" beneficiary will be seen not as Russia but as Estonia's own security services and government. In that case, the GRU achieves a second "result": in addition to controversy over a border closure, suspicion shifts toward the state itself.

More disappointed people will inevitably join in. Trust will erode for a time, while fertile ground will be created for other, perhaps future, conspiracy theories. In a democratic country with freedom of speech and a strong internet connection, this effect spreads at the speed of light, pausing only occasionally to pick up a few absurd comments along the way.

Defense industry companies, meanwhile, will spend resources improving their security. Companies involved in projects supporting Ukraine will request confidentiality. Those demanding transparency in decision-making will call for the publication of company lists. And thus another "debate" begins, once again burdening people and organizations with unnecessary expenditures of time and effort.

At some point, the Latvian origin of the sabotage suspects may also become an issue, triggering criticism of Latvian institutions and reopening discussions about controls on the Estonia-Latvia border.

I do not know how much this operation cost the Russians, but we will likely spend considerably more on securing companies and on all the public discussion it generates. The effects, including distrust and resentment, may last far longer. Latvia, meanwhile, gains eight citizens who can be portrayed as suspicious elements, potentially prompting increased scrutiny of certain groups. That, in turn, consumes additional resources and further reduces trust within society. Each future operation of this kind only adds momentum to the information operation described above.

So perhaps this was not really a failure after all. We simply failed to see the true objective behind the smoke from the arson attack. Perhaps the GRU never planned it this way, but that is certainly how it turned out.

World.title: Al-Qasab Salt Season returns with heritage displays, food and family attractions
World.content:
The fourth Al-Qasab Salt Season began on Thursday in the town’s heritage village, celebrating more than three centuries of salt production in the Riyadh region.

Historically known as the “Village of Salt” and nicknamed the “City of White Gold,” the area has supplied salt for more than three centuries.

The season aims to promote salt production, which is celebrated as one of the region’s most renowned natural resources.

Annual sales of Al-Qasab salt exceed SR200 million ($53.3 million), representing about 5 percent of the Kingdom’s total salt production value of SR3.7 billion.

That salt is distributed both domestically and internationally and is prized for its high quality and nutritional value.

Under the patronage of Minister of Municipalities and Housing Majed Al-Hogail and in the presence of the Minister of Commerce Majid Al-Qasabi, visitors are invited to step back in time and experience the atmosphere of the town as it was in the late 18th and 19th centuries.

The season features about 50 local exhibitors and more thab 300 volunteers from the community.

The event is expected to attract more than 100,000 attendees to its various activities, while also empowering the private sector and fostering the development of tourism and national heritage.

The event highlights traditional salt extraction, a craft passed down through generations of Al-Qasab residents for more than 300 years.

Visitors can follow the salt production process at a model saltworks, from manual extraction from pits known locally as Jifar Al-Milh to purification, packaging and marketing. Visitors will be able to sample salt flakes and other salty goods.

The Culinary Arts Commission is showcasing innovative uses of local salt, including beef ribs and a millet-and-almond dessert, alongside gift boxes and samples of Al-Qasab salt flakes.

Visitors can also tour several palaces and museums in the heritage village and visit the Heritage Commission’s visitor center.

The space is family-friendly and features attractions such as a cultural theater, a salt-themed rest area, an arts zone as well as a children’s corner.

Other attractions include an equestrian competition, a classic car display and the Al-Qasab Salt Race on Nov. 21, with routes for families and runners.

The event runs until Nov. 28.

World.title: Middle East’s proposed transport corridors will benefit all
World.content:
Writing in 1919, British geographer Halford Mackinder, considered by many to be one of the architects of modern geopolitics, described the strategic importance of what he called the “world island” — the connected landmass of Asia, Europe and Africa. Sitting at the hinge of this so-called world island is the Middle East, making it one of the most strategic regions in the world. Yet, for too long, the region’s potential for global and regional transport has not been fully realized.

Moving beyond traditional discussions about which shipping lanes are open or closed, there are four recent initiatives worth examining: Iraq’s Development Road, the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, the Gulf Cooperation Council railway project and the proposed north-south railway corridor connecting Turkiye and Saudi Arabia through Syria and Jordan. If realized, these projects could make the Middle East one of the most important regions in the world for global transport and trade.

In fact, all four initiatives have seen important developments in recent weeks. In late October, Iraq announced further progress on the engineering designs for its Development Road project. On Nov. 5, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development published a major report examining the potential of the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor. On Nov. 8, the GCC member states signed an agreement in Bahrain reaffirming their commitment to a regional railway network. And, on Nov. 9, Syria and Jordan signed a memorandum of understanding to improve railway connectivity between the two countries.

The Iraqi Development Road, commonly referred to as the “dry canal,” is an ambitious project involving Iraq, Turkiye, Qatar and the UAE. The ultimate aim is to connect Iraq’s Grand Faw Port on the Gulf to European markets through Turkiye. Recently, the engineering designs for the approximately 1,200-km project entered their final stages, with the designs expected to be completed before the end of this year. Iraqi officials have indicated that the first phase could be finished as early as 2028, although other official projections suggest a longer timeline.

These projects could make the Middle East one of the most important regions in the world for global transport and trade Luke Coffey

This initiative seeks to put Iraq’s strategic position on a more stable footing, while bolstering Turkiye’s ambitions to become a regional transport hub. When completed, Iraqi officials estimate that cargo could reach European markets from the Middle East in just 25 days, compared with the 36 days required when using the Suez Canal.

However, as with all ambitious infrastructure projects, funding remains uncertain. The Development Road is estimated to cost about $17 billion and it remains unclear who will ultimately foot the bill.

Another major initiative is the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, or IMEC. The idea is to connect markets in South Asia to European and global markets by utilizing new transport infrastructure through the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Israel.

While this sounds good in theory, several geopolitical and physical obstacles must be overcome. First proposed in September 2023, enthusiasm for the project stalled following the outbreak of war in Gaza, although there has been renewed diplomatic interest in 2026. Also, Jordan remains the main rail gap along the route, with major investment and construction needed.

In addition, with everything happening around the Strait of Hormuz, it is right to question the wisdom of leaving Oman out of the initiative. Utilizing Oman’s Duqm Port would allow cargo to bypass the Strait of Hormuz altogether, providing another option for transporting goods into the Arabian Peninsula.

The third initiative is the GCC’s plan to connect all six member states by rail by December 2030. Already, Gulf officials estimate that the project is about 56 percent complete, although this figure includes planning, engineering and other preparatory work, in addition to actual railway construction. Such a network could play an important role not only in improving transport and trade among GCC members but also in connecting the broader Development Road and IMEC initiatives.

Some might view these different projects as competing with one another. But in reality, this is not a zero-sum game Luke Coffey

The fourth and final initiative, also focused on improving rail connections in the Middle East, is the Turkish-Saudi proposal to improve railway links between Anatolia and the Arabian Peninsula, based loosely on the old Hijaz Railway.

With this initiative, however, the consequences of years of civil war in Syria are being felt. The biggest gap in the proposed railway network remains between Syria and Jordan. Turkiye is already working to restore railway connections to Aleppo but about 400 km of missing or damaged rail infrastructure remains along the broader route through Syria toward the Jordanian border.

Earlier this month, Syria and Jordan signed a memorandum of understanding covering railway rehabilitation and feasibility studies for the construction of a railway connecting Damascus and Amman.

Because the original Hijaz Railway used narrow-gauge tracks, while the proposed modern freight corridor would require standard-gauge infrastructure, this is not simply a matter of renovating an older railway line. Instead, significant sections of new railway infrastructure will have to be constructed.

Some might view these different projects as competing with one another. But in reality, this is not a zero-sum game. Although geopolitical rivals Turkiye and Israel are advocating different trade routes through the Iraqi Development Road and IMEC, the two initiatives could ultimately complement each other. Both major rail projects can also complement the Development Road and IMEC and, with some strategically placed branch lines, could even connect these different initiatives.

Having multiple options for transporting goods across the Middle East would help reduce dependence on any single route, while providing alternatives when geopolitical tensions or other disruptions threaten global commerce. It is the global consumer and the international economy that benefit from redundancy and diversity in trade routes.

Therefore, while there is considerable discussion about keeping shipping lanes open across the broader Middle East, policymakers should not overlook the region’s potential to serve as the transport hinge connecting Asian, European and African markets to the global economy.

World.title: Connectivity a new pillar in EU-Turkiye ties
World.content:
In Brussels on Monday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan highlighted regional connectivity as a potential area for constructive cooperation between Turkiye and the EU, given the importance of transport and energy.

Turkiye brings several connectivity initiatives to the table in its discussions with the EU. These include the Middle Corridor, Iraq’s Development Road project, the Four Seas Initiative, the Hijaz railway project and the Global Gateway. These initiatives share a common strategic aim: to connect Asia to Europe. Turkiye plays a significant role in each of these interconnected initiatives.

Ankara shares the concerns of the EU regarding the disruptions that this year’s escalations have caused in the Strait of Hormuz, Bab Al-Mandab Strait, Red Sea and Black Sea. These disruptions affect the connectivity chain between the Gulf and Europe. Within this context, Turkiye places itself as a cross-regional hub that connects Europe to the Gulf, the Caucasus and Central Asia through alternative corridors. In Fidan’s words: “We need to take responsibility commensurate with this role, both by proposing solutions and by taking the lead.” Turkiye’s incentives extend beyond its sense of regional responsibility, as there is also a significant economic opportunity it is keen not to miss.

Turkiye last month inaugurated a new EU-backed railway section near its border with Bulgaria, marking a key step in the bloc’s efforts to strengthen transport links with Central Asia and reduce shipping times along the Middle Corridor. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos attended the opening in person to indicate the importance both Ankara and Brussels attach to the railway.

Turkiye places itself as a cross-regional hub that connects Europe to the Gulf, the Caucasus and Central Asia Dr. Sinem Cengiz

The European Commission described the railway as the largest EU-Turkish infrastructural project undertaken so far and the first concrete outcome of its cross-regional connectivity agenda, which aims to boost transport, energy and connectivity between Europe and Central Asia through the South Caucasus and the Black Sea region.

Turkiye has significant leverage in the South Caucasus, having close political and energy relations with Azerbaijan, functioning ties with Georgia and having embarked on a normalization track with Armenia. For Europe, Turkiye’s geostrategic position in the Black Sea and geopolitical significance in the South Caucasus are the key motivations to push for a connectivity agenda with Ankara.

Over the past two decades, Turkiye-EU relations have been characterized by stagnation due to the stalled accession process, a lack of progress on visa liberalization and customs union modernization, and other foreign policy issues. However, connectivity is emerging as a new and positive agenda for engagement between the two sides, even though this is driven by necessity.

The EU acknowledges the increasing Turkish involvement in regional connectivity initiatives. Iraq signed a deal with Turkiye for the Development Road project, also known as the “dry canal,” which seeks to connect the Grand Faw Port in southern Iraq with Turkiye and eventually European markets through a network of roads, railways and energy links. Although the project, in which two Gulf states are also involved, faces some internal and external challenges, it would serve as a significant connectivity corridor if it were to come to fruition.

There is also the Syrian-proposed Four Seas Initiative, which is an alternative trade and connectivity route aimed at linking the region with Europe via Turkiye. The Four Seas Initiative seeks to position Syria as a connecting point between four major geographical areas: the Gulf, the Mediterranean, the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. Turkiye lies at the center of this initiative. This is why Ankara supports Syrian and Iraqi stability.

The Middle Corridor is another promising route for linking Europe to Central Asia and beyond. The Development Road, within this context, connects Basra to Turkiye and extends to the Middle Corridor. These projects seek to bypass disrupted maritime chokepoints.

Within these projects, Turkiye has the potential to emerge as a strategic partner — some even call it an energy gatekeeper — for the EU, using its location and political ties with regional states as significant tools.

Turkiye has the potential to emerge as a strategic partner — some even call it an energy gatekeeper — for the EU Dr. Sinem Cengiz

Europe previously considered the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, known as IMEC, as the key route for connectivity. However, since the start of the Gaza war in 2023, this project, in which Israel is a significant link, has been declining in relevance. This has pushed the EU to reassess its strategic options, although it also views the other routes as complementary to the IMEC. Thus, it appears the EU is seeking a multicorridor strategy. This would still be a gain for Turkiye because the IMEC was set to bypass the country altogether — a move seen as problematic by Ankara as it would undermine its strategic position as a bridge between Asia and Europe.

Certain developments, such as the US-Iran war, the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the growing insecurity around maritime chokepoints, have severely affected regional connectivity. However, other developments, such as the fall of the Assad regime in Syria and the new Iraqi approach, offer significant opportunities for Turkiye in particular.

EU officials have highlighted that relations with Turkiye are progressing on two separate tracks: while the accession process is stalled, significant opportunities remain under the connectivity agenda. This is a clear example of compartmentalization in international relations. Could progress in the second track open doors for the first track to advance? That cannot be assumed, as it is a far more complicated issue that has several variables.

Dr. Sinem Cengiz is a Turkish political analyst who specializes in Turkiye’s relations with the Middle East.
