NEW DELHI: SpiceJet's worsening cash crunch is disrupting flight operations, with the airline cancelling a large number of scheduled flights amid mounting financial difficulties.Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport has issued an advisory warning passengers that some SpiceJet flights may be affected, urging them to contact the airline directly for the latest updates on their flight status and travel plans."Please note, due to operational challenges being faced by SpiceJet Airlines, some flights may be impacted. Passengers are requested to contact SpiceJet directly for the latest information regarding their flight status and travel plans. Thank you for your patience and understanding," the airport said.The advisory comes as SpiceJet grapples with a deepening financial crisis and mounting flight cancellations. Despite receiving approval from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) to operate around 66 flights daily during the winter schedule, the airline has been operating barely 15 flights a day while continuing to accept bookings across its published schedule, according to an ET report.The carrier is also facing difficulties in keeping its aircraft operational. Six planes recently taken on lease remain grounded over unpaid dues, while Moldova-based FLYONE terminated its agreement to lease three aircraft to SpiceJet on Monday, citing outstanding payments.Amid the financial strain, SpiceJet's board has approved a proposal to raise up to Rs 5,500 crore. However, an ET report cited airline executives as warning that the carrier could be forced to shut down if fresh funds are not infused within a week.The DGCA has issued a show-cause notice to the airline for failing to maintain its approved schedule. However, the regulator has not yet barred SpiceJet from accepting bookings for future flights. A senior DGCA official said the civil aviation ministry would have to decide whether to suspend the airline's operations.

World.title: Economic losses from Indonesia fires could reach $30 billion, research shows
World.content:
Wildfires that tore through Indonesian forest and peatland areas this year could cost the Southeast Asian country more than $30 billion, the co-author of a study on the subject said on Friday (November 20, 2026).

Losses of physical assets and from disrupted economic activity alone would cost an estimated 340 trillion rupiah ($18.6 billion), according to new research by the Jakarta-based Center of Economic and Law Studies (CELIOS).

That was equal to about 2.69% of Indonesia's GDP, the CELIOS report said.

It said additional health costs from acute respiratory infections caused by the wildfires on Indonesia's Borneo, Sumatra and Papua islands could be as high as 225 trillion rupiah ($12.3 billion).

"There are also economic costs borne by the public, both directly and indirectly," CELIOS director Nailul Huda, a co-author of the report, told AFP.

Wildfires have burned through 2.88 million hectares (7.1 million acres) so far in 2026, according to the Nusantara Atlas deforestation monitor, an area 18 times the size of London.

Indonesia experiences fires every dry season, but this year's blazes have been particularly severe.

Researchers said last week that a strong El Nino weather phenomenon, climate change, deforestation and peatland drainage for mining and plantations have supercharged this year's fire season.

The fires emitted a foul haze that made hundreds of thousands of people in Indonesia ill and drifted as far as Malaysia and Singapore.

World.title: Cheetah brought from Botswana gives birth to four cubs at Kuno
World.content:
A two-and-a-half-year-old cheetah, KOMG 3, brought from Botswana, gave birth to four healthy cubs in the wild at Madhya Pradesh’s Kuno National Park on Friday (November 20, 2026), Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav said.

Calling the development a matter of pride for Madhya Pradesh and the entire country, Chief Minister Mohan Yadav said it was a historic achievement for Project Cheetah.

In a post on X, Bhupender Yadav said KOMG 3 is the first cheetah from Botswana to give birth in India.

“This is a landmark moment for Project Cheetah and a proud milestone in India’s journey towards restoring a viable cheetah population,” he added.

This is the second recorded birth in the wild since the reintroduction programme began in 2022.

With these four new arrivals, India’s cheetah population has risen to 62, including 43 Indian-born individuals.

“Every such birth strengthens our hope, deepens our commitment, and reminds us that conservation is a journey of patience, perseverance and collective effort,” Mr. Yadav said.

He also acknowledged the dedication, commitment and hard work of project managers, veterinarians, frontline forest staff and everyone working tirelessly for the success of Project Cheetah.

In a statement, CM Mohan Yadav said, “This is a matter of pride for Madhya Pradesh and the entire country. The birth of cubs in India for the first time by a female cheetah from Botswana is a historic achievement of Project Cheetah.

“This is an important and encouraging step towards restoring a viable cheetah population in India. KOMG 3, a female cheetah, gave birth to four healthy cubs in natural conditions after spending more than four months in the wild.”

He said this significant success was achieved due to the dedication, tireless hard work, and commitment of officials involved in the management of Project Cheetah, wildlife experts, veterinarians and frontline forest workers.

Madhya Pradesh is continuously achieving new milestones in the field of wildlife conservation and biodiversity promotion, he added.

World.title: Excise crackdown in Sabarimala: 96 COTPA cases registered
World.content:
The Excise department in Keralam has launched a crackdown on substance abuse during the Sabarimala Mandala pilgrimage season. As part of the drive launched under the aegis of the Assistant Excise Commissioner (Pamba), based in three temporary range offices established at Sannidhanam, Pamba, and Nilakkal, as many as 96 cases under COTPA (the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act) have been registered, collecting a fine of ₹19,200 and seizing 300 grams of tobacco products.

Given the strict ban on the sale and consumption of all forms of alcohol, narcotics and prohibited tobacco products at Sannidhanam, Pamba and along the pilgrimage routes, the Excise Department is conducting rigorous inspections in the region. A round-the-clock control room has also been set up to coordinate enforcement activities.

Department officials said the inspections would be intensified in the coming days.

The public is advised to register any complaints or grievances through the Sannidhanam Excise grievance redressal number: 04735 202203.

World.title: YSRCP accuses NDA government of leaving over ₹8,700 crore in fee reimbursement dues
World.content:
The YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) has accused the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) coalition government of leaving more than ₹8,700 crore in fee reimbursement and hostel maintenance dues, challenging Education Minister Nara Lokesh to reconcile his claims on payments with the figures in the government’s budget documents.

Addressing a press conference on Friday (November 20, 2026), YSRCP Political Affairs Committee member Duvvuri Krishna said the government was responsible for paying about ₹11,700 crore towards 12 quarters under the Vidya Deevena and Vasathi Deevena schemes. However, its expenditure in 2024-25 and 2025-26 amounted to only about ₹3,000 crore, according to budget figures, he alleged.

Mr. Krishna said the previous YSRCP government had spent ₹12,350 crore on fee reimbursement between 2019-20 and 2023-24 and another ₹4,850 crore on hostel and food expenses under Vasathi Deevena. It had also cleared ₹2,006 crore in fee reimbursement arrears left by the previous TDP government, he said.

Rejecting Mr. Lokesh’s allegation that the previous government had left ₹3,900 crore in dues, he said only ₹708 crore pertaining to the third quarter of 2023-24 remained unpaid because of the election code.

Questioning the Minister’s claim that ₹1,665 crore had been released in 2025-26, Mr. Krishna said the revised budget estimates showed only ₹1,200 crore. He also pointed to discrepancies in the figures cited by the Minister and those presented in the budget for tribal welfare, minority welfare and Economically Weaker Section categories.

World.title: 'If we have water, will give to T.N.' says Shivakumar after SC verdict on Cauvery dispute | LIVE
World.content:
The Supreme Court dismissed Tamil Nadu’s application in the decades-old Cauvery water-sharing dispute claiming a shortfall of 11.719 thousand million cubic feet in the Cauvery river water, according to the State’s formula. Karnataka had opposed the application on the ground that the CWMA had not ordered it. The judgment was pronounced by a Bench led by Justice Vikram Nath.

Also read | Tamil Nadu’s claim of Cauvery backlog and the Supreme Court’s response | Explained

Tamil Nadu has also accused Karnataka of withholding water despite having sufficient reserves, pointing to a combined reservoir storage of approximately 49 tmcft, which it maintained was adequate to meet its water-sharing obligations to the lower riparian State.

Earlier, Karnataka, in an affidavit filed before the Supreme Court, had argued that Tamil Nadu had been allocated the lion’s share of 404.25 tmcft on account of its historic irrigation claims, while Karnataka received only 284.75 tmcft out of the 483 tmcft available up to Billigundulu, without adequately accounting for its drought-prone areas.

World.title: Pregnant woman dies of suspected dengue in Erode district
World.content:
A 39-year-old seven-month pregnant woman died while undergoing treatment at the Coimbatore Medical College Hospital on Thursday (November 19, 2026), with dengue suspected to be the cause of death.

Gandhimathi, wife of Karthikeyan, hailed from Marappampalayam near Sivagiri and was residing at Velampalayam near Modakkurichi.

She developed fever recently and initially underwent treatment at a private hospital. She was subsequently admitted to the Government Erode Medical College Hospital in Perundurai and later shifted to the Coimbatore Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment. She died at the hospital on Thursday.

Her death has caused concern among residents of Velampalayam. Health Department officials have begun inspecting the area and are taking preventive measures against dengue, including steps to check the spread of the disease.

World.title: 4,962 acres land in 90 villages need to be acquired for 201-km RRR’s southern section: Officials inform Telangana CS
World.content:
Telangana Chief Secretary Sanjay Jaju reviewed the progress of land acquisition for the 201- kilometre-long southern part of the Regional Ring Road (RRR) and the proposed radial roads.

He held the review with Hyderabad Metropolitan Development Authority (HMDA) Metropolitan Commissioner Sarfraz Ahmed, Invest Telangana CEO Ajit Reddy and other senior officials in Hyderabad on Thursday (November 19, 2026). Discussions were also held on the Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) signed during the 2025 Investors Summit.

Officials informed the Chief Secretary that 4,962 acres of land spread across 90 villages in six districts need to be acquired for the RRR southern section. Mr. Jaju directed the district Collectors concerned to expedite the issuance of preliminary notifications for the radial roads and ensure that the project is completed within the stipulated timelines.

The Chief Secretary also reviewed the status of MoUs signed during the 2025 Investors Summit, along with the proposals being considered for the upcoming Invest Telangana Global Summit. Industries Department officials were directed to designate dedicated departmental officers for each sector to closely monitor the proposals and ensure their effective implementation on the ground.

World.title: Farmers’ body calls public hearing on Greenko project expansion a ‘farce’, seeks its cancellation
World.content:
The Andhra Pradesh Rythu Sangham has demanded the cancellation of the public hearing conducted on November 19 at Pinnapuram village in Panyam mandal of erstwhile Kurnool district on the proposed expansion of Greenko’s pumped storage power project, alleging that residents of the affected villages were deliberately excluded.

In a statement on Friday (November 20, 2026), the association’s State president V. Krishnaiah and secretary K. Prabhakar Reddy alleged that the public hearing on the proposal to enhance the project’s power generation capacity from 1,200 MW to 1,600 MW was a farce, as people from Pinnapuram and Gumitham Thanda, the villages directly affected by the project, were not allowed to participate.

They alleged that the exercise was conducted outside Pinnapuram village under police protection, with people brought from Kurnool and Nandyal towns and existing employees of Greenko being used to create the impression of public participation.

The leaders alleged that Kurnool District Collector A. Siri, Pollution Control Board officials and representatives of Greenko conducted the hearing without allowing the affected villagers to express their views. They demanded that the proceedings be scrapped and a fresh hearing be held with the participation of all affected residents.

According to them, the government had already taken over approximately 7,500 acres belonging to Pinnapuram and another 1,000 acres associated with Gumitham Thanda for the Greenko project. The lands had reportedly been under the cultivation and possession of farmers for more than a century, but the Revenue authorities had failed to recognise their rights, they alleged.

The association leaders claimed that the government had taken possession of the lands without paying compensation, citing the absence of formal title documents, thereby rendering farmers and agricultural labourers dependent on them landless and without livelihoods.

They also said that more than 8,000 cattle, buffaloes, sheep and goats in the region depended on these lands for grazing and fodder. The diversion of the lands for the project had adversely affected the livelihoods of farming families and the availability of grazing resources for livestock, the leaders alleged.

The leaders accused the government and officials of prioritising the interests of Greenko over the livelihoods of local communities and environmental protection. They said the proposed expansion would further aggravate the difficulties faced by people in the affected villages.

The association leaders demanded that the government cancel the November 19 public hearing, recognise the rights of people over the lands they had been using for generations and ensure livelihood security for farmers and agricultural workers. They also called for measures to protect the environment and safeguard grazing resources.

World.title: Pakistan’s natural resources worth $8-10tr at 'most conservative estimate', says Dar
World.content:
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Friday said that the estimated worth of minerals, hydrocarbons and other natural resources in Pakistan was between $8 trillion and $10tr.

And this was the “most conservative estimate”, he said while addressing a ceremony held in Karachi to mark the arrival of a Turkish seismic research vessel, Oruc Reis.

The vessel, which arrived on Thursday, will be used for offshore oil and gas exploration in Pakistan.

Dar began his address by welcoming the leadership and professionals of the Turkish Petroleum, as well as the captain, crew and seismic research team of Oruc Reis, and termed the occasion a “historic moment”.

He noted that Oruc Reis brought “Turkish scientific expertise together with the experience and capabilities of our national energy companies to advance exploration in Pakistan’s offshore domain”.

Dar added, “Every successful journey of exploration begins with knowledge. The data gathered by this vessel may deepen our understanding of the geological structures beneath the seabed and provide a stronger basis for Pakistan’s future exploration plan.”

He described offshore exploration as “complex, capital-intensive and inherently uncertain”.

And a seismic survey could not guarantee a commercial discovery, he continued. “But no discovery can be made without seismic and exploration,” he stressed, adding that today, Pakistan was taking that step with “confidence, responsibility and the prayers of our people”.

He said Pakistan sought a long-term energy partnership with Turkiye, encompassing offshore exploration, minerals and renewable energy.

“You all have witnessed three memorandums of understanding signed between the relevant Turkish and Pakistani agencies.

“We want Pakistani geologists and engineers to work very closely with their Turkish counterparts. We want our universities and research institutions to develop partnerships in marine, geoscience and offshore engineering,” he said.

He assured “our Turkish partners and brothers” that the government of Pakistan would extend every appropriate facilitation to the “very important mission” to be undertaken by Oruc Reis.

“All offshore activities must observe the highest standards of maritime safety and environmental protection. Our seas are an economic asset, but they are also a national trust. Development and environmental stewardship must proceed together,” he stressed.

Dar further said that the Turkish energy minister told him that the seismic mission would take around five to six months. “I said, you won’t be allowed to leave unless you give us good news of a real discovery,” he added.

He said he would come across people who described Pakistan as a country in a debt trap.

He went on to say the estimated value of the country’s natural resources, including mines and minerals, hydrocarbons, gemstones and rare earth materials, far exceeded its debt burden.

“Sometimes people talk about Pakistan being in debt, being a heavily indebted country, or being in a debt-trap; I always negate that,” he said, adding that Pakistan was endowed with abundant natural resources.

He thanked the Turkish government and people for standing alongside Pakistan and described the arrival of the Oruc Reis as another example of the two countries’ partnership.

The arrival of the Oruç Reis vessel follows the government’s revival of offshore exploration efforts after a gap of nearly two decades. The Offshore Bid Round 2025 was launched in January last year, offering 40 offshore blocks in the Indus and Makran basins for petroleum exploration.

Turkish Petroleum Offshore Company (TPOC), a subsidiary of Turkish Petroleum Corporation, has partnered with local state-owned energy companies, including Oil and Gas Development Company Limited (OGDCL), Mari Energies and Pakistan Petroleum Limited (PPL), for exploration activities in three blocks.

It holds a 25 per cent interest and operatorship in the Eastern Offshore Indus-C block in the Arabian Sea, alongside stakes in two onshore blocks.

Pakistan’s offshore zone covers around 300,000 square kilometres, but only 18 wells have been drilled there since independence in 1947. A basin study by US firm DeGolyer and MacNaughton has identified significant untapped hydrocarbon potential in the country’s offshore basins.

World.title: On North Waziristan visit, CDF Munir vows to eliminate terrorism, preserve peace in KP
World.content:
Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir reaffirmed on Friday the security force’s “unwavering resolve” to decisively eliminate terrorism and preserve peace and stability of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in close coordination with law enforcement agencies (LEAs).

The CDF said this during a visit to Miranshah in KP’s North Waziristan, the military media wing said in a statement.

“He reaffirmed the unwavering resolve of the Security Forces, in close coordination with law enforcement agencies, to decisively eliminate the menace of terrorism and preserve the hard-earned peace and stability of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa,” the statement by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) quoted him as saying.

He also appreciated the “brave police force” in KP and expressed pride in its resilience and sacrifices against terrorism and Fitna-al-Khawarij — a term the state uses for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan.

During the visit, the CDF was given a comprehensive briefing on “the prevailing security situation, ongoing intelligence-based operations and measures being undertaken to consolidate the gains achieved through sustained counter terrorism efforts and ensure lasting peace and stability in the area”, the ISPR statement said.

It added that CDF Munir also interacted with officers and troops and appreciated their “high level of preparedness, professionalism and unwavering commitment to the defence and security of the motherland”.

Upon his arrival in Miranshah, the CDF was received by the Peshawar Corps commander and later laid a floral wreath at Yadgar-i-Shuhada to pay homage to the “supreme sacrifices of the shuhada (martyrs) of the Pakistan Army”, the statement said.

His visit to Miranshah comes a day after he visited Turbat in Balochistan, where, too, he was briefed on the prevailing security environment, operational preparedness and ongoing operations against externally sponsored terrorism.

Security forces continue to carry out counterterrorism action in KP and Balochistan, the two provinces that have been particularly affected by terrorism in Pakistan.

On Saturday, ISPR said four troops, including a major, were martyred while 24 terrorists were killed in IBOs in Balochistan and KP’s North Waziristan. Furthermore, last week, 74 terrorists were killed in IBOs in KP and Balochistan.

Meanwhile, the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based independent think tank monitoring conflict and security developments, has reported encouraging trends in the two provinces in its monthly assessment for October.

Pakistan overall witnessed a significant decline in terrorism-related violence during October, with attacks falling by 37 per cent, deaths resulting from these attacks declining by 57pc, and injuries decreasing by 71pc compared to September, the report said.

It added that the improvement was particularly pronounced in Balochistan and mainland KP.

“Balochistan recorded a substantial reduction in militant violence, with attacks declining by 46pc, from 132 in September to 71 in October. Deaths resulting from militant attacks decreased from 136 to 44, a reduction of approximately 68pc, while injuries declined from 63 to 37, representing a decrease of 41pc,” the report said.

Regarding mainland KP, it said a “significant decline” was witnessed in terrorism.

PICSS recorded 40 attacks during October, compared with 58 in September, representing a reduction of 31pc. Meanwhile, deaths resulting from these attacks declined from 90 to 38, a decrease of approximately 58pc, while injuries fell from 165 to 19, representing a reduction of 88pc.

The merged districts of KP recorded 30 attacks during October, compared with 34 in September, and deaths resulting from these attacks decreased from 33 to 25, while injuries increased from 11 to 13, the report said.

In October, the federal government also imposed emergency and governor’s rule in KP, citing the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”.

World.title: Musadik Malik arrives in New Delhi to attend SCO dialogue forum
World.content:
Federal Minister for Climate Change and Environmental Coordination Dr Musadik Malik arrived in New Delhi on Friday to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum.

His visit is a first by a Pakistani minister since former foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari attended the SCO meeting in the Indian state of Goa in May 2023, and two years after India’s Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar attended the bloc’s meeting in Islamabad in 2024.

Musadik was received at the airport by Pakistan’s Chargé d’Affaires Saad Waraich, according to the Pakistan High Commission in India.

Dr Malik will lead the Pakistan delegation at the forum, being held from Nov 20 to Nov 22.

The gathering will bring together representatives from Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) member states to discuss issues related to civilisational dialogue and cultural understanding, the Foreign Office said in an earlier statement.

“The government of Pakistan remains committed to promoting dialogue among civilisations and fostering people-to-people contacts within the SCO framework in a spirit of mutual respect,” the statement said.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is also scheduled to address the “Civilisational Dialogue Forum” of the 10-member regional bloc.

The forum was proposed by Modi at the SCO Council of Heads of State summit in Tianjin, China, in September 2025.

Recent high-level engagements between Pakistan and India have largely taken place under the SCO framework; for instance, Bilawal’s visit in 2023 and Jaishankar’s in 2024.

But neither visit had featured formal bilateral talks.

More recently, India’s SCO National Coordinator Alok Dimri visited Islamabad in late September for a preparatory meeting ahead of the next SCO Council of Heads of State summit.

“This is my first time on Pakistani soil; these SCO-related programmes will continue throughout the year and culminate in the Islamabad summit,” the Indian official told PTV News at the time.

Pakistan has assumed the rotating chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for the 2026-27 term and is scheduled to host the organisation’s summit in Islamabad in August 2027.

Relations between India and Pakistan have remained strained, particularly since the four-day military conflict in May 2025, with official engagement largely confined to multilateral forums.

Additional input from AFP

World.title: Two Pakistani schools earn global recognition at World’s Best School Prizes 2026
World.content:
Two Pakistani schools — a private institution in Lahore and a government-run high school in Hyderabad — have earned international recognition after being named among the leading institutions in their respective categories at the World’s Best School Prizes 2026, organised by T4 Education.

T4 Education is an international organisation that recognises outstanding educational institutions from around the world. The World’s Best School Prizes are regarded as among the most prestigious global awards in education. The prizes recognise schools across five categories: Community Collaboration, Environmental Action, Innovation, Overcoming Adversity and Supporting Healthy Lives.

This year, thousands of public and private schools from around the world submitted applications. Following an extensive evaluation process, an international panel of experts selected the winners in each category.

Pakistan was represented by two schools in the global competition: TNS Beaconhouse in Lahore, and Govt Girls High School Tando Mir Ghulam Hussain in Hyderabad.

The TNS Beaconhouse was announced as the winner of the “Supporting Healthy Lives” category.

The school has more than 1,100 students across kindergarten, primary and secondary levels and was recognised for its approach to supporting neurodivergent learners.

“TNS Beaconhouse, an independent kindergarten, primary and secondary school in Lahore, Pakistan, is challenging one of the country’s most deeply rooted educational barriers by reimagining how mainstream schools include neurodivergent learners through a wellbeing-led design that puts confidence, inclusion and agency first,” said the organisation.

The United Kingdom’s Swiss Cottage School, Development and Research Centre, won the “Community Collaboration” category, while Hyderabad’s Govt Girls High School Tando Mir Ghulam Hussain secured a place among the world’s top three schools in the same category.

On its website, T4 Education recognised the Hyderabad girls’ school for “spearheading a revolutionary learning model that empowers vulnerable and working girls who are unable to attend full school hours to continue learning without stepping away from the social realities that shape their lives”.

It said that the school was located in an underprivileged area where access to education was limited and girls were expected to contribute to household income or take on household responsibilities.

“Recognising that fixed schedules, rigid policies and a standardised curriculum of conventional approaches only deepen exclusion, the school has redesigned its structure to fit the lived reality of its students through a flexible, context-responsive model that prioritises continuity of learning over compliance,” it said.

T4 Education added that the school had employed a dual-shift system, allowing students to attend school either in the morning or the evening, with girls who work or support their families during the day being able to attend in the afternoon.

“In a community where education for girls has historically been undervalued, the school has invested heavily in building trust with families,” it added.

Teachers also conduct home visits for counselling sessions to help parents recognise the value of long-term education for their daughters.

“By involving families, the deeply rooted beliefs of early marriage and placing work over learning are being consistently challenged, and there has been a noticeable shift in the perception of gender value across the community.”

T4 Education said that within one year, school enrolment had increased by 90 per cent and attendance had improved by 80pc.

“Girls who once struggled to attend regularly are now actively participating in class, speaking confidently, and engaging with learning,” it added.

Furthermore, parents were now increasingly supportive of girls’ education with 80pc prioritising education over child labour.

World.title: Pakistan cruise to eight-wicket win over Sri Lanka to seal Test series 1-0
World.content:
Pakistan wrapped up an eight-wicket victory over Sri Lanka in the second and final Test, chasing down a target of 90 in just 13 overs to seal the two-match series 1-0 on Friday.

The hosts needed only 90 minutes on the fourth morning to complete the job after Mohammad Abbas dismissed the last Sri Lankan batter to end the visitors’ second innings at 316.

It was Pakistan’s first Test win since they beat the West Indies in the summer and their first series victory in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle.

The result was also just their third win in 11 matches in the current cycle, following draws against South Africa and the West Indies and series defeats in Bangladesh and England.

The first Test against Sri Lanka, also played in Rawalpindi, had ended in a draw.

Sri Lanka, who had resumed at 309-9, added seven runs before Asitha Fernando was trapped lbw for two by Abbas. Fernando reviewed the decision, but ball-tracking showed the delivery clipping the top of middle stump.

Abbas finished with three wickets for 55 runs from 34 overs, including 15 maidens. Aamer Jamal also claimed three wickets for 67, while Razaullah took two for 116 and Saqib Khan one before being sidelined by a hamstring injury.

Sri Lanka’s total left Pakistan needing 90 for victory, with Milan Rathnayaka unbeaten on 66 from 88 balls, including 12 fours.

His fighting innings had been central to a recovery after the visitors were dismissed for 98 in their first innings and conceded a 227-run lead when Pakistan replied with 325.

Pakistan’s pace attack had made full use of a green-tinged pitch to bowl Sri Lanka out cheaply on the opening day and put the hosts firmly in control.

The tourists began their second innings 153 runs behind and slipped to 10-2, but half-centuries from Kusal Mendis (53), Sonal Dinusha (54) and Rathnayaka helped them reach 316 and avoid an innings defeat.

Their 235-run effort on the third day briefly revived the contest, although the eventual target remained modest.

Pakistan began the chase positively, with Azan Awais and Tayyab Arif putting on 18 for the opening wicket. The stand ended when Lahiru Kumara bowled Tayyab for 13, with the batter beaten by movement off the pitch after striking three fours.

Azan was joined by Mohammad Taha, but the latter’s stay was brief. Asitha Fernando trapped him lbw for four, and Taha’s review failed as the ball was shown to be clipping leg stump. Pakistan were 37-2, but Sri Lanka could not build on the breakthrough.

Aamer was promoted up the order and turned the chase into a brisk finish. He struck 34 not out from 22 balls, hitting five fours and a six, and added an unbroken 53 with Azan for the third wicket.

Aamer attacked from the outset, taking boundaries off Fernando and Kumara before finishing the match with a four off Prabath Jayasuriya. Azan remained unbeaten on 32 from 36 balls, with five fours, as Pakistan reached 90-2 in 13 overs.

World.title: Pakistan 'unequivocally' condemns Houthi attack on Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper
World.content:
Pakistan on Friday “unequivocally” condemned a Houthi attack on Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, which serves as the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund.

“This act of aggression constitutes a grave violation of the sovereignty of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” the Foreign Office (FO) said in a statement condemning Thursday’s attack, without naming the tower.

Saudi state-run news agency SPA reported, citing the kingdom’s civil defence, that the attack caused material damage to several floors of the building and nearby buildings, but no injuries were reported. The statement carried by the SPA did not identify the tower, but an accompanying photograph published by the agency showed the Public Investment Fund Tower.

The strike blew out windows across seven to eight floors of PIF Tower, bending parts of its metal facade. It was the second time in less than two weeks that a Houthi attack damaged a landmark in Riyadh’s financial district, with state oil company Aramco’s building hit in a Nov 8 attack.

The Houthis have been firing at Saudi airports and oil infrastructure since Yemen’s frozen civil war reignited in July amid the US-Iran conflict.

The renewed fighting has shattered a UN-brokered truce reached in 2022 that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital, Sanaa.

Pakistan, which is party to two defence agreements along with Saudi Arabia — the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and the Saudi Mutual Defence Agreement that empower the parties to treat an attack on any one of them as an attack on all — has expressed its solidarity with the kingdom amid the escalation.

In its statement on Friday regarding Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the FO said: “The continued targeting of civilian infrastructure and economic facilities endangers innocent lives and poses a serious threat to regional peace and security. Such reprehensible attacks must cease forthwith.”

It added that Pakistan stood firmly with the government and people of Saudi Arabia. “It supports the kingdom’s legitimate right to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and to safeguard its citizens and residents. Pakistan has been and will continue to make all efforts for achieving lasting peace and stability in the region,” the statement said.

World.title: NCCIA arrests suspect over alleged sale of stolen US government data in Karachi
World.content:
The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) arrested a suspect allegedly involved in the illegal acquisition, possession and sale of sensitive and confidential data belonging to US government agencies, law enforcement organisations and private companies, according to an agency statement issued on Friday.

A criminal case has been registered at the NCCIA Police Station in Karachi under Sections 3 (unauthorised access to an information system or data), 4 (unauthorised copying or transmission of data), 13 (electronic forgery), 14 (electronic fraud) and 16 (unauthorised use of identity information) of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), 2016, as amended in 2025.

The investigation revealed that the suspect operated under the online alias “DP BRUCE” and allegedly used the cybercriminal platform LeakBase and Telegram to advertise and sell stolen databases containing sensitive information.

“The compromised data allegedly included information relating to prominent US government institutions, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), US Department of State, Department of Defence, and various US police departments, along with data associated with private businesses,” the press release stated.

According to the agency, further investigations revealed that the suspect allegedly received payments for the stolen data through cryptocurrency transactions, including Bitcoin.

The press release added that, acting on “credible information”, an NCCIA Karachi team conducted a raid in Karachi’s Manzoor Colony area and arrested the suspect on November 11.

During the investigation, a laptop belonging to the suspect was also seized.

“Preliminary technical examination revealed multiple databases and files apparently containing sensitive information associated with US government agencies, law enforcement departments, and other organisations,” the agency said.

Digital evidence also pointed to the use of online platforms for the alleged sale and distribution of stolen data.

“NCCIA Karachi remains committed to combating cybercrime, dismantling networks involved in the illegal trade of stolen data, and taking strict legal action against individuals involved in national and transnational cybercriminal activities,” the agency said.

A day earlier, the agency claimed to have uncovered an extensive financial network allegedly involved in illegal online betting and gambling, fraudulent business operations and suspected money laundering, with an estimated transaction exposure of up to Rs1 trillion.

Earlier this month, NCCIA reportedly arrested 130 suspects, including nine women and four foreign nationals, during multiple operations against international cyber fraud networks, illegal call centres, the sale of citizens’ personal data and online blackmailing.

World.title: US religious freedom panel says India is targeting minorities in voter roll revisions
World.content:
India has escalated its targeting of religious minorities during a voter list revision that struck off tens of millions of names nationwide, a US panel on religious freedom said on Thursday.

“The Indian govt is targeting Muslim citizens by removing them from voter rolls, calling them ‘foreigners’, and now illegally deporting them,” Asif Mahmood, the chair of the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), said in a statement.

India’s voter list revision removed 130 million names, roughly the population of Mexico, in the largest deletion of voters in the country’s history.

Data shows the omissions disproportionately affect Muslims, India’s largest minority, who have faced what rights groups describe as exclusionary policies and rising discrimination since Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) took power in 2014.

India’s Election Commission says it was removing duplicate, deceased, shifted and otherwise ineligible voters and that anyone excluded in error can pursue appeals.

The revision has become entangled with a separate drive to identify and expel suspected illegal immigrants, even though removal from the rolls does not itself establish that someone is a foreigner.

“The Indian government’s expulsion of its own citizens based on their Muslim faith is a shocking escalation of tactics that target religious minorities,” said Gene Mills, a commissioner on the US panel.

Mills urged the State Department to designate India as a “country of particular concern”.

USCIRF is a bipartisan body of the US government that monitors religious freedom around the world and makes policy recommendations, which are not binding. Washington has not acted on its recent recommendations on India.

India’s foreign ministry has cast USCIRF as biased. New Delhi has repeatedly dismissed such criticism and called it interference in the country’s internal affairs. The Indian embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

The voter roll revisions sparked protests in recent weeks, with opposition groups and student demonstrators saying the revisions affected those unlikely to vote for the Hindu nationalist BJP. Rights experts condemned India’s crackdown on the protests.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last month the issue was a “domestic political matter” and Washington would not comment on it.

UN experts and human rights groups say abuse of minorities has risen under Modi.

They point to rising hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law that the UN calls “fundamentally discriminatory,” the demolition of Muslim-owned properties, the removal of Muslim-majority Kashmir’s autonomy and anti-conversion legislation that challenges freedom of belief.

India’s government denies being discriminatory and says its policies, including food subsidy programs and electrification drives, benefit all communities.

Civil rights advocates have also been critical of the treatment of Muslims in the US while noting a rise in Islamophobia in recent years and documenting escalating anti-Muslim rhetoric from Republicans during election campaigns.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
