World.title: Anthropic’s post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
World.content:
FILE PHOTO: An Anthropic, PBC (ANT) sign at One Times Square on the day Anthropic holds their initial public offering (IPO) at the NASDAQ Market site in New York City, US, November 19, 2026. REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton/File Photo

Anthropic could offer an early read on investor appetite for the sector after a turbulent stretch, with a sustained decline likely to deepen concerns over lofty valuations and massive AI spending

Anthropic shares fell 6% in premarket trading on Friday, November 20, pulling back after a strong market debut that vaulted the AI lab into the ranks of the most valuable US companies but failed to revive investor enthusiasm for the sector.

Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic could offer an early read on investor appetite for the sector after a turbulent stretch, with a sustained decline likely to deepen concerns over lofty valuations and massive AI spending.

The stock was at $91.24, below Thursday’s close, giving Anthropic a fully diluted valuation of about $1.7 trillion and a market capitalization of $1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding.

The shares are likely to remain in focus for signs of volatility as the initial euphoria surrounding the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.

“A decline in share value is normal following a high-profile listing, but we don’t know if that decline will be in line with other IPOs or more volatile, and that should raise alarms for investors,” said Tejal Patel, executive director at the SOC Investment Group.

Anthropic shares closed on Thursday at 13% below their opening price, reinforcing concerns trading could remain volatile in the first few weeks as some investors seek quick gains.

“We would not describe the valuation as cheap. At this valuation, the growth plan is largely priced in,” said Harrison Rolfes, senior research analyst of private company coverage at PitchBook.

“Large IPOs have historically delivered modest returns in their first year.”

The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which could provide the next major test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public next year.

Wall Street’s main indexes ended sharply lower on Thursday, and futures pointed to another day of declines on Friday.

Parallels with SpaceX

Anthropic’s IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which went public in June after the second-biggest IPO on record.

While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX’s sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing.

“There’s going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don’t think there’s any need to get on it on the first trade,” said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co.

Retail investors traded about $772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012.

Competition could also weigh on investor sentiment.

Apple is developing an AI agent that can perform tasks on behalf of users, entering a market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms, Bloomberg News reported on Friday. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tubig Pilipinas secures up to P900-million investment from Maharlika
World.content:
The transaction is expected to give MIC a 9.9% ownership stake in Tubig Pilipinas if it invests the full P900 million

MANILA, Philippines – Sovereign wealth fund Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC) is investing up to P900 million in water utilities firm Tubig Pilipinas Holdings Inc.

MIC signed a convertible note agreement with Tubig Pilipinas on Friday, November 20, with an initial investment of P450 million. It comes with an option to put in another P450 million through a follow-on offering targeted for the first quarter of 2027.

The transaction is expected to give MIC a 9.9% ownership stake in Tubig Pilipinas if it invests the full P900 million.

According to its Philippine Stock Exchange disclosure, the funding will be used to “accelerate water infrastructure expansion,” particularly in underserved communities.

In a separate statement, MIC confirmed the agreement, with its outgoing president and chief executive Rafael “Joel” Consing Jr. describing the investment as part of the sovereign wealth fund’s strategy related to infrastructure.

“This partnership fits a deliberate pattern. Power for the islands. New port cities. Now, water. Power and water are what every community needs to function; ports are what connect them to growth,” Consing said.

Tubig Pilipinas operates water supply and distribution projects outside major metropolitan areas through its operating subsidiary, Tubig Pilipinas Group. Its portfolio includes water supply projects in Bacolod City, Negros Occidental, and water distribution systems in Trece Martires, Cavite; San Jose City, Nueva Ecija; Coron, Palawan; and Catbalogan, Samar.

The company itself is relatively new to the stock market in its present form, having completed a backdoor listing by acquiring the dormant Coal Asia Holdings earlier this year and rebranded it into TUBIG.

Its shares, however, have been suspended from trading since October 19 after a share-swap transaction reduced its public float to 10.64%, below the PSE’s 20% minimum requirement.

The Maharlika deal also comes just days before Consing’s term ends on November 23.

Consing earlier told reporters that MIC was working on two or three additional investments that could be announced before the end of 2026.

Since its establishment in 2023, Maharlika has invested in port operator Asian Terminals Inc., electricity-grid holding firm Synergy Grid and Development Philippines, and short-term financing for Petron, among others.

Still, the sovereign wealth fund has been exceedingly cautious in deploying its capital. As of end-September 2026, it had invested P24.7 billion, about a third of its initial P75 billion, while retaining P53.67 billion in cash and cash equivalents. – Rappler.com

World.title: Quezon residents seek answers over environmental risks of 50,000-hog piggery
World.content:
THREATENED. A creek near the 50,000-hog piggery in San Antonio, Quezon, is among the waterways residents fear could be contaminated by wastewater from the facility.

Residents near a 50,000-hog piggery in San Antonio, Quezon, raise concerns over potential water contamination, threats to farms and livelihoods, and the lack of answers from government agencies

Conclusion

QUEZON PROVINCE, Philippines – For residents living near a sprawling piggery designed to accommodate up to 50,000 hogs, the concern is no longer just the loss of agricultural land. It is whether the facility’s waste management system can protect their water sources, farms, and livelihoods, and whether government agencies will act if those safeguards fail.

The 12-hectare development of Mighty Livestock Farms in Barangay Callejon, San Antonio, Quezon, has raised concerns among residents of surrounding communities who rely on nearby irrigation waterways and groundwater for farming and household use.

The project has also become a source of frustration for former rice farmhands who found temporary employment during its construction, only to abruptly lose their jobs.

For Emma Alday, a resident in her eighties whose farm lies just 250 meters from the development, the controversy has become a prolonged struggle to obtain answers from government agencies responsible for protecting agricultural land, farmers, and the environment.

Threat to water, farms, and communities

Beyond the loss of productive agricultural land, residents fear the environmental consequences of a facility designed to accommodate as many as 50,000 pigs.

Alday estimates that each hog could produce approximately five kilograms of waste daily. Using that figure, the facility could potentially generate as much as 250,000 kilograms, or 250 metric tons, of waste every day if operating at full stocking capacity.

“Siguradong maaapektuhan ang aming water. Kahit sabihin nilang modern na. The air, and the langaw. We will only find out when it starts,” Alday said.

(Our water will definitely be affected, even if they say the facility is modern. The air quality will also be affected, as well as attract flies.)

For residents who rely on nearby waterways for irrigation and groundwater for household use, these are not abstract concerns.

Former construction worker Arnel Las, who previously worked as a farmhand in the ricefields, said the proposed waste-treatment facilities are situated near agricultural areas and waterways.

“Yung tubigan namin mismong kalapit ng piggery. Yung lagoon ang nagpapatubig sa palay. Yung lagoon nila 20 meters, hindi nilagyan ng flooring, talagang lupa, kaya derecho yun sa palayan,” he alleged.

(Our irrigation waterway is right next to the piggery. The lagoon supplies water to the rice fields. Their lagoon is 20 meters and has no concrete flooring – it is just bare earth, so the water goes straight into the ricefields.)

Las also expressed concern about the potential impact on drinking water.

“Ang tubig na aming iniinom ay mula sa poso, kaya makakaapekto rin sa amin (The water we drink comes from a hand pump, so we will also be affected).”

According to Las, the communities potentially affected include barangays San Juan, San Francisco, Behia, Callejon, Sinturisan, and Briones, which he said share interconnected irrigation waterways.

Whether wastewater from the facility could seep into surrounding soil and groundwater, and whether its waste-treatment system can safely handle the expected volume, are among the questions residents want the Department of Environment and Natural Resources-Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) to answer.

The EMB issued an Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC) for the project on October 24, 2023, covering a total land area of 113,973 square meters, or approximately 12 hectares.

The ECC identifies the development as a Livestock Farm Project with a maximum stocking capacity of 50,000 hogs at any given time.

However, an ECC does not, by itself, establish that a facility will have no adverse environmental impact. Rather, it sets environmental conditions and commitments with which the project proponent must comply.

For residents, the pressing question is whether those safeguards are sufficient and who will be held accountable if they fail.

Promises against environmental violations

The municipal government of San Antonio maintains that Mighty Livestock Farms has complied with the documentary requirements for its development.

In an interview, Sangguniang Bayan Secretary Carlo Katigbak said the municipality has mechanisms to act against establishments that violate environmental regulations.

“Although nabibigyan sila ng authority to operate, once na nagkaroon ng non-compliances, nagkakaroon ng immediate action talaga ang local government unit,” he said.

(Although they are granted the authority to operate, the local government unit takes immediate action once there are any instances of non-compliance.)

He added that the municipality could revoke a company’s license to operate or business permit if violations were established.

“In case magkaroon ng mga violation may mga recourse din ang municipio such as revocation of license to operate or business permit, mahigpit po ang local government sa mga ganitong bagay lalo na kung may kinalaman sa environment.”

(In case of violations, the municipality has recourse, including revoking the license to operate or the business permit. The local government is strict on these matters, especially when they involve the environment.)

The assurances, however, have not dispelled residents’ concerns about the potential impact on irrigation waterways, groundwater, and neighboring farms.

Farmers turned workers, then left without jobs

The controversy has also taken a human toll on former rice farmers who found temporary employment during the first two years of the piggery’s construction.

Las said he and other residents initially believed that a feed mill would be built on the property.

“Ang sabi nila ay feedmill ang itatayo, nung binubuo na, piggery na (They said a feed mill would be built, but by the time construction began, it was a piggery),” he said.

After working on the construction site for nearly two years, Las said he and several other workers were abruptly dismissed.

“Kami po ay tinanggal ng walang sinabi. Nakatira doon mismo sa sitio na pinagtrabahuhan namin. Kami rin ang mga dating farmhands sa ricefields.”

(We were dismissed without being given any explanation. We lived right there in the sitio where we worked. We were also former farmhands in the ricefields.)

He said some employment benefits, including their 13th-month pay, remained unsettled at the time of the interview.

“Nag-report po kami sa San Antonio Mayor’s Office noong September, sabi sa amin tatawagan kami pero hanggang ngayon ay wala naman tumawag sa amin. Lumapit din kami sa aming barangay kagawad pero wala din.”

(We reported the matter to the San Antonio Mayor’s Office in September. We were told they would call us, but no one has contacted us to this day. We also approached our barangay councilor, but nothing came of it.)

Another former worker, Kenneth Ocampo, said 16 workers were dismissed after being told that the company needed to reduce its workforce because of financial constraints.

“Nagbabawas daw po sila ng trabahador dahil wala na silang pasahod. Ngayon nabalitaan namin, nagdadagdag naman sila. Sabi kasi priority kaming mismong taga doon, pero bakit naman po kami pa mismo ang tinanggal. Ang tinira nila ay yung mga taga malayong lugar,” he lamented.

(They said they were reducing their workforce because they could no longer afford to pay the workers. Now we’ve heard they are hiring more people. They said residents from the area would be given priority, so why were we the ones who were dismissed? They kept workers from faraway places.)

He said the workers were never given a clear explanation for their dismissal.

“Siguro po may nagawa kaming mali, pero hindi naman dapat na basta-basta na lang kami tatanggalin, dapat kausapin nila kami kung bakit.”

(Maybe we did something wrong, but they shouldn’t have just dismissed us without explanation. They should have talked to us and told us why.)

Today, Ocampo survives on occasional jobs, a far cry from the regular income he once earned.

The workers’ accounts raise additional questions about the impact of the development on residents who previously depended on the land for their livelihoods.

They appealed to the President and got no response

As early as three years ago, Alday and other concerned residents began organizing opposition to the project.

They gathered approximately 300 signatures from residents of San Antonio and neighboring Tiaong and sent a petition to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr..

“Ang pangunahing pagkain natin ay BIGAS (Our staple food is rice),” the petition emphasized, warning of the continuing loss of ricefields.

The appeal, dated November 28, 2024, did reach the national government.

A memorandum dated January 27, 2025, signed by DAR-Calabarzon Director Cupido Gerry Asuncion, documents the referral of Alday’s complaint from the Presidential Action Center through the DAR Central Office to the provincial office in Quezon.

The memorandum specifically directed the provincial office to respond to Alday and report any action taken. But Alday says the referral has not resulted in a satisfactory response.

“So I was asking the DAR people kung ano ang gagawin nilang pagkilos, eh ang dami daw nilang ginagawa kaya hindi nila mabigyan ng attention up to now, so wala,” she recalled.

(So I asked the DAR personnel what action they would take, but they said they had so much work that they had been unable to attend to the matter up to now. So nothing has happened.)

She also approached the EMB office in Lucena, whose personnel visited the project site and inspected the biogas and lagoon facilities.

“Yung EMB na Lucena all they do is investigate and report to the region (The EMB office in Lucena only investigates and reports to the regional office),” she said.

For Alday, the visits, referrals, and repeated follow-ups have yet to produce clear answers to the concerns she has raised.

The difficulty in obtaining answers is not confined to the affected residents.

In an effort to establish the facts and present all sides, Rappler contacted the Department of Environment and Natural Resources–Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) IVA, the National Irrigation Administration (NIA) in Quezon, the Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) Quezon, and Mighty Livestock Farms through email and/or phone.

Rappler subsequently followed up with all four parties on several occasions. Yet more than two weeks after the initial inquiries, none had responded to questions concerning matters that fall directly within the mandates of the government offices approached or to the allegations involving the company’s development.

Who protects the farmers?

For Alday, the fight has become an exhausting search for accountability. She has spent the past two years writing letters, visiting government offices, following up on referrals, and asking questions she believes should have been answered long ago. Her efforts have taken her from local offices to regional agencies and even to the Office of the President.

Yet the central questions remain unanswered. How was irrigated riceland allowed to give way to a 50,000-head piggery? Were the farmers’ rights adequately protected? Were surrounding communities properly informed and consulted? Can the facility’s waste-management system safeguard the waterways and groundwater on which nearby residents depend?

And perhaps most importantly, why has it been so difficult for ordinary citizens to obtain clear explanations from the very institutions mandated to protect agricultural land, farmers, and the environment?

For Alday and the residents who joined her appeal, the answers remain elusive even as the development that prompted their concerns continues to take shape. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Pinoy Criminology] Killing of judges threatens the rule of law
World.content:
A country that cannot protect its judges cannot promise its people a fair hearing, a just decision, or the rule of law

Another judge has fallen to assassins, and another court has been left to mourn. Judge Joseph Wee Sit, presiding over Branch 2 of the Regional Trial Court in Isabela City, Basilan, was shot dead in Zamboanga City on November 12. He was a young judge, only a little over a year into service on the bench, with his life and public service still opening before him.

This should outrage not only the legal profession, but the entire Filipino community. The killing is horrifying on its own, but it also carries a danger beyond one family’s grief. Every bullet fired at a judge is a threat to the institution that must decide disputes by law.

Whether this killing was intended to intimidate the judiciary remains for investigators to establish. But we cannot pretend an attack on a judge is merely a private crime, detached from public office. Judges sometimes confront politically charged, contested cases, where their decisions threaten interests powerful enough to answer law with force.

That possibility makes the killing all the more urgent to investigate, without prematurely declaring who ordered it or why. A murder can terrorize a court before its motive becomes known, because judges understand the warning implicit in violence.

The judiciary is supposed to be impartial and independent. Judges swear to decide cases on their merits, on the facts presented, and the law that governs them. They must be able to rule without fear or favor, even when their decisions anger the powerful or disappoint the public. When judges know that their lives, limbs, and careers are on the line, safety can begin to shape judgment. Then decisions are made not on merit, but on power; that is rule by men, not rule of law.

I have written about judgments arriving after 21 years, people trapped in judicial limbo, and detention prolonged by vacancies and delay. Those problems may look different from the murder of a judge, but they expose the same fragility. A court cannot guard liberty when it lacks time, personnel, and resources to hear cases fairly and promptly. Nor can the public trust justice when the law’s guardians are left vulnerable, unsupported, or pressured by political power. The judge should be the immediate guardian of liberty, and accountability separates justice from mere force.

That protection begins before a judge enters the courtroom. It begins with the appointment process, where judicial posts must never become prizes in partisan warfare. If lawyers must beg political patrons for judicial posts, obligations and loyalty tests can precede their first ruling. That is an unfair burden to place on young, idealistic lawyers, then send them to decide cases affecting the lives and fortunes of powerful people. Appointments must rest on merit alone, measured through integrity, ability, experience, and the courage to apply law equally.

The Judicial and Bar Council must be strengthened in its work of recruiting, selecting, and recommending judges and justices. Malacañang, as the final appointing authority, must respect the council’s merit-based recommendations and choose the most qualified candidates. That principle has too often remained aspirational, invoked in speeches but weakened by political calculation. An appointment system based on merit gives judges legitimacy and weakens patrons’ leverage over the bench. It also assures the public that judicial office is earned through qualification and service, rather than political loyalty.

We must also strengthen the judiciary after appointment. Congress and the presidency must provide more judges, court staff, functioning offices, and dependable operational budgets. Judges cannot deliver justice effectively when they lack the personnel, equipment, and basic resources to do their work. Courts should not have to depend on mayors, governors, or legislators for support that belongs to the national government. Local officials must respect independence, while the national government ensures judges never depend on local favor.

Protection must be real, sustained, and visible, especially for judges serving in places where cases carry exceptional risks. That means assessing threats, protecting court personnel, and coordinating security without letting security arrangements compromise judicial independence.

The investigation must establish who killed Judge Wee Sit, identify any instigators, and determine whether the attack was connected to his work. The Supreme Court has mobilized its judicial marshals to work with law enforcement, a necessary step toward accountability. The state must also stand with his family and every judge who returns to court despite danger.

Otherwise, judges will be reduced from instruments of law to instruments of the powerful. Disgruntled politicians, criminals, and businessmen will learn that terror can clear a judge from their path. Young lawyers attracted to public service will see that idealism can cost them their lives, while the state offers little protection.

That is how fear enters the courtroom, and how justice quietly yields to those who can threaten it. A country that cannot protect its judges cannot promise its people a fair hearing, a just decision, or the rule of law. – Rappler.com

Raymund E. Narag, PhD, is an associate professor in criminology and criminal justice at the School of Justice and Public Safety, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale.

World.title: FACT CHECK: PhilHealth not offering P5,000 cash aid under YAKAP
World.content:
PhilHealth has no program that automatically provides cash assistance to all its members

Claim: The Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) will provide P5,000 cash aid to all its members through its Yaman ng Kalusugan Program (YAKAP).

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: Facebook user Cres Jhoerax Vlog posted a video bearing the claim on November 20. The video claims that all PhilHealth members — regardless of whether they are active or inactive paying members — are eligible for the supposed P5,000 cash payout.

It also claims that even those without a Member Data Record or ID are eligible for the cash assistance.

“Nasa aming post ang registration, ang mga requirement, at iba pang detalye. Paki-share po sa iba, para mas marami ang makaalam at makapag-register nang maaga. Mag-follow sa amin at i-share ang balitang ito,” a narrator says in the video.

(Our post contains information regarding registration, requirements, and other details. Please share it with others so that more people can be informed and register early. Follow us and share this news.)

The video has garnered over 100 comments and 200 shares as of writing. Other users have reposted the video bearing the same claim.

The facts: PhilHealth has debunked circulating posts claiming that YAKAP provides cash aid to members.

The agency clarified that it has no program offering cash assistance to all its members, as its mandate is to provide health insurance coverage and access to healthcare services.

The health insurer urged the public to be wary of posts promising unconditional cash assistance or announcing supposed payout schedules accompanied by dubious registration links, particularly those that did not come from any of PhilHealth’s official accounts.

YAKAP is PhilHealth’s national primary care benefit package, giving its members free access to primary care services at accredited clinics. It is an improved version of its Konsulta program.

The program’s benefits include free checkups, laboratory tests, medicines, and cancer screening tests.

AI-generated video, dubious info: The videos about the supposed cash aid are AI-generated. Detection tool HumanMeter flagged one of the videos as 95% likely to be AI-generated, while HiveModeration gave an AI likelihood score of 94.7%.

Meanwhile, similar videos about PhilHealth’s supposed P5,000 cash aid mistakenly reference “AKAP” — referring to the Ayuda para sa Kapos ang Kita Program of the Department of Social Welfare and Development.

Though this program provided cash assistance, it was intended for individuals whose income is insufficient to meet their basic needs. The program has been discontinued as of 2026 and is not affiliated with PhilHealth.

Cash aid fact checks: Rappler has debunked false claims about cash aid and government subsidy programs:

– Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: How many workers does Sara-linked firm Cale88 have? Records don’t match.
World.content:
ANSWERING QUESTIONS. Trade Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo testifies during the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on November 20, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines – The company originally owned by Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, Mans Carpio, came under scrutiny on the 45th day of the impeachment trial, with questions emerging over its actual workforce.

The defense team’s witness, Trade Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo, said on Friday, November 20, that Cale88 had 201 employees as of 2024, based on Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) records.

The figure contrasts with its filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, which indicated that it had no “rank-and-file” employees and no “manpower complement” in 2024.

Rodolfo said DTI records also showed that the company declared 115 direct laborers and three indirect workers the previous year, with labor expenses amounting to P3.5 million.

Prosecution spokesman Zia Alonto Adiong, at a press conference, suggested that the company may be violating labor laws because of the poossibly extremely low wages.

“If we sum it up, and divide P3.1 million by 115 employees, annually, each one receives P27,066. Divide that by 12 months, and it shows each employee is paid P2,255 monthly. That’s about P75 per day. This is way below the annual wage order for Region XI,” Adiong said.

Play Video

Senator Raffy Tulfo asked how the Board of Investments made sure that Cale88’s declarations were truthful.

“That is what they submitted, notarized. That is compared with the audited financial statement,” Rodolfo said.

He added that they can check a company’s manpower records deeper if they avail of corporate income tax exemptions.

“There is a requirement there for a certificate of good standing from SSS. Included in what SSS submits is a master list of those whose contributions are being paid,” Rodolfo said.

“Maybe that’s why they are not availing of tax holiday so they don’t have to give those documents. Therefore, they may not have those many employees,” Tulfo said.

Rodolfo confirmed that Cale88 did not apply for incentives such as VAT zero-rating, but added that he did not know why, despite their importance to exporting businesses. – Rappler.com

World.title: Climbing up a Pangasinan hill, in the dark, to hear Rina’s story
World.content:
Upper middle income? Our field work in Pangasinan is proof that statistics cannot tell us what it feels like to live in a house without electricity

“Neighbors” is Rappler People section’s space for community and human interest stories told in a personal way.

PANGASINAN, Philippines – There are moments during the field work with University of Santo Tomas (UST) student researchers that made me stop and think about the lack of social justice in this part of the world. This is a story about one of those moments.

We agreed not to film the encounter that I am about to narrate regardless of how tempting it was to capture the drama of the situation. Lest you forget, we are researchers, not content creators. We are after the truth, not validation.

The scene I am referring to is that of Gabrielle (interviewer) and Rina (interviewee). Please note that I am not using the real name of the respondent to protect her privacy. The women are about the same age, but they were born in two separate social classes.

Gabrielle is studying at UST, whereas Rina was forced to stop schooling to prioritize her work as a canteen staff in Urdaneta City. Gabrielle is busy chasing her dreams, studying culinary arts in the oldest existing university in Asia with the help of some of the country’s best academicians. Meanwhile, Rina is busy trying to survive. She works so that she could help feed her mom, dad, and siblings.

If Gabrielle is reaching for her brightest stars, Rina only wants to survive. In this economy, Rina surely knows how to be realistic. Maybe her only prayer right now is to have electricity in their house one day. “Kung nakaluwag-luwag (once we can afford it),” as old people say. The sight was heart-wrenching, to say the least.

On October 3, we made our way up the hill to Rina’s house, where her family lives. By the time we arrived, the sun was already giving way to darkness. The family cannot afford electricity, so darkness is simply not the absence of light inside their house. It is part of their everyday life. At night, the family has only the stars and a few solar-powered lights to illuminate their home. Using Rina’s surroundings as a backdrop, you can almost hear Coldplay’s “Yellow” or Joey Ayala’s “Buwan, Buwan” playing.

We interviewed the family after sunset. We watched as darkness slowly enveloped the house, as insects and animals began announcing their presence nearby. Perhaps, they are nature’s natural sensors, knowing the arrival of strangers. Their sounds may mean welcome. Or threat.

The transition from day to night has a strange effect on someone’s psyche when you are in the wild, especially in unfamiliar terrain. As a probinsiyano (man from the province), I found it strangely comforting. For my five companions, however, it was a different story. They came from the brightest metropolis in the country. I could sense how tense they were throughout the entire ordeal.

Pero, in fairness, hindi nagpatinag ang mga estudiyante ng USTe. Dala-dala nila ang mga flashlights ng kani-kanilang iPhone para suungin ang dilim. Nagmukha kaming mga gamu-gamo sa tuktok ng napakadilim na munting burol. Napakatapang pa rin ng mga researchers sa kabila ng ‘di pangkaraniwang kaba na hirap din nilang itago. Takot na takot sila, pero sumulong at tumuloy pa rin.

(To be fair to the UST students [I accompanied], they were not discouraged. The held their iPhones’ flashlights through the dark. We looked like fireflies atop a really dark hill. The researchers braved the way, despite the fear they tried hard to hide. They were so afraid, yet they soldiered on.)

Your professors must be so proud of you, mga kapatid (brothers and sisters). Go, USTe!

Anyway, the next house with a television and WiFi was almost a kilometer away from Rina’s house. To be honest, the house where we conducted our field work was quite literally in the middle of nowhere. The scene looked like something from the 1970s, during the heydays of FPJ Productions. It was the setting that could easily be made romantic and cinematic on film. But life taught me that some things are only romantic when you are watching them from a safe distance. In reality, the place was malamok (mosquito-infested). It was mainit (hot) even at nighttime. And it was quite creepy.

During the entire interview, I couldn’t stop thinking about the insanity of it all. Only last July, our President Bongbong Marcos bragged that the country had achieved the upper-middle-income status after nearly four decades. I do not doubt the statistics. What I doubt is whether the statistics tell the whole story. Because whatever this achievement means to the country, it means very little to the people I encountered during our field work.

Ilang taon ko na ring sinusundan ang kuwento ng mga tao sa likod ng tradisyong panagliyab, pero mas tumatanda lang sila at mas nangayayat. Ang pag-asenso ay napakamailap pa rin sa kanila kahit pa nagpapakahirap sila araw-araw at gabi-gabi.

(For years, I have been following the story of the people behind the panagliyab tradition. They are getting older, and thinner. Having a comfortable life remains elusive for them although they work hard day and night.)

(According to Lokalpedia, panagliyab is the tradition of “processing the sap of the silag, or buri palm.”)

Kung kailan pa tayo nagkaroon ng upper-middle-income status — whatever that means — ‘tsaka naman naging mas kalunos-lunos ang kalagayan ng mga managliyab na nakilala ko. Mas mahina na ngayon si Laki Berting na 78 anyos na. Hindi ko na rin mahanap ang mga ibang aking nakapanayam noong 2024. Hindi ko na alam kung buhay pa ba silang lahat.

(When we finally achieved the upper-middle-income status — whatever that means — that’s when the living conditions of the traditional artisans that I met more deplorable. Laki Berting, who is 78, has grown weaker. I can’t find anymore those I interviewed in 2024. I don’t even know if they are still alive.)

Lagi nating naririnig sa balita na gumaganda naman daw ang ekonomiya, pero bakit tila dumarami pa rin ang katulad ni Rina? Bakit kailangan pa ring umakyat sa puno ng mga silag ang isang 78-anyos na lolo para lamang manatiling buhay? Gusto lang naman daw niyang tulungan ang kanyang mga apo na ulila na sa ama. Upper-middle-income na nga ba talaga tayo? Bakit parang ang mahal pa ring mabuhay sa Pilipinas? Minsan, nakakapagod na ring magtanong nang magtanong. Wala rin kasing malinaw na sagot. Basta, ang mahalaga ay upper-middle-income na raw tayo.

(We often hear in the news that our economy is improving, but why does it seem that there are more people like Rina? Why does a 78-year-old grandfather have to climb up buri palm trees just to earn a living? He said he just wanted to support his grandchildren who had lost their father. Are we really an upper-middle-income country? Why does it feel like it’s difficult to survive in the Philippines? Sometimes, I get tired of asking questions. There are no clear answers anyway. The government just insists, we’re upper-middle-income.)

Mas madali na lang talagang mahalin ang ating kapwa-tao. Sa dulo naman ay tayo-tayo rin lang ang magtutulungan. Silver lining na lang maituturing na may mga tulad nina Gabrielle, Francine, Jaime, Kath, at Phia na handang tumapak sa putikan at literal na umakyat sa madilim na burol para kumalap ng mga datos upang maging batayan ng katotohanang ibabahagi nila sa Maynila. Napakahusay ng mga magulang at guro na nagpalaki sa mga batang mananaliksik na aking sinamahan sa loob ng dalawang araw. Lumaki po sila nang napakaayos at napakarangal. Mapalad lang din ako at nakilala ko sila.

(What’s easier to do is to love our fellowmen. In the end, we’ve only got each other to help. I consider it a silver lining that there are students like Gabrielle, Francine, Jaime, Kath, and Phia who were willing to walk in the mud and climb up a dark hill to gather data on which they would base the truth that they would share in Manila. I admire the parents and teachers who raised these young researchers whom I guided for two days. They grew up decent and honorable. I’m blessed I got to know them.)

At the end of the day, these young researchers sought the welfare of the managliyab. They showed us that helping them and preserving the tradition should be an ultimate priority because a tradition cannot survive if we do not value the people who carry it. May panagliyab live on despite the increasing challenges.

I pray that researchers will not get tired of listening to the stories of people from the lowest ranks of the social ladder. Especially today, when the statistics serves as the sole basis of all the official pronouncements, it does not help to be so gullible. Statistics can tell us that the economy is growing, that the country has moved up another rung on the economic ladder, and that we are now upper-middle-income.

But statistics cannot tell us what it feels like to live in a house without electricity, and they certainly cannot tell us whether people like Rina feel that the country is progressing. Sometimes, these figures are seemingly out of touch, misleading, and simply fail to capture the truth. Hence, we need to engage with one another more than ever before to find the truth for ourselves. And sometimes, the only way to find the truth is to climb that dark mountain ourselves. – Rappler.com

Julius B. Cayabyab is an instructor at Pangasinan State University. His work in higher education informs his perspectives on issues concerning education, society, culture, and community development.

World.title: Witness can’t explain why VP-linked Calle88’s bank inflows exceeded sales
World.content:
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian —File photo by Niño Jesus Orbeta (INQUIRER)

MANILA, Philippines — An official of the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) could not think of any reason why the company owned by Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, would have received inward remittances totaling P776.64 million when its declared sales revenue only amounted to P208.49 million.

Questions about the huge gap between the reported bank deposits to Carpios’ Cale88 Foods Corp. and its declared sales hounded Trade Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo, who’s also the managing head of the Bureau of Investments (BOI), when he testified for the defense in Duterte’s impeachment trial on Friday.

The prosecution has accused the vice president of amassing unexplained wealth, failing to fully disclose her assets, and engaging in business activities while in office.

Article continues after this 

Citing Anti-Money Laundering Council records, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian noted the huge gap between the reported funds flowing into the firm and its audited sales from 2022 to 2025.

READ: Kapunan questions P568-M gap between Cale88 sales, bank inflows

“Mayroon bang undervaluing of sales, hindi ho nagdedeklara ng tama? Base ho sa inyong analysis, alam ko matagal na kayo sa DTI at kabisado nyo yung mga ganito nag-a-apply ng incentives. Anong possible reason? Ang layo ng numbers,” Gatchalian asked.

(Could there have been an undervaluation of sales, or a failure to declare the full amount? Based on your analysis, and given your years of experience at the DTI and your familiarity with companies applying for incentives, what could explain such a significant discrepancy in the figures?)

He said the amount would still not reach P776 million even if the supposed P20 million in advances from shareholders were included.

Article continues after this 

At this point, the witness conceded that he could not see any reason why the company’s inflows would have exceeded its sales.

“Dun sa operations po nung kumpanya at saka po dun sa mga sinabmit nila sa aming dokumento, wala akong makitang rason para tumaas po sila ng more than dito po sa declared sales revenue po nila na sinambit sa amin,” said Rodolfo.

Article continues after this 

(“Based on the company’s operations and the documents it submitted to us, I see no reason why its sales should exceed the declared sales revenue it reported to us.)

For 2023 and 2025, Cale88 reported combined sales of approximately P41 million, based on the bank certificates it submitted to the BOI, the witness added.

The firm’s supposed highest export sales were reported in 2024 at P150 million, according to Rodolfo.

Senator-Judge Bam Aquino pursued Gatchalian’s line of questioning, noting the firm’s reported losses based on Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) records:

P42,255 in 2022

P1.88 million in 2023

P61.5 million in 2024

P48,000 in 2025

The witness SAID, however, THAT the company had an income of P375,000 in 2025, the same year it changed its ownership.

READ: Cale88 had ‘unrecorded’ change in ownership in 2025

“Well, sa BIR submission to this court, it was negative P48,000. But in any case, lugi yung kumpanya,” Aquino said.

(“Well, based on the BIR’s submission to this court, it was negative P48,000. But in any case, the company was operating at a loss.)

The witness agreed with Aquino’s remark that Cale88 was losing money.

“Ang hindi ko na lang talaga maintindihan, yung AMLC inflow na nabanggit ni Senator Sherwin kanina at nabanggit ni Senator Risa (Hontiveros),” Aquino said.

(What I really cannot understand is the AMLC inflows mentioned earlier by Senator Sherwin and Senator Risa [Hontiveros].)

“P700 million yung pumasok, of which 315 million ay galing sa China. Napag-uusapan yan pero 208 million lang yung declared na kinita? And you cannot hazard a guess kung paano nangyari yun?” he asked further.

(Some P700 million came in, of which P315 million came from China. This has been brought up, yet the company declared only P208 million in earnings. Can you offer any explanation as to how that could have happened?”)

Responding to this, Rodolfo said the amount should have been P208 million based on Cale88’s operations and documents submitted to the BOI.

“Masasabi ko lang po, Honorable Judge, is dun po sa pagkakaalam namin ng operation nila at saka mga declaration nila sa amin, wala silang ibang source of income kundi itong operation lang po na ito,” he said.

(“All I can say, Your Honor, is that based on our understanding of their operations and the declarations they submitted to us, they have no other source of income apart from this particular business operation.)

“Kaya po kung tatanungin niyo ako kung ano dapat yung pumapasok sa kanila, ito lang pong amount na ito. As to the other sources, I would be purely guessing,” Rodolfo added.

(“So, if you ask me how much they should be receiving, it should only be this amount. As to the other sources, I would be purely guessing.)

* * *

World.title: Marcos brings investment commitments, free trade deal from China trip
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. —AFP file photo

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is back in Manila on Friday evening following a three-day trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China.

The aircraft carrying the Philippine delegation landed at the Villamor Air Base in Pasay City at 6:01 p.m.

In his arrival statement, Marcos enumerated the “concrete results” yielded from his three-day visit.

Article continues after this 

“At the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting, I spoke for an open, fair, and rules-based trading system and shared the gains that have made the Philippines an upper-middle-income economy and given us the widest free trade network in our history,” he said.

He called on fellow Apec leaders to recognize each other’s educational and professional qualifications so that skills and talent of Filipinos can move across the region.

As chair of the recently concluded Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit and Related Summit, Marcos also presented to Apec leaders the digital economy framework agreement signed by the Asean.

Marcos also said he encouraged them to bring affordable digital tools and artificial intelligence to micro, small, and medium enterprises.

When it comes to the rapidly developing artificial intelligence (AI) Marcos told the leaders that it needs to earn public trust.

Article continues after this 

“Our region needs interoperable, human-centric approaches to its governance,” he also said.

Additionally, Marcos emphasized that the oceans of Asia-Pacific are a source of livelihood for fisherfolk and highways of trade for all Apec nations.

Article continues after this 

“Keeping them secure and in accordance with international law, including Unclos, protects the supply chains of which all our economies depend,” he said.

During his trip, the Philippines and Chile concluded negotiations on free trade through the signing of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement.

This is the Philippines’ first-ever bilateral free trade agreement with a Latin American nation.

Business gains from Apec

Marcos secured an initial $87 million commitment from China’s C&U Group for the development of a 20-hectare facility in Alitagtag, Batangas.

This is set to become the largest production base outside China and the only manufacturing facility in Southeast Asia.

He also met with Ming Yang Smart Energy Group Chairman Zhang Chuanwei and discussed wind energy projects and planned investments in the Philippines.

The discussions covered the proposed establishment of an Operations and Maintenance Center and potential localization of renewable energy services.

Marcos also had separate meetings with BYD Founder and Chairman Wang Chuanfu for the company’s business plans.

World.title: P97-B slashed from DPWH budget in Senate appropriations bill
World.content:
Sen. JV Ejercito — INQUIRER / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — Approximately P97 billion was slashed from the budget of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in the Senate 2027 General Appropriations Bill, Sen. JV Ejercito said on Friday.

Ejercito, head of the Senate finance panel, revealed the budget cut after he filed on Friday afternoon Senate Committee Report No. 131.

“P97 billion worth of projects were deleted from the DPWH budget. Ito po ang resulta ng pag-scrutinize ng Senate the past few weeks,” Ejercito said in a press briefing.

Article continues after this 

(P97 billion worth of projects were deleted from the DPWH budget. This is the result of the Senate’s scrutiny over the past few weeks.)

According to the senator, the finance panel made such deletions and were mostly reallocated to foreign-assisted projects (FAPs).

An estimated P68.8 billion was restored for the FAPs, including a P4.7 billion restored for the Metro Manila Subway Project, which was cut in the House GAB. Another P30 billion was reallocated to the North-South Commuter Railway.

In addition, P33 billion was placed in DPWH FAPs including the Cavite-Bataan bridge, and the Laguna Lakeshore Highway.

As for other sectors, the health sector was proposed to have a P52-billion budget increase – P19.8 billion is for PhilHealth, P9.6 billion for the Department of Health, P5.49 billion for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, P1.09 billion for health promotion, and P1.5 billion for immunization programs.

Article continues after this 

Ejercito also shared that the funding placed in the Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (Maifip) program was realigned to the Zero Balance Billing project.

Meanwhile, the finance committee proposed a P15.3 billion increase for the education sector. This includes an additional P11.8-billion funding for the Department of Education, of which P11 billion is for the Universal Feeding Program for Kinder 1 to Grade 1 students.

Article continues after this 

There was also a proposed increase worth P2.8 billion for state universities and colleges.

READ: Senate told: Over P1 trillion in proposed 2027 budget is ‘pork’

In agriculture, an additional P48.62 billion budget was proposed, of which P4.4 billion would be for the National Rice Program.

A P5.56-billion increase was also proposed for the defense sector, including a P750 million budget for developing critical infrastructure at the Kalayaan Group of Islands in Palawan. The P50 billion funding for the Armed Forces of the Philippines’ Modernization Program was also included.

Furthermore, the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration, under the Senate’s proposal, received a P650 million increase for its emergency repatriation fund in case of a crisis.

World.title: DOH monitors monkey‑linked malaria cases in Northern Palawan
World.content:
The Department of Health in Mimaropa is monitoring cases of malaria caused by a monkey‑borne parasite in Northern Palawan, particularly in the municipalities of Roxas and San Vicente. INQUIRER FILES

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Department of Health in Mimaropa is monitoring cases of malaria caused by a monkey‑borne parasite in northern Palawan, particularly in the municipalities of Roxas and San Vicente.

Malaria attributed to the parasite Plasmodium knowlesi has been confirmed after an assessment conducted together with experts from the World Health Organization and the Pilipinas Shell Foundation Inc., according to Oscar Macam Jr., DOH vector‑borne disease coordinator in Mimaropa.

Plasmodium knowlesi originates in monkeys and is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes.

Article continues after this 

READ: WHO approves first malaria treatment for infants

“The mosquito that carries human malaria is also the one that transmits this parasite. The parasite really comes from monkeys and is transferred to humans. But there has not yet been any situation where Plasmodium knowlesi spreads from human to human. Usually it is monkey to human, but there is still no human‑to‑human transmission,” Macam explained.

Macam noted that Plasmodium knowlesi malaria is documented in Malaysia, and because of Palawan’s proximity to the country, heightened vigilance is necessary.

The Research Institute for Tropical Medicine (RITM) has validated four to five cases in Roxas town and 10 cases in San Vicente. Mimaropa, or Region IV-A, comprises Oriental and Occidental Mindoro, Marinduque, Palawan, and Romblon.

The health department is also coordinating with veterinary experts and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to gather data on monkey populations, especially in northern Palawan, to understand transmission risks.

Article continues after this 

“The monkeys’ territory appears to be mostly in the north, though I am not saying there are none in the south. I believe the population is larger in the north. We are working with DENR to obtain data on monkey numbers, which may help our monitoring efforts,” Macam said.

DOH Mimaropa is also scheduled to conduct further surveillance in Puerto Princesa City around the second week of January, in coordination with the City Health Office./coa

World.title: Phivolcs: ‘Moderately strong’ 4.3 quake felt in Iloilo City
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — A “moderately strong” tremor was felt in Iloilo City on Friday morning following a Magnitude 4.3 earthquake south of Anilao town, according to state seismologists.

The tectonic earthquake occurred on 5:11 a.m. four kilometers (km) south of Anilao town with a depth of 22 km, per the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) report on Friday afternoon.

An Intensity IV (moderately strong) was felt in Iloilo City.

Article continues after this 

Phivolcs also received reports of felt intensities in the following areas:

Intensity III (weak): Cuartero and Dao towns in Capiz; Nueva Valencia and Sibunag towns in Guimaras; City of La Carlota, City of Talisay and City of Bago, in Negros Occidental; Bacolod City

Intensity II (slightly felt): Manapla town in Negros Occidental,

Intensity I (scarcely perceptible): City of Roxas in Capiz; City of Canlaon, Negros Oriental

Here are the instrumental intensities recorded by Phivolcs:

Intensity IV (moderately strong): Buenavista and Jordan towns in Guimaras; City of Passi in Iloilo; City of Bago, Negros Occidental

Intensity III (weak): Tapaz town in Capiz; Nueva Valencia, in Guimaras; City of La Carlota in Negros Occidental

Intensity II (slightly felt) Jamindan and President Roxas, in Capiz; San Lorenzo town in Guimaras; Iloilo City and Bacolod City

Intensity I (scarcely perceptible): City of Roxas in Capiz

Felt intensity is the ground shaking actually felt and reported by the people through the Phivolcs Earthquake Intensity Scale while instrumental intensity was indicated by the ground shaking intensity measured by the intensity meters in and around the epicentral area. /ms

World.title: Zamboanga del Sur town shortlisted for national literacy award
World.content:
Aurea Jean Allado-Abad, chair of the National Literacy Awards Board of Evaluators, told the Inquirer on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, that the validation team looked beyond basic reading and writing to assess how the local government’s programs translate into real community impact. (Photo by Leah D. Agonoy)

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur — With a tight local budget and backed by out-of-pocket contributions from municipal workers, the Municipality of Kumalarang in Zamboanga del Sur province is making its fourth bid for top honors at the 2026 National Literacy Awards (NLA).

National evaluators from the Department of Education’s (DepEd) Literacy Coordinating Council (LCC) visited the town this week to validate its grassroots programs, placing Kumalarang among the top five national contenders in the fourth- to fifth-class municipality category.

The biennial awards recognize local government units (LGUs), non-government organizations, and higher education institutions for initiatives that help universalize literacy and eradicate illiteracy.

Article continues after this 

READ: Angara launches search for literacy champions through 2026 NLA

For the 2026 cycle, Kumalarang is competing against four other shortlisted municipalities from Misamis Oriental, Laguna and Sorsogon provinces, and the Cagayan Valley region.

Aurea Jean Allado-Abad, chair of the NLA Board of Evaluators, told the Inquirer on Thursday that the validation team looked beyond basic reading and writing to assess how the local government’s programs translate into real community impact.

“Kumalarang had a holistic program,” Allado-Abad said, noting that the town integrated financial, safety, and health literacy, among others, alongside formal education in partnership with DepEd and other national agencies.

While Kumalarang has been named a national contender three times before without clinching the top spot, Allado-Abad said that the LGU acted on recommendations from earlier evaluations—including reforms in local taxation and improvements to its community weaving school.

Article continues after this 

“Right now, they did all those. All of those now have innovations,” she added.

Mayor Ruel Molina attributed the town’s consistent national shortlisting to treating literacy as a moral obligation rather than a political showcase or a quest for trophies.

Article continues after this 

“This is not about the award, this is not about the recognition,” Molina said in a mix of Cebuano and English. “Our programs here are not just on paper, and they are not for politics. They are for the people, with no political boundaries.”

Molina acknowledged that Kumalarang is still faced with a significant number of residents struggling with illiteracy, prompting the LGU to stretch its limited resources. Because literacy initiatives lack dedicated national funding, municipal employees routinely pool their own money to travel to barangays every Thursday to teach and provide small incentives for learners.

READ: 4.5M struggling readers improve literacy skills in SY 2025-2026 – DepEdTo sustain access to higher education, the mayor said he realigned the LGU’s third- and fourth-quarter maintenance and other operating expenses, and suspended official travel funds to keep the Kumalarang Community College (KCC) running. KCC offers completely free tuition and miscellaneous fees to local students.

KCC is an LGU-run school that started operations last August 2026.

To ensure the school survives changes in political leadership, Molina said KCC has been institutionalized through a municipal ordinance that cannot be easily revoked.

“Building this is like setting the pillars of a house. If you build the foundation well, no matter what storm or season comes, it will not be shaken,” Molina said.

During the validation, evaluators also visited the local women weavers association—a sector Molina emphasized as proof that literacy underpins every aspect of local development, including disaster preparedness and livelihood.

“Could they weave properly if they did not know how to count?” the mayor asked.

Looking ahead, Molina said he is willing to forgo immediate financial returns if these educational investments help elevate Kumalarang into a first-class municipality over the next five to ten years.

READ: DepEd urged to focus on students’ reading comprehension

World.title: Calapan back on 4‑day workweek, trims fiesta and Christmas events
World.content:
The Calapan City government is shifting to a four‑day work week and scaling back upcoming fiesta and Christmas celebrations to keep its finances afloat amid soaring fuel prices, a weak peso, and the threat of El Niño.

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The city government is shifting to a four‑day work week and scaling back upcoming fiesta and Christmas celebrations to keep its finances afloat amid soaring fuel prices, a weak peso, and the threat of El Niño.

City Administrator Angel Navarro said in a message on Friday that Calapan’s 2026 budget of P1.6 billion was prepared last year when diesel stood at P63 per liter, and the US dollar traded at P57 to P58.

Today, diesel sells for P90 to P100 per liter while the peso has weakened past the P63 mark, driving up local inflation and putting significant strain on the city’s expenditures.

Article continues after this 

READ: Keep Christmas parties simple as peak of Super El Niño looms – Palace

“The expenditure plan was realistic then, but the situation has changed drastically since,” Navarro said.

While the exact savings from the reduced work schedule have yet to be quantified, Navarro emphasized that the cutback is necessary to ensure “the last‑quarter budget lasts until the end of this year.”

In tandem with the shorter workweek, several fiesta programs have been cancelled, including the Little Mr. and Ms. Calapan pageant. Nightly shows at the Calapan Christmas Village will also be reduced, and last year’s Christmas decorations will be reinstalled to cut costs.

Navarro stressed that the Christmas Village tradition will continue, but in a humbler version.

“We are reusing last year’s decorations so we can save without abandoning our tradition of lifting the spirit of Calapan residents as we face the troubled situation of our time,” Navarro said./coa
