World.title: US Warns Against ‘Politicization’ of ICJ, Studying Myanmar Ruling
World.content:
WASHINGTON—The U.S. State Department reacted with caution to the International Court of Justice’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, saying Washington was examining the decision while stressing the need to avoid “politicization” of the body.

Washington’s wary response comes as the United States determined in 2022 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people.

But it has more recently pushed back on another case before the top UN court, involving accusations by South Africa that US ally Israel perpetrated genocide in Gaza.

“The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ,” said a State Department spokesperson on Thursday.

“We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications,” the official added, referring to the Myanmar ruling.

The US statement comes as the top UN court ordered refugees to be given safe passage home and awarded compensation.

The decision marked the first time in its 80-year history that ICJ judges determined a state committed genocide. It is likely to be viewed as justice for Rohingya victims of Myanmar’s deadly 2017 crackdown on the mostly Muslim minority.

The US official said Thursday: “We express our support for the people of Burma and share the grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups.”

The official also called for more burden-sharing in the humanitarian response for Rohingya refugees.

For more than one million Rohingya living in the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh, the landmark ruling offered hope for accountability.

World.title: Five Key Points From Historic ICJ Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands—The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority—the first time the UN top court has determined a state responsible for the world’s worst crime.

Here are the key points from the 191-page ruling, which took nearly three hours to read out in court and is the second-longest in the ICJ’s 80-year history.

Genocide

This was what the hundreds of thousands of Rohingya victims were waiting for: did the atrocities they suffered clear the high bar under international law to be labelled a genocide?

In the end, the ICJ—known for dressing up its rulings in impenetrable legalese—was refreshingly clear.

Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State,” said the ruling, which was passed by nine votes to six.

By the same margin, the court found Myanmar had failed in its obligations under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention to prevent the crime.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to take “immediate and effective steps” to prosecute and punish anyone suspected of genocidal acts.

Myanmar must stop any ongoing acts of genocide and prevent similar violations of the Convention in future.

To prove genocide, judges have to be satisfied not only that genocidal acts have occurred but also there was intention to destroy a given community—a notoriously tricky legal hurdle.

However, the judges ruled that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people.

Safe return

Having concluded that genocide occurred, the court also issued rulings on the consequences for Myanmar—so-called “remedies” in the legal jargon.

It ordered several actions from Myanmar.

The authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.

They must also “return or replace in kind all individual and collective property” that was lost in the violent crackdown.

The Rohingya must also be offered “physical and psychological rehabilitation” for the harms they suffered, the judges ruled.

Reparations

The Rohingya are entitled to “adequate compensation” for the harms caused by the genocide.

The ICJ did not set an amount, saying that would be determined at a later phase.

It gave Myanmar two years to file a report setting out the “amount and modalities” of compensation.

After receiving the report, the ICJ will decide whether Myanmar’s proposal is sufficient.

Investigations

The ICJ is a court that settles disputes between countries, unlike its neighbor the International Criminal Court, which weighs individual responsibility.

However, the ICJ ruling tasks Myanmar with conducting a “prompt” investigation into anyone suspected of committing genocidal acts.

Judges ruled that previous efforts in Myanmar to probe atrocities were insufficient.

“Myanmar has not genuinely investigated or, if warranted, prosecuted its soldiers and commanders and punished them,” the ICJ said.

Scale of killings

The court said that an estimate of at least 10,000 deaths in the crackdown, established by an independent UN fact-finding mission, was “supported by the record.”

“The evidence before the court demonstrates the pervasive and lethal nature of the violence… and establishes that thousands of Rohingya civilians were killed by the Myanmar security forces,” said the ICJ.

The court said there were approximately 815,000 Rohingya in Rakhine State at the time of the crackdown, meaning those killed constituted 1.2 percent of the population.

The majority of the survivors fled to neighboring Bangladesh.

The ICJ also said there were at least 1,834 acts of rape during the 2017 “clearance operations.”

World.title: ICJ Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
World.content:
The United Nations’ top court, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017, in a historic decision.

In the case brought by the Gambia, the ICJ delivered the first ruling in its 80-year history finding a state responsible for committing genocide.

“The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said, delivering the court’s verdict.

Iwasawa said around 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the 2017 “clearance operations,” which also involved widespread sexual violence and violence against children, as the Rohingya fled en masse to Bangladesh.

“Records also contain evidence of intentional targeting of the Rohingya population,” Iwasawa said.

The court found that Myanmar deliberately targeted the approximately 815,000 Rohingya who lived in northern Rakhine before the operation.

Rohingya villages were systematically destroyed and their populations replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, the ICJ said, ruling that the only reasonable inference was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.

The ICJ president said Myanmar had failed to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible for acts punishable under Article III of the Genocide Convention.

The Myanmar military also disseminated and promoted hate speech in a systematic and coordinated way during the 2017 operation, the court said.

The court ordered Myanmar to cease any ongoing violations of its obligations under the Genocide Convention and to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of those who fled the violence to their homes. It also ruled that Myanmar must investigate suspected perpetrators and prosecute and punish those found responsible, and provide compensation. The amount would be determined in future proceedings, it said.

The ruling cannot be appealed. Rather than prosecuting individuals, the verdict determined that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide.

As a result of the military operation in Rakhine, over one million Rohingya now live in what is effectively the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh. For some of them, the case offered a glimmer of hope for accountability.

“I want justice,” a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor told AFP before the verdict in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family.

“There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this,” she said, requesting anonymity.

“This is a historic ruling. For the first time, the World Court has found a state responsible for committing genocide—and the man who commanded those operations is now Myanmar’s president,” said Richard Horsey, senior adviser for Asia at the International Crisis Group.

Horsey pointed out that the court lacks the power to enforce the orders contained in its ruling.

“What matters now is whether the governments engaging Naypyitaw are prepared to attach any cost to ignoring it,” he said.

Myanmar should comply with the court’s judgment and end its oppression of the Rohingya, said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.

“Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” she said.

Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, said international governments should not welcome putschist president and former Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw a campaign of crimes against humanity and other crimes under international law against the Rohingya.

“Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar,” she said.

All other states, including members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, must also uphold these obligations under the Genocide Convention and general international law, taking every measure within their power to prevent and punish genocide, Callamard said.

She urged the UN Security Council to impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court.

The Myanmar military’s 2017 “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee amid widespread killings, sexual violence and arson attacks, according to UN investigations.

World.title: 4,500 Myanmar Refugees to Get Thai Job Training Under $3m Project
World.content:
Japan has agreed to back employment training for 4,500 Myanmar refugees and their families in Thailand under a 478-million-yen (US$ 3 million) project implemented by the International Labor Organization (ILO).

Funded by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the two-year project announced Tuesday will also incorporate training for trainers, job-matching services, and outreach to employers including Japanese companies.

It will cover residents of border camps in Tak, Mae Hong Son, Kanchanaburi, and Ratchaburi provinces, aiming to serve high labor demand in Kanchanaburi as well as Chonburi and Rayong, where Japanese businesses are concentrated.

More than 100,000 refugees are currently sheltering in nine temporary camps along the Thai-Myanmar border, according to the Border Consortium (TBC), the main provider of food and shelter in the camps.

The refugees continue to face “significant resource pressure” due to international funding cuts, leading to reduction of food rations, medical services, and other basic assistance, with “no clear sign of reversal,”

the group’s 2026 mid-year report said.

Thailand granted Myanmar refugees the right to work outside their camps in August 2025 after funding collapsed following the USAID freeze. Since then, more than 6,000 have entered the workforce. Feedback has been mixed, with some complaining of language barriers, skill mismatches and unstable working hours.

“Some don’t have steady jobs, working for just a few days every month and surviving on meager wages,” a manager at Maela Camp in Tak Province told The Irrawaddy, citing testimony from returnees.

“We interview them and ask why they returned. They mention discrimination due to the language barrier.”

He said refugees receive a one-day orientation before joining the workforce covering their legal rights, minimum wage, work permit rules, workplace safety, and how to get help if they face abuse on the job.

However, information gaps and inconsistencies between employment brokers and employers often leave workers facing unexpected working conditions.

Announcing the project on Tuesday, the ILO said employers would support both recruitment and integration of refugees into the workforce.

The project “will help displaced persons access safe and decent jobs, while supporting employers to meet their labor needs,” ILO Thailand country director Xiaoyan Qian said at the signing ceremony.

A Karenni resident of a Mae Hong Son camp welcomed the initiative as a pathway to employment. “I hope the training will instill the basic skills needed to join the workforce,” he told The Irrawaddy, admitting it was the first he had heard of the project.

Separately, the Mae La camp official said a Japanese organization was scheduled to visit for a meeting that could be linked to the project.

Thailand relies heavily on migrants from Myanmar to fill labor shortages in key industries like construction, agriculture, and hospitality. The UNHCR and rights groups have welcomed Thailand’s decision to grant refugees labor rights as a win-win for both sides.

World.title: Regime Media Censor Min Aung Hlaing’s Swipes at China, Thailand
World.content:
Myanmar’s state-run newspapers have censored remarks by junta chief Min Aung Hlaing that appeared to blame China for the initial success of Operation 1027, and accuse Thailand of facilitating “illegal trade” through resistance-held territory, despite devoting six pages to coverage of his more than two-hour address to the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament.

In Wednesday’s speech, the junta boss delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on Operation 1027, the Brotherhood Alliance offensive that led to the collapse of the regime’s Northeastern Regional Military Command in Lashio and marked one of the most humiliating military setbacks of the post-coup period.

Without explicitly naming Myanmar’s giant neighbor, Min Aung Hlaing emotionally suggested the offensive was made possible by outside backing.

Recalling the launch of the offensive on Oct. 27, 2023, he said the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) conducted the surprise attack with superior manpower, weapons and technological assistance from “certain people.”

“I was traveling at the time. I received a phone call very early in the morning saying fighting had broken out. I immediately took out a map to assess the size of their forces. The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he stated during his speech.

“There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” he said.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country involved, few observers were left in doubt about the target of his remarks. Among Myanmar political watchers and the public alike, the comments were widely interpreted as a thinly veiled swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance during the northern Shan offensive.

The comments echoed earlier complaints by Min Aung Hlaing during the height of Operation 1027, when he publicly alleged that the MNDAA had used Chinese-made drones and advanced technology in attacks on regime positions.

The junta chief also turned his fire on Thailand, accusing Thai authorities of encouraging cross-border commerce through resistance-controlled territory.

Referring to his Nov. 12 meeting with Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, Min Aung Hlaing complained that despite discussions on using official border crossings, reports of what he called illegal trade were still reaching him.

“Recently, the Thai foreign minister came and discussed border crossings with me. I said Bridges No. 1 and No. 2 at Myawaddy are open and Tachileik is open, so use those official gates and not the illegal ones. But they are still supporting the illegal gates,” he said.

He accused Thai authorities of allowing goods to move through crossings linked to what he called “insurgents” because they offered easier access for both imports and exports.

The accusation came despite Thailand being one of the strongest advocates of maintaining engagement with Naypyitaw and pushing for Myanmar’s eventual reintegration into regional bloc the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

Yet neither the China-related remarks nor the criticism of Thailand were reported in Thursday’s editions of Kyemon, Myanma Alin and the English-language Global New Light of Myanmar.

The state newspapers carried extensive coverage of the speech across six full pages. However, the politically sensitive comments about Beijing and Bangkok were conspicuously absent.

Instead, the papers highlighted Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks on issues ranging from egg prices and coffee plantations to livestock breeding and other routine administrative matters.

Given the prominence accorded to far less consequential sections of the speech, the absence of his remarks on China and Thailand appears difficult to explain as an editorial decision based on length alone.

While Min Aung Hlaing continues to nurse grievances over Operation 1027, his regime remains heavily dependent on Beijing for diplomatic backing, economic support and political legitimacy. At the same time, it can ill afford a rupture with Thailand, a crucial neighbor that remains one of the regime’s few channels for regional engagement, analysts said.

World.title: What’s at Stake in Myanmar’s ICJ Trial for Genocide?
World.content:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has begun the session that will deliver a landmark ruling in the case brought by the Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya.

This is the first time in history that Myanmar faces a court ruling on these crimes, not as a criminal case against individuals but to determine whether it bears responsibility for genocide as a state.

What to look for in today’s ICJ judgment

In 2017, the Myanmar military’s “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee widespread killings, sexual violence and arson attacks, according to UN investigations.

In 2019, the Gambia—which ratified the Genocide Convention in 1978—filed a case at the ICJ with the backing of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya violated the convention.

In December 2019, when the ICJ held hearings on Gambia’s request for provisional measures to protect the thousands of Rohingya remaining in Myanmar, Aung San Suu Kyi decided to lead Myanmar’s legal defense as state counsellor and foreign minister.

The following month, the ICJ ordered Myanmar to prevent all genocidal acts against the Rohingya and to take steps to preserve evidence related to the case.

Since 2022, Myanmar has been represented at The Hague by the military regime that seized power in the 2021 and is led by Min Aung Hlaing, who had overseen the atrocities as military chief.

In July 2022, the ICJ rejected Myanmar’s preliminary objections and ruled that the case could move forward. It took until August 2023 for the Myanmar regime to submit its reply to the Gambia’s original legal argument, known as a “memorial.” The Gambia submitted its reply in May 2024.

In January this year, the ICJ held three weeks of so-called “merits hearings” with arguments, evidence, witnesses, and an expert from both sides. Eleven countries—Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, the Maldives, Slovenia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Belgium, and Ireland—were permitted to intervene on treaty interpretation under Article 63.

On Thursday, the ICJ delivers its final judgment concluding the proceedings. There is no possibility of appeal.

What is the Gambia asking the ICJ to do?

The Gambia has asked the ICJ to find Myanmar responsible for multiple violations of the Genocide Convention, including committing, conspiring to commit and failing to prevent genocide, and failing to prosecute those suspected of committing it.

It has also asked the court to order Myanmar to end these violations, introduce specific legislation criminalizing genocide, prosecute alleged perpetrators, and prevent direct and public incitement to genocide.

The Gambia is also seeking reparations for Rohingya victims, such as ensuring the “safe and dignified” return of refugees as well as financial compensation and other forms of reparation.

Although the Gambia is not directly affected by the alleged genocide, it claims the legal right to seek reparations on behalf of the Rohingya victims in its capacity as a signatory to the convention. Myanmar disputes this position.

The Gambia has further asked the court to find that Myanmar failed to comply with its January 2020 provisional measures order and to require guarantees that such violations will not happen again.

What if Myanmar defies the ICJ ruling?

If Myanmar fails to comply with any ICJ judgment against it, the other party can turn to the UN Security Council, which may recommend or decide on measures to enforce it, in accordance with UN Charter article 94(2). The UNSC has never acted on this discretionary power, and Myanmar has two powerful allies in permanent UNSC members China and Russia.

What is the situation in Myanmar?

Besides the Rohingya genocide case, the Min Aung Hlaing regime faces lawsuits in six countries for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity since the 2021 coup.

The regime continues to hold political prisoners, including Aung San Suu Kyi, and has killed more than 8,600 civilians and detained over 32,000 people since the coup, according to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners.

Millions of young people have fled to other countries due to forced conscription, security fears, and a lack of jobs amid inflation, widespread crime, and escalating conflict across the country.

The civilian death toll continues to grow amid daily regime airstrikes and ground attacks in resistance-held territory.

World.title: Min Aung Hlaing Accuses Thailand of Aiding ‘Illegal’ Border Trade
World.content:
Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing on Wednesday accused Thai authorities of facilitating “illegal” cross-border trade through resistance-controlled areas, ignoring his request to conduct it only through border checkpoints his military regime still controls.

In a marathon speech in the rubberstamp Parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing complained that he had raised the issue in a meeting with Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow on Nov. 12 but was still getting reports of illegal trade on Wednesday morning.

“Recently, the Thai foreign minister came and discussed border crossings with me. I said Bridges No. 1 and No. 2 at Myawaddy are open and Tachileik is open, so use those official gates and not the illegal ones. But they are still supporting the illegal gates,” he said.

He accused Thai authorities of allowing goods to move through crossings linked to what he called “insurgents” for both import and export because they offer easier access.

The regime itself controls only the three major trade gateways he mentioned: the two Thai–Myanmar Friendship Bridges in Myawaddy in Karen State and Tachileik in eastern Shan, plus Kawthoung in Tanintharyi Region in the deep south. The rest are now under the control of ethnic armed organizations that are fighting the putschist regime.

The regime routinely brands commerce through them as “smuggling” since it cannot collect much-needed tax, but businesses using the official channels also have to put up with growing regime chicanery and extortion.

Although the regime reopened the No. 2 Friendship Bridge in May after nearly a year of disruption caused by fighting, traders say trade remains constrained by import-license requirements, foreign-exchange controls and lengthy approval procedures. Importers must obtain licenses and show export earnings funneled through the regime-controlled official banking system before bringing goods into Myanmar, a process that often causes significant delays.

That has increased costs and slowed shipments. Currency volatility has added further pressure, making it increasingly difficult for importers to price goods and maintain working capital. The kyat has steadily weakened against Thai baht, Chinese yuan and U.S. dollar over the past month.

In August, the regime lodged a formal protest when Thai business representatives attended the opening of a border security and trade facility in Thaw Le Hta in Hpapun Township controlled by the Karen National Union (KNU). The area lies by the Salween River which forms the natural border between Myanmar and Thailand.

The protest letter urged Bangkok to prevent any economic, social or political engagement with KNU and warned that the military would target resistance supply routes.

Relations between the neighbors swiftly turned sour in recent weeks, despite efforts by the Thai government to ease the Myanmar regime’s way back into ASEAN. Bangkok is furious that recent regime airstrikes and shelling against the Karen resistance have spilled over the border.

On Oct. 31, the Myanmar military carried out airstrikes in the Thaw Le Hta area that damaged structures on the Thai side, prompting a protest from Bangkok and calls by Thai residents for a 10-km safety buffer zone along the river.

In a meeting with Royal Thai Army Commander-in-Chief Pana Claewplodtook, Myanmar Deputy Commander-in-Chief Kyaw Swar Lin also attempted to shift the blame on Thailand for online scam operations in Myawaddy, calling on Bangkok to do more to cut off essential supplies to scam syndicates operating in Karen State.

The regime has repeatedly sought to blame Thailand for the flourishing fraud industry on the border. Since early 2025, regime officials have argued that the scam compounds relied on electricity, internet connections and other logistical support from the Thai side.

Min Aung Hlaing is desperate to cut off revenue streams for resistance forces that are now able to tax border trade instead of the regime along much of the country’s borders with Thailand, China, Bangladesh and India.

World.title: Top UN Court to Rule on Whether 2017 Rohingya Crackdown Was Genocide
World.content:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands—The top United Nations court will Thursday decide whether Myanmar committed genocide against the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority with its brutal 2017 crackdown that forced hundreds of thousands to flee the country.

For the more than one million Rohingya now living in the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh, the landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice offers a glimmer of hope for accountability.

“I want justice,” a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor told AFP in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family.

“There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this,” she said, requesting anonymity.

Survivors of the violence brought with them harrowing tales of gang rapes, mass executions, and barely believable cruelty towards families and children.

Far from the squalor of the refugee camps, in the gothic splendour of the Peace Palace in The Hague, a panel of 15 judges has been weighing for seven years whether Myanmar’s actions constitute genocide.

The case has been brought by Gambia under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, which requires any state to bring a case against another it suspects of breaching the international agreement set up after World War II.

While the ICJ has no way of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing.

He commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy which may be complicated by the ruling.

Myanmar has always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

“Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein,” its representative Ko Ko Hlaing told judges during hearings on the case in January.

‘Targeted for destruction’

Gambia’s justice minister said the country filed the case “after reviewing credible reports of the most brutal and vicious violence imaginable inflicted upon a vulnerable group that had been dehumanised and persecuted for many years.”

Gambia has the “full backing and support” of the 57-member Organization of Islamic Cooperation for its efforts at the ICJ, said the minister, Dawda Jallow.

“It is not about esoteric issues of international law, it is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” added Jallow.

“The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

The ICJ has only once before found that a genocide has taken place, the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia.

Genocide is notoriously difficult to prove in international law because the Convention requires proof of a specific “intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.”

Gambia argued during the hearings that genocidal intent was clear from the “organized nature and execution” of the crackdown, its “extreme brutality”, the “pervasive sexual violence”, and the targeting of children.

Legal experts are watching the case closely for clues as to how the ICJ will handle another seminal case before it—accusations by South Africa that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

“How the court applies and interprets its current jurisprudence in Gambia’s case against Myanmar will shape ongoing and future proceedings in relation to similar claims,” said Human Rights Watch.

Survivor Mohammed Osman said he was hoping the verdict would allow him to go back home and perform last rites for his parents and younger brother killed by the Myanmar military.

“They shot my father dead, forced my mother into a house with a few other women, raped them and burnt down our homestead,” Osman, 20, told AFP.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Develop Unified Investment Tools for Agriculture by 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan will develop a unified set of investment instruments for the agricultural sector by the end of the first quarter of 2027 to improve access to long-term financing and simplify procedures for farmers, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said at a Nov. 20 third Forum of Agricultural Workers.

According to him, the government will work with the Baiterek holding company and financial regulators to prepare the proposal. Tokayev also noted that existing financing instruments offered by the Agrarian Credit Corporation and KazAgroFinance involve lengthy application reviews, complicated procedures and insufficient digitalization. The new framework is expected to make credit decisions more transparent, shorten application processing times and reduce administrative barriers.

Tokayev also called for a special program to improve agricultural productivity, developed jointly with international financial institutions. It should provide long-term financing, technical and expert support, and access to modern technologies and scientific developments, drawing on international experience.

He highlighted artificial intelligence as one of the tools that could help Kazakhstan strengthen its position in global food production.

“Leading global companies in the field of artificial intelligence recently advised us to focus on introducing AI into agriculture, as forecasts for global food security are unfortunately pessimistic,” Tokayev said.

He pointed to the potential impact of the El Niño climate phenomenon and said Kazakhstan could use its agricultural resources and AI technologies to become a major global food supplier.

“Why not? I believe this task should be addressed primarily to the government and the relevant departments,” he said.

Agricultural output and processing

Tokayev said Kazakhstan had made significant progress in agriculture over the past seven years. Food production increased by 28%, while 1,630 investment projects worth a combined 2.7 trillion tenge (US$5.2 billion) were launched.

Agricultural exports doubled to nearly $7 billion, with processed products accounting for 52% of total exports. The country harvested 24.5 million tons of agricultural crops during the latest autumn harvest campaign.

Tokayev also emphasized the need to expand deep processing of agricultural products to reduce dependence on food imports. Over the past three years, domestic food production increased by nearly 15%, including a 36% rise in vegetable oil production and a 25% increase in meat and dairy production.

He called on the government to promptly assess potential food-processing projects and begin their implementation.

Rural development and accountability

President Tokayev also cited rural development initiatives, saying that 921 projects worth 173 billion tenge (US$336 million) were implemented in nearly 500 villages last year. Water supply systems were modernized in 277 settlements. However, he questioned whether the reported figures fully reflected the results on the ground and called for a detailed assessment of the work.

“Previously, we were presented with a beautiful, almost perfect picture. And, frankly, we were all genuinely pleased with it. Then we looked for convenient excuses, saying that we had not been given accurate statistics, and simply put the issue aside. Such an approach is unacceptable in the future,” he said.

Tokayev also stressed that public officials must be judged by their current performance and adherence to the law, regardless of their previous achievements or qualifications.

“Many times I have said, and I will remind you again: the principle of Law and Order, enshrined in the Constitution, is immutable and applies equally to all citizens, regardless of their credentials or position in society,” he said.

He described encroachment on public funds and violations of constitutional norms as serious crimes against the state, adding that the government would continue its efforts to combat corruption.

At the same time, Tokayev reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s commitment to attracting foreign investment, supporting business activity and improving the investment climate.

“Our strategic course involves both creating a favorable investment environment and strengthening the institutional foundations for doing business in the country without obstacles,” he said.

World.title: Kazakhstan Discusses International Water Organization Proposal With UN Regional Envoy
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan discussed advancing its proposal to establish an International Water Organization within the United Nations system during a meeting between First Deputy Foreign Minister Yerzhan Ashikbayev and the UN Secretary-General’s Special Representative and Head of the UN Regional Center for Preventive Diplomacy for Central Asia (UNRCCA) Kakha Imnadze on Nov. 19.

The talks focused on regional developments and prospects for cooperation between Kazakhstan and the UN in preventive diplomacy, security and sustainable development.

Ashikbayev noted the positive dynamics of interstate relations in Central Asia, saying that deeper political dialogue, stronger mutual trust and expanded regional cooperation frameworks create favorable conditions for addressing common challenges.

The meeting also addressed nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation, particularly in light of two anniversaries this year: the 35th anniversary of the closure of the Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site and the 20th anniversary of the signing of the Treaty on a Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone in Central Asia.

They also discussed reforming the UN and adapting the organization to contemporary global challenges. In the context of the UN80 Initiative, they emphasized the importance of close cooperation between UNRCCA and the UN Regional Center for the Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan, based in Almaty.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the sides reaffirmed their shared interest in strengthening cooperation to promote lasting peace, stability and sustainable development across Central Asia.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Constitutional Reform: Importance of Strong Institutions and Rule of Law
World.content:
I have followed Kazakhstan’s political and constitutional reforms with particular interest. As an expert in constitutional law, I regard the reform process initiated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev as a significant stage in the country’s constitutional development. Its emphasis on institutional renewal, a more balanced exercise of public authority, the protection of human rights and the strengthening of constitutional safeguards merits serious attention and recognition.

The nationwide referendum held on March 15 gave Kazakhstan’s citizens an opportunity to express their will on the new Constitution, which entered into force on July 1 and marks an important milestone in the constitutional development of the republic.

The new constitutional framework affirms the importance of human dignity, fundamental rights and freedoms, the supremacy of the Constitution and the accountability of public institutions. The lasting significance of these constitutional commitments will depend on their consistent implementation by every branch of government and on the development of a legal culture grounded in respect for both the letter and the spirit of the Constitution.

Constitutional justice is central to that undertaking. In a constitutional democracy, a Constitutional Court serves as one of the most important guardians of constitutional principles and values, and helps ensure that legislation and the exercise of public authority remain within constitutional limits. It also provides an institutional safeguard for the rights and freedoms guaranteed to individuals. For this role to be fully realized, constitutional review must be accessible, effective, impartial, independent of political influence and exercised with the highest authority of the Constitutional Court.

The success of constitutional reform must therefore be assessed not only by the provisions adopted, but also by the strength and integrity of the institutions entrusted with their implementation. A sound democratic constitutional order requires separation of powers, effective checks and balances, protection of individual rights and freedoms, respect for legal equality, non-discrimination and other forms of justice, legal certainty and, last but not least, accountable public administration. These are enduring principles, and their practical application must remain a continuing responsibility of state authorities.

From the point of view of further constitutional and social developments in Kazakhstan, it is encouraging that some important matters have been set out in President Tokayev’s State of the Nation Address of October 28, entitled “Kazakhstan’s Current Priorities in a New Historical Cycle.” His vision connects economic modernization, infrastructure renewal, technological progress, social welfare and institutional reform. Particularly important is the recognition that sustainable growth must be supported by the rule of law, effective public administration and a predictable and efficient legal environment – conditions that enable investment and innovation while ensuring that progress benefits the people.

The development of digital technologies and artificial intelligence makes this discussion all the more pressing. Innovation should be guided by a careful balance between opportunity and responsibility, with due regard for human rights, ethical standards, public safety and the rule of law. A human-centred and human-controlled approach to technological change is essential if its benefits are to be broadly shared and public trust maintained. In this respect, it is of utmost importance that humanity, by ethical, political and legal means, prevents artificial intelligence from prevailing over humans.

The author is Professor Dr Miro Cerar, Dean and Full Professor, Faculty of Law at University of Ljubljana. He served as the Prime Minister of the Republic of Slovenia (2014–2018) and the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Slovenia (2018–2020).

World.title: Women in Central Asia Work Longer but Earn Less, Gender Gap Report Shows
World.content:
ASTANA – Women in Central Asia continue to earn less than men despite progress in formal employment, while unpaid household responsibilities add significantly to their working hours, highlighting persistent gender inequalities across the region.

Finprom reported these findings on Nov. 16, citing materials from the General Confederation of Trade Unions and the World Inequality Report 2026, which examines changes in women’s employment, earnings and working hours over the past 25 years.

Informal employment declines, but challenges remain

Between 2000 and 2025, the share of women working exclusively in households declined across CIS countries, reflecting a broader shift toward formal employment.

Armenia recorded the sharpest decline, from 37.3% to 4.9%, while the figure fell to 9.8% in the Kyrgyz Republic and 1.7% in Uzbekistan. Azerbaijan remained an exception, with 37.1% of women still working in households.

In Kazakhstan, the estimated share dropped to 0.08% in 2025. However, experimental data from the Bureau of National Statistics presents a different picture: the share of women employed in the informal sector declined from 39.3% in 2010 to 11.2% in 2024.

Informal employment often leaves women without paid leave, sick leave, pension contributions and other social protections.

Wage gap persists across regions

Women have made progress in closing the earnings gap, but parity remains distant. According to the World Inequality Report 2026, women in Central Asia and Russia earned nearly 75% of men’s average earnings in 2025, up from 62% in 2000. The global average stood at 71%.

In Kazakhstan, women’s wages amounted to 71.8% of men’s earnings in 2025, meaning women earned 28.2% less on average. The indicator declined by 3.2 percentage points over five years.

Part of the difference reflects women’s concentration in lower-paying industries. Around 80.3% of employed women in Kazakhstan worked in services, compared with 60.4% of men. Meanwhile, men were more represented in industry and construction, accounting for 27.2% of male employment, compared with 11% among women.

The gap also varies considerably by sector. Women’s earnings approached parity with men’s in construction, public administration and administrative services, reaching 94%-98%. In education, women earned 1.5% more than men.

However, in financial and insurance activities, women’s earnings amounted to just 69.3% of men’s, despite the sector having among the highest average salaries.

Unpaid work widens inequality

The report highlights the unequal burden of unpaid domestic work. In Central Asia and Russia, women worked an average of 53 hours a week in 2025, compared with 40 hours for men. Yet only 21 hours of women’s work were paid, while men recorded 30 paid hours. Including unpaid work, the gender gap in hourly earnings reached 51%.

Kazakhstan’s statistics show a similar pattern. Employed women spend an average of two hours and 15 minutes a day on household work, 3.2 times as much as men. On weekends, the gap widens to more than five hours for women, compared with two hours and 16 minutes for men.

The figures suggest that reducing gender inequality requires not only better access to paid employment and equal pay, but also a fairer distribution of unpaid household responsibilities.

World.title: Dimash Qudaibergen Plans to Record Song in Spanish for Mexican Fans
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen plans to record a song in Spanish for his Spanish-speaking fans, including audiences in Mexico, he said during a press conference in Mexico City ahead of two concerts on Nov. 19 and 20, reported the DimashNews agency.

“I would like to try making something in Spanish in the near future for all my Spanish-speaking fans. And, of course, for the Mexican audience, because I believe they deserve it,” Qudaibergen said. He added that he hoped to find someone who could help him with Spanish pronunciation and release the song soon.

The singer arrived in Mexico City on Nov. 18, where he was welcomed by large crowds of fans carrying Kazakh and Mexican flags. Fans greeted him with the chant “¡Dimash, hermano! ¡Ya eres mexicano!” (Dimash, brother! You are Mexican now!). Qudaibergen opened the sunroof of his car, stood up and personally greeted the crowd.

Mexico City is the fourth stop on the Mexican leg of his DIMENSIONS world tour, following performances in Merida, Monterrey and Guadalajara.

During the press conference, Qudaibergen said returning to Mexico a year after his first solo concert in the country was particularly meaningful.

“Last year, after performing in Mexico, I told my concert directors: ‘We absolutely have to come back here! If possible, let’s organize the next concert as soon as we can.’ And now we are here again!” he said.

A musical connection with Mexico

Qudaibergen also shared some of his favorite Spanish-language songs, including “Historia de un Amor,” “Bésame Mucho” and “Porque aún te amo” by Argentine singer Luciano Pereyra.

The singer also explained the concept behind his DIMENSIONS tour. The title reflects different aspects of human personality and the musical diversity of his work, which brings together classical music, pop, rock, jazz and rap.

Speaking about the role of music, Qudaibergen said he hoped his performances would remind audiences of the importance of peace and love. He cited his song “The Story of One Sky” as a message against war and “Mahabbat Ber Magan,” which means “Give Me Love,” as an expression of love.

He also emphasized the importance of family and personal values, saying that as he grew older, he came to see family, good relationships and striving to be a good person as more important than music.

Photo exhibition celebrates cultural ties

A photo exhibition dedicated to Qudaibergen’s career opened in Mexico City on Nov. 19, the day of his first concert in the capital as part of the DIMENSIONS tour.

The exhibition was presented at the historic Casa de Carranza Museum. It traces the singer’s artistic journey through photographs documenting significant moments in his career and his contribution to promoting Kazakh culture internationally.

The exhibition was organized by Mexican fans with the support of the museum. Its opening brought together Kudaibergen’s mother, singer Svetlana Aitbayeva, Kazakhstan’s Consul in Mexico Daniyar Karatayev and his wife.

Aitbayeva thanked the Mexican fans, known as Dears, for their efforts in preparing the exhibition and praised their dedication to her son’s music. She said Mexico held a special place in her family’s heart, adding that each visit was accompanied by warm emotions and that they missed the country and its people when they were away.

She also highlighted the shared values of Kazakh and Mexican cultures, including peace, unity, respect for family and traditions.

Qudaibergen’s two DIMENSIONS concerts in Mexico City were scheduled for Nov. 19 and 20, concluding the Mexican leg of his world tour.

He previously performed his first solo concert in Guadalajara on Nov. 17 at Auditorio Telmex, where the show sold out.

World.title: Tokayev Signals Further Expansion of International University Campuses in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to launch several campuses of international universities in Astana next year, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said during a roundtable with heads of international organizations and leading foreign universities on Nov. 19.

Tokayev said the initial stage of cooperation with foreign universities had been completed, with the necessary infrastructure established and partnership agreements formally signed. The next priority is to move beyond institutional arrangements toward joint research, technology development and practical solutions addressing the needs of Kazakhstan’s economy.

“I hope that next year we will launch several campuses here in Astana. This work must certainly continue, because it is a top priority for us,” Tokayev said, adding that he was ready to support any university interested in opening a branch in Astana or other regions of Kazakhstan.

Strengthening international research cooperation

Addressing representatives of international organizations and universities, Tokayev said growing geopolitical tensions were increasingly affecting scientific and technological cooperation.

“Scientific cooperation is increasingly viewed through the lens of security. Advanced achievements are less often perceived as a common good and increasingly become instruments of competition,” he said, noting that artificial intelligence, new materials, energy technologies and biotechnology were transforming economies, labor markets and education systems.

According to him, human capital development, education, science and innovation were central to Kazakhstan’s national strategy and had been enshrined in the Constitution as strategic priorities for the first time in the country’s history.

Water security and engineering education

Tokayev identified water security as one of the priority areas for international scientific cooperation, describing it as a matter of economic and social stability for Central Asia.

He highlighted the need for joint efforts in managing transboundary rivers, developing modern monitoring systems, introducing water-saving technologies and advancing science-based water diplomacy. Kazakhstan is counting on the expertise and capabilities of the United Nations University in this area.

Another priority is training specialists for the country’s large-scale infrastructure modernization. Tokayev referred to the People’s Construction initiative, which he said encompasses not only individual construction projects but a broader renewal of national infrastructure, including energy, nuclear power, transport, water management and digital infrastructure.

He called on international partners to contribute to training a new generation of engineers, technical specialists and researchers, as well as conducting applied research in these fields.

“The basic principle of this nationwide initiative is very simple: ‘Build, and build again,’” Tokayev said, describing the initiative as Kazakhstan’s response to the challenges of the artificial intelligence era.

Integrating AI into education and research

President Tokayev also called for the integration of artificial intelligence into education and science, emphasizing that its adoption should go beyond purchasing software. He said this would require updated curricula, teacher training, reliable digital infrastructure and clear principles for the responsible use of AI.

Tokayev invited participants to identify obstacles to international cooperation, including financial constraints, administrative procedures and barriers to academic mobility. He also called for concrete proposals and commitments that could translate the discussion into joint projects in the near future.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Aviation Ambitions, Digital Progress and Tourism Appeal
World.content:
ASTANA — The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest explores prospects for direct flights to the United States, tokenized government bonds, growing international cooperation, tourism achievements, and Kazakhstan’s rise in the UN e-government ranking.

Kazakhstan expects FAA blessing for direct US flights ahead of Trump-hosted G20 meeting

Kazakhstan hopes to get a coveted US safety rating in time for a December G20 summit that ​the Central Asian country’s president is expected to attend in Miami at ‌the invitation of host President Donald Trump, Reuters reported on Nov. 18.

Talgat Lastayev, vice minister of transport for Kazakhstan, said on Tuesday he is expecting news in December on whether his country will get a category 1 safety rating ​that would allow direct flights to the United States.

Starting direct US flights would ​be a boost for landlocked Kazakhstan, which is banking on investment in ⁠its fast-growing aviation system to drive air traffic and develop its resource-rich economy.

Kazakhstan sets Q1 2027 target for tokenized sovereign bonds after $22 million note test

Kazakhstan’s central bank plans to issue tokenized government bonds in the first quarter of 2027 with the Finance Ministry, Governor Timur Suleimenov said, after a debut sale of blockchain-recorded central bank notes this month, reported BigGo finance on Nov. 15.

The November auction placed 50 billion tenge (US$110.9 million) of 91-day notes at a weighted average yield of 15.72%, with only 10 billion tenge ($22.2 million) in tokenized form. The sale ran on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange’s digital asset platform, which uses the Solana blockchain, with BitGo providing custody. Key terms of the bond issue, including size, date, platform and yield, have not been disclosed. Inflation has slowed for 12 straight months to 9.2%, against a 5% target for 2028.

Kazakhstan and Belgium target investment and transport links after royal visit

EU Reporter published an article on Nov. 18 about Kazakhstan and Belgium strengthening economic cooperation following the royal visit, with a focus on investment, Middle Corridor development, critical minerals, transport infrastructure, and research partnerships.

Kazakhstan and Belgium are moving to turn a year of intensive diplomacy into closer economic cooperation, with investment, transport and critical minerals leading the agenda after October’s first Belgian state visit to Kazakhstan.

Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi met Belgium’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot in Brussels on Nov. 17 to discuss how to implement agreements reached during President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to Belgium in June and the subsequent visit of King Philippe and Queen Mathilde to Kazakhstan.

According to Kazakhstan’s embassy in Brussels, 40 documents were announced during the royal visit, including 16 commercial agreements and 22 agreements between universities and research institutions. A cooperation roadmap signed by the two foreign ministries covers 2027-2029, providing for regular consultations and closer coordination.

Kazakhstan and UN University to establish regional research hub in Almaty

As part of the third Strategic Partners Forum in Astana, a ceremony was held to exchange the Agreement between the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of Kazakhstan and the United Nations University on the establishment of a regional research hub, according to the press service of the President of Kazakhstan, reported Trend on Nov. 19.

Addressing the forum, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said that locating the hub in Almaty would demonstrate international recognition of Kazakhstan’s scientific potential and create new opportunities for cooperation with other educational and research institutions.

Kazakhstan’s Charyn Canyon ranks among world’s top 20 as tourist numbers surge fifteenfold

Charyn Canyon in southeastern Kazakhstan has ranked 17th in the Worldworthy 100: Canyons & Gorges 2026 international ranking. It was the only destination in Central Asia to make the list of 100 canyons and gorges across 46 countries. The Grand Canyon in the United States ranked fourth, while Letchworth Gorge in New York State took first place, reported The Times of Central Asia on Nov. 13.

Visitor numbers at Charyn Canyon have increased more than fifteenfold over the past five years, rising from 16,105 in 2020 to 249,928 in 2025. The number of visitors more than doubled from 117,793 in 2024.

Charyn is located approximately 200 kilometers east of Almaty, Kazakhstan’s largest city. The canyon stretches for 154 kilometers along the Charyn River. Its best-known section is the Valley of Castles, where reddish rock formations resemble fortress walls, towers, and palaces.

Kazakhstan rises to 16th in UN e-government ranking

Kazakhstan has climbed from 24th to 16th place in the United Nations E-Government Development Index (UN EGDI), entering the highest rating category for the first time, according to the country’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, Trend reported on Nov. 20.

Kazakhstan improved its position by eight places over two years, with the UN describing the progress as one of the most significant among leading countries. It has become the first country in Central Asia to enter the highest rating category.

The highest rating category comprises 21 countries with the world’s most advanced e-government systems. Kazakhstan is now in the same group as South Korea, Denmark, Singapore, the United Kingdom, Estonia, and the United States. In 2026, only three countries – Kazakhstan, Ireland, and Poland – entered this category for the first time.

World.title: Kazakhstan Rises to 16th Place in UN E-Government Development Index
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has climbed to 16th place in the 2026 United Nations E-Government Development Index (EGDI), entering the highest rating group for the first time, according to the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development’s press service.

The country’s EGDI score increased from 0.9009 in 2024 to 0.9363, compared with the global average of 0.6675. The highest group, known as Very High (VH), includes 21 countries with the world’s most advanced e-government systems.

Kazakhstan is now ranked alongside countries including South Korea, Denmark, Singapore, the United Kingdom, Estonia and the United States. It is one of three countries, together with Ireland and Poland, to have entered the group for the first time in 2026.

Over the past two years, Kazakhstan has moved ahead of Sweden, Germany, Ireland, New Zealand, Austria and Japan, which ranked above it in 2024. It remains the highest-ranked country in Central Asia.

Progress across key indicators

The country advanced from 41st to 13th place globally in mobile connectivity and internet accessibility. Its telecommunications infrastructure indicator reached a level comparable to Estonia’s, according to the ministry.

Digital literacy increased approximately 1.5 times, while Kazakhstan’s position in education and skills improved from around 42nd to 28th place. The country’s legal framework for digital government also received the UN’s highest assessment.

The report emphasizes the integration of government platforms, digital identification systems, mobile services and public service centers as important elements of Kazakhstan’s digital government model.

Building a digital government

Kazakhstan’s digital transformation has been guided by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s goal of turning the country into a fully digital state within three years. He also declared 2026 the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence.

This year, Kazakhstan introduced a new-generation e-government platform, which the ministry says has been rebuilt using modern technologies to improve its reliability and resilience to emerging threats. Government databases have also been integrated, allowing public services to retrieve the information they need without requiring citizens to collect certificates, scan documents or submit the same information repeatedly.

More services are moving entirely online. For citizens who prefer in-person assistance, the government is developing AI-powered service centers, which provide self-service facilities supported by artificial intelligence. Businesses can also use the eGov Business platform to reduce reliance on paper-based procedures.

More than 90% of public services are now available online in Kazakhstan. The eGov.kz portal has more than 16.4 million registered users. Between January and October 2026, the government provided more than 51 million services through eGov, with nearly two-thirds accessed through smartphones. Alongside digital services, the government has focused on expanding internet access, improving mobile connectivity across the regions and strengthening citizens’ digital skills.

Next steps

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said the ranking reflects long-term institutional efforts rather than individual technology projects.

“The ranking has never been an end in itself; it is the result of extensive systemic work. (…) The results came from a systematic approach, not individual projects. The UN assesses not websites, but how the government works as a whole,” he said.

Madiyev added that the focus on artificial intelligence had proved effective by reducing administrative burdens and allowing people to devote more time to strategic and creative tasks.

“Our next task is to build a government that reaches out to people before they even think of turning to it,” he said.

The UN E-Government Survey is published every two years by the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs. It assesses 193 UN member states based on three main dimensions: online services, telecommunications infrastructure and human capital. Countries are classified into four groups and 16 rating classes, with the Very High group representing the most advanced e-government systems.

World.title: Georgian and Russian representatives meet in Minsk: Reaction in Tbilisi
World.content:
Georgian and Russian representatives meet in Minsk

On 19 November, Georgian Prime Minister’s Special Representative for Relations with Russia and First Deputy Foreign Minister Giorgi Zurabashvili met Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin in Minsk.

In official statements issued following the meeting, the Russian side described it as part of the “resumed direct dialogue” between Russia and Georgia.

The Georgian government, meanwhile, said in a brief statement that the two sides had “reached a number of agreements”.

This was the first meeting of its kind since Giorgi Zurabashvili’s appointment as special representative. It drew strong criticism in Tbilisi, with former diplomats and experts viewing it as the restoration of direct dialogue with Russia.

What the official statements say

The Russian Foreign Ministry published a brief statement on its website, consisting of just a few paragraphs. The opening paragraph said that the “meeting took place as part of the resumed direct dialogue between Russia and Georgia”.

According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, the two sides discussed trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian cooperation, as well as regional security issues.

Moscow said the two sides had reached “a number of practical agreements” and agreed to maintain contact. However, the ministry did not specify what exactly these agreements concerned.

The Georgian government’s statement was published slightly later. Its content was almost identical to that of the Russian Foreign Ministry.

According to official Tbilisi, Zurabashvili and Galuzin discussed trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian relations, as well as existing challenges in these areas.

“The need to continue dialogue in order to achieve concrete results was emphasised,” the statement said.

The talks also touched on regional security:

“Particular attention was paid to the importance of the Geneva International Discussions as the main format for resolving outstanding issues between Russia and Georgia, as well as for discussing security and humanitarian matters.”

The statements issued by both countries noted that the heads of the delegations had thanked the Belarusian side for its assistance in organising the Russian-Georgian meeting.

The two sides also agreed to maintain contacts with a view to further developing relations between Russia and Georgia.

What is new about the meeting: Format, venue and expanded mandate

Zurabashvili-Galuzin meeting. Photo: Russian Foreign Ministry

On 21 October 2026, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze appointed Giorgi Zurabashvili as his special representative for relations with Russia. Zurabashvili also retained his position as first deputy foreign minister.

At the time of his appointment, Kobakhidze said the special representative’s responsibilities would include not only trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian issues, as before, but also the peaceful resolution of the conflict with Russia.

Since 2012, talks with Russia on trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian issues had been held in the so-called Karasin–Abashidze format. Georgia was represented by the prime minister’s special representative, Zurab Abashidze, while Russia was represented by Deputy Foreign Minister Grigory Karasin. The meetings were held mainly in Prague.

In parallel with this format, the Geneva International Discussions were established after the 2008 war as the only international negotiating format in which Georgia and Russia participate alongside representatives of the EU, UN, OSCE and US.

The Geneva Discussions address security and humanitarian issues, including the situation in Georgia’s occupied territories.

“Agreeing to move meetings from Prague to Minsk is a diplomatic mistake”: Reactions from Tbilisi

Russia had been calling for the Geneva talks to be moved to Minsk for many years. The new format of dialogue with Russia, the venue of the meeting and the possible expansion of Zurabashvili’s mandate have therefore drawn particular criticism in Tbilisi.

Former Georgian ambassador to Russia Valeri Chechelashvili said that agreeing to move the meetings from Prague to Minsk was a diplomatic mistake:

“Mikhail Galuzin is a very experienced diplomat with very clear positions on Abkhazia and Tskhinvali. He says they are Russia’s allies, that Russia must take care of them, and so on. Giorgi Zurabashvili has been entrusted with a difficult task!”

According to Chechelashvili, it is unclear who decided to expand the negotiating mandate and how that decision was made. The former diplomat believes the public should be given more information about such changes:

“The meetings in the Karasin-Abashidze format have exhausted their mandate, as Irakli Kobakhidze told us. But the mandate of the current meetings has been expanded: it covers not only trade, transport and cultural relations, but is also supposed to contribute to conflict resolution. This is somewhat surprising, because a mandate cannot be changed unilaterally. So someone, somewhere, has been negotiating with the Russians, and we know nothing about it.”

Security expert Giorgi Shaishmelashvili believes the new format could be a step towards restoring institutional diplomatic relations with Russia:

“The ruling Georgian Dream party has prepared everything needed to move to a new stage in relations with Russia, which will ultimately mean the restoration of diplomatic relations with Russia. What difference does it make whether you go to Minsk or Moscow?”

Political analyst Vakhtang Dzabiradze believes the meeting in Minsk could be an interim stage and does not rule out Giorgi Zurabashvili travelling to Moscow in the future:

“Minsk is a temporary venue for the meetings. Eventually, they will move to Moscow if things continue this way and Georgian Dream does not change its political course. Today, the authorities’ talk about the Geneva format is purely a propaganda manoeuvre. They want Georgian society to talk less about the fact that the country’s political direction has changed. Today, even geographically, it is clear that the foreign policy orientation has shifted northwards.”

Dzabiradze also believes that the Geneva International Discussions format has effectively already been abolished.

The Georgian Diplomatic Society also believes that the meeting is another clear indication of a change in Georgia’s foreign policy course:

“Expanding the mandate of the Georgian prime minister’s special representative to include the peaceful resolution of the Russian-Georgian conflict, and appointing the incumbent first deputy foreign minister to this position, can be regarded as a form of restoration of diplomatic relations. This contradicts Georgia’s previously stated approach and, at the same time, jeopardises the international format of the Geneva talks.”

According to the diplomats, Georgian Dream’s dialogue with Russia serves to normalise relations on Russia’s terms rather than achieve the de-occupation of Georgia’s occupied territories.

World.title: ‘What special status does the Russian language have?’: Russian-language education debated again in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Russian-language education in Azerbaijan

A lawmaker from the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Hikmat Babaoglu (Mammadov), has proposed reviewing state funding for Russian-language school education. He made the proposal on 16 November during a plenary session of the Milli Majlis, Azerbaijan’s parliament, as lawmakers discussed the 2027 state budget.

According to Babaoglu, 157,000 pupils study in Russian-language classes, compared with 1.57 million in Azerbaijani-language classes. The state spends 2,000 manats (around $1,177) a year on each pupil.

The MP stressed that “national identity and national ideology are shaped through education”. He also questioned whether Azerbaijan had any state-funded schools that taught in English or Chinese:

“Why is that? It is something worth thinking about.”

He said a similar situation existed in higher education.

Over the past two years, the future of Russian-language education in Azerbaijan has repeatedly come under discussion. This time, however, a lawmaker from the ruling party raised the issue from the parliamentary podium and backed his argument with budget figures. This raises a question:

Is this a debate about education spending, or does it reflect relations between Baku and Moscow?

What do the figures tell us?

According to the figures cited by the MP, around 9% of all schoolchildren in Azerbaijan study in Russian-language classes. Based on his estimate of annual spending per pupil, the state spends approximately 314 million manats a year on Russian-language education.

Elshan Azim, head of School No. 35 in the Kalbajar district, cited the same figure. He said that the government allocates 314 million manats a year to Russian-language education, while schools for internally displaced people receive 188 million manats (around $184.7 million). Comparing the two amounts, he stressed:

“For 30 years, these schools have played an important role in preserving the folklore, music, national values and spiritual heritage of their regions.”

Azim argues that if the authorities close schools to save public money, they should assess Russian-language schools by the same criteria.

In recent years, authorities have closed hundreds of small schools in rural areas or merged them with other educational institutions because they had too few pupils. Judging by the headteacher’s remarks, the future of schools for internally displaced people is also under discussion.

The Ministry of Education has not yet commented on the MP’s remarks.

What has the ministry said previously?

In July 2025, rumours spread widely that the authorities might close Russian-language classes. Messages in parents’ WhatsApp groups claimed that schools teaching in Russian would switch to Azerbaijani within three years. The Ministry of Education denied these reports. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova also dismissed them as “fake news” and said Moscow remained in constant contact with Baku on the issue.

In June 2026, Education Minister Emin Amrullayev said that closing Russian-language classes had “never been on the agenda”. He said it was “technically impossible” to shut them down “as early as tomorrow”, adding that parents themselves chose the language of instruction. However, he did not rule out restructuring for “objective reasons”, such as a decline in pupil numbers or a shortage of teachers.

Babaoglu’s proposal, however, concerns a different issue. The MP is not calling for Russian-language classes to close. Instead, he is questioning whether the state should continue to fund them.

Against the backdrop of improving relations with Moscow

The MP’s remarks come amid a period of improving relations between Baku and Moscow. In December 2024, an AZAL passenger plane crashed, killing 38 people. In April 2026, the two sides acknowledged in a joint statement that Russian air defence systems had unintentionally shot down the aircraft.

In September, Azerbaijan placed three Russian propagandists – Semyon Uralov, Ivan Knyazev and Alexey Chadayev – on its wanted list over public calls for a violent change of government. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador over the matter. Moscow dismissed their remarks as “personal opinions”.

Babaoglu did not mention Russia in his speech. He justified his proposal by referring to the need to preserve “national identity” and concerns over public spending. Moscow has not yet responded to his remarks.

The draft 2027 state budget contains no separate proposal to change the funding arrangements for Russian-language education. The government has also not responded to the issue raised by the MP.

Russian-language education in Azerbaijan

World.title: ‘Your own husband could be human trafficker’: tackling human trafficking in Armenia
World.content:
Every life matters: how people and animals save each other in Armenia

Over the past four years, Armenia has recorded 109 cases of human trafficking. Reports by international organisations show that Armenia is making efforts to prevent human trafficking. However, the government has scaled back its anti-trafficking efforts in the legal sphere.

We tell personal stories, present figures and facts about the scale of human trafficking in Armenia, and examine programmes that support victims.

Married to the enemy?

“My husband would drive me to different addresses in his car. He would wait in the car until I finished work and came out. He would take all the money from me right there in the car, then drive me to the next address,” Anna (not her real name, at her request) recalls.

Anna describes providing sexual services as her work. She says her husband had never been particularly keen on working. After they married, he decided to use his wife’s previous experience in the sex trade to support the family. The situation did not change even after they had a child.

Family life became hell not only for Anna but also for their child.

“I worked day and night. I had no right to complain or refuse. And it wasn’t just sexual exploitation. I also faced physical, psychological and economic abuse. I lived in constant fear and anxiety. He could beat me or insult me in front of other people, then show me affection, try to win me over and say that we were a family. But the very next day, he would take me to other men again. Sometimes I wouldn’t see my child for several days. Different women I didn’t know would look after them,” Anna says.

Years of exploitation, extreme physical and mental exhaustion, beatings and emotional suffering – but above all, anxiety about her child – drove Anna to flee her husband and report him to the police.

Anna says she found the decision difficult:

“The police force is made up mostly of men. I found it difficult to tell them all the details of what had happened to me – the abuse and the sexual services I had to provide. It felt as though I was going through it all over again. I was overwhelmed by shame, but I knew I had no other choice.”

The police offered to take her to a shelter for victims of human trafficking. Anna agreed, and she still lives there.

Shelter residents and those who do not “save” them

The NGO Sexual Violence Crisis Centre provides victims of human trafficking with shelter and support in dealing with the problems they face. In 2025, the government fully covered the shelter’s operating costs. It also signed its first three-year contract with the centre, allowing it to continue its work on a full scale.

Over the years, social worker Mané Chobanyan has witnessed many tragic stories while working with victims:

“The hardest part of social work is accepting that you are not a saviour. One of its principles is that you must not make decisions on behalf of the people you support. As a professional, I can only guide them and show them the options available. I can never influence their decisions. Of course, this can be very difficult at times. You can never be sure that months or even a year of work will not go to waste – that someone leaving the shelter will not return to the same path, trust an abuser or trafficker again, and end up in the same situation.”

Even so, she has no regrets about the effort she puts into helping these people change their lives.

Mané says an atmosphere of fear and intimidation sometimes forces people to remain in situations where traffickers exploit them. This happens most often to victims of labour exploitation. Given their vulnerable position, the prospect of losing their jobs frightens them more than anything else.

“When we work with people who have experienced sexual exploitation, we mainly try to show them that they can change their circumstances and find another job. In cases of labour exploitation, our priority is to inform people about their rights,” she explains.

With financial support from the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, the Sexual Violence Crisis Centre provides more than just shelter. It also offers psychological and medical care, legal advice and other assistance. Mané says many shelter residents have told her that they would have tried to escape their situations sooner if they had known about the support programmes available.

Anyone who finds themselves in a situation that resembles human trafficking or exploitation can contact the NGO Sexual Violence Crisis Centre for help on +374 77 991280.

US State Department and GRETA say government efforts remain insufficient

The US State Department publishes an annual report on human trafficking worldwide. The Council of Europe’s Group of Experts on Action against Trafficking in Human Beings (GRETA) also publishes a report every four years.

Both reports say that the Armenian government does not fully meet the minimum standards for combating human trafficking, although it has made considerable efforts in this area.

The US State Department welcomed the government’s decision to draw up a new national action plan for 2026–2028, although the authorities have yet to adopt it. However, the report considers the country’s efforts in the legal sphere insufficient.

Articles 188 and 189 of Armenia’s Criminal Code criminalise both sexual and labour trafficking.
