World.title: Coroner reopens investigation into Victorian police officer's suicide
World.content:
Victorian State Coroner Liberty Sanger has announced she is reopening the investigation into the 2019 suicide of Melbourne police sergeant Shona O'Connor, following new information raised in a Four Corners program about her death.

Changes to Victorian law that took effect on November 1, 2026, allow the Coroners Court to "act on its own motion" and reopen an investigation if it is satisfied there are new facts and circumstances that make reopening it appropriate; the court no longer requires someone else, such as a family member, to apply.

The investigation into Shona's death will be one of the first under the amendment to the Coroner's Act.

Four Corners' investigation, Unprofessional, found allegations that Shona had been bullied and was subjected to sexually harassing comments at the Melton police station in Melbourne's west.

It also revealed that Victoria Police had not provided key evidence to the coroner, including a statement from Shona's Local Area Commander saying she had complained of bullying a month before her death.

In her determination released on Friday, Ms Sanger said: "On 9 November, 2026, the ABC Four Corners episode titled 'Unprofessional' aired. During that episode, reference was made to a statement of Inspector Zorka Dunstan, including that approximately a month prior to Shona's suicide 'Sergeant Shona O'Connor made an allegation of bullying by Simon [Payne] and I asked for evidence of this at the time. I informed her that pending the information provided, that I would action the complaint appropriately'."

Ms Sanger made the point that "the Coronial Brief filed with the Coroners Court of Victoria, and considered by Coroner Katherine Lorenz, did not contain any statement from Inspector Zorka Dunstan".

She said the court only received the statement, which was written in September 2020, on November 12, 2026 — three days after Unprofessional was broadcast.

"On the basis of the statement of Inspector Zorka Dunstan, and the evidence contained therein, I am satisfied that these new facts and circumstances make it appropriate to re-open the investigation so that further investigation can be undertaken in respect of these matters."

Inside the 'boys' club' within Victoria Police When a police officer with more than two decades' service took her life, it set a young detective down a path that would leave him disillusioned about the force's culture and accountability.

Shona's sister, Reschelle O'Connor, and father Michael O'Connor tells Four Corners they thanked the coroner for making this decision.

"For the whistleblowers who have been so courageous, we thank them on behalf of the family and it's wonderful that the coroner of her own accord has reopened the investigation," Mr O'Connor says.

"We've lost our daughter, a mother, a sister and now there's a chance to have the full evidence produced to give us some real answers."

Reschelle says the outcome is needed "so that a fuller understanding of what has taken place can then be made public".

Shona, a mother of three, had wanted to join the police force since she was in preschool. (Supplied)

"Now we don't have to jump through hoops and my sister can get the justice that is deserved and also help other people from encountering the same thing or similar issues.

"That's the transparency that we need for change."

Four Corners has heard from 48 currently serving and former members of Victoria Police in response to the program, many of whom allege bullying, sexual harassment, sexual assault and corruption in the force.

Many are women and are devastated by Shona's story.

A number of them say they have received redress under the Restorative Engagement and Redress Scheme, set up by Victoria Police, which compensates current and former employees of the force who had experienced workplace sex discrimination and sexual harassment.

Reschelle says she is not surprised so many police have come forward and that her sister would feel "absolutely vindicated" by the coroner's decision.

"This didn't happen in isolation," she says.

"She would absolutely want this to be brought to the court of public opinion.

"I think given that you've had all of these other people come forward, the last things she would want is for anyone to suffer in her footsteps if this [coronial investigation] can bring some justice to the ones that are currently living it, that would be the purpose served."

Detective Sergeant Jacob Laidlaw, who investigated the aftermath of Shona's death for the Victoria Police integrity unit Professional Standards, but ultimately retired due to ill health after his treatment in the force, welcomes the coroner's decision.

"I'm just grateful that Shona's finally being heard," says Mr Laidlaw, who first raised Shona's death with the program.

"And I think this sets a precedent, moving forward.

"Victoria Police withheld material from the court that could have provided answers to the family — I'm glad they might come closer to closure.

"All the facts and circumstances will now be produced and that should have happened from the start."

In a statement, Commissioner Mike Bush told Four Corners Victoria Police "fully supports the coroner's decision to re-open its investigation into Shona's death".

"We will work closely with the coroner on the next steps and provide whatever assistance is required," Commissioner Bush said.

World.title: Qld jockey loses bid to reduce jail time after strangling woman
World.content:
A prominent Queensland jockey who admitted to almost killing a woman by strangling her until she saw "stars", has lost his bid to appeal his sentence.

Corey John Bayliss pleaded guilty to two charges, including strangulation and threatening to distribute a prohibited visual recording.

In September he was handed a two-year sentence, suspended after four months.

According to court documents, in June 2023, when Bayliss was 24-years-old, he returned home after a drinking session, and an argument broke out between him and a woman.

He later began calling her derogatory names, then grabbed her by the throat, "pushed her down against the bed", and choked her to the point she could not breathe.

The woman began to "see stars", with Bayliss continuing to strangle her for a further 10 seconds until another person in the house yelled at him to stop.

Bayliss left the room, with the woman then phoning her sister and locking herself in an ensuite until he left the house.

Days later Bayliss tried to apologise, and admitted to choking her in texts, writing: "I almost f***ing killed you", and "I'm so sorry".

She later moved interstate, but in November the following year Bayliss contacted her again, this time calling her a "pathetic c***" and threatening to release a video of her naked and showering if she did not send text messages to two people to "correct a misunderstanding".

He outlined what he wanted the woman to write in the messages, if she wanted to prevent the video being distributed.

She went to the police soon after, with officers interviewing Bayliss the following year.

During the interview he admitted to pinning her to the bed, saying he "snapped" and had a "blackout moment".

He was arrested and charged but released on bail.

When sentenced in September this year, the judge described the 27-year-old's offending as "very serious", "extreme and violent".

"The applicant only released his hold when (someone else in the home) screamed", he said.

"The messages threatening to distribute the intimate recording also included a threat to distribute even after the complainant had complied."

According to the judge, the texts left the woman in "great fear".

In handing down his two-year sentence, suspended after four months, the judge said Bayliss was receiving a "reduced" period of imprisonment due to his early guilty plea, his remorse, and cooperation with police.

"His career in the racing industry was affected by the suspension of his licence to ride when he was charged," a court document states.

"He had not been able to work as a jockey since then and this had been a significant deterrent as he was a highly regarded and talented rider."

It said racing stewards would decide whether Bayliss is able to acquire a licence again in future, and since the violent attack he had seen a psychologist to confront the "violent impulse" that led to the offending.

Today, the Court of Appeal in Brisbane handed down its decision. (ABC News: Demi Lynch)

After the court matter, Bayliss made an attempt to appeal his sentence, arguing they were "manifestly excessive", as he was required to "serve time in actual custody".

Today, the Court of Appeal in Brisbane handed down its decision.

The sentence for his video threat charge was set aside, while his application to appeal his strangulation sentence was rejected.

World.title: Teenager arrested after plea for information about 'Onepercent' profile
World.content:
A teenager has been arrested after a police appeal for information about the identity behind the username "Onepercent".

Last month, Armed Crime Squad detectives released the usernames of several people they alleged were the taskmasters who orchestrated a series of firebombings and extortions on bars, clubs and restaurants across Melbourne earlier this year.

This afternoon, a 17-year-old boy was arrested after his home was searched.

Police allege they found a traffickable quantity of cocaine, three phones and cash.

They are investigating whether the boy ran the profile "Onepercent", who they allege coordinated a number of attacks, including a fire that destroyed two vehicles on Severn Street in Moonee Ponds in March, an arson at a York Street bar in South Melbourne on April 15, and an aggravated home invasion on Sandown Road in Springvale several days later.

They will also investigate whether the boy commissioned a second attack on the home on April 22, which they are treating as a mistaken-identity kidnapping.

Police say a 34-year-old victim suffered serious injuries to his lower body and the partial amputation of one of his fingers.

A 19-year-old Tarneit man was charged over the incident.

Police are investigating whether the teenager organised a number of fires in Melbourne this year. (Facebook: Fire Rescue Victoria)

Detectives are also investigating whether the boy was behind an arson at a Williamstown ice cream store in March.

The Nelson Place fire caused more than $600,000 worth of damage and police allege it endangered the lives of a number of residents living above the shop.

Two Melbourne men, a 22-year-old and a 24-year-old, were charged over the fire.

Operation Eclipse began in late April with the task of identifying a range of serious and organised crime syndicates believed to be involved in a series of offending linked to hospitality venues.

It involved specialist detectives from the Gang Crime Squad, Armed Crime Squad, and Arson and Explosives Squad.

"Offences such as arson and kidnapping are not low-level offences," Detective Inspector Graham Banks said.

"They are violent crimes that can have life-changing consequences for victims and create fear within our community."

Police continue to appeal for information about the incidents and other crimes targeting hospitality venues.

World.title: Lloyd Rayney files legal action against Facebook giant Meta
World.content:
Former Perth barrister Lloyd Rayney is hoping to force tech giant Meta to hand over the identities of people he believes may have defamed him online.

Mr Rayney, whose wife Corryn was killed in August 2007, was found not guilty of her murder in 2012 — a verdict upheld on appeal.

Ms Rayney's body was found buried in Kings Park, more than a week after she vanished after attending a boot-scooting class in Bentley.

Lloyd Rayney and his late wife Corryn Rayney. (Supplied: WA Supreme Court)

This week Mr Rayney lodged an application in the Federal Court to compel Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to reveal the identities of people who may have been involved in defamatory Facebook comments against him.

"The request for identity information is connected to an intention to issue defamation proceedings against all those liable for damages arising from the online mob attacks suffered by Mr Rayney," his lawyer Roger Blow said.

" This application is only about my client identifying people as potential defendants where he can't already identify them. "

It is understood the comments were made in three separate Facebook groups, including one in August.

Meta has been contacted for comment.

In 2017, five years after Mr Rayney was found not guilty, he was awarded a total of $2.6 million after he sued the WA Police for naming him, in the weeks after his wife's death, as the "prime" and "only" suspect.

Lloyd Rayney outside court after he won a $350,000 defamation payout plus interest in 2022. (ABC News: Joanna Menagh)

In 2022, the Supreme Court found forensic investigator Mark Reynolds defamed Mr Rayney by suggesting he "murdered his wife and got away with it" at a university forum.

Mr Rayney is no longer a lawyer, having been struck off in 2020 for secretly recording his wife's conversations and then giving false evidence about it in court.

World.title: Australian Rohingya hope world will listen after UN court's genocide ruling
World.content:
There were celebrations in suburban Brisbane last night as the International Court of Justice delivered its judgement that Myanmar had committed genocide against the country's Rohingya people.

Robi Alam, president of the Rohingya United Youth Network, said members had gathered at the group's Logan youth centre to watch the proceedings.

He said they were in touch with relatives and friends back in the Cox's Bazar refugee camp in Bangladesh where "thousands and thousands" were gathered to watch the hearing.

"A lot of them were in tears," he said.

"We also had a couple of brothers that were crying [here] last night, because this means that … it feels like the world will finally listen."

Members of the Rohingya United Youth Network gathered to watch the ICJ's genocide ruling. (Supplied: Rohingya United Youth Network)

The United Nations' court found that a campaign mounted by Myanmar's security forces that killed thousands and perpetrated widespread sexual violence against the long-persecuted Rohingya Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to genocide.

It was the first time the court held a state responsible for committing genocide.

The government said the campaign in Myanmar's western Rakhine State was launched in response to a series of guerilla-style attacks by a Rohingya militant group.

Rohingya people adjust to life in Australia The Rohingya, a Muslim ethnic group, have suffered killings, forced evictions and other atrocities.

The army conducted massive "clearance operations" that targeted Rohingya villages. Survivors described massacres, rape, arson and looting.

According to the court, about 10,000 Rohingya people were killed and more than 700,000 forced to flee to Bangladesh.

The military insisted the Rohingya had burned their own homes and the government said there was no direct evidence of genocidal intent.

Robi Alam welcomed the ICJ's ruling but said it was not the end of the story. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

Mr Alam was born in a camp in Bangladesh and came as a refugee to Australia with his family when he was 10.

He said that he grew up like many Rohingya young people hearing stories of persecution, loss and displacement.

"For our parents and grandparents, this judgement represents recognition of the suffering they endured," he said.

"For my generation, it represents hope that our children may one day inherit a future different from the one we were born into."

Sydney Rohingya youth leader, Asma Nayim Ullah, who fled Myanmar with her family and arrived as a refugee in Australia when she was 10, said that justice was long-awaited.

Asma Nayim Ullah says she's relieved following the UN court's ruling. (ABC News: Rex Siu)

"This is recognition that what we were saying wasn't false claims, or being accused that we were burning down our own homes by the Myanmar government. Finally this is being recognised as a genocide," said Ms Nayim Ullah, who is co-founder of the Australian Rohingya Women's Development Organisation (ARWDO).

"I'm relieved that we have finally reached this milestone together as it has been a long journey."

Whether that recognition translates into lasting change is another question.

Four years after the military operation targeting the Rohingya, a military coup sparked a civil war that is still wracking the country.

For most of her life, Asma was a citizen of nowhere As a Rohingya person from Myanmar, Asma was denied an official nationality, and since living in Australia has faced a unique set of challenges.

One of Ms Nayim Ullah's family members remained in Myanmar until a recent wave of attacks by the Myanmar military drove her to flee.

"Obviously, we don't want to live in camps, but for us to go back it needs to be safe," she said.

"I welcome the opportunities this verdict presents to secure justice and hold Myanmar accountable.

"The priority now is determining our next steps and what actions can we take to support Rohingya communities who remain displaced without safety and dignity."

What happens now?

The top UN court said Myanmar must allow the "safe and dignified return to their place of residence and the reunification of families for the Rohingya displaced as a result of Myanmar's wrongful acts".

It also said Myanmar had an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined at a later date.

Myanmar's historic genocide verdict at UN court The top United Nations court has ruled that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar's security forces against the Rohingya Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

These orders are legally binding, but the court has no enforcement powers of its own.

Sydney-based immigration lawyer Ko Ko Aung said the decision was symbolic, and what it would mean for the many Rohingya refugees still living in camps was unclear.

He said the facts in the case were obvious but the bar to prove genocide was high.

"I believe it is [thanks to] the real hard work of everybody involved in documenting and all the evidence that has been produced for so many years," he said.

Robi Alam is president of the Rohingya United Youth Network. (Supplied.)

Mr Alam said that while the judgement was welcome, it would not restore citizenship, return stolen homes or bring displaced families back together.

"The international community, including Australia, must now translate this judgement into meaningful action through diplomatic pressure, accountability, humanitarian assistance and support for a safe, voluntary and dignified return to Myanmar when conditions allow," he said.

A statement from Foreign Minister Penny Wong said Australia had "consistently condemned the Myanmar military's grave human rights abuses and called for those responsible to face justice".

Senator Wong said Australia had committed more than $1.26 billion in humanitarian assistance to people affected by the crisis in Myanmar and Bangladesh, including Rohingya refugees and their host communities, since 2017.

"We call on Myanmar to comply fully with the Court's judgement and its obligations under international law," she said.

World.title: Xi wants stronger bonds with Australia as Albanese defends Putin rebuke
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalChina relations Xi wants stronger bonds with Australia as Albanese defends Putin rebuke Natassia Chrysanthos Updated November 20, 2026 — 9:04pm ,first published 3:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Shenzhen/Beijing: Chinese President Xi Jinping said he wants to see stronger cultural ties between the people of Australia and China as he hailed a “full turnaround” in diplomatic relations between the two nations while meeting Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Albanese met Xi on Friday morning at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, the sprawling complex where the Chinese president hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for historic trilateral talks the night before. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese meets with China’s President Xi Jinping at the Kylin State Guest House. AAP The Australian prime minister said it was a “positive thing” that the three leaders had had the meeting and there was “a positive declaration to come out of it, including on nuclear weapons and nuclear proliferation”. Albanese had this week backed the talks between Xi, Trump and Putin, saying it was better to have dialogue than conflict, but followed through on his commitment to use his attendance at this week’s APEC conference to express Australia’s opposition to Russia’s war in Ukraine.



The prime minister used his official address to APEC’s leaders’ session on Thursday to directly call on Putin to end the conflict. Sources in the room said Albanese looked at Putin, and the Russian president looked down, as the prime minister gave this speech. Reflecting on that moment on Friday, Albanese said: “Well, he [Putin] certainly heard it, as did others in the room. I have a responsibility to put Australia’s position clearly and directly, and that is what I did.” Loading “I made very clear to President Putin directly yesterday that he needs to stop his war, and he needs to stop it now,” Albanese said. “This has now gone on for longer than I’ve been prime minister … with a devastating human impact, with a significant loss of life on both sides of the conflict, but also with a significant economic impact on the world, and Australia’s position is very clear.”





Even so, Xi and Albanese talked up cultural ties between their two nations in public remarks before Friday’s bilateral talks. “We have jointly promoted the full turnaround of China-Australia relations, and exchanges and cooperation in various fields between our two countries have continued to deepen,” Xi said, according to a translation of his comments. “China-Australia friendship is what the people want, and we should strengthen people-to-people exchanges ... I will work with you in the spirit of equality, seeking common ground despite differences, and mutually beneficial co-operation.” Chinese President Xi Jinping speaks during the plenary meeting at the APEC summit. Ng Han Guan/Pool AP via AP Xi said he had recently been “very touched” to receive a letter from Australian exchange students about their experience in China. “I believe our young people should have more exchanges and get to know each other better,” he said.



Albanese also praised the improvement in Australia’s relationship with China, which hit a low under the Morrison government because of its push for a COVID-19 inquiry, leading to punitive tariffs on key Australian exports. “Some 25 per cent of Australian exports come to this one destination [China], but importantly as well, the improvement in relations has meant people-to-people engagement across the business community,” Albanese said. “A stable and productive relationship is in the interests of both of our nations, particularly given that one in four jobs in Australia depends upon trade, and what we’ve seen with the resumption of trade across so many products is major advantages. “We have different political systems, different histories, but that doesn’t mean that you can’t have constructive dialogue. And that’s what Australia seeks.”



Clean energy, AI to be new opportunities Speaking later in Beijing at the start of his meeting with Li, who is the second-most powerful figure in the Chinese government, Albanese flagged artificial intelligence and clean energy as potential areas for co-operation. In a statement released after the talks, the two countries said they had agreed to establish an AI dialogue to share their views on safety, governance and application. Business leaders from ANZ, GrainCorp, Rio Tinto and SunCorp were among the Australians who sat down with Chinese executives for a roundtable with Li and Albanese later on Friday evening. Li told Albanese that the China-Australia relationship had benefited from positive momentum and deepening co-operation.



“These achievements have not come easily. They are the result of our joint efforts,” he said. Li said he agreed with Albanese, who had referenced the need to maintain stable relationships amid destabilising forces in international relations. “Facts have shown that a more mature, stable and productive China-Australia relationship will not only benefit the two countries, but also the region and beyond,” Li said. At the roundtable, Business Council of Australia president Geoff Culbert said both countries’ business communities were committed to strengthening their relationships at a time of growing global uncertainty. Culbert named AI, green energy, industrial decarbonisation, agriculture, education, health, and professional services as the key areas of commercial opportunity. World.content:
NationalNSWNote From The Editor Many reporters won’t touch this issue. We’re determined to shine a light Jordan Baker November 20, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Over the past year, the Herald has published many outstanding photographs. Some of those were celebrated on Thursday night at the Walkley Awards, when Sam Mooy won for his essay on the death of Kimanjayi Little Baby and the riots that followed, and Edwina Pickles was named Nikon photographer of the year for the image she captured of a devastated police officer in Bondi, moments after an alleged gunman was shot. I would like to bring your attention to another remarkable photograph we published on Monday. The image, by the brilliant Steven Siewert, features the eye of a woman looking through an opening in a patched-up perspex wall. Her fingers grip the sides. Five teens charged with the murder over a fatal drive-by shooting were mentioned in court for the first time on Friday, following raids and arrests on Thursday morning. The five 16-year-old boys stand accused of three counts of attempted murder and one count of murder, arson and unlawful use of a motor vehicle following the fatal shooting of 19-year-old Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau on October 24. Loading None of the teenagers applied for bail on Friday, and were expected to remain in custody over the Christmas period. Schuster-Togiatau was one of four people struck outside Loganholme pub Fitzy’s during a community boxing event, after a car allegedly pulled up outside the building and an occupant fired shots from the passenger window.



The 19-year-old Jimboomba local was struck in the head and neck, succumbing to her injuries five days later. Kane Barrett, Brodie Blackwood and Zach Uchtman also suffered gunshot injuries, and were treated in hospital over the days following the shooting. The car officers suspected was involved in the shooting was found torched several suburbs over. On Thursday, police arrested five juveniles in relation to a fatal drive-by shooting in Loganholme last month. 9news On Thursday, close to one month after the shooting, more than 50 police officers raided five homes and arrested the five 16-year-old boys.



Detective Inspector Ian Galpin told media on Thursday the investigation had suspected two of the accused teenagers had been behind the wheel, but indicated others in the group were “involved in a different capacity”. They each received five charges, including murder. Nine reported one of the five charged teenagers appeared in Brisbane Childrens’ Court on Friday, while the other four remained in their cells. Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau, 19, succumbed to her injuries five days after she was shot in the head outside a Loganholme pub. GoFundMe Parents of the five 16-year-olds appeared in court, where the boy mouthed “I love you” to his mother as he was escorted from the courtroom.



His case was adjourned until later in the month, when an application for DNA testing from police would be due before the court. Another of the five had his case adjourned while the court sought a language interpreter. On Thursday Galpin said the investigation was continuing and did not rule out additional arrests. World.title: Five of the best homes for sale in Melbourne’s inner north
World.content:
PropertyNewsVictoria residential property Five of the best homes for sale in Melbourne’s inner north Shona Hendley November 20, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. With a mix of walkability, community, character, culture, and proximity to the CBD, Melbourne’s inner-northern suburbs tick many boxes. From the historic Victorian terraces of Parkville to the leafy pockets of Alphington, here are five of the best homes for sale across Melbourne’s inner north. 884 Drummond Street, Carlton North This semi-detached Edwardian home sits on a leafy Carlton North street, within walking distance of Princes Park, Rathdowne Village, and local schools.



Built in about 1907, the home retains its period character, including a traditional return entry, a wide hallway, and a formal living room with a fireplace and a marble mantel. Modern updates include a kitchen with marble benchtops, quality appliances, and a breakfast bar overlooking an al fresco area with a remote-controlled awning and a courtyard garden. Other features include the attic, hydronic heating, heated floors and towel rails. 8 Keith Street, Alphington This Mason Bright architect-designed home sits directly opposite Pitcher Park in Alphington, close to Darebin Parklands and Fairfield station. With high ceilings, natural light, warm neutral colours, designer lighting and cathedral ceilings upstairs, the interiors are elegant and inviting.



The home features a seven-star energy rating, 6.63kW of solar power, double glazing, heat-pump hot water, and six-zone Daikin heating and cooling. Highlights include Volakas Gold marble in the kitchen, an open-plan living, dining, and kitchen area, sliding doors that open onto the al fresco with a motorised shade roof and built-in barbecue, and a heated pool and spa. 104 Kellett Street, Northcote Designed by Taouk Architects, this brand-new residence sits in a quiet pocket of Northcote, close to Northcote Aquatic Centre, local parks, and schools.



Set across two levels, the home prioritises natural light and a strong connection to the outdoors, evident in the open-plan layout and full-height stackable sliding doors that open to a north-facing undercover al fresco area. The exteriors are another highlight, with the al fresco area including an outdoor kitchen, plus a landscaped courtyard and pool. Other features include the kitchen with a butler’s pantry, a remote double garage, and custom built-in cabinetry throughout. 88 Fyffe Street, Thornbury Set on about 713 square metres in Thornbury, this art deco-style home is close to Merri Creek, Thornbury station, and the St Georges Road bike path, and is zoned for Bell Primary School and Coburg High School.



The home features four bedrooms, two on the ground floor and two on the upper floor, and a light-filled open-plan living and dining area, with a large granite kitchen also on the ground floor. Outside, there is a large paved entertainment area with a barbecue bench and a north-facing rear garden. 151 Park Drive, Parkville Conveniently located on the city’s edge, this Parkville home is within easy reach of a host of attractions, including the University of Melbourne, Royal Park, Princes Park, and Queen Victoria Market. It is also zoned for University High School and North Melbourne Primary School.



The home itself is a Victorian balcony terrace with original details and plenty of natural light. It features a traditional arched hallway, formal living and dining, and an open fireplace, plus a spacious open-plan kitchen, dining, and living area at the rear. Another highlight is the rear garden with a remote roller door opening to the rear right-of-way and reserve.

World.title: Xi wants stronger bonds with Australia as Albanese defends Putin rebuke
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalChina relations Xi wants stronger bonds with Australia as Albanese defends Putin rebuke Natassia Chrysanthos Updated November 20, 2026 — 9:04pm ,first published 3:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Shenzhen/Beijing: Chinese President Xi Jinping said he wants to see stronger cultural ties between the people of Australia and China as he hailed a “full turnaround” in diplomatic relations between the two nations while meeting Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Albanese met Xi on Friday morning at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, the sprawling complex where the Chinese president hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for historic trilateral talks the night before. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese meets with China’s President Xi Jinping at the Kylin State Guest House. AAP The Australian prime minister said it was a “positive thing” that the three leaders had had the meeting and there was “a positive declaration to come out of it, including on nuclear weapons and nuclear proliferation”. Albanese had this week backed the talks between Xi, Trump and Putin, saying it was better to have dialogue than conflict, but followed through on his commitment to use his attendance at this week’s APEC conference to express Australia’s opposition to Russia’s war in Ukraine.



The prime minister used his official address to APEC’s leaders’ session on Thursday to directly call on Putin to end the conflict. Sources in the room said Albanese looked at Putin, and the Russian president looked down, as the prime minister gave this speech. Reflecting on that moment on Friday, Albanese said: “Well, he [Putin] certainly heard it, as did others in the room. I have a responsibility to put Australia’s position clearly and directly, and that is what I did.” Loading “I made very clear to President Putin directly yesterday that he needs to stop his war, and he needs to stop it now,” Albanese said. “This has now gone on for longer than I’ve been prime minister … with a devastating human impact, with a significant loss of life on both sides of the conflict, but also with a significant economic impact on the world, and Australia’s position is very clear.”





Even so, Xi and Albanese talked up cultural ties between their two nations in public remarks before Friday’s bilateral talks. “We have jointly promoted the full turnaround of China-Australia relations, and exchanges and cooperation in various fields between our two countries have continued to deepen,” Xi said, according to a translation of his comments. “China-Australia friendship is what the people want, and we should strengthen people-to-people exchanges ... I will work with you in the spirit of equality, seeking common ground despite differences, and mutually beneficial co-operation.” Chinese President Xi Jinping speaks during the plenary meeting at the APEC summit. Ng Han Guan/Pool AP via AP Xi said he had recently been “very touched” to receive a letter from Australian exchange students about their experience in China. “I believe our young people should have more exchanges and get to know each other better,” he said.



Albanese also praised the improvement in Australia’s relationship with China, which hit a low under the Morrison government because of its push for a COVID-19 inquiry, leading to punitive tariffs on key Australian exports. “Some 25 per cent of Australian exports come to this one destination [China], but importantly as well, the improvement in relations has meant people-to-people engagement across the business community,” Albanese said. “A stable and productive relationship is in the interests of both of our nations, particularly given that one in four jobs in Australia depends upon trade, and what we’ve seen with the resumption of trade across so many products is major advantages. “We have different political systems, different histories, but that doesn’t mean that you can’t have constructive dialogue. And that’s what Australia seeks.”



Clean energy, AI to be new opportunities Speaking later in Beijing at the start of his meeting with Li, who is the second-most powerful figure in the Chinese government, Albanese flagged artificial intelligence and clean energy as potential areas for co-operation. In a statement released after the talks, the two countries said they had agreed to establish an AI dialogue to share their views on safety, governance and application. Business leaders from ANZ, GrainCorp, Rio Tinto and SunCorp were among the Australians who sat down with Chinese executives for a roundtable with Li and Albanese later on Friday evening. Li told Albanese that the China-Australia relationship had benefited from positive momentum and deepening co-operation.



“These achievements have not come easily. They are the result of our joint efforts,” he said. Li said he agreed with Albanese, who had referenced the need to maintain stable relationships amid destabilising forces in international relations. “Facts have shown that a more mature, stable and productive China-Australia relationship will not only benefit the two countries, but also the region and beyond,” Li said. At the roundtable, Business Council of Australia president Geoff Culbert said both countries’ business communities were committed to strengthening their relationships at a time of growing global uncertainty. Culbert named AI, green energy, industrial decarbonisation, agriculture, education, health, and professional services as the key areas of commercial opportunity. World.title: Irony at play with the grievance parties
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Irony at play with the grievance parties November 20, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Annika Smethurst (“Teal movement faces test in a changed political environment”, 18/11) reports that traditional areas of teal policy strength have been overshadowed and that independent candidates have missed the current zeitgeist issues, namely crime and cost of living. Because here, and in most countries, wages are not keeping up with the cost of everything. The reason is mostly related to high fuel prices affecting costs, especially so for Australia at the end of a long supply chain. Until the wars we have no control over are finished, this will continue. It seems ironic that many will vote for a grievance party and will elect people who have no solutions and who will probably last a single term. The community independents have proved their worth with allegiance only to their electorates.

Helen Hook, Black Rock Have voters stopped listening?

So the Coalition’s solution to the housing issue is mostly a return to urban sprawl (“Voters back more housing to be built in the outer suburbs″⁣, 14/11). It’s surprising that voters from the urban fringes, who appear highly disgruntled about issues such as traffic congestion and a lack of services, would vote for more of the same. It poses the question, have voters in these areas just stopped listening and thinking about what’s being offered. What they want is change and the details don’t matter. The problem with this is that the details do matter. You don’t solve a problem by simply doing more of the same. We often hear from outer urban voters that they are neglected and yet there is nothing on offer when Jess Wilson’s solution is more housing and logically more congestion and a scramble for limited services in these areas. If voters stop listening, thinking and scrutinising and just vote on grievance then they might find that four years will drift by while they just get more of the same.

Michael Cormick, Carnegie The wrongs overshadow the rights

Whatever Ben Carroll and his party may have done right in past terms is now unfortunately overshadowed by what’s been done wrong in this one.

David Johnston, Healesville



Pickering’s pickle on nuclear energy

One Nation’s man in Victoria (″⁣How Warren Pickering wants to soften One Nation and smash rivals″⁣, 20/11) says he “wants to see the true state of the budget after the election before getting policies costed”. How, then, to explain such certainty around nuclear energy? The party would end Victoria’s ban on nuclear energy “so that the state can consider modern nuclear technology as part of a proper, technology-neutral energy mix”. Nuclear has been considered by energy experts and scientists, and has been found to be the most costly option, especially for a nation with no history of the technology. A “technology-neutral” approach would include at least a recognition of the success of our renewables adoption. But One Nation disputes human-caused global warming and Pickering vows he will not “answer to the cult of climate change”.

Fiona Colin, Malvern East THE FORUM A private forum?

So Cricket Australia’s grand solution to this mess is that any interested parties voluntarily testify to a closed, supervised forum, with any results to be released at its discretion. The word “forum” originally meant a public place. No danger of that here.

Henry Woolley, East Keilor What of sledging?

Cricket has a long history in Australia and the phrase “it is not cricket” has been passed into the vernacular to mean play by the rules. But sandpapering the ball “is not cricket”. But polishing the ball is.

Is sledging not in the same class as ball tampering? It would be called bullying in the workplace and its sole aim is to unsettle the batsman and give the fielding team an advantage.

Adrian Tabor, Point Lonsdale Watch the women

I follow and support the Australian women’s cricket team. They are friendly, amusing, play fair and are dominant in world cricket. A joy to watch.

Peter Williams, Alphington



Cricket’s fallout

A quick perusal of the articles and letters correspondents in The Age has one wondering, if a nuclear weapon were dropped on an Australian city would it command as many column inches as sandpapergate?

James Ischia, Hawthorn East An inspiring legacy

When I read about Sharman Stone I said, Wow (″⁣Former MP Stone bows out on her own terms″⁣, 20/11). What an amazing woman and her work with abortion reform and her commitment to break with conservative thinking regarding embryonic stem-cell research and reducing suffering with medical cannabis made her a strong advocate for women. She was described as having stubborn independence.

She left this world a better place and now her decision to use voluntary assisted dying shows her determination to make her own decision and leave this world on her own terms.

Julie Ottobre, Brunswick East Discordant trio

The Three Tenors burst into our consciousness in 1990. They were Jose Carreras (Spain), Placido Domingo (Spain) and Luciano Pavarotti (Italy). And by their work they gave many of us a lot of pleasure.

Today we have another triumvirate striding the world stage, Vladimir Putin (Russia), Donald Trump (US) and Xi Jinping (China). So what are they giving us and what should we call them?

Henry Haszler, Eltham Not a fan

If anything, I view the frenzied celebration of Grand Theft Auto VI not as the shared cultural moment and relationship education opportunity columnist Alice Clarke does (Comment, 20/11), but as diagnostic of a mass societal illness we deny we have.

Beyond the obscenity of investing billions of dollars to fuel corporate profit from the glamorisation of violence, there is the almost blanket adulation of media complicit in this dismal phenomenon.

To have the game ennobled as somehow worthy only heightens a sickening sense of a society that has lost its bearings.

Clarke’s praise of the game feels something like squeezing a laudable anti-smoking message from an ad featuring the Malboro Man.

I agree we should be in search of shared cultural moments, but ones that celebrate human meaning, not immersive virtual despair.

Darren Lewin-Hill, Northcote Scrap the activity laws

There are many Melburnians unfamiliar with the extent of Labor’s Activity Centres planning laws. Media coverage tends to focus on the core business and retail areas affected. Many are unaware that the residential areas affected and which surround the cores are kilometres wide.

In the case of Bayside, the new Inner Catchment residential area now allows for residential buildings up to six storeys and the new Outer Catchment residential area now allows for buildings up to four storeys. These areas are extensive throughout Bayside and actually form one area stretching across the Activity Centres of North Brighton, Middle Brighton, Hampton and Sandringham.

They have the potential to destroy these Bayside suburbs as we now know them. Other Melbourne suburbs are also detrimentally affected by these new controls.

Many Melbourne people are also unaware that these changes allow a speculative developer, satisfying bare minimum standards, to be given the go ahead, taking away the right of the local council or those affected to object. A new government should scrap these Activity Centres, effective from day one!

John Isaac, Brighton



Economy blues

Maybe the Reserve Bank will now be satisfied with causing struggling families financial stress and many to become unemployed. In the meantime, large corporations send jobs offshore.

Arthur Pritchard, Ascot Vale Our new plates

With the advent of Christmas spirit, and of holiday travel on our roads, a seasonal variant for our number plates could read: Victoria – The Holey State.

Brian Jacka, Kew Well done, PM

At the leaders’ summit, it looks like Anthony Albanese has done what former prime minister Tony Abbott boasted he would do and then didn’t. In his speech Albanese called out Vladimir Putin directly and to his face – a very clear shirt-fronting – about ending the Ukraine war immediately. Well done, PM.

Robyn Westwood, Heidelberg Heights And not so well done

I wonder if it even crossed the mind of Anthony Albanese that being photographed alongside the man responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians, could be seen as a betrayal of Ukrainians everywhere. It certainly doesn’t look like he did.

Chris Burgess, Port Melbourne Grandstanding galore

The Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump love fest on the sidelines of APEC was merely a distraction and a chance for Trump to big note himself. Was there mention of the war in Ukraine and in the Middle East in their communique? No. Was there a plan to reduce nuclear arms? No. What we did get was the push for more fossil fuel, so it is safe to assume that these three don’t see global warming as an issue.

These meetings are normally choreographed and have agreed to outcomes worked out behind the scenes. This one looked hastily called and what we saw was two leaders allowing another, who has just had a humiliating defeat, to grandstand. Why Xi and Putin agreed to meet is a matter of conjecture, but surely, they got something out of it more than watching a lame duck president make a fool of himself yet again. He doesn’t need their help to do that.

Greg Tuck, Warragul



Terrifying image

There was a time when a photo of an amicable meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the US would have made me think I was watching the world becoming a safer place.

Now I feel like I’m watching the genesis of a terrifying global triumvirate agreeing on the mutual benefits of their association.

Stephen Farrelly, Donvale Digital memories

I am intrigued by the faith that many readers have in artificial intelligence. The ″⁣memories″⁣ of Claude, chatGTP, et al, are limited to what exists digitally. The feeds that come to you from (anti)social media would indicate that some flaws are still in evidence.

Richard McLoughlin, Dromana Truth in illustration

After years of enjoyment from illustrator Matt Golding, I believe I was treated to his most compelling, truthful and unfortunately accurate depiction in his take on the ball tampering saga this week.

David West, Essendon Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING



World affairs

Vladimir Putin’s army invades Ukraine causing death, pain, trauma and destruction and US President Donald Trump calls him “a friend”? Words fail me.

Warwick Spinaze, Rosebud Could someone tell Donald Trump that Vladimir Putin doesn’t have friends, only patsies that he can use for his own benefit.

Michael Brinkman, Ventnor If only telling Vladimir Putin directly, face to face, to end his war would make a difference. And pigs might fly.

Marie Nash, Balwyn So three blokes get together and reckon they will change the UN, ICC, etc sounds like a boozy Wednesday afternoon lunch to me.

James Lane, Hampton East The International Criminal Court claimed to be “out of control”? Coming from those three immunity claimants, I don’t think so.

Alan McLean, Queenscliff



Cricket

Time, surely, to call stumps on sandpapergate. Please.

Raeleene Gregory, Ballarat East Cricket: it’s only a game, you know.

Keith Fletcher, Glenlyon Why is it legal to shine one side of the ball but illegal to scratch the other side of the ball?

Bruce Hartnett, Alphington As the ancients said: Truth is the daughter of time.

Robert Gray, Glen Iris Furthermore

It’s long overdue that businesses sending jobs offshore for cheaper labour, should need to prove it’s in the national interest.

Perhaps someone could come up with a list of companies that outsource their labour overseas, so I have a more comprehensive list of companies to avoid.

I don’t know what you are paying Nick McKenzie, but you should double it (″⁣McKenzie takes Gold Walkey″⁣, 20/11). The dude is a phenomenon.

Five teens charged with the murder over a fatal drive-by shooting were mentioned in court for the first time on Friday, following raids and arrests on Thursday morning. The five 16-year-old boys stand accused of three counts of attempted murder and one count of murder, arson and unlawful use of a motor vehicle following the fatal shooting of 19-year-old Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau on October 24. Loading None of the teenagers applied for bail on Friday, and were expected to remain in custody over the Christmas period. Schuster-Togiatau was one of four people struck outside Loganholme pub Fitzy’s during a community boxing event, after a car allegedly pulled up outside the building and an occupant fired shots from the passenger window.



The 19-year-old Jimboomba local was struck in the head and neck, succumbing to her injuries five days later. Kane Barrett, Brodie Blackwood and Zach Uchtman also suffered gunshot injuries, and were treated in hospital over the days following the shooting. The car officers suspected was involved in the shooting was found torched several suburbs over. On Thursday, police arrested five juveniles in relation to a fatal drive-by shooting in Loganholme last month. 9news On Thursday, close to one month after the shooting, more than 50 police officers raided five homes and arrested the five 16-year-old boys.



Detective Inspector Ian Galpin told media on Thursday the investigation had suspected two of the accused teenagers had been behind the wheel, but indicated others in the group were “involved in a different capacity”. They each received five charges, including murder. Nine reported one of the five charged teenagers appeared in Brisbane Childrens’ Court on Friday, while the other four remained in their cells. Vana-Reese Schuster-Togiatau, 19, succumbed to her injuries five days after she was shot in the head outside a Loganholme pub. GoFundMe Parents of the five 16-year-olds appeared in court, where the boy mouthed “I love you” to his mother as he was escorted from the courtroom.



His case was adjourned until later in the month, when an application for DNA testing from police would be due before the court. Another of the five had his case adjourned while the court sought a language interpreter. On Thursday Galpin said the investigation was continuing and did not rule out additional arrests. World.title: Pacific countries among minority voting with Israel against Palestinian rights at UN
World.content:
Several Pacific Island countries have joined a small minority of countries voting with Israel against a United Nations (UN) resolution on the right of Palestinian people to self-determination.

The Pacific countries also swam against the tide of the international community on a series of other UN resolutions related to Palestinian people or territory.

In total, 162 countries voted in favour of the United Nations General Assembly Fourth Committee resolution on the right of Palestinian people to self-determination.

Four of the six countries who voted with Israel and the United States against the resolution were from the Pacific: Papua New Guinea, Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia and Naoero.

Three Pacific countries abstained: Fiji, Samoa and the Marshall Islands.

Meanwhile, several Pacific Islands nations against the resolution on assistance to Palestinian refugees in the form of operations of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency mandate, which was supported by 143 countries.

Fiji, Tonga, Palau and Micronesia were among nine countries who voted against it, alongside the United States and Israel - those abstaining included Samoa, PNG and the Marshall Islands.

A resolution on the rights of Palestinian people over their natural resources was supported by 155 countries.

However, Naoero, Palau, Fiji, Tonga and Micronesia were among the nine countries who voted against the resolution, with Samoa, the Marshall Islands and PNG abstaining.

Similarly, on the UN resolution to declare Israeli settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory as illegal, a core of Israel's staunchest Pacific allies again voted with it.

In total, 143 voted in favour of the resolution which aimed to stop the expansion of illegal Israeli settlements and uphold international law.

The eleven countries voting against the resolution included Palau, Micronesia, Tonga and Fiji - those abstaining included Samoa, the Marshall Islands, Naoero and PNG.

Another resolution addressing Israeli settlement activities in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (including East Jerusalem) and the occupied Syrian Golan, was supported by 149 countries.

But Fiji, Tonga, Micronesia and Palau were among the seven countries who voted against, with Israel.

World.title: Police given special powers after gang firearm incidents in Gisborne region
World.content:
Police have been given special powers to search the vehicles of suspected gang members, as well as seize firearms and weapons in the Gisborne region.

A series of gang incidents in the area have led to police being issued a gang conflict warrant, granting them the extra powers.

Four people have received injuries following the incidents, which involved firearms.

Tairāwhiti's area commander, Inspector Danny Kirk, said police were "sending a clear message" to gang members.

"Unlawful behaviour, and the harm that it brings, will not be tolerated.

"Our tight-knit community can be reassured that we are working to keep Tairāwhiti safe and to prevent further harm."

Bullets through a window, people with 'gunshot wounds'

On Friday night, police explained the series of gang-linked events that led to the gang conflict warrant being issued.

Around 9.30pm on Saturday, police responded to a report of a firearm being discharged towards a residential address on Wainui Road in Kaiti.

"Bullets have gone through a window, and we understand pellets from a firearm have struck two people.

"This was an incredibly distressing incident for those injured, and the others present at the address."

Just before 1am on Sunday, police were called by a person driving on State Highway 2, south of Wairoa.

They said they had been shot at, and they were being chased by a vehicle.

"The victim was uninjured and managed to get away from the offenders, and the Police Communicator guided them to Wairoa to be met by officers," Kirk said.

Also on Sunday, around 5.10am, police responded to an incident near the Stanley Road footbridge in Te Hāpara.

"Police arrived at the scene and located two people at a nearby property with what appeared to be gunshot wounds."

The offenders had fled the scene.

"One person was transported the hospital in serious condition, and the other person was transported in moderate condition."

Both have since been discharged.

The fourth incident occurred around 11.30pm on Monday. Police were called to Justin Street after a firearm was reportedly discharged at a property.

The offenders fled the scene. Police believe they are connected to a gang and had thought someone else was living at the property.

Gang vehicles searched, weapons seized

An operation is underway to investigate the incidents, Kirk said.

Police were " committed to holding those responsible for these offences to account".

Authorities would be out in the communities following the issuing of the warrant, "ready to respond to any unlawful behaviour by gangs and anyone who believed they are above the law".

Additional staff from other police districts have been brought into the Tairāwhiti area to help enforcement activity against gangs.

"With the gang conflict warrant's special powers, police have stopped and searched several vehicles driven by, or connected to, gang members," Kirk said.

"This has resulted in the seizure of weapons including a sword, axe, ammunition, methamphetamine, and drug paraphernalia," Kirk said.

Police have also found a pump action shotgun, two loaded firearms, a 12-gauge semiautomatic sawn-off shotgun, knuckle dusters and other drug utensils throughout the week, following searches of multiple properties and vehicles.

As of Friday night, nine people have been taken into custody.

They include:

A 22-year-old man charged with unlawful possession of a firearm

25-year-old man, a patched gang member, has been charged with possession of an offensive weapon and possession of ammunition

A 25-year-old man charged with unlawful possession of firearms, ammunition and methamphetamine

A 27-year-old man charged with possession of offensive weapon, unlawful possession of ammunition and firearms

A 27-year-old man charged with unlawful possession of a firearm and ammunition

A 28-year-old woman charged with possession of methamphetamine and drug utensils

A 29-year-old gang associate charged with possession of an offensive weapon, possession of cannabis, possession of utensils for drug use and driving while forbidden.

A 30-year-old patched gang member charged with possession of methamphetamine and drug utensils

A 36-year-old man charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition.

Kirk urged the community to report "anything suspicious" to police - even if they did so anonymously.

World.title: Unions, IT expert warn of health sector's reliance on Microsoft after outage
World.content:
An IT expert says a recent streak of software outages shows the risk of essential public services like health putting too many eggs into one basket.

The Public Service Association says hospitals should consider back-up communication systems to be just as important as emergency power generators.

Surprise IT failures have caused chaos around the world in recent days, including a worldwide Microsoft outage, a series of mishaps in the United States, and cyber-attacks impacting hundreds of websites including Zoom and the BBC.

Audio player for " Streak of software outages prompts calls for back up systems " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2712060%2Funions-it-expert-warn-of-health-sector-s-reliance-on-microsoft-after-outage

Streak of software outages prompts calls for back up systems Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Cogent chief information security officer Tony Grasso said it pointed to an increasingly vulnerable internet.

"I don't think they're related, it's just that we are still very vulnerable in a variety of ways and as we outsource more and more of our computing, we become more and more vulnerable," he said.

Grasso said New Zealand, in particular, relied on providers based in other countries to keep its services running.

"Where New Zealand went wrong is that we went, on premise: servers are bad, because they cost money, and the cloud is good," he said.

"It's true that you outsource, effectively, all of your maintenance and patching and all of the problems that can happen, but then when Microsoft has that problem you've got no way to fix it."

Grasso said his mother-in-law experienced the impacts of the Microsoft outage up-close.

"My mother-in-law was going in for surgery and she can't have that surgery because the email that was coming from the specialist that gives them details wasn't there," he said.

"When you have situations like that, then just relying on email and one provider... You need to find a different way to communicate, even if it's just picking up the damn phone and calling."

Association of Salaried Medical Specialists executive director Sarah Dalton said the outage was a major headache for hospital staff.

"In terms of trying to provide patient care, or do any number of tasks, there would be issues with accessing referrals, lab records, any document that was sent from another hospital or another part of the health system most likely, anything that was email related," she said.

Public Service Association national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said it wasn't right for New Zealand's health system to be reliant on an overseas company.

"IT systems in hospitals are part of life saving clinical care, they shouldn't be relying solely on Microsoft's systems to operate, particularly for important things like prescriptions, lab results, and information about what's happening in theatre. We need much stronger resilience," she said.

It wasn't the first time New Zealand hospitals had been disrupted by IT issues in 2026.

Another outage in July forced health workers in the Waikato district to use pen and paper, and that came after a similar outage in January impacted hospitals in the upper North Island.

In the same way hospitals had back-up generators for power outages, Fitzsimons said they needed other ways for staff to communicate during IT outages.

"They need to consider much more than electricity generation back-up. Satellite technology and other communication resilience needs to be factored into the equation here," she said.

"The consequences of getting this wrong could result in lives being lost."

Health NZ director of digital operations James Allison said the Microsoft outage caused "minimal disruption" and didn't cause any delays to clinical operations.

"Where email is commonly used to communicate with patients or providers, we used alternative contact methods such as phone calls, fax, or printing of physical forms, to minimise any disruption," he said.

"We are continuing to stabilise and modernise our technology through the Health Digital Investment Plan. The first major investments under the plan have been approved, supporting work to strengthen core digital infrastructure and systems and improve digital services for patient care."

Allison said Health NZ had Starlink and satellite phones set up strategically around the country as emergency backup communications.

World.title: Pacific rugby preview: Fiji, Samoa and Tonga set for big weekend of tests
World.content:
The Flying Fijians have a chance to get their first win in the Nations Championship this weekend, when they meet Italy in Udine on Sunday morning.

Head coach Jake White has retained the core of the side that lost 43-15 to Ireland last weekend, with a few changes to the starting lineup and the bench.

In the Nations Cup competition, both Tonga and Samoa have made changes to their lineups as well, heading into their final internationals for the current series.

Tonga will take on Hong Kong China in Hong Kong on Saturday night, while Samoa will meet Spain in Malaga on Sunday morning.

Options and balance

Fiji v Italy

Kick off: 5:40am NZDT, Sunday, 22 November

Venue: Bluenergy Stadium, Udine

As they close off their preparation for Italy, White has stated that options taken during the game and stirking a balance between flair and structure are two key areas the team will need to improve on.

He pointed to the team's decision to take a penalty tap instead of a scrum against Ireland when the pressure was on last weekend as an example of something that could have been differently approached.

He said in an interview during the week that the difference between competing at the highest level and learning how to win can sometimes come down to a single decision.

"When an option to take a scrum on the 60th minute, we take a tap-free kick," White said.

He believes a scrum could have forced Ireland into defending a more demanding situation.

He also stressed the fact that the Flying Fijians must learn to balance their natural attacking instincts with structured play.

He said the players, led by the leaders, need to know when to do what, adding that the players revert to their own plays when under pressure at times.

"Whereas Fiji, we still caught in between the way the game should be played and the way they have historically played it," he said.

"Now, just got to try and get those two closer together because we can't be seduced by space."

Flying Fijians head coach Jake White Fiji Rugby

For the clash against Italy he has named former England number eight Nathan Hughes again at number eight, having made his debut there against France in their first game two weekends ago.

Also given a run in the starting lineup is giant lock forward Setaraki Turagacoke.

On the bench comes France-based Etonia Waqa and Marika Parker, who is set to make his debut for the Fijians.

Hooker Tevita Ikanivere, who lost a number of throws last weekend, and halfback Frank Lomani, blamed for aimless kicks against Ireland, have both been retained for the game.

The centre pairing of Josua Tuisova and Seteraki Bituniyata has also been retained.

Former All Black Ngani Laumape will debut for Tonga against Hong Kong China on Saturday night.

Laumape has been named at inside centre for the clash, pairing Fetuli Paea.

Head coach Tevita Tuifua and assistant Nili Latu have given the Manawatu player his opportunity to show his experience in the Tongan jersey.

"He is an experience player and knows Test rugby situations," Tuifua said.

"This is his chance to show himself in the team."

His former All Blacks teammate Malakai Fekitoa played against Georgia last week.

Changes have also been made in the forward pack, with Justin Mataele replacing Veikoso Poloniati in the second row, while Otunuku Jr Pauta comes in for Lotu Inisi at number eight.

Veteran halfback Sonatane Takulua pairs young Manu Vunipola as the new halves combination.

Hong Kong China have made some minor changes from the side beaten 38-17 by Canada last weekend.

Hong Kong China have lost five of their last six matches, including each of their last three and will look to avoid more than four consecutive losses for the first time since a six-game stretch between 2014 and 2015.

Tonga won their only previous match against Hong Kong China, defeating them 44-22 in a play-off game in Australia to qualify for Rugby World Cup 2023.

Third consecutive win

Manu Samoa will look to maintain their recent form after racking up big wins over Zimbabwe and Portugal in their last two games.

A third consecutive win on the go is what the team will be aiming for when they take on the Spanish.

Samoa have won each of their last two matches in Europe and could make it three straight wins on European soil for the very first time.

Three former All Blacks and a former Wallaby are all in the match-day 23.

Prop Scott Sio packs down again in the starting lineup, joined by utility back Shane Stevenson, who moves to wing from fullback and Josh Ioane, who starts at flyhalf.
